items.q: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain for 20 minutes. He has no allergies and no history of GI bleeding. Which medication should the EMT give first?
items.x: Aspirin reduces mortality in ACS by blocking platelet aggregation and should be given early when there are no contraindications.
items.a: Chewable aspirin 162-324 mg
w: Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg
Enteric-coated aspirin 81 mg
Chewable ibuprofen 200-400 mg

items.q: The primary reason aspirin is given to a patient with suspected ACS is to:
items.x: Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent; it keeps the clot from growing but does not dissolve it.
items.a: Prevent platelets from clumping and enlarging the clot
w: Dissolve the clot that is blocking the coronary artery
Dilate the coronary arteries to improve blood flow
Relieve the chest pain by blocking pain signals to the brain

items.q: Which form of aspirin is preferred for suspected ACS?
items.x: Chewing non-enteric-coated aspirin gives the fastest antiplatelet effect.
items.a: Chewable, non-enteric-coated
w: Enteric-coated, swallowed whole
Extended-release, swallowed whole
Non-coated, swallowed whole

items.q: Which finding is a contraindication to giving aspirin?
items.x: Known aspirin allergy is a contraindication. Taking daily low-dose aspirin is not a reason to withhold a chewed dose for ACS.
items.a: A known allergy to aspirin
w: A systolic pressure below 100
Sildenafil use in the past day
A daily low-dose aspirin regimen

items.q: A 15-year-old with a flu-like illness asks for aspirin for a fever. Aspirin should be avoided because of the risk of:

items.a: Reye syndrome
w: Guillain-Barre syndrome
Kawasaki disease
Stevens-Johnson syndrome

items.q: A patient with chest pain reports vomiting dark coffee-ground material this morning. With regard to aspirin, you should:
items.x: Active GI bleeding is a contraindication to aspirin.
items.a: Withhold it because of possible active GI bleeding
w: Give it since chest pain takes priority over the bleed
Give half the usual dose to limit further GI bleeding
Give it once the vomiting has settled for an hour

items.q: How long does a single dose of aspirin affect platelets?
items.x: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, so the effect lasts the platelet's lifespan.
items.a: For the life of the platelet (about 7-10 days)
w: Until the drug is cleared (about 4-6 hours)
For one full day (about 24 hours per dose)
Until the liver recovers (about 2-3 days)

items.q: Aspirin belongs to which drug class when given for ACS?
items.x: In ACS, aspirin works as an antiplatelet agent.
items.a: Antiplatelet
w: Anticoagulant
Thrombolytic
Vasodilator

items.q: Which classic symptom suggests aspirin (salicylate) overdose?

items.a: Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
w: Slow, shallow breathing (bradypnea)

Pinpoint pupils (miosis)

items.q: Before assisting a patient with nitroglycerin, the EMT must confirm:

items.a: Not give nitroglycerin in any form
w: Give it, since six hours is long enough

Give the spray form instead of a tablet

w: Dilating the airways and increasing oxygen to the heart
Slowing the heart rate and decreasing its oxygen demand
Blocking platelets and keeping the clot from growing

items.q: The usual dose of sublingual nitroglycerin is:

items.a: 0.4 mg
w: 4 mg
40 mg

Allergenic

items.a: Every 3-5 minutes up to the protocol maximum
w: Every 1-2 minutes up to the protocol maximum
Every 10-15 minutes up to the protocol maximum
Every 3-5 minutes until the pain fully resolves

Oxygen saturation

items.a: Sublingual
w: Oral (swallowed)
Intranasal
Transdermal

w: 4-8 grams
50-60 grams
100-120 grams

w: 3 mg

w: 0.3 mg adult auto-injector

w: Give labetalol IV to bring the systolic pressure down
Hyperventilate to an EtCO2 of 25 mmHg to lower the ICP
Give mannitol for a presumed rise in intracranial pressure

items.q: A head-injured 22-year-old has been on Diprivan at 80 mcg/kg/min for 3 days. He develops a Brugada-like ECG, lactate 6, CK 9000 and K 6.1. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: 80 mcg/kg/min is 4.8 mg/kg/hr, above the roughly 4 mg/kg/hr threshold linked to PRIS: metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmia and heart failure. Stop the propofol. NMS needs a dopamine antagonist and lead-pipe rigidity.
items.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Rhabdomyolysis from paralysis alone
Refeeding syndrome from the lipid

items.q: During RSI, fentanyl 250 mcg is pushed rapidly before the paralytic. The chest becomes rigid, BVM ventilation is impossible and SpO2 is falling. What is the best action?
items.x: Opioid-induced chest wall and glottic rigidity responds quickly to neuromuscular blockade, which was already planned. Naloxone works more slowly and removes the analgesia the patient needs for intubation.
items.a: Give the paralytic and intubate
w: Give naloxone IV, then resume BVM
Place a supraglottic airway and bag harder
Give midazolam IV to relax the chest

items.q: A septic patient with lactate 9 on maximal norepinephrine receives Ketalar 2 mg/kg. BP falls from 84/50 to 60/30. What is the best explanation?
items.x: Ketamine supports BP only indirectly, by releasing catecholamines. When stores are exhausted, its direct myocardial depressant effect appears, so reduce the dose in profound shock. Morphine, not ketamine, is the classic histamine releaser.
items.a: Catecholamine depletion unmasks ketamine's direct negative inotropy
w: Ketamine releases histamine and causes vasodilatory collapse
Ketamine-induced laryngospasm caused a hypoxic cardiovascular collapse
An allergic reaction to the benzethonium chloride preservative

items.q: An 80-kg patient received rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg 3 minutes ago. Intubation failed, and the team decides on immediate pharmacologic reversal. What is the labeled Bridion dose?
items.x: The label uses 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal after 1.2 mg/kg rocuronium. 2 and 4 mg/kg are for moderate and deep block at later times, and neostigmine cannot reverse a deep block. Reversal does not replace a surgical airway if oxygenation fails.
items.a: 16 mg/kg IV
w: 2 mg/kg IV
4 mg/kg IV
0.07 mg/kg neostigmine IV

items.q: A 74-year-old with cirrhosis and a creatinine of 3.2 needs post-intubation sedation for a 3-hour transfer. Which agent is most likely to accumulate and prolong sedation?
items.x: Midazolam relies on hepatic CYP3A4, and its active glucuronide metabolite builds up in renal failure. Propofol is cleared quickly, including by extrahepatic routes, so it does not accumulate in the same way.
items.a: Midazolam infusion
w: Fentanyl small boluses
Propofol infusion
Ketamine single bolus

items.q: An 8-year-old boy with no known history is intubated with succinylcholine. Within minutes his QRS widens, T waves peak, and he goes into VF. What is the most likely undiagnosed condition?
items.x: The boxed warning describes acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia in children with undiagnosed myopathies. Treat with calcium, insulin and dextrose. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency causes only prolonged apnea.
items.a: Duchenne muscular dystrophy with hyperkalemic rhabdomyolysis
w: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency causing prolonged apnea and paralysis
Malignant hyperthermia presenting as an isolated arrhythmia
Myasthenia gravis causing resistance to succinylcholine

items.q: A GCS 6 TBI patient has BP 88/50. A partner objects to ketamine because it raises ICP. What is the best response?
items.x: The old ICP data came from spontaneously breathing patients. With controlled ventilation, ketamine does not raise ICP, and keeping BP up protects cerebral perfusion pressure. Propofol-induced hypotension is the bigger threat to the injured brain.
items.a: Ketamine does not worsen ICP with controlled ventilation
w: Ketamine is unsafe, so give full-dose propofol to protect the ICP
Ketamine is acceptable only after mannitol has been given first
Ketamine is safe in TBI only at very high doses

items.q: A patient with known critical aortic stenosis has BP 96/60 and HR 78 and needs intubation. Which induction agent best preserves hemodynamics?
items.x: Etomidate has the least effect on SVR and contractility. Propofol drops SVR, which a fixed outflow obstruction cannot tolerate. Ketamine's tachycardia shortens diastole and raises myocardial oxygen demand in severe AS.
items.a: Etomidate
w: Propofol
Ketamine
Midazolam

items.q: Levophed is running through a peripheral IV in the hand. The site becomes blanched, cool and firm. What is the best management?
items.x: The label calls for phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10 mL saline infiltrated into the area as soon as possible to reverse alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Hyaluronidase is for nonvasoconstrictive extravasations such as hyperosmolar fluids.
items.a: Stop the drip, aspirate, and infiltrate phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10 mL saline
w: Pull the catheter at once and apply warm compresses as the only care
Inject hyaluronidase subcutaneously around the site of infiltration
Apply nitroglycerin paste and keep infusing through the same site

items.q: Phentolamine reverses alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Extravasation of which infusion acts through a different receptor and responds poorly to it?
items.x: Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic blocker. Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through V1 receptors, which phentolamine does not block.
items.a: Vasopressin
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Epinephrine

items.q: After an anterior STEMI, a patient has BP 84/58, HR 112, cool mottled skin, lactate 5 and crackles. What is the best initial vasoactive strategy?
items.x: In hypotensive cardiogenic shock, norepinephrine restores perfusion pressure with fewer arrhythmias than dopamine. Dobutamine alone can lower BP, and phenylephrine raises afterload on a failing LV.
items.a: Norepinephrine, then add dobutamine once MAP is supported
w: Dobutamine alone to improve cardiac output and tissue perfusion
High-dose dopamine as the only vasoactive agent
Phenylephrine to restore coronary perfusion pressure

items.q: A patient with known hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy has been vomiting. BP is 78/50, HR 128, and the systolic murmur is louder. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Dynamic LVOT obstruction worsens with inotropes, tachycardia, low preload and low afterload. A pure alpha agonist plus volume opens the outflow tract. Inotropes and vasodilators make the obstruction worse.
items.a: Neo-Synephrine plus a fluid bolus
w: Dobutamine infusion
Push-dose epinephrine
Nitroglycerin to unload the stiff LV

items.q: Giapreza is added for refractory vasodilatory shock. Which precaution does its label specifically emphasize?
items.x: Thrombotic events were more common with angiotensin II in its pivotal trial, and the label recommends VTE prophylaxis. Cyanide toxicity is a nitroprusside concern.
items.a: Thromboembolism, so give concurrent VTE prophylaxis
w: Cyanide toxicity, so trend lactate and acid-base status
Digital ischemia, so give it through a central line only
Adrenal suppression, so add stress-dose hydrocortisone

items.q: Methylene blue is considered for refractory vasoplegia after cardiac surgery. The patient takes sertraline daily. What is the major concern?
items.x: Methylene blue is a potent MAO-A inhibitor and carries a boxed warning for serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. It also falsely lowers SpO2 readings, which can be mistaken for hypoxemia.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome from MAO-A inhibition
w: Methemoglobinemia from the SSRI interaction
Hemolysis from oxidative red cell injury
Torsades from additive QT prolongation

items.q: After a C5 spinal cord injury, a patient has BP 76/40 and HR 44 despite fluids. Which single vasoactive agent fits best?
items.x: Neurogenic shock with bradycardia needs both vascular tone and chronotropy. Phenylephrine often worsens the bradycardia through a baroreceptor reflex.
items.a: Norepinephrine, adding beta-1 chronotropy to alpha tone
w: Phenylephrine, raising SVR without changing the heart rate
Vasopressin, correcting the bradycardia through V1
Dobutamine, raising SVR through beta-2 stimulation

items.q: A patient with pulmonary hypertension and RV failure on Primacor 0.375 mcg/kg/min becomes hypotensive at 74/40. Which addition makes the most sense?
items.x: Vasopressin restores SVR and RV coronary perfusion without raising pulmonary vascular resistance much. Large fluid loads over-distend the failing RV and worsen septal shift, and phenylephrine raises PVR.
items.a: Vasopressin, which raises SVR with little effect on PVR
w: Phenylephrine, which lowers PVR more than it raises the SVR
A 2-liter crystalloid bolus to load the dilated RV
A higher milrinone dose to unload the right ventricle

items.q: A patient on metoprolol has anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension after three IM epinephrine doses and an epinephrine infusion. Which drug should be added?
items.x: Glucagon raises cAMP independently of beta receptors and is the guideline adjunct for beta-blocked patients with refractory anaphylaxis. Steroids do not act fast enough to work as pressors.
items.a: Glucagon IV
w: Atropine IV
Calcium chloride IV
Diphenhydramine IV

items.q: A crewmember makes push-dose epinephrine by drawing 1 mL from a 1 mg/mL vial into 9 mL saline, believing it is 10 mcg/mL, then gives 1 mL. How much was given?
items.x: 1 mg in 10 mL is 100 mcg/mL. The usual protocol mix uses 1 mL of the 0.1 mg/mL cardiac syringe in 9 mL saline to make 10 mcg/mL. Concentration mix-ups are a classic push-dose error.
items.a: 100 mcg, a tenfold overdose
w: 10 mcg, the intended protocol dose
1 mcg, a tenfold underdose
1000 mcg, a hundredfold overdose

items.q: A patient with an aortic dissection is started on Nipride without a beta-blocker, and HR rises to 128. Why is this a problem?
items.x: Vasodilators trigger reflex tachycardia and a higher dP/dt, which propagates the tear. Beta-blockade, e.g., esmolol to HR under 60, comes first per guideline, then a vasodilator if BP remains high.
items.a: Reflex tachycardia raises shear force on the aortic wall
w: Nitroprusside directly stimulates beta-1 receptors
Early cyanide toxicity is causing a compensatory sinus tachycardia
The tachycardia is harmful only if MAP drops below 65

items.q: A 26-year-old has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240 with varying QRS morphology. BP is 118/70. Which drug is best?
items.x: Irregular, very fast, changing wide complexes suggest pre-excited AF (WPW). AV nodal blockers can speed conduction down the accessory pathway and cause VF. Procainamide or cardioversion is preferred.
items.a: Procainamide infusion
w: Diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV
Metoprolol 5 mg IV

items.q: A heart transplant recipient has a narrow-complex SVT at 190. How should the adenosine dose be adjusted per guideline?
items.x: Denervated transplanted hearts have exaggerated, prolonged responses to adenosine, so guidelines reduce the dose. Doubling it risks prolonged asystole.
items.a: Lower the first dose (e.g., 3 mg), since the denervated heart is hypersensitive
w: Double the first dose to 12 mg, since the heart lacks vagal innervation
Avoid adenosine entirely and give verapamil as the first-line agent
Use standard 6 mg and 12 mg dosing, since transplant does not matter

items.q: A patient with SVT takes several home medications. Which one would most blunt the effect of Adenocard?
items.x: Methylxanthines such as theophylline and caffeine competitively block adenosine receptors, so larger doses may be needed. Dipyridamole blocks adenosine uptake and greatly potentiates it.
items.a: Theophylline
w: Dipyridamole
Carbamazepine
Lisinopril

items.q: A 70-kg patient has stable monomorphic VT at 170 with BP 110/70. What is the labeled Cordarone IV regimen?
items.x: The label gives 150 mg over 10 minutes, then 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min. The 300 mg push is the ACLS dose for pulseless VF or VT and can cause hypotension in a perfusing patient.
items.a: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 hr, then 0.5 mg/min
w: 300 mg rapid IV push, then 150 mg rapid IV push 3-5 min later
5 mg/kg IV over 2 minutes, repeated twice as needed
1 g IV over 1 hour, then 0.5 mg/min for 24 hours

items.q: A patient with a long baseline QTc has recurrent, self-terminating polymorphic VT with twisting QRS axis. BP is adequate between runs. What is the best first treatment?
items.x: Per ACLS, torsades responds to magnesium, and raising the heart rate shortens the QT. Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol all prolong the QT and can worsen torsades.
items.a: Magnesium 2 g IV, then overdrive pacing or isoproterenol if needed
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes to suppress the runs
Procainamide 20 mg/min until the QRS widens by 50 percent
Sotalol 1.5 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes for rhythm control

items.q: Corvert is given to convert recent-onset atrial flutter. Which monitoring does its label require?
items.x: Ibutilide causes polymorphic VT in a small percentage of patients, usually within hours of the infusion. Correct potassium and magnesium first and have a defibrillator ready.
items.a: Continuous ECG for at least 4 hours
w: Continuous ECG for at least 30 minutes
Serum drug levels at 2 and 4 hours
Invasive blood pressure for 4 hours

items.q: A patient with known EF 20% has AF at 160, BP 98/62 and crackles. Which rate-control drug is most likely to cause decompensation?
items.x: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and are avoided in decompensated HFrEF. Amiodarone and digoxin are the usual options, with cardioversion for instability.
items.a: Cardizem
w: Amiodarone
Digoxin
Magnesium sulfate

items.q: A patient with a regular wide-complex tachycardia, presumed to be SVT with aberrancy, collapses after verapamil. What is the most likely mechanism?
items.x: Most regular wide-complex tachycardias are VT. Calcium channel blockers given in VT cause profound hypotension and collapse. Treat wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise.
items.a: Verapamil caused vasodilation and negative inotropy during VT
w: Verapamil turned SVT with aberrancy directly into VF
Verapamil prolonged the QT interval and caused torsades
Verapamil blocked sodium channels and widened the QRS complex further

items.q: A patient in AF at 180 has BP 70/40 and is confused. Per ACLS, what is the appropriate biphasic electrical therapy?
items.x: Unstable AF needs synchronized cardioversion, starting around 120-200 J biphasic per ACLS and the device maker. An unsynchronized shock can land on the T wave and cause VF.
items.a: Synchronized 120-200 J
w: Unsynchronized 120-200 J
Unsynchronized 360 J
Synchronized 2 J/kg

items.q: A patient has third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape at 30 and BP 70/40. Why is atropine likely to fail?
items.x: A wide escape rhythm suggests block at or below the His-Purkinje system, which vagal blockade cannot help. Move quickly to pacing or an epinephrine or dopamine infusion.
items.a: The block is infranodal, below vagal influence
w: The block is at the AV node, above vagal reach
The escape focus is junctional, so it is maximal
The ischemia has depleted acetylcholine stores

items.q: A patient remains in VF after multiple shocks, epinephrine, and amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg. Which electrical change has RCT support for refractory VF?
items.x: The DOSE-VF trial found that anterior-posterior vector change and double sequential external defibrillation improved survival. Long pauses in CPR before shocks reduce the chance of success.
items.a: Vector change or double sequential defibrillation
w: Escalating single shocks to 400 J with one defibrillator
Switching to unsynchronized monophasic 200 J shocks
Pausing CPR for 30 seconds before each shock

items.q: A patient with ICD shocks has received 6 shocks for recurrent VT in one hour despite amiodarone. He is awake and terrified between episodes. Which adjunct best targets the cause?
items.x: Electrical storm feeds on catecholamines: each shock and the patient's fear trigger more VT. Sedation and beta-blockade, e.g., esmolol or propranolol, break the cycle. Epinephrine and isoproterenol fuel it.
items.a: Deep sedation plus beta-blockade to blunt sympathetic drive
w: Epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes between episodes
Isoproterenol infusion to suppress the ventricular ectopy and pauses
Calcium chloride 1 g IV to stabilize the cardiac membrane

items.q: An 80-kg patient on warfarin has an intracranial hemorrhage with INR 5.2. Per the Kcentra label, what is the best reversal?
items.x: The labeled dosing is 25 units/kg for INR 2 to under 4, 35 units/kg for INR 4-6 and 50 units/kg for INR over 6, with a max per tier. Vitamin K is given with it. Many protocols use a fixed dose instead.
items.a: 35 units/kg 4F-PCC (2800 units) plus vitamin K 10 mg slow IV
w: 25 units/kg 4F-PCC (2000 units) with no vitamin K given at all
50 units/kg 4F-PCC (4000 units) with FFP 15 mL/kg added
10 units/kg 4F-PCC (800 units) plus protamine 50 mg IV

items.q: Why is IV vitamin K given together with 4F-PCC for warfarin reversal?
items.x: The factors in PCC, especially factor VII, have short half-lives, and the INR rebounds unless the liver resumes making functional factors. PCC factors are already carboxylated and do not need vitamin K to work.
items.a: PCC wears off in hours; vitamin K restores factor synthesis over 12-24 hr
w: Vitamin K binds warfarin in the plasma and speeds its renal clearance from blood
Vitamin K is needed to activate the clotting factors in the PCC vial
Vitamin K prevents the thrombotic complications caused by PCC

items.q: A 72-year-old on dabigatran has a traumatic subdural hematoma. What is the labeled Praxbind dose?
items.x: The label dose is 5 g, given as two consecutive 2.5 g infusions or bolus injections. Idarucizumab binds dabigatran with very high affinity and reverses it within minutes.
items.a: 5 g IV as two 2.5 g vials
w: 2.5 g IV, repeated in 12 hours
50 units/kg IV based on weight
1 mg per 100 mg of dabigatran

items.q: A patient on Eliquis has a life-threatening GI bleed, and andexanet is not available. Which option is reasonable per guideline?
items.x: Guidelines accept 4F-PCC as an off-label option for factor Xa inhibitor bleeding when andexanet is unavailable. Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran, and vitamin K does nothing for a direct Xa inhibitor.
items.a: 4F-PCC (off-label, e.g., 50 units/kg)
w: Idarucizumab 5 g IV
Protamine 1 mg per 100 units
Vitamin K 10 mg slow IV with fresh plasma

items.q: A heparin infusion at 1200 units/hr was stopped just before an emergency. Using a common guideline that counts heparin given in the last 2.5 hours, what is the protamine dose?
items.x: 1200 units/hr x 2.5 hr = 3000 units. At about 1 mg protamine per 100 units of heparin, that is 30 mg, under the 50 mg labeled single-dose maximum.
items.a: 30 mg
w: 12 mg
50 mg
120 mg

items.q: Which patient is at highest risk of a severe reaction to protamine?
items.x: Prior exposure to protamine-containing insulin (NPH), fish allergy, vasectomy and prior protamine exposure increase the risk of anaphylaxis and pulmonary hypertensive reactions. Give it slowly and be ready to treat reactions.
items.a: A diabetic who has used NPH insulin for years
w: A patient with a documented penicillin allergy
A patient on long-term warfarin for AF
A patient with prior heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

items.q: A patient who got Lovenox 1 mg/kg 4 hours ago is now bleeding significantly. What is true about reversal?
items.x: Per the enoxaparin label, protamine 1 mg per 1 mg given within 8 hours neutralizes anti-IIa activity but only about 60% of anti-Xa activity. Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
items.a: Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin gives only partial reversal
w: Protamine completely reverses enoxaparin, just as it does heparin
Idarucizumab 5 g IV completely reverses enoxaparin
Vitamin K 10 mg IV reverses enoxaparin within hours

items.q: After 8 units of blood products over 40 minutes, a trauma patient's QT lengthens and BP falls despite more products. iCa is 0.82 mmol/L. What is the cause and fix?
items.x: Citrate preservative binds ionized calcium, causing hypotension, poor contractility, coagulopathy and a long QT. Calcium replacement is part of massive transfusion protocols.
items.a: Citrate chelating calcium; give calcium chloride 1 g IV
w: Hyperkalemia from stored blood; give insulin and dextrose
Hypothermia from cold products; warm them and give TXA
An acute transfusion reaction; stop products and give epinephrine

items.q: Compared with 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate, how much elemental calcium does 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride provide?
items.x: 1 g of calcium chloride has about 13.6 mEq of calcium, versus about 4.65 mEq in 1 g of calcium gluconate. Chloride is also more irritating to veins, so a central or large, secure line is preferred.
items.a: About 3 times more (13.6 vs 4.65 mEq)
w: About the same, since both are 10% solutions
About one-third as much as the gluconate
About 10 times more than the gluconate

items.q: A trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock was injured 3.5 hours ago and has not had TXA. What did CRASH-2 find about starting TXA this late?
items.x: In CRASH-2, TXA started more than 3 hours after injury was linked to more deaths from bleeding, so it is given only within 3 hours of injury. Blood clots (vascular occlusive events) were not increased.
items.a: It was linked to more deaths from bleeding
w: It was safe but no longer reduced bleeding deaths
It caused more blood clots than early dosing
It worked only when the fibrinogen level was low

items.q: Cyklokapron 1 g is pushed IV over 1 minute instead of over 10 minutes. Which effect does the label warn of with rapid injection?
items.x: Rapid IV injection of tranexamic acid can cause hypotension. Infuse it no faster than about 100 mg/min.
items.a: Hypotension
w: Seizures
Thrombosis
Bronchospasm

items.q: A patient with a penetrating torso injury and no head injury has BP 82/50 after 2 units of blood. Surgery is 40 minutes away. What is the best resuscitation target?
items.x: Until bleeding is controlled, damage control resuscitation accepts a lower BP with blood products to avoid dislodging clot and diluting clotting factors. This does not apply to TBI, where hypotension worsens outcomes.
items.a: Permissive hypotension, SBP about 80-90
w: Norepinephrine to a MAP of 65 first
2 liters of crystalloid to restore a normal BP
Push-dose phenylephrine to SBP 120

items.q: A patient with active heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is on warfarin and needs emergency reversal. Which product does its own label contraindicate?
items.x: Kcentra contains a small amount of heparin and is contraindicated in known HIT. FFP or other strategies are used instead, together with vitamin K.
items.a: Kcentra
w: Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Fresh frozen plasma

items.q: A patient on Pradaxa with acute kidney injury has a major bleed, and idarucizumab is unavailable. Which therapy can remove the drug?
items.x: Dabigatran has low protein binding and is renally cleared, so hemodialysis removes much of it. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are highly protein-bound and are not dialyzable.
items.a: Hemodialysis
w: Plasmapheresis
Protamine IV
Charcoal hemoperfusion only

items.q: A patient with an amitriptyline overdose has QRS 148 ms, BP 80/50 and is seizing. What is the best immediate treatment?
items.x: Hypertonic sodium and alkalemia overcome TCA sodium channel blockade. Benzodiazepines treat the seizures. Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker, and physostigmine can cause asystole in TCA toxicity.
items.a: Benzodiazepine plus sodium bicarbonate IV
w: Phenytoin load plus amiodarone for the wide QRS
Physostigmine for the anticholinergic toxidrome signs
Flumazenil to reverse a possible benzodiazepine

items.q: A TCA overdose patient is intubated after bicarbonate boluses. Which ventilator strategy is best?
items.x: Acidemia increases TCA binding to sodium channels and widens the QRS. A drop in minute ventilation after intubation can rapidly worsen the cardiotoxicity. Target a pH of about 7.45-7.55 per toxicology guidance.
items.a: Avoid hypoventilation; keep the pH mildly alkalemic
w: Permissive hypercapnia for lung-protective ventilation
Hypoventilate to retain CO2 and offset the bicarbonate
Any rate is fine; ventilation does not affect TCA toxicity

items.q: A TCA overdose patient still has QRS 160 ms and runs of VT after the pH reaches 7.55. Which antiarrhythmic is preferred?
items.x: Lidocaine is a fast on-off sodium channel blocker that can displace the TCA and is the preferred second-line agent. Class IA and IC drugs add to the sodium channel blockade, and sotalol prolongs the QT.
items.a: Lidocaine
w: Procainamide
Flecainide
Sotalol

items.q: After an amlodipine overdose, BP is 70/40, HR 58 and glucose 310 despite fluids and calcium. Which therapy is the best next step?
items.x: CCB toxicity blocks insulin release and leaves the heart starved of glucose. High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy (toxicology protocol, off-label, e.g., 1 unit/kg bolus then an infusion) improves contractility. The hyperglycemia is a marker of severity, not a reason to withhold insulin.
items.a: High-dose insulin with dextrose per protocol
w: Give more calcium only, because the glucose is already high
Atropine every few minutes as the main therapy
Glucagon IV as the definitive therapy

items.q: After glucagon 5 mg IV for propranolol toxicity, which adverse effect should the crew prepare for first?
items.x: Large glucagon doses (an off-label toxicology use) commonly cause vomiting, which is dangerous in an obtunded patient. Pretreat with an antiemetic and protect the airway. Glucagon raises glucose.
items.a: Vomiting with aspiration risk
w: Severe rebound hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia with peaked T waves
Bronchospasm and wheezing

items.q: Which beta-blocker in overdose is most likely to cause seizures and QRS widening?
items.x: Propranolol is lipophilic and blocks sodium channels, causing seizures and a wide QRS that may respond to bicarbonate. Sotalol's distinct danger is QT prolongation and torsades.
items.a: Propranolol
w: Atenolol
Metoprolol succinate ER
Sotalol

items.q: A 70-kg patient has an acute digoxin ingestion with a serum level of 12 ng/mL. How many DigiFab vials does the label formula give?
items.x: Vials = (level in ng/mL x weight in kg)/100 = 840/100 = 8.4, rounded up to 9. Each vial binds about 0.5 mg of digoxin.
items.a: 9 vials
w: 6 vials
12 vials
20 vials

items.q: A patient on chronic digoxin has nausea, yellow-tinged vision, a junctional rhythm at 38 and K 5.9. What is the best definitive treatment?
items.x: The hyperkalemia comes from Na-K ATPase poisoning, and Fab reverses both the dysrhythmia and the potassium shift. Digoxin's large volume of distribution makes dialysis ineffective, and pacing can trigger arrhythmias in the irritable myocardium.
items.a: Digoxin immune Fab, which also corrects the potassium
w: Calcium chloride 1 g IV, then insulin and dextrose infusions
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate plus hemodialysis
Transcutaneous pacing as the definitive treatment

items.q: After DigiFab, a lab reports a total serum digoxin level of 25 ng/mL. What does this mean?
items.x: Most immunoassays measure total digoxin, including inactive drug bound to Fab, so levels rise after treatment and are unreliable for days. Follow the clinical response instead.
items.a: Expected: the assay counts Fab-bound digoxin
w: Fab failed, so give a double dose at once
The patient has taken more digoxin
A lab error, so repeat it in 1 hour to redose

items.q: An enclosed-space fire victim has GCS 8, BP 82/50, lactate 11 and SpCO 18%. What is the best antidote plan?
items.x: A lactate above about 8 in smoke inhalation strongly suggests cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin (5 g per label) does not impair oxygen delivery. Nitrites create methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen carrying in a patient who already has carboxyhemoglobin.
items.a: Cyanokit 5 g IV over 15 min with 100% oxygen
w: Sodium nitrite then thiosulfate with 100% oxygen
Methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV with 100% oxygen
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg for the acidosis

items.q: Which finding is expected after hydroxocobalamin and could mislead the receiving team?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin's red color interferes with colorimetric labs and co-oximetry and can trigger blood-leak alarms on dialysis machines. It tends to raise BP, not lower it. Draw labs before giving it if possible.
items.a: Red skin and urine with falsely abnormal labs and co-oximetry
w: Blue-gray skin with a falsely low SpO2 reading on pulse oximetry
Profound bradycardia that needs atropine
Hypotension that needs vasopressor support

items.q: A patient on propofol and dopamine infusions needs Cyanokit. How should it be given?
items.x: The label lists physical incompatibility with many drugs, including propofol, dopamine, dobutamine, diazepam, sodium thiosulfate and blood products. Use a dedicated line.
items.a: Through a separate IV line
w: Piggybacked into the propofol line
In the same bag as sodium thiosulfate

items.q: A carbon monoxide-poisoned patient has SpO2 99% on a standard pulse oximeter. Why can this be misleading?

items.q: A patient with liver failure and anuric kidney failure needs a paralytic infusion for ARDS. Which agent is best?
items.x: Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which does not depend on the liver or kidneys. Vecuronium's active metabolite and pancuronium accumulate in renal failure, and rocuronium is cleared by the liver.
items.a: Nimbex
w: Vecuronium
Pancuronium
Rocuronium

items.q: A patient with ARDS got vecuronium for 3 days plus high-dose methylprednisolone. After the drugs stop, there is profound flaccid weakness. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Aminosteroid paralytics combined with corticosteroids are a classic cause of ICU-acquired myopathy. Limit how long paralytics are used and monitor depth with train-of-four.
items.a: Critical illness myopathy
w: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency
Guillain-Barre syndrome
Central pontine myelinolysis

items.q: Which factor is most likely to PROLONG rocuronium paralysis during transport?
items.x: Magnesium reduces acetylcholine release and potentiates nondepolarizers. Aminoglycosides and hypothermia do this too. Chronic anticonvulsants and burns cause resistance.
items.a: A magnesium infusion
w: Chronic phenytoin use
Recent major burns
Mild hyperthermia

items.q: At a cabin altitude of 8000 feet, what happens to an air-filled ETT cuff inflated at sea level?
items.x: Boyle's law: at about 565 mmHg, gas expands roughly 35%. Check cuff pressure with a manometer during ascent and descent, or fill the cuff with saline.
items.a: Cuff pressure rises, risking tracheal injury
w: Cuff pressure falls, risking an air leak
Cuff volume shrinks, risking aspiration
Cuff pressure stays the same in flight

items.q: A patient needs FiO2 0.40 at sea level. What FiO2 is needed for the same PAO2 at a cabin altitude of about 8000 feet (565 mmHg)?
items.x: Dalton's law: FiO2 x 760 / 565 = 0.40 x 1.35, or about 0.54. Watch for desaturation as cabin pressure falls.
items.a: About 0.54
w: About 0.45
About 0.30
About 0.70

items.q: An amiodarone infusion will run for 4 hours by peripheral line. Which preparation follows the label?
items.x: Concentrations over 2 mg/mL need a central line because of phlebitis risk. Infusions over 2 hours need non-PVC or DEHP-free containers because amiodarone leaches plasticizer.
items.a: Concentration up to 2 mg/mL, with non-PVC tubing
w: Concentration up to 6 mg/mL, with non-PVC tubing
Concentration up to 2 mg/mL, in normal saline only
Concentration up to 4 mg/mL, with standard PVC tubing

items.q: Sodium bicarbonate is pushed through the IV line already running norepinephrine. What are the two main problems?
items.x: Catecholamines are inactivated in alkaline solutions, and pushing anything through a pressor line flushes a bolus of drug into the patient. Bicarbonate with calcium is the combination that precipitates.
items.a: Pressor inactivation and a pressor bolus
w: Calcium precipitate and a blocked line
Pressor potentiation and a sodium load
Line clotting and a delayed bicarb effect

items.q: A nitroglycerin infusion seems less effective than expected at the programmed dose. Which equipment factor may explain this?
items.x: Nitroglycerin is absorbed by PVC, so the delivered dose can be lower until binding sites saturate. Use the tubing the manufacturer recommends and titrate to effect.
items.a: Drug absorbed into PVC tubing
w: Drug degraded by cabin light
Drug bound to the glass bottle
Drug trapped by the in-line filter

items.q: Anectine is stored in an unrefrigerated flight bag. What does the label say about storage?
items.x: Multi-dose succinylcholine vials are stable up to 14 days at room temperature. Track out-of-fridge dates and replace stock, since heat in aircraft and vehicles speeds degradation.
items.a: Stable 14 days at room temperature; date the vial
w: Stable 24 hours at room temperature; date the vial
Stable 90 days at room temperature; date the vial
Stable until the printed expiration; no dating needed

items.q: A smoke inhalation patient will get both hydroxocobalamin and blood products. How should they be given?
items.x: The hydroxocobalamin label lists blood products among its incompatibilities, so give it through its own line. Draw baseline labs first because of colorimetric interference.
items.a: Separate IV lines
w: The same line, one after another
The same line, with a saline flush
A Y-site on the same blood tubing

items.q: An awake ventilated patient has HR 118 and BP 160/90 and is fighting the vent. The crew wants to paralyze without changing sedation. What should happen first?
items.x: Paralysis without adequate sedation and analgesia causes awareness and is a never-event. Fighting the vent is often pain, anxiety, hypoxia or a mechanical problem that paralysis would hide.
items.a: Optimize analgesia and sedation first
w: Paralyze first and add sedation afterward
Treat the BP and HR first, then paralyze
Raise the set rate and volume first

items.q: A 64-year-old man has had substernal pressure for 30 minutes. He is diaphoretic; BP 148/90, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air. He has no allergies or bleeding history. What is the best next action?
items.x: Early chewed aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and is indicated for suspected ACS when no contraindication exists. Oxygen is not needed when SpO2 is normal, and enteric coating delays absorption.
items.a: Have him chew non-enteric-coated aspirin per protocol
w: Place him on a nonrebreather mask before any medication
Wait for ALS to obtain a 12-lead before giving aspirin
Have him swallow an enteric-coated aspirin tablet whole

items.q: After chewing aspirin, a 60-year-old chest pain patient has an SpO2 of 98% on room air, is speaking in full sentences, and has clear lung sounds. Which oxygen decision is most appropriate?
items.x: Oxygen is given for hypoxia or respiratory distress per protocol; routine high-flow oxygen in a well-oxygenated ACS patient offers no benefit. Keep reassessing SpO2 and start oxygen if it falls.
items.a: Withhold supplemental oxygen and keep monitoring SpO2
w: Apply a nonrebreather at high flow for all chest pain
Apply a nasal cannula at low flow as a routine step
Give oxygen now so it is running before nitroglycerin

items.q: A 58-year-old woman with chest pressure and nausea reports black, tarry stools for the past two days. BP 118/74, HR 104. She has no drug allergies. Regarding aspirin, the EMT should:
items.x: Black, tarry stools suggest active GI bleeding, a contraindication to aspirin, and the tachycardia adds concern for blood loss. A smaller dose or a different route does not remove the antiplatelet bleeding risk.
items.a: Withhold aspirin and report the finding to medical direction
w: Give full-dose aspirin because chest pain outweighs any bleeding risk
Give half of the usual aspirin dose to limit bleeding risk
Give aspirin rectally so it bypasses the stomach entirely

items.q: A 9-year-old was found with an open bottle of his grandmother's aspirin 2 hours ago. He now has ringing in his ears, vomiting, and rapid deep breathing. What is the best interpretation and action?
items.x: Tinnitus, vomiting, and hyperventilation after an aspirin ingestion point to salicylate toxicity, which can worsen over hours. It needs poison control input and hospital evaluation, not home observation.
items.a: Likely salicylate toxicity; contact poison control and transport
w: Likely hyperventilation from fear; coach slow breathing and recheck
Likely stomach irritation only; give milk and observe at home
Likely too late for harm at 2 hours; advise parents to observe

items.q: Ten minutes after chewing aspirin for chest pain, a 66-year-old man reports mild heartburn. Vitals are unchanged and he has no rash, swelling, or wheezing. This is best interpreted as:
items.x: GI upset and heartburn are common aspirin side effects. Without hives, swelling, wheezing, or hypotension there is no allergic reaction, and heartburn does not rule out ACS.
items.a: An expected GI side effect; continue care and reassess
w: An early allergic reaction; request ALS for epinephrine
A sign of GI bleeding; report it and expect black stools
Evidence the pain is reflux; downgrade the transport priority

items.q: Five minutes after chewing aspirin, a 55-year-old chest pain patient develops generalized hives, wheezing, and a BP that drops from 142/88 to 86/52. What is the priority?
items.x: Hives, wheezing, and hypotension after a drug indicate anaphylaxis, which is treated per protocol (including epinephrine) with ALS support. Nitroglycerin would worsen the hypotension.
items.a: Treat as anaphylaxis per protocol and request ALS
w: Treat as cardiogenic shock; lay him flat and request ALS
Assist with his nitroglycerin for the ongoing chest pain
Treat as an aspirin side effect; give oxygen and monitor

items.q: A 72-year-old man with chest pain becomes confused and can no longer follow commands or swallow reliably before you give aspirin. What should you do about the aspirin?
items.x: Aspirin for ACS is chewed and swallowed, so it requires an alert patient who can protect the airway. A declining mental status makes airway management the priority and oral medication an aspiration risk.
items.a: Withhold oral aspirin and manage his airway first
w: Place the tablets in his cheek and let them dissolve
Have a family member help him chew the tablets slowly
Crush the tablets in water and pour them into his mouth

items.q: A 61-year-old woman with chest pain took her usual low-dose aspirin this morning. Why does the ACS protocol still call for chewed aspirin now?
items.x: A daily low dose gives partial, slower platelet inhibition. The larger chewed dose is absorbed quickly and gives rapid, near-complete inhibition during the acute event.
items.a: A larger chewed dose blocks platelets faster and more fully
w: The morning tablet has already worn off the platelets by now
Chewed aspirin opens the blocked coronary artery directly
A second dose thins the blood by lowering clotting factors

items.q: A 70-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness, facial droop, and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. He has no chest pain. His wife asks you to give him aspirin. You should:
items.x: Prehospital aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS, not stroke; a stroke may be hemorrhagic, and slurred speech raises swallowing concerns. Rapid transport for imaging is the priority.
items.a: Withhold aspirin and transport rapidly to a stroke center
w: Give chewed aspirin because it helps prevent stroke
Give chewed aspirin only if his blood pressure stays above 160 systolic
Give aspirin with water since he cannot chew well

items.q: You are assessing a 67-year-old with chest pain before giving aspirin. Which history finding is the most important reason to withhold it?
items.x: Hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs is a contraindication, and a prior reaction to ibuprofen suggests NSAID sensitivity. A statin, a prior stent, or a recent meal are not contraindications.
items.a: Lip swelling the last time she took ibuprofen
w: Heartburn the last time she took an aspirin
A daily low-dose aspirin taken this morning
A daily clopidogrel tablet for a cardiac stent

items.q: You gave aspirin to a 63-year-old with chest pain. During transport he becomes unresponsive, pulseless, and apneic. What is your next action?
items.x: Cardiac arrest takes priority over every medication decision; immediate high-quality CPR and early defibrillation are what change survival. No oral or sublingual medication is given to a pulseless patient.
items.a: Begin chest compressions and apply the AED
w: Ventilate with a BVM and recheck the pulse in two minutes
Request ALS and continue transport with oxygen applied
Assist with his nitroglycerin and recheck for a pulse

items.q: A 52-year-old man has chest pain that began while shoveling snow. He took acetaminophen at home for the pain. He has no allergies or bleeding history. Regarding aspirin, the best action is:
items.x: Acetaminophen has no antiplatelet effect, so it does not replace aspirin for suspected ACS. Waiting or reducing the dose delays a proven early treatment.
items.a: Give chewed aspirin; acetaminophen is not an antiplatelet
w: Withhold aspirin because he already took a pain reliever at home today
Give only half the aspirin dose to avoid an overdose
Wait to see whether the acetaminophen relieves the pain

items.q: A 45-year-old with chest pain has a history of asthma but has taken aspirin many times without wheezing or rash. She is not wheezing now. What is the best action?
items.x: Asthma alone is not a contraindication; aspirin-induced asthma or NSAID hypersensitivity is. Because she has tolerated aspirin before, give it and watch for bronchospasm, a known serious side effect.
items.a: Give aspirin per protocol and monitor for bronchospasm
w: Give half the usual aspirin dose because of her asthma
Assist with her albuterol inhaler first, then give aspirin
Give aspirin only after ALS arrives to manage her airway

items.q: At a family gathering, a 62-year-old has crushing chest pain and a 14-year-old has fever, sore throat, and body aches. Both ask for aspirin. Which plan is correct?
items.x: Aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS in the adult, but it is avoided in children and teens with viral illness because of Reye syndrome. Withholding it from the adult delays a key ACS treatment.
items.a: Aspirin for the adult per protocol, but not the teenager
w: Aspirin for both patients, since each of them is unwell and in pain
Aspirin for the teenager only, who is at lower risk
Withhold aspirin from both until hospital arrival

items.q: A 76-year-old man taking glipizide was found confused with a glucose of 44 mg/dL. After oral glucose he is alert with a glucose of 98 mg/dL and wants to refuse transport. What concern should guide your advice?
items.x: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide can cause prolonged, recurrent hypoglycemia, especially in older adults living alone. Oral glucose works quickly but briefly, so transport and observation are strongly advised.
items.a: His low glucose may return for hours, so transport is advised
w: His glucose is now normal, so a meal at home is enough care
His glipizide wears off quickly, so recurrence is unlikely
His oral glucose will keep working until his next meal

items.q: You are about to give oral glucose to a confused diabetic woman (glucose 39 mg/dL) when she becomes unresponsive with gurgling respirations. What is your next action?
items.x: Oral glucose requires a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Once she is unresponsive with gurgling, airway management and ALS for IV dextrose take priority; oral gel risks aspiration.
items.a: Suction and manage the airway; do not give oral glucose
w: Rub a small amount of gel on her gums while suctioning
Place her on her side and put the gel inside her cheek
Insert an oral airway and squeeze the gel beside it

items.q: A 7-year-old with type 1 diabetes is pale, sweaty, and irritable after soccer practice but answers questions and swallows normally. Glucose is 52 mg/dL. What is the best action?
items.x: A child who is awake and able to swallow can receive oral glucose for symptomatic hypoglycemia. Insulin would worsen the low glucose, and rest alone does not correct it.
items.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
w: Give a diet soda and a snack, then recheck glucose
Request ALS for IV dextrose before giving anything oral
Have him rest and recheck glucose in fifteen minutes

items.q: A 45-year-old found confused in a parked car smells of alcohol and has slurred speech. His friend says he is diabetic. What is the most important step before deciding on treatment?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic intoxication, and the two often coexist. A glucose reading decides whether oral glucose is indicated; assuming intoxication can miss a treatable emergency.
items.a: Check his blood glucose with a glucometer
w: Give oral glucose based on his history
Ask his friend how much alcohol he drank
Perform a stroke scale assessment

items.q: A 28-year-old diabetic has vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath odor, and mild confusion. Glucose reads 480 mg/dL. What is the best action?
items.x: Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to glucose, and these findings suggest DKA, which needs hospital care. Oral glucose would raise an already high glucose, and vomiting increases aspiration risk.
items.a: Withhold oral glucose, give supportive care, and transport
w: Give oral glucose because confusion suggests a low sugar
Give oral fluids to replace what he lost by vomiting
Help him take his own insulin before transport

items.q: Fifteen minutes after oral glucose, a 60-year-old diabetic remains confused and her repeat glucose is still 46 mg/dL. She can still swallow. What is the best next step?
items.x: Persistent hypoglycemia calls for a repeat dose per protocol while she can still swallow, plus ALS for IV dextrose. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia, and waiting prolongs brain glucose deprivation.
items.a: Repeat oral glucose per protocol and request ALS
w: Request ALS and give nothing more by mouth meanwhile
Give her a sandwich now in place of more oral glucose
Wait another 15 minutes for the first dose to work

items.q: A 68-year-old with diabetes has new left-sided weakness and slurred speech. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. Why can a low glucose produce stroke-like findings?
items.x: Neurons have almost no glucose stores. Hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits that look like a stroke and resolve once glucose is restored.
items.a: Brain cells run on glucose and fail when it runs low
w: Low glucose makes blood clot inside the brain's arteries
Insulin narrows the arteries on one side of the brain
Low glucose raises the pressure inside the skull

items.q: An 81-year-old nursing home resident with dementia is more confused than usual, according to staff. Glucose is 54 mg/dL. She has a weak cough and chokes when drinking water. Which is the best decision?
items.x: Oral glucose requires the ability to swallow and protect the airway; a weak cough and choking on liquids indicate aspiration risk. ALS can give IV dextrose instead.
items.a: Avoid oral glucose and request ALS for IV dextrose
w: Give small amounts of gel inside her cheek while seated
Thicken the gel with juice so she can swallow it safely
Give the gel slowly while a partner suctions her mouth

items.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant and takes insulin for gestational diabetes is shaky, sweaty, and anxious but alert. Glucose is 50 mg/dL. What is the best action?
items.x: Symptomatic hypoglycemia in an alert pregnant patient is treated with oral glucose, which also protects the fetus. Supine positioning late in pregnancy can cause hypotension, so the left side is preferred.
items.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
w: Request ALS for IV dextrose because she is pregnant
Give half the usual oral glucose to protect the fetus
Place her on her left side and recheck in 15 minutes

items.q: Which patient is the best candidate for EMT-administered oral glucose?
items.x: Oral glucose is for symptomatic hypoglycemia in a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Unresponsiveness, hyperglycemia, and a normal glucose are all reasons not to give it.
items.a: An alert, sweaty diabetic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL
w: A diabetic responsive only to pain, glucose 35 mg/dL
A confused diabetic with a glucose of 420 mg/dL
A drowsy diabetic who gags on sips, glucose 48 mg/dL

items.q: A known diabetic is sweaty and confused but able to swallow, and your glucometer has failed. He took insulin and skipped lunch. Following typical protocols, the best action is:
items.x: Many protocols allow oral glucose for a diabetic with signs of hypoglycemia when glucose cannot be measured; it is low risk in a patient who can swallow, while delay risks brain injury. Insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.
items.a: Give oral glucose per protocol, then reassess mental status
w: Request ALS and give nothing until a reading is available
Treat as a possible stroke, since glucose is unconfirmed
Give him a full meal in place of the oral glucose gel

items.q: A 50-year-old with chronic alcohol use is confused and sweaty after days of not eating. Glucose is 46 mg/dL. He can follow commands and swallow. What is the best action?
items.x: Hypoglycemia is treated regardless of diabetic history; poor intake and alcohol use deplete glucose stores. Naloxone is not indicated without signs of opioid toxicity.
items.a: Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck
w: Request ALS for IV dextrose, since he is not diabetic
Treat as alcohol intoxication and transport on his side
Give oral fluids only, since oral glucose is for diabetics

items.q: A 60-year-old diabetic with a glucose of 38 mg/dL receives oral glucose. Ten minutes later she is alert with a glucose of 112 mg/dL, but she still has slurred speech and a new right facial droop. What does this suggest?
items.x: Focal deficits that persist after glucose is corrected suggest a stroke, not hypoglycemia. More glucose is not indicated with a normal reading, and time to stroke care matters.
items.a: A possible stroke needing rapid stroke-center transport
w: Slow recovery from hypoglycemia needing more oral glucose
Lingering hypoglycemia effects that clear within the hour
A seizure aftereffect needing routine transport only

items.q: A 19-year-old type 1 diabetic collapsed during a marathon. She is awake, confused, and sweaty, and she can swallow. Glucose is 55 mg/dL; HR 118. What is the best initial treatment?
items.x: Exercise can drop glucose in insulin-dependent diabetics; she is symptomatic and able to swallow, so oral glucose is indicated. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
items.a: Give oral glucose per protocol, then recheck glucose
w: Give water only, since exertion explains her symptoms
Cool her first, then check glucose again in 15 minutes
Request ALS for IV fluids and give nothing by mouth

items.q: An insulin-dependent diabetic who is awake but very confused will not open her mouth for oral glucose and keeps turning her head away. What is the best action?
items.x: Oral glucose requires a cooperative patient who can swallow; forcing it risks aspiration and injury. ALS can give IV dextrose while you protect the airway.
items.a: Do not force it; protect the airway and request ALS
w: Slip a little gel inside her cheek with a tongue depressor
Have a family member hold her head while you give the gel
Recheck in 15 minutes and try the gel again without ALS

items.q: A 35-year-old diabetic who took insulin is anxious, pale, and sweaty with a pulse of 112. She is alert, and her glucose is 61 mg/dL. Her friend says it is a panic attack. What is the best action?
items.x: Sweating, pallor, anxiety, and tachycardia with a low glucose after insulin indicate symptomatic hypoglycemia. Treat it now rather than waiting for neurologic decline.
items.a: Treat the low glucose with oral glucose per protocol
w: Coach slow breathing and recheck glucose in 15 minutes
Request ALS for IV dextrose since she is still alert
Offer water and transport her for an anxiety evaluation

items.q: A 19-year-old with a known peanut allergy ate a cookie 15 minutes ago. He has diffuse hives, abdominal cramping, and has vomited twice. Breathing is unlabored; BP 118/76. He has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
items.x: Skin plus GI involvement after a known allergen exposure meets anaphylaxis criteria even without airway or BP changes. Early epinephrine is safer than waiting for airway compromise or shock.
items.a: Assist with his auto-injector because two systems are involved
w: Monitor closely, since breathing and blood pressure are normal
Request ALS for an antihistamine before using his auto-injector
Assist with the auto-injector only if wheezing or stridor develops

items.q: A 10-year-old (35 kg) has anaphylaxis from a bee sting. His parent holds his own prescribed 0.3 mg auto-injector and a younger sibling's 0.15 mg device. Which is appropriate?
items.x: The 0.3 mg auto-injector is for patients 30 kg or more, and it is prescribed to this child. The 0.15 mg device is for 15-30 kg and belongs to someone else.
items.a: The child's own 0.3 mg auto-injector
w: The sibling's 0.15 mg auto-injector
Both devices, one into each thigh
The 0.15 mg device first, then the 0.3 mg

items.q: Three minutes after an auto-injector, a 45-year-old with anaphylaxis says her heart is pounding and her hands are shaking. HR 118, BP 128/80, and her wheezing has decreased. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Tachycardia, palpitations, and tremor are common epinephrine side effects, and improving wheezing with a normal BP shows it is working. Repeat dosing is based on persistent anaphylaxis, not on side effects.
items.a: Expected epinephrine effects with a good response
w: An early biphasic reaction needing a second auto-injector
An epinephrine overdose needing urgent medical direction
Developing shock, since her heart rate is now above 100

items.q: Twenty minutes after an auto-injector, a patient's hives and wheezing had resolved. During transport her voice becomes hoarse, wheezing returns, and BP falls to 88/56. What is the best action?
items.x: Epinephrine wears off and anaphylaxis can recur; returning airway signs and hypotension call for a repeat dose per protocol and ALS. Albuterol alone does not treat airway swelling or shock.
items.a: Give a second auto-injector per protocol and request ALS
w: Assist with her albuterol inhaler and request ALS
Give high-flow oxygen and lay her flat until arrival
Wait for ALS, since epinephrine was given 20 minutes ago

items.q: A patient in anaphylaxis is wearing heavy jeans and has stridor. Which approach to her auto-injector is best?
items.x: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh and can be given through clothing to avoid delay. Removing clothing wastes time, and other sites are not the recommended location.
items.a: Inject the anterolateral thigh, through clothing if needed
w: Expose the thigh fully first, then inject the outer thigh
Inject the deltoid, which is easier to reach than the thigh
Inject the upper outer buttock, through clothing if needed

items.q: A 30-year-old asthmatic is wheezing after eating at a restaurant. Which additional finding most strongly suggests anaphylaxis rather than an asthma flare?
items.x: Hives and lip swelling with wheezing after a possible allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis, which needs epinephrine. An inhaler history, a mild tachypnea, or a night cough do not distinguish the two.
items.a: New hives and lip swelling
w: A heart rate of 118 at rest
Wheezing heard in both lungs
Speaking in short phrases only

items.q: A teenager in anaphylaxis with stridor and BP 80/50 has only an auto-injector that expired two months ago. ALS is 15 minutes away. What is the best action?
items.x: A recently expired auto-injector usually retains much of its potency, and in a life-threatening reaction with no alternative, medical direction may approve its use rather than a 15-minute delay. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
items.a: Contact medical direction about using the expired device
w: Wait for ALS to arrive with an in-date epinephrine dose
Give high-flow oxygen only, since the device has expired
Use the device in the deltoid, where absorption is faster

items.q: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant develops hives, wheezing, and BP 84/50 after a dose of an antibiotic. She has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
items.x: There is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and maternal shock threatens the fetus. Left lateral positioning prevents the uterus from compressing the vena cava.
items.a: Give epinephrine and position her on her left side
w: Give oxygen, tilt her left, and let ALS decide on epinephrine
Give epinephrine and lay her flat on her back with legs raised
Give oxygen and call her obstetrician before any epinephrine

items.q: After assisting with an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, which reassessment finding best shows the drug is working?
items.x: Improving airway sounds and blood pressure show that anaphylaxis is being reversed. A rising heart rate, tremor, and local pallor are side effects, not measures of response.
items.a: Stridor resolves and BP rises to 112/70
w: Heart rate rises from 110 to 126
Hands become shaky and tremulous
The injection site is pale and sore

items.q: A 68-year-old with coronary disease received an auto-injector for anaphylaxis. His wheezing has improved, but he now reports new chest pressure; HR 128, BP 176/98. What is the best action?
items.x: Chest pain and severe hypertension are serious epinephrine adverse effects that need ALS or medical direction input. A second dose is not indicated because the anaphylaxis is improving.
items.a: Report the chest pain to ALS or medical direction
w: Give a second auto-injector, since symptoms persist
Assist with nitroglycerin before contacting anyone
Reassure him that this is expected and needs no report

items.q: A 35-year-old in anaphylaxis becomes unresponsive and pulseless before you can use her auto-injector. What is your immediate priority?
items.x: Once she is pulseless, high-quality CPR and early defibrillation come first; ALS gives arrest-dose epinephrine IV or IO. Compressions should not be delayed for an IM injection, which is poorly absorbed without circulation.
items.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED
w: Give the auto-injector, then start CPR
Open the airway and give rescue breaths
Give the auto-injector and recheck a pulse

items.q: A 40-year-old with no known allergies has hives, stridor, and BP 80/48 after a wasp sting. Your ambulance carries epinephrine auto-injectors under local protocol. He has no prescription. What is the best action?
items.x: First-time anaphylaxis is still anaphylaxis; when the service stocks auto-injectors, protocol allows the EMT to give one without a prior prescription. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
items.a: Give the ambulance auto-injector per protocol
w: Remove the stinger and apply a cold pack to the site first
Give high-flow oxygen and leave epinephrine to ALS
Lay him flat, raise his legs, and recheck in 5 minutes

items.q: After epinephrine, an anaphylaxis patient's stridor is improving, but SpO2 is 89% and she is working hard to breathe. Which oxygen decision is best?
items.x: Hypoxia with increased work of breathing calls for high-concentration oxygen and readiness to assist ventilations. Epinephrine treats the cause but does not replace oxygen or ventilatory support.
items.a: Give high-concentration oxygen; be ready to ventilate
w: Give a second auto-injector now to raise the SpO2
Apply a nasal cannula at low flow and recheck SpO2
Assist with an albuterol inhaler before any oxygen

items.q: A 50-year-old with a shellfish allergy has hives only on her forearms and mild itching after dinner. Breathing is normal, BP 134/82, and she has no GI symptoms. She has her auto-injector. What is the best plan?
items.x: Localized skin findings alone, with normal breathing and BP, do not meet anaphylaxis criteria. Reassess often and give epinephrine promptly if other systems become involved.
items.a: Monitor closely and be ready to give epinephrine
w: Assist with her auto-injector now, given her allergy
Advise an antihistamine at home with no reassessment
Request ALS to start epinephrine before symptoms spread

items.q: A 9-year-old (32 kg) in anaphylaxis received his 0.3 mg auto-injector 10 minutes ago. Stridor is worse and he is pale and lethargic. No second injector is on scene, and ALS is 8 minutes out. What is the best action?
items.x: A used auto-injector cannot deliver another dose. Airway support, oxygen, and an urgent ALS update for further epinephrine are the priorities; albuterol does not treat upper airway swelling.
items.a: Support the airway, give oxygen, and update ALS
w: Try the used auto-injector again in the other thigh
Assist with an albuterol inhaler in place of epinephrine
Sit him fully upright and wait for ALS before acting

Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before giving any treatment

items.q: You have given 100 mL of D10 to a hypoglycemic 66-year-old woman. Her glucose rose from 31 to 64 mg/dL, but she is still confused. What should you do next?
items.x: D10 is titrated in 5-10 g (50-100 mL) aliquots until glucose is normal and mental status improves. A glucose still in the low 60s with persistent confusion means treatment is not finished.
items.a: Give another D10 aliquot and reassess glucose and mental status
w: Switch to oral glucose gel now that the glucose is above 60
Give IM glucagon as well, since the D10 has been too slow
Finish the bag wide open, then recheck at the hospital

items.q: A 71-year-old man has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. BP is 178/96 and his blood glucose is 312 mg/dL. A bystander says "he is diabetic, give him sugar." What is the best action?
items.x: Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to dextrose, and the glucose reading rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of his deficits. Giving sugar to a hyperglycemic stroke patient may worsen outcome and delays stroke care.
items.a: Withhold dextrose and treat as a possible stroke with rapid transport
w: Give D10 because diabetics with altered speech are usually hypoglycemic
Give oral glucose because it is safer than IV dextrose
Give a half dose of D50 to be safe and recheck

items.q: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days. She is lethargic, her glucose is 38 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. What is the best treatment?
items.x: For infants and children, D10 at 5-10 mL/kg IV is the listed dose. A lethargic child cannot safely take oral glucose, and an adult D50 dose is far too concentrated and too large for a 16 kg child.
items.a: D10 IV at 5-10 mL/kg, then recheck glucose
w: Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Undiluted D50, the full 50 mL by slow IV push
IM glucagon 1 mg instead of IV dextrose

items.q: A 49-year-old woman woke up after IV D10 and now has a glucose of 118 mg/dL. Which finding is most concerning?
items.x: Swelling, coolness and blanching at the site suggest extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis with dextrose. Stop the infusion at that site; hunger and resolving sweating are expected after correction.
items.a: Swelling, coolness and blanching around the IV site
w: A mild headache she rates 2 out of 10
Hunger and asking for something to eat right away
Mild sweating that is now resolving

items.q: You are titrating D10 for a 62-year-old hypoglycemic man. After 150 mL, he is alert, oriented and his glucose is 142 mg/dL. What should you do now?
items.x: Dextrose is stopped when glucose is normal and mental status has improved. Pushing the full bag regardless of response risks hyperglycemia, which is the most common side effect.
items.a: Stop further dextrose and keep reassessing glucose and mental status
w: Infuse the rest of the 250 mL bag to complete the full dose
Give IM glucagon to prevent the glucose from dropping again
Switch to D50 so the remaining full dose can be given faster

items.q: A 40-year-old man of unknown history is found unresponsive in his apartment. RR is 14 and deep, SpO2 97%, pupils midsize and there is no trauma. Before giving any medication, what is the most important step?
items.x: Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible cause of unresponsiveness, and a glucose check guides whether dextrose is needed. His breathing is adequate and his pupils are not pinpoint, so naloxone is not indicated.
items.a: Check a blood glucose level
w: Obtain a 12-lead ECG tracing
Establish a large-bore IV line
Search the scene for pill bottles

items.q: A 6-year-old with type 1 diabetes received D10 at the pediatric dose. Ten minutes later she is still lethargic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
items.x: Persistent hypoglycemia with altered mental status means the dose was not enough, so a repeat per protocol is indicated. A lethargic child still cannot protect her airway for oral glucose.
items.a: Repeat dextrose per protocol and recheck glucose and mental status
w: Consider her treated and transport without further medication
Give oral glucose now because she has already had IV dextrose
Change to undiluted adult D50 because the D10 did not work at all

items.q: An 84-year-old malnourished woman with a glucose of 36 mg/dL received glucagon 1 mg IM 15 minutes ago because no IV could be placed. Her glucose is now 37 mg/dL and she is still unresponsive. What does this most likely mean, and what is next?
items.x: Glucagon works by releasing stored glycogen, so malnourished patients may not respond. When glucose does not rise within 15 minutes, dextrose by IV or IO is needed.
items.a: Her glycogen stores are likely depleted; obtain IV or IO access for dextrose
w: The glucagon needs another 30 minutes to peak; keep monitoring only
The dose was too small for her; repeat glucagon IM and transport
The glucagon was injected too shallow; give oral glucose gel instead

items.q: A 52-year-old man with a known pheochromocytoma is unresponsive with a glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is the best plan?
items.x: Pheochromocytoma is a contraindication to glucagon because it can trigger a dangerous catecholamine surge. Dextrose can be given IO, and oral glucose is unsafe in an unresponsive patient.
items.a: Avoid glucagon and obtain IO access to give dextrose per protocol
w: Give glucagon IM because it is the standard choice when an IV fails
Give oral glucose gel because he cannot get glucagon
Give glucagon at half the usual dose to limit side effects

items.q: A 27-year-old diabetic received glucagon 1 mg IM. He is now awake, oriented, swallowing normally and his glucose is 92 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.x: The effect of glucagon is short and uses up glycogen, so glucose can fall again. Once he can swallow, oral carbohydrates help maintain the glucose; another glucagon dose is not indicated.
items.a: Give oral carbohydrates and continue to monitor during transport
w: Give a second glucagon dose to keep the glucose from falling
Start an IV and give dextrose to rebuild his glycogen stores
Keep him NPO during transport because glucagon causes vomiting

items.q: You are called for several diabetic patients at the same event. Which one is the best candidate for IM glucagon?
items.x: Glucagon is indicated for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. The alert patient can take oral glucose, the patient with an IV should get IV dextrose, and the hyperglycemic patient needs no glucose-raising drug.
items.a: Unresponsive, glucose 29 mg/dL, no IV obtainable
w: Alert, glucose 58 mg/dL, asking for juice
Confused, glucose 45 mg/dL, with a patent IV already in place
Alert, glucose 240 mg/dL, nauseated

items.q: A parent gave a 9-year-old 3 mg of nasal glucagon 5 minutes before you arrived. The boy is starting to stir and moan but cannot answer questions. What is the best next action?
items.x: The child is responding, so the priority is airway protection (vomiting is common), a glucose recheck and reassessment. A drowsy child cannot safely take oral glucose, and repeating glucagon this early is not indicated.
items.a: Recheck glucose, protect the airway and reassess as the drug takes effect
w: Give IM glucagon now because the nasal form is unreliable in children
Give oral glucose gel right away while he is starting to stir
Give a second nasal dose now, since the first has not woken him

items.q: A confused 45-year-old has a glucose of 33 mg/dL and a patent, flushing IV. Your partner hands you glucagon. What is the best response?
items.x: Glucagon is meant for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. With a working IV, dextrose acts faster and does not depend on liver glycogen.
items.a: Give IV dextrose instead, since IV access is available
w: Give the glucagon IM since it avoids any IV-related complications
Give glucagon IV push followed by oral glucose
Give both glucagon and dextrose to speed recovery

items.q: A 67-year-old diabetic has new left arm weakness and facial droop that started an hour ago. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. He cannot swallow safely and no IV can be started. What is the best action?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke, and focal deficits may resolve once glucose is corrected. With no IV and an unsafe swallow, glucagon is the appropriate route, followed by a neurologic reassessment.
items.a: Give glucagon IM and recheck glucose and neurologic signs
w: Give oral glucose gel in the cheek, since he is still conscious
Transport rapidly to a stroke center and recheck glucose en route
Treat as a stroke first and let the hospital correct the glucose

items.q: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain. BP is 150/90 and HR 84. He says he took tadalafil (Cialis) about 30 hours ago. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
items.x: Tadalafil lasts longer than other PDE-5 inhibitors, so nitrates are withheld for 48 hours. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
items.a: Withhold it; tadalafil within 48 hours is a contraindication
w: Give it, since more than 24 hours have passed since his last dose
Give a half dose and lay him flat to prevent hypotension
Give it only if his systolic pressure stays above 120

items.q: A 63-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has chest pressure. BP is 132/78 and HR 92. Her medication list includes riociguat. What should you do about nitroglycerin?
items.x: Riociguat is listed with the PDE-5 inhibitors as a nitroglycerin contraindication because the combination can cause severe hypotension. A normal BP does not remove that risk.
items.a: Withhold nitroglycerin and continue ACS care and transport
w: Give nitroglycerin since her BP is above 90 systolic
Give nitroglycerin but only one dose
Give nitroglycerin and start a fluid bolus at the same time

items.q: A 74-year-old man with chest pain says his BP is "always around 160." Today it is 118/70 with HR 96. He is pale and diaphoretic. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
items.x: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated with SBP under 90 or more than 30 below baseline. A drop of over 40 from his usual pressure suggests poor perfusion, so a vasodilator could cause collapse.
items.a: Withhold it; his BP is more than 30 below his baseline
w: Give it, since his systolic is well above 90
Give it, since a lower BP shows his heart workload is now reduced
Give two doses quickly before his BP drops further

items.q: Two minutes after SL nitroglycerin, a 66-year-old woman becomes pale and lightheaded. HR falls from 78 to 44 and BP from 128/80 to 76/40. What is happening, and what should you do?
items.x: Sudden bradycardia with hypotension after nitroglycerin is a known Bezold-Jarisch reaction. Further nitrates are withheld, and supine positioning with a fluid bolus per protocol supports her pressure.
items.a: Bezold-Jarisch reaction; lay her supine, no more nitro, fluids per protocol
w: Normal nitrate effect; sit her upright and give the next dose on schedule
Worsening infarction; give another nitroglycerin dose to relieve ischemia
Allergic reaction; lay her supine and give IM epinephrine per protocol

items.q: A 61-year-old man has received three SL nitroglycerin doses over 15 minutes. Pain is 5 out of 10, BP is 140/86 and HR 82. What is the best next action?
items.x: The FDA label allows up to three doses in 15 minutes, so further doses need protocol or medical control direction. Persistent pain points to ongoing ischemia that needs rapid transport, not a larger dose.
items.a: Hold more SL doses unless protocol or medical control directs; transport
w: Give a fourth dose right away, since his BP is still above 90 systolic
Double the next dose, since the first three were not enough
Stop treatment entirely because the medication has failed

items.q: After one SL nitroglycerin, a 57-year-old woman's chest pain goes from 7 to 0 out of 10. BP is 130/80 and HR 76. What should the AEMT do now?
items.x: Nitroglycerin is stopped once pain is relieved, so more doses add risk without benefit. Relief with nitroglycerin does not rule out ACS, so she still needs transport and monitoring.
items.a: Hold further doses and keep monitoring during transport
w: Give the second dose in 5 minutes to complete the series
Give two more doses to prevent the pain from returning
Cancel transport since the pain is fully relieved

items.q: A 69-year-old man with chest pain is ready for nitroglycerin. Which finding is most important to address before you give it?
items.x: Severe bradycardia is a listed contraindication, and adding a vasodilator can drop his BP further. The other findings do not change the decision to give nitroglycerin.
items.a: HR of 42 with dizziness
w: HR of 96 with anxiety
BP of 148/92 in both arms
RR of 22 with clear lungs

items.q: A 64-year-old man is given a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet but chews and swallows it. Why does swallowing make the tablet much less effective?
items.x: Swallowed nitroglycerin goes through the liver first, which removes most of it. Under the tongue it is absorbed straight into the bloodstream.
items.a: The liver removes most of it on the way in
w: Stomach acid converts the drug into an inactive salt
The drug only works where it touches the tongue
Swallowed tablets are absorbed too fast to last

items.q: Five minutes after nitroglycerin, a 59-year-old woman says her chest pain went from 8 to 4, but she now has a pounding headache and flushing. BP is 138/84. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: Headache and flushing are common, expected effects of vasodilation. Her BP is stable and pain is improving, so a repeat dose per protocol is reasonable.
items.a: An expected side effect; reassess and repeat per protocol
w: An allergic reaction; give no more doses and give IM epinephrine
A sign of excessive dosing; lay her flat and give a fluid bolus
A hypertensive response; give the next dose early to lower BP

items.q: A 55-year-old man has chest pain that suggests ACS. BP is 142/88. He has asthma and says that aspirin once caused a severe asthma attack. What is the best decision?
items.x: Aspirin-induced asthma is a listed contraindication because aspirin can cause severe bronchospasm in these patients. A smaller dose does not prevent the reaction.
items.a: Withhold aspirin and continue other ACS care
w: Give aspirin, since the benefit in ACS outweighs the risk
Give one 81 mg tablet instead of the full dose
Give aspirin with albuterol ready in case he wheezes
