A 55-year-old with a dislocated shoulder and BP 138/86

items.q: A 300-lb man with severe facial burns, a short neck and stridor is combative. The crew has no supraglottic airway or surgical airway kit, and it is a 5-minute transport to a trauma center. A partner suggests rocuronium so he can be intubated. What is the best decision?
items.x: Inability to manage the airway is a contraindication to paralytics; a predicted difficult airway with no rescue option can turn into a fatal cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate event. A smaller dose does not preserve safe breathing.
items.a: Do not paralyze without a rescue plan; support and transport
w: Give rocuronium, since paralysis makes intubation easier
Give rocuronium at half dose to keep some breathing
Give rocuronium now, then decide on a backup plan only if he desaturates

items.q: After RSI with rocuronium, two intubation attempts fail. SpO2 drops to 85%, and BVM ventilation with two providers and an OPA is difficult. What is the best next step?
items.x: Rocuronium paralysis lasts a long time, so spontaneous breathing will not return soon; oxygenation through a supraglottic airway is the priority. Repeated attempts during desaturation worsen hypoxia.
items.a: Place a supraglottic airway and ventilate
w: Wait for the rocuronium to wear off
Keep attempting intubation until successful
Give naloxone to restore breathing

items.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient missed two sessions and is now obtunded with vomiting. The monitor shows peaked T waves and a wide QRS. You are preparing for RSI. Which paralytic decision is best?
items.x: Known or suspected hyperkalemia contraindicates succinylcholine, which raises potassium and can trigger arrest. Rocuronium does not raise potassium; a smaller succinylcholine dose does not remove the risk.
items.a: Use rocuronium instead of succinylcholine
w: Use succinylcholine at the usual RSI dose
Use succinylcholine at a reduced dose
Give succinylcholine IM to slow absorption

items.q: A 77-year-old was hospitalized for a stroke 3 weeks ago, has been bedbound since, and now has aspiration pneumonia with worsening hypoxia that requires RSI. Which finding most affects your paralytic choice?
items.x: Stroke with immobilization for more than 48-72 hours contraindicates succinylcholine because of the risk of severe hyperkalemia. Age and pneumonia do not change the paralytic choice.
items.a: Immobility since the stroke weeks ago
w: Age over 75 years
Pneumonia as the underlying cause of his hypoxia
Prior use of aspirin for stroke

items.q: Before RSI, a 24-year-old's mother tells you that her brother developed a dangerously high fever and stiffness during surgery under general anesthesia. What is the best decision about succinylcholine?
items.x: A family history of malignant hyperthermia is a contraindication to succinylcholine. Antipyretics and dose reduction do not prevent a malignant hyperthermia reaction.
items.a: Avoid it because of possible malignant hyperthermia risk
w: Give it as planned, since the reaction occurred in another relative
Give it but pre-treat with acetaminophen
Give a smaller dose and watch the temperature

items.q: During transport, a patient intubated and paralyzed with vecuronium suddenly loses the EtCO2 waveform, SpO2 falls from 98% to 86%, and HR drops from 96 to 58. Sedation is running and the next vecuronium dose is due. What is the best action?
items.x: Loss of the EtCO2 waveform with falling SpO2 and bradycardia suggests a dislodged tube or disconnection, and a paralyzed patient cannot breathe on his own. Redosing vecuronium or adjusting sedation ignores the airway emergency.
items.a: Hold the dose and check the tube and circuit now
w: Give the vecuronium dose on schedule
Increase the sedation infusion rate
Give atropine and continue as planned

items.q: After midazolam and fentanyl for procedural sedation, a 52-year-old's RR drops to 6, SpO2 to 87%, and EtCO2 rises to 62. What is the first action?
items.x: Combined benzodiazepine and opioid sedation can cause respiratory depression; airway support and ventilation come first. Reversal agents may follow, but they do not replace immediate ventilation.
items.a: Open the airway and assist ventilation with BVM
w: Give flumazenil IV to reverse the midazolam effect right away
Give naloxone IN and wait for the response
Increase oxygen by nonrebreather and observe

items.q: An intubated trauma patient needs post-intubation sedation. His BP is 76/40 and HR 132 despite fluids. Which sedation plan is best?
items.x: Midazolam can cause hypotension and shock is a relative contraindication, so ketamine is a better sedative in the hypotensive patient. Withholding sedation risks awareness, especially if the patient is paralyzed.
items.a: Ketamine per protocol rather than a midazolam bolus
w: A midazolam bolus followed by a continuous midazolam infusion
No sedation until the BP is normal
A midazolam bolus plus fentanyl for analgesia

items.q: After ketamine for a painful dislocation reduction, a 34-year-old is frightened, crying and describing terrifying visions. Vitals are stable and airway is patent. What is the best management?
items.x: This is a ketamine emergence reaction; a calm environment and, if needed, a small benzodiazepine dose per protocol can help. Naloxone has no effect on ketamine.
items.a: Reduce stimulation; small benzodiazepine dose per protocol
w: Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effect
Give a repeat ketamine dose to deepen sedation
Physically restrain the patient and give haloperidol IV

items.q: A 66-year-old COPD patient on CPAP was given lorazepam for anxiety. He is now drowsy with RR 9, EtCO2 70 and SpO2 86%. What is the best next step?
items.x: CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing, alert patient; with hypoventilation and rising EtCO2, he needs assisted ventilation. Increasing the CPAP pressure does not fix hypoventilation from respiratory depression.
items.a: Remove CPAP and ventilate with BVM
w: Increase the CPAP pressure to improve ventilation
Give a second lorazepam dose
Switch to a nonrebreather

items.q: A 40-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis has a dislocated shoulder with severe muscle spasm. A partner suggests diazepam to relax the muscles. What is the best decision?
items.x: Myasthenia gravis is a contraindication to diazepam, which can worsen muscle weakness and breathing. IM diazepam is absorbed erratically and does not avoid the problem.
items.a: Avoid diazepam because of her myasthenia gravis
w: Give diazepam because it relaxes skeletal muscle
Give diazepam IM since IM is safer
Give diazepam with fentanyl for synergy

items.q: After a rapid IV push of a large fentanyl dose, a patient becomes apneic. You cannot ventilate with the BVM, and the chest wall is stiff. What is the best action?
items.x: Chest wall rigidity is a known serious effect of fentanyl; it is treated with naloxone or a paralytic per protocol along with continued ventilation. It is not a dystonic reaction.
items.a: Chest wall rigidity: naloxone or a paralytic per protocol
w: Push harder on the BVM until the chest rises
Give more fentanyl to relax the muscles
Give IV diphenhydramine for a presumed dystonic reaction

items.q: A 6-year-old (22 kg) with an obvious forearm deformity is screaming and has no IV access; two IV attempts have failed. What is the best analgesia plan?
items.x: Intranasal fentanyl gives fast analgesia without IV access and avoids a painful IO for an isolated limb injury. Delaying analgesia for IV access is unnecessary.
items.a: Intranasal fentanyl per protocol
w: Wait until IV access is obtained
IO fentanyl through a tibial needle
IM morphine at the adult dose

items.q: A 48-year-old with a tibia fracture received two doses of fentanyl. Pain is now 6/10, but she is drowsy though rousable, with RR 10 and SpO2 92%. What is the best next step?
items.x: RR around 10 with oversedation is a stop point for fentanyl, so hold doses and watch ventilation closely. Full-dose naloxone is not needed while she is breathing and rousable.
items.a: Withhold more fentanyl, stimulate her and monitor EtCO2
w: Give a third fentanyl dose since pain persists
Give naloxone 2 mg IV for full and rapid reversal of the opioid
Switch to morphine and give a full dose

items.q: Four patients each need fentanyl for pain. Which patient needs the most caution?
items.x: An older patient with chronic lung disease who also takes a benzodiazepine is at highest risk of opioid respiratory depression. The healthy patients with normal vitals carry much less risk.
items.a: An 82-year-old on home O2 for COPD who takes a nightly benzodiazepine
w: A 30-year-old with a kidney stone and normal vital signs
A 25-year-old with an ankle fracture and BP 130/82
A 45-year-old with a shoulder dislocation and no medical history

items.q: A 29-year-old with three rib fractures is in an acute asthma attack with diffuse wheezing and SpO2 90%. He asks for pain relief. Which plan is best?
items.x: Acute or severe asthma is a contraindication to morphine without airway support, and histamine release can worsen bronchospasm. Fentanyl with close monitoring and treatment of the asthma is a safer plan.
items.a: Avoid morphine; fentanyl per protocol and treat the asthma
w: Give morphine since it also reduces air hunger
Give morphine and diphenhydramine together
Give a full morphine dose so he can take deep, effective breaths

items.q: After morphine for a hip fracture, an 81-year-old's BP falls from 124/80 to 86/58. RR is 16, SpO2 96%, and she is alert. What is the best next step?
items.x: Hypotension is a stop point for morphine; manage with positioning and fluids. With normal breathing and alertness, naloxone is not indicated and would remove her analgesia.
items.a: Stop morphine, position supine and give fluid per protocol
w: Give naloxone IV to reverse the hypotension from the morphine
Give the next morphine dose for pain control
Give epinephrine IM for possible anaphylaxis

items.q: During an interfacility transfer, a patient's next hydromorphone dose is due. She is hard to arouse, with RR 11 and SpO2 91%. What is the best decision?
items.x: RR below 12 and excessive sedation are hold criteria for hydromorphone. A scheduled order does not override clear signs of opioid toxicity.
items.a: Hold the dose and notify the sending provider
w: Give the dose since it is ordered on schedule
Give half the dose and recheck in 30 minutes
Give the dose and add naloxone at the same time

items.q: A 6-year-old weighing 20 kg improved after nebulizers for an asthma attack. Medical direction orders dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, but she has vomited twice and has no IV access. What is the best action?
items.x: 0.6 mg/kg for 20 kg is 12 mg, and the IM route avoids losing an oral dose to vomiting. A 1.2 mg dose is a tenfold error, and waiting delays a drug that already takes hours to work.
items.a: Give 12 mg IM
w: Give 12 mg PO now
Give 1.2 mg IM
Wait for IV access at the hospital

items.q: After 0.4 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient now has RR 14, SpO2 96%, and responds to voice but is drowsy. What is the best next step?
items.x: Naloxone is titrated to adequate ventilation, not full wakefulness. Extra doses risk acute withdrawal, vomiting and agitation without improving safety.
items.a: Monitor; no more naloxone is needed now
w: Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Give a second, larger IV dose to prevent relapse
Give naloxone IM to extend the effect

items.q: After 2 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient vomits, becomes agitated, and has crackles with SpO2 84% and pink frothy sputum. What is the best next step?
items.x: Pulmonary edema is a serious naloxone effect; oxygenation and ventilation support are the priority, and more naloxone is not indicated. The low SpO2 is from pulmonary edema, not recurrent opioid toxicity.
items.a: Support oxygenation and ventilation; give no more naloxone
w: Give another naloxone dose IV for recurrent opioid toxicity
Give midazolam to control the agitation
Give furosemide and repeat the naloxone

items.q: A 40-year-old was intubated using succinylcholine 8 minutes ago and faces a 60-minute transport. Tube placement is confirmed and sedation and analgesia have been given, but he is starting to move against the ventilator. Medical direction orders ongoing paralysis. Which is best?
items.x: A longer-acting nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium maintains paralysis once placement and sedation are assured. Repeated succinylcholine can cause bradycardia and hyperkalemia, and etomidate is a sedative, not a paralytic.
items.a: Rocuronium per protocol
w: Repeat succinylcholine every 5 minutes
An etomidate infusion for paralysis
Naloxone to reduce the movement

items.q: A 72-year-old with renal colic has normal renal function, no bleeding history, and takes no NSAIDs. Medical direction approves ketorolac. Which single IV dose is appropriate?
items.x: Patients 65 and older get a reduced single dose of 15 mg IV. Higher doses are for younger adults and raise the risk of renal and GI harm.
items.a: 15 mg IV
w: 30 mg IV push
60 mg IV
60 mg IM

items.q: A 54-year-old with renal colic takes daily aspirin for a heart stent and had a bleeding ulcer last year. Which analgesic decision is best?
items.x: History of GI bleeding and concurrent aspirin use are contraindications to ketorolac. A reduced dose does not remove the bleeding risk.
items.a: Withhold ketorolac and consider an alternative
w: Give ketorolac since renal colic responds well to NSAIDs
Give ketorolac at a reduced dose
Give ketorolac with ondansetron

items.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin fell and has a wrist fracture and a mild headache. She asks for something other than opioids. What is the best decision?
items.x: Coagulopathy and possible intracranial bleeding are contraindications to ketorolac. The IM route does not reduce bleeding risk.
items.a: Avoid ketorolac due to bleeding risk and possible head bleed
w: Give ketorolac since she clearly wants to avoid opioids
Give ketorolac IM to reduce bleeding risk
Give ketorolac and recheck her neuro status

items.q: A 34-year-old with an ankle sprain asks for ibuprofen. She has asthma that previously worsened after taking aspirin. What is the best decision?
items.x: Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma is a contraindication to ibuprofen because of cross-reactivity. Having albuterol ready does not make the drug safe.
items.a: Withhold ibuprofen because of NSAID-sensitive asthma
w: Give ibuprofen since it is a different drug from aspirin
Give ibuprofen with albuterol on standby
Give a smaller ibuprofen dose

items.q: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks of pregnancy has severe back pain after a fall. She has no allergies. Which pain medication decision is best?
items.x: Ibuprofen is contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy. Acetaminophen is a safer option, and changing the route does not remove the fetal risk.
items.a: Avoid ibuprofen; consider acetaminophen per protocol
w: Give ibuprofen since she has no allergies
Give ibuprofen IV to bypass the GI tract
Give a double dose of ibuprofen for a faster, stronger effect

items.q: A 55-year-old with known cirrhosis and jaundice has a painful wrist fracture. Which analgesic decision is best?
items.x: Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease contraindicates acetaminophen. The IV route does not bypass liver metabolism.
items.a: Avoid acetaminophen because of his active liver disease
w: Give acetaminophen since it is gentle on the stomach lining
Give IV acetaminophen to bypass the liver
Give acetaminophen with a reduced interval

items.q: A 24-year-old with a sprained knee asks for IV acetaminophen. She says she took several OTC cold remedies today and is unsure how much acetaminophen they contained. What is the best decision?
items.x: Many OTC products contain acetaminophen, and reaching the daily max is a stop point. Hold until the total is known; changing the route or halving the dose does not prevent exceeding it.
items.a: Hold acetaminophen until the total dose is known
w: Give the full IV dose for her pain
Give half the IV dose as a precaution
Give acetaminophen PO instead of IV to be safer

items.q: Medical direction orders promethazine for a 40-year-old woman with severe motion sickness and repeated vomiting. Her only IV is a small catheter in the back of her hand. What is the best route?
items.x: IM is the preferred route for promethazine; IV use, especially through small hand veins, risks severe tissue injury, and SQ injection is contraindicated. If given IV it must be diluted and slow.
items.a: Deep IM injection into a large muscle
w: Undiluted IV push through the hand IV
SQ injection in the back of the upper arm
Rapid IV push followed by a fast flush

items.q: A 34-year-old man is found in a bathroom with a syringe nearby. He is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, RR 4, SpO2 78% and HR 112. Your partner is preparing naloxone. What should you do right now?
items.x: Hypoxia is the immediate threat, so ventilation comes first and continues while naloxone is drawn up. Waiting for naloxone to work while he stays apneic and hypoxic wastes critical minutes.
items.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen while naloxone is prepared
w: Give naloxone first and wait for him to breathe on his own
Intubate him before any naloxone is given so the airway is secure
Place him in the recovery position and apply a nonrebreather mask

items.q: A 45-year-old woman who takes methadone was found with RR 6. After titrated IV naloxone she has RR 14, SpO2 96% and is awake. She now wants to refuse transport. What is your main concern?
items.x: Methadone has a long duration while naloxone wears off much sooner, so respiratory depression can return after the crew leaves. Withdrawal from naloxone is unpleasant but short-lived and is not the main danger.
items.a: Methadone can outlast naloxone, so breathing may slow again
w: Naloxone will cause several days of severe opioid withdrawal
Naloxone often causes a delayed hypertensive crisis
She must receive a full second dose before she can refuse

items.q: A 2-year-old weighing 12 kg got into a grandparent's oxycodone. He is limp with RR 6 and pinpoint pupils. You are ventilating with a BVM. Using the PALS full-reversal dose, how much naloxone do you give?
items.x: The PALS full-reversal dose is 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg), so 12 kg x 0.1 mg = 1.2 mg. A flat adult dose ignores the weight-based calculation, and ventilation continues until breathing is adequate.
items.a: 1.2 mg IV, IO, IM or IN
w: 0.12 mg IV and wait 30 minutes
2 mg IV regardless of weight
4 mg IN as for an adult

items.q: A 26-year-old woman took an unknown amount of amitriptyline. She had one brief seizure. HR 128, BP 84/50, QRS 148 ms, and she is ventilating adequately on a BVM. What is the best next medication?
items.x: A wide QRS with hypotension after a tricyclic overdose reflects sodium channel blockade, and bicarbonate is the antidote. Procainamide and amiodarone can worsen sodium channel or QT toxicity in this setting.
items.a: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Procainamide infusion for the wide QRS
Physostigmine to reverse anticholinergic signs

items.q: A 40-year-old man with a tricyclic overdose has a QRS of 138 ms. He is unresponsive with RR 6 and SpO2 88%. Before you give sodium bicarbonate, what is the priority?
items.x: Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate: the CO2 produced by bicarbonate builds up and worsens acidosis unless the patient is ventilated. Giving it to a hypoventilating patient undercuts the treatment.
items.a: Secure ventilation, because bicarbonate creates CO2 that must be exhaled
w: Give the bicarbonate first, since the wide QRS is the bigger and more urgent threat
Give midazolam first to prevent seizures during the infusion
Obtain an ABG on arrival before deciding on any bicarbonate

items.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has Kussmaul breathing, a glucometer reading of HI, HR 124 and BP 98/60. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Your partner suggests sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis. What is best?
items.x: DKA is treated with fluids and later insulin, and routine bicarbonate is not indicated without a specific reason such as hyperkalemic ECG changes or arrest. Rapid breathing here is compensation, not a reason to give bicarbonate.
items.a: Withhold bicarbonate and give an isotonic fluid bolus per protocol
w: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV to correct the acidosis
Give bicarbonate only if the respiratory rate keeps increasing
Give bicarbonate first and then start IV fluids once the blood pH improves

items.q: After IV glucagon for a propranolol overdose, a 58-year-old man's HR rises from 38 to 58 and BP improves, but he becomes drowsy and starts vomiting. What is the best action?
items.x: Nausea and vomiting are common glucagon effects, and a drowsy patient is at risk of aspiration, so airway protection comes first. Vomiting is not an allergy, and charcoal is contraindicated with altered mental status.
items.a: Position him and suction to protect the airway; consider an antiemetic
w: Stop all glucagon since vomiting means he is allergic to it
Give atropine to treat the vagal response that is causing all the vomiting
Give activated charcoal now that his heart rate has improved

items.q: A 62-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes was unresponsive with BG 32 and no IV access. Fifteen minutes after glucagon 1 mg IM she is awake, alert and swallowing, with BG 88. What is the best next step?
items.x: Glucagon raises glucose briefly by releasing stored glycogen, so an awake patient who can swallow should get oral carbohydrates to keep the glucose up. A repeat dose is not needed when she can eat.
items.a: Give oral carbohydrates now that she can swallow safely
w: Give a second glucagon dose to prevent recurrence
Withhold food because glucagon causes vomiting
Stop monitoring her since her glucose is now normal

items.q: A 62-year-old dialysis patient has missed two treatments. He is weak, HR 48, BP 88/50, and the ECG shows a very wide QRS with peaked T waves. What is the first medication?
items.x: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes calls for calcium first to stabilize the heart muscle. Atropine and amiodarone do not address the cause, and albuterol shifts potassium but does not protect the heart quickly enough by itself.
items.a: Calcium chloride 1 g IV slow push
w: Atropine 1 mg IV for the bradycardia
Amiodarone 150 mg IV for the wide QRS
Albuterol nebulizer as the only treatment

items.q: You are giving calcium chloride slowly through a hand IV for a verapamil overdose. The patient reports severe burning, and the site is swollen and pale. What should you do?
items.x: Calcium chloride can cause tissue necrosis when it extravasates, and extravasation is a reason to stop. Finish the dose through a new large, secure line such as a large vein or IO.
items.a: Stop giving it at that site because of extravasation
w: Speed up the push so the dose finishes sooner
Flush the line hard and continue at the same site
Finish the dose, then elevate the hand on arrival

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with hyperkalemia had a wide QRS and peaked T waves. After calcium gluconate IV the QRS narrows. What is the best interpretation and plan?
items.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes but does not lower serum potassium. The patient still needs treatments that move potassium into cells, such as albuterol per protocol, with continuous monitoring.
items.a: The heart is stabilized, but potassium is unchanged; add shifting therapy
w: The potassium is now corrected, so no further treatment is needed
The improvement means the diagnosis was wrong and the calcium was not actually needed
Calcium has lowered potassium, so stop cardiac monitoring

items.q: A patient with hyperkalemic ECG changes is receiving calcium gluconate IV. Midway through the dose, the heart rate drops from 72 to 46 and she feels lightheaded. What should you do?
items.x: Bradycardia is a serious calcium side effect and a reason to stop, often from pushing it too fast. Speeding it up or switching to the stronger chloride salt would make the problem worse.
items.a: Stop the calcium and reassess the rhythm and blood pressure
w: Push the rest of the calcium quickly to finish the dose
Give atropine and keep giving calcium at the same rate
Switch to calcium chloride and push it faster

items.q: A farmworker sprayed with pesticide has drooling, wheezing, copious bronchial secretions, SpO2 86% and HR 52. After the first IV atropine dose, HR is 118 but the lungs are still wet with secretions. What next?
items.x: In organophosphate poisoning the goal of atropine is drying of the airway secretions, not heart rate. Tachycardia is expected and is not a reason to stop while the lungs are still wet.
items.a: Give more atropine, doubling the dose, until secretions dry
w: Stop atropine because the heart rate is now over 100
Switch to albuterol to dry the bronchial secretions
Give atropine only if the heart rate falls below 60

items.q: You are first on scene where two field workers are vomiting and drooling after a crop-spraying accident. Their clothes are soaked with chemical. What do you do first?
items.x: Organophosphates are absorbed through the skin, so unprotected rescuers can be poisoned too. Responder safety and decontamination come before atropine, which is given as soon as it is safe.
items.a: Put on PPE and decontaminate the patients before treating
w: Give each patient atropine IM right away, before anything else
Start IVs in both patients inside the ambulance at once
Assist ventilation first, then remove the clothing later

items.q: An organophosphate-poisoned patient has dry lungs after repeated atropine doses, but he has muscle twitching, increasing weakness and shallow breaths. What is the best next step?
items.x: Atropine treats muscarinic effects such as secretions but does nothing for nicotinic muscle weakness. Pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase and can improve muscle strength, while ventilation is supported as needed.
items.a: Give pralidoxime to treat the nicotinic muscle weakness
w: Give more atropine until the twitching stops completely
Give midazolam, because the twitching is a seizure
Give calcium chloride for the muscle cramps and twitching

items.q: A 20-kg child has organophosphate poisoning with weakness and fasciculations after atropine. Medical control orders IV pralidoxime. Which order fits the dosing range?
items.x: Pediatric IV dosing is 20-50 mg/kg (max 2 g) infused over 15-30 minutes, so 20 kg gives 400-1,000 mg. A rapid push of a full adult dose exceeds the weight-based range and the administration time.
items.a: 400-1,000 mg IV infused over 15-30 minutes
w: 2 g IV as a rapid push over 1 minute
100 mg IV infused slowly over about 2 full hours
1,800 mg IV push every 5 minutes

items.q: A 44-year-old electroplating worker suddenly collapsed at work after a chemical spill. He had a seizure, BP is 80/50, he is gasping, and SpO2 reads 99%. Coworkers mention a bitter almond odor. What is the priority antidote?
items.x: Sudden collapse, seizure and shock with a normal SpO2 after an industrial exposure suggests cyanide, which blocks oxygen use in the cells. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide; naloxone and atropine do not treat cellular poisoning.
items.a: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes
w: Naloxone 2 mg IN for possible opioid use
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV push
Atropine 2 mg IV for the collapse

items.q: After hydroxocobalamin for smoke inhalation, a patient's skin and urine turn red and BP rises from 96/60 to 148/88. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: Red skin and urine and a rise in blood pressure are common effects of hydroxocobalamin. They are not signs of allergy or treatment failure, though the color can interfere with some monitors and labs.
items.a: Expected effects of the drug; continue care and monitoring
w: A severe allergy that needs epinephrine IM right away
Worsening carbon monoxide levels that need a second 5 g dose of the drug
Kidney failure, so stop all IV fluids immediately

items.q: A 24-year-old man used methamphetamine. He is agitated and paranoid, HR 150, BP 190/110, temp 40.2 C (104.4 F). He has IV access. What is the best first medication?
items.x: Benzodiazepines are first-line for stimulant toxicity: they calm the patient and lower heart rate, blood pressure and heat production. Beta blockers are avoided as initial therapy in stimulant toxicity.
items.a: Midazolam per protocol to reduce agitation and sympathetic drive
w: Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower his blood pressure quickly
Labetalol IV to bring the blood pressure down to normal
Haloperidol alone to control the paranoia and the agitation

items.q: A 35-year-old man received midazolam 5 mg IM for violent agitation. Ten minutes later he is calm but snoring, with RR 8 and SpO2 89%. What is the next step?
items.x: Respiratory depression is the main danger of sedation, so airway support and capnography come first. Flumazenil is generally avoided in the field because it can trigger seizures, and more sedation would make things worse.
items.a: Open the airway, assist with a BVM and monitor EtCO2
w: Give a second midazolam dose since the first one worked
Leave him supine in restraints and recheck at the hospital
Give flumazenil IV to completely reverse the midazolam

items.q: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg with a fever has been having a generalized seizure for 7 minutes. There is no IV access yet. What is the best action?
items.x: A seizure longer than 5 minutes needs a benzodiazepine whatever the cause, and IN or IM midazolam avoids the delay of IV access. Antipyretics do not stop an active seizure.
items.a: Give midazolam IN or IM using weight-based dosing
w: Wait for it to stop, since febrile seizures are harmless
Give rectal acetaminophen first to treat the fever
Start an IV before giving any seizure medication

items.q: A 38-year-old man in status epilepticus received lorazepam 4 mg IV. After 10-15 minutes of observation he is still having a generalized seizure, SpO2 94% with assisted ventilation and BP 142/88. What is next?
items.x: The lorazepam label allows one repeat 4 mg dose after a 10-15 minute observation period if seizures continue. Waiting longer lets status epilepticus cause more injury.
items.a: Repeat lorazepam 4 mg IV once
w: Wait another 30 minutes before any further dose
Give naloxone in case this is an opioid overdose
Give a fluid bolus before any more anticonvulsant

items.q: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD is restless and anxious. SpO2 84%, RR 8, EtCO2 68. His family asks you to give him something to calm him. What is best?
items.x: His restlessness comes from hypercapnic respiratory failure, and severe respiratory insufficiency without airway support is a contraindication to lorazepam. A sedative could cause respiratory arrest; he needs ventilatory support.
items.a: Withhold lorazepam and assist ventilation for the hypercapnia
w: Give lorazepam IV so that he can better tolerate the oxygen mask and calm down
Give lorazepam IM since the IM route is less sedating
Give lorazepam and recheck the EtCO2 in 30 minutes

items.q: A 52-year-old man stopped drinking alcohol 2 days ago. He has tremors, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, HR 128, BP 172/100 and temp 38.3 C (100.9 F). What is the best medication?
items.x: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam treat alcohol withdrawal and prevent seizures. Haloperidol alone lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat the withdrawal itself.
items.a: Diazepam IV, then reassess and repeat per protocol
w: Haloperidol IM as the only agent for hallucinations
Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower BP
Naloxone IN in case he took opioids along with alcohol

items.q: An 8-year-old weighing 25 kg has been seizing for 6 minutes, and there is no IV access. Your service carries diazepam rectal gel. Which dose matches the label for this age?
items.x: Rectal gel dosing is 0.3 mg/kg for ages 6-11 years, so 25 kg x 0.3 = 7.5 mg. The 0.5 mg/kg dose is for ages 2-5, and 0.2 mg/kg is for age 12 and older.
items.a: 7.5 mg PR (0.3 mg/kg)
w: 12.5 mg PR (0.5 mg/kg)
5 mg PR (0.2 mg/kg)
25 mg PR (1 mg/kg)

items.q: A 55-year-old malnourished man with heavy alcohol use is confused, with a glucose of 42 mg/dL. Why is thiamine given along with the dextrose?
items.x: Thiamine is needed for glucose metabolism in the brain. In a depleted patient a glucose load uses up what little is left, so thiamine is given too, without delaying the dextrose.
items.a: Thiamine is a cofactor needed to use the glucose load
w: Thiamine raises blood glucose by releasing liver glycogen
Thiamine prevents the dextrose from damaging the vein
Thiamine reverses the sedating effect of the alcohol

items.q: A 49-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is ataxic and confused, with nystagmus. After dextrose his BG is 112, but the confusion, nystagmus and ataxia persist. What should you consider next?
items.x: Confusion, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities in a malnourished drinker suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, which is treated with thiamine 100 mg IV. More dextrose is not needed with a normal glucose.
items.a: Thiamine 100 mg IV for possible Wernicke encephalopathy
w: Another D50 dose since the confusion persists
Naloxone 2 mg IV for possible opioid co-ingestion
Haloperidol IM to manage the confusion

items.q: A 1-year-old weighing 10 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea. She is lethargic and not feeding, with BG 34. You have IV access. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Infants and young children get dilute dextrose (D10) by weight to avoid vein injury and large osmotic loads. Oral glucose is unsafe in a lethargic child who cannot protect the airway.
items.a: D10 IV dosed at 5-10 mL/kg
w: D50 25 g IV push as for an adult
Oral glucose gel between her cheek and gum
Withhold dextrose and give a fluid bolus

items.q: A 66-year-old man who takes glipizide was found confused with BG 36. After D50 he is alert with BG 104. He wants to refuse transport. What is the key concern?
items.x: Sulfonylureas act for many hours and can cause hypoglycemia to come back after a single dextrose dose. These patients need observation, so the crew should strongly encourage transport.
items.a: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia often returns after dextrose
w: D50 will cause dangerous hyperglycemia within the hour
Glipizide will interact with the D50 to cause dangerously low potassium
His glucose will stay normal for the rest of the day

items.q: A 71-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech that started 40 minutes ago. BP 168/94. Her glucometer reads 38 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke, so it must be found and treated first; the deficits often resolve once glucose is restored. Aspirin and BP lowering are not field stroke treatments here.
items.a: Treat the hypoglycemia with dextrose and reassess her deficits
w: Transport to a stroke center without treating the glucose
Lower her blood pressure first, then recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
Give aspirin for the stroke while the glucose is rechecked

items.q: A 28-year-old man is naked, sweating, screaming and fighting police. Temp is 40.5 C (104.9 F), and he cannot be safely approached for IV access. What is the best medication strategy?
items.x: Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia needs fast chemical sedation, and IM ketamine works quickly without IV access. Prone restraint without sedation risks sudden death, and IV or oral routes are not practical.
items.a: Ketamine IM per protocol for rapid, safe sedation
w: Haloperidol IV once an IV is started in the field
Keep him prone in restraints until he tires out
Midazolam PO mixed in a drink to calm him down

items.q: Minutes after IM ketamine for agitation, a patient develops high-pitched stridor, chest retractions, and SpO2 dropping to 84%. What should you do?
items.x: Laryngospasm is a serious ketamine complication, and positive pressure ventilation with a jaw thrust usually breaks it. Naloxone does not reverse ketamine, and the prone position makes airway management harder.
items.a: Jaw thrust and BVM with positive pressure for laryngospasm
w: Give a second ketamine dose to deepen the sedation
Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effects
Place him prone and apply a nonrebreather mask

items.q: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is confused and agitated after a fall. He is pulling at his IV. Medical control asks what agent you plan to use. What is the key consideration?
items.x: Parkinson's disease is a contraindication to haloperidol because blocking dopamine can sharply worsen rigidity and mobility. Look for causes of delirium and use other approaches or agents per protocol.
items.a: Avoid haloperidol; it can severely worsen his parkinsonism
w: Give haloperidol IV because it acts faster in the elderly
Give double the usual haloperidol dose because of his tremor
Haloperidol is preferred since he has a movement disorder

items.q: Twenty minutes after IM haloperidol for agitation, the monitor shows a QTc of 520 ms and short runs of polymorphic VT. The patient has a pulse. What is the best action?
items.x: QT prolongation is a serious haloperidol effect and a reason to stop; polymorphic VT with a long QT (torsades) is treated with magnesium. Amiodarone further prolongs the QT.
items.a: Withhold more haloperidol and give magnesium per protocol
w: Give a second haloperidol dose to prevent more agitation
Give amiodarone to suppress the polymorphic VT runs
Ignore the runs since they are self-terminating

items.q: A 30-year-old woman is severely agitated after an argument. Her 12-lead shows a QTc of 480 ms. Droperidol is in your agitation protocol. What is best?
items.x: A QTc over 450 ms in a female is a contraindication to droperidol, which carries a QT prolongation risk. A lower dose or another route does not remove that risk.
items.a: Withhold droperidol and use a benzodiazepine per protocol
w: Give droperidol IM, since the IM route avoids QT effects
Give droperidol at half the usual dose with monitoring
Give droperidol and repeat the 12-lead at the hospital

items.q: Twenty minutes after droperidol for vomiting, a 22-year-old woman is very restless, keeps standing up and says she feels like she has to keep moving. Vitals are stable. What is happening?
items.x: Akathisia is a common droperidol side effect and a reason to stop further doses; it is often treated with diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine per protocol. Giving more droperidol would make it worse.
items.a: Akathisia from the droperidol; stop it and treat per protocol
w: Worsening anxiety that needs a second, larger droperidol dose to control it
A normal sign that the nausea is resolving
An allergic reaction that needs IM epinephrine

items.q: A 27-year-old woman who delivered 4 days ago has a severe headache and had a generalized seizure at home. BP is 164/108. She is now postictal. What is the best medication?
items.x: Eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, and magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to treat and prevent seizures. Blood pressure control alone does not prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures.
items.a: Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV over 15-20 minutes
w: Labetalol alone, since the pregnancy is over
Dextrose, because seizures after delivery are hypoglycemic
Diphenhydramine for a postpartum migraine

items.q: During a magnesium loading dose for eclampsia, a patient feels warm and flushed and is sweating. RR is 18 and patellar reflexes are present. Which action of magnesium explains this?
items.x: Magnesium relaxes vascular smooth muscle, so warmth and flushing are expected. Toxicity shows first as lost reflexes, then slowed breathing.
items.a: Vasodilation from relaxed vascular smooth muscle
w: Early respiratory muscle weakness from toxicity
An allergic release of histamine from mast cells
Blockade of the sweat glands' muscarinic receptors

items.q: A woman has just delivered a full-term infant. The uterus remains large, with the fundus above the umbilicus, and you feel what may be another fetus. Bleeding is moderate. Your partner draws up oxytocin. What is best?
items.x: A possible second twin is a contraindication: oxytocin could clamp the uterus down on an undelivered infant. Give it only after all infants are delivered.
items.a: Withhold oxytocin until a second twin is ruled out
w: Give oxytocin 10 units IM to control the bleeding now
Give oxytocin IV fast to speed delivery of the placenta
Give oxytocin, then perform fundal massage firmly

items.q: After oxytocin 10 units IM and fundal massage for postpartum bleeding, the uterus is firm at the umbilicus, but a steady stream of bright red blood continues. HR 112. What should you do next?
items.x: Once the uterus is firm, ongoing bleeding suggests another source such as a laceration, which needs direct pressure. More oxytocin targets uterine tone, which is already good.
items.a: Look for a perineal laceration and apply direct pressure
w: Give more oxytocin, since a firm uterus means it is not working
Vigorously massage the fundus for another 15 minutes
Have her sit upright to slow down the flow of blood

items.q: A woman delivered 40 minutes ago. Despite oxytocin and fundal massage she is still bleeding heavily. HR 124, BP 86/50. Your protocol includes TXA. What is the correct administration?
items.x: For postpartum hemorrhage, TXA is given as 1 g IV over 10 minutes, and the dose can be repeated if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. A rapid push can cause hypotension.
items.a: 1 g IV infused over 10 minutes
w: 1 g IV as a rapid push over 30 seconds
2 g IM divided into both thighs
100 mg IV infused over 8 hours

items.q: A trauma patient is receiving TXA. The first part of the dose was pushed over about 30 seconds, and BP falls from 104/68 to 82/50. Which property of TXA explains the fall?
items.x: TXA given too quickly can drop the blood pressure, which is why it is infused over about 10 minutes. It stabilizes clots; it does not dissolve them.
items.a: Rapid IV injection can cause brief hypotension
w: TXA dissolves clots and restarts the bleeding
TXA blocks alpha receptors in the blood vessels
TXA triggers anaphylaxis in most trauma patients

items.q: A 30-week pregnant woman in preterm labor received terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ by medical control order. Now her HR is 128, and she reports chest tightness. What is the best action?
items.x: A maternal HR over 120 or chest pain is a reason to stop terbutaline. Repeating the dose increases the risk of dysrhythmia and cardiac ischemia.
items.a: Withhold further terbutaline and obtain a 12-lead
w: Give the second dose since contractions persist
Give a fluid bolus and then repeat the dose
Give metoprolol to slow her heart rate

items.q: A woman at 31 weeks has regular contractions. Medical control is discussing terbutaline when you see the infant's head crowning with each contraction. What should you do?
items.x: Delivery is imminent, so trying to stop labor is no longer appropriate and could delay care. The crew should prepare for a preterm delivery and neonatal resuscitation.
items.a: Prepare for delivery; do not attempt tocolysis
w: Give terbutaline SQ quickly to stop the delivery
Have her cross her legs while terbutaline is drawn up
Give terbutaline and transport in the left lateral position

items.q: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg ate a peanut cookie. He has hives, wheezing and vomiting, BP 70/40. Using 1 mg/mL epinephrine, what is the correct initial dose?
items.x: Children under 30 kg receive 0.01 mg/kg IM, so 22 kg gives 0.22 mg. The 1 mg/mL concentration is never given IV push, and antihistamines do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
items.a: 0.22 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
w: 0.22 mg IV push of the 1 mg/mL solution
0.5 mg IM in the deltoid muscle
Diphenhydramine first, then epinephrine

items.q: A 9-year-old in anaphylaxis received IM epinephrine 6 minutes ago. She is still wheezing with hives, and BP is 76/44. What is the best next action?
items.x: IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5-10 minutes when anaphylaxis persists, along with fluids for hypotension. Antihistamines and steroids are slow adjuncts that do not reverse shock.
items.a: Repeat IM epinephrine and give fluids per protocol
w: Wait 20 minutes for the first dose to fully work
Give diphenhydramine instead of more epinephrine
Give methylprednisolone and wait for it to work

items.q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, stridor at rest, suprasternal retractions and SpO2 93%. Symptoms began suddenly overnight after a mild cold. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Croup with stridor at rest is treated with nebulized racemic epinephrine to reduce swelling in the upper airway. Albuterol treats lower airway bronchospasm, and agitating the child can worsen the obstruction.
items.a: Nebulized racemic epinephrine and calm transport
w: Nebulized albuterol for the noisy breathing
Inspect the throat with a tongue blade first
Nebulized saline only, since croup resolves

items.q: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with high fever, a muffled voice and soft stridor. He looks toxic. Your partner wants to start a nebulizer and an IV. What is best?
items.x: Drooling, toxic appearance and tripod positioning suggest epiglottitis, where agitation can cause complete obstruction. Avoid upsetting procedures, keep him in a position of comfort, and prepare for a difficult airway.
items.a: Keep him calm with the parent and transport quickly
w: Start the IV first, then give racemic epinephrine
Lay him flat and give racemic epinephrine by mask
Look in his throat to confirm the diagnosis first

items.q: A 3-year-old has a barking cough at night but no stridor at rest, normal work of breathing and SpO2 98%. What is the most appropriate medication?
items.x: Mild croup without stridor at rest benefits from a single dose of dexamethasone, which reduces airway swelling over hours. Racemic epinephrine is reserved for stridor at rest or respiratory distress.
items.a: Dexamethasone PO per weight-based dosing
w: Nebulized racemic epinephrine right away
Nebulized albuterol every 20 minutes
IM epinephrine in the lateral thigh

items.q: A 46-year-old woman with vomiting and diarrhea remains hypotensive after 2 L of fluid. Her medication list shows long-term daily prednisone for lupus, and she missed doses while sick. What does this finding change?
items.x: Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, so illness with missed doses can cause adrenal crisis that does not respond to fluids. A corticosteroid such as dexamethasone (4 mg IV per protocol) is indicated.
items.a: Consider adrenal crisis and give dexamethasone per protocol
w: It changes nothing, since steroids do not affect shock
Stop all fluids, since prednisone causes fluid retention
Give extra potassium for steroid-induced hypokalemia

items.q: A 5-year-old weighing 18 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for a day. She is alert, mildly dehydrated, and has no IV. Your protocol allows ODT ondansetron. What is the correct dose?
items.x: For children 15-30 kg, the ODT dose is 4 mg. The 2 mg dose is for 8-15 kg, and 8 mg is above the range for her weight.
items.a: 4 mg ODT
w: 2 mg ODT
8 mg ODT
0.4 mg ODT

items.q: An 18-month-old has been vomiting for 6 hours and is mildly dehydrated. A parent asks if you can give promethazine like the older sibling got. What is the best response?
items.x: Promethazine is contraindicated in children under 2 years because of fatal respiratory depression. An age-appropriate antiemetic such as ondansetron per protocol is the alternative.
items.a: Promethazine is contraindicated under age 2 because it can stop breathing
w: Promethazine is safe at half the adult dose in any toddler
Promethazine is fine in toddlers as long as it is given deep IM rather than IV
Promethazine can be given if the child weighs over 10 kg

items.q: A 72-year-old woman with prior abdominal surgery has a distended abdomen, no bowel movement for 3 days, and is vomiting foul brown fluid. What is the best decision about metoclopramide?
items.x: GI obstruction is a contraindication to metoclopramide because it increases gut movement. The surgical history and feculent vomiting strongly suggest obstruction.
items.a: Withhold it because of suspected bowel obstruction
w: Give 10 mg IV to speed up stomach emptying
Give it IM so that it bypasses the gut
Give it only after a fluid bolus is complete

items.q: A 30-year-old woman took a handful of her amitriptyline 45 minutes ago. On arrival she is drowsy, slurring words and her GCS is 11. She is not intubated. What is the best decision about activated charcoal?
items.x: Altered mental status without a protected airway is a contraindication because of aspiration risk, which is especially high with a tricyclic that can cause sudden seizures and coma. A smaller dose does not solve the airway problem.
items.a: Withhold charcoal because she cannot protect her airway
w: Give charcoal right away while she can still swallow
Give charcoal mixed with soda to improve its taste
Give half the charcoal dose to lower aspiration risk

items.q: A 3-year-old drank from a bottle of lamp oil 20 minutes ago. He is coughing and mildly tachypneic but alert. The parent asks about the charcoal they read about online. What is best?
items.x: Hydrocarbons are a contraindication to charcoal: it does not bind them well and vomiting increases aspiration risk. The cough already suggests aspiration, so watch his breathing closely.
items.a: Do not give charcoal; it does not help and raises aspiration risk
w: Give charcoal 1 g/kg PO right away to bind the lamp oil before it is absorbed
Give charcoal after making the child vomit
Give charcoal through an NG tube to protect the lungs

items.q: A 33-week pregnant woman has a severe headache and BP 172/114. She uses an albuterol inhaler for asthma and wheezed last week. Medical control asks about labetalol. What is your best response?
items.x: Labetalol blocks beta-2 receptors and is contraindicated in asthma or reactive airway disease because it can cause bronchospasm. Another antihypertensive should be chosen per medical control.
items.a: Asthma is a contraindication; request an alternative agent
w: Labetalol is safe in asthma when it is given slowly IV
Give labetalol with albuterol to prevent bronchospasm
Give labetalol IM instead of IV to avoid bronchospasm

items.q: A preeclamptic patient received labetalol 20 mg IV for BP 170/112. Ten minutes later, BP is 146/94 and HR has fallen to 52. Your protocol calls for 40 mg next if BP is still above goal. What is best?
items.x: An HR under 60 is a stop criterion for labetalol, and 146/94 is already out of the severe range that requires urgent treatment. Further beta blockade could cause symptomatic bradycardia or heart block.
items.a: Hold further labetalol because of the bradycardia
w: Give the 40 mg dose since BP is still above 140
Give atropine and then the 40 mg dose of labetalol
Give 80 mg now to reach the BP goal faster

items.q: A 7-year-old weighing 20 kg ate shrimp and has itchy hives on the trunk. Lungs are clear, no swelling of the lips or tongue, no vomiting, BP 104/66, HR 108. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Isolated hives without airway, breathing, GI or circulation involvement is a mild allergic reaction that is treated with an antihistamine, with monitoring for progression to anaphylaxis. IV epinephrine is reserved for refractory shock.
items.a: Diphenhydramine and close monitoring for any progression
w: Epinephrine IV push of the cardiac-arrest syringe to stop the reaction
Nebulized albuterol to prevent future wheezing
No treatment, since hives alone never progress

items.q: An 18-month-old weighing 11 kg had a 2-minute generalized seizure with fever. On arrival she is crying and moving all limbs, with normal breathing, SpO2 98% and temp 39.4 C (102.9 F). What is the best approach?
items.x: A short febrile seizure that has stopped does not need a benzodiazepine; acetaminophen is given for comfort but does not prevent recurrence. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome.
items.a: Withhold benzodiazepines; treat fever for comfort and transport
w: Give IN midazolam now to prevent another seizure
Give acetaminophen now, since it reliably prevents the seizure from recurring
Give aspirin for the fever during transport

items.q: A 58-year-old with urosepsis has MAP 56, HR 118 and lactate 4.8 after an initial crystalloid bolus. Her lungs now have faint crackles. Only an 18 g antecubital IV is available, and a central line will take 45 minutes. What is the best next step?
items.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock and can be started through a secure proximal peripheral IV with close site checks. Waiting 45 minutes for a central line prolongs hypoperfusion, and more fluid is risky once crackles appear.
items.a: Start peripheral norepinephrine and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
w: Wait for the central line, then start norepinephrine
Start peripheral phenylephrine and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
Give another crystalloid bolus and recheck the lactate

items.q: You pick up a 31-year-old with an open-book pelvic fracture. BP is 74/40 and HR 138. The referring facility started norepinephrine but has not given any blood. What should change first?
items.x: Hypovolemic hypotension is a contraindication to norepinephrine unless used briefly while volume is restored. This patient needs hemorrhage control and blood; raising the pressor dose squeezes an empty tank.
items.a: Give blood and bind the pelvis before relying on the pressor
w: Double the norepinephrine rate to reach a MAP of 65 or greater
Add vasopressin so norepinephrine can be weaned
Give push-dose phenylephrine and keep the current plan

items.q: Twenty minutes into transport, the MAP of a patient on norepinephrine falls from 70 to 46 over 2 minutes. The patient just had a line change at the referring bedside. HR and rhythm are unchanged. What is the best first action?
items.x: A sudden MAP drop right after a line change with no other change points to an interrupted or disconnected pressor. Restoring flow fixes the cause; adding drugs before checking the line treats the wrong problem.
items.a: Trace the line and pump to confirm the drip is infusing
w: Give a rapid fluid bolus and recheck the pressure
Add a vasopressin infusion as a second pressor
Double the norepinephrine rate on the pump

items.q: A 64-year-old has ROSC after VF arrest. He is intubated and unresponsive with BP 78/48 (MAP 58) and HR 96. What is the best hemodynamic plan?
items.x: Post-arrest hypotension worsens brain injury; a titrated vasopressor infusion to MAP 65 or greater is standard. Arrest-dose epinephrine pushes are for pulseless patients and cause wild swings, and permissive hypotension applies to bleeding trauma, not post-arrest care.
items.a: Start a norepinephrine infusion and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
w: Start a dobutamine infusion and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
Give crystalloid boluses alone until the MAP is 65 or greater
Accept the current MAP to limit myocardial oxygen demand

items.q: A septic patient remains at MAP 58 on high-dose norepinephrine plus vasopressin. Bedside echo shows a poorly contracting left ventricle, and her extremities are cold. Which addition best fits?
items.x: She needs both more pressure and more contractility, which epinephrine provides (labeled for septic shock). Dobutamine adds inotropy but often lowers BP further when the MAP is already below goal.
items.a: Add an epinephrine infusion titrated to MAP
w: Add dobutamine and titrate to cardiac output
Add phenylephrine for more alpha tone
Add milrinone to lower the afterload

items.q: A patient on an epinephrine infusion for septic shock develops frequent multifocal PVCs during transport. MAP is 72. A point-of-care potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. What is the most likely contributor?
items.x: Hypokalemia and dysrhythmias are listed serious effects of epinephrine through beta-2 driven cellular potassium uptake. Replace potassium per protocol and reassess whether the dose can come down.
items.a: Epinephrine-driven shift of potassium into cells
w: Epinephrine-driven loss of potassium in the urine
Vasopressin-driven shift of potassium into cells
Lactate-driven shift of potassium out of cells

items.q: Two minutes after intubation with propofol, a 70-year-old's BP falls from 104/62 to 68/40. HR is 108 and the tube position is confirmed. What is the best immediate treatment while an infusion is being prepared?
items.x: Post-induction hypotension needs prompt vasoactive support; push-dose epinephrine per protocol bridges until an infusion runs. More propofol worsens the vasodilation that caused the drop.
items.a: Push-dose epinephrine 10-20 mcg IV, repeated per protocol
w: Epinephrine 1 mg IV push, repeated every 3-5 minutes
Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the thigh, repeated once
Atropine 0.5 mg IV push, repeated per protocol

items.q: A 4-year-old with septic shock has had repeated fluid boluses. He is still lethargic with HR 168, cool mottled legs, capillary refill 5 seconds and a narrow pulse pressure. Which vasoactive agent fits this cold-shock picture best?
items.x: Fluid-refractory cold shock in children reflects low cardiac output with high resistance, and epinephrine adds inotropy plus pressure. A pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or vasopressin raises afterload on a struggling heart.
items.a: An epinephrine infusion
w: A norepinephrine infusion
A phenylephrine infusion
A vasopressin infusion

items.q: A septic patient is on norepinephrine and vasopressin. After source control and fluids, MAP is now 88 and rising. Which drip should be weaned first?
items.x: When MAP is well above goal, catecholamines are tapered first, and vasopressin is usually weaned last. Stopping both at once risks rebound hypotension.
items.a: Norepinephrine
w: Vasopressin
Both together
Whichever began last

items.q: During a 3-hour transfer, a patient on norepinephrine and vasopressin develops several new findings. Which one is most concerning?
items.x: Mesenteric ischemia is a serious effect of vasopressin (and catecholamines), and pain with a climbing lactate is an early warning. A mild sodium change or slightly slower HR does not change the plan right now.
items.a: New severe abdominal pain with a rising lactate
w: A drop in HR from 104 to 92 with a stable MAP
Sodium falling from 139 to 133 mEq/L
Cool, pale fingertips with intact pulses

items.q: Four patients need vasoactive support during interfacility transfer. In which patient would vasopressin as the only agent most likely lower cardiac output?
items.x: Vasopressin is a pure vasoconstrictor that can decrease cardiac output; without inotropy it can lower output in a failing heart and worsen cardiogenic shock. In vasodilatory states, which are labeled indications, it restores tone without that drawback.
items.a: Cardiogenic shock with a low ejection fraction
w: Septic shock already on norepinephrine
Post-cardiotomy vasoplegia with good LV function
Vasodilatory shock with warm, flushed skin

items.q: A 77-year-old with known severe aortic stenosis is intubated. Afterward, BP is 78/44 and HR 92 in sinus rhythm. Which drug best fits her physiology right now?
items.x: With fixed outflow obstruction, she needs diastolic pressure for coronary flow and a slower HR for filling, and pure alpha agonism with reflex slowing does both. Inotropes and chronotropes shorten filling time, and vasodilators can cause collapse.
items.a: Phenylephrine
w: Dobutamine
Epinephrine
Milrinone

items.q: A patient with an EF of 15% gets several phenylephrine boluses for post-intubation hypotension. BP rises to 112/70, but HR falls to 48, SpO2 drops and new crackles appear. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Phenylephrine can lower cardiac output (a listed serious effect) and causes reflex bradycardia. In a weak heart the BP looks better while forward flow and oxygenation worsen, so an agent with inotropy fits better.
items.a: Afterload rose and cardiac output fell; change to an inotropic pressor
w: Reflex bradycardia with a good response; continue the boluses
Aspiration during intubation; the drug effect is unrelated
Preload is now too low; give a fluid bolus and repeat the dose

items.q: A septic patient was started on dopamine at the referring hospital. During packaging she develops atrial fibrillation at 164 with frequent PVCs. MAP is 64. What is the best change?
items.x: Tachydysrhythmias are a stop criterion for dopamine, which causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, the first-line agent in septic shock. Beta-blocking a septic patient on a failing pressor risks collapse.
items.a: Switch from dopamine to norepinephrine
w: Add amiodarone and continue the dopamine
Add an esmolol infusion for rate control
Switch from dopamine to epinephrine

items.q: A 72-year-old has symptomatic bradycardia at 36 with BP 76/40 and confusion. Atropine has failed, and transcutaneous pacing gives only intermittent capture despite pad and output changes. What is the best next drug per ACLS?
items.x: ACLS lists dopamine (or epinephrine) infusion when atropine fails and pacing is not effective. More atropine past the max adds little, and amiodarone or diltiazem would slow conduction further.
items.a: A dopamine infusion titrated to HR and BP
w: A norepinephrine infusion titrated to MAP
A glucagon bolus followed by an infusion
A phenylephrine infusion titrated to BP

items.q: Three days after an MI, a 67-year-old has BP 98/64, HR 102, cool clammy skin, falling urine output and bibasilar crackles. MAP is 75. Which agent best addresses the main problem?
items.x: This is low-output cardiogenic shock with acceptable BP, so contractility is the target. Pure vasoconstrictors raise afterload on a failing ventricle, and nitroprusside with a borderline BP risks hypotension.
items.a: Dobutamine

Vasopressin
Nitroprusside

items.q: Dobutamine is started for cardiogenic shock with an initial BP of 92/60. Ten minutes later, BP is 76/42 and HR 128. What is the best next step?
items.x: Dobutamine can cause hypotension through beta-2 vasodilation, a stop criterion, so its dose is reassessed while a vasopressor such as norepinephrine restores MAP. Raising dobutamine worsens both the tachycardia and the vasodilation.

w: Increase dobutamine to raise cardiac output
Change dobutamine to milrinone at once
Give a large crystalloid bolus and recheck

items.q: A septic patient has reached MAP 68 on norepinephrine after adequate fluids. Lactate keeps rising, the skin stays mottled, and echo shows a severely depressed LV. Which addition best fits?
items.x: With the MAP at goal but low output, an inotrope addresses the real deficit. Pushing the MAP higher or adding pure vasoconstriction does not fix a weak pump.
items.a: Add dobutamine to improve cardiac output
w: Raise norepinephrine until the MAP reaches about 85
Add vasopressin for more vascular tone
Give another large fluid bolus

items.q: A 59-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy on high-dose home carvedilol is in low-output cardiogenic shock with BP 94/58. Dobutamine has had little effect. Which agent is most likely to work?
items.x: Milrinone raises contractility through PDE-3 inhibition, which bypasses beta receptors blocked by carvedilol. Increasing a beta agonist against a full blockade adds little inotropy.
items.a: Milrinone

Higher-dose dobutamine
Phenylephrine

items.q: During an interfacility transfer, a patient on milrinone becomes hypotensive at 80/44 with new runs of ventricular ectopy. What is the best response?
items.x: Hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias are stop criteria for milrinone. A vasopressor supports MAP while the effect fades; a repeat load or a higher rate makes both problems worse.
items.a: Reduce or stop milrinone per orders and support MAP with a pressor
w: Continue milrinone unchanged and add dobutamine for the low MAP
Increase milrinone to raise cardiac output and suppress ectopy
Continue milrinone unchanged and give amiodarone for the ectopy

items.q: A 66-year-old with pneumonia and septic shock needs RSI. BP is 86/52 and HR 124 (shock index about 1.4) on low-dose norepinephrine. Ketamine is chosen. What is the best dosing approach?
items.x: In shock, a lower induction dose limits hemodynamic collapse, while a full (or higher) paralytic dose ensures good conditions because slow circulation delays onset. Cutting the paralytic invites a failed first pass.
items.a: Reduce the induction dose and give a full paralytic dose
w: Give the full induction dose and reduce the paralytic
Give a full induction dose and skip the paralytic to avoid apnea
Reduce both drugs to half their usual dose

items.q: A 52-year-old with a type A aortic dissection is in severe distress, hypoxic and needs intubation. BP is 192/110 and HR 112 despite an esmolol infusion. Which induction agent would most likely raise aortic wall stress?
items.x: Ketamine's sympathetic surge raises BP and HR, and severe hypertension is a stop criterion, which can extend a dissection. Agents that blunt or do not raise sympathetic tone fit better here.
items.a: Ketamine
w: Etomidate
Propofol at a reduced dose
Midazolam with fentanyl

items.q: An intubated trauma patient on norepinephrine has BP 92/56 and needs sedation for a 90-minute flight. He was induced with ketamine and paralyzed with rocuronium. Which sedation plan best fits his hemodynamics?
items.x: Ketamine (per protocol infusion range) keeps sympathetic tone, so it suits a pressor-dependent patient. Propofol and large benzodiazepine boluses deepen hypotension, and a paralyzed patient always needs sedation and analgesia.
items.a: A ketamine infusion with fentanyl as needed
w: A propofol infusion with fentanyl as needed
A dexmedetomidine infusion after a full load
Repeat rocuronium doses with fentanyl alone

items.q: A septic patient has been on a propofol infusion at the referring facility. While on the transport ventilator, BP drifts from 104/60 to 82/48 and HR is 112. Sedation is deep (RASS -5). What is the best adjustment?
items.x: Hypotension and oversedation are stop criteria for propofol. Lowering it and using an analgesia-first approach (with pressor support as needed) protects BP; large benzodiazepine boluses also drop BP.
items.a: Lower the propofol and shift to analgesia-first sedation
w: Keep the propofol rate and add a fentanyl infusion
Change propofol to midazolam at an equal depth
Keep the propofol rate and give a fluid bolus

items.q: Propofol is the only induction agent available for a 74-year-old with GI bleeding who needs intubation. BP is 88/56 after 2 units of blood. What is the best approach?
items.x: Propofol's labeled induction dose for unstable patients is 0.5-1 mg/kg, with vasopressor support at hand. A full dose risks arrest, and paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
items.a: Give a reduced dose with a pressor ready
w: Give the standard dose with a pressor ready
Give the standard dose after a fluid bolus
Give a near-standard dose with fentanyl to blunt the response

items.q: A 41-year-old with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis is intubated for respiratory failure before transfer. Which sedation agent should be avoided for the infusion?
items.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that can raise triglycerides and cause pancreatitis (listed serious effects), so it is a poor choice in triglyceride-driven pancreatitis. The other agents lack that lipid load.
items.a: Propofol
w: Fentanyl
Ketamine
Dexmedetomidine

items.q: A 69-year-old in cardiogenic shock (BP 82/50, HR 108, crackles) needs RSI. Which induction choice best preserves hemodynamics?
items.x: Etomidate has little effect on contractility or vascular tone, which suits a patient with a failing heart. Propofol, induction-dose midazolam and fentanyl pretreatment all lower BP in a patient with no reserve.

w: Propofol at a reduced weight-based dose
Midazolam at the standard induction dose

items.q: Seconds after etomidate is pushed and before rocuronium takes effect, the patient has jerking movements of the arms. SpO2 is 96%. What is the most likely explanation and response?
items.x: Myoclonus is a common effect of etomidate and resolves with paralysis. Treating it as a seizure delays the airway, and malignant hyperthermia is linked to succinylcholine and volatile agents, not etomidate.
items.a: Myoclonus from etomidate; proceed with the intubation
w: Seizure from etomidate; give lorazepam and delay intubation
Light anesthesia; give a second full dose of etomidate
Hypoxic posturing; bag the patient before going further

items.q: A 100-kg patient in cardiogenic shock with a low cardiac output needs RSI. Which rocuronium dose best ensures fast intubating conditions?
items.x: Low output slows drug delivery to muscles, so the upper RSI dose (1.2 mg/kg) gives faster onset. The lower doses are labeled for intubation but onset is slower, which matters most in a patient with little reserve.
items.a: 1.2 mg/kg IV
w: 0.45 mg/kg IV
0.6 mg/kg IV
0.1 mg/kg IV

items.q: A 63-year-old dialysis patient with sepsis missed two sessions. He needs RSI for hypoxic respiratory failure. K is 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves. Which paralytic plan is best?
items.x: Known hyperkalemia is a contraindication to succinylcholine, which raises potassium further and can cause arrest. Rocuronium avoids that risk; calcium or a lower dose does not make succinylcholine safe here.
items.a: Rocuronium at a full RSI dose
w: Succinylcholine after calcium pretreatment
Succinylcholine at a reduced RSI dose
Vecuronium at a standard intubating dose

items.q: A 48-year-old has been bedbound in an ICU for 3 weeks after a stroke and now needs reintubation before transfer. Which paralytic consideration matters most?
items.x: Stroke and immobilization over 48-72 hours upregulate receptors and can cause a severe potassium surge with succinylcholine, even with a normal baseline K. A nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium avoids that.
items.a: Prolonged immobilization and stroke make succinylcholine unsafe
w: Prolonged immobilization and stroke make rocuronium unsafe
A normal potassium on arrival makes succinylcholine safe
Prolonged immobilization causes succinylcholine resistance

items.q: After intubation for ARDS, a 45-year-old is fighting the vent with HR 124 and BP 156/92. He is on a midazolam infusion only. What is the best next step?
items.x: An endotracheal tube is painful, and analgesia-first sedation treats the cause of the distress. Paralyzing him or raising only the benzodiazepine leaves pain untreated, and labetalol hides the signs.
items.a: Add analgesia with fentanyl, then reassess sedation
w: Add vecuronium, then reassess the ventilator
Increase midazolam, then reassess sedation
Add labetalol, then reassess the HR and BP

items.q: A 71-year-old with septic shock has BP 84/50 and HR 126 before RSI. Your protocol lists fentanyl pretreatment as an option. What is the best decision?
items.x: Fentanyl pretreatment blunts sympathetic tone, which this shock patient depends on; hypotension is a stop criterion. It suits hypertensive patients such as TBI or dissection, not septic shock.
items.a: Omit fentanyl pretreatment in this hypotensive patient
w: Give fentanyl pretreatment to blunt the heart rate of 126
Give fentanyl pretreatment and lower the paralytic dose
Replace fentanyl pretreatment with an esmolol bolus

items.q: An intubated patient in cardiogenic shock on norepinephrine becomes agitated during the flight. BP is 88/54. Which sedation choice is most likely to worsen his hemodynamics?
items.x: Shock is a relative contraindication to midazolam, and large boluses cause hypotension in a patient without reserve. Small, titrated analgesic doses or ketamine better protect BP.
items.a: Repeated large midazolam boluses
w: Small fentanyl doses titrated to effect
A low-dose ketamine infusion
Small midazolam doses with fentanyl

items.q: A post-arrest patient on norepinephrine (MAP 72) has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on the transport ventilator. He has not received a paralytic since intubation. What is the best action?
items.x: Post-arrest seizures worsen brain injury and need treatment; a benzodiazepine is first-line, with close BP monitoring because of hypotension risk. A paralytic stops movement but not seizure activity in the brain.
items.a: Give midazolam IV titrated while watching BP
w: Give rocuronium to stop the motor activity
Give propofol IV boluses until movement ends
Give levetiracetam alone as the first agent

items.q: A post-arrest patient on a dexmedetomidine infusion during transfer develops HR 42 in sinus rhythm with BP 82/50. What is the best first action?
items.x: Bradycardia under 50 with hypotension is a stop criterion for dexmedetomidine. Raising the rate or giving a load (which can cause sinus arrest or hypertension then hypotension) worsens the problem.
items.a: Stop the dexmedetomidine infusion
w: Give atropine and continue the infusion
Give a fluid bolus and recheck the BP
Start dopamine and continue the infusion

items.q: A patient with ARDS is on a rocuronium infusion for a long flight. The only sedation running is dexmedetomidine at a low rate. What is the main concern?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine gives light, rousable sedation and does not reliably provide the deep sedation a paralyzed patient needs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk of rocuronium, so deep sedation and analgesia must be in place.
items.a: Sedation may be too light, risking awareness under paralysis
w: Sedation may be too deep, risking bradycardia under paralysis
Dexmedetomidine may potentiate rocuronium and delay recovery
Rocuronium may mask shivering, so the dose should be lowered

items.q: After ROSC from VF, a 70-year-old is in complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 38, BP 78/40 and occasional PVCs. The referring team asks about an amiodarone infusion. What is the best response?
items.x: Third-degree AV block without a pacemaker is a contraindication to amiodarone, which could suppress the escape rhythm. The priority is rate support with pacing or a chronotrope.
items.a: Withhold amiodarone and treat the bradycardia with pacing
w: Start amiodarone at the maintenance rate with no bolus
Start lidocaine instead to suppress the PVCs
Start amiodarone once atropine has raised the rate

items.q: A patient on an amiodarone infusion for recurrent VT has BP 82/50 and sinus rhythm at 50 during transport. Before the infusion, BP was 118/70 and HR 82. What is the best next step?
items.x: Hypotension and bradycardia are stop criteria for amiodarone. Continuing or re-bolusing makes both worse; stop the drip and discuss next steps.
items.a: Stop the amiodarone and notify medical control
w: Continue the same rate and add a dopamine infusion
Give another amiodarone bolus to keep the VT away
Continue the same rate since the VT is suppressed

items.q: An 82-year-old with heart failure has been on a lidocaine infusion for 12 hours after VT. During transfer he reports perioral numbness and ringing in the ears, then becomes confused with muscle twitching. What is the best action?
items.x: These are lidocaine toxicity signs, and heart failure plus older age reduce clearance. Stopping the drug and being ready for seizures is correct; more lidocaine would worsen CNS toxicity.
items.a: Stop the lidocaine and prepare to treat seizures
w: Halve the lidocaine rate and recheck in an hour
Continue lidocaine and give midazolam for twitching
Continue lidocaine and check a magnesium level

items.q: An intubated septic patient has pH 7.08, PaCO2 64 and HCO3 18. The ventilator is set to a low minute ventilation from the referring hospital. The referring physician suggests sodium bicarbonate. What should happen first?
items.x: Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate, which makes CO2 that must be exhaled. The acidosis here is largely respiratory, so fixing ventilation comes first.
items.a: Increase minute ventilation to clear CO2
w: Give bicarbonate first, then recheck the gas
Increase PEEP to improve the gas exchange
Give a fluid bolus to treat the acidosis

items.q: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is on a nitroglycerin infusion. During transport, BP falls from 168/96 to 86/50, HR rises to 118, the skin becomes cool and mottled, and crackles persist. What is the best change?
items.x: An SBP under 90 is a stop criterion for nitroglycerin. With poor perfusion and crackles, this has turned into cardiogenic shock and needs support of BP and output, not more preload reduction.
items.a: Stop the nitroglycerin and start inotropic or pressor support
w: Halve the nitroglycerin and give furosemide for the crackles
Keep the nitroglycerin and give a large fluid bolus for the BP
Change the nitroglycerin infusion to a nitroprusside infusion

items.q: A septic patient has received several liters of fluid. MAP is 58 on low-dose norepinephrine, SpO2 is 90% and new crackles are present. The referring team suggests furosemide. What is the best response?
items.x: Furosemide is held in hypotension because diuresis worsens perfusion. Raising the pressor supports MAP without more fluid; any diuresis can wait until the shock improves.
items.a: Hold furosemide and titrate the vasopressor up
w: Give furosemide now and recheck the MAP after
Give another fluid bolus before raising the pressor
Give albumin with furosemide to support the MAP

items.q: A septic patient has sinus tachycardia at 138 with MAP 62 on norepinephrine and a lactate of 5. A crewmember suggests esmolol to slow the HR. What is the best decision?
items.x: Sinus tachycardia in shock maintains cardiac output, and esmolol causes hypotension, a stop criterion. Treat the shock, not the heart rate.
items.a: Withhold esmolol; the tachycardia is compensatory
w: Start esmolol; the rate is raising oxygen demand
Give diltiazem; it lowers BP less than esmolol
Give adenosine; the rate suggests a reentrant SVT

items.q: A 76-year-old with a spontaneous ICH has SBP 186. The transfer orders call for a nicardipine infusion. Her chart shows advanced aortic stenosis. What is the best action?
items.x: Advanced aortic stenosis is a listed contraindication to nicardipine because fixed outflow cannot compensate for the drop in afterload. Clarify and pick an agent that fits her physiology.
items.a: Clarify the order since advanced AS is a contraindication
w: Start nicardipine at half the ordered rate and titrate slowly
Start nicardipine as ordered since ICH takes priority over AS
Substitute nitroprusside since it is safer in aortic stenosis

items.q: A 66-year-old with NSTEMI is on a heparin infusion during transfer. Mid-flight he reports a sudden severe headache and then develops left arm weakness. What is the best first action?
items.x: A new neuro change on heparin suggests intracranial bleeding, which is a stop criterion. More anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy could be fatal.
items.a: Stop the heparin and notify the receiving team
w: Halve the heparin and repeat the neuro exam
Continue the heparin and give aspirin for stroke
Continue the heparin and treat the BP first

items.q: A teenager in DKA is on an insulin infusion during transfer. A repeat potassium mid-flight is 3.1 mEq/L, and the patient has new PVCs. What is the best action?
items.x: Potassium under 3.3 is a stop criterion for insulin, which drives potassium into cells and can cause dysrhythmias. Replace potassium first, then resume insulin.
items.a: Hold insulin and replace potassium per protocol
w: Continue insulin and add potassium to the fluids
Halve the insulin rate and recheck in 2 hours
Continue insulin and give magnesium for the PVCs
