items.q: A post-arrest patient with GCS 3 starts bucking the ventilator with HR 132 and BP 172/96. The crew gives vecuronium only, saying he is comatose and needs no sedation. What is the main problem?
items.x: A rising HR and BP while bucking suggest arousal, and paralysis hides both comfort and seizure signs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk, so sedation and analgesia must be given.
items.a: He may be aware under paralysis without sedation
w: Vecuronium lasts too long for a post-arrest patient
Vecuronium will blunt the pressure response he needs
A GCS of 3 means the bucking is a spinal reflex only

items.q: A dialysis patient has ROSC after a brief arrest. During transfer, the QRS widens to 160 ms with peaked T waves. K is 7.4 mEq/L, and a central line is in place. What is the best first drug?
items.x: Calcium stabilizes the heart in hyperkalemia within minutes, and a central line suits calcium chloride, which can cause necrosis if it leaks. Antiarrhythmics do not address the cause.
items.a: Calcium chloride slowly via the central line
w: Sodium bicarbonate by IV push via the central line
Regular insulin with dextrose via the central line
Amiodarone slowly by infusion via the central line

items.q: A 4-year-old with septic shock gets a second dose of succinylcholine after a failed first attempt. HR drops from 140 to 66 with delayed capillary refill. SpO2 is 97% with good BVM ventilation. What is the best next step?
items.x: A repeat succinylcholine dose in a child commonly causes vagal bradycardia, and with oxygenation and ventilation confirmed, atropine treats it. Compressions are indicated only if HR falls below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
items.a: Give atropine IV per PALS dosing
w: Start chest compressions per PALS
Begin transcutaneous pacing at once
Give a fluid bolus per PALS dosing

items.q: A 32-year-old ejected from a vehicle 50 minutes ago has HR 128, BP 84/52 and a positive FAST. The ground crew gave TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes just before handoff. What should the flight crew do with TXA now?
items.x: Per CRASH-2 based protocols the 1 g load over 10 minutes is followed by 1 g over 8 hours. TXA is antifibrinolytic, not a pressor, so persistent hypotension is not a reason to stop it or to push another rapid bolus (rapid push causes hypotension).
items.a: Start the second 1 g as an infusion over 8 hours
w: Push the second 1 g as a bolus over 10 minutes now
Start the second 1 g only after 3 hours from injury
Give the second 1 g once a fibrinogen level is back

items.q: A 54-year-old with a sudden worst-ever headache has GCS 13 and BP 168/94. CT at the sending hospital shows a nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. A resident asks the crew to start TXA in flight to prevent rebleeding. What is the best response?
items.x: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a contraindication to TXA, and the 3-hour window applies to trauma, not to this indication. BP control and rapid transport to neurosurgery are the priorities.
items.a: Withhold TXA; SAH is a contraindication
w: Give TXA; it works within 3 hours of onset
Give TXA; rebleeding risk peaks in 24 hours
Delay TXA; give it once the SBP is under 140

items.q: A 25-kg 7-year-old struck by a car 40 minutes ago has HR 150, BP 78/40 and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Your pediatric trauma protocol includes TXA. Which loading dose fits?
items.x: Pediatric trauma protocols use 15 mg/kg over 10 minutes (max 1 g), here 375 mg, followed by 2 mg/kg/h. The adult 1 g or 2 g doses overshoot a 25-kg child, and a rapid push risks hypotension.
items.a: 375 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg/h
w: 250 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg/h
750 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg/h
1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours

items.q: Forty-five minutes into a TXA maintenance infusion, a trauma patient without head injury has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Glucose is 112 and SpO2 is 97%. What is the best interpretation and action?
items.x: Seizures are a listed serious adverse effect of TXA, so the infusion is stopped, the seizure treated, and medical control informed. Assuming it is unrelated and continuing, or giving more TXA, ignores a known drug toxicity.
items.a: A known TXA adverse effect; stop it and treat the seizure
w: An occult head injury; continue TXA and treat the seizure
A sign of blood loss; continue TXA and give more volume
A calcium drop from blood; continue TXA and give calcium

items.q: A dialysis patient with K 7.2 had a QRS of 160 ms. After calcium gluconate the QRS narrows to 110 ms and peaked T waves persist. What is the most important next step?
items.x: Calcium only stabilizes the cardiac membrane for a short time and does not lower potassium, so a shifting agent such as insulin with dextrose is next. Furosemide is not useful in an anuric dialysis patient.
items.a: Shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose
w: Repeat calcium until the T waves return to normal
Remove potassium with furosemide through the kidneys
Bind potassium in the gut with an exchange resin

items.q: A 20-kg child with renal failure has K 7.4, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Per PALS, which calcium gluconate dose is appropriate?
items.x: PALS calcium gluconate for hyperkalemia is 60 mg/kg (max 3 g), 1.2 g for 20 kg. The tempting 20 mg/kg figure is the calcium chloride dose, which contains about three times more elemental calcium per gram.
items.a: 1.2 g (60 mg/kg) IV/IO given slowly
w: 400 mg (20 mg/kg) IV/IO given slowly
3 g (the adult dose) IV/IO given slowly
120 mg (6 mg/kg) IV/IO given slowly

items.q: A 41-year-old industrial worker splashed hydrofluoric acid on two fingers. The skin looks almost normal, but he reports severe pain out of proportion to the findings. After copious irrigation, what is the best next treatment?
items.x: Fluoride ions bind calcium and cause deep tissue injury with pain out of proportion; topical calcium gluconate binds fluoride. Opioids alone treat the symptom but not the ongoing chemical injury.
items.a: Apply calcium gluconate gel to the burn
w: Apply a silver sulfadiazine dressing to the burn
Apply a sodium bicarbonate paste to the burn
Apply a lidocaine gel dressing to the burn

items.q: A 66-year-old with K 7.3 and a QRS of 150 ms is getting calcium chloride 1 g by slow push through a forearm IV. Halfway through, the site becomes swollen, pale and painful. The QRS has narrowed to 124 ms. What is the best action?
items.x: Extravasation is a stop point for calcium chloride, which causes tissue necrosis, but the hyperkalemia still needs membrane stabilization, so the dose is completed through a new, reliable large vein. Pushing more drug or fluid into the infiltrated site worsens the injury, and calcium chloride is not given IM.
items.a: Stop the push at that site and give the rest through new access
w: Slow the push at that site and finish the rest of the dose
Flush that site with saline and give the rest more slowly
Give the rest of the calcium chloride IM in the thigh

items.q: A 60-year-old with a verapamil overdose has HR 40 and BP 72/40. After calcium chloride 1 g IV the BP rises to 90/56, then falls back to 74/42 fifteen minutes later. What is the best next step?
items.x: In calcium channel blocker overdose, calcium is given as 1-2 g every 10-20 minutes because the response is often transient. A temporary response shows benefit, not failure, and switching salts adds nothing.
items.a: Repeat calcium chloride; its effect is often brief
w: Switch to calcium gluconate; chloride has failed
Give atropine alone; calcium rarely works twice
Start glucagon alone; it is the verapamil antidote

items.q: A 34-week preeclamptic patient is on magnesium 2 g/h for transfer. Which new finding should prompt the crew to stop the infusion first?
items.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity and appears before respiratory depression; it is a listed stop point. Flushing, warmth and nausea are common expected effects.
items.a: Patellar reflexes that were present are now absent
w: Facial flushing and warmth after the loading dose
Urine output of 40 mL/h over the past two hours
Respiratory rate of 14 with mild drowsiness

items.q: A 30-week patient with severe preeclampsia has been on magnesium 2 g/h for 3 hours after a full load. Mid-flight she has a second eclamptic seizure. Reflexes were present and RR was 16 just before. What is the best next action?
items.x: Recurrent eclamptic seizures on maintenance therapy are treated with an additional magnesium bolus per protocol while supporting the airway, with toxicity checks afterward. Magnesium is not abandoned for phenytoin, and an antihypertensive does not stop a seizure.
items.a: Protect the airway; give another magnesium bolus per protocol
w: Protect the airway; switch from magnesium to phenytoin
Protect the airway; double the magnesium infusion rate
Protect the airway; give hydralazine before more magnesium

items.q: A 30-kg 9-year-old with severe asthma has poor air movement and SpO2 89% despite continuous albuterol, ipratropium and steroids. Which magnesium dose is appropriate?
items.x: Pediatric magnesium for asthma is 25-50 mg/kg IV over 15-30 minutes (max 2 g), here 750-1,500 mg. The 4 g dose is an eclampsia load, and a rapid push risks hypotension and bradycardia.
items.a: 750-1,500 mg IV over 15-30 minutes
w: 150-300 mg IV over 15-30 minutes
750-1,500 mg IV push over 1 minute
3,000-4,000 mg IV over 15-30 minutes

items.q: A 36-week patient with severe preeclampsia is about to receive magnesium for seizure prophylaxis. Which history finding most changes the plan?
items.x: Heart block is a listed contraindication to magnesium, which slows AV conduction, so this needs a different plan with medical control. Diabetes, prior surgery and asthma do not contraindicate magnesium.
items.a: Known third-degree heart block without a pacemaker
w: Chronic hypertension treated with labetalol
Gestational diabetes treated with insulin
Seizure disorder treated with levetiracetam

items.q: After a field delivery of one infant, the mother's abdomen stays distended, the fundus is well above the umbilicus and fetal parts are palpable. Bleeding is moderate and the placenta has not delivered. A partner draws up oxytocin 10 units IM. What is the best action?
items.x: A possible second twin is a listed contraindication; oxytocin could contract the uterus around an undelivered infant. A fundus well above the umbilicus with palpable fetal parts after one birth suggests another fetus, so it must be excluded first.
items.a: Withhold oxytocin until a second fetus is ruled out
w: Give oxytocin IM now since bleeding is the priority
Give oxytocin once the placenta has delivered
Give oxytocin IV instead for a more titratable effect

items.q: A patient with postpartum hemorrhage has a boggy uterus after placental delivery. HR is 122 and BP 92/58. Two IV attempts have failed and the IO is not yet placed. What is the best oxytocin decision?
items.x: Oxytocin 10 units IM is an accepted PPH route and should not be delayed for access. An IV push risks hypotension and tachycardia, and 40 units is the amount mixed into an infusion bag, not an IM dose.
items.a: Give 10 units IM now while vascular access continues
w: Wait for IO access, then give 10 units by IV push
Give 40 units IM now to match the IV infusion bag
Give misoprostol first while vascular access continues

items.q: Ten minutes after carboprost 250 mcg IM for atony, a patient with no known asthma develops wheezing, RR 30 and SpO2 dropping from 97% to 88%. What is the best next action?
items.x: Bronchospasm and hypoxemia are listed stop points for carboprost, even without an asthma history. Treating the airway takes priority over repeating a drug that is causing it.
items.a: Stop further carboprost and treat the bronchospasm
w: Repeat carboprost on schedule and give albuterol
Treat as pulmonary edema and give furosemide
Treat as anaphylaxis and continue the carboprost

items.q: Twenty minutes after methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM for atony, a postpartum patient has crushing chest pain and BP 174/110. HR is 96. What is the best next action?
items.x: Chest pain and severe hypertension are listed stop criteria; methylergonovine can cause coronary vasospasm. Repeating the dose or dismissing the pain as cramping misses a serious adverse effect.
items.a: Stop further doses; treat as coronary vasospasm
w: Repeat the dose; treat the BP with labetalol
Change to carboprost; treat the pain as cramping
Continue the doses; treat as a pulmonary embolus

items.q: A patient with PPH from atony is vomiting repeatedly and cannot hold anything in her mouth. Oxytocin is running. Which misoprostol route fits best per ACOG/WHO?
items.x: Rectal misoprostol 800-1,000 mcg avoids the oral route in a vomiting patient. Misoprostol has no IV form, 200 mcg QID is the ulcer dose, and 250 mcg IM is carboprost.
items.a: 800-1,000 mcg rectally, once
w: 600 mcg orally, once
800 mcg sublingually, once
200 mcg rectally, once

items.q: A 66-year-old being transferred for a large PE has HR 112 and BP 118/76. The chart notes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia 18 months ago. The sending order is a heparin bolus and infusion. What is the best action?
items.x: A history of HIT is a listed contraindication to heparin, and a lower dose or a different route does not remove that risk. Medical control should order an alternative anticoagulant.
items.a: Withhold heparin and request a non-heparin anticoagulant
w: Give heparin since HIT antibodies fade after 100 days
Give enoxaparin instead since it is not unfractionated heparin
Give the heparin infusion without the bolus and watch platelets

items.q: Two hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization, a patient on a heparin infusion during transfer develops a firm, enlarging groin swelling. HR has risen from 78 to 112 and BP has fallen from 132/80 to 96/60. What is the best first action?
items.x: An expanding hematoma with rising HR and falling BP is active bleeding, a stop point for heparin, and manual pressure just above the arterial puncture controls the source. Giving fluid while the anticoagulant keeps running treats the numbers, not the bleed.
items.a: Stop the heparin and hold firm pressure above the puncture site
w: Halve the heparin and place a pressure dressing over the swelling
Continue the heparin and give a fluid bolus for the blood pressure
Give protamine first and then reassess the groin after landing

items.q: A 90-kg patient with NSTEMI needs heparin started for transfer per the ACC/AHA ACS regimen. What initial dosing is correct?
items.x: The ACS regimen is 60 units/kg (max 4,000) then 12 units/kg/h (max 1,000/h), so both values are capped for a 90-kg patient. 5,400 units ignores the caps, and 7,200 units uses the VTE nomogram.
items.a: 4,000-unit bolus, then 1,000 units/h
w: 5,400-unit bolus, then 1,080 units/h
7,200-unit bolus, then 1,620 units/h
10,000-unit bolus, then 2,000 units/h

items.q: Forty minutes into an alteplase infusion for ischemic stroke, the patient reports a sudden severe headache, vomits, and her NIHSS rises by 6 points. What is the best immediate action?
items.x: New headache, vomiting and neurologic decline are listed stop criteria for alteplase and suggest hemorrhage. Treating the nausea or slowing the drip leaves a thrombolytic running into a possible bleed.
items.a: Stop the infusion; treat as intracranial hemorrhage
w: Slow the infusion; recheck the NIHSS in 15 minutes
Finish the infusion; treat the nausea and headache
Pause the infusion; restart it if the BP is normal

items.q: A 71-year-old with sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia 1 hour ago is a possible alteplase candidate. Glucose is 42 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
items.x: Glucose under 50 is listed as a stroke thrombolytic exclusion because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke. Treat it and reassess; if deficits persist with normal glucose, the stroke pathway continues.
items.a: Treat the hypoglycemia and reassess the neuro exam
w: Start alteplase now and treat the glucose afterward
Treat the hypoglycemia and start alteplase together
Cancel the stroke alert and treat the glucose alone

items.q: An acute ischemic stroke patient within 2 hours of onset has BP 170/92, glucose 130, and platelets 82,000 on labs. What is the alteplase decision?
items.x: Platelets under 100,000 are a listed contraindication. Meeting the BP goal does not override it, and a reduced dose does not make a contraindicated thrombolytic safe.
items.a: Withhold alteplase; the platelet count excludes it
w: Give alteplase; the BP is below the 185/110 limit
Give alteplase; platelets exclude it only below 50,000
Give alteplase; glucose is the only lab needed first

items.q: A 74-kg patient with an anterior STEMI is 3 hours from the nearest PCI center, and the decision is made to give TNKase. What is the correct dose?
items.x: The STEMI dose is weight-banded: 70-79 kg receives 40 mg as a single bolus. 20 mg is the stroke dose for that weight band, and 0.9 mg/kg over 60 minutes is the alteplase stroke regimen.
items.a: 40 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
w: 35 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
45 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
50 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds

items.q: A 58-year-old with inferior ST elevation has tearing chest pain radiating to the back, BP 168/90 in the right arm and 128/70 in the left. PCI is 3 hours away. What is the best decision?
items.x: Suspected aortic dissection is a listed contraindication; a dissection can extend into a coronary ostium and mimic STEMI. Lowering the BP does not make a thrombolytic safe.
items.a: Withhold tenecteplase and treat as suspected aortic dissection
w: Give tenecteplase since PCI is more than 120 minutes away
Give tenecteplase once the SBP is below 140 in both arms
Give heparin and aspirin now and defer tenecteplase to PCI

items.q: Twenty minutes after tenecteplase for STEMI, the chest pain eases, ST elevation falls by more than half, and a wide regular rhythm at 82 appears. BP is 128/76 and the patient is alert. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: An accelerated idioventricular rhythm with pain relief and ST resolution suggests reperfusion; it is usually benign in a stable patient. A rate of 82 is not VT, and tenecteplase is a single-bolus drug that is not repeated.
items.a: Probable reperfusion rhythm; monitor closely without treating
w: Slow ventricular tachycardia; give an amiodarone bolus now
Failed reperfusion; prepare a second tenecteplase dose
Complete heart block with escape; begin pacing at once

items.q: A 6-week-old infant with bronchiolitis is being intubated for transport. A crew member suggests ketamine as the induction agent. What is the main concern with this choice?
items.x: Age under 3 months is a ketamine contraindication, so another agent should be chosen per protocol. The ICP concern is outdated, and IV dosing is not the issue.
items.a: Ketamine is contraindicated under 3 months of age
w: Ketamine is contraindicated in bronchiolitis
Ketamine is contraindicated under 10 kg
Ketamine is contraindicated without atropine

items.q: A 5-year-old receiving ketamine for burn dressing sedation develops a high-pitched inspiratory noise, then silent chest movement and SpO2 falling from 98% to 86%. What is the best immediate action?
items.x: Laryngospasm is a listed ketamine stop point. It is managed first with airway positioning and positive pressure, then further steps per protocol. Naloxone does not reverse ketamine, and albuterol does not treat laryngospasm.
items.a: Stop ketamine; jaw thrust and positive-pressure ventilation
w: Stop ketamine; nebulized albuterol and high-flow oxygen
Stop ketamine; naloxone and a non-rebreather mask
Stop ketamine; nebulized epinephrine and blow-by oxygen

items.q: A 58-year-old in atrial flutter at 150 with BP 86/52 receives a reduced propofol dose and is cardioverted to sinus rhythm at 84. Two minutes later she is apneic, SpO2 is falling from 98% to 89% and the capnography waveform is flat. BP is 102/64. What is the best next action?
items.x: Apnea is a common effect of propofol and there is no reversal agent; because the drug is short-acting, assisted ventilation bridges her until spontaneous breathing returns. Oxygen without ventilation does not treat apnea, and naloxone and flumazenil do not act on propofol.
items.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask until breathing returns
w: Apply a non-rebreather mask until the SpO2 recovers
Give flumazenil IV and repeat until breathing returns
Perform RSI with a paralytic before the SpO2 falls more

items.q: A 20-kg 6-year-old has scald burns to both legs and severe pain. IV access has failed twice, and the IO is reserved for resuscitation. Which analgesic plan fits?
items.x: Intranasal fentanyl 1.5-2 mcg/kg (30-40 mcg for 20 kg) gives fast analgesia without IV access. 100 mcg is an adult-sized dose, and delaying analgesia in a burned child is not appropriate.
items.a: Fentanyl 30-40 mcg intranasally
w: Fentanyl 100-150 mcg intranasally
Fentanyl 5-10 mcg intranasally
Morphine 10 mg intramuscularly

items.q: A non-intubated 45-year-old with rib fractures received fentanyl 50 mcg twice during the flight. He is now hard to rouse with RR 8, SpO2 89% and EtCO2 58. What is the best next action?
items.x: RR under 10-12 with falling SpO2 and rising EtCO2 are fentanyl stop points. Ventilate and reverse; more oxygen does not fix hypoventilation, and a benzodiazepine would deepen respiratory depression.
items.a: Stop fentanyl, support ventilation, and give naloxone
w: Raise oxygen flow, lower the fentanyl dose, and recheck
Apply a non-rebreather, stimulate him, and recheck EtCO2
Start BiPAP, continue fentanyl, and add ketorolac

items.q: A 67-year-old with a COPD flare is on BiPAP for transfer. His PaCO2 is improving, but he is agitated and keeps pulling at the mask. HR is 96, BP 142/84 and SpO2 91%. Which sedation plan best fits?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine calms with little respiratory depression, so it suits a non-intubated hypercapnic patient, and skipping the load limits bradycardia and transient hypertension. Benzodiazepine boluses, propofol and stacked opioid doses can suppress the respiratory drive he depends on.
items.a: A low-dose dexmedetomidine infusion without a load
w: A midazolam infusion after a loading bolus
A propofol infusion at an ICU sedation rate
A fentanyl infusion after a loading bolus

items.q: A 24-year-old with a severe TBI has a dilated right pupil, BP 192/104, HR 48 and irregular respirations. A partner draws up labetalol for the BP. What is the best response?
items.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing (Cushing triad) with a blown pupil mean herniation. Lowering the BP would cut cerebral perfusion, and bradycardia is a listed labetalol stop point.
items.a: Withhold it; treat the herniation, not the BP
w: Give it; an SBP above 180 worsens the bleeding
Give it with atropine; treat the BP and the HR
Use nicardipine; it lowers BP without slowing HR

items.q: A 64-year-old with a spontaneous ICH is on nicardipine at 12.5 mg/h with a target SBP of 130-150. During the flight SBP falls to 108, HR is 104 and she is newly more drowsy. What is the best action?
items.x: A BP below target is a stop point for nicardipine, and overshooting in ICH can reduce cerebral perfusion, which may explain the new drowsiness (expansion of the bleed must also be considered). Lower is not better once below goal, and a second antihypertensive drops the BP further.
items.a: Reduce or pause the nicardipine and recheck the BP and neuro exam
w: Continue the nicardipine rate, since a lower BP limits the bleeding
Continue the nicardipine and add labetalol for the tachycardia
Continue the nicardipine and give a fluid bolus to raise the SBP

items.q: A 30-year-old with an isolated TBI was just intubated. BP falls from 118/70 to 82/48 with HR 96, attributed to induction drugs and positive pressure. What is the best immediate step while the cause is addressed?
items.x: Even one hypotensive episode worsens TBI outcomes, so post-intubation hypotension is corrected quickly; push-dose phenylephrine is used per protocol. Permissive hypotension is for penetrating torso trauma, not TBI.
items.a: Give push-dose phenylephrine per protocol to restore MAP
w: Accept the BP, since permissive hypotension limits bleeding
Give mannitol per protocol to protect cerebral perfusion
Give more sedation per protocol to blunt the ICP response

items.q: A 100-kg patient with a TBI is still seizing after two doses of midazolam. The physician orders a levetiracetam load for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus. Which dose matches the ESETT approach?
items.x: ESETT dosing is 60 mg/kg with a 4,500 mg maximum, so a 100-kg patient receives 4,500 mg. 6,000 mg ignores the cap, and 500 mg is the routine maintenance dose.
items.a: 4,500 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
w: 6,000 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
2,000 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
1,000 mg IV over 10-15 minutes

items.q: A 12-kg toddler with croup has stridor at rest and retractions. Racemic epinephrine is not stocked, so the crew uses 1 mg/mL epinephrine by nebulizer per croup guidelines. What volume is correct?
items.x: The croup dose is 0.5 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL (max 5 mL). For 12 kg this would be 6 mL, so the 5 mL cap applies. 0.12 mL is the IM anaphylaxis dose, and 0.5 mL is the racemic dose.
items.a: 5 mL nebulized
w: 6 mL nebulized
0.12 mL nebulized
0.5 mL nebulized

items.q: Thirty minutes after nebulized racemic epinephrine, a 3-year-old with croup has no stridor at rest and SpO2 98%. No steroid has been given. What is the best plan?
items.x: Racemic epinephrine wears off and stridor can return, so the child needs observation and a corticosteroid for longer-lasting relief. Scheduled repeat nebs and albuterol do not address the airway edema.
items.a: Give dexamethasone and keep watching for rebound stridor
w: Give no steroid and keep watching for rebound stridor
Give a second racemic epinephrine dose to prevent rebound
Give nebulized albuterol and keep watching for wheezing

items.q: A 12-kg toddler found with a relative's methadone had RR 4 and pinpoint pupils. After naloxone 1.2 mg IV he woke and cried. Forty minutes into the flight he is drowsy again with RR 8. What is the best explanation and action?
items.x: Methadone has a much longer duration than naloxone, so resedation is expected and needs repeat dosing or an infusion. Improvement after the first dose confirms the opioid effect.
items.a: Methadone outlasts naloxone; redose per protocol
w: Naloxone caused withdrawal; give no further doses
Naloxone failed; look for a non-opioid ingestion
Naloxone is still active; check a glucose instead

items.q: A 15-kg 3-year-old has seized for 7 minutes during an interfacility transfer, and the peripheral IV has infiltrated. Per protocol, which first anticonvulsant is best?
items.x: Intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg) is fast and needs no IV; for 15 kg that is 3 mg. 10 mg is the adult maximum, and waiting for IV access prolongs the seizure.
items.a: Midazolam 3 mg intranasally
w: Midazolam 10 mg intranasally
Midazolam 0.5 mg intranasally
Diazepam 3 mg intramuscularly

items.q: A 24-year-old took amitriptyline 40 minutes ago. GCS has fallen from 15 to 11 during transport preparation and the gag reflex is weak. She is not intubated. What is the charcoal decision?
items.x: Altered mental status without a protected airway is a listed contraindication because of aspiration risk. A TCA patient can deteriorate quickly, so the airway and sodium bicarbonate readiness come first.
items.a: Withhold it; her airway is not protected
w: Give it PO; she is still within the first hour
Give it by NG tube; the tube lowers aspiration risk
Give half PO; a smaller volume is safer to swallow

items.q: A 20-kg 5-year-old pulled from a house fire has GCS 9, BP 70/40, and suspected cyanide toxicity. What is the hydroxocobalamin dose?
items.x: Pediatric dosing is 70 mg/kg (max 5 g) over 15 minutes, 1.4 g for 20 kg. 5 g is the adult dose, and a push over 1 minute does not match the labeled infusion time.
items.a: 1.4 g IV over 15 minutes
w: 5 g IV over 15 minutes
2.5 g IV over 15 minutes
0.7 g IV over 15 minutes

items.q: Twenty minutes into the IV NAC loading dose for acetaminophen overdose, a patient develops flushing, hives and mild wheezing. BP is 118/72. What is the best action?
items.x: Anaphylactoid reactions are rate-related; the standard approach is to pause, treat and restart slower. Stopping permanently leaves the overdose untreated, and charcoal will not replace NAC.
items.a: Pause, treat the reaction, then restart slower
w: Switch to activated charcoal, then recheck levels
Continue, give diphenhydramine, then recheck
Continue, then slow down if the BP drops

items.q: After physostigmine for anticholinergic delirium, a patient becomes calm, then develops HR 46, drooling, vomiting and new wheezing. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: Bradycardia, salivation, vomiting and bronchospasm are cholinergic effects and listed physostigmine stop points. Anticholinergic toxicity causes tachycardia and dry skin, the opposite picture.
items.a: Cholinergic excess from physostigmine; stop it and treat
w: Returning anticholinergic toxicity; give another dose
Allergic reaction to physostigmine; give epinephrine IM
Aspiration during the delirium; give albuterol and watch

items.q: A farmer with organophosphate poisoning received atropine until his secretions dried and his lungs cleared. He now has muscle fasciculations and weak respiratory effort. What is the best next step?
items.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but not nicotinic weakness and fasciculations, which pralidoxime targets. More atropine will not restore muscle strength once secretions are dry.
items.a: Give pralidoxime and prepare ventilatory support
w: Give more atropine until the fasciculations stop
Give glycopyrrolate and prepare ventilatory support
Give diazepam for the twitching and recheck effort

items.q: An intubated TCA overdose patient has received several sodium bicarbonate boluses and is on a bicarbonate infusion. The QRS has narrowed from 146 to 104 ms, and the arterial pH is now 7.58. What is the best plan for the bicarbonate?
items.x: A narrowed QRS and a pH above the 7.45-7.55 goal are stop points for bicarbonate; more alkalosis lowers potassium and ionized calcium and can provoke dysrhythmias. Bicarbonate resumes if the QRS widens again once pH allows, and hypoventilating the patient to make room for more is not standard care.
items.a: Stop further bicarbonate and keep monitoring the QRS
w: Give another bolus to bring the QRS below 100 ms
Double the infusion and keep monitoring the QRS
Lower the vent rate so more bicarbonate can be given

items.q: A dialysis patient with K 7.0 and peaked T waves has received calcium. The plan is insulin with dextrose to shift potassium. Which insulin dose fits for renal failure?
items.x: In renal failure the hyperkalemia dose is reduced to 5 units with 25 g dextrose because insulin clears slowly. Insulin without dextrose risks hypoglycemia, and 1 unit/kg is the HIET dose for toxicology.
items.a: 5 units IV with 25 g dextrose
w: 10 units IV without dextrose
5 units SQ with 25 g dextrose
20 units IV with 25 g dextrose

items.q: A dialysis patient who makes no urine has K 6.9 and mild crackles. A crew member suggests furosemide 80 mg IV to remove potassium. What is the best response?
items.x: Anuria is a listed contraindication; a loop diuretic needs functioning kidneys to work. This patient needs potassium shifting and urgent dialysis instead.
items.a: Withhold it; anuria is a contraindication
w: Give it; the crackles show fluid overload
Double it; failing kidneys need a higher dose
Give it with saline; flow carries potassium out

items.q: A 22-year-old runner collapsed in a marathon. He is confused with core temp 41.4 C (106.5 F), HR 150 and BP 98/58. A partner suggests IV acetaminophen 1,000 mg for the fever. What is the best response?
items.x: Heat stroke is not a fever driven by the hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics do not work; rapid cooling is the treatment. Liver injury is also common in heat stroke and adds acetaminophen risk.
items.a: Rapid cooling; antipyretics do not work here
w: Acetaminophen first; cool him if it fails
Acetaminophen with cooling; it adds benefit
Dantrolene instead; it stops muscle heat

items.q: A 38-year-old motorcyclist has GCS 5, a fixed dilated left pupil and an open femur fracture. After intubation, BP is 74/40 and HR 138. Medical control asks about hyperosmolar therapy for suspected herniation. Which plan is best?
items.x: Mannitol is contraindicated in severe hypovolemia and its diuresis worsens hypotension, which itself injures the brain; hypertonic saline per protocol lowers ICP without the diuretic volume loss. Herniation is urgent, but giving mannitol in hemorrhagic shock compounds secondary brain injury.
items.a: Avoid mannitol; restore perfusion and use hypertonic saline per protocol
w: Give mannitol now; herniation outweighs the low blood pressure
Give mannitol with furosemide; the pair lowers ICP more strongly
Delay all ICP treatment; give crystalloid until the SBP is normal

items.q: A 70-kg intubated TBI patient is finishing a mannitol dose started 30 minutes ago at the sending facility. Since it began, the Foley has drained 900 mL, BP has fallen from 134/82 to 92/58 and HR has risen from 88 to 116. What is the best next step?
items.x: Mannitol's osmotic diuresis can cause dehydration and hypotension, and hypotension is a stop criterion; the lost volume must be replaced to protect cerebral perfusion. Clamping the catheter does not stop the diuresis, and a vasopressor does not make continuing the drug safe.
items.a: Stop the mannitol, replace volume with isotonic fluid and reassess
w: Finish the mannitol, start a vasopressor and reassess the BP
Finish the mannitol, give furosemide for the kidneys and reassess
Slow the mannitol, limit further IV fluid and reassess

items.q: During an interfacility transfer of a TBI patient who has had several mannitol doses, the latest labs show serum osmolality 326 mOsm/kg and sodium 151. The sending physician asks whether the next scheduled dose should be given in flight. What is the best response?
items.x: Serum osmolality above 320 is a stop criterion for mannitol because of the risk of dehydration and renal injury. Slowing the infusion or adding water still delivers the osmotic load the threshold is meant to prevent.
items.a: Hold the dose and notify medical control, since osmolality is above 320
w: Give the dose, since sodium is still below the limit of 160
Give half the dose, since osmolality is only slightly high
Give the dose with extra isotonic fluid to offset the osmolality

items.q: A 74-year-old with severe heart failure fell and now has GCS 7 with a new dilated right pupil. After intubation, pink frothy secretions fill the ETT, crackles are heard bilaterally and SpO2 is 86% on FiO2 1.0. Which finding most changes the hyperosmolar plan?
items.x: Mannitol is contraindicated in pulmonary edema or severe heart failure because its osmotic shift first expands intravascular volume; withhold it and discuss alternatives with medical control. Age alone does not change the dose in the drug data.
items.a: The pulmonary edema, which contraindicates mannitol
w: The age of 74, which calls for a reduced dose
The GCS of 7, which predicts a poor response
The dilated pupil, which calls for a larger dose

items.q: An intubated TBI patient is receiving mannitol every 6 hours during a long transfer. Which new finding is most concerning and calls for stopping the drug and notifying medical control?
items.x: Anuria is a contraindication and a stop criterion: mannitol is cleared by the kidneys, so it accumulates and can cause volume overload and renal injury. Brisk urine output is the expected effect, and an osmolality of 306 is below the 320 stop threshold.
items.a: No urine output for the past hour despite a patent catheter
w: Urine output of 350 mL in the hour after the latest dose
Serum osmolality of 312 mOsm/kg on the most recent lab
Serum sodium of 148 mEq/L on the most recent lab draw

items.q: A TBI patient with signs of herniation is receiving 3% saline per protocol through a 20-gauge hand IV. Ten minutes later the site is swollen, pale and painful, and the infusion is slowing. What is the best next step?
items.x: IV infiltration ends a 3% saline infusion because hypertonic fluid in the tissues causes pain and tissue injury; therapy resumes through new reliable IV or IO access per protocol. Flushing and resuming at an infiltrated site pushes more hypertonic fluid into the tissue.
items.a: Stop the infusion at that site, notify the provider and get new access
w: Flush the IV with saline and resume the 3% at the same site
Slow the infusion and apply a warm pack to the swollen hand
Continue the infusion and elevate the hand until landing

items.q: A 52-year-old with TBI is on a 3% saline infusion per protocol with an ordered sodium goal. Baseline sodium was 139. A repeat sodium 2 hours later is well above the ordered goal, and the intubated patient has stable vital signs. What is the best action?
items.x: A sodium rise faster than the planned correction is a hold criterion for 3% saline because of the risk of hypernatremia. Stable vital signs do not make an overshoot safe, and adding a diuretic does not address the excess sodium load.
items.a: Hold the infusion and notify the provider of the sodium result
w: Continue the infusion and recheck the sodium in 2 hours
Slow the infusion and report the sodium result at handoff
Continue the infusion and add furosemide as a sodium offset

items.q: A 4-hour interfacility transfer is arranged for a TBI patient on a 3% saline infusion per protocol. Point-of-care testing is available on the aircraft. Which value is most important to recheck during the flight?
items.x: Serum sodium is checked every 2 to 4 hours during 3% saline to catch hypernatremia or an overly fast rise. Glucose matters in TBI, but it does not track the main risk of this drug.
items.a: Serum sodium, every 2 to 4 hours during the infusion
w: Serum potassium, every 2 to 4 hours during the infusion
Blood glucose, every 30 to 60 minutes during the infusion
Serum lactate, every 2 to 4 hours during the infusion

items.q: An 81-year-old with a subdural hematoma and a history of heart failure is receiving 3% saline per protocol. Twenty minutes in, RR rises to 32, crackles appear in both bases and SpO2 falls from 95% to 88%. What is the best next step?
items.x: New pulmonary edema ends a 3% saline infusion; hypertonic saline expands intravascular volume and can cause fluid overload, especially in heart failure. Switching to normal saline would add even more volume.
items.a: Stop the infusion, support oxygenation and notify the provider
w: Slow the infusion, give a bronchodilator and recheck the SpO2
Change to normal saline at the same rate and notify the provider
Finish the infusion, raise the oxygen flow and recheck at landing

items.q: A TBI patient with a blown pupil has a serum sodium of 140. A new crew member objects to 3% saline because its label lists normal sodium as a contraindication. What is the best response?
items.x: The label covers sodium depletion; using 3% saline to lower ICP is an established off-label use, so dosing follows protocol and medical direction. Applying the sodium-depletion label limits or waiting for hyponatremia would delay needed ICP treatment.
items.a: Its ICP use is off-label; give it per protocol and medical direction
w: The label is absolute; do not give it and continue the transport
The label allows it; give it once the sodium falls below 135
The label limits it; give it only at the slow sodium-loss rate

items.q: A 76-year-old on warfarin with a large intracerebral hemorrhage is ready for transfer. The 4F-PCC infusion finished 10 minutes ago, but no vitamin K appears on the medication record. What is the best action before departure?
items.x: The label pairs 4F-PCC with concurrent vitamin K: PCC replaces factors quickly, but that effect is temporary while warfarin persists, so vitamin K is needed to sustain reversal. Repeating PCC adds thrombotic risk without addressing the ongoing warfarin effect.
items.a: Ensure IV vitamin K is given, as the label pairs it with PCC
w: Ensure a second PCC dose is ready, as its effect fades in hours
Take no action, as PCC fully replaces the need for vitamin K
Ensure oral vitamin K is given, as IV dosing is for surgery only

items.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin with septic shock has an INR of 4.8, oozing from every line site, platelets 38,000, a low fibrinogen and schistocytes on the smear. The sending team asks about 4F-PCC before transport. Which finding most argues against it?
items.x: DIC is a label contraindication to 4F-PCC because concentrated clotting factors can worsen thrombosis, so the decision goes to medical control. An INR of 4 to 6 is within the labeled dosing range.
items.a: The picture of DIC, a label contraindication to PCC
w: The septic shock, a label contraindication to PCC
The INR above 4, a level PCC is not labeled to treat
The warfarin use, a reason to give vitamin K alone

items.q: A 79-year-old on warfarin with a major GI bleed is receiving 4F-PCC with vitamin K. Near the end of the infusion he develops new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. BP is 148/86. What is the best next step?
items.x: New neurologic deficits during PCC suggest thromboembolism such as stroke, a known serious effect, so the infusion is stopped and the provider notified. Protamine reverses heparin and does not reverse PCC.
items.a: Stop the infusion, assess for stroke and notify medical control
w: Finish the infusion, assess for stroke and notify on arrival
Slow the infusion, recheck the INR and continue if it is high
Finish the infusion, then give heparin for the likely clot

items.q: A warfarin patient with a traumatic subdural hematoma received 4F-PCC and IV vitamin K before a 90-minute transfer. Point-of-care INR testing is available on the aircraft. When is a repeat INR most useful to judge the response?
items.x: The label calls for an INR at baseline and about 30 minutes after the infusion to confirm reversal. Waiting 24 hours misses the window in which PCC's effect should be measured, and warfarin effect is tracked by INR, not aPTT.
items.a: About 30 minutes after the PCC infusion is complete
w: About 6 hours after the PCC infusion is complete
About 12 hours after the vitamin K dose is given
Right at the midpoint of the PCC infusion

items.q: A 130-kg patient on warfarin has a life-threatening retroperitoneal bleed with an INR of 4.5. A partner calculates 4,550 units of 4F-PCC. Per the 4F-PCC (Kcentra) label, what is the correct dose?
items.x: For an INR of 4 to 6, the label dose is 35 units/kg with weight counted only up to 100 kg, so the maximum is 3,500 units. Using actual body weight overdoses the patient and adds thrombotic risk.
items.a: 3,500 units, because dosing uses weight only up to 100 kg
w: 4,550 units, because dosing follows actual body weight
2,500 units, because an INR below 6 uses the lowest tier
5,000 units, because a life-threatening bleed uses the top tier

items.q: A 74-year-old with atrial fibrillation fell and has an expanding epidural hematoma. His pill organizer holds dabigatran, metoprolol and atorvastatin. The sending ED stocks andexanet alfa, 4F-PCC and idarucizumab. Which is the targeted reversal?
items.x: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Andexanet reverses the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban and has no effect on dabigatran.
items.a: Idarucizumab 5 g IV
w: Andexanet alfa high-dose bolus
4F-PCC 50 units/kg IV
Protamine 50 mg slow IV

items.q: A 66-year-old on dabigatran for atrial fibrillation received idarucizumab for a traumatic splenic bleed. Two hours into the transfer, bleeding is controlled, but she develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, HR 124, BP 132/78 and SpO2 falling from 97% to 88%. What should the crew suspect first?
items.x: Reversal removes dabigatran's protection against clotting in a patient with atrial fibrillation, and thrombosis is a known serious effect; sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxia suggests PE. Rebleeding would cause hypotension, not sudden pleuritic pain and hypoxia with a stable BP.
items.a: A thromboembolic event now that anticoagulation is reversed
w: An allergic reaction to the earlier idarucizumab dose
Recurrent splenic bleeding irritating the left diaphragm
A rebound in dabigatran effect as the reversal wears off

items.q: After idarucizumab is given for dabigatran-associated bleeding, the receiving team asks which coagulation tests best reflect the reversal. What is the best answer?
items.x: Dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin, so the aPTT and thrombin time track its effect and its reversal. INR tracks warfarin, and anti-Xa activity relates to heparin and factor Xa inhibitors.
items.a: aPTT and thrombin time
w: INR and prothrombin time
Anti-Xa level and INR
Fibrinogen and D-dimer

items.q: A 70-year-old on apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. A partner, seeing anticoagulant reversal on the idarucizumab box, prepares the 5 g dose. What is the best response?
items.x: Idarucizumab binds only dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors; apixaban reversal uses andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC per protocol. Pairing it with protamine adds risk without reversing apixaban.
items.a: Withhold it; use andexanet or PCC per protocol for apixaban
w: Give it; it reverses all of the direct oral anticoagulants
Give it; add PCC per protocol to cover any remaining apixaban
Withhold it; use protamine per protocol for factor Xa inhibitors

items.q: A dabigatran patient with a life-threatening GI bleed is ordered idarucizumab. During a hurried loading, the partner has given one 2.5 g vial and is preparing to depart. What is the best action?
items.x: The labeled dose is 5 g, supplied as two 2.5 g vials; giving only one leaves reversal incomplete in a life-threatening bleed. Waiting for labs delays reversal, and PCC is not the targeted agent for dabigatran.
items.a: Give the second 2.5 g vial so the full 5 g dose is complete
w: Depart now, since one 2.5 g vial is the complete labeled dose
Give the second vial only if bleeding continues after landing
Give 4F-PCC in place of the second vial during the flight

items.q: A 62-year-old on a heparin infusion after a cardiac procedure develops an expanding groin hematoma. During IV protamine, BP drops from 126/78 to 80/48, HR falls to 52 and his face is flushed. What is the best next step?
items.x: Hypotension, bradycardia and flushing are recognized protamine reactions and hold criteria; stopping the drug, supporting perfusion and notifying the provider comes first. That these effects are common does not make continuing safe once the patient is unstable.
items.a: Stop the protamine, support BP and notify the provider
w: Continue the protamine, give atropine and recheck the BP
Finish the protamine, then give a fluid bolus for the BP
Continue the protamine, since flushing is an expected effect

items.q: A 58-year-old with an NSTEMI is being flown on a heparin infusion. Midway through the flight he becomes confused, vomits and develops a new dilated left pupil with BP 196/104. What is the best first action?
items.x: Suspected intracranial hemorrhage on heparin calls for stopping the source first, with protamine reversal to follow per order. Giving protamine while heparin keeps infusing works against itself.
items.a: Stop the heparin infusion and notify medical control
w: Halve the heparin infusion and treat the BP with labetalol
Continue the heparin infusion and give mannitol per protocol
Continue the heparin infusion and treat as an embolic stroke

items.q: A 66-year-old man with diabetes treated with NPH insulin is receiving protamine for heparin reversal. Within minutes he develops diffuse hives, wheezing and BP 74/40. What is the best next step?
items.x: Anaphylaxis is the serious adverse effect of protamine, so the drug is stopped and epinephrine given. An antihistamine alone does not treat the hypotension or bronchospasm.
items.a: Stop the protamine and treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine
w: Slow the protamine and treat the hives with diphenhydramine
Stop the protamine and treat with IV methylprednisolone alone
Finish the protamine and treat the BP with a fluid bolus

items.q: An 83-year-old on warfarin has a subdural hematoma with an INR of 3.6. A crew member suggests protamine because it is the reversal agent carried on the aircraft. What is the best response?
items.x: Protamine reverses heparin and partially reverses enoxaparin; warfarin reversal uses 4F-PCC with vitamin K. Giving protamine here adds hypotension and anaphylaxis risk with no benefit.
items.a: Withhold it; protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin
w: Give it; protamine partly reverses most anticoagulants
Give it; protamine bridges until vitamin K takes effect
Give half; protamine carries more risk in older patients

items.q: A patient on a heparin infusion received protamine for bleeding at a femoral sheath site, and the bleeding has slowed. Which test best confirms the reversal at the transfer handoff?
items.x: The aPTT reflects unfractionated heparin effect and is the lab used to follow protamine reversal. The INR tracks warfarin and does not confirm heparin reversal.
items.a: aPTT
w: INR
Platelet count
Fibrinogen level

items.q: A 69-year-old on rivaroxaban is being flown for an unrelated cardiac workup. She develops a nosebleed that stops after 10 minutes of direct pressure, with stable vital signs and normal mentation. What is the best plan for andexanet alfa?
items.x: Andexanet is indicated for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding; a controlled nosebleed does not justify its thromboembolic risk. Being on a factor Xa inhibitor is not by itself an indication.
items.a: Do not give it; the bleed is neither life-threatening nor uncontrolled
w: Give the low-dose regimen to keep the bleed from recurring in flight
Give the high-dose regimen, since rivaroxaban is a factor Xa inhibitor
Give 4F-PCC instead, since it carries less clot risk than andexanet

items.q: A patient on apixaban with an intracerebral hemorrhage received andexanet alfa before transfer. The receiving team plans to order a commercial anti-Xa level to judge the reversal. What is the best handoff point?
items.x: Commercial anti-Xa assays are unreliable after andexanet, so reversal is judged by hemostasis, the clinical picture and hemoglobin. Acting on those results could lead to inappropriate redosing or early restarting of anticoagulation.
items.a: Commercial anti-Xa assays are unreliable after andexanet
w: A near-zero anti-Xa level means apixaban can be restarted
A high anti-Xa level means a second full dose is required
The anti-Xa level should be repeated every 15 minutes

items.q: A 77-year-old on rivaroxaban with a life-threatening GI bleed is on the andexanet infusion after the bolus. Forty minutes later he reports crushing chest pain, and the monitor shows new ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What is the best next step?
items.x: MI is a known serious thromboembolic effect of andexanet and a stop criterion. Anticoagulating a patient with an active major bleed is a medical control decision, not a reflex, and continuing the infusion ignores the stop criterion.
items.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider of a possible MI
w: Continue the infusion and give aspirin for a possible MI
Continue the infusion and give a heparin bolus for the MI
Slow the infusion and give nitroglycerin for the chest pain

items.q: A 64-year-old on apixaban with a traumatic intracranial bleed received the low-dose andexanet bolus at the sending hospital, and the 4 mg/min infusion has run for 20 minutes when the aircraft arrives. What is the best plan?
items.x: The bolus is followed by an infusion for up to 120 minutes to sustain reversal; stopping or pausing it lets anticoagulant activity return. Switching to the high-dose rate changes the ordered regimen without an indication.
items.a: Continue the infusion in flight for up to 120 minutes total
w: Disconnect it for flight, since the bolus gives the full reversal
Switch to the 8 mg/min rate to finish before landing
Pause the infusion for transport and restart it at the receiving ED

items.q: An 82-year-old on rivaroxaban has a life-threatening bleed, and the low-dose andexanet regimen is ordered. A partner plans to push the 400 mg bolus over 2 minutes to save time. What is the best response?
items.x: The labeled low-dose regimen is a 400 mg bolus at 30 mg/min (about 13 minutes) followed by 4 mg/min for up to 120 minutes. Skipping the bolus or stretching it over 2 hours delays reversal in a life-threatening bleed.
items.a: Give the bolus at 30 mg/min, then start the 4 mg/min infusion
w: Push it over 2 minutes, since the rate does not matter for a bolus
Give the full 400 mg as a slow infusion over 2 hours instead
Skip the bolus and start the 8 mg/min infusion directly

items.q: At 1500 you are dispatched to a two-car crash on a four-lane interstate. A fire engine is already parked angled across the left lane just upstream of the wrecked vehicles. Where should you position the ambulance?
items.x: The fire apparatus acts as the upstream block, so the ambulance parks downstream of the scene where loading is protected. Parking upstream or beside the wreck in an open lane puts the crew and patient in the path of traffic.
items.a: Beyond the crash, downstream of the engine, so it is shielded
w: Upstream of the fire engine to add a second barrier to traffic
In the open right lane alongside the wreck for faster loading
On the grass median directly across from the crash site

items.q: At 2200 you arrive at a single-vehicle crash on an unlit two-lane highway. Traffic is still moving past the scene in both directions. Before stepping out of the ambulance, what is the most important personal protective step?
items.x: Being struck by traffic is a leading cause of EMS roadway deaths, so high-visibility apparel is required before working near moving traffic. Gloves and eye protection are needed before patient contact but do not address the traffic hazard.
items.a: Put on a high-visibility safety vest
w: Put on exam gloves and eye protection
Turn on the scene and loading lights
Put on a helmet and extrication gloves

items.q: You arrive at a car that struck a utility pole in a rural area at night. A power line is lying across the hood, and the alert driver says his leg hurts. What is the best action?
items.x: A downed line can energize the car and the ground around it; the occupant is safest inside while the crew stays outside the hazard zone until the utility company de-energizes it. EMS gear is not rated electrical protection, and moving the line is never an EMS task.
items.a: Tell him to stay in the car, stay back, and request the utility company
w: Have him open the door and jump clear of the car with both feet together
Use a dry wooden pike pole to move the line off of the hood
Approach the car in rubber boots and gloves to assess his leg

items.q: You are first on scene at a rollover of a tanker truck on a state highway. A liquid is pooling under the trailer and the driver is slumped in the cab. You can see an orange-bordered diamond placard but cannot read it from your position. What should you do first?
items.x: Hazardous materials scenes are approached from uphill and upwind at a distance; binoculars allow identification so the Emergency Response Guidebook can set isolation distances. Moving closer or sending anyone toward the leak risks more victims.
items.a: Stop uphill and upwind, read it with binoculars, use the ERG
w: Drive closer so the placard number can be read and reported to dispatch
Walk to the cab to check the driver while holding your breath
Have a bystander read the placard while you get the stretcher

items.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a man who collapsed inside a manure pit. On arrival, a family member says a second man went in to help him and also collapsed. Both are visible at the bottom and are not moving. What is the best action?
items.x: Confined spaces like manure pits can contain toxic gases and low oxygen; a second collapsed rescuer confirms a deadly atmosphere. Only rescuers with supplied air and confined-space training enter; a surgical mask gives no protection.
items.a: Do not enter; request fire and technical rescue with SCBA
w: Enter quickly with a surgical mask to drag out the nearer man
Lower a crew member on a rope to check both men's breathing
Have the family member lower a ladder so you can climb down

items.q: You enter a home for a 66-year-old man with COPD who is short of breath. He is wearing a nasal cannula from his home oxygen concentrator and is lighting a cigarette. What should you do first?
items.x: Oxygen strongly supports combustion, and an open flame near a cannula can cause facial burns or a fire. Eliminating the ignition source is a scene safety step that comes before patient assessment.
items.a: Have him put out the cigarette before anything else
w: Turn off the concentrator and let him finish smoking
Switch him to your portable oxygen tank right away
Begin the primary assessment while he finishes it

items.q: You are assigned to the rehab and treatment area at a working house fire. A firefighter tells you a resident may still be inside a back bedroom. You are wearing standard EMS gear. What is your role?
items.x: Interior search and rescue in a burning structure requires turnout gear, SCBA, and fire training. The EMT's role is to be ready in a safe treatment area to receive the patient once firefighters remove them.
items.a: Stay in the treatment area and prepare to receive the patient
w: Go to the back window to call out to the resident
Follow the attack crew to help carry the resident out
Move the stretcher to the back door to save time

items.q: You are dispatched to a home for a 34-year-old woman with a headache. As you step through the front door, the carbon monoxide monitor clipped to your bag starts alarming. What is the best action?
items.x: A personal CO alarm means the environment is unsafe. The crew exits, helping occupants out if it can be done quickly, and requests the fire department to meter and ventilate; staying inside to treat exposes the crew.
items.a: Leave the home, help occupants out, and request fire
w: Silence the monitor and continue to the patient while watching it
Open a window in the living room and then assess the patient there
Place oxygen on the patient and treat her inside the home

items.q: You are dispatched to a warehouse for a worker who is "stuck" to an electrical panel. On arrival, a coworker says he is still in contact with the panel and shaking. What is the best action?
items.x: Rescuers must not touch a patient in contact with an energized source. Power is shut off by qualified personnel first; improvised insulators and medical gloves do not protect against industrial voltages.
items.a: Have qualified staff shut off the power first
w: Push him away from the panel using a dry wooden broom handle
Pull him off by his clothing while wearing exam gloves
Grab his ankle quickly and pull him away from the panel

items.q: You are dispatched to a golf course. A group of four golfers was struck by lightning; the storm is still overhead. Two are moaning, and two are motionless and not breathing. After moving everyone to a safe location, who should receive care first?
items.x: In lightning strikes, reverse triage applies: patients in respiratory or cardiac arrest often respond to prompt care, while those moaning are breathing and less likely to die. Crew safety from the ongoing storm comes first.
items.a: The two motionless, apneic golfers
w: The two moaning golfers, per standard triage
The moaning golfer with the worst burns
No one until all four have been tagged

items.q: You arrive at a home for a 40-year-old woman with a nosebleed. While you are assessing her, her husband walks in holding a kitchen knife and shouts at you to leave. What is the best action?
items.x: When the scene becomes unsafe mid-call, the crew retreats to a safe location and requests law enforcement. Disarming a person is not an EMS task, and continuing care with a weapon present risks the crew.
items.a: Leave with your partner and request law enforcement
w: Back into another room and continue treating her
Calmly explain your role and ask him to put it down
Have your partner stay while you go radio for police

items.q: You are dispatched to a reported shooting outside a nightclub. Dispatch states police are en route and the scene is not yet secure. What should you do?
items.x: Responders stage a safe distance away and out of view until law enforcement secures the scene. Arriving early, even quietly, risks injury or creating more patients.
items.a: Stage out of sight nearby until police report the scene secure
w: Drive to the front door with lights off to avoid drawing attention
Park at the scene and wait in the ambulance with the doors locked
Go to the scene because a shooting victim needs care immediately

items.q: Police secure an apartment and you enter for a man who is pulseless and apneic with obvious signs of death and a gunshot wound to the head. How should you manage the scene?
items.x: At a crime scene with obvious death, EMS confirms death, limits personnel, and disturbs nothing beyond what care requires. Touching the weapon or moving the body can destroy evidence; anything moved should be reported to police.
items.a: Use one path in and out and disturb as little as you can
w: Start CPR and move him to the hallway for more space
Secure the handgun in your kit for the officers
Cover him with a sheet and tidy the items nearby

items.q: You are treating a 24-year-old man with a stab wound to the chest. Police say this is a crime scene. You need to expose the wound. How should you remove his shirt?
items.x: Cutting around a stab or bullet hole preserves evidence while still allowing full exposure. Patient care still comes first, but avoiding the defect is easy and protects the investigation.
items.a: Cut around, not through, the hole in the fabric
w: Cut straight through the hole to save time
Pull the shirt off over his head to keep it whole
Leave the shirt on and assess only by palpation

items.q: A 22-year-old woman reports being sexually assaulted 1 hour ago and is calm. She asks if she can shower before going to the hospital. What is the best response?
items.x: Showering, changing, or using the bathroom can destroy evidence, so the EMT gently asks her to avoid this. Clothing is placed in separate paper bags because plastic traps moisture and degrades evidence.
items.a: Ask her not to shower, change, or wash before the exam
w: Let her shower but place her clothes in a plastic trash bag
Let her shower because her comfort comes before evidence
Ask her to wash her hands only and then change her clothes

items.q: You are dispatched to a rural home for a man with a dog bite to the arm. As you pull into the driveway, the caller yells that the dog is still loose in the yard. What should you do?
items.x: An uncontrolled aggressive animal makes the scene unsafe. The crew stays in the vehicle until the animal is secured, asking the patient to come out only if that can be done safely.
items.a: Stay in the ambulance and request animal control or police
w: Walk quickly from the ambulance to the porch with your jump kit
Use your stretcher as a shield while you move toward the house
Have your partner distract the dog while you go into the house

items.q: You are dispatched to a campground for a 14-year-old bitten on the ankle by a snake. The father says the snake is still under the picnic table next to the boy. What is the best action?
items.x: The snake is a continuing hazard, so the patient is moved away before care. Killing or capturing it risks more bites; a photo from a safe distance is enough if identification is needed.
items.a: Move the boy away from the table, then assess him
w: Kill the snake and bring it for identification
Assess the boy in place while a partner watches the snake
Photograph the snake up close before moving the boy

items.q: You are first on scene where a school bus collided with a pickup truck. Many children are crying, several are walking around, and the pickup driver is not moving. What is your first priority as the first arriving unit?
items.x: At a multiple-casualty incident, the first unit establishes command, estimates the number of patients, requests resources early, and begins triage. Stopping to treat one patient leaves everyone else unassessed.
items.a: Size up, request more units, and begin triage
w: Begin care on the unmoving pickup driver
Treat the children who are crying loudest
Load the most injured child and transport

items.q: At an MCI, you ask everyone who can walk to move to a marked area by the fire engine. Twelve patients walk there. Using START triage, how are they categorized?
items.x: In START, patients who can walk are initially triaged as minor (green) and moved to one place, but they must be reassessed because some may deteriorate.
items.a: Minor (green), with reassessment later
w: Delayed (yellow), pending secondary triage
Immediate (red), since they may worsen
Their category is not assigned until all are assessed

items.q: During START triage, an adult is breathing at 36 breaths per minute. Radial pulse is present and he follows commands. What is his triage category?
items.x: In START, a respiratory rate over 30 in an adult places the patient in the immediate category without further assessment.
items.a: Immediate (red)
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

items.q: During START triage, a woman is breathing 24 times per minute, follows commands, and cannot walk. Her radial pulse is absent. What is her triage category?
items.x: In START, an absent radial pulse (or capillary refill over 2 seconds) indicates poor perfusion and makes the patient immediate, even if breathing and mental status are acceptable.
items.a: Immediate (red)
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

items.q: During START triage, a man with a leg injury cannot walk. He breathes 20 times per minute, has a radial pulse, and correctly follows commands. What is his triage category?
items.x: A non-ambulatory patient with a respiratory rate of 30 or less, a radial pulse, and the ability to follow commands is delayed in START.
items.a: Delayed (yellow)
w: Immediate (red)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

items.q: During START triage, an unresponsive adult is not breathing. You reposition the airway and she begins breathing at 12 per minute. What should you do?
items.x: In START, a patient who begins breathing after airway repositioning is immediate. The triager tags and moves on rather than staying to provide prolonged care.
items.a: Tag her immediate (red) and move on
w: Tag her expectant (black) and move on
Stay with her and assist ventilations
Tag her delayed (yellow) and move on

items.q: During JumpSTART triage at a daycare fire, a 3-year-old is not breathing after airway positioning but has a palpable pulse. What should you do next?
items.x: JumpSTART recognizes that apnea in children is often respiratory. An apneic child with a pulse receives 5 rescue breaths; if breathing resumes, the child is immediate, and if not, expectant.
items.a: Give 5 rescue breaths, then reassess breathing
w: Tag her expectant (black) and move to the next child
Begin CPR and stay with her until she is transported
Tag her immediate (red) without any breaths

items.q: You arrive at a two-car crash. The driver of one car says she was alone, but you see an empty child safety seat in the back with a sippy cup on the floor. What should you do?
items.x: Determining the number of patients is part of scene size-up. An empty car seat with signs of recent use suggests a possibly ejected or wandering child who must be searched for promptly.
items.a: Ask about a child and search for another patient
w: Finish treating the driver, then ask about the seat
Take her word and note the car seat in your report
Ask police to look for a child when they arrive

items.q: You are dispatched to a crash on a rural two-lane road. A pickup rolled several times, and the unrestrained driver was ejected. He is confused, and the nearest trauma center is a 60-minute drive away. Which resource should you request early?
items.x: An ejection with altered mental status is a high-risk mechanism. With a long ground transport, early air medical activation shortens time to definitive trauma care.
items.a: Air medical transport
w: A second BLS ambulance
A heavy rescue for extrication
A police crash reconstruction unit

items.q: You are guiding an air medical helicopter to a landing zone in a field. The aircraft has landed and the rotors are still turning. How should you approach the aircraft?
items.x: The tail rotor and the downhill side are danger zones. Approach only when the flight crew signals, from the front in the pilot's view, and keep equipment low.
items.a: From the front, in view of the pilot, only when signaled
w: From the rear, so you do not distract the pilot
From the uphill side with the stretcher raised
Any time, as long as you crouch below the rotors

items.q: You arrive at a car that struck a tree. The driver is trapped with her legs pinned under the dashboard, and the front airbags did not deploy. Which action improves crew safety?
items.x: Undeployed airbags can deploy unexpectedly and injure anyone in their path. Rescuers stay out of the deployment zone and request fire/rescue for extrication and vehicle stabilization.
items.a: Avoid the airbag deployment path and request fire/rescue
w: Disconnect the battery yourself, then work at the wheel
Reach across the steering wheel to hold her head still
Work in front of the dash, since undeployed bags are inert

items.q: You are assessing a driver with neck pain who is still seated in his car, not trapped, when you notice smoke and then flames coming from the engine compartment. Fire is still 5 minutes out. What is the best action?
items.x: When an immediate threat such as fire develops, an emergency move takes priority over full spinal precautions. Waiting or using time-consuming devices could cost the patient and crew their lives.
items.a: Perform an emergency move and get him out now
w: Apply a collar before moving him from the car
Continue assessment until fire arrives
Use a short spine board to remove him slowly

items.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a 52-year-old man pinned under an overturned tractor. He is conscious and in pain. Bystanders are trying to lift the tractor with a farm jack. What is the best size-up action?
items.x: An unstable vehicle can shift and crush rescuers or the patient. Lifting requires trained crews with proper cribbing and equipment, so EMS stops unsafe efforts and requests fire/rescue.
items.a: Request fire/rescue and have bystanders stop
w: Help the bystanders so the lift is quick and even
Have them lift slowly while you slide him out
Give oxygen under the tractor while they lift it

items.q: At a construction site, a worker is buried to his waist after a trench wall collapsed. Coworkers are digging him out by hand from inside the trench. What is the best action?
items.x: Trenches often collapse again, and machinery vibration increases the risk. Rescuers stay out, nearby equipment is shut down, and a trench rescue team is requested to shore the walls.
items.a: Get everyone out and request trench rescue
w: Enter the trench to assess his airway and breathing
Have coworkers keep digging while you request rescue
Use the site excavator to clear soil from around him

items.q: You arrive at a city park in winter. A 9-year-old boy has fallen through the ice of a pond about 30 feet from shore and is clinging to the edge. What is the best action?
items.x: The rescue sequence is reach, throw, row, go. Rescuers without ice rescue training and equipment stay on shore and request a specialized team; walking or crawling onto ice risks a second victim.
items.a: Reach or throw from shore and request water rescue
w: Crawl out flat on the ice to spread your weight
Walk out with a rope tied around your waist
Send a bystander out with a ladder to reach him

items.q: During a heavy rainstorm, you see a car stalled in fast-moving water over a low-water crossing. The driver is on the roof waving. What should you do?
items.x: Moving water just a few inches deep can knock a person down, and a little more can float a vehicle. Responders without swift water training stay out and request a specialized team.
items.a: Stay out of the water and request swift water rescue
w: Wade in tethered to your partner to reach the car
Drive the ambulance through the water to reach him
Tell him to swim to you while you hold a rope

items.q: You are dispatched to a clinic for a 45-year-old man with a 3-week cough, night sweats, weight loss, and blood in his sputum. What PPE is most appropriate?
items.x: These findings suggest tuberculosis, an airborne disease. Providers wear a fit-tested N95 respirator, and the patient wears a surgical mask if tolerated to reduce spread.
items.a: An N95 respirator for you, and a surgical mask on him
w: A surgical mask for you, and an N95 respirator on him
Gloves only, since he is not actively bleeding
A gown and gloves, without any mask or respirator

items.q: You are dispatched to a home for a 58-year-old man vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. What PPE should you put on before contact?
items.x: Splashing body fluids require gloves and eye and face protection, with a gown if heavy soiling is likely. An N95 is for airborne pathogens and does not protect against splashes to the eyes.
items.a: Gloves plus eye and face protection
w: Gloves only, changed after patient care
Gloves and an N95 respirator only
Gloves and a gown, without face protection

items.q: You are dispatched to a home for a woman in active labor. She is crowning on arrival. What is the most appropriate PPE?
items.x: Childbirth involves large amounts of blood and amniotic fluid that can splash, so full standard precautions with gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection are appropriate.
items.a: Gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection
w: Gloves only, since birth is not an exposure
A mask and gloves, without eye protection
An N95 respirator and gown, without gloves

items.q: You are dispatched to a bank mailroom. A worker opened an envelope containing white powder, and three workers nearby have mild cough. What is the best action?
items.x: An unknown powder is a possible hazardous or biological agent. Exposed people are isolated to prevent spread, and hazmat manages decontamination; EMS should not handle the substance or contaminate its unit.
items.a: Isolate the area, keep people in place, and request hazmat
w: Move the workers outside to fresh air and treat them there
Bag the envelope in gloves and a mask, then request hazmat
Evacuate the building through the mailroom and request police

items.q: You arrive at a rental house for a 30-year-old man with a burn on his hand. Inside you smell a strong chemical odor and see glass jars, tubing, and camp stove fuel on the kitchen table. What is the best action?
items.x: These findings suggest a clandestine drug lab, which can contain toxic, flammable, or explosive chemicals. The crew withdraws, removes the patient if it can be done safely, and requests law enforcement and hazmat without touching anything.
items.a: Leave with the patient if possible and request police and hazmat
w: Treat him in the kitchen while your partner opens the windows
Move the jars to the sink so no one knocks them over
Turn off the stove and remove the tubing before assessing him

items.q: You are dispatched to a farm for a 28-year-old field worker with vomiting and excessive drooling. His clothing is wet with a pesticide sprayed an hour ago. What should happen before he is loaded into the ambulance?
items.x: A contaminated patient can expose the crew and ambulance. Gross decontamination by removing clothing and washing the skin, done with proper PPE, comes before transport.
items.a: Remove his clothing and decontaminate him
w: Give oxygen and load him to save time
Wrap him in a sheet to contain the pesticide
Rinse his hands and face, then load him

items.q: You are treating a 19-year-old man with a seizure at an outdoor concert. A crowd gathers, and several people begin shouting and shoving toward your crew. What is the best action?
items.x: When a crowd becomes hostile, the scene is no longer safe. Moving quickly to the ambulance and leaving the area while requesting law enforcement protects both the crew and the patient.
items.a: Move him to the ambulance quickly and request police
w: Finish the assessment in place and request police
Ask the crowd to step back and continue care
Have bystanders form a ring around your crew

items.q: You are dispatched to a high school football game for a player who was hit and is now lying motionless on the field. His teammates say he hit the other player helmet first. What does the mechanism suggest?
items.x: A helmet-first collision transmits axial load to the cervical spine. The mechanism alone raises suspicion for spinal injury, guiding precautions before moving him.
items.a: Possible spinal injury needing motion restriction
w: A probable concussion needing only a sideline check
A stinger injury that resolves without any precautions
Heat exhaustion needing cooling and oral fluids

items.q: You are dispatched for an 81-year-old woman found at the bottom of her stairs. She says she "got dizzy and then fell." How should you approach her care?
items.x: In older adults, a fall may be caused by a medical problem such as an arrhythmia or stroke. Both the mechanism of injury and the nature of illness must be evaluated.
items.a: Assess both the injuries and the cause of the dizziness
w: Focus on the injuries, since trauma takes priority
Focus on the dizziness, since she is awake and talking
Focus on home hazards, since most falls are trips

items.q: You are dispatched to an apartment for a 6-year-old with a broken arm. The parents give different stories about how it happened, and you notice bruises in different stages of healing on his back. Which action is most appropriate?
items.x: Inconsistent stories and multiple bruises in different stages suggest abuse. The EMT provides care, documents facts without accusing, and reports as required by law; confronting caregivers can make the scene unsafe.
items.a: Treat him, document objectively, and report per local law
w: Ask the parents directly whether they hurt him
Treat him and report only if the hospital agrees
Treat him and document your opinion that it is abuse

items.q: You are dispatched to a public pool for a lifeguard who collapsed in the pump room. Other staff report a strong chlorine smell and coughing near that room. What is the best action?
items.x: Chlorine gas is a respiratory hazard, and a collapsed person in the room confirms dangerous levels. EMS stays out and requests responders with SCBA; a surgical mask provides no protection against gas.
items.a: Keep everyone away and request fire and hazmat
w: Enter the pump room with a surgical mask to remove him
Open the pump room door wide to vent the gas out
Turn off the chlorinator and then remove the lifeguard

items.q: You are dispatched to a two-story home that partially collapsed after a gas explosion. A woman is calling for help from under debris inside. What is the best action?
