items.x: A partly collapsed structure with a gas leak risks further collapse and explosion. EMS stays out and requests fire, the gas utility, and structural collapse rescue; shutting off the gas does not make the structure stable.
items.a: Stay out and request fire, the gas utility, and collapse rescue
w: Enter carefully to reach her and assess her airway first
Shut off the gas meter and then go in to get her out
Clear debris from the doorway to make a path in to her

items.q: A CNA is helping four residents who all take warfarin. Which finding should be described to the nurse first?
items.x: Dark tarry stool suggests bleeding into the gut, which is a much larger bleed than the bruising and gum oozing that are common on warfarin. The CNA describes what was seen; the nurse decides what happens next.
items.a: Dark, tarry stool in the bedpan
w: A new bruise on the shin from a walker
Pink-tinged gums after tooth brushing
A brief nosebleed that has now stopped

items.q: A resident on warfarin has started eating a large spinach salad every day. Which part of this does the nurse need to know about?
items.x: Warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, so a steady vitamin K intake keeps the INR steady. It is a sudden large change in intake, not greens themselves, that shifts the level.
items.a: The large daily amount of a vitamin K food
w: The calories in the dressing she adds to it
The fiber content of the raw greens
The iron in the dark green leaves

items.q: While shaving a resident who takes warfarin, the CNA should use:
items.x: Electric razors lower the risk of cuts and bleeding in residents on blood thinners.
items.a: An electric razor
w: A new disposable razor
A safety razor with a guard
A multi-blade cartridge razor

items.q: A resident on apixaban has gums that bleed heavily during mouth care. The CNA should:
items.x: Apixaban (Eliquis) is a blood thinner. Bleeding gums should be reported, and a soft toothbrush should be used.
items.a: Stop, switch to a soft brush, and tell the nurse
w: Switch to a soft brush and chart it at shift end
Finish with foam swabs and recheck gums tomorrow
Rinse with cool water and keep brushing gently

items.q: A resident on apixaban fell and hit her head two hours ago and says she feels fine. Which new finding should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
items.x: A rising level of drowsiness points to bleeding inside the skull, which an anticoagulant such as apixaban makes more likely and which can appear hours after a fall that looked minor.
items.a: She is harder to wake than she was at lunch
w: She has a small bruise forming on her forehead
She says her neck feels stiff after the fall
She asks for acetaminophen for a headache

items.q: Two residents have black stools. One takes daily aspirin and one takes a ferrous sulfate tablet. What should the CNA tell the nurse?
items.x: Iron can darken stool harmlessly, but aspirin can cause stomach bleeding, which also looks black and tarry. The CNA cannot tell them apart at the bedside, so both get described to the nurse.
items.a: Both stools, because color alone does not sort out the cause
w: Only the aspirin resident, since iron always darkens the stool
Only the iron resident, since aspirin does not affect stool
Neither, because black stool is expected with both pills

items.q: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is commonly used to:
items.x: Acetaminophen is a pain reliever and fever reducer.
items.a: Relieve mild pain and reduce fever
w: Relieve pain and reduce joint swelling
Reduce fever and prevent blood clots
Relieve severe pain and aid sleep

items.q: A resident is scheduled for acetaminophen and also takes hydrocodone-acetaminophen for pain. Why does the nurse want to know about every dose the resident gets?
items.x: Many combination pain pills contain acetaminophen, and the total from all sources is capped at about 3000 to 4000 mg a day in adults because higher totals injure the liver.
items.a: The two products add up toward a daily acetaminophen limit
w: Acetaminophen cancels out the pain relief from the hydrocodone
Taking both at once raises the risk of stomach bleeding
Acetaminophen makes hydrocodone leave the body faster

items.q: Metformin is used to treat:
items.x: Metformin lowers blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes.
items.a: Type 2 diabetes
w: Type 1 diabetes
Low blood sugar
High cholesterol

items.q: A resident who started metformin has loose stools and an upset stomach. The CNA should:
items.x: Stomach upset and diarrhea are common metformin side effects and should be reported. The CNA does not change medicines.
items.a: Report both symptoms to the nurse promptly
w: Offer only clear liquids until it settles
Chart the stools and report in the morning
Reassure her it is expected and will pass

items.q: A resident on insulin is shaky, sweaty, and confused before lunch. The CNA should first:
items.x: These are signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). The CNA should get the nurse right away and follow the care plan.
items.a: Stay with the resident and call the nurse
w: Help the resident to the dining room early
Check the resident's pulse and recheck later
Get the resident a diet soda from the pantry

items.q: The care plan for a resident on insulin says to give 4 ounces of juice for signs of low blood sugar. The resident is sweaty and shaky but alert. The CNA should:
items.x: The CNA follows the care plan for a hypoglycemia snack and reports to the nurse. The CNA never gives insulin.
items.a: Give the juice per the care plan and tell the nurse
w: Give the juice per the care plan and chart it at shift end
Give a sugar-free drink instead and then tell the nurse
Give the juice and send the resident on to the dining room

items.q: A resident was given lispro insulin and then ate none of lunch. About how soon would the CNA expect signs of low blood sugar?
items.x: Lispro is rapid-acting: it starts working in roughly 15 minutes and peaks about 1 hour after the injection, so a skipped meal shows up quickly, unlike long-acting insulins that peak many hours later.
items.a: Within about 15 to 60 minutes
w: Within about 6 to 8 hours
Within about 10 to 12 hours
Within about 18 to 24 hours

items.q: A resident who gets NPH insulin is very hard to wake at 3 a.m. and is sweating. The CNA should:
items.x: Low blood sugar can happen overnight with intermediate-acting insulin. Trouble waking is an emergency.
items.a: Call the nurse to the room right away
w: Change the damp gown and recheck soon
Try to give juice by mouth right away
Note it for the morning nurse's report

items.q: Glipizide is a diabetes pill that can cause:
items.x: Glipizide makes the pancreas release more insulin, so low blood sugar is a key risk, especially if meals are missed.
items.a: Low blood sugar
w: High blood sugar
Low blood pressure
A slow heart rate

items.q: A resident who ate only a few bites of breakfast takes glipizide, and her roommate who also ate little takes metformin. Which resident should the CNA mention to the nurse first, and why?
items.x: Glipizide makes the pancreas release insulin whether or not food was eaten, so a missed meal can cause hypoglycemia. Metformin rarely causes low blood sugar by itself.
items.a: The glipizide resident, because that pill can drop blood sugar on its own
w: The metformin resident, because metformin also lowers blood sugar on its own
The glipizide resident, because glipizide needs food to be absorbed
Neither, because both pills are safe when a meal is skipped

items.q: The CNA checks a resident's blood sugar as delegated and gets a reading of 52. The CNA should:
items.x: A low reading must be reported right away. Only trained, delegated CNAs check glucose, and they always report results.
items.a: Report the result to the nurse at once
w: Write it down and report it at shift change
Recheck it in two hours before telling anyone
Give a snack and report it only if still low

items.q: A resident on lisinopril says the room spins when she first stands. What should the CNA measure and report to make this useful to the nurse?
items.x: Orthostatic readings show the drop that happens on standing. A fall of about 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic on standing is the finding the nurse is looking for.
items.a: Blood pressure and pulse lying down and then standing
w: Blood pressure in both arms while she is sitting quietly
Pulse before and after she walks down the hall
Temperature and pulse once she is back in bed

items.q: Lisinopril is used to treat:
items.x: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure and protects the heart and kidneys.
items.a: High blood pressure
w: Low blood pressure
A fast heart rate
High cholesterol

items.q: A resident on lisinopril has sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. The CNA should:
items.x: Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue (angioedema) is a rare but dangerous lisinopril reaction that can block the airway.
items.a: Call for the nurse to come immediately
w: Offer ice chips and recheck in a while
Sit the resident up and chart it later
Ask if the resident ate something new

items.q: Amlodipine is a medicine for:
items.x: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure.
items.a: High blood pressure
w: High cholesterol
A slow heart rate
Fluid in the legs

items.q: A resident on amlodipine has swelling in both ankles. Which additional observation would make the nurse most concerned about something beyond the amlodipine?
items.x: Amlodipine commonly causes ankle edema by dilating blood vessels in the legs, without fluid in the lungs. Breathlessness lying flat points to fluid overload from the heart instead.
items.a: New shortness of breath when lying flat
w: Shoes feeling snug by the end of the day
Sock marks on both lower legs at bedtime
Swelling that is equal on the right and left

items.q: A CNA takes vital signs before the morning metoprolol. Which set should be reported to the nurse before the dose is given?
items.x: Metoprolol slows conduction through the heart, and doses are commonly held for a rate under 60. A rate of 48 crosses that line even though the blood pressure looks fine.
items.a: Pulse 48 and regular, blood pressure 118/70
w: Pulse 72 and regular, blood pressure 128/78
Pulse 88 and regular, blood pressure 140/86
Pulse 64 and regular, blood pressure 110/68

items.q: A resident on furosemide will likely need to:
items.x: Furosemide (Lasix) is a water pill that increases urine output, so toileting help is often needed.
items.a: Use the bathroom more often
w: Rest in bed after each dose
Avoid potassium-rich foods
Be weighed just once a month

items.q: The care plan for a resident on furosemide says daily weights. The CNA should weigh the resident:
items.x: Daily weights must be consistent (same time, scale, and clothing) so changes in fluid can be seen.
items.a: At the same time each day on the same scale
w: At the same time each day on any free scale
At any time of day as long as the scale is the same
On the same scale whenever the legs look swollen

items.q: A resident on daily weights for furosemide weighed 162 pounds yesterday. Which weight today should the CNA report to the nurse?
items.x: A gain of about 2 to 3 pounds in a day is roughly 1 to 1.5 liters of retained fluid, which is the usual threshold for reporting. Small up-and-down changes of a pound are ordinary.
items.a: 165 pounds
w: 163 pounds
162 pounds
161 pounds

items.q: A resident on furosemide is on intake and output (I&O). The CNA should:
items.x: Accurate I&O helps the nurse see whether the water pill is working and if the resident is dehydrated.
items.a: Measure and record all fluids taken in and urine passed
w: Measure and record urine passed but only drinks at meals
Record all fluids taken in and estimate the urine passed
Measure and record everything except soups and gelatin

items.q: Bumetanide, like furosemide, is a:
items.x: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that removes extra fluid, so I&O and daily weights matter.
items.a: Water pill (diuretic)
w: Heart pill (beta blocker)
Potassium pill (supplement)
Blood thinner (anticoagulant)

items.q: A resident with heart failure is on daily weights. Which finding tells the nurse the most about fluid building up?
items.x: Daily weight is the most sensitive measure of fluid gain and changes before swelling or breathlessness is obvious; 4 pounds is about 2 liters of fluid.
items.a: A 4 pound weight gain over two days
w: Reporting feeling tired in the afternoon
Needing two pillows instead of one at night
Ankles that look puffy after sitting up

items.q: Spironolactone is a water pill that can raise potassium. A CNA should report:
items.x: High potassium can cause weakness and heart rhythm problems. Report these signs.
items.a: Muscle weakness or an irregular pulse
w: Frequent urination in the morning
A dry cough or a stuffy nose
Constipation or a dry mouth

items.q: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a water pill. It is best for residents to take it in the morning so that:
items.x: Diuretics increase urination, so morning dosing helps prevent nighttime trips to the bathroom and falls.
items.a: They are not up at night to urinate
w: It is absorbed best with breakfast
Their blood pressure peaks at noon
Their potassium stays up overnight

items.q: Digoxin is a heart medicine. A CNA should report if the resident has:
items.x: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and vision changes can be signs of digoxin toxicity.
items.a: Nausea, poor appetite, or seeing yellow-green halos
w: Dry mouth, thirst, or passing more urine than usual
A stuffy nose, sneezing, or itchy and watery eyes
Sore gums, a metallic taste, or hair that is thinning

items.q: The nurse asks the CNA to count an apical or radial pulse before the resident's digoxin. The CNA should:
items.x: Counting a full minute is accurate and important because digoxin can slow or change the heart rhythm.
items.a: Count for one full minute and report it
w: Count for 30 seconds and double it
Count for 15 seconds and multiply by four
Count for one minute after the dose is given

items.q: Potassium chloride is given to residents who:
items.x: Diuretics like furosemide can lower potassium, so a potassium supplement is often added.
items.a: Have low potassium, often from water pills
w: Have low sodium, often from drinking water
Have high potassium, often from kidney disease
Have low calcium, often from thin bones

items.q: A resident says the potassium chloride tablet is too large to swallow. What should the CNA tell the nurse about why this matters?
items.x: Most oral potassium chloride is extended release, and crushing it dumps the whole dose onto the stomach lining and can cause ulceration. The nurse or pharmacy can switch to a liquid or powder form.
items.a: The tablet is extended release and cannot simply be crushed
w: The tablet can be chewed but must not be swallowed whole
The tablet must dissolve under the tongue to work properly
The tablet should be split and taken on an empty stomach

items.q: Four residents on atorvastatin report aches. Which complaint should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
items.x: Statin muscle injury is symmetrical and affects the large muscles, and dark urine suggests myoglobin from breaking down muscle, which can damage the kidneys. One-sided aches after activity point to strain.
items.a: Aching weakness in both thighs with dark brown urine
w: Soreness in one shoulder after a physical therapy session
Stiff knees that loosen up after walking in the morning
A sore calf the day after a long walk outdoors

items.q: A resident asks for grapefruit juice at breakfast. She takes simvastatin and her roommate takes pravastatin. Which should the CNA raise with the nurse?
items.x: Grapefruit blocks the CYP3A4 enzyme that clears simvastatin, so levels rise and muscle injury becomes more likely. Pravastatin is not cleared by that enzyme.
items.a: The simvastatin resident, because grapefruit raises its blood level
w: Both residents, because grapefruit blocks every statin in the same way
The pravastatin resident, because grapefruit weakens that drug
Neither, because grapefruit only matters with blood thinners

items.q: Levothyroxine is used to treat:
items.x: Levothyroxine (Synthroid) replaces thyroid hormone when the thyroid is underactive.
items.a: An underactive thyroid
w: An overactive thyroid
Low blood sugar
Weak, thin bones

items.q: After meals, a resident with heartburn should be positioned:
items.x: Staying upright after meals helps keep stomach acid from coming back up.
items.a: Sitting upright for at least 30 minutes
w: Lying on the right side for 30 minutes
Lying flat with the legs raised on pillows
Reclined all the way back for 30 minutes

items.q: Pantoprazole is in the same group as omeprazole and is used to:
items.x: Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that lowers stomach acid.
items.a: Reduce stomach acid
w: Coat the stomach lining
Speed stomach emptying
Relieve nausea quickly

items.q: Famotidine (Pepcid) is used to:
items.x: Famotidine blocks acid production and treats heartburn and ulcers.
items.a: Lower stomach acid
w: Soften hard stool
Stop loose stools
Relieve nausea

items.q: Docusate is a stool softener. The CNA can help it work by:
items.x: Stool softeners pull water into stool; enough fluid makes them work better.
items.a: Offering fluids as allowed by the care plan
w: Offering it with milk at the bedtime snack
Keeping the resident resting after the dose
Limiting fiber so the stool stays small

items.q: A resident on docusate has not had a bowel movement in 4 days. The CNA should:
items.x: The CNA tracks and reports bowel movements. Treatment is decided by the nurse.
items.a: Report the lack of stools to the nurse today
w: Offer prune juice and wait a few more days
Chart it and keep giving extra fluids
Ask the resident to try again after supper

items.q: A resident on senna has cramping and many watery stools today. The CNA should:
items.x: Too many loose stools can lead to dehydration. The CNA reports it so the nurse can review the laxative.
items.a: Report the diarrhea to the nurse
w: Offer extra fluids and chart it later
Give bananas and rice at the next meal
Tell her cramping is expected with senna

items.q: Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX) is a powder that is:
items.x: MiraLAX is mixed with liquid and draws water into the bowel to soften stool.
items.a: Mixed in a drink to treat constipation
w: Mixed in a drink to treat loose stools
Mixed in a drink to replace potassium
Mixed in food to thicken thin liquids

items.q: Milk of Magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) is commonly used for:
items.x: Magnesium hydroxide is a laxative and antacid.
items.a: Constipation or upset stomach
w: Diarrhea or stomach cramps
Low calcium or weak bones
Nausea or motion sickness

items.q: Bisacodyl is a laxative that may come as a suppository. A CNA should:
items.x: Inserting medicated suppositories is medication administration and is usually outside the CNA role.
items.a: Not insert it unless state rules and training allow
w: Insert it only when the resident asks for it directly
Insert it as long as the nurse is busy with others
Leave it at the bedside for the resident to insert

items.q: A resident on lactulose has frequent soft stools. The CNA should especially:
items.x: Frequent stools can break down skin. Good perineal care and reporting skin changes help prevent pressure sores.
items.a: Give good perineal care and watch the skin
w: Limit fluids until the stools are firmer
Double the briefs to protect the linen
Offer rice and bananas to firm the stool

items.q: A resident who takes oxycodone often has which bowel problem?
items.x: Opioids slow the bowels and commonly cause constipation. Track and report bowel movements.
items.a: Constipation
w: Diarrhea
Black stool
Incontinence

items.q: A resident on oxycodone is very sleepy, hard to wake, and breathing 8 times a minute. The CNA should:
items.x: Slow breathing and trouble waking are signs of opioid overdose, a medical emergency.
items.a: Call the nurse immediately and stay
w: Raise the head of the bed and recheck soon
Shake the resident awake and offer fluids
Chart the rate and tell the nurse at rounds

items.q: A resident on hydrocodone-acetaminophen (Norco) should be watched for:
items.x: Hydrocodone is an opioid. Sleepiness, dizziness, falls, and constipation are common concerns.
items.a: Drowsiness, dizziness, and constipation
w: Restlessness, diarrhea, and fast breathing
Stomach bleeding, bruising, and black stool
Dry cough, ankle swelling, and a slow pulse

items.q: A resident waiting for a dose of hydrocodone says the pain is 8 out of 10. Which description would be most useful to the nurse?
items.x: A location, a quality and a time course let the nurse judge whether this is the expected pain or something new, such as a fracture or an abdomen that has become rigid. A number alone does not.
items.a: Where the pain is, what it feels like, and when it started
w: That the resident seems to be in a great deal of discomfort
That the resident has asked about pain twice today
That the resident rates the pain higher than yesterday

items.q: A resident on morphine has pinpoint pupils and shallow breathing. The CNA should:
items.x: Small pupils, slow or shallow breathing, and sleepiness are signs of opioid overdose.
items.a: Get the nurse to the room right away
w: Raise the head of the bed and recheck
Wake the resident and offer some fluids
Count the breathing again in an hour

items.q: A resident wears a fentanyl patch. Which thing noticed during the bath should be mentioned to the nurse because it can raise the amount of drug absorbed?
items.x: Heat increases blood flow and the rate drug crosses the skin, so a heating pad over a fentanyl patch can cause a dangerous rise in absorption. Normal bathing and a 72 hour wear time are expected.
items.a: A heating pad has been left on over the patch site
w: The patch has been in place for about two days
The patch is on the upper back rather than the chest
The resident showered with warm water this morning

items.q: A CNA finds a used fentanyl patch on the bed linen. Why does the CNA handle it with gloves rather than bare fingers?
items.x: A patch is built as a drug reservoir and a good deal of fentanyl remains when it comes off, so skin contact can dose the person handling it. The nurse witnesses disposal.
items.a: A used patch still holds drug that absorbs through skin
w: A used patch has adhesive that irritates bare skin
A used patch carries germs from the resident's skin
A used patch must be counted before it is touched

items.q: A resident has chest pain and asks the CNA to hand over the nitroglycerin bottle on the nightstand. The CNA should:
items.x: Chest pain is an emergency. The CNA stays with the resident and gets the nurse, who handles the medicine.
items.a: Stay and call the nurse right away
w: Hand over the bottle and get the nurse after
Take a set of vital signs before calling anyone
Help the resident lie flat and recheck shortly

items.q: After a resident gets nitroglycerin, the CNA should watch for:
items.x: Nitroglycerin can drop blood pressure and cause headache and dizziness, so help prevent falls.
items.a: Dizziness, headache, or low blood pressure
w: Slow pulse, cough, or high blood pressure
Nausea, drowsiness, or slowed breathing
Shakiness, sweating, or low blood sugar

items.q: Isosorbide mononitrate is taken daily to:
items.x: Long-acting nitrates like isosorbide help prevent angina episodes.
items.a: Prevent chest pain
w: Relieve chest pain fast
Prevent blood clots
Lower cholesterol

items.q: After an albuterol treatment, a resident says his heart is racing and his hands are shaky. The CNA should:
items.x: A fast heart rate and shakiness are common albuterol side effects. Report them to the nurse.
items.a: Report both symptoms to the nurse now
w: Have him rest and recheck him at lunch
Offer a second puff to open the lungs
Tell him it is expected and move on

items.q: A resident with COPD uses tiotropium every morning and also has an albuterol inhaler. He is more short of breath than usual. What is true about the tiotropium?
items.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting bronchodilator taken once a day to prevent symptoms; albuterol is the rescue inhaler that works in minutes. Knowing which is which tells the nurse what the resident needs now.
items.a: It is a daily maintenance inhaler, not a rescue inhaler
w: It should be given a second time whenever breathing worsens
It works within a minute or two of being inhaled
It replaces the albuterol inhaler once started

items.q: A resident uses a steroid inhaler (fluticasone). Afterward, the resident should usually:
items.x: Rinsing after inhaled steroids helps prevent thrush (a yeast infection of the mouth).
items.a: Rinse the mouth and spit
w: Rinse the mouth and swallow
Avoid water for an hour
Use the albuterol next

items.q: Which is the most important oxygen safety rule?
items.x: Oxygen feeds fire. No smoking, candles, or flames near oxygen, and secure tanks upright.
items.a: No smoking or open flames near oxygen
w: Keep the tank at least half full at all times
Change the nasal cannula at every shift
Keep the tubing off the floor at all times

items.q: A resident on 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula is more short of breath. Which observation should the CNA report along with the breathlessness?
items.x: A kink stops flow no matter what the flowmeter reads, and checking the delivery path is within the CNA role. Prongs curve down by design, and a raised head of the bed helps rather than hurts.
items.a: The tubing is kinked under the wheel of the recliner
w: The resident wears the cannula with the prongs curved down
The concentrator has been running since early this morning
The head of the bed is raised about 30 degrees

items.q: A resident's family member lights a candle in a room where oxygen is in use. The CNA should:
items.x: Open flames near oxygen can cause a fire. The candle must be put out.
items.a: Ask them to put it out right away and explain why
w: Move the candle across the room and explain why
Turn the oxygen off until the candle burns out
Let the nurse know about it at the next rounds

items.q: Where should a portable oxygen tank be kept?
items.x: Tanks should be secured so they cannot fall and be damaged.
items.a: Secured upright in a holder or cart
w: Standing free in a corner of the room
Propped upright against the bed frame
Laid on the bed beside the resident

items.q: A resident on donepezil has nausea, diarrhea, and a slow pulse. The CNA should:
items.x: Donepezil can cause stomach upset and a slow heart rate. These signs should be reported.
items.a: Report these signs to the nurse
w: Offer clear fluids and recheck her later
Chart the stools and tell the day shift
Count the pulse again after she has rested

items.q: Memantine (Namenda) is used to treat:
items.x: Memantine is given for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease.
items.a: Alzheimer's dementia
w: Parkinson's disease
Major depression
Trouble sleeping

items.q: A resident on sertraline says she wants to end her life. The CNA should:
items.x: Any talk of suicide must be reported immediately. The CNA should not leave the resident alone.
items.a: Stay with her and tell the nurse right away
w: Tell the nurse once her morning care is done
Ask her family to come and sit with her
Leave to get the nurse while she rests alone

items.q: A resident recently started an antidepressant (escitalopram). The CNA should report:
items.x: Changes in mood, behavior, or new confusion should be reported, especially when a medicine is new.
items.a: New confusion, falls, or mood changes
w: No lift in mood after the first two days
A better appetite at the evening meal
Wanting to join the afternoon activity

items.q: Mirtazapine may be given to an older resident for depression. A common side effect is:
items.x: Mirtazapine often causes drowsiness and weight gain, so watch for falls.
items.a: Sleepiness and increased appetite
w: Insomnia and decreased appetite
Diarrhea and steady weight loss
Tremor and a fast, pounding pulse

items.q: A resident takes trazodone at bedtime for sleep. The CNA should:
items.x: Trazodone can cause drowsiness and dizziness, raising the fall risk at night.
items.a: Use fall precautions if the resident gets up at night
w: Raise all four side rails so the resident stays in bed
Wake the resident every two hours to check alertness
Keep the room fully lit so the resident sleeps lightly

items.q: An 84 year old resident was started on lorazepam yesterday. Which change should the CNA describe to the nurse first?
items.x: New unsteadiness is the finding that predicts a hip fracture, and benzodiazepine effects are stronger and last longer in older adults. Sleeping a little longer and less anxiety are expected effects.
items.a: Unsteady walking with two near falls today
w: Sleeping about an hour longer this morning
Asking for help to the bathroom at night
Feeling less worried than she did last week

items.q: A resident who takes alprazolam is drowsy at breakfast and keeps nodding off with food in her mouth. Which risk should the CNA act on first?
items.x: A sedated resident cannot protect her airway, so aspiration is the immediate danger. Feeding stops and she is positioned upright while the nurse is told about the sedation.
items.a: Choking and aspiration while she is being fed
w: Dry mouth from the medicine at breakfast
Losing weight from a poor appetite over several weeks
Spilling hot coffee on her lap at the table

items.q: A resident takes zolpidem at bedtime. Which observation from the night shift is most important for the CNA to pass on?
items.x: Zolpidem can cause complex sleep behaviors such as walking or eating with no recall, which carry a real injury risk and are a reason the drug is reconsidered. Falling asleep in about 20 minutes is the expected effect.
items.a: Walking in the hall at 2 a.m. with no memory of it
w: Fell asleep about 20 minutes after taking the pill
Slept through the night without getting up
Woke once to use the bathroom and went back to sleep

items.q: Temazepam is a sleeping pill. Because of this medicine, the CNA should:
items.x: Sleeping pills raise fall risk. Keep the bed low, the call light close, and the path lit.
items.a: Keep the call light within reach at night
w: Raise every side rail on the bed at night
Offer extra fluids just before bedtime
Wake the resident every hour for safety

items.q: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is an antipsychotic. The CNA should watch for:
items.x: Quetiapine causes sedation and low blood pressure on standing, increasing fall risk.
items.a: Sleepiness and dizziness when standing
w: Weight loss and low blood sugar readings
Bleeding gums and easy bruising on arms
Loose stools and frequent urination

items.q: A resident on haloperidol has new stiffness, shuffling, and lip smacking. The CNA should:
items.x: Antipsychotics can cause movement side effects. These must be reported.
items.a: Report the movements to the nurse
w: Chart them as part of her dementia
Offer range of motion until they ease
Remind her gently to relax her mouth

items.q: Antipsychotics such as risperidone should never be used in a nursing home to:
items.x: Using medicines to control behavior for staff convenience is a chemical restraint and is not allowed.
items.a: Keep a resident quiet for staff convenience
w: Treat a diagnosed mental illness as ordered
Help with hallucinations that frighten the resident
Treat symptoms that put the resident or others at risk

items.q: Gabapentin is often used for nerve pain. A common side effect is:
items.x: Gabapentin can cause dizziness and drowsiness, raising fall risk in older adults.
items.a: Dizziness and sleepiness
w: Stomach bleeding and heartburn
Trouble sleeping and jitters
A dry cough and hoarseness

items.q: A resident on tamsulosin gets dizzy getting out of bed. The CNA should:
items.x: Tamsulosin can cause low blood pressure on standing. The resident should dangle first and rise slowly.
items.a: Have him sit on the edge of the bed first
w: Have him stand at once and hold the bed rail
Have him drink a glass of water before rising
Have him keep his head down as he stands up

items.q: Oxybutynin is used for an overactive bladder. A CNA might notice:
items.x: Oxybutynin is anticholinergic and often causes dry mouth, constipation, and confusion in older adults.
items.a: Dry mouth and constipation
w: Drooling and loose stools
Sweating and watery eyes
Thirst and more urination

items.q: A resident on prednisone should be watched for:
items.x: Steroids raise blood sugar, weaken the immune system, and can thin the skin.
items.a: Higher blood sugar and infection
w: Lower blood sugar and weight loss
Lower blood pressure and a slow pulse
Higher potassium and loose stools

items.q: A resident started on cephalexin today has a new red, itchy rash on the chest. The CNA should:
items.x: A new rash after starting an antibiotic may be an allergic reaction and must be reported.
items.a: Report the rash to the nurse right away
w: Apply lotion and recheck the rash tomorrow
Chart the rash and report it at shift change
Ask whether she has had this rash before

items.q: A resident on nitrofurantoin has dark brown urine. The CNA should:
items.x: Nitrofurantoin can darken urine, but any color change should be reported so the nurse can check.
items.a: Report the color change to the nurse
w: Offer cranberry juice and recheck later
Chart the output without noting the color
Tell her it means the infection is worse

items.q: A resident on amoxicillin suddenly has hives, wheezing, and a swollen face. The CNA should:
items.x: These are signs of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is an emergency.
items.a: Call for the nurse immediately
w: Offer cool cloths for the itching
Sit the resident up and recheck soon
Ask what the resident ate at lunch

items.q: A resident on ciprofloxacin complains of new pain in the back of the ankle. The CNA should:
items.x: This antibiotic can rarely damage tendons. New tendon pain should be reported.
items.a: Report the ankle pain to the nurse
w: Apply a warm pack and recheck it tomorrow
Have him walk gently to loosen the ankle
Chart it once the antibiotic is finished

items.q: A resident on clindamycin has had several watery, foul smelling stools. Which action by the CNA matters most for keeping it from spreading?
items.x: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol does not kill, so physical removal by washing with soap and running water is what stops transmission. The organism is not spread through the air.
items.a: Washing hands with soap and water after each contact
w: Using the alcohol hand rub between each resident contact
Wearing a surgical mask while in the room
Changing gloves only when they look soiled

items.q: After caring for a resident with C. diff, the CNA should clean hands with:
items.x: Alcohol rubs do not kill C. diff spores. Washing with soap and water removes them.
items.a: Soap and water
w: Alcohol hand rub
A bleach wipe
Water alone

items.q: Nystatin is used to treat:
items.x: Nystatin is an antifungal used for thrush and yeast infections of the skin.
items.a: Yeast (fungal) infections such as thrush
w: Bacterial infections such as strep throat
Viral infections such as cold sores
Dry mouth caused by other medicines

items.q: The nurse has just given a resident nystatin oral suspension for thrush. What should the CNA do next?
items.x: Nystatin works by touching the fungus directly, so it is swished and held in the mouth and food and drink are kept back for about 30 minutes to keep from washing it away.
items.a: Hold food and fluids for about 30 minutes afterward
w: Offer a large glass of water to rinse it down
Give mouth care with mouthwash right after
Serve the meal tray while the mouth is still wet with it

items.q: A resident takes alendronate (Fosamax). The CNA should help the resident:
items.x: Alendronate can irritate the esophagus. Staying upright helps it go down and reduces irritation.
items.a: Stay upright for 30 minutes after the pill
w: Lie down for 30 minutes after the pill
Eat breakfast right along with the pill
Take the pill with juice in place of water

items.q: Alendronate is used to treat:
items.x: Alendronate helps strengthen bones and lowers fracture risk.
items.a: Weak, thin bones (osteoporosis)
w: Stiff, sore joints (arthritis)
Low blood calcium (hypocalcemia)
Painful swollen toes (gout)

items.q: Calcium carbonate (Tums) may be given for bones or heartburn. A common side effect is:
items.x: Calcium carbonate often causes constipation, so bowel movements should be tracked.
items.a: Constipation
w: Diarrhea
Drowsiness
Dry cough

items.q: A resident on ferrous sulfate (iron) has dark green-black stools. The CNA should:
items.x: Iron often turns stools dark, but black stools can also mean bleeding. The CNA reports it so the nurse can decide.
items.a: Report the stool color to the nurse
w: Chart it as a normal stool for her
Offer prune juice to lighten the stool
Tell her it means she is bleeding

items.q: Ferrous sulfate is given to treat:
items.x: Iron tablets help the body make red blood cells.
items.a: Low iron (anemia)
w: Low potassium
Low vitamin B12
Low calcium

items.q: Allopurinol is used to prevent:
items.x: Allopurinol lowers uric acid levels to prevent gout flares.
items.a: Gout attacks
w: Osteoarthritis pain
Bladder infections
Muscle spasms

items.q: Meloxicam is an anti-inflammatory pain medicine. The CNA should report:
items.x: Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can cause stomach bleeding, so pain or black stools should be reported.
items.a: Stomach pain or black stools
w: Easier movement of the knees
Taking the pill with a snack
Less swelling in the fingers

items.q: Clopidogrel (Plavix) increases the risk of:
items.x: Clopidogrel keeps platelets from sticking, so watch for bruising and bleeding.
items.a: Bleeding
w: Blood clots
Low blood sugar
Constipation

items.q: A CNA finds a tablet on the floor by a resident's bed. Besides handing it to the nurse, what information is most useful to give?
items.x: The nurse needs to know whose dose may have been missed and roughly when, so the right medication record can be checked. Appearance alone does not identify a tablet reliably.
items.a: Which resident's room it was in and when it was found
w: That the tablet is white and oval in shape
That the floor had been mopped earlier in the same shift
That the resident says she took all her pills

items.q: A CNA finds several pills tucked inside a resident's pillowcase. Which detail is most important for the nurse to hear?
items.x: Pills from several passes means doses have been missed repeatedly, which changes what the nurse checks: a blood pressure that has drifted up, a missed anticoagulant, a skipped antibiotic course.
items.a: Pills from more than one medication pass are present
w: That the pillowcase had been changed the day before that
The resident has a private room on the unit
The resident takes her pills with applesauce

items.q: A resident refuses her morning pills. Which part of the refusal is most important for the CNA to pass along?
items.x: Residents may refuse, and the nurse needs to know which drug was missed and why: a skipped levothyroxine matters differently from a skipped stool softener, and nausea or trouble swallowing can be fixed.
items.a: Which pills she refused and the reason she gave
w: That she refused at about the usual time
That she has refused once before earlier this month
That she was polite about refusing them

items.q: In most states, giving residents their medicines is the job of the:
items.x: CNAs do not give medicines unless they are certified as medication aides under state rules.
items.a: Licensed nurse or certified medication aide
w: CNA with the most years of experience
Any staff member the nurse has asked
Family member who visits at mealtimes

items.q: A nurse asks the CNA to give a resident their pills while the nurse is busy. The CNA is not a medication aide. The CNA should:
items.x: Giving medicines is outside the CNA scope of practice unless the CNA is certified to do so.
items.a: Politely refuse and explain it is outside the CNA role
w: Give the pills since the nurse is the one delegating
Hand the pill cup over and let the resident take them
Give them only if the nurse has already poured them

items.q: A CNA finds a full pill cup on a resident's overbed table an hour after the medication pass. Why does the nurse need to know?
items.x: Medications are charted when they are handed over, so an untouched cup means the record and reality no longer match. The nurse has to find out which drugs were missed before the next dose is due.
items.a: The dose is recorded as given but was not taken
w: The pills will have gone bad sitting in the open air
The cup should have been returned to the cart
The resident may want them later in the day

items.q: A CNA should never crush a resident's pills because:
items.x: Crushing is medication administration, and long-acting or coated pills can become unsafe if crushed.
items.a: CNAs do not handle medicines, and some pills must not be crushed
w: Crushing pills is allowed only when the resident asks for it
Crushed pills always work too slowly to be of any real use
CNAs may crush only vitamins, and those must be mixed in food

items.q: Which sign of an allergic reaction should the CNA report to the nurse right away?
items.x: Hives, swelling, and trouble breathing can mean a dangerous allergic reaction.
items.a: Hives and trouble breathing
w: Mild nausea after a pill
Drowsiness after a dose
Dry mouth and thirst

items.q: A resident is on fall precautions because of a new blood pressure medicine. The CNA should:
items.x: Medicines that lower blood pressure can cause dizziness. Fall precautions keep the resident safe.
items.a: Keep the bed low and help the resident stand slowly
w: Raise all side rails and remind them to stay in bed
Keep the bed high so standing takes less effort
Place the walker across the room to slow them down

items.q: A CNA notices a new side effect after a resident's medicine changes. The CNA should:
items.x: The CNA observes and reports. The nurse and prescriber decide what to do.
items.a: Report it to the nurse and document as directed
w: Document it and watch for a few more days
Ask the resident whether to tell the nurse
Tell the family so they can call the doctor

items.q: A nurse delegates several tasks to a CNA. Which one is within the CNA role?
items.x: CNAs measure, observe, record and report. Interpreting the reading, holding a dose and teaching about medication are nursing judgment; the CNA's number is what the nurse acts on.
items.a: Recording a blood pressure before an antihypertensive dose
w: Judging whether that blood pressure is safe for the next dose
Deciding to hold the dose when the reading is low
Teaching the resident why the dose was held today

items.q: A resident on several medicines is suddenly confused this afternoon after being clear at breakfast. Which quick check is within the CNA role and most useful to the nurse?
items.x: An abrupt change over hours is delirium rather than dementia, and low blood sugar, fever and low oxygen are the fast reversible causes. Reading the record and judging the cause belong to the nurse.
items.a: A set of vital signs and a delegated blood glucose
w: A review of the medication record for new drugs
A judgment about whether this is dementia worsening
A call to the family to ask about her usual behavior

items.q: The best way for a CNA to help prevent constipation in a resident on pain medicine is to:
items.x: Fluids, fiber, and activity help prevent opioid constipation. The CNA does not give laxatives.
items.a: Offer fluids and high-fiber foods as allowed
w: Offer low-fiber foods and extra milk
Encourage rest in bed after each meal
Offer fluids only with the meal trays

items.q: Before and after helping with any care, including care near medicines, the CNA should:
items.x: Hand hygiene is the most important way to prevent the spread of infection.
items.a: Perform hand hygiene
w: Put on clean gloves
Put on a clean gown
Use a paper towel

items.q: A resident takes several medicines that can cause dizziness. Before walking, the CNA should first have the resident:
items.x: Dangling before standing lets blood pressure adjust and helps prevent falls.
items.a: Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment
w: Stand and begin walking without a pause
Take a few deep breaths while lying flat
Drink a glass of water while lying down

items.q: A resident's daughter asks the CNA what her mother's new pill is for. The CNA should:
items.x: Questions about medicines are answered by the nurse. The CNA also protects the resident's privacy.
items.a: Refer the question to the nurse
w: Tell her what the resident told you
Look it up and explain it to her
Say you think it is for her heart

items.q: A resident who just got a new medicine has trouble breathing and a swollen throat. The CNA's first action is to:
items.x: Possible anaphylaxis is an emergency. The CNA should call for help and stay with the resident.
items.a: Call for help and stay with the resident
w: Leave the room to find the nurse quickly
Lay the resident flat and raise the legs
Give sips of water to open the throat

items.q: A resident receiving medicines through a feeding tube should be positioned:
items.x: Raising the head of the bed helps prevent aspiration during and after tube feeding.
items.a: With the head of the bed raised
w: Flat on the back with a pillow
On the left side with the bed flat
With the foot of the bed raised

items.q: A resident coughs and chokes on her pills every morning. Which observation would be most useful for the nurse deciding on a safer plan?
items.x: Coughing on thin liquids and not on thicker textures points to the kind of swallowing problem a speech evaluation can confirm, and it tells the nurse whether a liquid form or thickened liquids would help.
items.a: She coughs on thin liquids but not on pureed food
w: She prefers to take her pills just before breakfast
She takes seven tablets at the morning pass
She drinks from a cup rather than a straw

items.q: A resident refuses the bedtime snack ordered to prevent low blood sugar overnight. What should the CNA record and report?
items.x: The nurse uses the time and the actual intake to judge the risk of a low glucose during the night, which may mean a glucose check or a change in the evening insulin.
items.a: The refusal, the time, and what she did eat
w: That the snack was offered as the order states
That the resident said she was not hungry
That the snack was left at the bedside

items.q: A client is due for both digoxin and metoprolol, and the apical pulse is 56. Which statement about the hold parameters is correct?
items.x: Both a cardiac glycoside and a beta blocker slow conduction through the AV node, so a rate under 60 is the usual threshold for holding either drug and reporting. A rate of 56 crosses it for both.
items.a: Both drugs are commonly held below 60 beats per minute
w: Digoxin is held below 60 beats per minute and metoprolol below 40
Metoprolol is held below 60 and digoxin below 50
Neither drug has a heart rate hold parameter

items.q: A client taking digoxin reports nausea, poor appetite, and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. The nurse recognizes these as:
items.x: GI upset and visual changes such as yellow-green halos are classic early signs of digoxin toxicity; hold the dose and report the findings.
items.a: Possible signs of digoxin toxicity
w: Expected early effects of digoxin therapy
Signs of a low digoxin blood level
Symptoms of worsening heart failure

items.q: Which lab result places a client taking digoxin at greatest risk for toxicity?
items.x: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmias.
items.a: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
w: Potassium 5.1 mEq/L
Calcium 8.6 mg/dL
Magnesium 2.0 mEq/L

items.q: A client with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has taken digoxin for a week. Which finding best shows the drug is doing its job?
items.x: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node and improves contractility, so the rate comes down and heart failure symptoms ease. It is not a blood pressure drug and does not change potassium.
items.a: A resting rate of 78 and easier breathing when flat
w: A blood pressure that fell from 140/88 to 118/74
A weight that has gone up two pounds since admission
A potassium that rose from 3.4 to 4.0 mEq/L

items.q: A client with severe digoxin toxicity and a dangerous dysrhythmia is expected to receive which antidote?
items.x: Digoxin immune Fab binds digoxin and reverses life-threatening toxicity.
items.a: Digoxin immune Fab
w: Calcium gluconate
Glucagon
Protamine sulfate

items.q: The nurse sees an order for potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push. The nurse should:
items.x: Potassium given by IV push can cause fatal cardiac arrest; it must be diluted and infused by pump per policy.
items.a: Question the order, because potassium is never given IV push
w: Give it slowly over 2 minutes through the existing IV line
Dilute it in saline and give it over 5 minutes
Give it IV push only if the client is on a continuous cardiac monitor

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking oral potassium chloride liquid?
items.x: Liquid potassium irritates the GI tract; dilute it and take it with or after meals.
items.a: Dilute it in juice or water and take it with food
w: Take it undiluted and follow it with a sip of water
Dilute it in water and take it on an empty stomach
Dilute it in juice and take it at bedtime lying down

items.q: Four clients have an order for oral potassium chloride. Which one should the nurse ask about before giving the dose?
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, so a supplement on top of it pushes an already high level toward dangerous hyperkalemia. The other three are losing potassium, which is why the supplement is ordered.
items.a: The client on spironolactone with a potassium of 5.2 mEq/L
w: The client on furosemide today with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L
The client with vomiting and a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L
The client on a thiazide with a potassium of 3.4 mEq/L

items.q: A client is ordered IV furosemide 80 mg. Over how long should the nurse plan to give it, and why?
items.x: The usual limit is 4 mg per minute, so 80 mg runs over about 20 minutes. Rapid IV administration causes tinnitus and hearing loss, and the risk rises with aminoglycosides or kidney impairment.
items.a: About 20 minutes, because a fast push can damage hearing
w: About 2 minutes, because that rate is safe for any dose
About 20 minutes, because a fast push can damage the liver
About 4 hours, because a fast push can damage the kidneys

items.q: Which statement by a client taking furosemide indicates the need for more teaching?
items.x: Loop diuretics are taken in the morning to avoid nighttime urination and lost sleep.
items.a: I will take my water pill right before I go to bed.
w: I will weigh myself every morning before breakfast.
I will get up slowly when I stand from the chair.
I will eat foods like bananas and oranges each day.

items.q: A client receiving furosemide should report which finding to the nurse immediately?
items.x: Muscle cramps and weakness may signal hypokalemia.
items.a: Leg cramps along with muscle weakness
w: More urine output soon after each dose
Mild thirst with a dry mouth after doses
A weight one pound lower than yesterday

items.q: A client with diabetes is started on hydrochlorothiazide. The nurse should reinforce closer monitoring of:
items.x: Thiazides can cause hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, and increased uric acid.
items.a: Blood glucose, because thiazides can raise it
w: Blood glucose, because thiazides can lower it
Potassium, because thiazides can raise it
Hearing, because thiazides can damage it

items.q: A client taking spironolactone asks about using a salt substitute. The nurse should advise the client to:
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing; potassium-based salt substitutes can cause hyperkalemia.
items.a: Avoid salt substitutes, because most contain potassium
w: Use salt substitutes freely, because they contain no sodium
Use salt substitutes, because the drug wastes potassium
Avoid salt substitutes, because most are high in sodium

items.q: A client taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry, tickling cough. The nurse should:
items.x: ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough from bradykinin buildup; the provider may switch to an ARB.
items.a: Report it, because it is a common ACE inhibitor effect
w: Report it, because it is an early sign of angioedema
Offer a cough syrup, because it clears in a few days
Reassure the client, because it fades within a week

items.q: A client who started lisinopril three days ago has swelling of the lips and tongue, with no hives and no wheeze. Which feature points to drug-induced angioedema rather than an allergic reaction?
items.x: ACE inhibitor angioedema comes from bradykinin rather than histamine, so it causes deep non-itchy swelling with no urticaria and responds poorly to antihistamines. It can appear days to months after starting.
items.a: Swelling without hives or itching
w: Swelling that came on within minutes
Swelling with a widespread red rash
Swelling that improves with an antihistamine

items.q: A client took the first dose of lisinopril this morning. When is the blood pressure most likely to fall the furthest?
items.x: Oral lisinopril starts working in about an hour and peaks around 6 hours, so first-dose hypotension shows up the same day. The drop is largest in clients who are volume depleted or already on a diuretic.
items.a: Within about 1 to 6 hours after the dose
w: Within about 5 to 15 minutes of the dose
About 12 to 24 hours after the dose
Only after a full week of daily doses

items.q: A client taking enalapril tells the nurse she has just learned she is pregnant. The nurse should:
items.x: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal kidney toxicity.
items.a: Notify the provider, because ACE inhibitors can harm the fetus
w: Reassure her, because the risk is only in the first trimester
Notify the provider, because the dose must be raised in pregnancy
Reassure her, because enalapril is the preferred drug in pregnancy

items.q: Which lab value is most important to monitor for a client taking losartan?
items.x: ARBs can cause hyperkalemia, especially with kidney impairment or potassium supplements.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum sodium
Serum calcium
Serum magnesium

items.q: A client is switched from metoprolol tartrate twice daily to metoprolol succinate once daily. What should the nurse reinforce about the new tablet?
items.x: Metoprolol succinate is an extended-release tablet, so chewing or crushing it releases the whole day of drug at once. Scored succinate tablets may be split in half but not crushed.
items.a: Swallow it whole or split it only on the score line
w: Crush it and mix it with soft food if needed
Take it twice daily, just like the old tablet
Split it into quarters for easier swallowing

items.q: Which statement by a client taking metoprolol indicates that teaching was effective?
items.x: Abruptly stopping beta blockers can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and angina.
items.a: I will not stop this medicine suddenly on my own.
w: I will take it only on days my pressure is high.
I will check my pulse once a month at the clinic.
I will double the next dose if I miss one.

items.q: A client with diabetes takes atenolol. The nurse reinforces that this drug may:
items.x: Beta blockers can mask tachycardia and tremor from hypoglycemia; sweating usually remains.
items.a: Hide the fast heartbeat that warns of low blood sugar
w: Hide the sweating that warns of low blood sugar
Cause a rapid heartbeat when blood sugar is low
Make insulin wear off sooner after each meal

items.q: The nurse reviews the history of a client with a new order for propranolol. Which condition should the nurse report before giving the drug?
items.x: Nonselective beta blockers can cause bronchospasm in clients with asthma.
items.a: Asthma
w: Migraine
Anxiety

0.5 tablet
1 tablet

150 mg

339 kg
64 kg

items.q: While preparing medications, the nurse drops a tablet on the floor. The nurse should:
items.x: A contaminated dose is discarded per policy; controlled substances need a witnessed waste.
items.a: Discard it per policy and obtain a new dose
w: Wipe it with an alcohol pad and give the dose
Return it to the drawer for the next shift
Discard it and record the dose as given

items.q: When instilling eye drops, the nurse should:
items.x: Afterward, gentle pressure on the inner corner of the eye limits systemic absorption.
items.a: Drop the medication into the lower conjunctival sac
