Drop the medication at the inner corner of the open eye
Drop the medication under the lifted upper eyelid

items.q: To give ear drops to a 2-year-old, the nurse should pull the pinna:
items.x: In children under 3, pulling the pinna down and back straightens the ear canal.
items.a: Down and back
w: Up and back
Straight up and forward
Forward

items.q: When giving an IM injection using the Z-track method, the nurse should:
items.x: Z-track seals the drug in the muscle and prevents leakage into the subcutaneous tissue.
items.a: Pull the skin aside, inject, and release it after removing the needle
w: Pull the skin aside, inject, and release it before removing the needle
Pull the skin aside, inject, and massage the site after removing the needle
Pinch the skin up, inject, and release it after removing the needle

items.q: Which site is preferred for an IM injection in most adults?
items.x: The ventrogluteal site is away from major nerves and blood vessels.
items.a: Ventrogluteal
w: Dorsogluteal
Vastus lateralis
Rectus femoris

items.q: A pregnant client asks which over-the-counter drug is generally preferred for a mild headache. The nurse reinforces that it is usually:
items.x: NSAIDs are generally avoided in pregnancy, especially after 20 weeks.
items.a: Acetaminophen
w: Ibuprofen (Advil)
Naproxen sodium
Low-dose aspirin

items.q: A nurse is titrating a continuous heparin infusion by protocol. Which result shows the infusion is in the usual therapeutic range?
items.x: Heparin is titrated to an aPTT about 1.5 to 2.5 times control, roughly 60 to 90 seconds in most labs. The INR tracks warfarin rather than heparin, and a normal platelet count says nothing about whether the dose is therapeutic.
items.a: aPTT 68 seconds
w: aPTT 26 seconds
INR 2.4
Platelet count 310,000/mm3

items.q: Heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W is ordered to infuse at 1,000 units/hr. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
items.x: 25,000 units / 250 mL = 100 units/mL; 1,000 units/hr divided by 100 units/mL = 10 mL/hr.
items.a: 10 mL/hr
w: 25 mL/hr
100 mL/hr
4 mL/hr

items.q: A heparin protocol calls for 18 units/kg/hr for a client weighing 80 kg. The bag contains 25,000 units in 500 mL. What rate should the nurse program?
items.a: 28.8 mL/hr
w: 14.4 mL/hr
57.6 mL/hr
36 mL/hr

items.q: A heparin bolus of 80 units/kg is ordered for a client who weighs 80 kg. The vial contains 5,000 units/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up?
items.x: 80 units x 80 kg = 6,400 units; 6,400 divided by 5,000 units/mL = 1.28 mL.
w: 6.4 mL

items.q: The nurse prepares protamine sulfate for a client with a heparin overdose. Which administration technique is correct?
items.x: Rapid protamine can cause severe hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylactoid reactions; it is given slowly IV.
items.a: Give it slowly IV, no faster than 5 mg per minute
w: Give it rapidly IV push so it binds heparin quickly
Add it to the running heparin bag so the two drugs neutralize
Give it deep IM in the ventrogluteal site to avoid hypotension

items.q: The nurse teaches a client to self-inject enoxaparin at home. Which statement indicates that the client understands the teaching?
items.x: The air bubble is left in to keep all the drug in the tissue; rubbing and aspirating increase bruising.
items.a: I will leave the air bubble in the prefilled syringe.
w: I will rub the site well afterward to spread the drug.
I will inject it into my thigh muscle at a 90-degree angle.
I will pull back on the plunger to check for blood first.

items.q: A client receiving enoxaparin for 7 days has new lab results. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
items.x: A platelet drop of more than 50% suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prompt evaluation.
items.a: Platelets fell from 240,000 to 90,000/mm3
w: aPTT of 34 seconds compared with 31 seconds at baseline
Hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dL, unchanged from admission
Serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL

items.q: A client received enoxaparin and had an epidural catheter removed earlier today. Which finding requires immediate action?
items.x: Neuraxial anesthesia with low-molecular-weight heparin can cause a spinal or epidural hematoma; new neurologic deficits are an emergency.
items.a: New numbness and weakness in both legs
w: Mild soreness at the former catheter site
A small bruise at the abdominal injection site
Pain rated 3 out of 10 on the incision

items.q: A client is started on warfarin while the heparin infusion continues. Why is heparin kept running for about five more days?
items.x: Warfarin blocks new synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X, but factor II already in the blood has a half-life near 60 hours, so full effect takes about 5 days. The INR can look therapeutic from loss of factor VII before the client is truly anticoagulated.
items.a: Warfarin needs days to deplete circulating clotting factors
w: Warfarin cannot be absorbed until all heparin is fully cleared
Heparin raises the INR so the warfarin dose can be set
Heparin protects the stomach from warfarin irritation

items.q: A client on warfarin has an intracranial hemorrhage and an INR of 4.5. Which treatment should the nurse prepare to give?
items.x: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding is reversed rapidly with prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K for sustained effect.
items.a: Four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K
w: Protamine sulfate IV and hold the next dose
Oral vitamin K alone, then recheck the INR in 24 hours
Idarucizumab 5 g IV with a platelet transfusion

items.q: Which statement by a client taking warfarin indicates a need for further teaching?
items.x: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase bleeding risk with warfarin and should be avoided.
items.a: I can take ibuprofen when my arthritis flares up.
w: I will keep my intake of green leafy vegetables about the same.
I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor.
I will tell my dentist that I take a blood thinner.

items.q: The nurse is preparing IV phytonadione for a client with a high INR. Which action is correct?
items.x: IV vitamin K can cause severe anaphylactoid reactions, so it is diluted and infused slowly.
items.a: Dilute it and infuse slowly while watching for anaphylaxis
w: Give it undiluted by rapid IV push over about 30 seconds
Mix it directly into the client's running heparin infusion
Give it with protamine at the same time to speed reversal

items.q: A client taking dabigatran has a life-threatening GI bleed. Which reversal agent should the nurse expect to give?
items.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that specifically binds and reverses dabigatran.
items.a: Idarucizumab
w: Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione
Andexanet given with vitamin K

items.q: Which statement by a client starting apixaban shows correct understanding?
items.x: Apixaban does not require INR monitoring; stopping abruptly, doubling doses, or adding aspirin increase the risk of clotting or bleeding.
items.a: I will not need routine INR blood tests.
w: I can stop it a day before dental work on my own.
If I miss a dose I will take two doses the next time.
I should add a daily aspirin for extra clot protection.

items.q: A client is prescribed rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for atrial fibrillation. What should the nurse include in teaching?
items.x: The 15 mg and 20 mg doses are taken with food, usually the evening meal, for proper absorption.
items.a: Take it with your evening meal
w: Take it on an empty stomach at bedtime
Have your INR checked weekly for the first month
Eat the same amount of vitamin K every day

items.q: A client in DKA has a glucose of 540 mg/dL and a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. Which order should the nurse implement first?
items.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells; starting it with a potassium below 3.3 mEq/L can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
items.a: Potassium replacement before starting insulin
w: Regular insulin infusion started right away
Sodium bicarbonate by IV push for acidosis
Insulin glargine subcutaneously now

items.q: A client with DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 240 mg/dL, but the anion gap is still open. Why is dextrose added while the insulin continues?
items.x: Glucose corrects before the acidosis does. Insulin must continue until ketone production stops and the gap closes, so dextrose is added to keep the glucose from falling too far.
items.a: Insulin is still needed to stop ketone production
w: Dextrose is needed to close the anion gap directly
Insulin no longer lowers glucose at this level
Dextrose prevents insulin from lowering potassium

items.q: An insulin infusion of 100 units of regular insulin in 100 mL NS is ordered at 0.1 units/kg/hr for a 70 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
items.x: 0.1 x 70 = 7 units/hr; the concentration is 1 unit/mL, so 7 mL/hr.
items.a: 7 mL/hr
w: 0.7 mL/hr
70 mL/hr
14 mL/hr

items.q: Which insulin can the nurse give as a continuous IV infusion?
items.x: Regular insulin is the standard IV insulin; long-acting and cloudy insulins are never given IV.
items.a: Regular human insulin
w: Insulin glargine
Insulin NPH (isophane suspension)
Insulin detemir

items.q: A client's fingerstick glucose is 52 mg/dL. The client is alert and able to swallow. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: An alert client who can swallow gets 15 g of simple carbohydrate, then a recheck in 15 minutes.
items.a: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
w: Give glucagon 1 mg IM in the thigh
Start D50 IV push through the hand vein
Provide a full meal tray with a protein snack

items.q: A client with diabetes is unresponsive with a glucose of 38 mg/dL and has no IV access. Which action is best?
items.x: Glucagon works without IV access; vomiting is common, so the client is placed on the side.
items.a: Give glucagon 1 mg IM and turn the client to the side
w: Place glucose gel in the cheek and recheck in 15 minutes
Give regular insulin subcutaneously and recheck in an hour
Start an IV and wait for a repeat glucose before treating

items.q: The nurse is giving 50% dextrose IV for severe hypoglycemia. Which action is most important?
items.x: D50 is hypertonic and a vesicant; extravasation can cause tissue necrosis.
items.a: Confirm a patent, free-flowing IV before pushing
w: Give it IM if the IV site looks slightly puffy
Push it through the smallest available hand vein
Mix it with regular insulin in the same syringe

items.q: A client with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state has a glucose of 960 mg/dL and dry mucous membranes. What is the priority intervention?
items.x: Severe dehydration is the main problem in HHS; isotonic fluid replacement comes first.
items.a: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride as ordered
w: Give regular insulin by IV push
Start oral fluids every hour
Give sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis

items.q: An order reads potassium chloride 40 mEq in 100 mL NS over 1 hour through a peripheral IV. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Peripheral potassium is usually limited to about 10 mEq/hr; 40 mEq/hr is unsafe without central access and cardiac monitoring.
items.a: Clarify the order because the rate is unsafe
w: Give it as ordered on an infusion pump
Run it over 30 minutes to finish it sooner
Give it as ordered but check the site every hour

items.q: Before starting IV potassium chloride, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Potassium is excreted by the kidneys; giving it with poor urine output can cause hyperkalemia.
items.a: Urine output of at least 30 mL/hr
w: Serum calcium level from yesterday
Blood glucose within normal limits
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants

items.q: Potassium chloride 20 mEq in 100 mL is ordered to infuse over 2 hours. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
items.x: 100 mL over 2 hours = 50 mL/hr, which delivers 10 mEq/hr.
items.a: 50 mL/hr
w: 100 mL/hr
20 mL/hr
25 mL/hr

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client taking oral potassium chloride tablets?
items.x: Oral potassium irritates the GI tract; taking it with fluid and food reduces ulceration.
items.a: Take it with a full glass of water after meals
w: Take it on an empty stomach first thing in the morning
Crush the extended-release tablet into pudding
Take it with a salt substitute to boost the effect

items.q: A client with preeclampsia is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding requires immediate action?
items.x: Absent reflexes and respiratory depression signal magnesium toxicity.
items.a: Respirations 10/min and absent patellar reflexes
w: Blood pressure 146/94 mm Hg and mild headache
Patellar reflexes 2+ and urine output 50 mL/hr
Facial flushing and a feeling of warmth

items.q: A client on a magnesium sulfate infusion becomes lethargic with a respiratory rate of 8/min. After stopping the infusion, which drug should the nurse prepare?
items.x: Calcium gluconate antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction.
items.a: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV given slowly
w: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV push
Potassium chloride 20 mEq IV
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 30 seconds

items.q: Which finding in a client receiving magnesium sulfate increases the risk of toxicity?
items.x: Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys; output under 30 mL/hr allows it to accumulate.
items.a: Urine output of 80 mL over 4 hours
w: Deep tendon reflexes of 2+ bilaterally
Respiratory rate of 16/min
Serum magnesium of 5.5 mg/dL

items.q: A 4 g magnesium sulfate loading dose is ordered over 20 minutes. The bag contains 40 g in 1,000 mL. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
items.x: 40 g/1,000 mL = 0.04 g/mL; 4 g = 100 mL; 100 mL over 20 minutes = 300 mL/hr.
items.a: 300 mL/hr
w: 100 mL/hr
200 mL/hr
400 mL/hr

items.q: After the loading dose, magnesium sulfate is ordered at 2 g/hr. The bag is 40 g in 1,000 mL. What rate should the nurse program?
items.x: 2 g divided by 0.04 g/mL = 50 mL/hr.
items.a: 50 mL/hr
w: 20 mL/hr
80 mL/hr
25 mL/hr

items.q: The nurse is monitoring an oxytocin induction. Which contraction pattern meets the definition of tachysystole?
items.x: Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over a 30-minute window, and it is the reason oxytocin is titrated down or stopped. Contractions every 3 minutes is only 3 to 4 per 10 minutes, the usual goal in active labor.
items.a: More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes over 30 minutes
w: Contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 seconds
Contractions lasting 70 seconds with full relaxation between
A 20-minute stretch with no contractions recorded at all

items.q: A postpartum client has received high-dose oxytocin for 12 hours. She reports headache and confusion, and urine output has dropped. Which laboratory value should the nurse check?
items.x: Oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect and can cause water intoxication with hyponatremia.
items.a: Serum sodium
w: Serum magnesium
Platelet count
Liver enzymes

items.q: A client is receiving terbutaline for preterm labor. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the next dose?
items.x: Terbutaline is a beta-agonist; maternal tachycardia over about 120/min warrants holding it.
items.a: Maternal heart rate of 132/min
w: Maternal heart rate of 96/min
Mild tremor of both hands
Blood glucose of 118 mg/dL

items.q: Which statement by a client in preterm labor shows understanding of betamethasone?
items.x: Antenatal corticosteroids speed fetal lung maturity and reduce respiratory distress syndrome.
items.a: This shot helps my baby's lungs mature before birth.
w: This shot will stop my contractions within an hour.
This medicine prevents my baby from getting an infection.
This shot lowers my blood pressure during labor.

items.q: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM is ordered for postpartum hemorrhage. Which charted finding should the nurse question before giving it?
items.x: Methylergonovine is an ergot vasoconstrictor, so it is avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia because of stroke and severe hypertension. Asthma is the limit on carboprost, not on this drug, and anemia with heavy blood loss is the reason it was ordered.
items.a: A blood pressure of 162/98 mm Hg
w: A hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL
A history of well-controlled asthma
An estimated blood loss of 900 mL

items.q: A postpartum client with hemorrhage has a history of asthma. Which uterotonic order should the nurse question?
items.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha that can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma.
items.a: Carboprost tromethamine IM
w: Oxytocin by IV infusion
Misoprostol given rectally
Tranexamic acid given IV

items.q: A client has a dinoprostone vaginal insert for cervical ripening and now has contractions every 90 seconds. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Tachysystole with dinoprostone is managed by removing the insert.
items.a: Remove the vaginal insert
w: Start an oxytocin infusion at 2 milliunits/min
Give a second insert to finish ripening
Have the client walk to promote dilation

items.q: A peripheral norepinephrine infusion has infiltrated and the hand is pale, cool, and mottled. Which drug is infiltrated into the site to limit tissue loss?
items.x: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker, so it reverses the intense alpha-mediated vasoconstriction causing the ischemia. Hyaluronidase disperses other extravasations but does not relieve vasospasm, and protamine and calcium reverse heparin and calcium channel blockers.
items.a: Phentolamine
w: Protamine sulfate
Hyaluronidase
Calcium gluconate

items.q: Norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 8 mcg/min. What rate should the nurse program?
items.x: 4 mg/250 mL = 16 mcg/mL; 8 mcg/min divided by 16 mcg/mL = 0.5 mL/min; 0.5 mL/min x 60 = 30 mL/hr.
items.a: 30 mL/hr
w: 15 mL/hr
60 mL/hr
0.5 mL/hr

items.q: Dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
items.a: 15 mL/hr
w: 24 mL/hr
30 mL/hr
7.5 mL/hr

items.q: Dobutamine 500 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 10 mcg/kg/min for a 60 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
items.a: 18 mL/hr
w: 36 mL/hr
30 mL/hr
9 mL/hr

items.q: A client with cardiogenic shock is started on dobutamine. Which finding best shows the drug is working?
items.x: Dobutamine increases contractility and cardiac output, which improves kidney perfusion.
items.a: Urine output rises from 15 to 45 mL/hr
w: Heart rate rises from 90 to 135/min
Lung crackles extend higher on the posterior chest
Skin becomes cooler and more mottled at the knees

items.q: Vasopressin 20 units in 100 mL is ordered at 0.03 units/min for septic shock. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
items.x: 20 units/100 mL = 0.2 units/mL; 0.03 x 60 = 1.8 units/hr; 1.8 divided by 0.2 = 9 mL/hr.
items.a: 9 mL/hr
w: 1.8 mL/hr
15 mL/hr
6 mL/hr

items.q: After an IV phenylephrine bolus for hypotension, which finding should the nurse expect and monitor?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-agonist; the rise in BP can trigger a reflex drop in heart rate.
items.a: Reflex bradycardia
w: Rebound tachycardia
Bronchospasm
Hypoglycemia

items.q: A client has anaphylaxis after an IV antibiotic. Which epinephrine order should the nurse anticipate first?
items.x: IM epinephrine 1 mg/mL (0.3 to 0.5 mg) in the thigh is first-line for anaphylaxis; the cardiac arrest dose is not used.
items.a: 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution IM in the lateral thigh
w: 1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL solution by rapid IV push
0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL solution subcutaneously in the arm
0.1 mg of 1 mg/mL solution IV push undiluted

items.q: Adenosine 6 mg is ordered for a client with stable SVT. Which technique is correct?
items.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly via rapid push and flush.
items.a: Rapid IV push followed by a 20 mL saline flush
w: Slow IV push over 2 minutes into a hand vein
Dilute in 50 mL and infuse over 10 minutes
Give IM in the deltoid and repeat in 5 minutes

items.q: Right after adenosine, the monitor shows a 4-second pause and the client reports chest heaviness and flushing. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Transient asystole, flushing, and chest pressure are expected and resolve within seconds.
items.a: Continue monitoring; these effects are expected and brief
w: Start chest compressions right away and call a code blue
Give atropine IV push right away to treat the long pause
Give a second, larger dose of adenosine immediately

items.q: A client taking oral amiodarone for 6 months reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Pulmonary fibrosis is a serious amiodarone toxicity and requires prompt evaluation.
items.a: Report it as possible pulmonary toxicity
w: Tell the client it is a common cold symptom
Advise doubling fluids and using a humidifier
Suggest taking the dose at bedtime with food

items.q: A client on warfarin is started on amiodarone. Which effect should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR; the warfarin dose often must be reduced.
items.a: INR increases
w: INR decreases
Serum potassium rises sharply
Serum glucose falls sharply

items.q: A client in atrial fibrillation with RVR is ordered a diltiazem infusion. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the infusion?
items.x: Diltiazem lowers BP; hypotension is an indication to stop and notify the provider.
items.a: Blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg
w: Heart rate of 108/min
Blood pressure of 112/70 mm Hg
Mild headache and flushing

items.q: Diltiazem 125 mg in 125 mL is ordered at 10 mg/hr. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?
items.x: 125 mg/125 mL = 1 mg/mL, so 10 mg/hr = 10 mL/hr.
items.a: 10 mL/hr
w: 12.5 mL/hr
1 mL/hr
5 mL/hr

items.q: Which serum digoxin level falls within the usual therapeutic range for an adult treated for heart failure?
items.x: The target for heart failure is about 0.5 to 0.9 ng/mL, and levels above 2.0 ng/mL are associated with toxicity. The window is narrow, which is why hypokalemia and falling renal function matter so much with this drug.
items.a: 0.8 ng/mL
w: 2.4 ng/mL
4.0 ng/mL
0.1 ng/mL

items.q: A client taking digoxin and furosemide reports nausea and seeing yellow halos. Which lab result is most important for the nurse to check?
items.x: Hypokalemia from loop diuretics increases digoxin toxicity.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum sodium
Serum albumin
Serum phosphorus

items.q: After a client receives digoxin immune Fab for toxicity, which finding should the nurse monitor closely?
items.x: As digoxin is bound and the Na-K pump recovers, potassium shifts back into cells and can drop.
items.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hyperglycemia
Hypercalcemia

items.q: An infant is ordered digoxin 0.04 mg PO. The elixir contains 50 mcg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
items.x: 0.04 mg = 40 mcg; 40 divided by 50 mcg/mL = 0.8 mL.
items.a: 0.8 mL
w: 0.4 mL
8 mL

items.q: Which action is correct when giving a nitroprusside infusion?
items.x: Nitroprusside breaks down in light; it is protected and given on a pump with arterial BP monitoring.
items.a: Cover the bag with an opaque sleeve
w: Infuse it by gravity without a pump
Mix it in a bag with dobutamine
Give it as a bolus before each titration

items.q: A client has been on nitroprusside for 3 days. Which finding suggests cyanide toxicity?
items.x: Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis, confusion, and hemodynamic instability.
items.a: Rising lactate with metabolic acidosis
w: Low blood glucose with shakiness and sweating
Bradycardia with tall, peaked T waves on the ECG
Rising hemoglobin with flushed, ruddy skin color

items.q: A client with chest pain took tadalafil about 30 hours ago. How does this change the plan for sublingual nitroglycerin?
items.x: Tadalafil is the long-acting PDE-5 inhibitor, so nitrates are held 48 hours, while sildenafil and vardenafil require 24 hours. Both drug classes act on the nitric oxide pathway, and together they cause profound hypotension.
items.a: Nitrates are avoided for 48 hours after tadalafil
w: Nitrates are safe once 12 hours have fully passed
Tadalafil has no meaningful interaction with nitrates
Nitrates may be given at half the usual dose

items.q: A client is taught to use sublingual nitroglycerin at home. Which statement shows correct understanding?
items.x: Up to three doses 5 minutes apart is the standard home regimen, with 911 called if pain persists after the first dose. Taking the tablets together or driving oneself both risk syncope from the abrupt fall in blood pressure.
items.a: I can take one tablet every 5 minutes for up to three doses
w: I can take three tablets at once for faster relief
I should wait 15 minutes between tablets so my pressure holds
I should take one tablet and then drive myself to the hospital

items.q: A client using a nitroglycerin transdermal patch asks why it must be removed at night. What is the best response?
items.x: A nitrate-free interval of 10 to 12 hours prevents tolerance to nitrates.
items.a: A daily patch-free period helps prevent tolerance
w: It keeps your blood sugar from dropping overnight
It stops the patch from causing nightmares
Your heart does not need oxygen while you sleep

items.q: After receiving furosemide 120 mg IV push, a client reports ringing in the ears. What does the nurse suspect?
items.x: High-dose IV furosemide given too fast can cause ototoxicity; rates are generally no faster than 4 mg/min.
items.a: Ototoxicity from overly rapid administration
w: An expected sign that the diuretic is working
An allergic reaction to sulfa components
Hyperkalemia from the large single dose

items.q: Two clients receive diuretics for heart failure. Which pairing of drug and expected potassium change is correct?
items.x: Furosemide blocks the sodium-potassium-2-chloride transporter in the loop, so potassium is lost in the urine. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone in the distal tubule and spares potassium, which is why hyperkalemia is its major risk.
items.a: Furosemide lowers potassium and spironolactone raises it
w: Furosemide raises potassium and spironolactone lowers it
Both furosemide and spironolactone lower potassium
Neither drug changes potassium when renal function is normal

items.q: Which finding best shows IV furosemide is effective for a client with heart failure?
items.x: Reduced fluid overload is shown by weight loss and improved lung sounds.
items.a: Fewer crackles and a 1.5 kg weight loss
w: Blood pressure rising from 110 to 140 systolic
Serum potassium falling from 4.2 to 3.4
Heart rate increasing from 76 to 98/min

items.q: A client taking lisinopril is started on spironolactone. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Both drugs raise potassium; potassium salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.
items.a: Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
w: Increase your intake of bananas and oranges
Take a potassium supplement each morning
Expect your potassium level to fall

items.q: A client who started lisinopril 3 days ago has a swollen tongue and lips and a hoarse voice. What is the priority action?
items.x: Angioedema can obstruct the airway; airway protection comes first and the ACE inhibitor is stopped.
items.a: Assess the airway and call the rapid response team
w: Give the next lisinopril dose with diphenhydramine
Apply ice packs to the lips and recheck in 1 hour
Document the finding and notify the provider in the morning

items.q: A client taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry cough. Which change should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, causing cough; ARBs do not affect bradykinin.
items.a: Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker
w: Adding a cough suppressant and continuing lisinopril
Doubling the lisinopril dose at bedtime
Switching to a different ACE inhibitor

items.q: Which statement by a woman taking losartan requires follow-up by the nurse?
items.x: ARBs and ACE inhibitors cause fetal harm; pregnancy plans require a medication change.
items.a: We are planning to get pregnant in a few months.
w: I check my blood pressure at home every morning.
I stand up slowly when I get out of bed.
I avoid potassium-rich salt substitutes.

items.q: Which medication order should the nurse question for a client with asthma?
items.x: Nonselective beta blockers block beta-2 receptors in the lungs and can trigger bronchospasm.
items.a: Propranolol 40 mg PO twice daily
w: Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily
Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily
Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg PO daily

items.q: A client with type 1 diabetes is starting metoprolol. Which statement shows understanding?
items.x: Beta blockers mask adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor and tachycardia; sweating may still occur.
items.a: My shakiness and racing heart may not warn me of low sugar.
w: Metoprolol will lower my blood sugar so I need less insulin.
I should stop insulin on days I take metoprolol.
I need to eat extra sugar with every metoprolol dose.

items.q: After IV labetalol for severe hypertension, which action is most important before the client gets up?
items.x: Labetalol has alpha-blocking effects that cause orthostatic hypotension and fall risk.
items.a: Check for orthostatic hypotension
w: Check the blood glucose level
Auscultate bowel sounds
Measure the urine specific gravity

items.q: When should the nurse draw a vancomycin trough level?
items.x: A trough reflects the lowest level and is drawn just before the next dose, usually before the fourth dose. Many hospitals now dose vancomycin by AUC monitoring instead of troughs alone, so follow facility protocol.
items.a: Within 30 minutes before the next dose
w: Exactly 1 hour after the infusion ends
Halfway through the infusion
Any time during the day shift

items.q: Ten minutes into a vancomycin infusion a client has flushing of the face and neck with a stable blood pressure. What explains this reaction?
items.x: Vancomycin infusion reaction is a direct, non-immune mast cell release tied to how fast the drug is given, so it can be resumed over at least 60 minutes after an antihistamine. Because it is not IgE-mediated it is not a true allergy.
items.a: Direct mast cell histamine release from the infusion rate
w: An IgE-mediated allergy that bars vancomycin for his life
Bacterial endotoxin released as organisms are killed
Vasodilation caused by the sodium in the diluent

items.q: Gentamicin is infused over 30 minutes. When should the nurse draw the peak level?
items.x: The peak for an IV aminoglycoside is drawn about 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion is complete.
items.a: 30 minutes after the infusion ends
w: Right before the infusion starts
4 hours after the infusion ends
Halfway through the 30-minute infusion

items.q: A client has received gentamicin for 6 days. Which finding is most important to report?
items.x: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic; a rising creatinine requires dose adjustment or a different drug.
items.a: Creatinine rising from 0.8 to 1.9 mg/dL
w: Mild nausea after meals
Temperature down from 38.9 to 37.2 C (102-99 F)
White blood cell count down to 9,000/mm3

items.q: A client says penicillin gave him a flat itchy rash as a child, with no swelling or trouble breathing. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is ordered. What does this history mean?
items.x: A childhood maculopapular rash without urticaria, angioedema or airway involvement is a low-risk label, and most such clients tolerate penicillins; documented anaphylaxis is what bars the class. Clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor and does not change allergy risk.
items.a: A rash alone is low-risk and the drug is often given
w: Any penicillin history rules out every beta-lactam antibiotic
The clavulanate component removes the risk of a reaction
A test dose will confirm whether he can tolerate the drug

items.q: A client with a creatinine clearance of 22 mL/min is ordered ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours. Which order should the nurse question?
items.x: Ceftriaxone is largely eliminated in bile, so its dose is not routinely adjusted for renal function. Cefepime is renally cleared, and at this clearance it accumulates and causes encephalopathy and myoclonus; most other cephalosporins also need adjustment.
items.a: The cefepime, which requires a renal dose adjustment
w: The ceftriaxone, which requires a renal dose adjustment
Both orders, since neither drug is used in renal failure
Neither order, since cephalosporins are cleared by the liver

items.q: A client takes ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO twice daily along with calcium carbonate, a multivitamin with iron, and a stool softener. How should the nurse schedule them?
items.x: Divalent and trivalent cations such as calcium, iron, magnesium and zinc chelate fluoroquinolones in the gut and can cut absorption by more than half. The usual spacing is 2 hours before or 6 hours after the cation.
items.a: Give the ciprofloxacin 2 hours before the calcium and iron
w: Give all of the medications together with a full glass of milk
Crush the ciprofloxacin and mix it in applesauce with the iron
Give the ciprofloxacin with the antacid to protect the stomach

items.q: A client on clindamycin for 8 days has had 6 watery stools today. Which result would confirm the suspected cause?
items.x: Clindamycin strips anaerobic gut flora and carries one of the highest risks of C. difficile colitis, which is diagnosed by stool toxin or toxin-gene testing. A normal white count and a negative occult blood test do not rule it out.
items.a: Stool positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin
w: Stool culture growing only normal gut flora organisms
A white blood cell count of 9,000/mm3
A stool sample negative for occult blood

items.q: Which statement indicates that the client understands teaching about metronidazole?
items.x: Metronidazole with alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.
items.a: I will avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after.
w: I can have a glass of wine with dinner once in a while.
I will take each dose on an empty stomach with a glass of milk.
I will stop taking it as soon as the diarrhea starts to improve.

items.q: A client who takes valproic acid for seizures is started on meropenem. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Carbapenems sharply lower valproic acid levels and can lead to breakthrough seizures.
items.a: A large drop in the valproic acid level
w: A sharp rise in valproic acid levels with toxicity risk
Reduced meropenem effect against the current infection
Increased bleeding risk from added platelet dysfunction

items.q: A client on a morphine PCA is difficult to arouse, has pinpoint pupils, and a respiratory rate of 7/min. What is the nurse's first action?
items.x: Opioid-induced respiratory depression requires stopping the opioid and reversing it with naloxone while supporting breathing.
items.a: Stop the PCA and prepare naloxone
w: Lower the PCA dose and recheck in 1 hour
Raise the head of bed and apply oxygen
Notify the provider and document findings

items.q: A family member is seen pressing the PCA button while the client sleeps. What should the nurse do?
items.x: PCA by proxy bypasses the built-in safety of sedation (a sedated client cannot press the button) and can cause overdose and respiratory depression.
items.a: Explain that only the client should press it
w: Thank them for helping keep the client's pain controlled
Ask them to press it only every 2 hours while the client sleeps
Increase the PCA lockout interval on the pump to be safe

items.q: A client's respirations improved after naloxone for opioid overdose. Which is the priority ongoing assessment?
items.x: Naloxone's duration is shorter than many opioids, so sedation and respiratory depression can return.
items.a: Watch for respiratory depression returning
w: Watch for hypoglycemia over the next hour
Watch for urinary retention
Watch for a rash at the IV site

items.q: Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV is ordered. The vial contains 2 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
items.x: 0.5 mg divided by 2 mg/mL = 0.25 mL.
w: 0.5 mL
2.5 mL
0.4 mL

items.q: A client with a fentanyl transdermal patch now has a fever of 39.4°C. What is the nurse's primary concern?
items.x: Heat increases skin blood flow and fentanyl absorption, raising the risk of respiratory depression.
items.a: Increased drug absorption and oversedation
w: Decreased drug absorption and increased pain
Loss of patch adhesion and detachment
Conversion of fentanyl to an inactive form

items.q: A client on methadone maintenance is admitted. Which finding requires the nurse to notify the provider before the next dose?
items.x: Methadone prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes.
items.a: QTc interval of 520 milliseconds
w: Constipation for the past 2 days despite docusate
Pupils 3 mm and reactive to light
Respiratory rate of 16/min

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client discharged on scheduled oxycodone?
items.x: Opioid-induced constipation does not resolve over time, so a bowel regimen is started along with the opioid.
items.a: Take a stool softener and a stimulant laxative daily
w: Take it with a glass of wine in the evening to help you relax
Take an extra tablet whenever the pain breaks through
Drive as usual once the first dose has started working

items.q: A client taking sertraline is prescribed tramadol. Which findings should the nurse teach the client to report?
items.x: Tramadol combined with an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome; tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold.
items.a: Agitation, sweating, and muscle twitching
w: Drowsiness and dry mouth during the first few days
Mild constipation and nausea
Itching without a rash

items.q: Flumazenil is ordered for a client oversedated with lorazepam who has taken benzodiazepines daily for 10 years. What is the nurse's primary concern?
items.x: Flumazenil can trigger abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal and seizures in clients who use benzodiazepines chronically.
items.a: It may precipitate seizures
w: It may cause respiratory depression
It may increase sedation
It may cause severe hypertension

items.q: During moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl, which finding requires immediate intervention?
items.x: A rising end-tidal CO2 with a low respiratory rate indicates hypoventilation, often before SpO2 falls.
items.a: EtCO2 rising from 38 to 58 mm Hg with an RR of 6/min
w: Responding to voice and following simple commands
SpO2 of 96% on 2 L via nasal cannula with even breaths
Heart rate decreasing from 92 to 80/min after the dose

items.q: Which action is correct when maintaining a propofol infusion?
items.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that supports bacterial growth, so strict aseptic technique and hang-time limits apply.
items.a: Change the tubing and bottle every 12 hours
w: Mix it with the client's antibiotic infusion
Keep an opened vial at the bedside for 24 hours
Use it as the client's only pain medication

items.q: A ventilated client on propofol is grimacing and has a heart rate of 118/min after turning. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Propofol has no analgesic properties, so pain must be treated separately.
items.a: Assess for pain and give the ordered analgesic
w: Increase the propofol because it relieves pain
Document it as an expected response to turning
Give a paralytic to stop the grimacing

items.q: A client is sedated on a dexmedetomidine infusion in the ICU. How does this drug differ from a propofol or midazolam infusion?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist, so clients stay rousable and keep their respiratory drive, which is why it is used during ventilator weaning. Its hallmark adverse effects are bradycardia and hypotension, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines instead.
items.a: It sedates with little respiratory depression
w: It raises both the heart rate and blood pressure
It gives deep sedation with full amnesia
It can be reversed with flumazenil

items.q: A client sedated with ketamine in the ED is emerging from sedation, appears frightened, and is hallucinating. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Emergence reactions are managed with a calm, quiet environment and, if needed, a benzodiazepine.
items.a: Reduce stimulation and prepare a benzodiazepine
w: Turn on bright lights and speak loudly to reorient the client
Give a second full dose of ketamine by IV push
Restrain all four limbs and leave the room

items.q: After rapid sequence intubation with etomidate, a client with sepsis remains hypotensive. Which effect of etomidate may be contributing?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits cortisol synthesis, which may worsen hypotension in septic shock.
items.a: Adrenal suppression
w: Histamine release
Malignant hyperthermia
Hyperkalemia

items.q: For which client should the nurse question an order for succinylcholine for intubation?
items.x: Succinylcholine raises serum potassium and can cause cardiac arrest in clients with hyperkalemia or with crush or burn injuries after the first day.
items.a: A client with a potassium level of 6.1 after a crush injury
w: A client with pneumonia and a potassium level of 4.0
A client with a drug overdose and a normal potassium level
A client with an acute asthma attack and normal labs

items.q: Shortly after receiving succinylcholine, a surgical client develops jaw rigidity, a sharp rise in EtCO2, and tachycardia. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: These are early signs of malignant hyperthermia; dantrolene is the antidote.
items.a: Stopping triggering agents and giving dantrolene
w: Giving more succinylcholine to relieve the rigidity
Giving acetaminophen and using cooling blankets only
Giving naloxone to reverse the sedation

items.q: A client is intubated and receiving a continuous rocuronium infusion. What is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Paralytics provide no sedation or analgesia; a paralyzed client must be sedated to prevent awareness.
items.a: Ensuring ongoing sedation and analgesia
w: Checking for intact cough and gag reflexes
Encouraging deep-breathing exercises
Keeping the client NPO because of aspiration risk

items.q: Which teaching is essential for a female client who received sugammadex at the end of surgery?
items.x: Sugammadex binds progestogens and reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness, similar to a missed dose.
items.a: Use a backup birth control method for 7 days
w: Avoid dairy products and leafy greens for 48 hours
Expect your urine to turn orange for a day
Take your birth control pill twice tomorrow

items.q: A train-of-four test is performed on a client receiving vecuronium. Which result typically reflects the target level of blockade?
items.x: One or two twitches usually reflect adequate blockade without excessive paralysis.
items.a: 1 to 2 twitches out of 4
w: 0 twitches out of 4
4 strong twitches out of 4
3 to 4 twitches with fade

items.q: Neostigmine is given to reverse neuromuscular blockade. Why is glycopyrrolate given with it?
items.x: Neostigmine also increases acetylcholine at muscarinic sites; an anticholinergic prevents bradycardia and excess secretions.
items.a: To prevent bradycardia
w: To prevent hypertension
To speed reversal
To prevent hypoglycemia

items.q: Which action is correct when giving IV phenytoin?
items.x: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions and causes hypotension and dysrhythmias if given too fast.
items.a: Dilute in normal saline; give no faster than 50 mg/min
w: Mix in D5W and infuse as fast as the client tolerates
Give it IM in the deltoid if the IV is not patent
Dilute it in lactated Ringer's and push over 1 minute

items.q: A client with a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL has a total phenytoin level reported as 9 mcg/mL. Why may this level be misleading?
items.x: Phenytoin is about 90 percent albumin bound and only the free fraction is active. With low albumin, less drug is carried in the bound pool, so the total reads low while the free level may be in range; the quoted 10 to 20 mcg/mL range assumes normal albumin.
items.a: Low albumin lowers the total while free drug is therapeutic
w: Low albumin raises the total level and hides a low free level
Phenytoin is not protein bound, so albumin has no effect
Phenytoin levels are only valid when drawn after a meal

items.q: Which statement by a client taking long-term phenytoin indicates correct understanding?
items.x: Gingival hyperplasia is common; switching brands or stopping abruptly can change drug levels or cause seizures.
items.a: "I will brush and floss carefully every day."
w: "I can switch brands whenever one is cheaper."
"I can stop it once I have been seizure-free for a month."
"I will take an antacid with each dose."

items.q: What is an advantage of fosphenytoin over IV phenytoin?
items.x: Fosphenytoin is water-soluble, causes less purple glove syndrome, and can be infused at up to 150 mg PE/min.
items.a: It can be infused faster with less tissue injury
w: It never requires blood level monitoring
It can be mixed with any IV fluid in the line
It cannot cause hypotension or dysrhythmias

items.q: Which report from a client taking levetiracetam should the nurse follow up on?
items.x: Levetiracetam can cause irritability, depression, and suicidal thoughts.
items.a: "I have been feeling angry and hopeless."
w: "I feel a little sleepy in the afternoon."
"I have had a slight headache this week."
"I am a bit dizzy when I first stand up."

items.q: A client taking valproic acid reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and vomiting. What does the nurse suspect?
items.x: Valproic acid carries boxed warnings for pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity.
items.a: Pancreatitis
w: Viral gastroenteritis
An expected adjustment effect
Drug-induced kidney stones

items.q: Which finding in a client taking carbamazepine should the nurse report immediately?
items.x: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
items.a: Fever, sore throat, and a blistering rash
w: Mild drowsiness during the first week
Slight dizziness when standing
Mild nausea when a dose is taken on an empty stomach

items.q: A client starts lamotrigine on a schedule that raises the dose slowly over about 6 weeks. What is the reason for the slow titration?
items.x: The risk of serious rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, rises with rapid dose escalation, so the manufacturer's schedule takes about 6 weeks to reach maintenance. Adding valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, so the starting dose is halved.
items.a: It lowers the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
w: It lets the kidneys adapt to clearing the drug
It prevents withdrawal seizures between doses
It allows a blood level to be checked each week

items.q: A client on maintenance lithium has a level of 1.6 mEq/L. Which finding fits this level?
items.x: Maintenance levels run about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L, and 1.5 to 2.0 mEq/L brings coarse tremor, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. A fine tremor and polyuria occur at therapeutic levels, while seizures and stupor appear above roughly 2.5 mEq/L.
items.a: Coarse hand tremor and nausea
w: A fine tremor present since the first week
Seizures and a decreased level of consciousness
Polyuria and thirst since the drug was started

items.q: Which statement by a client taking lithium indicates a need for further teaching?
items.x: Low sodium intake causes lithium retention and toxicity.
items.a: "I am going to start a low-salt diet."
w: "I will drink about 2 to 3 liters of fluid daily."
"I will have my blood level checked as ordered."
"I will call if I have vomiting or diarrhea."

items.q: A client taking lithium has several new orders. Which order should the nurse question?
items.x: NSAIDs decrease lithium clearance and raise lithium levels.
items.a: Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours
Docusate 100 mg twice daily
Famotidine 20 mg twice daily

items.q: A client taking clozapine reports a sore throat and a fever of 38.6°C. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia; signs of infection require an urgent ANC.
items.a: Check the most recent absolute neutrophil count
w: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours
Encourage warm saltwater gargles
Hold fluids to reduce secretions

items.q: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 104 F, lead-pipe rigidity, and a creatine kinase of 4,200 units/L. Which syndrome do these findings fit?
items.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome brings fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a high creatine kinase from muscle breakdown, and it builds over days. Serotonin syndrome instead causes hyperreflexia, clonus and diarrhea and appears within hours.
items.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome from an SSRI
An acute dystonic reaction
Tardive dyskinesia of the tongue

items.q: A client given haloperidol develops sudden twisting of the neck and upward rolling of the eyes. Which order should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Acute dystonia is treated with an anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine or benztropine.
items.a: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV or IM
w: Haloperidol 5 mg IM now
Lorazepam 0.5 mg PO at bedtime
Naloxone 0.4 mg IV push

items.q: Which monitoring is most important for a client taking olanzapine long-term?
items.x: Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine cause weight gain, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
items.a: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipids
w: Monthly serum lithium levels
Daily peak flow readings
Hearing tests and eye exams every 6 months

items.q: An 80-year-old client is started on quetiapine. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
items.x: Quetiapine causes orthostatic hypotension and sedation, which increase the risk of falls in older adults.
items.a: Rise slowly from a lying or sitting position
w: Take it with grapefruit juice
Avoid all dairy products
Expect reddish-orange urine for a few days

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give about ziprasidone?
items.x: Ziprasidone absorption roughly doubles with food; the drug also prolongs the QT interval.
items.a: Take it with a meal
w: Take it on an empty stomach
Take it with an antacid
Crush it in applesauce

items.q: A client recently started on sertraline along with another serotonergic drug has agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and leg clonus. What does the nurse suspect?
items.x: Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome; NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity and slowed reflexes.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Acute dystonic reaction
Anticholinergic toxicity

items.q: Which statement by a client starting fluoxetine indicates a need for further teaching?
items.x: Antidepressants should not be stopped abruptly, and their full effect takes several weeks.
items.a: "I can stop it as soon as I feel better."
w: "It may take several weeks to feel the full effect."
"I will report any thoughts of hurting myself."
"I will take it in the morning if it keeps me awake."

items.q: A client taking phenelzine ate aged cheese and salami and now has a severe occipital headache and a BP of 210/120 mm Hg. What does the nurse suspect?
items.x: MAOIs taken with tyramine-rich foods can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.a: Hypertensive crisis
w: Serotonin syndrome
Orthostatic hypotension
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

items.q: A client taking fluoxetine is to be switched to an MAOI. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Because of fluoxetine's long half-life, about 5 weeks must pass before an MAOI is started to prevent serotonin syndrome.
items.a: A washout period of about 5 weeks
w: Starting the MAOI the next morning
Taking both drugs together for 1 week
A washout period of 24 hours

items.q: For which client should the nurse question an order for bupropion?
items.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in clients with eating disorders or seizure disorders.
items.a: A client with bulimia nervosa
w: A client trying to quit smoking
A client with seasonal depression
A client taking an SSRI who has low sexual desire

items.q: Which adverse effect of trazodone should the nurse teach a male client to report immediately?
items.x: Priapism is a rare but serious emergency with trazodone.
items.a: An erection lasting more than 4 hours
w: Mild morning drowsiness
Dry mouth during the day
Mild dizziness when standing up quickly

items.q: Which parameter should the nurse monitor in a client taking high doses of venlafaxine?
items.x: Venlafaxine can cause sustained, dose-related hypertension.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Serum potassium
Blood glucose
Hearing acuity

items.q: Which order should the nurse question for an 84-year-old client?
items.x: Diphenhydramine is on the Beers list because of anticholinergic effects such as confusion, falls, and urinary retention.
items.a: Diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime for sleep
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours for pain
Melatonin 3 mg at bedtime for sleep
Polyethylene glycol 17 g daily for constipation

items.q: A newly admitted 82-year-old client takes glyburide. Why should the nurse discuss this drug with the provider?
items.x: Glyburide is on the Beers list because of prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults.
items.a: It causes prolonged hypoglycemia
w: It causes severe hyperkalemia
It raises the risk of lactic acidosis
It often causes severe weight loss

items.q: An 88-year-old client asks for temazepam for sleep. Which risk should the nurse discuss with the provider?
items.x: In older adults, benzodiazepines increase the risk of falls, fractures, and delirium.
items.a: Falls and confusion
w: Hypertensive crisis
Severe hyperglycemia
Excessive daytime energy

items.q: Which statement indicates that the client understands teaching about zolpidem?
items.x: Zolpidem can cause next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors; it is taken only at bedtime.
items.a: "I will take it right before bed when I can sleep 7 to 8 hours."
w: "I will take it with a glass of wine so it works faster tonight."
"I can safely drive to work about 2 hours after I take it."
"I will take an extra tablet if I wake up at 3 AM and cannot sleep."

items.q: A client has taken prednisone 40 mg daily for 4 months and asks why the dose is being stepped down over weeks. What is the best response?
items.x: Daily steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis after about 2 to 3 weeks, so an abrupt stop can cause adrenal crisis with hypotension, weakness and hypoglycemia. The taper gives endogenous cortisol production time to recover.
items.a: Your adrenal glands need time to make cortisol again
w: The drug must clear slowly to protect your kidneys
Stopping quickly would make your blood sugar drop fast
A slow taper keeps the medicine from upsetting you

items.q: A client on long-term prednisone has been NPO for 2 days and is now confused with a BP of 78/40 mm Hg. Which drug should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Missed steroid doses can cause adrenal crisis, which is treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids.
items.a: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
w: Dexamethasone 4 mg PO
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg PO
Prednisone 5 mg PO

items.q: A client without diabetes is receiving high-dose IV methylprednisolone. Which finding is most important to monitor?
items.x: Corticosteroids cause hyperglycemia that may require insulin coverage.
items.a: Blood glucose
w: Serum calcium
Hearing acuity
Serum ammonia

items.q: A client on high-dose dexamethasone for cerebral edema is also started on pantoprazole. What is the reason for the second drug?
items.x: Glucocorticoids reduce mucosal prostaglandins and impair healing, so ulcer and GI bleeding risk rises, particularly at high dose or alongside an NSAID. Acid suppression is added for that reason, not to change absorption or glucose.
items.a: Steroids raise the risk of gastric ulceration and bleeding
w: Pantoprazole improves the absorption of dexamethasone tablets
Pantoprazole prevents the steroid from raising glucose
Steroids cause reflux by relaxing the lower esophagus

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client taking levothyroxine?
items.x: Food, calcium, and iron reduce levothyroxine absorption.
items.a: Take it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
w: Take it together with your calcium and iron to improve absorption
Take it at bedtime with a full meal and a glass of milk
Skip doses on days when you feel full of energy and restless

items.q: An older adult with coronary artery disease recently started levothyroxine. Which finding requires immediate action?
items.x: Levothyroxine increases cardiac oxygen demand and can trigger angina or dysrhythmias.
items.a: Chest pain and a heart rate of 118/min
w: Mild fatigue and feeling cold in the first week
Weight loss of 0.5 kg in a month
Feeling less cold than before

items.q: Which finding should the nurse teach a client taking propylthiouracil to report immediately?
items.x: PTU carries a boxed warning for severe liver injury.
items.a: Dark urine and yellowing of the skin
w: Mild itching of the arms without a rash
Feeling warm in a hot room
A metallic taste in the mouth

items.q: A client taking methimazole develops a sore throat and fever. Which lab should the nurse expect to be ordered?
items.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis.
items.a: Complete blood count with differential
w: Thyroid-stimulating hormone level
Serum calcium and phosphorus level
Hemoglobin A1C and fasting glucose
