Note the appointment on the unit calendar only

items.q: A resident uses oxygen at home from a concentrator. Which thing in his room should the CNA report as unsafe?
items.x: Petroleum products on the face near oxygen are a fire hazard, and a water-based lubricant is used instead. A cotton blanket, humidifier water and clearance around the unit are all normal.
items.a: A petroleum jelly jar at the bedside for his lips
w: A cotton blanket folded at the foot of the bed
Water in the humidifier bottle on the concentrator
The concentrator placed about 2 feet away from the wall

items.q: A resident takes digoxin and furosemide. Which group of findings should the CNA bring to the nurse first?
items.x: Nausea, loss of appetite and yellow-green visual changes are classic digoxin toxicity, and furosemide makes it more likely by lowering potassium. The other groups are common complaints and not signs of toxicity.
items.a: Nausea, poor appetite, yellow halos
w: Dry mouth, thirst, and pale colored urine
A sore throat, a stuffy nose, and sneezing
Mild ankle swelling by the end of the day

items.q: A resident has two insulin pens in the refrigerator. One looks clear and one looks milky white. What should the CNA do?
items.x: NPH is a suspension and is normally cloudy, while glargine and the rapid-acting insulins are clear, so cloudiness alone does not mean a spoiled pen. Preparing insulin is a licensed task, so the CNA reports what is seen.
items.a: Tell the nurse how each pen looks and give neither
w: Shake the milky pen until the liquid looks clear again
Throw out the milky pen because insulin should be clear
Warm the milky pen in her hands until it turns clear

items.q: A resident on clopidogrel has bleeding gums after brushing. The CNA should:
items.x: Clopidogrel increases bleeding. Gentle oral care and reporting is the right approach.
items.a: Report it and use a soft toothbrush
w: Chart it and switch to mouthwash only
Rinse with salt water and recheck later
Brush as usual and mention it next week

items.q: A resident takes alendronate for her bones. After the dose she should:
items.x: Alendronate can injure the esophagus. Staying upright with plain water afterward is the key instruction.
items.a: Stay upright for at least 30 minutes with a full glass of water
w: Take it with a large glass of milk at bedtime instead
Lie down flat for at least 30 minutes after the dose to rest
Take it with all of her other pills at lunch time with food

items.q: A resident starting tamsulosin is at risk for what?
items.x: Tamsulosin relaxes blood vessels as well as the prostate and commonly causes a drop in blood pressure on standing.
items.a: Dizziness and falls when standing up
w: Constipation and a very dry mouth
Swollen ankles and a slow pulse
A dry cough and a hoarse voice

items.q: The LVN is asked to give subcutaneous enoxaparin. Which technique is correct?
items.x: The air bubble in a prefilled enoxaparin syringe is intentional. The abdomen is the usual site, and rubbing increases bruising.
items.a: Give it in the abdominal fat, without expelling the air bubble from a prefilled syringe
w: Expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe first, then inject into the abdominal fat
Inject it into the deltoid muscle at a 90-degree angle to the skin surface
Massage the injection site firmly afterward to help spread the dose

items.q: An LVN notices a patient on long-term phenytoin has swollen, overgrown gums. This is:
items.x: Gingival hyperplasia is a classic long-term effect of phenytoin and prompts dental care and a conversation with the provider.
items.a: A known effect of phenytoin that should be reported
w: A sign of phenytoin toxicity that needs a level today
An allergic reaction to phenytoin that needs treatment
A sign of low folate that is unrelated to phenytoin

items.q: A patient on lithium has been vomiting with diarrhea for two days. What is the concern?
items.x: Lithium is handled by the kidney alongside sodium. Dehydration and sodium loss raise levels into the toxic range.
items.a: Lithium levels can rise dangerously with fluid and sodium losses
w: Lithium levels can fall too low with fluid and sodium losses
Lithium is lost in the stool, so an extra dose will be needed
Lithium levels stay steady, but potassium can fall dangerously

items.q: What should the LVN reinforce with a patient starting metronidazole?
items.x: Metronidazole with alcohol can cause a severe flushing, vomiting reaction.
items.a: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for several days afterward
w: Avoid dairy products during treatment and for two hours after
Avoid direct sunlight during treatment and for a week afterward
Avoid alcohol only for the first two days of the treatment

items.q: Which instruction is correct for a patient taking oral iron?
items.x: Iron absorbs best without food, though it may be taken with food if it upsets the stomach. Black stool is expected.
items.a: It is absorbed better on an empty stomach, and stools may turn black
w: It is absorbed better with a glass of milk, and stools may turn black
It is absorbed better on an empty stomach, and black stools mean bleeding
It is absorbed better with an antacid, and stools may turn pale

items.q: A patient takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. How is it usually dosed?
items.x: Daily dosing of weekly methotrexate is a well-known fatal medication error.
items.a: Once a week, on the same day
w: Once a day, at the same time
Twice a day, with a meal
Once a month, at the clinic

items.q: Which instruction fits a patient starting spironolactone?
items.x: Spironolactone keeps potassium in the body, and salt substitutes are usually potassium chloride.
items.a: Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless the provider says otherwise
w: Use a salt substitute in place of table salt to help lower the blood pressure
Eat extra bananas and oranges each day to replace the potassium that is lost
Take a daily potassium supplement with it unless the provider says otherwise

items.q: An EMT is treating a 58-year-old with crushing chest pain. Which aspirin instruction is correct?
items.x: Chewing non-enteric aspirin gets it into the bloodstream fastest. Enteric coating delays absorption when minutes matter.
items.a: Have the patient chew 162 to 324 mg of non-enteric aspirin
w: Have the patient swallow 324 mg of enteric-coated aspirin whole
Have the patient chew a single 81 mg aspirin as the full dose
Have the patient chew 650 mg of non-enteric aspirin at once

items.q: Which patient with chest pain should an EMT not give aspirin to?
items.x: Active bleeding is the contraindication. Age, prior aspirin use and symptom duration are not.
items.a: One with an active gastrointestinal bleed
w: One who took a daily low-dose aspirin today
One with asthma who tolerates aspirin
One who takes clopidogrel for a stent

items.q: An EMT finds a patient breathing 4 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. What comes first?
items.x: Opioid overdose kills through hypoventilation. Ventilation fixes the problem that is killing the patient; naloxone follows.
items.a: Open the airway and ventilate, then give naloxone
w: Give naloxone, then ventilate if there is no response
Apply a nonrebreather mask, then give naloxone
Start chest compressions, then give naloxone

items.q: After intranasal naloxone, a patient is awake and refusing transport. Which fact best supports the need to be seen at a hospital?
items.x: Naloxone wears off sooner than most opioids do, so breathing can slow again after the patient looks fine. It does work on long-acting opioids; it simply wears off well before they do.
items.a: Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes, less than most opioids
w: Naloxone works for about a day, but withdrawal follows
Naloxone has little effect on long-acting opioids
Naloxone itself slows breathing as the dose wears off

items.q: An EMT gives an epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. Where is it placed?
items.x: The anterolateral thigh gives the fastest absorption and is the standard site.
items.a: The outer mid-thigh, through clothing if needed
w: The deltoid, with the sleeve rolled up first
The upper outer buttock, through clothing
The abdomen, two inches from the navel

items.q: A 10-year-old weighing 22 kg needs an epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. Which strength fits?
items.x: The junior auto-injector covers roughly 15 to 30 kg.
items.a: The 0.15 mg junior auto-injector
w: The 0.3 mg adult auto-injector
Two 0.15 mg junior auto-injectors
Either strength; age matters more than weight

items.q: An EMT assists a patient with her own albuterol inhaler. What should be checked first?
items.x: Assisting with a patient's own medication means confirming it is theirs, current, and not already overused.
items.a: That it is her own prescription, in date, and within her doses
w: That her pulse is under 100, because albuterol raises heart rate
That she has eaten, because albuterol can upset the stomach
That she rinsed her mouth, because albuterol causes thrush

items.q: A patient with asthma has used her inhaler six times in an hour and is now quiet with little air movement. What does the quiet chest mean?
items.x: A silent chest in asthma is an ominous sign of severe obstruction, not improvement.
items.a: She is moving too little air to wheeze, which is worse than wheezing
w: Her bronchospasm is easing, so the inhaler is finally working
She has used too much albuterol, which is suppressing her breathing
Her airways have opened, though her chest muscles are now fatigued

items.q: An EMT has a conscious hypoglycemic patient who can swallow and protect her airway. What is appropriate?
items.x: Oral glucose is within EMT scope when the patient can swallow safely.
items.a: Oral glucose gel or another oral sugar source
w: Intravenous dextrose through a large-bore line
Glucagon intramuscularly into the outer thigh
Nothing by mouth until a paramedic arrives

items.q: Why should oral glucose not be given to an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient?
items.x: An unresponsive patient cannot protect the airway, so anything placed in the mouth risks aspiration.
items.a: It can be aspirated into the lungs
w: It is absorbed too slowly from the cheek
It can trigger vomiting on waking up
It needs stomach acid to be activated

items.q: An EMT is asked to assist a chest pain patient with his own nitroglycerin. Which finding makes this unsafe?
items.x: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors with nitrates can cause profound hypotension.
items.a: He took sildenafil last night
w: His systolic blood pressure is 150
He took aspirin ten minutes ago
He takes a daily beta blocker

items.q: Before assisting with nitroglycerin, an EMT should confirm what?
items.x: Nitroglycerin drops blood pressure, so a minimum systolic is the standard check.
items.a: A systolic blood pressure above the protocol's minimum
w: A 12-lead tracing that confirms an acute STEMI pattern
A pain score that is rated at least moderate in severity
An oxygen saturation that is within the normal range

items.q: A COPD patient is breathless with a saturation of 86 percent. What should the EMT do?
items.x: Hypoxia is treated. The old fear of giving any oxygen in COPD has been replaced by titration to a target.
items.a: Give oxygen titrated toward the target range in protocol
w: Give high-flow oxygen regardless of the saturation
Give no oxygen and coach pursed-lip breathing
Give low-flow oxygen and never increase the rate

items.q: For which ingestion is activated charcoal least useful?
items.x: Charcoal does not bind caustics, and it obscures the view for endoscopy while risking a dangerous vomit.
items.a: A caustic drain cleaner
w: Aspirin tablets taken 30 minutes ago
A large ingestion of an antidepressant
Acetaminophen taken within the hour

items.q: A patient with a known bee allergy is stung and has only localized swelling with no other symptoms. What is appropriate?
items.x: Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis, meaning systemic involvement, not for a local reaction alone.
items.a: Monitor closely; epinephrine is for systemic reactions
w: Give the auto-injector now because of the known allergy
Give an antihistamine and release the patient from care
Apply a constricting band above the sting and transport

items.q: An AEMT establishes an IV on an unresponsive patient with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. What is appropriate?
items.x: With intravenous access and an unresponsive patient, IV dextrose is the AEMT-level treatment.
items.a: Intravenous dextrose, with the concentration and volume per protocol
w: Intramuscular glucagon only, keeping the dextrose in reserve for later
Oral glucose gel placed between the cheek and the gum to absorb
A saline bolus first, with a repeat glucose check before any dextrose

items.q: Why is dextrose given through a well-running, well-secured line?
items.x: Concentrated dextrose is a vesicant, and extravasation causes significant local damage.
items.a: Infiltration of concentrated dextrose can cause severe tissue injury
w: A slow line lets the dextrose be metabolized before it reaches the brain
A positional line makes the measured glucose read falsely high afterward
A loose line lets air enter with the thick solution and cause embolism

items.q: When is glucagon the better choice for hypoglycemia?
items.x: Glucagon is the route-of-last-resort option when access cannot be obtained.
items.a: When no intravenous or intraosseous access can be obtained
w: When the patient is alert but refuses to take oral glucose
When intravenous dextrose has already been given once
When the patient is malnourished with low glycogen stores

items.q: What limits how well glucagon works?
items.x: Glucagon mobilizes stored glycogen. With no stores, it does little.
items.a: It needs glycogen stores, which are depleted in starvation and alcoholism
w: It needs working insulin, which is absent in most type 1 diabetic patients
It needs intact muscle perfusion, which is lost in all hypoglycemic patients
It needs a recent meal, which supplies the glucose that it then releases

items.q: An AEMT has intravenous access on an apneic opioid overdose. How should naloxone be titrated?
items.x: Titrating to breathing avoids precipitating severe withdrawal and agitation.
items.a: In small increments, to restore adequate breathing rather than full alertness
w: As one large push given quickly, to restore full alertness right away
In small increments, repeated until the pupils return to normal size
In small increments, but only after an advanced airway is in place

items.q: A patient with severe asthma has had three albuterol treatments with little improvement. What else is commonly added at this level?
items.x: Combining ipratropium with albuterol improves bronchodilation in severe exacerbations.
items.a: Ipratropium with the albuterol
w: Levalbuterol with the albuterol
Inhaled steroid with the albuterol
Oral theophylline after the albuterol

items.q: An inferior wall infarct patient becomes profoundly hypotensive after nitroglycerin. What is the likely explanation?
items.x: Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent, and nitrates can drop the pressure sharply.
items.a: A right ventricular infarct, which depends on preload that nitroglycerin removes
w: A left ventricular infarct, which nitroglycerin weakens by slowing the rate
A reflex tachycardia, which empties the ventricle and drops the pressure
A nitrate allergy, which dilates the vessels within minutes of the dose

items.q: In anaphylaxis with hypotension that persists after two intramuscular epinephrine doses, what is the next step at an advanced level?
items.x: Anaphylactic shock is distributive, and volume is a key part of the treatment.
items.a: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid alongside further epinephrine
w: Oral antihistamines and a steroid in place of further epinephrine
Nebulized albuterol alone while waiting for the epinephrine to peak
Intravenous push of the intramuscular epinephrine concentration

items.q: A patient has vomiting after a head injury. What is the main reason to treat it?
items.x: Controlling vomiting in head injury protects the airway and avoids pressure spikes.
items.a: Vomiting raises intracranial pressure and threatens the airway
w: Vomiting lowers blood pressure and worsens cerebral perfusion
Vomiting causes dehydration that worsens the brain swelling
Vomiting masks the pupil changes used to track the injury

items.q: A flight nurse transports a patient on a norepinephrine infusion. What is the most important preparation before lift-off?
items.x: Pump failure in flight with no backup is a known and preventable critical event.
items.a: Confirm pump battery charge, line security and a backup plan for infusion failure
w: Raise the infusion rate before loading to offset the pressure change at altitude
Convert the infusion to scheduled push-dose boluses so the pump is free in flight
Move the infusion to the most distal peripheral line to keep the other lines free

items.q: Why is a central line preferred for norepinephrine in transport?
items.x: Vasopressor extravasation is a serious injury, and transport increases the risk of line problems.
items.a: Extravasation from a peripheral line causes tissue necrosis, and a moving aircraft makes dislodgement more likely
w: Peripheral veins constrict at cabin altitude, so drug delivery from a peripheral line becomes unreliable in flight
Central delivery reaches the heart sooner, and a peripheral infusion cannot be titrated quickly enough in flight
Central lines allow central venous pressure monitoring, which is needed to titrate norepinephrine safely in flight

items.q: A ventilated patient on rocuronium becomes tachycardic and hypertensive during flight. What should the flight nurse consider first?
items.x: A paralyzed patient cannot show distress except through vital signs. Awareness under paralysis is the first thing to exclude.
items.a: Inadequate sedation and analgesia under paralysis
w: Rocuronium wearing off as the muscle tone returns
Early malignant hyperthermia from the paralytic
A histamine reaction to the last rocuronium dose

items.q: Which transport patient makes succinylcholine a poor choice?
items.x: Up-regulated receptors after burns, denervation and prolonged immobility cause a dangerous potassium release.
items.a: A patient several days after a major burn or spinal cord injury
w: A patient in the first hour after a major thermal burn injury
A patient with a head injury and a recently eaten full meal
A patient with chronic kidney disease and a normal potassium

items.q: Why is ketamine often favored for induction in transport?
items.x: Hemodynamic stability is the main reason it is chosen in an unstable transport patient.
items.a: It tends to preserve blood pressure and respiratory drive compared with other agents
w: It lowers intracranial pressure and cerebral oxygen demand more than other agents do
It dries airway secretions and blunts laryngeal reflexes, which eases laryngoscopy
It has a faster onset than other agents and causes no emergence reactions on waking

items.q: A ventilated transport patient is on a fentanyl infusion. What is the altitude-related concern?
items.x: The drug behaves normally. Boyle's law effects on trapped gas are what change with altitude.
items.a: Expanding gas can change cuff pressure and pneumothorax size, so the whole picture changes, not the drug
w: Fentanyl clearance falls at cabin altitude, so the infusion rate should be reduced once the aircraft is in flight
Fentanyl causes chest wall rigidity more often at altitude, so a paralytic infusion is added before the flight
Lower cabin pressure slows the pump delivery, so the fentanyl rate should be increased during the climb

items.q: A flight nurse is transporting a hemorrhaging trauma patient 90 minutes by air. What is the preferred resuscitation?
items.x: Crystalloid dilutes clotting factors. Blood is the resuscitation fluid for hemorrhage.
items.a: Blood products rather than crystalloid, with tranexamic acid if within the window
w: Crystalloid titrated to a normal systolic pressure, with blood products on arrival
Colloid as the first fluid, with blood products once the pressure stops responding
Vasopressors to maintain perfusion pressure, with blood products if they fail

items.q: What is the key timing point for tranexamic acid in trauma?
items.x: Early administration is what drives the mortality benefit; later administration loses it.
items.a: Benefit is greatest when given early, within about three hours of injury
w: Benefit is greatest when given after the first units of blood are running
Benefit is the same at any time within the first day after the injury
Benefit is greatest when given once bleeding is controlled surgically

items.q: A head-injured patient shows a blown pupil in flight. What does hypertonic saline do?
items.x: Osmotic therapy buys time to definitive care; it does not treat the lesion.
items.a: Draws water out of brain tissue to reduce intracranial pressure as a temporizing measure
w: Constricts cerebral vessels to reduce intracranial blood volume as a temporizing measure
Lowers cerebral metabolic demand to protect brain tissue until surgical decompression
Promotes a brisk diuresis that lowers blood volume and so reduces intracranial pressure

items.q: A hypotensive patient needs sedation in flight. Why is propofol often avoided?
items.x: Propofol's hemodynamic effects are the limiting factor in an unstable patient.
items.a: It causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, worsening hypotension
w: It causes adrenal suppression, which worsens hypotension in shock states
It causes histamine release and bronchospasm, worsening the hypotension
It causes a catecholamine surge followed by a rebound drop in pressure

items.q: A flight nurse transports a patient on a heparin infusion who develops a falling platelet count. What is the concern?
items.x: HIT is a prothrombotic state despite the low platelets, and heparin must be stopped.
items.a: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which causes clotting rather than bleeding
w: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which causes bleeding rather than clotting
Disseminated intravascular coagulation caused directly by the heparin itself
Heparin overdose, which consumes platelets and calls for protamine reversal

items.q: A DKA patient is transported on an insulin infusion. What must the flight nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Insulin-driven hypokalemia is the dangerous and preventable event in DKA transport.
items.a: Potassium and glucose, since insulin drives potassium into cells
w: Sodium and glucose, since insulin drives sodium into the cells
Glucose and ketones, since insulin clears both at the same rate
Magnesium and glucose, since insulin wastes magnesium in urine

items.q: A pre-eclamptic patient on magnesium loses her patellar reflexes in flight. What does that indicate?
items.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the early warning sign of magnesium toxicity, and calcium gluconate is the antidote.
items.a: Rising magnesium toxicity, which precedes respiratory depression
w: A therapeutic magnesium level, which confirms seizure protection
Worsening pre-eclampsia, which precedes an eclamptic seizure
Falling serum calcium, which precedes tetany and laryngospasm

items.q: A massively transfused patient becomes hypotensive with a prolonged QT in flight. What should be considered?
items.x: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and the resulting hypocalcemia impairs contractility and coagulation.
items.a: Citrate-induced hypocalcemia from the transfusion
w: Hyperkalemia from the stored red blood cell units
Citrate-induced hypermagnesemia from the plasma
Dilutional hyponatremia from the blood products

items.q: A flight nurse transports a patient with acute pulmonary edema on a nitroglycerin infusion. What is the main benefit?
items.x: Nitroglycerin works by unloading the ventricle, which is why it helps before any diuretic does.
items.a: Reduced preload and afterload, which unloads the failing left ventricle
w: Increased contractility, which raises output from the failing ventricle
A brisk diuresis, which removes the excess fluid from the flooded lungs
Slowed heart rate, which lengthens filling time for the left ventricle

items.q: A flight nurse is asked to start a peripheral epinephrine infusion for refractory shock. What is the practical concern?
items.x: Peripheral vasopressors are used in transport with close monitoring and a plan to convert to central access.
items.a: Extravasation risk and the need for frequent site checks and a plan for central access
w: Reduced drug effect peripherally and the need for a higher rate until central access is placed
Arrhythmia risk from peripheral delivery and the need to use only a hand or wrist vein
Slower onset from a peripheral vein and the need for a loading bolus before the infusion

items.q: A client on a weight-based heparin infusion has an aPTT of 128 seconds (goal 60-85 per the nomogram) and new oozing from the gums. Vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: A supratherapeutic aPTT with minor bleeding is handled by the nomogram hold and rate decrease with close monitoring. Protamine is reserved for serious bleeding or overdose.
items.a: Hold the infusion for the time the nomogram specifies, then restart at the lower rate
w: Give protamine sulfate IV now and discontinue heparin for the rest of the stay
Continue the current rate and redraw the aPTT in 6 hours to confirm the value
Cut the rate in half without stopping it and report the aPTT result at the morning rounds

items.q: A client on a heparin infusion has a platelet count fall from 240,000 to 105,000/mm3. Which added detail most supports heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
items.x: HIT is an antibody reaction that appears on about day 5 to 10, with a fall of more than 50 percent and new clot rather than bleeding. A drop within hours is usually nonimmune and transient.
items.a: It began on day 6 and the left calf is swollen
w: It began within 6 hours of the first heparin bolus
There is new oozing from the gums and the IV sites
The count fell while the aPTT stayed below the goal

items.q: A client in DKA has glucose 486 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 8 mEq/L. Why does the insulin infusion wait?
items.x: Per ADA guidance insulin is delayed until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L, because insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can cause a fatal arrhythmia. Fluid and potassium replacement come first.
items.a: Insulin drives potassium into the cells
w: Insulin cannot work in a low potassium state
The bicarbonate must be corrected first
The glucose must be lowered with fluid first

items.q: Four hours into a DKA insulin infusion, glucose is 212 mg/dL and the anion gap is still 19. What does the open gap show about the insulin's work?
items.x: The anion gap tracks ketoacids. A gap that is still open means the insulin has more to do, even though the glucose is near target.
items.a: Ketone production is not yet switched off
w: The insulin has stopped working on glucose
The kidneys are no longer clearing glucose
Potassium has shifted fully out of the cells

items.q: A client whose DKA has resolved is to change from the IV insulin infusion to subcutaneous Lantus. Which plan is safest?
items.x: IV insulin has a half-life of minutes, so basal insulin must overlap the drip by 1-2 hours to prevent rebound hyperglycemia and ketosis. Stopping the drip first leaves a gap with no insulin on board.
items.a: Give the glargine, then stop the infusion about 2 hours later
w: Stop the infusion first, then give glargine once the client eats
Stop the infusion and give the glargine at the very same moment
Give glargine and keep the infusion running for another 24 hours

items.q: A client is on insulin lispro with meals and insulin glargine at bedtime. Breakfast trays will be 45 minutes late. Which dose does the delay change?
items.x: Lispro starts within about 15 minutes and peaks in 1 to 2 hours, so it is timed within 15 minutes of food. Glargine is a peakless basal insulin given on a fixed schedule regardless of meals.
items.a: The lispro, because it acts in about 15 minutes
w: The glargine, because it peaks at the morning meal
Both doses, because each is matched to food intake
Neither dose, since glucose is checked before both

items.q: Which statement by a client starting Lantus shows a need for more teaching?
items.x: Glargine must never be mixed with another insulin because mixing changes its acidic solution and its long action. It is clear, so it needs no rolling, and basal insulin usually continues on sick days.
items.a: I can draw up my Lantus and NovoLog together to save an injection
w: I give the Lantus at about the same time every day, even on sick days
I do not need to roll or shake the Lantus pen before I inject it
I keep the pen I am using at room temperature and date it when opened

items.q: A client received NPH and regular insulin at 0730, ate half of breakfast, and refused lunch. When is this client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia?
items.x: NPH peaks about 4-12 hours after injection, so a missed lunch puts the risk in the afternoon. Regular insulin peaks in 2-4 hours and is long gone by 0300.
items.a: Mid-afternoon, when the NPH effect peaks
w: Within 15 minutes of the morning injection
Around 0300, when the regular insulin peaks
Only right before lunch, when regular peaks

items.q: An order reads: potassium chloride 40 mEq in 100 mL IV over 1 hour via the forearm peripheral IV on a med-surg unit. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Most policies cap peripheral potassium at about 10 mEq/h outside monitored units, and 40 mEq/h risks arrhythmia and vein injury. Potassium is never given by IV push or by gravity.
items.a: Clarify the order, because the rate exceeds the usual peripheral limit
w: Give it as ordered on an infusion pump, checking the IV site every 15 minutes
Run it by gravity with a roller clamp so it can be stopped quickly
Give it as a slow IV push over 5 minutes through the same catheter

items.q: Four clients each have potassium chloride 10 mEq IV ordered for a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. Which order should the nurse question first?
items.x: Potassium leaves the body almost entirely through the kidneys, so new oliguria with a doubled creatinine turns replacement into hyperkalemia. The other three have ordinary reasons to run low and need the dose.
items.a: Urine output 12 mL/h, creatinine risen to 2.1 mg/dL
w: Taking furosemide 40 mg daily with a magnesium of 1.9
Taking metoprolol with a heart rate of 58 beats a minute
Vomiting for 2 days with a bicarbonate of 32 mEq/L

items.q: A monitored client has potassium 6.4 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves. The rider is stopped and three more orders arrive. Which one protects the heart fastest?
items.x: Calcium does not lower the potassium at all; it restores the gap between resting and threshold potential in the myocardium within minutes. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium in 15 to 30 minutes, and polystyrene and diuresis remove it slowly.
items.a: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV
w: Insulin with dextrose IV
Oral sodium polystyrene
Furosemide 40 mg by IV push

items.q: A client on magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia has a serum magnesium of 9.5 mg/dL. Which finding fits that level?
items.x: Reflexes disappear around 8 to 10 mg/dL, which is why they are the hourly bedside check. Respiratory depression comes near 12, cardiac arrest above 25, and flushing with drowsiness fits the therapeutic 4 to 7 range.
items.a: Patellar reflexes that can no longer be elicited
w: A respiratory rate that has fallen to 8 per minute
Complete heart block on the cardiac monitor
Flushing and warmth with mild drowsiness only

items.q: A client on a magnesium sulfate infusion has these findings. Which one places her at greatest risk of magnesium toxicity?
items.x: Magnesium is cleared only by the kidneys, so renal impairment lets it build up. Flushing during the bolus is expected, and 2+ reflexes and a level of 5.8 mg/dL are within usual targets.
items.a: Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with falling urine output
w: Patellar reflexes 2+ and equal on both sides
Flushing and warmth during the loading dose
A serum magnesium of 5.8 mg/dL per protocol

items.q: A client on magnesium sulfate for severe preeclampsia has an emergency cesarean under general anesthesia with rocuronium. What should the PACU nurse watch for most closely?
items.x: Magnesium reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and potentiates nondepolarizing blockers, so residual paralysis and respiratory depression are the risk. Rocuronium does not trigger malignant hyperthermia.
items.a: Prolonged weakness and hypoventilation from potentiated blockade
w: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the two drugs used together
Rebound hypertension as the paralytic wears off in the first hour
Seizure activity caused by rocuronium lowering seizure threshold

items.q: A post-op client on IV morphine has SpO2 95 percent on 2 L oxygen and a respiratory rate of 12. Which finding most predicts respiratory depression?
items.x: On the Pasero sedation scale, unintended sleepiness during conversation is the point at which the opioid is reduced, because sedation precedes respiratory depression. Miosis, itching and pain relief are expected effects.
items.a: Falling asleep mid-sentence
w: A pain score that has dropped from 8 to 3
Pupils that are 2 mm and equally reactive
Itching across the chest and upper arms

items.q: An opioid-naive 80-year-old's order reads Dilaudid 4 mg IV every 4 hours PRN pain. Yesterday she received morphine 4 mg IV. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Hydromorphone is roughly 5-7 times as potent as morphine, and the labeled IV starting range for opioid-naive adults is 0.2-1 mg. A milligram-for-milligram swap is a classic fatal error.
items.a: Question the order, as the dose is far above opioid-naive starting doses
w: Give it as ordered, since it matches the morphine dose she tolerated
Give it as ordered but over 5 minutes with an oxygen saturation probe
Give half now and the other half in an hour if pain is not relieved

items.q: A client with renal failure on IV morphine received naloxone for RR 6/min and became alert. Ninety minutes later the RR is again 6/min. What best explains this?
items.x: Naloxone acts for about 30-90 minutes, shorter than many opioids, and morphine's active metabolite builds up in renal failure. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
items.a: Naloxone wore off before the opioid and its active metabolite did
w: The client developed tolerance to naloxone after a single dose
A new problem such as a stroke is the most likely cause of this
The naloxone dose was too high and caused rebound sedation

items.q: A hospice client on high-dose opioids for bone cancer pain is arousable only to pain with RR 7/min. Per your protocol, how should naloxone be given?
items.x: In opioid-tolerant clients, small titrated doses reverse respiratory depression without causing severe withdrawal and a pain crisis. Hospice status alone does not forbid treating an unintended overdose.
items.a: Dilute it and give small increments, titrated to the breathing rate
w: Give 2 mg IV push rapidly, repeating every 2 minutes until fully alert
Give 4 mg intranasally, then hold all opioids for the next 24 hours
Do not give naloxone at all, because the client is receiving hospice

items.q: A client with a fentanyl 50 mcg/h patch has several new orders. Which one should the nurse question first?
items.x: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, which can raise fentanyl levels and cause fatal respiratory depression (boxed warning). The other drugs do not affect fentanyl metabolism.
items.a: Clarithromycin 500 mg PO twice daily
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours
Docusate sodium 100 mg PO twice daily
Famotidine 20 mg PO twice daily now

items.q: A client wearing a Duragesic patch develops a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and becomes hard to arouse with RR 9/min. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Heat and fever increase transdermal fentanyl absorption and can cause overdose. The patch is removed, the client stimulated, and the provider notified.
items.a: Fever increased drug absorption through the skin
w: Sepsis is causing encephalopathy without opioid effect
The patch was worn past 72 hours and began to leak
The fever lowered the opioid's protein binding

items.q: A client on methadone 120 mg daily is admitted with pneumonia. QTc 498 ms, K 3.2 mEq/L, Mg 1.5 mg/dL. Levofloxacin and ondansetron are ordered. What is the priority action?
items.x: Methadone, levofloxacin and ondansetron all prolong QT, and low potassium and magnesium add to torsades risk. Abruptly holding methadone causes withdrawal and does not quickly shorten the QT.
items.a: Report the QT risk and request electrolyte replacement before the doses
w: Give both drugs and recheck the ECG in the morning per the routine unit protocol
Give the methadone later today to make room for the new medications
Give the ondansetron now and the levofloxacin after the next ECG

items.q: Which statement by a client discharged on OxyContin shows a need for more teaching?
items.x: Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the whole dose at once and can cause a fatal overdose.
items.a: If it is hard to swallow, I can crush it into some applesauce
w: I will not drink any alcohol while I am taking this medicine
I will keep it locked up and away from my grandchildren at home
I will add fiber and a stool softener while I take this medicine

items.q: A client who uses illicit fentanyl wants to begin buprenorphine-naloxone in the ED. Before the first dose, which finding matters most?
items.x: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist that displaces full agonists, so it precipitates withdrawal unless the client is already in moderate withdrawal. A fixed 72-hour wait or a negative screen is not required.
items.a: Objective signs of moderate withdrawal on the COWS scale
w: A urine drug screen that is negative for fentanyl now
At least 72 hours since the last use of any fentanyl
A normal liver panel drawn earlier during the visit

items.q: A client on warfarin has an INR of 11.4 and no signs of bleeding. What does the nurse anticipate per current guidelines?
items.x: With an INR above 10 and no bleeding, guidelines advise holding warfarin and giving low-dose oral vitamin K. IV vitamin K with PCC is reserved for major bleeding.
items.a: Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
w: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus 4-factor PCC
Hold one dose, then resume the same dose
Transfuse 2 units of fresh frozen plasma

items.q: A client with a stable INR on warfarin is prescribed an antibiotic for a UTI. Which choice should prompt the nurse to request closer INR monitoring?
items.x: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main pathway for S-warfarin, and can sharply raise the INR. The others have little effect on warfarin.
items.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim DS)
w: Nitrofurantoin monohydrate (Macrobid)
Cephalexin (Keflex) four times daily
Fosfomycin as a single oral dose sachet

items.q: A client has enoxaparin ordered every 12 hours for DVT. Creatinine clearance is 24 mL/min. Why does this clearance matter for enoxaparin?
items.x: Enoxaparin is cleared by the kidneys. Below a clearance of 30 the label reduces the frequency to once daily to avoid accumulation and bleeding.
items.a: The kidneys clear it, so it accumulates and bleeding risk rises
w: The kidneys activate the drug, so it will not work at this level
The drug injures the kidneys further at any dose that is given
The drug binds creatinine and falsely raises the reported level

items.q: A client with an epidural catheter received enoxaparin 40 mg subcut at 2100. Anesthesia asks when the catheter may be removed. What should the nurse say?
items.x: The label calls for at least 12 hours between a prophylactic dose and catheter removal, and at least 4 hours after removal before the next dose, to limit the risk of spinal hematoma and paralysis.
items.a: At 0900, 12 hours after the dose
w: At 0100, about 4 hours after the dose
At 2130, once the site stops oozing
At 0300, about 6 hours after the dose

items.q: A client is 40 minutes into an alteplase infusion for stroke. Which finding means the infusion is stopped and an emergent head CT is obtained?
items.x: Sudden headache, vomiting and neurologic decline during thrombolysis suggest intracranial hemorrhage, the feared complication. Minor oozing, nausea and a pressure under 180/105 are managed without stopping the drug.
items.a: Headache, vomiting, and a GCS fall of 3 points
w: Oozing from the antecubital venipuncture site
A blood pressure that has risen to 176/98 mm Hg
A transient nausea with no change in the neuro exam

items.q: Two stroke clients both have a BP of 196/108. One received alteplase an hour ago and one did not. How do their targets differ?
items.x: AHA guidance keeps BP at or below 180/105 for 24 hours after a lytic to limit hemorrhage, and allows up to 220/120 when no lytic was given. The 185/110 figure is the threshold before the lytic is started.
items.a: The treated client is kept at or below 180/105
w: The treated client is kept at or below 220/120 instead
Both clients are kept at or below 185/110
Neither client has the pressure lowered at all

items.q: During alteplase for stroke, a client develops swelling of the tongue and lip on one side. Which home medication most increases the risk of this reaction?
items.x: Orolingual angioedema during alteplase is more common in clients on ACE inhibitors, because both raise bradykinin activity.
items.a: Lisinopril
w: Metformin
Atorvastatin
Amlodipine

items.q: A norepinephrine infusion has extravasated into the forearm, which is pale and cool. Which antidote does the nurse expect to infiltrate into the site?
items.x: Phentolamine reverses the alpha-mediated vasoconstriction that is starving the tissue of blood. Hyaluronidase is used for vinca and nutrition extravasation, thiosulfate for mechlorethamine, and dexrazoxane for anthracyclines.
items.a: Phentolamine, an alpha blocker
w: Hyaluronidase, which spreads the drug out in tissue
Sodium thiosulfate, which binds the drug locally
Dexrazoxane, which protects the tissue from injury

items.q: A client on norepinephrine titrated to MAP 65 or higher has an arterial line reading 76/42 (MAP 53) with a flattened waveform. Cuff BP is 112/66 and mentation is unchanged. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: A damped arterial waveform underreads systolic pressure, and titrating to a false reading causes harmful vasoconstriction. Correlate with the cuff and fix the line first.
items.a: Troubleshoot the line: flush, level and zero it
w: Increase the norepinephrine to bring MAP above 65
Add vasopressin and report refractory shock now
Give a 1 L crystalloid bolus while awaiting orders

items.q: A client has received Nipride for 3 days. New findings: confusion, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, falling bicarbonate, and venous blood that looks bright red. What should the nurse suspect?
items.x: Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis and high venous oxygen content. The infusion is stopped and hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate given.
items.a: Cyanide toxicity from nitroprusside metabolism
w: Thiocyanate retention from mild renal impairment
Methemoglobinemia from the nitrite ions released
Septic shock that has gone unrecognized for days

items.q: A client with chest pain took a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor last night. How long are nitrates withheld?
items.x: Tadalafil has a half-life near 17.5 hours against roughly 4 hours for sildenafil, so the nitrate-free interval is 48 hours after tadalafil and 24 hours after sildenafil. A nitrate inside that window can cause profound hypotension.
items.a: 48 hours for tadalafil and 24 for sildenafil
w: 24 hours for either drug, since both are short acting
48 hours for either drug, since both are long acting
12 hours for tadalafil and 48 for sildenafil

items.q: A client with an inferior STEMI has BP 92/58, clear lungs, JVD, and ST elevation in lead V4R. Why is nitroglycerin a problem here?
items.x: ST elevation in V4R with clear lungs and raised neck veins points to right ventricular infarction, which fills by volume, so a venodilator drops cardiac output sharply. A fluid bolus is given instead.
items.a: A right ventricular infarct needs preload
w: Nitrates block conduction through the AV node
Nitrates raise oxygen demand in the right heart
A right ventricular infarct causes pulmonary edema

items.q: A client in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 152 has a Cardizem bolus and drip ordered. Which finding should make the nurse question the order?
items.x: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers depress contractility and can cause decompensation in HFrEF; amiodarone or digoxin is usually chosen instead.
items.a: Heart failure with an ejection fraction of 20 percent
w: An irregularly irregular rhythm on the cardiac monitor
BP of 118/76 mmHg with brisk capillary refill
Taking apixaban daily for stroke prevention at home

items.q: An amiodarone maintenance infusion arrives mixed at 3.6 mg/mL. The client has only a 20-gauge forearm IV. What should the nurse do?
items.x: The label calls for a central line when concentrations exceed 2 mg/mL because of phlebitis risk, and amiodarone infusions use an in-line filter.
items.a: Clarify it, because this concentration needs central access
w: Give it, since amiodarone is safe through any peripheral catheter
Give it through the forearm IV and check the site every 4 hours
Give it through the forearm IV after removing the in-line filter

items.q: A client on digoxin reports nausea and yellow-tinged vision. Apical HR 54. Digoxin level 1.4 ng/mL, K 2.9 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding to the sodium-potassium pump, so toxicity can occur with a normal level. Levels are drawn at least 6 hours after a dose.
items.a: Hold digoxin and report possible toxicity from the low potassium
w: Give the digoxin, since the level is within the reference range
Give digoxin and an antiemetic, then recheck the level in 6 hours
Hold digoxin and request a level drawn 2 hours after the next dose

items.q: Four hours after DigiFab for digoxin toxicity, the HR and potassium have normalized, but the total digoxin level rose from 4.1 to 9.8 ng/mL. What does this mean?
items.x: Most assays measure total digoxin, including drug bound to Fab, so levels rise after treatment and are unreliable. The clinical response guides care.
items.a: It is expected, since the assay also counts Fab-bound drug
w: Fab failed, so a second full dose is needed right away
The sample was drawn from the line used to infuse the Fab
Toxicity is worsening and the client now needs dialysis

items.q: An 86-year-old on digoxin 0.25 mg daily has a creatinine clearance that has fallen to 28 mL/min. Which new findings most suggest toxicity?
items.x: In older adults digoxin toxicity often shows first as anorexia, nausea and confusion, well before bradycardia, and reduced renal clearance lets the drug build up. A heart rate above 60 does not rule it out.
items.a: Loss of appetite with confusion
w: A heart rate of 64 and a dry mouth
A dry cough with new ankle swelling
Thirst with frequent urination at night

items.q: A client in SVT takes dipyridamole. Adenosine is about to be given. What should the nurse anticipate per ACLS?
items.x: Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake and potentiates it, so ACLS suggests a reduced first dose of 3 mg. Caffeine and theophylline have the opposite effect.
items.a: A smaller first dose, since dipyridamole boosts its effect
w: A larger first dose, since dipyridamole blocks its effect
The usual dose, since there is no interaction between them
Avoiding adenosine, since the pair is fully contraindicated

items.q: A client with BP 214/124 and an acute asthma flare with diffuse wheezes has IV labetalol ordered. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Labetalol blocks beta-2 receptors and can worsen bronchospasm; agents such as nicardipine or clevidipine avoid this. Labetalol is not cardioselective.
items.a: Question the order because of the bronchospasm
w: Give it, since labetalol is cardioselective
Give it right after an albuterol treatment
Give half the dose and recheck in 10 minutes

items.q: A client on Diprivan at 70 mcg/kg/min for 4 days has new findings: lactate 6.1, CK 9,400, K 6.0, and a new RBBB pattern. What should the nurse suspect?
items.x: Prolonged high-dose propofol can cause metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and heart failure. The infusion is stopped and the provider notified.
items.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Central line-associated sepsis
Malignant hyperthermia crisis

items.q: A propofol bottle and its tubing were spiked 14 hours ago and 40 mL remain. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that supports bacterial growth, so the label requires discarding the bottle and tubing 12 hours after spiking.
items.a: Replace the bottle and the tubing
w: Let it run until the bottle is empty
Replace the bottle but keep the tubing
Add a new filter and keep it running

items.q: A client needs sedation but has borderline hypotension and a heart rate of 50. Which difference between dexmedetomidine and propofol matters most here?
items.x: As an alpha-2 agonist, dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia and hypotension but little respiratory depression, which is why it can sedate an unintubated client. With a rate of 50 already, that bradycardia is the limiting problem.
items.a: Dexmedetomidine slows the heart rate further
w: Dexmedetomidine depresses respiration far more
Dexmedetomidine raises the blood pressure
Dexmedetomidine has no effect on heart rate

items.q: A client is scheduled for sedation with IV midazolam. Which home medication should the nurse report to the anesthesia team?
items.x: Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, the main pathway for midazolam, so sedation becomes deep and prolonged and the plan has to change. The other three do not inhibit that pathway.
items.a: Ritonavir, taken as part of an HIV regimen
w: Levetiracetam, taken twice daily for seizures
Metformin, taken twice daily with the meals
Rosuvastatin, taken each evening at bedtime

items.q: A client who took an unknown number of pills is sedated. The QRS is 140 ms, and the family says she takes alprazolam daily. Flumazenil is ordered. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A wide QRS suggests a tricyclic co-ingestion, and both TCAs and chronic benzodiazepine use make flumazenil-induced seizures likely.
items.a: Question the order because of seizure risk
w: Give it, since a benzodiazepine is likely
Give it slowly over 30 seconds with suction
Give it, then prepare activated charcoal

items.q: A client on a Nimbex infusion has HR 128, BP 172/98, and tears on the cheeks. Train-of-four is 1/4. What do these findings suggest?
items.x: Paralytics provide no sedation or analgesia, so tachycardia, hypertension and tearing in a paralyzed client suggest awareness or pain. A TOF of 1/4 shows the blockade is adequate.
items.a: Inadequate sedation or pain control
w: Too little neuromuscular blockade
Early neuromuscular blocker toxicity
Expected autonomic effects of paralysis

items.q: A 28-year-old who takes oral contraceptives received Bridion at the end of surgery. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen, so the label treats it like a missed pill and advises a nonhormonal backup method for 7 days.
items.a: Use a backup birth control method for 7 days
w: No change is needed with the contraceptive pill
Stop taking the contraceptive pill for a week
Take two contraceptive pills tomorrow morning

items.q: During surgery with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, which finding is often the earliest sign that dantrolene will be needed?
items.x: Malignant hyperthermia raises CO2 production first. Hyperthermia and myoglobinuria are later findings.
items.a: Rising EtCO2 despite more ventilation
w: Temperature of 40 C (104 F) with heavy sweating
Dark brown urine in the Foley drainage bag
Bradycardia and widening pulse pressure

items.q: Vancomycin 1 g IV is run over 30 minutes. The client develops flushing of the face and neck and itching. BP is 108/68 with no wheezing. What should the nurse do?
items.x: This is the vancomycin infusion reaction from histamine release at fast rates; the label calls for infusion over at least 60 minutes. It is not a true allergy.
items.a: Stop it, notify, then resume at a slower rate
w: Give epinephrine IM for suspected anaphylaxis
Stop it and chart vancomycin as an allergy
Continue it and give acetaminophen for comfort

items.q: A 10-day-old infant receiving calcium-containing parenteral nutrition is ordered ceftriaxone. What should the nurse do?
items.x: In neonates, ceftriaxone with calcium-containing IV solutions can form fatal precipitates in the lungs and kidneys even through separate lines, so the label contraindicates it.
items.a: Question the order because of the calcium
w: Give it through a separate IV line instead
Flush with saline between the two infusions
Give it, since neonates tolerate ceftriaxone

items.q: A client on sertraline is started on Zyvox. Two days later the client is agitated and sweaty, with temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F) and inducible clonus. What is most likely?
items.x: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor that, with SSRIs, can cause serotonin syndrome. Clonus and hyperreflexia separate it from NMS, which causes rigidity.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
A linezolid drug allergy
Sepsis from the VRE infection

items.q: A client with eGFR 38 on metformin is scheduled for a CT with IV iodinated contrast. What does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: With eGFR 30-60, the label says stop metformin at or before the contrast study and restart 48 hours later if renal function is stable, because AKI can lead to lactic acidosis.
items.a: Hold metformin at the scan, then recheck eGFR in 48 h
w: Continue metformin, since it does not affect the kidneys
Stop metformin permanently because of this eGFR level
Hold it only on the morning of the scan, then resume it

items.q: An 82-year-old taking glyburide has recurrent hypoglycemia overnight after D50 at midnight. CrCl is 35 mL/min. What should the nurse expect?
items.x: Glyburide has active metabolites that build up in renal impairment, causing prolonged hypoglycemia that outlasts a D50 bolus. The Beers criteria advise avoiding it in older adults.
items.a: Prolonged monitoring and a dextrose infusion
w: One more dose of D50, then discharge home
Glucagon IM to prevent another low tonight
A glucose recheck only at 0600 with breakfast

items.q: A client on Jardiance, NPO 2 days after surgery, has glucose 178 mg/dL, pH 7.19, bicarbonate 11, and anion gap 22. What does the nurse suspect?
items.x: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with fasting or surgery; the label advises holding it 3 days before surgery.
items.a: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
w: Lactic acidosis from hypoperfusion
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Harmless starvation ketosis only

items.q: A client's stable lithium level was 0.8 mEq/L. After starting a new medication, a week later the client has coarse tremor, vomiting and confusion with a level of 1.9. Which new medication most likely caused it?
items.x: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can push levels into the toxic range, as can thiazides and ACE inhibitors.
items.a: Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours
w: Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours
Amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure
Omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast

items.q: Which statement by a client taking lithium shows a need for more teaching?
items.x: Low sodium intake makes the kidneys hold onto lithium and can cause toxicity. Sodium intake should stay consistent.
items.a: I will cut way back on salt to protect my heart
w: I will drink about 2 to 3 liters of fluid each day
I will call the clinic if I have vomiting or diarrhea
I will get my lithium level checked when I am told

items.q: A client on phenytoin has nystagmus and ataxia. The total level is 9 mcg/mL (range 10-20) and albumin is 2.0 g/dL. A dose increase is ordered. What should the nurse do?
items.x: With low albumin, more phenytoin is unbound, so the total level underestimates active drug. The clinical signs of toxicity matter more than the number.
items.a: Report the toxicity signs and ask about a free level
w: Give the higher dose, since the level is below range
Give the higher dose and recheck the total level tomorrow
Hold all phenytoin until albumin is replaced IV

items.q: IV phenytoin is to be given piggyback into a running line of D5W. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions, so it is given only with normal saline and the line is flushed before and after.
items.a: Flush with saline before and after the dose
w: Give it through the D5W line very slowly
Mix the phenytoin into the D5W bag first
Give it through the D5W line quickly

items.q: A client who was seizure-free on valproic acid is started on meropenem for pneumonia and has a seizure two days later. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Carbapenems sharply reduce valproate levels, and raising the valproate dose does not overcome this; a different antibiotic or antiseizure drug is needed.
items.a: Meropenem lowered valproate levels
w: Meropenem directly causes seizures
Pneumonia lowered seizure threshold
The valproate level rose too high

items.q: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F), rigidity, labile BP, and a CK of 12,000. Which finding separates this from serotonin syndrome?
items.x: Both syndromes cause fever, rigidity and autonomic instability, but neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, while serotonin syndrome gives clonus and hyperreflexia. Fever and a high CK occur in both.
items.a: Lead-pipe rigidity without clonus
w: A temperature above 40 C with sweating
A creatine kinase level in the thousands
Labile blood pressure with tachycardia

items.q: A 3-year-old weighing 14 kg has IV acetaminophen 210 mg every 4 hours ordered. What should the nurse do?
items.x: For ages 2-12 the label gives 15 mg/kg every 6 hours or 12.5 mg/kg every 4 hours, maximum 75 mg/kg/day. 210 mg every 4 hours is 90 mg/kg/day.
items.a: Clarify, since the daily total exceeds the label maximum
w: Give it as ordered, since each single dose is within range
Give it as ordered but only overnight while the child is awake
Give it orally instead at the same dose and the same interval

items.q: Four discharge prescriptions are being reviewed. For which client does the label contraindicate tramadol?
items.x: Tramadol is contraindicated under age 12, and after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy under 18, because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers convert it to a large opioid load. Renal impairment and an SSRI call for caution, not a ban.
items.a: A 7-year-old going home after a tonsillectomy
w: A 70-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 45
A 40-year-old taking sertraline for depression
A 55-year-old with a history of kidney stones

items.q: A parent of a 1-year-old says: When the children's ibuprofen runs out, I will give the same 5 mL using the infant drops. How should the nurse respond?
items.x: Infant drops are 50 mg per 1.25 mL, four times as strong as the 100 mg per 5 mL children's liquid, so 5 mL of drops would be 4 times the dose.
items.a: The infant drops are stronger, so the dose is different
w: That is right, because both forms have the same strength
That is right, as long as you give it with food or milk
Infant drops act faster, so give them half as often instead

items.q: An infant's order is digoxin 0.04 mg PO. The elixir is 0.05 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
items.x: 0.04 mg divided by 0.05 mg/mL is 0.8 mL; a decimal slip gives a 10-fold error. Pediatric digoxin doses need an independent double check.
items.a: 0.8 mL
w: 8 mL

items.q: A 79-year-old started oxybutynin a week ago and also takes diphenhydramine at night. She now has new confusion, constipation, and a bladder scan of 650 mL. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Both drugs are anticholinergic, and older adults are at high risk for delirium, urinary retention and constipation; the Beers criteria advise avoiding both.
items.a: Additive anticholinergic drug effects
w: An acute urinary tract infection
Early Alzheimer type dementia onset
Dehydration from poor oral fluid intake

items.q: A 76-year-old on lisinopril and furosemide starts OTC ibuprofen for arthritis. A week later the creatinine has doubled. What is the most likely mechanism?
items.x: This triple whammy lowers filtration: NSAIDs block prostaglandin dilation of the afferent arteriole, the ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, and the diuretic reduces volume.
items.a: NSAID afferent constriction plus ACE efferent dilation
w: Volume depletion caused by the furosemide alone
Allergic interstitial nephritis from the ACE inhibitor therapy
Direct tubular toxicity from the loop diuretic

items.q: Two nurses check a new heparin infusion. The bag reads 25,000 units in 250 mL. Which finding must be corrected before starting?
items.x: If the pump assumes 50 units/mL but the bag holds 100 units/mL, every rate it calculates delivers twice the ordered dose.
items.a: The pump concentration is set to 25,000 units in 500 mL
w: The order lists the client's weight in kilograms only
The aPTT is ordered for 6 hours after the infusion starts
The pump is using the drug library's heparin entry

items.q: Per the ICU protocol, norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 0.1 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
items.x: The concentration is 16 mcg/mL; 0.1 x 80 = 8 mcg/min = 480 mcg/h, and 480 divided by 16 is 30 mL/h.
items.a: 30 mL/h
w: 3 mL/h
0.5 mL/h
48 mL/h

items.q: Dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL is ordered at 5 mcg/kg/min for a 70 kg client. What rate should the nurse set?
items.x: The concentration is 1,600 mcg/mL; 5 x 70 = 350 mcg/min = 21,000 mcg/h, and 21,000 divided by 1,600 is 13.1 mL/h.
w: 1.3 mL/h
8.8 mL/h

items.q: At the start of the shift, which client should the nurse see first?
items.x: Sedation with snoring and a low RR on a PCA signals impending opioid respiratory depression. The other clients are in range or stable.
items.a: PCA client who is snoring and drifts off, RR 10

items.q: A 66-year-old man started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension later has a gout flare. Which set of laboratory changes is expected with this drug?
