5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone without others
Prochlorperazine, lorazepam, and dexamethasone only

items.q: A 54-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). ANC is 200/mm3. BP is 122/76 mm Hg, she has no catheter site infection, and lungs are clear. Which is the most appropriate empiric therapy?
items.x: High-risk febrile neutropenia requires prompt IV monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications such as instability or catheter infection.
items.a: Intravenous cefepime
w: Intravenous ceftriaxone
Intravenous vancomycin
Intravenous ertapenem

items.q: A 16-year-old boy with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Which medication is given 24 hours later to protect normal cells?
items.x: Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to rescue normal cells after high-dose methotrexate. Hydration, urine alkalinization, and level monitoring are also used.

Dexrazoxane
Folic acid

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is receiving IV cyclophosphamide. Which medication reduces her risk of hemorrhagic cystitis?
items.x: Acrolein, a cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide metabolite, injures the bladder. Mesna binds acrolein in the urine; hydration also helps.
items.a: Mesna
w: Leucovorin
Amifostine
Dexrazoxane

items.q: A 64-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has new back pain, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary retention. Which is the most appropriate immediate step while arranging urgent MRI of the spine?
items.x: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is treated with high-dose dexamethasone immediately, then urgent MRI of the whole spine and radiation or surgery.
items.a: Intravenous dexamethasone
w: Intravenous zoledronic acid
Intramuscular leuprolide
Intravenous hydromorphone

items.q: A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer starts scheduled oxycodone for pain. Which is the most appropriate bowel regimen to start at the same time?
items.x: Opioid-induced constipation should be prevented when opioids are started, using a stimulant laxative such as senna, with or without an osmotic laxative. Fiber can worsen it, and docusate alone is ineffective.
items.a: Scheduled senna

Scheduled docusate
As-needed bisacodyl

items.q: A 68-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min) has an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent crystals. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: Glucocorticoids are preferred for acute gout in advanced CKD. NSAIDs worsen kidney function, and colchicine requires dose reduction in CKD; hourly high-dose colchicine is no longer used.
items.a: Oral prednisone 30 to 40 mg daily for 5 days

Start allopurinol 300 mg daily alone

items.q: A 58-year-old man of Korean descent with CKD stage 3 has recurrent gout and tophi. Urate-lowering therapy is planned. Which test is recommended before starting allopurinol?
items.x: ACR recommends HLA-B*5801 testing before allopurinol in people of Korean descent with CKD 3 or worse and in those of Han Chinese, Thai, or African ancestry, because the allele predicts severe cutaneous reactions.
items.a: HLA-B*5801 testing

Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
24-hour urinary uric acid excretion

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis with high disease activity. Liver enzymes, creatinine, and CBC are normal. She does not drink alcohol. Which is the most appropriate initial DMARD?
items.x: ACR recommends methotrexate monotherapy as the first DMARD in RA with moderate to high disease activity, with folic acid to reduce adverse effects. Long-term glucocorticoids should be avoided.
items.a: Methotrexate with folic acid
w: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy
Adalimumab monotherapy
Prednisone monotherapy

items.q: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, and 1 day of blurred vision in the left eye. ESR is 98 mm/h. Temporal artery biopsy is scheduled for next week. Which is the most appropriate next step?
items.x: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms requires immediate high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone) to prevent permanent vision loss. Biopsy remains diagnostic for 2 weeks or more.
items.a: Start high-dose glucocorticoids now, before biopsy

Start low-dose prednisone daily

items.q: A 70-year-old woman has 2 months of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. ESR is 62 mm/h and CK is normal. She has no headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: Polymyalgia rheumatica responds rapidly to low-dose prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg daily with a slow taper. High doses are used for giant cell arteritis.
items.a: Prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg daily

Methotrexate monotherapy
Oral naproxen 500 mg twice daily alone

items.q: A 26-year-old woman with SLE has hematuria, proteinuria of 2.5 g/day, and rising creatinine. Kidney biopsy shows class IV lupus nephritis. Which is the most appropriate induction therapy with glucocorticoids?
items.x: Mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids is used to induce remission in proliferative lupus nephritis. Belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor may be added.
items.a: Mycophenolate mofetil
w: Azathioprine
Methotrexate
Hydroxychloroquine

items.q: A 48-year-old woman has a duodenal ulcer and a positive H. pylori stool antigen. She received clarithromycin for sinusitis last year. She has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: ACG prefers bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days for treatment-naive H. pylori infection, especially with prior macrolide exposure, because clarithromycin resistance is common.
items.a: Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days
w: PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 7 days
PPI and amoxicillin for 5 days
Levofloxacin alone for 10 days

items.q: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis has hematemesis. BP is 92/58 mm Hg and pulse 116/min. He is given blood transfusions with a hemoglobin target of 7 g/dL. Which is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy before endoscopy?
items.x: Suspected variceal bleeding is treated with a vasoactive agent such as octreotide and antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone, followed by endoscopy within 12 hours. Nonselective beta blockers are avoided acutely.
items.a: Octreotide infusion and IV ceftriaxone
w: Pantoprazole infusion and IV vitamin K
Oral propranolol and IV ceftriaxone
Octreotide infusion and oral nadolol

items.q: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a second episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy despite adherence to lactulose with 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Which is the most appropriate addition?
items.x: Rifaximin added to lactulose reduces recurrent hepatic encephalopathy and hospitalization. Long-term metronidazole is neurotoxic, protein restriction is not recommended, and benzodiazepines precipitate encephalopathy.
items.a: Add rifaximin
w: Add long-term metronidazole three times daily
Restrict dietary protein to 0.5 g/kg/day
Add lorazepam at night for agitation

items.q: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Ascitic fluid has 640 neutrophils/mm3. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL and bilirubin is 4.2 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin. With creatinine above 1 mg/dL or bilirubin above 4 mg/dL, albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces kidney failure and death.
items.a: IV cefotaxime plus albumin on days 1 and 3

Oral norfloxacin daily
Large-volume paracentesis and IV furosemide

items.q: A 32-year-old woman has mildly to moderately active ulcerative colitis extending to the splenic flexure with 4 bloody stools daily. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
items.x: Oral 5-ASA (2 g or more daily) combined with rectal mesalamine is first-line for mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis. Steroids are for induction only and antibiotics have no role.

Oral prednisone with rectal mesalamine
Oral azathioprine with rectal mesalamine

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with heavy alcohol use has jaundice, fever, and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 14 mg/dL, AST 220 U/L, and ALT 90 U/L. Maddrey discriminant function is 48. Infection and GI bleeding are excluded. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: Prednisolone improves short-term survival in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (discriminant function 32 or more or MELD above 20). Prednisolone is used rather than prednisone because it does not require hepatic activation.
items.a: Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days

N-acetylcysteine alone
Infliximab infusion

Direct toxicity to cerebellar Purkinje cells

items.q: A 70-year-old man with CKD has weakness. Potassium is 7.4 mEq/L and ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Which is the most appropriate first medication?
items.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes in hyperkalemia with ECG changes. Insulin with glucose and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and binders, diuretics, or dialysis remove it.
items.a: Intravenous calcium gluconate

Intravenous furosemide
Patiromer orally with a recheck in 6 hours

items.q: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is confused and dehydrated. Calcium is 14.6 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.x: Severe hypercalcemia of malignancy is treated with IV isotonic saline, calcitonin for rapid effect, and a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid or denosumab for sustained control. Thiazides raise calcium.

Oral alendronate and increased fluid intake
Hydrochlorothiazide and oral fluids

items.q: A 62-year-old man on long-term omeprazole and furosemide has potassium 2.9 mEq/L despite 3 days of oral potassium chloride. Magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
items.x: Hypomagnesemia causes renal potassium wasting through ROMK, making hypokalemia refractory until magnesium is replaced. PPIs and loop diuretics both cause hypomagnesemia.
items.a: Intravenous magnesium sulfate

Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV loading dose
Diazepam 10 mg orally, may repeat once

items.q: After lorazepam, seizures continue. Which second-line loading dose is appropriate?
items.x: Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg are second-line options.
items.a: Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV
w: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg orally
Levetiracetam 6 mg/kg IV
Fosphenytoin 5 mg PE/kg IV

items.q: A patient has a hypertensive emergency with a BP of 220/130 mm Hg and encephalopathy. What is the initial blood pressure goal?
items.x: Rapid overcorrection risks ischemia; reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then gradually.
items.a: Lower MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour
w: Lower BP to 120/80 within the first hour
Lower MAP by 50% within 30 minutes
Avoid any blood pressure lowering for 24 hours

items.q: A patient on lithium is started on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. What is the main concern?
items.x: ACE inhibitors, thiazides, and NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance and increase toxicity risk.
items.a: Increased lithium levels and toxicity
w: Decreased lithium levels and relapse
Unchanged lithium levels with hyponatremia
Unchanged lithium levels with hyperkalemia

items.q: When should a lithium level be drawn after a dose change?
items.x: Lithium levels are drawn 12 hours post-dose at steady state, about 5 days after a dose change.
items.a: A 12-hour trough about 5 days after the change
w: A 12-hour trough the morning after the change
A peak level 2 hours after the dose on day 5
A random level about 2 weeks after the change

items.q: Which labs should be monitored periodically in a patient on long-term lithium?
items.x: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism.
items.a: Renal function, TSH, and calcium
w: Liver enzymes, CBC, and ammonia
CBC, sodium, and liver enzymes
Renal function, TSH, and prolactin

items.q: A patient is starting amiodarone. What baseline monitoring is recommended?
items.x: Amiodarone causes thyroid, liver, and lung toxicity; baseline and periodic monitoring is required.
items.a: TSH, LFTs, chest x-ray, and PFTs
w: CBC, creatinine, CK, and a lipid panel
TSH, creatinine, lipase, and uric acid
LFTs, CBC, INR, and a urinalysis

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on weekly methotrexate. Which supplement and monitoring are standard?
items.x: Folic acid reduces toxicity; methotrexate needs CBC, liver, and renal monitoring.
items.a: Folic acid, CBC, LFTs, and creatinine
w: Vitamin B12, CBC, TSH, and creatinine
Folic acid, INR, lipase, and glucose
Vitamin D, CBC, calcium, and CK

items.q: A patient on methotrexate is prescribed TMP-SMX. What is the main risk?
items.x: TMP-SMX inhibits folate metabolism and reduces methotrexate clearance, causing pancytopenia.
items.a: Additive antifolate bone marrow suppression
w: Reduced methotrexate effect and an RA flare
Crystal nephropathy from the sulfonamide alone
Hepatotoxicity from CYP3A4 inhibition

items.q: A patient is being started on clozapine. What is the minimum ANC required to start it in the general population?
items.x: Clozapine requires an ANC of 1500 or more to start (1000 for benign ethnic neutropenia) because of agranulocytosis risk.
items.a: 1500 cells per microliter
w: 1000 cells per microliter
2000 cells per microliter
2500 cells per microliter

items.q: Three weeks into clozapine, a patient has fever, tachycardia, and chest pain. What should be checked?
items.x: Clozapine-induced myocarditis usually occurs in the first 4-8 weeks; troponin and CRP screen for it.
items.a: Troponin and CRP for myocarditis
w: CK and myoglobin for NMS
Lipase and amylase for pancreatitis
Clozapine level for dose toxicity

items.q: A patient started on atorvastatin develops mild muscle aches. What is the best next step?
items.x: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are evaluated with CK; mild cases can be managed by dose reduction or switching.
items.a: Check CK and consider a dose change or another statin
w: Check liver enzymes and continue the same statin dose
Change to gemfibrozil alone and recheck lipids later
Add niacin to the statin and recheck lipids in a month

items.q: A patient with heart failure on lisinopril is started on spironolactone. What should be monitored?
items.x: Spironolactone with ACE inhibitors increases hyperkalemia risk; check K and creatinine in a few days and periodically.
items.a: Potassium and creatinine
w: Sodium and uric acid
Magnesium and calcium
Glucose and lipid panel

items.q: A patient on digoxin is started on amiodarone. What adjustment is recommended?
items.x: Amiodarone raises digoxin levels; reduce digoxin and monitor levels.
items.a: Reduce the digoxin dose by about 50%
w: Increase the digoxin dose by about 25%
Reduce the amiodarone dose by about 50%
Keep both doses and check a level in a month

items.q: A patient on azathioprine is started on allopurinol for gout. What is the main concern?
items.x: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which metabolizes azathioprine, causing toxicity; reduce the azathioprine dose substantially or avoid the combination.
items.a: Myelosuppression from azathioprine buildup
w: Hepatotoxicity from allopurinol buildup
Gout flares from reduced allopurinol effect
Nephrotoxicity from xanthine crystals

items.q: A patient on dialysis is prescribed gabapentin 600 mg three times daily and becomes sedated. What is the problem?
items.x: Gabapentin is renally cleared and requires dose reduction in renal impairment.
items.a: Gabapentin accumulates and needs renal dosing
w: Gabapentin needs hepatic dosing, not renal dosing
Gabapentin is cleared too fast by each dialysis run
Gabapentin lowers the seizure threshold in ESRD

items.q: A patient ingested a large amount of acetaminophen 4 hours ago. When should NAC be started?
items.x: The 4-hour acetaminophen level is plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to guide NAC therapy.
items.a: If the 4-hour level is above the treatment line
w: Only once the AST or ALT begins to rise
If the level is still detectable at 8 hours
If activated charcoal cannot be given in time

items.q: A transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on rifampin. What is the expected effect?
items.x: Rifampin induces CYP3A4, reducing tacrolimus levels.
items.a: Tacrolimus levels fall and rejection risk rises
w: Tacrolimus levels rise and nephrotoxicity follows
Tacrolimus levels hold steady but rifampin levels fall
Tacrolimus levels fall only if rifampin is given IV

items.q: A structural analog of amiodarone was designed to reduce thyroid toxicity and shorten tissue accumulation. Which structural change most directly explains its lower thyroid toxicity?
items.x: Dronedarone lacks iodine and has a methanesulfonyl group that reduces lipophilicity, giving less thyroid toxicity and a much shorter half-life than amiodarone.
items.a: Removal of the iodine atoms from the molecule
w: Addition of a methylsulfonyl group to the molecule
Replacement of the iodine atoms with bromine atoms
Shortening of the butyl chain on the benzofuran ring

items.q: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation for 3 years has failed two cardioversions and is now managed with rate control only. His cardiologist plans no further rhythm attempts. Why is dronedarone inappropriate for him?
items.x: In PALLAS, dronedarone increased stroke, HF, and CV death in permanent AF, which is now a boxed-warning contraindication.
items.a: It increases death and stroke in permanent atrial fibrillation
w: It causes pulmonary fibrosis in most patients within 1 year
It must be started in hospital with 3 days of ECG monitoring
It is ineffective for rate control without added digoxin

items.q: A client is switched from amiodarone to dronedarone. Which monitoring need is reduced by that change?
items.x: Dronedarone was built without the iodine moiety of amiodarone, so thyroid dysfunction and pulmonary fibrosis are far less common. Liver injury, an early creatinine rise and QT prolongation still occur and are still followed.
items.a: Periodic thyroid studies and lung imaging
w: Periodic serum creatinine measurement
Periodic liver enzyme measurement
Periodic ECG review of the QT interval on telemetry

items.q: An IV class III antiarrhythmic converts atrial flutter to sinus rhythm. In addition to blocking the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, it has a second distinctive ionic action. Which action is it?
items.x: Ibutilide blocks IKr and activates the slow inward plateau sodium current, both of which prolong the action potential and QT interval.
items.a: Enhancement of the slow inward late sodium current
w: Activation of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel
Blockade of the funny current in the sinoatrial node
Stimulation of the cardiac sodium-potassium ATPase

items.q: A 58-year-old woman with atrial flutter of 12 hours' duration receives IV ibutilide and converts to sinus rhythm. Twenty minutes later she becomes unresponsive. Which rhythm is most likely?
items.x: Ibutilide causes torsades de pointes in about 2% of patients, usually within an hour of infusion and more often in women.
items.a: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation
w: Complete heart block with a narrow junctional escape
Sinus tachycardia from beta-adrenergic stimulation
Monomorphic VT from a scar-mediated reentry circuit

items.q: A client with recent-onset atrial fibrillation is ordered IV ibutilide. Which laboratory values should the nurse confirm are within normal limits before starting the infusion?
items.x: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia increase the risk of torsades de pointes with ibutilide and should be corrected before the infusion.
items.a: Potassium and magnesium
w: Sodium and chloride
Glucose and calcium
Hemoglobin and platelets

items.q: A class Ia antiarrhythmic is chosen for a patient with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the outflow tract gradient. Which property of this drug produces that benefit?
items.x: Disopyramide strongly reduces contractility, which lessens dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM; the same property worsens HFrEF.
items.a: Negative inotropic effect on ventricular myocardium
w: Anticholinergic effect on the sinoatrial node
Prolongation of the ventricular action potential
Sodium channel block slowing conduction velocity

items.q: A 71-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is started on disopyramide. Two days later he has suprapubic fullness and cannot void. What property of the drug best explains this?
items.x: Disopyramide has prominent anticholinergic effects that cause urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, and may precipitate angle-closure glaucoma.
items.a: Antimuscarinic blockade of the bladder detrusor
w: Alpha-1 agonist contraction of the bladder neck
Sodium channel blockade of the pelvic nerves
Negative inotropy lowering renal perfusion

items.q: A client receiving disopyramide has a QRS that increased from 0.09 to 0.13 seconds since the drug was started. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A QRS widening of more than 25% from baseline suggests sodium channel toxicity, so the dose is held and the provider notified.
items.a: Hold the dose and report the QRS change to the provider
w: Give the dose because the QRS remains under 0.20 seconds
Give the dose with milk to lessen the conduction effect
Hold the dose for 1 hour and then give it as scheduled

items.q: A patient with acute decompensated heart failure receives a recombinant peptide that binds natriuretic peptide receptor-A. Which second messenger mediates its vasodilating effect?
items.x: Nesiritide is recombinant BNP; NPR-A is a membrane-bound guanylate cyclase that raises cGMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
items.a: Increased cyclic GMP from particulate guanylate cyclase
w: Increased cyclic AMP from Gs-coupled adenylyl cyclase
Increased IP3 and calcium release from Gq signaling
Decreased cyclic GMP from phosphodiesterase activation

items.q: A 66-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure is started on nesiritide. Which adverse effect is most common and most likely to limit the infusion?
items.x: Hypotension is the most frequent adverse effect of nesiritide; it is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock and when SBP is below 100 mmHg.
items.a: Hypotension
w: Hypokalemia
Thiocyanate toxicity
Ventricular ectopy

items.q: A client is to begin a nesiritide bolus and infusion. Current vital signs are BP 94/58 mmHg, HR 92/min, and RR 24/min. What is the nurse's best action?
items.x: Nesiritide should not be started when systolic BP is below 100 mmHg because it can cause significant, prolonged hypotension.
items.a: Withhold the drug and notify the provider of the BP
w: Give the bolus and begin the infusion as ordered
Give the bolus only and hold the infusion for 1 hour
Begin the infusion at a double rate to skip the bolus

items.q: A patient with a hypertensive emergency and acute kidney injury receives an IV agent that dilates renal arterioles and increases sodium excretion. Which receptor does this drug activate?
items.x: Fenoldopam is a selective peripheral D1 agonist that raises cAMP in vascular smooth muscle, dilating renal and mesenteric arterioles.
items.a: Peripheral dopamine D1 receptor
w: Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor
Vascular beta-2 adrenergic receptor
Presynaptic dopamine D2 receptor

items.q: A 60-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency is treated with a fenoldopam infusion. Which adverse effect is a recognized dose-related consequence of this drug?
items.x: Fenoldopam can raise intraocular pressure and cause hypokalemia and reflex tachycardia; cyanide toxicity is associated with nitroprusside.
items.a: Increased intraocular pressure
w: Increased serum thiocyanate level
Increased serum potassium level
Decreased resting heart rate

items.q: A client has been receiving a fenoldopam infusion for 6 hours for severe hypertension. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor?
items.x: Fenoldopam commonly lowers serum potassium, often within the first 6 hours, so potassium should be checked and replaced as ordered.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum calcium
Serum amylase
Platelet count

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and an LVOT gradient of 80 mmHg is started on a drug that reduces actin-myosin cross-bridge formation. What is its molecular target?
items.x: Mavacamten is an allosteric, reversible inhibitor of cardiac myosin ATPase that reduces hypercontractility and LVOT obstruction.
items.a: Cardiac myosin ATPase
w: Cardiac troponin C
L-type calcium channel
Phospholamban protein

items.q: A patient with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is being considered for mavacamten. Which finding must be confirmed before therapy begins?
items.x: The boxed warning requires echocardiographic LVEF of at least 55% before starting because mavacamten can cause HF from systolic dysfunction.
items.a: Left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 55%
w: Left ventricular outflow gradient under 30 mm Hg
Resting sinus heart rate of at least 70 per minute
Corrected QT interval shorter than 450 milliseconds

items.q: A client on mavacamten for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes for the scheduled echocardiogram. Which result requires the drug to be interrupted?
items.x: Mavacamten reduces contractility by inhibiting cardiac myosin ATPase, so its REMS program requires serial echocardiograms and the drug is interrupted when LVEF falls below 50 percent. Atrial size and septal thickness are features of the disease, not stopping rules.
items.a: An LVEF of 45 percent
w: An LVEF of 62 percent
A left atrial size of 42 mm
A septal thickness of 18 mm

items.q: An oral heart failure drug increases cyclic GMP by directly stimulating the nitric oxide receptor, even when nitric oxide levels are low. Which enzyme does it act on?
items.x: Vericiguat stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase independently of NO and sensitizes it to endogenous NO, increasing cGMP.
items.a: Soluble guanylate cyclase
w: Phosphodiesterase type 5
Neutral endopeptidase
Membrane adenylyl cyclase

items.q: A 62-year-old man with HFrEF who was recently hospitalized is being started on vericiguat. Which of his current medications is contraindicated with it?
items.x: Vericiguat is contraindicated with other soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat because of additive hypotension.
items.a: Riociguat for pulmonary hypertension
w: Ambrisentan for pulmonary hypertension
Sacubitril-valsartan for heart failure
Ivabradine for resting tachycardia

items.q: A woman of reproductive age is starting vericiguat. Which teaching point is the priority for the nurse to include?
items.x: Vericiguat carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so pregnancy must be excluded and effective contraception used.
items.a: Avoid pregnancy and use effective contraception
w: Take each dose on an empty stomach at bedtime
Avoid foods high in potassium such as bananas
Expect orange urine during the first week of use

items.q: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and ascites develops hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury. He is treated with albumin plus a vasopressin analog. Which receptor mediates the main therapeutic effect of this drug?
items.x: Terlipressin is a V1-selective vasopressin analog; splanchnic vasoconstriction raises effective arterial volume and improves renal perfusion in hepatorenal syndrome.
items.a: V1 receptor on splanchnic vascular smooth muscle
w: V2 receptor on renal collecting duct principal cells
Alpha-1 receptor on systemic arteriolar smooth muscle
SSTR2 receptor on splanchnic endothelial cells

items.q: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis and hepatorenal syndrome-AKI is being considered for terlipressin. Which finding is a contraindication to starting it?
items.x: Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure and should not be started in patients with SpO2 below 90% or worsening respiratory symptoms.
items.a: Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
w: Serum sodium of 131 mEq/L
Serum creatinine of 3.4 mg/dL
Mean arterial pressure of 68 mm Hg

items.q: A client is starting terlipressin for hepatorenal syndrome. Which baseline assessment does the boxed warning drive?
items.x: Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure, so oxygenation and volume status are assessed before the first dose and the drug is avoided in patients who are hypoxic or fluid overloaded. Its V1 receptor action causes ischemic complications rather than QT change.
items.a: Oxygen saturation and volume status
w: Serum potassium and magnesium
A twelve-lead ECG with QT interval
A fasting lipid panel with an A1c and TSH

items.q: A 68-year-old hospitalized woman with SIADH and a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L is started on an IV drug that blocks vasopressin receptors. What is the mechanism by which this drug raises the serum sodium?
items.x: Conivaptan blocks V2 receptors, preventing cAMP-driven aquaporin-2 insertion and producing free water excretion (aquaresis); it also blocks V1a receptors.
items.a: Reduced aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct
w: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop
Increased aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex
Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel in the tubule

items.q: A 72-year-old man is admitted with a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L. Which clinical situation is a contraindication to treatment with IV conivaptan?
items.x: Conivaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia; it is used for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia.
items.a: Vomiting with dry mucosa and orthostasis
w: Small-cell lung cancer with euvolemia
Heart failure with peripheral edema
Postoperative nausea with normal volume

items.q: A client with euvolemic hyponatremia receives an IV conivaptan infusion. Which effect accounts for the rise in serum sodium?
items.x: Conivaptan blocks the V2 receptor in the collecting duct, so aquaporin-2 channels are withdrawn and solute-free water is excreted. That is an aquaresis rather than a diuresis, which is why fluid restriction is relaxed during the infusion to keep the sodium from climbing too fast.
items.a: Loss of free water without loss of sodium
w: Loss of sodium and water in about equal amounts
Increased renal reabsorption of sodium
Movement of sodium out of the cells

items.q: A 47-year-old man with acromegaly has persistent elevation of IGF-1 after transsphenoidal surgery. He is started on a monthly deep subcutaneous injection that inhibits growth hormone release. Which receptor does this drug activate?
items.x: Lanreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog that acts mainly at SSTR2 and SSTR5, a Gi-coupled receptor that suppresses GH secretion.
items.a: Somatostatin receptor subtype 2
w: Growth hormone receptor on hepatocytes
Dopamine D2 receptor on somatotrophs
GHRH receptor on anterior pituitary cells

items.q: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic small bowel neuroendocrine tumor and carcinoid syndrome has received lanreotide every 4 weeks for 1 year. Which adverse effect is most likely to develop with long-term use?
items.x: Somatostatin analogs reduce gallbladder contractility and cholecystokinin release, causing gallbladder sludge and gallstones.
items.a: Cholelithiasis
w: Nephrolithiasis
Peptic ulceration
Osteoporosis

items.q: A nurse is preparing to give lanreotide 120 mg to a client with a neuroendocrine tumor. Which administration technique is correct?
items.x: Lanreotide is given by deep subcutaneous injection in the superior external quadrant of the buttock, alternating sides; the site is not massaged.
items.a: Deep subcutaneous injection in the upper outer buttock
w: IV push over 2 minutes through a saline lock
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen with massage

items.q: A 35-year-old woman has fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide levels from an unresectable insulinoma. She is started on an oral drug that prevents insulin release. Which action describes this drug?
items.x: Diazoxide binds the SUR1 subunit and opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing beta cells and blocking insulin release, the opposite of sulfonylureas.
items.a: Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
w: Closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
Blocks GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells
Activates SSTR5 receptors on pancreatic delta cells

items.q: A 6-month-old infant with congenital hyperinsulinism has been treated with oral diazoxide for 4 months. Which adverse effect is most characteristic of this therapy?
items.x: Diazoxide commonly causes hypertrichosis and also fluid retention; infants are at risk for pulmonary hypertension.
items.a: Hypertrichosis
w: Gingival hyperplasia
Cholelithiasis
Polyuria

items.q: A nurse is teaching the parents of an infant started on diazoxide oral suspension for congenital hyperinsulinism. Which statement by a parent shows correct understanding?
items.x: Diazoxide can cause fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension in infants; respiratory distress or swelling must be reported promptly, and doses are measured with the dropper on a schedule.
items.a: I will report fast breathing or swelling right away
w: I will stop it if my baby grows extra body hair
I can measure the dose with a kitchen teaspoon
I will give it only when the sugar reading is low

items.q: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting, muscle weakness, and cardiomyopathy. Plasma carnitine is very low. Supplementation corrects his defect in which process?
items.x: Carnitine is required to carry long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation; deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and myopathy.
items.a: Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
w: Transport of pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix
Conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in cytosol
Transfer of reducing equivalents by the malate shuttle

items.q: A 24-year-old woman with epilepsy takes a large intentional overdose of valproic acid. She is lethargic, and her ammonia level is markedly elevated. Which therapy is most appropriate for the hyperammonemia?
items.x: Valproate depletes carnitine and impairs urea cycle function; IV levocarnitine is used for valproate-induced hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity.
items.a: IV levocarnitine
w: IV acetylcysteine
Oral lactulose
Oral rifaximin

items.q: A client on hemodialysis is prescribed IV levocarnitine. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.x: In end-stage renal disease, levocarnitine is given as a slow IV bolus over 2-3 minutes at the end of each dialysis session, since dialysis removes carnitine.
items.a: Give it as a slow IV bolus after the dialysis session
w: Give it before dialysis so the filter clears the excess
Mix it with the client's oral phosphate binder dose
Give it by rapid IV push during the first hour of dialysis

items.q: A 16-year-old with osteosarcoma develops acute kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate and has a markedly elevated plasma methotrexate level. He receives an IV enzyme. What is the mechanism of this drug?
items.x: Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) hydrolyzes methotrexate to inactive DAMPA and glutamate; leucovorin, by contrast, bypasses the DHFR block.
items.a: Cleaves the terminal glutamate from methotrexate
w: Bypasses dihydrofolate reductase by providing folate
Enhances renal tubular secretion of methotrexate
Inhibits thymidylate synthase in normal tissues

items.q: A 45-year-old man with lymphoma receives glucarpidase for toxic methotrexate levels and impaired renal function. Which statement about subsequent management is correct?
items.x: Glucarpidase degrades leucovorin, so leucovorin is separated by 2 hours but continued; immunoassays overestimate methotrexate for 48 hours due to DAMPA.
items.a: Leucovorin is continued but not within 2 hours of the dose
w: Leucovorin should be stopped once glucarpidase is given
Immunoassay methotrexate levels are reliable right away
Hemodialysis should be started at the same time as dosing

items.q: A nurse is giving glucarpidase to a client with methotrexate toxicity. The client is also scheduled for IV leucovorin. When should the leucovorin be given?
items.x: Leucovorin is a substrate for glucarpidase, so it should not be given within 2 hours before or after the glucarpidase dose.
items.a: At least 2 hours after the glucarpidase dose
w: Mixed with glucarpidase in the same syringe
Immediately before glucarpidase in the same line
Only after levels are undetectable on immunoassay

items.q: A 64-year-old man on a continuous 5-fluorouracil infusion receives the full 4-day dose in 4 hours due to a pump error. He is given an oral antidote. What is its mechanism?
items.x: Uridine triacetate is converted to uridine, and the resulting UTP competitively limits incorporation of the 5-FU metabolite FUTP into RNA of normal cells.
items.a: Uridine competes with fluorouridine triphosphate for RNA
w: It restores thymidylate synthase activity by binding 5-FU
It supplies reduced folate to stabilize thymidylate synthase
It increases dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity

items.q: A 59-year-old woman taking capecitabine develops severe diarrhea, mucositis, and neutropenia within 2 days of starting therapy. Genetic testing later shows dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency. Which is the most appropriate antidote?
items.x: Uridine triacetate treats early-onset severe toxicity from 5-FU or capecitabine within 96 hours; leucovorin potentiates 5-FU, and glucarpidase is for methotrexate.
items.a: Uridine triacetate
w: Leucovorin
Glucarpidase
Mesna

items.q: A client receiving uridine triacetate every 6 hours vomits 45 minutes after taking a dose. What should the nurse do?
items.x: The label directs that if vomiting occurs within 2 hours of a dose, a complete dose should be repeated as soon as possible, then the schedule continues.
items.a: Give another full dose as soon as possible
w: Wait and give the next dose on schedule
Give half a dose mixed with water instead
Give the next dose crushed in applesauce at bedtime

items.q: A 78-year-old woman taking apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. She receives a recombinant protein that lacks the Gla domain and has an inactivated active site. How does this agent restore hemostasis?
items.x: Andexanet alfa is a catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds apixaban and rivaroxaban, freeing native factor Xa to function.
items.a: It acts as a decoy that binds and sequesters the factor Xa inhibitor
w: It directly activates factor X to generate thrombin at the bleeding site
It replaces vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X in plasma
It binds the drug with a monoclonal antibody fragment and is renally cleared

items.q: A 70-year-old man on rivaroxaban receives andexanet alfa for a life-threatening GI bleed and hemostasis is achieved. Which complication carries a boxed warning for this agent?
items.x: Andexanet alfa has a boxed warning for thromboembolic and ischemic events, cardiac arrest and sudden death; anticoagulation should resume when appropriate.
items.a: Thromboembolic events, ischemic events and cardiac arrest
w: Anaphylaxis, serum sickness and antibody formation
Rebound bleeding, hemolysis and acute kidney injury
Fluid overload, pulmonary edema and lung injury

items.q: A 60-year-old man has persistent oozing after cardiac surgery with laboratory evidence of hyperfibrinolysis. He is given a lysine analog. What is its mechanism?
items.x: Aminocaproic acid occupies the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen, preventing its binding to fibrin and its activation to plasmin.
items.a: Blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, preventing plasmin formation
w: Directly inhibits thrombin and fibrin-bound thrombin
Replaces fibrinogen and factor XIII consumed during bypass surgery
Activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on platelets

items.q: A patient with severe hemophilia A is treated with aminocaproic acid for a prolonged dental bleed. Which condition is a contraindication to this drug unless heparin is also given?
items.x: Antifibrinolytics can cause dangerous thrombosis in active intravascular clotting such as DIC unless heparin is given concurrently.
items.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation with active clotting
w: Immune thrombocytopenia with active mucosal bleeding
Von Willebrand disease with recurrent epistaxis
Hepatic cirrhosis with a prolonged prothrombin time

items.q: A patient has received continuous aminocaproic acid for several days. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor for a characteristic adverse effect?
items.x: Prolonged aminocaproic acid can cause skeletal muscle weakness with necrosis and rhabdomyolysis, so CK should be monitored.
items.a: Creatine kinase
w: Serum amylase
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Serum ammonia

items.q: During PCI, a patient receives an IV antiplatelet agent with a half-life of 3 to 6 minutes that does not need hepatic activation. Which statement best describes this drug?
items.x: Cangrelor is an ATP analog that directly and reversibly blocks P2Y12 without metabolic activation, so platelet function returns within about 1 hour.
items.a: A direct, reversible antagonist of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
w: An irreversible prodrug inhibitor of the platelet P2Y12 receptor

items.q: A client taking quetiapine is dizzy when getting up. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Quetiapine can cause orthostatic hypotension. The LVN keeps the client safe and reports.
items.a: Help the client sit and report the finding
w: Walk with the client and document the finding
Reinforce that dizziness is expected and harmless
Give the next dose with food and recheck later

items.q: A client in septic shock is receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV. The nurse finds the site cool, pale and swollen. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Blanching and swelling at a vasopressor site suggest extravasation. Stopping the infusion, leaving the catheter to aspirate, and notifying the provider for an antidote such as phentolamine limits tissue necrosis.
items.a: Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place, and notify the provider
w: Apply a warm compress and keep the infusion running at the same rate
Elevate the arm and recheck the site again in one hour
Flush the catheter with saline to clear the medication from the vein

items.q: The provider prescribes phentolamine for a client whose norepinephrine infusion extravasated into the forearm. How does the nurse expect phentolamine to be given?
items.x: Phentolamine is infiltrated into the extravasated area to reverse local alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction. It is not given systemically for this purpose.
items.a: Infiltrated subcutaneously into the affected area
w: As a rapid IV push through the same IV catheter
As an intramuscular injection into the deltoid
As an oral dose once the client is able to swallow

items.q: A client has been receiving a propofol infusion for sedation for three days. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor?
items.x: Propofol is delivered in a lipid emulsion, so prolonged infusion can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Triglycerides are monitored during longer infusions.
items.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum ammonia level
Serum magnesium level
Hemoglobin A1C value

items.q: A client is receiving high-dose propofol for several days. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
items.x: Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and arrhythmias suggest propofol infusion syndrome, which can be fatal. Green urine and a milky emulsion are harmless and expected.
items.a: New metabolic acidosis with dark red-brown urine
w: Urine that has turned a light green color
A RASS score that is at the prescribed target
A milky white appearance of the infusion

items.q: A client receiving a dexmedetomidine infusion has a heart rate of 44 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 84/48 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Bradycardia and hypotension are the most common serious effects of dexmedetomidine and need prompt provider review. Increasing the dose would worsen them.
items.a: Report the bradycardia and hypotension to the provider
w: Increase the infusion rate to keep the client calm
Give an extra bolus to maintain the sedation level
Document the findings as an expected effect of the drug

items.q: The family of an intubated client asks why the client on dexmedetomidine opens the eyes when spoken to. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine produces arousable sedation with little respiratory depression. It is not a general anesthetic or a paralytic.
items.a: This medicine calms the client but still lets them wake easily
w: This medicine works like a general anesthetic with deep amnesia
This medicine slows breathing so the ventilator can do all the work
This medicine is a paralytic that keeps the client from moving

items.q: The nurse is caring for an intubated, sedated client on a fentanyl infusion. Which tool is most appropriate for assessing this client's pain?
items.x: The CPOT uses facial expression, movement, muscle tension and ventilator compliance, so it works for clients who cannot self-report. The GCS measures consciousness, not pain.
items.a: Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool
w: Numeric rating scale from 0 to 10
Wong-Baker FACES pain rating scale
Glasgow Coma Scale total score

items.q: Right after a rapid IV bolus of fentanyl, a client on a ventilator becomes hard to ventilate and the chest wall feels rigid. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Rapid high-dose fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity that impairs ventilation. Fentanyl causes little histamine release and does not trigger malignant hyperthermia.
items.a: Chest wall rigidity caused by rapid fentanyl dosing
w: An expected anxiety response to the ventilator mode
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the opioid dose
Bronchospasm caused by a large histamine release

items.q: A client is on a continuous midazolam infusion. Which newly prescribed medicine should prompt the nurse to watch for prolonged sedation?
items.x: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4, the main pathway for midazolam metabolism, which raises midazolam levels and prolongs sedation. The other drugs do not meaningfully affect midazolam.
items.a: Fluconazole
w: Pantoprazole
Acetaminophen
Enoxaparin

items.q: Flumazenil is prescribed for a client who is oversedated after midazolam. Which history is most important for the nurse to report before it is given?
items.x: Flumazenil can trigger seizures in clients on long-term benzodiazepines or with a seizure disorder. The provider needs this before reversal.
items.a: Long-term benzodiazepine use for a seizure disorder
w: An allergy to penicillin with a past skin rash
Short-term opioid use after a knee surgery last year
Hypothyroidism treated with daily levothyroxine

items.q: A postoperative client using a hydromorphone PCA is difficult to arouse with a respiratory rate of 6 per minute. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.x: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is treated by holding the opioid, supporting breathing, and giving naloxone per protocol. Waiting or only adjusting fluids delays rescue.
items.a: Pause the PCA, stimulate the client, and give naloxone per protocol
w: Raise the head of the bed and recheck the client in 30 minutes
Increase the IV fluid rate and reassess the oxygen saturation
Lower the PCA dose and teach the client to press the button less

items.q: Succinylcholine is planned for rapid sequence intubation. Which laboratory result should the nurse report to the provider before it is given?
items.x: Succinylcholine raises serum potassium and can cause dangerous hyperkalemia in a client who already has a high level. The other values are within or near normal range.
items.a: Potassium 6.4 mEq/L
w: Sodium 138 mEq/L
Glucose 142 mg/dL
Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL

items.q: Shortly after receiving succinylcholine, a client develops jaw rigidity, a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide and tachycardia. Which medicine does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: These signs suggest malignant hyperthermia, and dantrolene is the specific treatment. Neostigmine and sugammadex reverse nondepolarizing blockers.
items.a: Dantrolene
w: Neostigmine
Sugammadex
Phentolamine

items.q: A client on a ventilator is started on a rocuronium infusion. Which action is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Neuromuscular blockers provide no sedation or pain relief, so the client must be adequately sedated to prevent awareness. A paralyzed client cannot give a pain score or blink.
items.a: Confirm sedation and analgesia are running before and during paralysis
w: Assess pain hourly using the client's own numeric pain scale rating
Reduce the ventilator alarm volume since the client cannot move at all
Skip routine eye care because the client's blink reflex stays intact

items.q: The nurse performs train-of-four testing on a client receiving a cisatracurium infusion. What is the purpose of this assessment?
items.x: Train-of-four monitoring shows how deeply the muscles are blocked and guides titration. It does not measure sedation, pain or seizure activity.
items.a: To measure the depth of neuromuscular blockade
w: To measure how deeply the client is sedated
To detect nonconvulsive seizure activity early
To estimate the client's current level of pain

items.q: The spouse of a client receiving vecuronium asks whether talking to the client is pointless. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.x: Paralytics do not cause unconsciousness, and hearing may be preserved. Explaining care and speaking to the client is appropriate.
items.a: The client cannot move but may hear, so please talk to them
w: The client is fully unconscious and cannot hear anything
Talking may cause the client to fight the ventilator
Please wait to talk until the medicine is reversed

items.q: A female client received sugammadex to reverse rocuronium. She takes a daily oral contraceptive. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen and reduce hormonal contraceptive effect, so a backup method is advised for 7 days. Doubling doses is not recommended.
items.a: Use a nonhormonal backup method for the next 7 days
w: Skip tonight's pill and restart it tomorrow morning
No change is needed because the drugs do not interact
Double the next pill to make up for lost effect

items.q: A client in septic shock is receiving norepinephrine and vasopressin. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Vasopressin causes strong vasoconstriction that can lead to digital or mesenteric ischemia. The MAP and urine output show adequate perfusion.
items.a: Cool, mottled fingertips with slow capillary refill
w: A mean arterial pressure of 68 mm Hg on both drips
A urine output of 45 mL over the most recent hour
Warm, pink skin on the trunk with brisk capillary refill

items.q: A client has a titration order for norepinephrine to keep the mean arterial pressure at 65 mm Hg or higher. The current MAP is 58 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A MAP below the ordered goal calls for titrating upward within the prescribed parameters. Vasopressors are never bolused through the line.
items.a: Increase the rate within the ordered titration range
w: Decrease the rate to allow the pressure to settle
Give a manual bolus of the norepinephrine solution
Leave the rate unchanged and recheck in two hours

items.q: A client needs an IV antibiotic, and the only open lumen is the one running norepinephrine. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Flushing or interrupting a pressor line can bolus or interrupt the drug and cause dangerous swings in blood pressure. A separate line should be used.
items.a: Obtain another access line rather than use the pressor lumen
w: Pause the norepinephrine briefly while the antibiotic infuses
Flush the pressor lumen first, then give the antibiotic
Piggyback the antibiotic into the norepinephrine tubing

items.q: A client in shock is started on an epinephrine infusion. Which laboratory change does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Epinephrine stimulates glycogen breakdown and raises blood glucose; it can also raise lactate. It tends to shift potassium into cells rather than raise it.
items.a: Elevated blood glucose
w: Elevated serum potassium
Decreased serum sodium
Elevated serum calcium

items.q: A client in cardiogenic shock is receiving dobutamine. The heart rate rises from 98 to 138 beats per minute with frequent premature ventricular contractions. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Dobutamine can cause tachycardia and ventricular arrhythmias that increase oxygen demand. These changes need prompt provider review.
items.a: Notify the provider of the new tachycardia and ectopy
w: Increase the dobutamine to improve cardiac output further
Document the change as an expected drug response
Give a fluid bolus and recheck the rhythm in four hours

items.q: A client with heart failure is receiving milrinone. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to review because of how this drug is eliminated?
items.x: Milrinone is cleared by the kidneys, so renal impairment causes accumulation and more hypotension and arrhythmias. Creatinine guides dose adjustment.
items.a: Serum creatinine
w: Serum lipase
Serum albumin
Serum ammonia

items.q: A client receiving a phenylephrine infusion has a heart rate that drops from 88 to 46 beats per minute. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist; the rise in pressure triggers a baroreceptor-mediated drop in heart rate. It has little beta effect.
items.a: Reflex bradycardia from the rise in blood pressure
w: A direct beta-1 effect of phenylephrine on the heart
An early sign of phenylephrine extravasation
A sign that the infusion has run out

items.q: A client with an aortic dissection is on an esmolol infusion. The heart rate is 50 beats per minute and the blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. Which action is appropriate?
items.x: These values are below safe limits for a beta blocker. Esmolol is short acting, so holding titration per protocol and notifying the provider allows quick recovery.
items.a: Hold further titration per protocol and notify the provider
w: Increase the esmolol to reach a lower heart rate goal
Give a bolus of esmolol and recheck in five minutes
Continue at the same rate and document the readings

items.q: A client with a hypertensive emergency has a new order for clevidipine. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the drug and clarify the order?
items.x: Clevidipine is a lipid emulsion that contains soybean oil and egg lecithin, so it is contraindicated with these allergies. The high blood pressure is the reason for the order.
items.a: A documented allergy to soy and egg products
w: A documented allergy to sulfa antibiotics
A blood pressure of 212/118 mm Hg
A history of type 2 diabetes mellitus

items.q: A client has received nitroprusside for three days. Which finding suggests cyanide toxicity?
items.x: Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic metabolic acidosis. This is a key warning sign during prolonged or high-dose nitroprusside.
items.a: Worsening metabolic acidosis with rising lactate
w: Respiratory alkalosis with a low carbon dioxide
A rising serum sodium with low urine output
A falling blood glucose with diaphoresis

items.q: A client with chest pain is to start a nitroglycerin infusion. Which information must the nurse report before starting it?
items.x: Nitrates with a PDE-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil can cause severe hypotension. The other drugs do not interact this way.
items.a: The client took sildenafil the day before
w: The client takes atorvastatin every evening
The client takes daily low-dose aspirin
The client takes metformin with meals

items.q: A client receiving an amiodarone infusion for atrial fibrillation has a heart rate of 42 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?
items.x: IV amiodarone commonly causes hypotension and bradycardia. These findings need prompt provider review, not more drug.
items.a: Report the bradycardia and hypotension to the provider
w: Expect these findings and continue routine monitoring
Give a second amiodarone bolus to control the rhythm
Increase the infusion to restore sinus rhythm faster

items.q: A client on a heparin infusion for 6 days has a platelet count that has fallen from 240,000 to 98,000 per cubic millimeter. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A platelet drop of more than half after 5 to 10 days of heparin suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Heparin is held and the provider notified so a non-heparin anticoagulant can be ordered.
items.a: Notify the provider of possible HIT before giving the heparin
w: Continue the heparin and recheck the platelet count tomorrow
Give protamine now and then resume the heparin in one hour
Increase the heparin rate to prevent a new clot from forming

items.q: A client with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is started on argatroban. Which laboratory test does the nurse expect to guide titration?
items.x: Argatroban is titrated to the aPTT. A heparin-calibrated anti-Xa level does not measure direct thrombin inhibitors.
items.a: Activated partial thromboplastin time
w: Platelet count drawn once each day
Heparin-calibrated anti-factor Xa level
Fibrinogen level drawn every shift

items.q: Protamine is ordered to reverse heparin. Which history increases the client's risk for a serious reaction to protamine?
items.x: Prior exposure to protamine-containing insulin such as NPH raises the risk of hypersensitivity reactions to protamine. Fish allergy and vasectomy are other risk factors.
items.a: Daily use of NPH insulin for diabetes
w: Daily use of low-dose aspirin for the heart
A long history of migraine headaches
A known intolerance to lactose in milk

items.q: A client taking dabigatran arrives in the ICU with an intracranial hemorrhage. Which reversal agent does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Idarucizumab binds dabigatran and reverses its effect within minutes. Protamine reverses heparin and vitamin K reverses warfarin.
items.a: Idarucizumab
w: Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione
Aminocaproic acid

items.q: A client on warfarin with an INR of 6.8 has an active GI bleed, and prothrombin complex concentrate is ordered. Which other medicine does the nurse anticipate giving with it?
items.x: PCC replaces clotting factors quickly, but IV vitamin K is also needed to sustain reversal of warfarin.
items.a: IV phytonadione
w: IV protamine
IV idarucizumab
IV desmopressin

items.q: A client receiving an alteplase infusion for acute ischemic stroke develops a severe headache and vomiting. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: New headache, vomiting or neurologic decline during alteplase suggests intracranial bleeding. Stroke protocols direct stopping the infusion and getting an emergency CT.
items.a: Stop the alteplase infusion per protocol and notify the provider
w: Give an antiemetic and continue the infusion as ordered
Lower the head of the bed and recheck neuro signs in one hour
Give acetaminophen and continue routine monitoring

items.q: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has a regular insulin infusion ordered. The serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalemia. DKA protocols delay insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L.
items.a: Notify the provider of the potassium before giving the insulin
w: Start the insulin now and recheck the potassium in four hours
Start the insulin and give the potassium by IV push
Start the insulin at double the rate to fix the acidosis

items.q: A client in DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 240 mg/dL, but the anion gap remains open. What does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Insulin is continued until the ketoacidosis resolves, and dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycemia. The gap, not the glucose alone, guides when to stop the drip.
items.a: Adding dextrose to the IV fluids while insulin continues
w: Holding the insulin drip until the glucose rises again
Switching to subcutaneous insulin and holding all fluids
Giving sodium bicarbonate to close the open anion gap

items.q: A client has an order for potassium chloride 20 mEq per hour through a peripheral IV. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Most protocols limit peripheral potassium to 10 mEq per hour because of pain, phlebitis and arrhythmia risk. Higher rates need a central line and cardiac monitoring.
items.a: Clarify the order because it exceeds the peripheral rate limit
w: Give it as ordered using an infusion pump on the peripheral line
Give it as ordered and check the IV site for redness every hour
Dilute it in a smaller bag so it can run in at the ordered rate

items.q: A client with cerebral edema is receiving 3 percent sodium chloride. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Hypertonic saline raises serum sodium; frequent checks prevent overcorrection and complications. It is titrated to a sodium goal set by the provider.
items.a: Serum sodium
w: Serum calcium
Serum phosphorus
Serum albumin

items.q: A client with increased intracranial pressure is receiving mannitol. Before the next dose, which result should the nurse report?
items.x: A high serum osmolality raises the risk of kidney injury, and many protocols hold mannitol when it exceeds about 320 mOsm/kg. Good urine output is expected with an osmotic diuretic.
items.a: Serum osmolality of 325 mOsm/kg
w: Serum potassium of 4.1 mEq/L
Urine output of 120 mL per hour
Serum glucose of 118 mg/dL

items.q: During an IV vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and itching of the face and neck. The blood pressure is stable. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Flushing and itching with stable vital signs suggest vancomycin infusion reaction from a rate that is too fast. It is managed by slowing the rate, not epinephrine.
items.a: Notify the provider before continuing the infusion
w: Give IM epinephrine and call the rapid response team
Continue the infusion and apply a cool cloth to the skin
Increase the rate to finish the dose more quickly

items.q: A client is receiving vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam together. Which assessment is most important because of this combination?
items.x: The combination of vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam is linked to a higher rate of acute kidney injury. Creatinine and urine output are watched closely.
items.a: Daily creatinine and urine output for kidney injury
w: Daily liver enzymes for drug-induced hepatitis
Daily hearing checks for drug-induced hearing loss
Daily blood glucose checks for hypoglycemia

items.q: A client who takes valproic acid for seizures is started on meropenem. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Carbapenems markedly lower valproic acid levels, which can lead to breakthrough seizures. The combination is generally avoided.
items.a: A sharp drop in valproic acid levels with seizure risk
w: A sharp rise in valproic acid levels with toxicity risk
Reduced meropenem effect against the current infection
Increased bleeding risk from added platelet dysfunction

items.q: A client with acute kidney injury is receiving cefepime. The client becomes newly confused and has muscle twitching. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Cefepime can accumulate in renal impairment and cause encephalopathy, myoclonus and seizures. The provider must be notified to adjust or change therapy.
items.a: Report possible cefepime neurotoxicity to the provider
w: Document this as ICU delirium and reorient the client
Give a sedative to calm the client and recheck later
Increase the dose since this suggests worsening sepsis

items.q: A client is receiving amphotericin B. Which laboratory changes should the nurse expect to monitor for?
items.x: Amphotericin B damages renal tubules, causing potassium and magnesium wasting. Replacement is often needed during therapy.
items.a: Low potassium and low magnesium
w: High potassium and high calcium
Low sodium and high glucose
High phosphorus and low albumin

items.q: The nurse receives an order for amphotericin B without the formulation specified. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Conventional and lipid-based amphotericin have very different doses, and mix-ups have caused fatal overdoses. The order must be clarified before giving.
items.a: Hold and clarify whether conventional or lipid-based is intended
w: Give the conventional formulation since it is the standard
Give the lipid-based formulation since it is safer
Give whichever formulation the pharmacy has in stock

items.q: A client with pulmonary arterial hypertension is on a continuous epoprostenol infusion and needs an IV antibiotic. Which action is correct?
items.x: Interrupting or bolusing epoprostenol can cause rebound pulmonary hypertension or hypotension. It needs a dedicated line.
items.a: Use a separate line so the epoprostenol is never interrupted
w: Pause the epoprostenol briefly while the antibiotic infuses
Flush the epoprostenol line with saline before the antibiotic
Piggyback the antibiotic into the epoprostenol infusion tubing

items.q: A client with hepatorenal syndrome is ordered terlipressin. Before the dose, the client's oxygen saturation is 88 percent on room air. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Terlipressin can cause serious or fatal respiratory failure and should not be started when oxygen saturation is below 90 percent. The provider must reassess.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and apply oxygen afterward
Give the dose and recheck oxygen in four hours
Give half the dose and recheck the saturation

items.q: A client with end-stage kidney disease receiving IV morphine is increasingly drowsy and has new muscle twitching. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Morphine's active metabolites accumulate in kidney failure and cause sedation, myoclonus and respiratory depression. The provider may choose another opioid.
items.a: Report possible metabolite buildup to the provider
w: Give the next dose early to treat the twitching
Document this as normal sleep after pain relief
Encourage fluids to help flush out the drug

items.q: A client receiving bumetanide is being moved from the ICU to a step-down unit. What should the nurse teach the client?
items.x: Bumetanide is a potent loop diuretic that causes potassium loss and orthostatic hypotension. Cramps or weakness may signal hypokalemia.
items.a: Report muscle cramps or weakness and rise slowly when standing
w: Limit potassium-rich foods such as bananas while on this drug
Take extra doses if your ankles begin to swell during the day
Expect your urine output to decrease the longer you take it

items.q: A client in the emergency department has stable supraventricular tachycardia, and adenosine is ordered. How should the nurse give it?
items.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly through a proximal IV with an immediate rapid flush.
items.a: Rapid IV push followed at once by a rapid saline flush
w: Slow IV push over two minutes into a small hand vein
Diluted in 100 mL of saline and infused over 20 minutes
As an intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis

items.q: Before giving adenosine for supraventricular tachycardia, what should the nurse tell the client?
items.x: Adenosine often causes brief flushing, chest pressure, dyspnea and a feeling of doom, along with a short pause in the rhythm. Preparing the client lowers anxiety.
items.a: You may feel brief chest pressure or a sense of doom
w: You will feel drowsy and sleepy for several hours
You will need to lie flat in bed for the next six hours
You will have a metallic taste for about a full day

items.q: A client with supraventricular tachycardia is about to receive adenosine. Which home medicine should the nurse report because it increases adenosine's effect?
items.x: Dipyridamole blocks adenosine uptake and greatly enhances its effect, so a smaller dose is used. Theophylline and caffeine have the opposite effect.
items.a: Dipyridamole
w: Theophylline
Levothyroxine
Omeprazole

items.q: A client has a heart rate of 36 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg and is dizzy. Which medicine and dose does the nurse anticipate first?
items.x: ACLS guidelines list atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes up to 3 mg, as the first drug for symptomatic bradycardia. Epinephrine 1 mg push is the cardiac arrest dose.
items.a: Atropine 1 mg IV
w: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Epinephrine 1 mg IV push

items.q: An adult client has hives, wheezing and throat tightness after a bee sting. Which medicine and route does the nurse give first?
items.x: IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, and 1 mg IV push is a cardiac arrest dose.
items.a: Epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 0.5 mg IM in the thigh
w: Epinephrine 0.1 mg/mL, 1 mg by rapid IV push
Diphenhydramine 50 mg by slow IV push first
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV push right away

items.q: A client in ventricular fibrillation has received three shocks and epinephrine. Which antiarrhythmic dose does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: The first amiodarone dose in pulseless VF or VT is 300 mg IV or IO push. The 150 mg dose is the second dose or the stable-tachycardia dose.
items.a: Amiodarone 300 mg IV push
w: Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Adenosine 12 mg rapid IV push
Atropine 1 mg IV push

items.q: During a lidocaine infusion for ventricular arrhythmia, a client reports numb lips and ringing in the ears. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Perioral numbness and tinnitus are early signs of lidocaine toxicity, which can progress to seizures. The infusion should be held and the provider notified.
items.a: Notify the provider of possible toxicity before continuing the infusion
w: Reassure the client that these are expected and mild effects of lidocaine
Increase the infusion rate to better control the ventricular arrhythmia
Give a sedative as needed and continue the infusion at the same rate

items.q: A client with stable wide-complex tachycardia is receiving a procainamide infusion. The QRS widens from 0.10 to 0.16 seconds. What should the nurse do?
items.x: ACLS stopping points for procainamide include QRS widening of more than 50 percent, hypotension, or arrhythmia suppression. A widening QRS signals toxicity.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately before continuing the infusion
w: Continue the infusion because the rhythm has not yet converted
Increase the infusion rate so the rhythm will convert much sooner
Give adenosine by rapid IV push to slow the ventricular rate now

items.q: Why does the nurse prefer a central line or large vein when giving calcium chloride?
items.x: Calcium chloride is highly irritating and can cause tissue necrosis if it leaks. Calcium gluconate is less irritating for peripheral use.
items.a: It causes severe tissue injury if it extravasates
w: It must be given faster than a small vein allows
It causes hypercalcemia only when given peripherally
It loses potency when exposed to small vessels

items.q: A client's potassium is 7.1 mEq/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Which medicine does the nurse anticipate giving first?
items.x: IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes when hyperkalemia causes ECG changes. Insulin with dextrose and other measures then lower the potassium.
items.a: IV calcium gluconate
w: Oral sodium polystyrene
IV furosemide
IV potassium chloride

items.q: A client who took an overdose of amitriptyline has a QRS of 140 milliseconds and hypotension. Which medicine does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Sodium bicarbonate treats the sodium channel blockade that widens the QRS in tricyclic overdose. Physostigmine and flumazenil can cause seizures or arrhythmias in this setting.
items.a: IV sodium bicarbonate
w: IV physostigmine push
IV flumazenil bolus
IV procainamide drip

items.q: Sodium bicarbonate and calcium chloride are both ordered during a resuscitation. Which action is correct?
items.x: Bicarbonate and calcium form a calcium carbonate precipitate that can block the line. The line must be flushed between them or separate lines used.
items.a: Flush the line well between the two medicines
w: Mix them in one syringe to save time
Give them together through the same tubing
Give calcium chloride first without a flush

items.q: A client with diabetes is unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL and has an IV in place. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: An unresponsive client with severe hypoglycemia and IV access needs IV dextrose. Oral glucose is unsafe because the client cannot protect the airway.
items.a: Give IV dextrose per hypoglycemia protocol
w: Give oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before acting
Give a dose of regular insulin subcutaneously

items.q: The nurse is teaching the family of a client with type 1 diabetes how to use emergency glucagon. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Glucagon often causes nausea and vomiting, and a person who is not fully awake could aspirate. Turning them on their side protects the airway.
items.a: Turn the person on their side after giving it
w: Give it only after the person eats a snack
Give it only after checking a ketone level
Keep the person flat on their back afterward

items.q: A client with a beta-blocker overdose is receiving high-dose IV glucagon. Which adverse effect should the nurse be ready to manage?
items.x: Nausea and vomiting are common with high-dose glucagon, so the nurse protects the airway. Glucagon raises, not lowers, blood glucose.
items.a: Vomiting with risk of aspiration
w: Severe and prolonged hypoglycemia
Acute urinary retention with pain
Profuse watery diarrhea

items.q: A client who received hydroxocobalamin for smoke inhalation asks why the urine is red. What should the nurse say?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin is a red compound that colors the skin and urine; urine color can persist for up to several weeks. It is not a sign of bleeding.
items.a: This color change is expected and can last for weeks
w: This means the kidneys are bleeding and need testing
This means the drug is not working and must be repeated
This color change will fade within a few hours

items.q: The provider orders hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide poisoning. Which action should the nurse take before giving it, if it does not delay treatment?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin's red color interferes with many colorimetric lab tests, so baseline samples are drawn first when possible. Treatment should not wait on results.
items.a: Draw baseline blood samples for laboratory testing
w: Check a serum vitamin B12 level and wait for results
Obtain a urine drug screen and wait for results
Give oral activated charcoal to bind the cyanide

items.q: Sodium nitrite is being considered for a client with cyanide poisoning after a house fire. Which finding should the nurse report before it is given?
items.x: Sodium nitrite works by creating methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen delivery in a client who already has carbon monoxide poisoning. Hydroxocobalamin is usually preferred in smoke inhalation.
items.a: Carboxyhemoglobin level of 25 percent
w: Heart rate of 104 beats per minute
Serum glucose of 132 mg/dL
Temperature of 37.4 degrees C

items.q: A client with methemoglobinemia is to receive methylene blue. Which home medicine should the nurse report before it is given?
items.x: Methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase and can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs such as SSRIs. This is a boxed warning.
items.a: Sertraline
w: Lisinopril
Metformin
Atorvastatin

items.q: Which laboratory findings in a confused client would lead the nurse to anticipate fomepizole?
items.x: Ethylene glycol and methanol cause a high osmolar gap early and a high anion gap acidosis as toxic metabolites form. Fomepizole blocks their metabolism.
items.a: High anion gap acidosis with a high osmolar gap
w: Normal anion gap acidosis with low potassium
Respiratory alkalosis with a low carbon dioxide
Metabolic alkalosis with low chloride levels

items.q: During the loading infusion of IV acetylcysteine, a client develops flushing and a rash. Vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Anaphylactoid reactions such as flushing and rash are common during the IV loading dose. They are usually managed by pausing, treating with an antihistamine, and restarting per order.
items.a: Notify the provider before continuing the infusion
w: Continue the infusion at a faster rate to finish the dose
Document an allergy so the drug is never given again
Give IM epinephrine and prepare for intubation

items.q: Activated charcoal is ordered for a client who took an overdose 30 minutes ago. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold it and clarify the order?
items.x: Activated charcoal needs an intact or protected airway because aspiration can cause severe lung injury. A weak gag reflex is a contraindication without airway protection.
items.a: The client is drowsy and has a weak gag reflex
w: The client is alert and reports mild nausea
The client took the pills less than an hour ago
The client has a heart rate of 108 beats per minute

items.q: A client received digoxin immune fab for digoxin toxicity. Which laboratory monitoring is most important afterward?
items.x: As digoxin is reversed, potassium moves back into cells and can fall quickly. Serum digoxin levels are unreliable after fab because most assays measure bound drug.
items.a: Serum potassium for a sudden drop
w: Serum digoxin level to guide redosing
Serum calcium for a sudden rise
Serum sodium for a sudden drop

items.q: Physostigmine is being considered for a client with anticholinergic toxicity from an unknown ingestion. The ECG shows a QRS of 130 milliseconds. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A wide QRS suggests a tricyclic ingestion, and physostigmine can cause bradycardia, asystole or seizures in that case. The order must be clarified.
items.a: Clarify the order with the provider before giving the physostigmine
w: Give the physostigmine rapidly to reverse the delirium and agitation
Give the physostigmine and recheck the ECG again in four hours
Give the physostigmine along with a rapid dose of IV adenosine

items.q: A client with organophosphate poisoning is receiving repeated doses of IV atropine. Which finding best shows that atropine dosing is adequate?
items.x: The goal of atropine in organophosphate poisoning is dry lungs and easier breathing. Atropine does not reverse muscle twitching, which needs pralidoxime.
items.a: Drying of bronchial secretions
w: Return of normal pupil size
A heart rate below 60
Stopping of muscle twitching

items.q: Shortly after a bupivacaine nerve block, a client has a seizure followed by bradycardia and a widening QRS. Which medicine does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: These signs suggest local anesthetic systemic toxicity, and 20 percent lipid emulsion is the specific treatment along with airway and seizure management.
items.a: 20 percent lipid emulsion
w: Sodium nitrite infusion
Flumazenil IV push
Methylene blue infusion

items.q: A client who was revived with naloxone after an opioid overdose is now awake and wants to leave. What should the nurse explain?
