items.x: Naloxone's effect often lasts a shorter time than many opioids, so respiratory depression can return. Observation is needed, especially with long-acting opioids.
items.a: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so breathing may slow again
w: Naloxone will protect you from overdose for the next several days
Naloxone has fully cleared the opioid from your body by now
Naloxone makes it safe to use the same amount of opioid later

items.q: A client with suspected opioid dependence receives nalmefene for an overdose. Which effect should the nurse anticipate compared with naloxone?
items.x: Nalmefene lasts longer than naloxone, so precipitated withdrawal can also be prolonged. It does not remove the need for observation.
items.a: Withdrawal symptoms that may last longer
w: Withdrawal symptoms that end within minutes
No risk of opioid withdrawal at all
A shorter duration of overdose reversal

items.q: A client with acute ischemic stroke is being evaluated for tenecteplase. Which history must the nurse report to the provider immediately?
items.x: Any prior intracranial hemorrhage is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy. The other conditions do not prevent treatment.
items.a: A hemorrhagic stroke six months ago
w: A controlled history of hypertension
Type 2 diabetes treated with metformin
A knee replacement three years ago

items.q: A client receiving alteplase for acute ischemic stroke takes lisinopril at home. Which complication should the nurse watch for most closely because of this combination?
items.x: Orolingual angioedema is a known risk of alteplase, and it is more common in clients taking ACE inhibitors. The nurse watches the airway closely.
items.a: Swelling of the tongue and lips
w: Sudden severe rebound hypertension
Acute urinary retention and pain
Profound and sudden hypoglycemia

items.q: A client arrives with hemorrhage after a motor vehicle crash. Tranexamic acid is ordered. Which timing is most important?
items.x: Trauma research shows tranexamic acid reduces bleeding death when given within three hours of injury; later doses may cause harm.
items.a: Giving it early, within three hours of the injury
w: Giving it only after a blood transfusion is complete
Giving it only after the bleeding source is controlled
Giving it six hours after the injury for best effect

items.q: Labetalol IV is ordered for a client with a blood pressure of 210/120 mm Hg. The heart rate is 48 beats per minute. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Labetalol has beta-blocking effects that worsen bradycardia. The provider may choose a different agent such as nicardipine.
items.a: Notify the provider of the heart rate before giving the labetalol
w: Give the labetalol as ordered and recheck the vitals in 15 minutes
Give half the labetalol dose to protect the client's heart rate
Give the labetalol mixed with atropine in the same IV syringe

items.q: A client with an inferior STEMI has a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg, and right-sided ECG leads suggest right ventricular involvement. Sublingual nitroglycerin is ordered. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Nitrates can cause severe hypotension in right ventricular infarction and when systolic pressure is below 90 mm Hg. Fluids are often needed instead.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the nitroglycerin
w: Give the nitroglycerin and repeat it in 5 minutes
Give the nitroglycerin with the client sitting up
Give half the tablet and recheck the pressure

items.q: A client with a severe asthma attack is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which findings should the nurse monitor during the infusion?
items.x: IV magnesium can cause flushing, hypotension and, at high levels, loss of reflexes and respiratory depression. These are checked during the infusion.
items.a: Blood pressure, respiratory rate and reflexes
w: Blood glucose, temperature and pupil size
Urine color, skin turgor and bowel sounds
Oxygen saturation only at the end of the dose

items.q: A client receives etomidate for rapid sequence intubation. The nurse notices brief jerking movements of the arms. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Transient myoclonus is common after etomidate induction and is not a seizure. Etomidate does not trigger malignant hyperthermia.
items.a: Myoclonus, a known effect of etomidate
w: A generalized seizure needing lorazepam
Malignant hyperthermia from etomidate
An allergic reaction needing epinephrine

items.q: Ketamine is being considered for procedural sedation. Which client finding should the nurse report to the provider first?
items.x: Ketamine raises heart rate and blood pressure, so it is used cautiously or avoided when hypertension or ischemia could be dangerous.
items.a: Blood pressure of 202/118 mm Hg with chest pain
w: Heart rate of 88 beats per minute and regular
Oxygen saturation of 97 percent on room air
Mild anxiety and questions about the procedure

items.q: The ED team is preparing for rapid sequence intubation with succinylcholine. Which history should the nurse report to the provider before it is given?
items.x: After denervation injuries, burns or crush injuries, succinylcholine can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia. A nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium is often chosen instead.
items.a: Spinal cord injury three weeks ago
w: Ankle fracture three years ago
Seasonal allergies treated with loratadine
Appendectomy as a child

items.q: After rapid sequence intubation with etomidate and rocuronium, the client is motionless on the ventilator. What is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Rocuronium lasts much longer than etomidate, so a paralyzed client can be awake and in pain. Ongoing sedation and analgesia prevent awareness.
items.a: Make sure sedation and analgesia are started promptly
w: Delay sedation until the client starts to move
Assess pain by asking the client to squeeze a hand
Lower the ventilator alarm limits for comfort

items.q: A client is receiving propofol for procedural sedation in the ED. Which monitoring is most important?
items.x: Propofol can quickly cause apnea and hypotension. Capnography detects poor ventilation earlier than pulse oximetry alone.
items.a: Continuous capnography and pulse oximetry
w: Hourly fingerstick blood glucose checks
Serum triglyceride level before discharge
Full neurologic checks every four hours

items.q: Ceftriaxone IV is ordered for a client who has lactated Ringer's infusing in the only IV line. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Ceftriaxone can form a calcium precipitate with calcium-containing solutions such as lactated Ringer's. They must not be mixed or given at the same time in one line.
items.a: Avoid giving them at the same time through the same line
w: Mix the ceftriaxone directly into the lactated Ringer's bag
Piggyback the ceftriaxone into the running lactated Ringer's
Give the ceftriaxone by IV push into the same running line

items.q: Ondansetron IV is ordered for a vomiting client. Which laboratory results increase the client's risk of a serious adverse effect?
items.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, and low potassium or magnesium raises the risk of torsades de pointes. These should be corrected.
items.a: Low potassium and low magnesium
w: High sodium and high chloride
Low glucose and low calcium
High albumin and high protein

items.q: Ketorolac IV is ordered for a client with renal colic. Which home medicine should the nurse report before giving it?
items.x: Ketorolac inhibits platelets and raises bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants like warfarin. Tamsulosin is often used for kidney stones.
items.a: Warfarin
w: Levothyroxine
Montelukast
Tamsulosin

items.q: A client received IV hydromorphone for a fracture and is being discharged. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Hydromorphone causes sedation and slowed reactions, so driving is unsafe. Alcohol and sedatives add to respiratory depression.
items.a: Do not drive and have a responsible adult take you home
w: You may drive yourself home if you feel alert after an hour
A glass of wine at home tonight will help you get some sleep
Take an over-the-counter sleep aid tonight to help you rest

items.q: A client in status epilepticus receives IV lorazepam and the seizure stops. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
items.x: IV lorazepam can cause respiratory depression, especially after a seizure. Airway and breathing are checked first.
items.a: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
w: Pupil size and their reactivity to light
Blood glucose level and urine output
Skin color and capillary refill time

items.q: A client is discharged on levetiracetam after a first seizure. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Levetiracetam can cause behavioral changes, aggression, depression and suicidal thoughts. Seizure medicines must not be stopped without the provider.
items.a: Report mood changes, irritability or thoughts of self-harm
w: Stop the medicine once you have been seizure-free a week
Expect your urine to turn orange while on this medicine
Avoid green leafy vegetables while taking this medicine

items.q: An hour after IM haloperidol for agitation, a client's neck twists to one side and the eyes roll upward. Which medicine does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: These are signs of acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal reaction. An anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine or benztropine relieves it quickly.
items.a: Diphenhydramine IV or IM
w: Another dose of haloperidol
Dantrolene IV
Naloxone IV

items.q: Droperidol is ordered for a client with nausea and agitation. Which assessment should the nurse complete before giving it?
items.x: Droperidol has a boxed warning for QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. A baseline ECG helps identify clients at risk.
items.a: Review a baseline ECG for QT prolongation
w: Check the client's blood glucose level
Check the client's pupil response to light
Review the most recent liver enzymes

items.q: IM olanzapine has just been given to an agitated client. The provider now orders IV lorazepam as well. What should the nurse do?
items.x: IM olanzapine given with a parenteral benzodiazepine has been linked to dangerous cardiorespiratory depression. The combination is not recommended.
items.a: Clarify the order because the combination can depress breathing
w: Give the lorazepam right away to deepen the client's sedation
Give the lorazepam IM into the same site used for the olanzapine
Give both medicines again in one hour if agitation continues

items.q: An 82-year-old client received IV diphenhydramine for itching. Which finding should the nurse watch for most closely?
items.x: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and can cause confusion, falls and urinary retention in older adults.
items.a: New confusion and urinary retention
w: New diarrhea and abdominal cramps
New hyperactivity and weight loss
New bradycardia and hypoglycemia

items.q: A child with croup improves after a racemic epinephrine treatment. The parents ask to leave right away. What should the nurse explain?
items.x: Racemic epinephrine wears off within about two hours, and stridor can return. Observation for at least two hours is standard.
items.a: Your child needs to be watched for a few hours for returning symptoms
w: Your child can go home right now because the swelling is gone for good
Your child will need this same treatment every hour at home tonight
Your child should sleep in a cold room at home to keep swelling down

items.q: A client on telemetry has stable narrow-complex SVT at 190/min, and adenosine 6 mg IV is prescribed. Which administration technique should the nurse use?
items.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must be pushed rapidly and chased with a saline flush to reach the heart. A slow push or infusion lets it be metabolized before it works.
items.a: Rapid IV push at the closest port, then a fast 20 mL saline flush
w: Slow IV push over 2 minutes to reduce flushing and chest pressure
Dilute in 50 mL of saline and infuse over 15 minutes using a pump
Give into a distal hand vein, then flush slowly with 5 mL of saline

items.q: Immediately after adenosine IV push for SVT, the monitor shows about 4 seconds of asystole, then sinus rhythm at 88/min. The client is alert. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node, so a short pause before the rhythm returns is expected. The client is alert with a perfusing rhythm, so CPR, defibrillation and atropine are not indicated.
items.a: Continue monitoring, as a brief pause is expected with adenosine
w: Begin chest compressions and call a code for the asystole
Prepare to defibrillate the client at the highest energy setting
Give atropine IV push to prevent another episode of asystole

items.q: Adenosine is prescribed for a client with SVT. Which item in the client's history is most important to report to the provider before the dose?
items.x: Methylxanthines such as theophylline block adenosine receptors and can reduce its effect, and reactive airway disease raises bronchospasm risk. The other items do not affect adenosine.
items.a: Takes theophylline daily for chronic lung disease
w: Takes atorvastatin each night for high cholesterol
Has a documented allergy to penicillin
Takes omeprazole each morning for reflux

items.q: A client taking oral amiodarone for 8 months reports a new dry cough and shortness of breath on exertion. What is the nurse's priority action?
items.x: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary toxicity, which can be serious. New cough or dyspnea needs prompt evaluation, not reassurance.
items.a: Report the new respiratory symptoms to the provider promptly
w: Reassure the client that a cough is expected with this drug
Encourage an over-the-counter cough suppressant at bedtime
Teach the client to increase fluids to loosen secretions

items.q: A client is being discharged on long-term amiodarone. Which tests should the nurse expect to be monitored periodically?
items.x: Amiodarone can cause both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism and can injure the liver, so thyroid and liver tests are checked at baseline and over time.
items.a: Thyroid and liver function tests
w: Serum amylase and lipase levels
Serum uric acid and creatine kinase
Blood ammonia and lactate levels

items.q: A client stable on warfarin is started on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation. Which lab result should the nurse watch most closely in the following weeks?
items.x: Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism and can raise the INR and bleeding risk, so the INR is monitored closely and the warfarin dose often needs adjusting.
items.a: INR, because amiodarone can increase warfarin's effect
w: Serum sodium, because amiodarone causes major sodium loss
Platelet count, because amiodarone rapidly destroys platelets
Blood glucose, because amiodarone often causes hypoglycemia

items.q: The nurse is reinforcing discharge teaching for a client starting oral amiodarone. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Amiodarone causes photosensitivity and, over time, a blue-gray skin tint. Grapefruit juice raises amiodarone levels and doses should never be doubled.
items.a: Use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors
w: Drink grapefruit juice daily to improve absorption
Double the next dose if a dose is missed
Expect any skin color change to fade within a week

items.q: A client with heart failure is due for digoxin. The apical pulse counted for 1 full minute is 52/min. What should the nurse do?
items.x: An apical rate below 60/min in an adult is the usual parameter for holding digoxin and notifying the provider, because the drug slows AV conduction.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the pulse in 1 hour
Give half the dose and document the pulse
Have the client walk, then recount the pulse

items.q: The nurse reviews morning labs for a client receiving digoxin. Which result should be reported before giving the dose?
items.x: Low potassium increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmias. The other values are within normal limits.
items.a: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
w: Sodium 139 mEq/L
Magnesium 2.0 mg/dL
Calcium 9.4 mg/dL

items.q: Which report from a client taking digoxin is most suggestive of digoxin toxicity?
items.x: Visual changes such as yellow-green halos, along with nausea, anorexia and confusion, are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.
items.a: Seeing yellow-green halos around lights
w: Increased appetite over the past week
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Dry cough that is worse at night

items.q: A client with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is on a diltiazem infusion. The blood pressure falls to 82/48 mm Hg and the client is dizzy. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Diltiazem lowers blood pressure, and symptomatic hypotension requires holding the drip and prompt provider notification. Raising the head of the bed would worsen the dizziness.
items.a: Notify the provider before continuing the infusion
w: Increase the infusion rate to slow the heart rate
Give the next scheduled oral dose early
Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler

items.q: IV diltiazem is prescribed for rapid atrial fibrillation. Which item in the client's history should the nurse report before starting it?
items.x: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers depress contractility and should be avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. The other conditions do not affect the order.
items.a: Heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction
w: Hypothyroidism controlled with levothyroxine
Seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with a spray
Osteoarthritis of both knees

items.q: A client is admitted to telemetry to start dofetilide. Which assessments must be completed before the first dose?
items.x: Dofetilide is started in a monitored setting because it prolongs the QT interval. The dose depends on creatinine clearance and the baseline QTc.
items.a: QTc interval and creatinine clearance
w: Peak expiratory flow and oxygen saturation
Fingerstick glucose and hemoglobin A1C
Pupil response and level of consciousness

items.q: Two hours after a dose of sotalol, a client's QTc has risen from 440 ms to 540 ms. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Sotalol prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes. A QTc above 500 ms is a reason to hold and report.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the next dose
w: Give the next dose with food to slow absorption
Document this as an expected finding of sotalol
Give an extra potassium tablet and continue as ordered

items.q: Flecainide is prescribed for a client with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Which item in the history should the nurse report before the first dose?
items.x: Flecainide increased mortality in clients after myocardial infarction and is avoided in structural heart disease, so this history must be reported.
items.a: Myocardial infarction two years ago
w: Migraine headaches twice a month
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Hypothyroidism on daily replacement

items.q: A client has received an ibutilide infusion to convert atrial flutter. For which complication must the nurse monitor continuously for several hours afterward?
items.x: Ibutilide prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes, so continuous ECG monitoring is required for at least 4 hours after the infusion.
items.a: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
w: Severe rebound hypertensive crisis
Sudden profound hyperglycemia
Acute urinary retention and bladder spasm

items.q: A client receiving an IV lidocaine infusion for ventricular dysrhythmias becomes confused and reports numbness around the mouth. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Perioral numbness, confusion, tremor and slurred speech are early signs of lidocaine toxicity and can progress to seizures, so the provider must be notified.
items.a: Notify the provider of possible lidocaine toxicity
w: Document these findings as expected lidocaine effects
Increase the infusion to suppress the dysrhythmias
Give a dose of oral glucose and recheck in 15 minutes

items.q: A client with a recent MI is due for oral metoprolol. Vital signs are heart rate 48/min and blood pressure 88/56 mm Hg. What is the best action?
items.x: Bradycardia and hypotension are reasons to hold a beta blocker and contact the provider. The nurse does not change the dose independently.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck vital signs in 1 hour
Give the dose with a full glass of water
Give half the dose and document the vital signs

items.q: A client is being discharged on metoprolol succinate after an MI. Which teaching point should the nurse include?
items.x: Abrupt withdrawal of a beta blocker can cause rebound angina or MI. Extended-release tablets should not be crushed.
items.a: Take it every day, since suddenly missing doses can cause chest pain
w: Skip the dose on any day your heart rate is above 70 beats per minute
Crush the tablet and mix it with food if it is hard to swallow
Take an extra tablet whenever you feel your heart racing

items.q: IV metoprolol is prescribed for a client with rapid atrial fibrillation. Which assessment is most important immediately before giving the dose?
items.x: IV beta blockers can cause bradycardia and hypotension, so heart rate and blood pressure are checked right before and after each dose.
items.a: Heart rate and blood pressure
w: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Capillary refill in the toes
Urine specific gravity

items.q: During an IV procainamide infusion for stable wide-complex tachycardia, the QRS widens by more than 50% from baseline. What should the nurse do?
items.x: QRS widening of more than 50% is an endpoint for procainamide in ACLS, so the infusion is held and the provider notified.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately before continuing the infusion
w: Increase the infusion rate so the rhythm converts more quickly
Continue the infusion as ordered and recheck the ECG in 30 minutes
Give a bolus of IV potassium to narrow the widened QRS complex

items.q: Which finding is a common adverse effect the nurse should monitor for in a client taking amlodipine?
items.x: Peripheral edema is a common dose-related effect of amlodipine. Cough and hyperkalemia are linked to ACE inhibitors, and dihydropyridines do not usually slow the heart rate.
items.a: Swelling of the ankles and feet
w: Persistent dry hacking cough
Serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L
Resting heart rate of 46/min

items.q: A client given a second dose of lisinopril develops swelling of the lips and tongue and a hoarse voice. What is the nurse's priority action?
items.x: Angioedema from an ACE inhibitor can obstruct the airway. The nurse assesses the airway and gets emergency help.
items.a: Assess the airway and call the rapid response team
w: Give the next dose along with an oral antihistamine
Apply ice to the lips and recheck the swelling in 1 hour
Document it as an expected effect of the medication

items.q: Lisinopril is due for a client with heart failure. Today's potassium is 5.9 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: ACE inhibitors raise potassium. A level of 5.9 mEq/L is a reason to hold and notify. Bananas and salt substitutes add potassium.
items.a: Notify the provider of the potassium before giving the dose
w: Give the dose as ordered and recheck the potassium tomorrow
Give the dose with a banana to help balance the electrolytes
Give the dose and encourage salt substitutes with each meal

items.q: A client taking losartan is also prescribed spironolactone and oral potassium chloride. Which lab value is the priority to monitor?
items.x: An ARB, a potassium-sparing diuretic and a potassium supplement together greatly raise the risk of hyperkalemia.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum calcium
Serum albumin
Serum amylase

items.q: A client with heart failure is starting spironolactone. Which teaching point should the nurse include?
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium sparing, so potassium-containing salt substitutes can cause hyperkalemia.
items.a: Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
w: Eat extra potassium-rich foods every day
Expect weight loss of 2 kg each day
Take the dose at bedtime to avoid sleep loss

items.q: After IV hydralazine for severe hypertension, which finding should the nurse expect and monitor for?
items.x: Hydralazine is a direct arterial vasodilator. The drop in blood pressure triggers a reflex rise in heart rate.
items.a: Reflex tachycardia
w: Profound bradycardia
Hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia

items.q: A client has taken hydrochlorothiazide for several months. Which lab change should the nurse expect?
items.x: Thiazides cause loss of potassium and can raise glucose and uric acid. Sodium tends to fall, not rise.
items.a: Decreased serum potassium
w: Decreased serum glucose
Decreased serum uric acid
Increased serum sodium

items.q: A client taking isosorbide mononitrate asks whether sildenafil for erectile dysfunction is safe. What is the nurse's best response?
items.x: Nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors can cause profound, life-threatening hypotension, so the combination is contraindicated.
items.a: Taking them together can cause a severe drop in blood pressure
w: It is safe as long as you take the two drugs at least 1 hour apart
It is safe because the two drugs work on completely different organs
You can take it if you double your water intake on those days

items.q: A client with chest pain asks for prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin. Which assessment is most important before giving it?
items.x: Nitroglycerin causes vasodilation and can drop blood pressure, so blood pressure is checked before each dose.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Temperature
Pupil size
Blood glucose

items.q: A client with chest pain asks for sublingual nitroglycerin. The blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Nitroglycerin is generally held for systolic pressure below 90 mm Hg because it can worsen hypotension. The provider must be notified about ongoing chest pain.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the nitroglycerin
w: Give the nitroglycerin and recheck the pressure in 5 minutes
Give the tablet whole by mouth with a glass of water
Give two tablets at once to relieve the pain faster

items.q: A client receives IV labetalol for a hypertensive emergency. Which nursing action is most important after the dose?
items.x: IV labetalol can cause marked orthostatic hypotension, so the client stays supine and blood pressure is monitored closely.
items.a: Keep the client supine and monitor blood pressure closely
w: Walk the client in the hall to check for orthostatic dizziness
Check the client's blood glucose every 15 minutes for an hour
Give the client oral fluids to prevent dehydration and thirst

items.q: Propranolol is prescribed for a client with hypertension. Which item in the client's history is most important to report?
items.x: Propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker that can cause bronchospasm in clients with asthma.
items.a: Asthma with frequent wheezing
w: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
Osteoarthritis of the hip
History of kidney stones

items.q: A client taking clonidine for hypertension asks what happens if a few doses are missed. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Abrupt withdrawal of clonidine can cause rebound hypertension, so it must be tapered by the provider.
items.a: Missing doses suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound rise in blood pressure
w: Missing doses is harmless because the drug stays in your body for a week
Missing doses will cause your blood pressure to drop too low to stand
You may take all of the missed doses at once to catch up on the schedule

items.q: On day 6 of a heparin infusion, a client's platelet count has fallen from 250,000 to 95,000/mm3. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A platelet fall of more than 50% after 5 to 10 days of heparin suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs immediate provider evaluation.
items.a: Report the platelet drop to the provider promptly
w: Give the next heparin dose with dialysis as scheduled
Document it as an expected effect of dialysis
Apply ice packs to all of the injection sites

items.q: A client on a heparin infusion has an aPTT far above the target range and is bleeding from the gums. Which drug should the nurse expect to be available?
items.x: Protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
items.a: Protamine sulfate
w: Vitamin K injection
Idarucizumab
Andexanet alfa

items.q: A client on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 4.8 and no bleeding. The evening dose is due. What should the nurse do?
items.x: An INR of 4.8 is above the usual therapeutic range of 2 to 3. The dose is held and the provider decides on further management.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the INR in a week
Give half the dose and document the INR
Give the dose with vitamin K to balance it

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client starting warfarin. Which diet instruction is correct?
items.x: Consistent vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable. Sudden changes in green vegetable intake change warfarin's effect.
items.a: Keep your intake of leafy green vegetables about the same each week
w: Avoid eating all green vegetables for as long as you take warfarin
Eat extra spinach and kale on the days when your INR is low
Take a vitamin K supplement with each dose to protect your liver

items.q: A client taking apixaban asks what to take for knee pain. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.x: NSAIDs and aspirin add to bleeding risk with anticoagulants. Acetaminophen is preferred when used as directed.
items.a: Acetaminophen as directed is preferred over ibuprofen
w: Ibuprofen is fine as long as you take it with food
Naproxen twice daily is the safest choice for you
Aspirin is best because it also protects your heart

items.q: A client taking clopidogrel after a coronary stent has a new prescription for omeprazole. How does omeprazole interfere with clopidogrel?
items.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19. Omeprazole inhibits that enzyme, so less active drug is formed and platelet inhibition is weaker.
items.a: It inhibits CYP2C19, which activates clopidogrel
w: It raises stomach pH and blocks clopidogrel absorption
It induces CYP3A4, which clears clopidogrel faster
It competes with clopidogrel at the platelet receptor

items.q: A client started ticagrelor after an acute coronary syndrome. Which adverse effect is commonly reported with this drug?
items.x: Dyspnea is a common effect of ticagrelor. It is usually mild, but new or worsening dyspnea should be reported.
items.a: Shortness of breath
w: Persistent dry cough
Low blood glucose
Hair loss

items.q: A client receiving an eptifibatide infusion after a coronary intervention has a femoral sheath in place. Which assessment is most important?
items.x: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors increase bleeding risk, especially at the femoral access site.
items.a: Check the access site and distal pulses for bleeding
w: Check bowel sounds in all four quadrants every 2 hours
Check the pupils for size, equality and reaction to light
Check the skin of the trunk for a maculopapular rash

items.q: A client with acute decompensated heart failure is receiving high-dose IV furosemide. Which finding should the nurse report?
items.x: Rapid or high-dose IV furosemide can cause ototoxicity. Increased urine output, fewer crackles and weight loss are expected results.
items.a: New ringing in the ears
w: Increased urine output
Decreased crackles in the lungs
Weight loss of 1 kg overnight

items.q: Which assessment is the best indicator of fluid status for a client with heart failure on furosemide?
items.x: Daily weight is the most reliable measure of fluid gain or loss in heart failure.
items.a: Daily weight on the same scale at the same time
w: Skin turgor checked on the back of the hand daily
Color of the urine in the drainage collection bag
The client's report of thirst at the start of each shift

items.q: A client on furosemide has metolazone added for refractory edema. Which lab should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Adding a thiazide-like diuretic to a loop diuretic causes strong diuresis and can lead to severe hypokalemia.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum lipase
Serum ammonia
Serum troponin

items.q: A client taking enalapril is being switched to sacubitril-valsartan. Which action by the nurse is essential?
items.x: Sacubitril-valsartan with an ACE inhibitor raises the risk of angioedema, so a 36-hour washout is required.
items.a: Confirm 36 hours have passed since the last enalapril dose
w: Give both drugs together for the first week of treatment
Give the first dose 1 hour after the final enalapril dose
Give the two drugs on alternating days for the first 2 weeks

items.q: A client with advanced heart failure is receiving a milrinone infusion. Which assessment is most important?
items.x: Milrinone causes vasodilation and can cause hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias, so continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring are required.
items.a: Continuous ECG and frequent blood pressure checks
w: Hourly fingerstick blood glucose checks for the first day
Neurological checks with pupil response every hour
Daily full skin assessment for a rash or hives

items.q: A client on a dobutamine infusion has a heart rate that rises from 92 to 138/min with new frequent PVCs. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Dobutamine can cause tachycardia and ventricular dysrhythmias, which need prompt provider evaluation.
items.a: Notify the provider of the tachycardia and ectopy
w: Document this as the expected effect of the drug
Increase the infusion to improve cardiac output
Give the next dose of oral metoprolol early

items.q: A client starting ivabradine for heart failure asks about side effects. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Ivabradine can cause luminous phenomena (phosphenes), usually brief bright spots in vision. It slows the heart rate, so bradycardia is a concern.
items.a: Brief flashes of brightness in vision can occur
w: A dry cough means the medicine is working well
Expect a fast heart rate during the first week
Dark stools are expected while taking this drug

items.q: A client taking atorvastatin reports unexplained muscle pain and weakness with dark urine. What is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Muscle pain with dark urine may mean rhabdomyolysis, a rare but serious statin effect that needs prompt evaluation.
items.a: Report the symptoms to the provider promptly
w: Give the next dose with a full glass of extra water
Document them as expected effects of the drug
Give the next dose without food to ease the pain

items.q: The LVN is preparing to give digoxin to a client on the telemetry unit. Which data must the LVN collect first?
items.x: An apical pulse counted for a full minute is required before digoxin. A low rate is reported to the RN or provider before the dose is given.
items.a: Apical pulse for 1 full minute
w: Radial pulse for 1 full minute
Apical pulse for 30 seconds
Blood pressure in both arms

items.q: A client taking digoxin tells the LVN that food has no appeal and that he feels nauseated. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Anorexia and nausea are early signs of digoxin toxicity and must be reported before the dose.
items.a: Report the findings to the RN as possible toxicity
w: Offer crackers and give the digoxin dose as scheduled
Reinforce that nausea is an expected and harmless effect
Give the dose with a glass of milk to settle the stomach

items.q: Before giving oral metoprolol, the LVN finds a heart rate of 50/min and a blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Bradycardia and low blood pressure are reasons to hold a beta blocker and report. The LVN does not change the dose.
items.a: Report the findings to the RN before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the vital signs in 1 hour
Give the dose with extra fluids to raise the pressure
Give half the dose and document the vital signs

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for a client taking carvedilol. Which statement by the client needs more teaching?
items.x: Beta blockers must not be withdrawn abruptly because of rebound angina and tachycardia. The other statements are correct.
items.a: I can quit taking it once I feel better
w: I will take each dose with food
I may feel more tired for a few weeks
I will report a weight gain right away

items.q: A client taking lisinopril calls the LVN because the lips look swollen. What should the LVN do first?
items.x: Lip swelling may be angioedema, which can block the airway. The LVN checks breathing and gets help right away.
items.a: Check the airway and breathing and get the RN right away
w: Check the blood pressure and pulse and recheck in 15 minutes
Apply a cold pack to the lips and recheck in 30 minutes
Ask about new foods and document a possible food allergy

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a client with heart failure who takes furosemide. Which finding should be reported to the RN?
items.x: A rapid weight gain suggests fluid retention and worsening heart failure. The other findings are expected or normal.
items.a: Weight gain of 1.5 kg since yesterday
w: Weight loss of 0.5 kg since yesterday
Urine output of 60 mL in the past hour
Potassium of 4.1 mEq/L this morning

items.q: A client taking furosemide reports leg cramps and weakness. Which lab result should the LVN check for?
items.x: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, and muscle cramps and weakness are signs of hypokalemia.
items.a: Low potassium
w: High potassium
High calcium
High magnesium

items.q: The LVN notes that a client taking spironolactone has a potassium level of 5.8 mEq/L. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Spironolactone retains potassium. A high level is reported before the dose.
items.a: Report the result to the RN before giving the dose
w: Give the dose with a large glass of orange juice
Give the dose and recheck the lab again next week
Reinforce teaching about eating potassium-rich foods

items.q: A client taking amlodipine shows the LVN swelling of both ankles. Which is the best action?
items.x: Peripheral edema is a common effect of amlodipine and should be reported so the provider can evaluate it.
items.a: Report the swelling, as it is a known effect of amlodipine
w: Reinforce a low-salt diet, as it is caused by sodium intake
Request a diuretic order, as it is caused by fluid overload
Document the swelling, as it will fade with continued doses

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching about sublingual nitroglycerin. The client asks what to do if chest pain does not ease after the first tablet. Which reply is correct?
items.x: Current teaching is to call emergency services if chest pain is unimproved or worse 5 minutes after the first dose.
items.a: Call 911 if the pain is not better 5 minutes after the first dose
w: Call 911 only if the pain is not better after three tablets
Call your provider if the pain is not better after 15 minutes
Take a second tablet and rest 30 minutes before calling anyone

items.q: Which data should the LVN collect before giving a client a prescribed dose of sublingual nitroglycerin?
items.x: Nitroglycerin can drop blood pressure. A low pressure is reported before the dose.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Radial pulse
Oxygen saturation
Respiratory rate

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for a client on warfarin. Which client statement shows understanding?
items.x: Bleeding precautions are important with warfarin. Aspirin adds to bleeding risk and vitamin K intake should be consistent.
items.a: I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
w: I will cut all green vegetables out of my diet
I will use ibuprofen instead of aspirin for pain
I will take a missed dose along with the next one

items.q: The LVN reviews the chart of a client on warfarin. Which result should be reported before the evening dose?
items.x: An INR of 5.1 is well above the usual therapeutic range and increases bleeding risk.
items.a: INR of 5.1
w: INR of 2.9
aPTT of 32 seconds
Platelets of 165,000/mm3

items.q: The LVN is caring for a client on heparin. Which finding should be reported to the RN immediately?
items.x: Black tarry stools suggest gastrointestinal bleeding, which is a serious complication of anticoagulation.
items.a: Black tarry stools
w: Small bruise at an old IV site
aPTT within the target range
Mild soreness at the IV site

items.q: The LVN is giving subcutaneous enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe. Which technique is correct?
items.x: The air bubble in the prefilled syringe is left in, and the site is not rubbed, to reduce bruising.
items.a: Leave the air bubble in and do not rub the site
w: Expel the air bubble first and massage the site after
Inject into the deltoid muscle and rub the site gently
Aspirate before injecting the medicine into the abdomen

items.q: A client taking apixaban asks the LVN about pain relief for a headache. Which reply reinforces correct teaching?
items.x: NSAIDs and aspirin increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants. Acetaminophen is usually preferred.
items.a: Check with your provider, as acetaminophen is often preferred
w: Ibuprofen is the best choice to take with your blood thinner
Take aspirin, since it does not affect bleeding with this drug
Naproxen is safe as long as you take it with a full meal

items.q: A client taking clopidogrel after a stent placement says he plans to skip it before a dental cleaning. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Interrupting antiplatelet therapy after a stent raises the risk of stent thrombosis. Any interruption must be decided by the provider.
items.a: Report it to the RN, as only the provider can decide on a pause
w: Reinforce that a short pause is routine before any dental work
Suggest taking only the aspirin until the cleaning is finished
Advise calling the dentist, as the dentist decides on a pause

items.q: A client taking atorvastatin tells the LVN about new muscle aches in both thighs. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Muscle pain can signal statin myopathy and should be reported.
items.a: Report the muscle aches to the RN
w: Reinforce that aches fade with time
Suggest taking the dose at bedtime
Offer a warm pack and recheck later

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a client taking oral diltiazem. Which finding should be reported?
items.x: Diltiazem slows AV conduction and can cause bradycardia, which should be reported before the next dose.
items.a: Heart rate of 48/min
w: Heart rate of 62/min
Blood pressure of 110/68 mm Hg
Respirations of 18/min

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a client taking sotalol. Which client report should be reported right away?
items.x: Syncope may signal a dangerous dysrhythmia such as torsades de pointes, which sotalol can cause.
items.a: Fainting while walking to the bathroom
w: Mild fatigue in the late afternoon
Cold hands and feet in the morning
Trouble falling asleep some nights

items.q: A client on hemodialysis is prescribed calcium acetate. Which instruction should the nurse give about timing?
items.x: Phosphate binders work by binding dietary phosphorus in the gut, so they must be taken with meals.
items.a: Take it with each meal
w: Take it at bedtime on an empty stomach
Take it only on dialysis days
Take it 2 hours after meals

items.q: A client taking calcium acetate has new constipation, confusion and muscle weakness. Which lab result should the nurse check first?
items.x: Calcium-based binders can cause hypercalcemia, which presents with constipation, confusion and weakness.
items.a: Serum calcium
w: Serum sodium
Serum glucose
Serum albumin

items.q: A client in the dialysis unit has a potassium of 7.4 mEq/L with peaked T waves and a widening QRS. IV calcium chloride is prescribed. Which access is preferred?
items.x: Calcium chloride is very irritating and can cause severe tissue necrosis if it extravasates, so a central line is preferred when available.
items.a: A central venous catheter
w: A small hand vein with a 24-gauge catheter
A subcutaneous infusion site
The arterial needle of the dialysis circuit

items.q: What is the purpose of IV calcium in a client with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes?
items.x: IV calcium protects the heart from dysrhythmias within minutes but does not lower the serum potassium. Other treatments are needed to shift or remove potassium.
items.a: To stabilize the cardiac cell membrane
w: To move potassium into the cells
To remove potassium through the stool
To increase potassium loss in the urine

items.q: A client with hyperkalemia is to receive IV calcium gluconate and also takes digoxin. What should the nurse do?
items.x: IV calcium in a client on digoxin carries a risk of dysrhythmias. The nurse confirms the plan and keeps the client on continuous ECG monitoring.
items.a: Clarify the plan with the provider and use continuous ECG monitoring
w: Give the calcium rapidly so it works before the digoxin takes effect
Give the calcium and the scheduled digoxin dose together in one line
Give the calcium orally instead of by IV to avoid any interaction

items.q: IV calcium gluconate and sodium bicarbonate are both ordered for a client in acute kidney injury. Which action is correct?
items.x: Calcium and bicarbonate form an insoluble precipitate, so they are never mixed and the line is flushed between them.
items.a: Give them through separate lines or flush well between them
w: Mix them together in the same syringe to save time in the emergency
Give them together in one small minibag of normal saline
Give the calcium directly into the running bicarbonate infusion

items.q: A client with end-stage kidney disease is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which assessment is most important?
items.x: Clients with kidney failure cannot excrete magnesium well. Loss of reflexes and slow breathing are signs of toxicity.
items.a: Deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate
w: Bowel sounds and abdominal girth measurement
Pupil size and reaction to light
Skin turgor and moist mucous membranes

items.q: A client with chronic kidney disease asks about a magnesium-based laxative. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Impaired kidneys cannot excrete magnesium, so magnesium-containing products can cause hypermagnesemia.
items.a: Avoid magnesium laxatives and antacids unless your provider approves
w: Magnesium laxatives are the safest choice for clients with kidney disease
Take a magnesium laxative daily to help remove extra potassium
Use magnesium antacids in place of your prescribed phosphate binder

items.q: A client is prescribed patiromer for chronic hyperkalemia and also takes several oral drugs. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Patiromer can bind other oral drugs, so they are separated by at least 3 hours.
items.a: Separate other oral medicines by at least 3 hours
w: Take it together with all your other medicines at once
Take it only on days when you feel muscle weakness
Mix it with orange juice for the best possible effect

items.q: A client with a potassium of 7.0 mEq/L and ECG changes has patiromer ordered as the only treatment. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Patiromer has a delayed onset and is not for life-threatening hyperkalemia. Emergency treatment is needed.
items.a: Notify the provider, as patiromer acts too slowly for an emergency
w: Give the patiromer and recheck the potassium level in one week
Give the patiromer and allow the client to eat a normal diet today
Give double the patiromer dose so that it lowers potassium faster

items.q: A client has taken patiromer for several weeks. Which additional lab should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Patiromer can cause hypomagnesemia, so magnesium is monitored along with potassium.
items.a: Serum magnesium
w: Serum amylase
Serum ammonia
Serum lipase

items.q: A client with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L has IV potassium chloride ordered through a peripheral IV. Which action is correct?
items.x: IV potassium is never given by push. It is diluted and given by pump, and many policies limit peripheral infusions to 10 mEq per hour.
items.a: Infuse it diluted by pump, no faster than 10 mEq per hour
w: Give it undiluted by slow IV push over at least 5 minutes
Infuse it by gravity as fast as the IV line will allow
Add it to a hanging IV bag without inverting to mix it

items.q: Before giving IV potassium chloride to a client in acute kidney injury, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Potassium is cleared by the kidneys. Low urine output raises the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia, so it must be checked first.
items.a: Urine output over the past few hours
w: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Skin turgor over the inner forearm area
Capillary refill in the fingers and toes

items.q: A client on hemodialysis has an order for oral potassium chloride. Today's potassium is 5.6 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: The level is above normal. Giving potassium could cause dangerous hyperkalemia, so the nurse holds and notifies.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose with a large meal as ordered
Give the dose after dialysis instead of now
Give half the dose and document the reason

items.q: Which client statement shows understanding of teaching about sevelamer?
items.x: Sevelamer binds dietary phosphorus and is taken with meals. The tablets should not be crushed or chewed.
items.a: I will take it with my meals and swallow it whole
w: I will take it at bedtime with a snack
I will chew the tablets before swallowing
I will take it only when my phosphorus is high

items.q: A client with chronic kidney disease takes oral sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis. Which finding should the nurse report?
items.x: Sodium bicarbonate adds sodium, which can cause fluid retention and edema in kidney disease.
items.a: New edema and a weight gain of 2 kg
w: Serum bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L
Mild belching after each of the doses
Normal vesicular lung sounds

items.q: A client taking sodium zirconium cyclosilicate develops swelling of both legs. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate contains sodium and can cause edema, which should be reported.
items.a: Report the edema to the provider
w: Give the next dose with extra fluids
Document as unrelated to the drug
Elevate the legs and give double the dose

items.q: A client is prescribed sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and also takes oral drugs with pH-dependent absorption. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: SZC can change gastric pH and affect other drugs, so they are separated by at least 2 hours.
items.a: Take other oral medicines at least 2 hours before or after it
w: Take all of the medicines together at one time to save time
Take it only on the days that you have a dialysis treatment
Take it mixed with orange juice to help with its absorption

items.q: Finerenone is prescribed for a client with diabetic kidney disease. Which lab is most important to check before the first dose?
items.x: Finerenone can cause hyperkalemia. It should not be started if the potassium is above 5.0 mEq/L.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum lipase
Serum ammonia
Serum uric acid

items.q: A client taking finerenone asks about drinking grapefruit juice. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Finerenone is metabolized by CYP3A4. Grapefruit inhibits it and raises finerenone levels and the risk of hyperkalemia.
items.a: Avoid grapefruit juice, as it can raise drug levels
w: Grapefruit juice is fine if you drink it only at night
Grapefruit juice helps the medicine work much better
Drink grapefruit juice daily to lower your potassium

items.q: A client on finerenone has a potassium level of 6.0 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A potassium of 6.0 mEq/L is dangerous, and finerenone raises potassium. The dose is held and the provider is notified.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the potassium tomorrow
Give the dose with a high-potassium snack
Give half the dose and document the level

items.q: A client taking ferric citrate reports dark stools. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.x: Ferric citrate contains iron and commonly darkens stools. Signs of bleeding still need evaluation.
items.a: This iron binder often darkens stools, but report tarry or bloody stools
w: Dark stools mean a bleeding ulcer, so go to the emergency room right now
Dark stools mean you should take the medicine on an empty stomach instead
Dark stools mean the drug is not working and should be changed right away

items.q: A client on hemodialysis takes ferric citrate and is also receiving IV iron. Which lab should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Ferric citrate is absorbed and raises iron stores. With IV iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation are monitored to avoid iron overload.
items.a: Ferritin and transferrin saturation
w: Serum troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide
Serum amylase and lipase
Prothrombin time and INR

items.q: A client taking potassium citrate for kidney stones asks how to take it. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Potassium citrate is taken with meals or a snack and swallowed whole to reduce gastrointestinal irritation.
items.a: Take it with meals and swallow the tablet whole
w: Take it on an empty stomach at bedtime with water
Crush the tablet and mix it into soft food
Take it along with a potassium salt substitute

items.q: A client is prescribed sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
items.x: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is linked to intestinal necrosis. Severe abdominal pain needs immediate evaluation.
items.a: Severe abdominal pain and distention
w: One soft bowel movement after the dose
Mild nausea after the dose
Mild thirst during the afternoon

items.q: A client receiving sodium polystyrene sulfonate takes several other oral medicines. What should the nurse do?
items.x: The resin can bind other oral drugs, so they are separated by at least 3 hours, or 6 hours in clients with gastroparesis.
items.a: Give other oral medicines at least 3 hours before or after it
w: Mix the other oral medicines right into the resin suspension
Give all of the medicines together right after the same meal
Give the other oral medicines only once a day, at bedtime instead

items.q: A client with IgA nephropathy is starting sparsentan. Which lab test does the nurse expect to be monitored?
items.x: Sparsentan can cause liver injury, so liver tests are checked before and during treatment.
items.a: Liver aminotransferases
w: Serum amylase and lipase
Arterial serum ammonia
Thyroid antibody panel

items.q: A client with IgA nephropathy is prescribed sparsentan and is also taking losartan. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Sparsentan already blocks the angiotensin receptor, so it should not be combined with ARBs or ACE inhibitors.
items.a: Clarify the order, as sparsentan is not used with an ARB
w: Give both drugs together as ordered and monitor the BP
Give the losartan in the evening and sparsentan in the morning
Give the sparsentan with grapefruit juice to aid absorption

items.q: A female client of childbearing age is starting sparsentan. Which teaching is most important?
items.x: Sparsentan can cause embryo-fetal harm, so pregnancy must be avoided and reliable contraception used.
items.a: Use reliable contraception, as the drug can harm a fetus
w: Take a pregnancy test only if your period is late
Pregnancy is safe as long as you take folic acid
You can take the drug during pregnancy in the evening

items.q: A client starting atrasentan for IgA nephropathy asks what to report. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Endothelin receptor antagonists such as atrasentan can cause fluid retention, so edema and weight gain should be reported.
items.a: Report swelling of the legs or rapid weight gain
w: Report any increase in how often you urinate
Report a better appetite than before treatment
Report any mild thirst during the warm months

items.q: Before starting atrasentan in a female client of childbearing potential, which result must the nurse confirm?
items.x: Atrasentan can cause embryo-fetal harm, so pregnancy must be ruled out before starting.
items.a: A negative pregnancy test
w: A normal serum lipase
A normal hemoglobin A1C
A negative throat culture

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client prescribed sucroferric oxyhydroxide?
items.x: Sucroferric oxyhydroxide is a chewable phosphate binder that must be chewed and taken with meals.
items.a: Chew the tablet with meals
w: Swallow the tablet whole at bedtime
Take it on an empty stomach
Take it once weekly at dialysis

items.q: A client on lanthanum carbonate reports severe abdominal pain and vomiting. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Lanthanum can cause gastrointestinal obstruction and perforation, so severe pain and vomiting need prompt evaluation.
items.a: Report the symptoms to the provider promptly
w: Give the next dose with a full glass of extra water
Document them as expected effects of the drug
Give the next dose without food to ease the pain

items.q: A client taking lanthanum carbonate is scheduled for an abdominal X-ray. Why should the nurse inform the radiology staff?
items.x: Lanthanum is radiopaque and can show on abdominal X-rays, which could be confused with other findings.
items.a: Lanthanum can appear radiopaque on the image
w: Lanthanum makes the client allergic to contrast
Lanthanum must be held for 2 days before imaging
Lanthanum causes the X-ray to be falsely normal

items.q: A client with struvite stones from chronic urease-producing infections is prescribed acetohydroxamic acid. Which result is most important before the first dose in a woman of childbearing age?
items.x: Acetohydroxamic acid can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
items.a: Negative pregnancy test
w: Normal serum lipase
Normal urine color
Normal platelet count

items.q: A client taking acetohydroxamic acid reports calf pain and swelling. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Acetohydroxamic acid has been linked to deep vein thrombosis. Calf pain and swelling need evaluation.
items.a: Report the findings to the provider promptly
w: Massage the calf firmly to relieve the pain
Teach the client to increase walking each day
Document them as expected effects of the drug

items.q: Tromethamine is ordered for a client with severe metabolic acidosis. Which finding should the nurse report before starting it?

Vitamin K is needed only for babies born by cesarean or with forceps
Breast milk supplies all the vitamin K a newborn needs to clot well

items.q: After an epidural bolus of bupivacaine, a laboring client's blood pressure falls to 84/46 and the fetal heart rate slows. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Sympathetic block causes hypotension. Lateral positioning and a fluid bolus improve venous return and placental perfusion, then anesthesia is notified.
items.a: Turn the client to her side and increase IV fluids per protocol
w: Place the client flat on her back and raise both legs on pillows
Increase the epidural infusion rate so the client stays comfortable
Give oral fluids and recheck the blood pressure in 30 minutes

items.q: A client with a bupivacaine epidural reports a metallic taste, ringing in her ears and numb lips. What should the nurse do?
items.x: These are early signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, which can progress to seizures and cardiac arrest.
items.a: Notify anesthesia immediately of possible systemic toxicity
w: Reassure her that these are common and expected epidural effects
Increase the epidural rate to keep her more comfortable in labor
Offer ice chips for the taste and recheck her symptoms in 1 hour

items.q: A laboring client received IV fentanyl 20 minutes ago and is now quickly progressing to birth. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Opioids cross the placenta, and a dose close to birth can depress the newborn's breathing. The team prepares to support ventilation.
items.a: Tell the newborn team so they can prepare for respiratory depression
w: Give a second fentanyl dose now to cover the whole pushing stage
Plan to hold the baby's first feeding for 24 hours after birth
Plan to give the newborn naloxone routinely right after the birth

items.q: A postpartum client takes scheduled acetaminophen and asks if she can also take an over-the-counter cold medicine. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Combination products can lead to accidental acetaminophen overdose and liver damage.
items.a: Check labels because many products also contain acetaminophen
w: Any over-the-counter cold medicine is safe to add with this one
Take the cold medicine only with milk to protect your stomach
Double the acetaminophen dose if your cold symptoms get worse

items.q: A postpartum client is prescribed ibuprofen for afterbirth pain. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: NSAIDs can irritate the stomach, so taking them with food reduces GI upset.
items.a: Take it with food to lower stomach upset
w: Take it on an empty stomach for faster relief
Take it with an antacid that has aspirin
Lie flat for 30 minutes after each dose

items.q: A client is prescribed docusate after a fourth-degree laceration repair. Which statement shows correct understanding?
items.x: Docusate is a stool softener that reduces straining. It works over 1 to 3 days and needs good fluid intake.
items.a: This softens my stool so I do not strain
w: This medicine will cause a bowel movement within an hour
This medicine will treat my perineal pain
I should take this with very little fluid

items.q: A postpartum client is discharged on ferrous sulfate. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.x: Calcium, antacids and tea reduce iron absorption. Iron is best taken apart from them, ideally with vitamin C.
items.a: Do not take it at the same time as milk or antacids
w: Take it with a glass of milk to protect your stomach
Take it together with your calcium supplement daily
Take it with a cup of tea to help it absorb better

items.q: A breastfeeding client chooses medroxyprogesterone injection for birth control. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Medroxyprogesterone injection can lower bone mineral density. It is given every 3 months and is compatible with breastfeeding.
items.a: Get enough calcium and vitamin D and do weight-bearing exercise
w: Expect your periods to become very regular and light on this method
You will need a new injection every month to stay fully protected
This method will quickly dry up your breast milk supply for good

items.q: A preterm infant receiving caffeine citrate for apnea of prematurity has a resting heart rate of 196. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Caffeine can cause tachycardia. A sustained heart rate this high is reported before more doses are given.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the next dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the heart rate in 4 hours
Give the dose early to prevent apnea
Document this as an expected effect

items.q: Parents ask why their 29-week infant receives caffeine citrate. What should the nurse explain?
items.x: Caffeine citrate stimulates the respiratory center and is used to treat apnea of prematurity.
items.a: It stimulates breathing and reduces pauses in breathing
w: It helps the baby stay awake and alert for longer feedings
It helps the baby's lungs make more surfactant over time
It treats a bacterial infection in the baby's bloodstream

items.q: A preterm infant on caffeine citrate develops abdominal distension, feeding intolerance and blood in the stool. What should the nurse do?
items.x: These signs suggest necrotizing enterocolitis, which has been reported with caffeine citrate and needs urgent evaluation.
items.a: Notify the provider right away before continuing the feeding
w: Increase the feeding volume to help settle the baby's stomach
Give the next caffeine dose with the feeding and keep watching
Recheck the abdomen at the next scheduled care time and chart

items.q: Minutes after poractant alfa is given, an intubated preterm infant's chest rises more easily and SpO2 is 99% on 60% oxygen. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Surfactant quickly improves lung compliance. Oxygen and pressures must be weaned promptly to avoid hyperoxia and pneumothorax.
items.a: Prompt weaning of oxygen and ventilator pressures
w: Giving a second full dose of surfactant right away
Increasing the ventilator pressures to keep chest rise
Suctioning the endotracheal tube right now to clear it

items.q: During instillation of poractant alfa, the infant's heart rate falls to 80 and SpO2 drops. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Bradycardia and desaturation during dosing are managed by pausing and ventilating. Dosing resumes when the infant is stable.
items.a: Pause dosing and support ventilation until the infant is stable
w: Instill the rest of the dose quickly so it reaches both lungs
Suction the endotracheal tube to remove the surfactant now
Give atropine first and then continue the instillation as planned

items.q: A newborn with a ductal-dependent heart defect is started on alprostadil. Which equipment must be at the bedside?
items.x: Apnea is a boxed warning with alprostadil, especially in infants under 2 kg and in the first hour of infusion.
items.a: Equipment for bag-mask ventilation and intubation
w: A cooling blanket for the expected high temperature
A phototherapy light for the expected rise in bilirubin
An extra feeding pump for continuous gavage feeds

items.q: A newborn with coarctation of the aorta is receiving alprostadil. Which finding shows that the drug is working?
items.x: Alprostadil keeps the ductus arteriosus open, which improves blood flow to the lower body in coarctation.
items.a: Stronger femoral pulses and warmer legs
w: A lower and more regular heart rate
A higher body temperature and flushing
More frequent and looser yellow stools

items.q: A preterm infant is due for IV indomethacin for a patent ductus arteriosus. Urine output over the last 8 hours was 0.4 mL/kg/hr. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Indomethacin reduces kidney blood flow. The label says to hold the dose for marked oliguria and report it.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and increase IV fluids
Give the dose and recheck output in 12 hours
Give furosemide first, then the dose

items.q: Before each dose of IV indomethacin for a patent ductus arteriosus, which labs should the nurse review?
items.x: Indomethacin can reduce kidney function and impair platelet function, so creatinine and platelets are checked.
items.a: Serum creatinine and platelet count
w: Blood culture and C-reactive protein
Thyroid and liver panel
Bilirubin and blood type

items.q: A preterm infant receiving hydrocortisone for low blood pressure is prescribed indomethacin. Which complication should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Giving indomethacin with a corticosteroid raises the risk of spontaneous intestinal perforation in preterm infants.
items.a: Intestinal perforation
w: Low blood glucose
Hearing loss
High blood pressure

items.q: A preterm infant is receiving IV ibuprofen lysine for a patent ductus arteriosus. Which finding should the nurse report right away?
items.x: NSAIDs can cause GI bleeding and are linked to necrotizing enterocolitis. A quieter murmur may mean the ductus is closing.
items.a: Abdominal distension and bloody stools
w: A drop in heart rate during sleep
A soft heart murmur that is quieter
Urine output of 2 mL/kg/hr

items.q: A neonate is receiving IV acetaminophen around the clock. Which labs should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Acetaminophen can cause liver injury, so liver tests are watched with repeated dosing.
items.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum lipase level
Thyroid hormone levels
Hemoglobin A1c level

items.q: A newborn with suspected sepsis is prescribed IV ampicillin and gentamicin through one IV line. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Ampicillin inactivates aminoglycosides in the same solution, so they are given separately with a flush between.
items.a: Flush the line between the two drugs
w: Mix both drugs in one syringe
Give both drugs at the same time through a Y-site
Give gentamicin first with no flush

items.q: A trough level is prescribed for a neonate receiving gentamicin. When should the nurse draw it?
items.x: Trough levels are drawn just before the next dose to check that the drug is clearing and to limit toxicity.
items.a: Just before the next dose
w: Right after the dose ends
Two hours after the dose
At any time during the day

items.q: A neonate's gentamicin trough comes back higher than the target range. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A high trough raises the risk of kidney and ear damage, so the dose is held and reported.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the next dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the trough tomorrow
Give the dose over a longer time
Give half the dose

items.q: A neonate on gentamicin is also prescribed furosemide. Which effect should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Loop diuretics add to the ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity of aminoglycosides.
items.a: Increased risk of hearing damage
w: Lower blood glucose after feeds
Lower serum gentamicin levels
Increased muscle tone and jitters

items.q: During a vancomycin infusion, an infant develops redness of the face, neck and upper body. Blood pressure is stable. What should the nurse do?
items.x: This is a vancomycin infusion reaction related to fast infusion. It is managed by pausing and slowing the infusion.
items.a: Notify the provider before continuing the infusion
w: Give the rest of the dose as a slow IV push instead
Increase the rate to finish the infusion more quickly
Apply cool cloths and continue the infusion as ordered

items.q: A newborn is receiving high-dose IV acyclovir for herpes simplex virus. Which labs should the nurse monitor?
items.x: High-dose acyclovir in neonates can cause neutropenia and kidney injury.
items.a: Absolute neutrophil count and creatinine
w: Blood glucose and urine ketone levels
Serum magnesium and phosphate levels
Thyroid hormone and cortisol levels

items.q: A preterm infant receiving fluconazole is now prescribed midazolam. What should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and can raise midazolam levels, causing more sedation and respiratory depression.
items.a: More sedation and slower breathing than expected
w: Lower fluconazole levels and less antifungal effect
Higher blood glucose levels after each feeding
A faster heart rate and more irritability than usual

items.q: The nurse is teaching a breastfeeding parent how to give nystatin suspension for an infant's thrush. Which statement shows understanding?
items.x: Nystatin works by contact, so it is placed in the mouth after feedings. The parent's nipples may also need treatment.
items.a: I will put it inside each cheek after feedings
w: I will mix it into a full bottle of formula
I will give it right before each feeding
I will give it only when I see white patches

items.q: A newborn whose parents declined vitamin K is now 3 weeks old. Which finding should the nurse report right away?
items.x: These signs suggest vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can include bleeding in the brain.
items.a: Bleeding from the umbilical stump and a bulging fontanel
w: Yellow, seedy stools after each breastfeeding session
Tiny white bumps scattered across the nose and the chin
Sneezing several times a day with no fever or cough

items.q: A 10-day-old infant is discharged on oral erythromycin for pertussis exposure. What should the nurse teach the parents to report?
items.x: Oral erythromycin in young infants is linked to hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which causes projectile vomiting.
items.a: Forceful vomiting after feedings
w: Yellow seedy stools after feedings
Sleeping about 16 hours each day
Hiccups for a few minutes after feeding

items.q: An infant receiving a morphine infusion after surgery has a respiratory rate of 18 and SpO2 of 86%. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Morphine causes respiratory depression. The infant needs immediate stimulation and breathing support, then the provider is notified.
items.a: Stimulate the infant and support breathing
w: Document the findings and keep observing
Increase the morphine rate for comfort
Recheck the infant's vital signs in 30 minutes

items.q: The nurse is giving IV fentanyl to an intubated neonate. Which action helps prevent chest wall rigidity?
items.x: Rapid IV fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity, which makes ventilation hard. Slow administration lowers the risk.
items.a: Give the dose slowly over several minutes
w: Give the dose as a rapid push
Give the dose with a feeding
Give the dose into the endotracheal tube

items.q: Midazolam is prescribed for a preterm neonate. Which action is most important?
items.x: Some midazolam products contain benzyl alcohol, which is toxic to neonates. Rapid injection can cause severe hypotension.
items.a: Use a preservative-free product and give it slowly
w: Give it as a rapid IV push so it acts more quickly
Mix it with the next feeding to make it easier to give
Give it down the endotracheal tube for faster effect

items.q: An intubated infant on a dexmedetomidine infusion has a heart rate of 82, down from 140. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine can cause bradycardia and hypotension, which must be reported.
items.a: Notify the provider of the bradycardia
w: Increase the dexmedetomidine infusion rate
Give a bolus dose of dexmedetomidine now
Document the change as expected deep sleep

items.q: An infant receiving methadone for neonatal opioid withdrawal is very sleepy, feeds poorly and has shallow breathing. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Too much sedation means the dose may be too high. The dose is held and reported.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the next dose
w: Give the next methadone dose early as planned
Increase the feeding volume to boost the energy
Swaddle the infant snugly and recheck in 4 hours

items.q: Parents ask why clonidine for their infant's withdrawal is being lowered slowly. What should the nurse explain?
items.x: Abrupt withdrawal of clonidine can cause rebound hypertension and agitation, so it is weaned.
items.a: Ending it suddenly can cause rebound high blood pressure and agitation
w: Lowering it slowly helps the medicine work better against the withdrawal
It is lowered slowly because the infant has become addicted to the drug
Ending it suddenly can cause low blood sugar and very sleepy feedings

items.q: Before a dose of clonidine, an infant's heart rate is 88 and blood pressure is lower than usual. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Clonidine can cause bradycardia and hypotension, so the dose is held and reported.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the vitals in 1 hour
Give the dose along with the next feeding
Give half the dose and document the vitals

items.q: A neonate with seizures is receiving phenobarbital. Which test helps the provider adjust the dose?
items.x: Phenobarbital levels guide dosing and help prevent toxicity.
items.a: Phenobarbital drug level
w: Serum lipase level
Arterial blood ammonia
Urine culture results

items.q: Parents of an infant going home on levetiracetam ask about the medicine. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Seizure medicines are given on schedule, and abrupt withdrawal can trigger seizures.
items.a: Give it at the same times each day and do not end it suddenly
w: Give it only on the days when the baby is having seizures
Mix it with a small amount of honey to improve the taste
Lower the dose on your own whenever the baby seems fussy

items.q: An infant has a dopamine infusion through a peripheral IV. The site becomes pale and cool. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Dopamine extravasation can cause tissue necrosis. The infusion is stopped and phentolamine may be ordered.
items.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
w: Apply a warm pack and continue
Increase the infusion rate
Flush the IV with saline

items.q: An infant on a dobutamine infusion has a heart rate of 210. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Dobutamine can cause tachycardia and dysrhythmias. A heart rate this high must be reported.
items.a: Notify the provider
w: Increase the dobutamine rate
Give a fluid bolus
Document it as an expected effect

items.q: An infant is receiving a milrinone infusion after cardiac surgery. Which labs should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Milrinone is cleared by the kidneys and can cause thrombocytopenia, so platelets and renal function are watched.
items.a: Platelet count and serum creatinine
w: Serum ammonia and lactate levels
Thyroid hormone and cortisol levels
Serum lipase and amylase levels

items.q: An infant on a milrinone infusion has a mean arterial pressure below the prescribed target. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Milrinone dilates blood vessels and can cause hypotension, which needs provider evaluation.
items.a: Notify the provider of the low blood pressure
w: Increase the milrinone infusion rate by one step
Give a milrinone bolus from the bag on the pump
Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees and wait

items.q: During newborn resuscitation, when is IV epinephrine indicated?
items.x: Epinephrine is given when the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation and at least 60 seconds of compressions with 100% oxygen.
items.a: Heart rate below 60 after effective ventilation and 60 seconds of compressions
w: Heart rate below 100 after 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation
Oxygen saturation below the target range at 5 minutes despite oxygen given
Central cyanosis that persists at 1 minute of life with a normal heart rate

items.q: The nurse is drawing up IV epinephrine for newborn resuscitation. Which concentration should the nurse use?
items.x: Neonatal IV epinephrine uses the 0.1 mg/mL concentration. Using 1 mg/mL is a tenfold error.
items.a: 0.1 mg/mL (1 mg per 10 mL)
w: 1 mg/mL (1 mg per 1 mL)
Any concentration diluted with saline
The concentration used for anaphylaxis

items.q: An infant with chronic lung disease receives furosemide daily. Which lab result should the nurse report?
items.x: Furosemide wastes potassium. A potassium of 2.9 is low and can cause dysrhythmias.
items.a: Serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L
w: Serum sodium of 138 mEq/L
Serum calcium of 9.4 mg/dL
Blood glucose of 82 mg/dL

items.q: A neonate's IV prescription is D15W through a peripheral IV. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Dextrose above 12.5% is not infused peripherally because it can cause phlebitis and tissue injury. It needs central access.
items.a: Clarify the order before hanging the fluid
w: Hang the fluid at the prescribed rate
Dilute the bag with sterile water
Hang it and check the site every 4 hours

items.q: An infant is prescribed calcium gluconate and sodium bicarbonate through the same IV line. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Calcium and bicarbonate form a precipitate, so they are never mixed and the line is flushed between them.
items.a: Flush the line well between the two drugs
w: Draw up both drugs in one syringe
Run them together through a Y-site
Give the bicarbonate first with no flush

items.q: An infant receiving calcium gluconate through a peripheral IV has a swollen, pale IV site. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Calcium extravasation can cause tissue necrosis and calcification. The infusion is stopped and the provider is notified.
items.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
w: Flush the IV to clear the line
Apply a warm pack and continue the infusion
Elevate the limb and continue the infusion

items.q: Sodium bicarbonate is prescribed for a preterm infant with metabolic acidosis. What should the nurse confirm first?
items.x: Bicarbonate produces CO2, so ventilation must be adequate. It is also given slowly to lower the risk of brain bleeding.
items.a: That ventilation is adequate
