w: That a feeding has just been given
That the infant is in a prone position
That a blood culture has been drawn

items.q: An infant is on a regular insulin infusion for hyperglycemia. Which labs should the nurse check often?
items.x: Insulin can cause hypoglycemia and shifts potassium into cells.
items.a: Blood glucose and serum potassium
w: Serum calcium and phosphate levels
Thyroid hormone and cortisol levels
Serum ammonia and lactate levels

items.q: The nurse is preparing heparin for an infant's arterial line fluid. Which action is most important?
items.x: Serious neonatal heparin errors have come from using the wrong concentration. An independent double-check prevents them.
items.a: Check the heparin concentration with a second nurse
w: Use the heparin vial most often stocked on the unit
Confirm the heparin vial is at room temperature first
Choose the vial with the smallest volume to limit waste

items.q: An infant receiving heparin has a platelet count that has fallen by half over several days. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A large drop in platelets on heparin may mean heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
items.a: Notify the provider of the drop
w: Give the next dose as prescribed
Recheck the platelets next week
Increase the heparin to protect the line

items.q: A preterm infant is prescribed famotidine for suspected reflux. Which complication should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Acid suppression with H2 blockers in preterm infants is linked to higher rates of NEC and late-onset infection.
items.a: Signs of infection and necrotizing enterocolitis
w: Low blood pressure and flushing during the dose
High blood glucose levels after each feeding
Hearing loss found on the newborn hearing screen

items.q: Parents of a preterm infant going home on ferrous sulfate drops ask about safety at home. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of poisoning deaths in young children, so iron is stored safely.
items.a: Keep the iron locked away from children
w: Give an extra dose if the baby looks pale
Mix the full dose into every bottle
Expect the baby's stool to turn red

items.q: Atropine is given before a planned intubation of a neonate. What is the purpose?
items.x: Atropine blocks the vagal response to laryngoscopy, which can cause bradycardia.
items.a: To prevent bradycardia during intubation
w: To provide sedation for the procedure
To relax the airway muscles
To reduce the risk of infection

items.q: An intubated infant is about to receive rocuronium. What must the nurse ensure first?
items.x: Neuromuscular blockers do not sedate or relieve pain, so sedation and analgesia must be in place first.
items.a: That sedation and pain medicine have been given
w: That the infant has been fed within the last hour
That the cardiac monitor alarms are turned off
That the infant is breathing well on his own

items.q: An infant on a vecuronium infusion is started on gentamicin. What should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Aminoglycosides can increase and prolong the effect of neuromuscular blockers.
items.a: Longer and deeper muscle blockade
w: Lower blood glucose after feeds
A sudden rise in the heart rate
Lower serum gentamicin peak levels

items.q: A 2-year-old client weighing 12 kg is admitted with fever and has PRN acetaminophen ordered. The parent says a children's cold and flu liquid was given at home 2 hours ago. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Many combination cold products contain acetaminophen, and duplicate dosing is a common cause of pediatric liver injury. The nurse verifies the last acetaminophen dose and total daily amount before giving more.
items.a: Check the home product's ingredients for acetaminophen before giving the dose
w: Give the ordered dose now because the child's fever is above 38.5 C and rising
Give half of the ordered dose now to limit the total daily acetaminophen
Give ibuprofen instead because it works by a different mechanism of action

items.q: An adolescent client is admitted after an intentional ingestion of acetaminophen tablets about 6 hours ago and currently has no symptoms. Which laboratory result is most important for the nurse to track?
items.x: Early acetaminophen toxicity is often symptom-free, so treatment decisions rest on the serum level plotted against time since ingestion, along with liver enzymes. Electrolytes and pancreatic enzymes do not guide antidote therapy.
items.a: A serum acetaminophen level drawn with the exact time since ingestion
w: A serum sodium and potassium level drawn every 2 hours after admission
A serum amylase and lipase level drawn on admission and again at 24 hours
A complete blood count with a manual differential drawn on admission

items.q: A 4-year-old client with gastroenteritis has a temperature of 39.2 C, dry mucous membranes, and no urine output for the past 10 hours. PRN ibuprofen is ordered for fever. What is the nurse's best action?
items.x: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow, and a dehydrated child with no urine output is at risk for acute kidney injury. The nurse holds the dose and reports the findings so the provider can reassess.
items.a: Notify the provider about the signs of dehydration before giving the ibuprofen
w: Give the ibuprofen with a small snack to protect the child's stomach lining
Give the ibuprofen now and recheck the child's temperature again in 1 hour
Give the ibuprofen first and then encourage oral rehydration solution afterward

items.q: A 7-year-old client with an asthma exacerbation has received three albuterol nebulizer treatments. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?
items.x: A quiet chest with drowsiness and falling oxygen saturation signals poor air movement and impending respiratory failure. Tachycardia, tremor and jitteriness are expected albuterol effects.
items.a: Wheezing is no longer heard, the child is drowsy, and SpO2 is 88 percent
w: The heart rate is 132 per minute and the child has a fine hand tremor
The child says she feels jittery and cannot sit still in bed
The respiratory rate is 26 per minute with scattered expiratory wheezes

items.q: A 5-year-old client is receiving continuous albuterol nebulization in the pediatric unit. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells, and continuous use can cause hypokalemia with dysrhythmia risk. Glucose may also rise.
items.a: Serum potassium, because albuterol shifts potassium into the cells
w: Serum sodium, because albuterol causes the kidneys to retain water
Serum calcium, because albuterol increases calcium loss in urine
Serum magnesium, because albuterol blocks magnesium absorption

items.q: The nurse is reinforcing care for a child who receives ipratropium with albuterol by nebulizer and face mask. What should the nurse teach the parent?
items.x: Ipratropium is anticholinergic, and medication reaching the eyes can cause pupil dilation, blurred vision or eye pain. A good mask seal limits eye exposure.
items.a: Keep the mask fitted well because mist in the eyes can blur vision or dilate the pupils
w: Give the treatment only after meals because it causes severe nausea on an empty stomach
Expect the child to become drowsy for several hours after each treatment
Rinse the mask with the leftover medicine so the next dose works faster

items.q: A 2-year-old client with croup had stridor at rest that resolved after a racemic epinephrine nebulizer treatment 30 minutes ago. The parent asks to go home. What is the nurse's best response?
items.x: Racemic epinephrine works quickly but wears off within about 2 hours, and airway swelling can rebound. Children are observed for several hours after treatment before discharge.
items.a: The child needs to be watched for a few more hours because the stridor can return
w: The child can go home now because the stridor at rest has fully resolved with treatment
The child will need a nebulizer treatment every hour at home for the rest of the day
The child can go home as soon as she is able to drink a full cup of fluids by mouth

items.q: A parent of a toddler with croup asks why a single oral dose of dexamethasone was given. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Corticosteroids decrease airway inflammation and edema with an onset over hours and a long duration. They do not act on the virus and are not quick-relief bronchodilators.
items.a: It reduces swelling in the airway, and the effect builds over several hours
w: It opens the airway within a few minutes, much like a rescue inhaler would
It kills the virus that is causing the croup and shortens the whole illness
It loosens the thick mucus in the throat so the child can cough it up easily

items.q: A 6-year-old client on the pediatric unit eats a cookie containing peanuts and develops hives, wheezing, hoarseness and vomiting. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.x: Epinephrine IM in the mid-outer thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines, bronchodilators and steroids are adjuncts and do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
items.a: Give intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh
w: Give intravenous diphenhydramine and then reassess the airway
Start an albuterol nebulizer treatment for the wheezing
Give oral prednisolone and place the child on a monitor

items.q: A child in the pediatric unit is pulseless, and CPR is in progress with IO access in place. Which epinephrine regimen does the nurse anticipate according to PALS?
items.x: PALS uses epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration) IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes during pediatric cardiac arrest. The adult 1 mg dose is the maximum single dose.
items.a: 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO every 3 to 5 minutes
w: 0.1 mg/kg IV or IO every 10 minutes
0.01 mg/kg IV or IO given one time only
1 mg IV or IO for any weight every 3 to 5 minutes

items.q: An infant client has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 260 per minute, and adenosine is ordered. How should the nurse give the medication?
items.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly with a rapid push and flush, ideally through a site close to the heart.
items.a: As a rapid IV push followed immediately by a rapid saline flush
w: As a slow IV push over 2 minutes to lower the risk of low blood pressure
Diluted in a small bag of saline and infused over 10 to 15 minutes
As an intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis muscle

items.q: Right after a dose of adenosine for supraventricular tachycardia in a school-age client, the monitor shows a pause of several seconds before a sinus rhythm appears. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node, and a short pause or asystole of a few seconds is expected before the rhythm resumes. The nurse keeps watching the monitor and the child's responsiveness.
items.a: Continue monitoring, because a brief pause is an expected effect of adenosine
w: Begin chest compressions right away, because the child is now in asystole
Give a dose of atropine right away to speed the heart rate back up again
Prepare for synchronized cardioversion in case the pause happens again

items.q: A child with a perfusing ventricular tachycardia is receiving an amiodarone infusion. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
items.x: Hypotension and bradycardia are serious adverse effects of IV amiodarone and need prompt action. A fall in heart rate from the tachycardia toward normal is the intended response.
items.a: Blood pressure falls from 98/60 to 70/40 mm Hg with a slower heart rate
w: The child complains of a metallic taste in the mouth after the infusion began
The IV site has mild redness along the vein without swelling or any pain
The heart rate decreases from 180 to 120 per minute with a steady pressure

items.q: The nurse is caring for children with bradycardia. In which situation does the nurse expect atropine to be the preferred first medication?
items.x: PALS recommends atropine for bradycardia from increased vagal tone or primary AV block. Hypoxic bradycardia is treated with oxygenation and ventilation, and persistent bradycardia with poor perfusion is treated with CPR and epinephrine.
items.a: Bradycardia caused by increased vagal tone during intubation
w: Bradycardia caused by hypoxia in an infant with bronchiolitis
Bradycardia caused by hypothermia after a near-drowning
Bradycardia that persists after oxygen and adequate ventilation

items.q: A 3-month-old client has a point-of-care glucose of 38 mg/dL and receives an IV dextrose bolus. What is the nurse's next priority?
items.x: After treating hypoglycemia the nurse rechecks the glucose to confirm a response and to catch a rebound drop. A1C and urine ketones do not guide acute treatment.
items.a: Recheck the blood glucose about 15 to 30 minutes after the bolus
w: Draw a hemoglobin A1C to look for long-term glucose problems
Check the urine for ketones before offering the next feeding
Send a serum insulin level and wait for the result before rechecking

items.q: A 6-month-old client with hypoglycemia has peripheral IV access. Which dextrose concentration does the nurse expect for the IV bolus?
items.x: D10W is the usual concentration for IV bolus treatment of hypoglycemia in infants. Concentrated dextrose such as D50 is irritating to small peripheral veins and is not used in infants.
items.a: Dextrose 10 percent in water
w: Dextrose 50 percent in water
Dextrose 5 percent in normal saline
Dextrose 70 percent in water

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 10-year-old with type 1 diabetes how to give glucagon for severe hypoglycemia at school. Which instruction is most important to include?
items.x: Nausea and vomiting are common after glucagon, so a side-lying position protects the airway. A child who cannot swallow safely should never be given food or fluids by mouth.
items.a: Turn the child onto the side after giving it because vomiting is common
w: Give it only after trying to make the child swallow juice or glucose gel
Wait 30 minutes after giving it before calling for emergency help
Give it into a vein in the arm so that it works faster

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parents of a child with epilepsy how to give rectal diazepam for a prolonged seizure. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Benzodiazepines can depress breathing, especially after a long seizure, so parents watch respirations and call for help. Nothing goes in the mouth and the child is not restrained.
items.a: Watch the child's breathing after giving it and call 911 if breathing is slow or shallow
w: Give a second dose right away if the seizure has not stopped within 1 minute of the first
Give the child a full glass of water to drink as soon as the seizure jerking has ended
Hold the child's arms and legs firmly still until the medicine starts to take effect

items.q: A 4-year-old client is still seizing 5 minutes into a generalized seizure, and the nurse gives IV midazolam as ordered. Which assessment is the priority after the dose?
items.x: Midazolam can cause respiratory depression, especially combined with the postictal state. The nurse monitors breathing and oxygenation closely with ventilation equipment ready.
items.a: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and airway, with a bag-valve-mask at the bedside
w: Pupil size and reaction to light every 15 minutes, with a penlight at the bedside
Blood pressure in both arms to compare them, with a manual cuff at the bedside
Temperature every 15 minutes, because midazolam commonly causes a high fever

items.q: The parent of a 9-year-old who started levetiracetam 3 weeks ago says the child has become irritable and aggressive and cries easily. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Behavior and mood changes are known adverse effects of levetiracetam and need provider review. Antiseizure drugs are not stopped abruptly because of the risk of seizures.
items.a: Report the behavior changes to the provider and advise the parent not to skip doses
w: Reassure the parent that these changes are normal and will pass without any action
Suggest giving the dose at bedtime so the behavior changes are less noticeable
Advise the parent to cut the tablet in half until the mood changes have settled

items.q: A 5-year-old client after surgery received IV fentanyl and is now difficult to arouse with a respiratory rate of 8 per minute and SpO2 of 86 percent. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Airway and breathing come first, with ventilation support while naloxone is given as ordered. Waiting or giving anything by mouth to a sedated child is unsafe.
items.a: Open the airway and support breathing with a bag-valve-mask while naloxone is prepared
w: Recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes to see whether the breathing improves on its own
Sit the child upright and give oral fluids to help flush the opioid out of the body
Document the finding and plan to lower the next scheduled fentanyl dose by half

items.q: An adolescent client received naloxone for opioid toxicity after taking oxycodone and is now alert. What is the most important ongoing nursing assessment?
items.x: Naloxone's duration can be shorter than that of many opioids, so respiratory depression can recur. The nurse keeps monitoring level of consciousness and breathing.
items.a: Watch for returning sedation, because naloxone may wear off before the opioid does
w: Check the blood glucose every hour, because naloxone commonly causes low sugar
Watch for bleeding at IV sites, because naloxone lowers the platelet count
Check the temperature every hour, because naloxone often causes a high fever

items.q: A 7-year-old client is receiving IV ketamine for sedation during a fracture reduction. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate intervention?
items.x: Laryngospasm is a dangerous adverse effect of ketamine and presents with stridor and desaturation. Nystagmus, a dissociated stare and mild sympathetic stimulation are expected.
items.a: High-pitched inspiratory noise with a falling oxygen saturation
w: Eyes open with a fixed gaze and rhythmic eye movements
Mild increase in heart rate and blood pressure from baseline
Increased saliva in the mouth with a normal oxygen saturation

items.q: A 10-year-old client with severe asthma is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which assessment should the nurse monitor most closely during the infusion?
items.x: IV magnesium relaxes smooth muscle and can cause flushing and hypotension. The nurse also watches reflexes and breathing.
items.a: Blood pressure, because magnesium can cause hypotension and flushing
w: Blood glucose, because magnesium commonly causes hyperglycemia and thirst
Temperature, because magnesium commonly causes a high fever and chills
Pupil size, because magnesium commonly causes pupil dilation and blurring

items.q: A 12-year-old client with congenital long QT syndrome has IV ondansetron ordered for postoperative nausea. What is the nurse's best action?
items.x: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval and should be avoided in congenital long QT syndrome. The nurse holds it and asks the provider for a safer choice.
items.a: Clarify the order with the provider before giving the ondansetron
w: Give the ondansetron slowly over 15 minutes instead of 2 minutes
Give half the dose and reassess the nausea in 30 minutes
Give the ondansetron and place the child on continuous pulse oximetry

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 4-year-old with vomiting how to give ondansetron orally disintegrating tablets at home. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: ODT tablets dissolve on the tongue and are swallowed with saliva, so they work for a child who cannot keep fluids down. Handle them with dry hands because they break down when wet.
items.a: Place the tablet on the tongue with dry hands and let it dissolve before swallowing
w: Crush the tablet and stir it into a full glass of milk so the child drinks it all
Have the child chew the tablet well and then drink a full cup of water right after
Place the tablet between the cheek and gum and keep it there for 30 minutes

items.q: A 3-year-old client receives diphenhydramine for itching from hives. An hour later, which finding should the nurse recognize as a known adverse effect in young children?
items.x: Young children can have a paradoxical excitatory reaction to first-generation antihistamines instead of drowsiness. Anticholinergic effects cause dryness and urinary retention, not the opposite.
items.a: Restlessness, excitability and trouble sleeping
w: Bradycardia with a heart rate in the 60s and 70s
Increased urine output with very frequent voiding
Excess tearing of the eyes and a constant runny nose

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parent of a toddler who receives nebulized budesonide twice a day with a face mask. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Inhaled corticosteroid left on the face or in the mouth can cause skin irritation and oral thrush. Budesonide is a daily controller medicine, not a rescue treatment.
items.a: Wipe the child's face and give a drink or rinse the mouth after each treatment
w: Use the treatment only on days when the child is actively coughing or wheezing
Give the treatment right before the child lies down for a nap or for bedtime
Mix the budesonide with tap water in the cup to make each treatment last longer

items.q: The parent of an 8-year-old taking montelukast for asthma reports the child has been having vivid nightmares and says she wishes she were not alive. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Montelukast has a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thinking. These symptoms need prompt provider evaluation.
items.a: Notify the provider promptly about the neuropsychiatric symptoms
w: Reassure the parent that nightmares are common and will fade
Suggest giving the dose in the morning instead of the evening
Tell the parent to double the dose of the rescue inhaler at night

items.q: A 6-year-old client with nephrotic syndrome has taken high-dose prednisolone daily for the past 3 weeks and is due for an MMR vaccine. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Live vaccines are generally deferred in children on high-dose systemic steroids for 2 weeks or longer because of immune suppression. The nurse holds it and clarifies the plan.
items.a: Notify the provider about the steroid course before giving the vaccine
w: Give the vaccine as scheduled, because steroids do not affect live vaccines
Give the vaccine with a dose of acetaminophen to prevent a fever afterward
Give the vaccine today and then skip the next morning dose of the steroid

items.q: The parent of a child who has taken daily prednisolone for 2 months calls to say a classmate has chickenpox and the child sat next to the classmate yesterday. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Children on long-term corticosteroids can develop severe or fatal varicella and may need post-exposure prophylaxis, which is time sensitive. Steroids must not be stopped abruptly.
items.a: Notify the provider today about the exposure
w: Tell the parent to watch for a rash and call if one appears
Tell the parent to stop the prednisolone until the risk passes
Advise the parent to give a dose of acetaminophen tonight

items.q: Parents of a newborn in the nursery tell the nurse they want to decline the vitamin K injection. What information should the nurse share?
items.x: Newborns are born with low vitamin K stores, and refusing the dose raises the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can be intracranial. It does not prevent jaundice.
items.a: Newborns have low vitamin K, and without it they can have serious bleeding, including in the brain
w: Vitamin K is given mainly to prevent newborn jaundice and yellow skin during the first week of life
Vitamin K is only needed when the mother had a cesarean birth or a very long and difficult labor
Vitamin K can safely be given later, as long as it is given before the baby's first checkup

items.q: A 3-year-old client receiving amoxicillin for otitis media develops hives and swelling of the lips 20 minutes after a dose. What should the nurse do after checking the airway?
items.x: Hives with lip swelling shortly after a dose suggest an IgE-mediated allergy that can progress to anaphylaxis. The provider must be notified and doses held, and related penicillins are not given without an order.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately and hold further doses
w: Give the next dose with diphenhydramine to prevent hives
Document a mild rash and continue the course
Switch the child to amoxicillin-clavulanate at the next dose

items.q: The parent of a 2-year-old starting amoxicillin-clavulanate asks how to reduce stomach upset and diarrhea. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Taking amoxicillin-clavulanate at the start of a meal improves tolerance and absorption of clavulanate. Doses should not be changed, and mixing into a full bottle risks an incomplete dose.
items.a: Give each dose at the start of a meal or feeding
w: Give each dose on an empty stomach at bedtime
Give each dose mixed into a full bottle of formula
Give only half of each dose until the diarrhea improves

items.q: A 10-day-old neonate on the pediatric unit has IV ceftriaxone ordered and is also receiving an IV fluid that contains calcium. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Ceftriaxone must not be given with IV calcium-containing solutions in neonates, even through separate lines, because fatal precipitates have formed in the lungs and kidneys.
items.a: Notify the provider about the calcium-containing fluid before giving the ceftriaxone
w: Give the ceftriaxone through the same IV line right after a brief saline flush
Give the ceftriaxone through a separate IV site at the same time as the fluid
Give the ceftriaxone as ordered and draw a serum calcium level 1 hour later

items.q: A 2-week-old client is receiving ampicillin and gentamicin for suspected sepsis. Which laboratory results should the nurse review before the next gentamicin dose?
items.x: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic, and its dosing is guided by drug levels and kidney function.
items.a: The gentamicin trough level and serum creatinine
w: The serum glucose and ionized calcium level
The liver enzymes and total serum bilirubin
The ampicillin peak level and platelet count

items.q: An infant receiving gentamicin is now also prescribed IV furosemide for fluid overload. Which risk should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Loop diuretics add to the ototoxic and nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. The nurse monitors urine output, creatinine and drug levels.
items.a: Increased risk of hearing loss and kidney injury
w: Increased risk of low blood sugar and seizures
Increased risk of bleeding and bruising
Increased risk of rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome

items.q: The parent of a 7-year-old taking cefdinir for sinusitis says the child also takes an iron supplement every morning. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Iron supplements bind cefdinir and reduce its absorption, so doses are separated by about 2 hours. Iron can also turn stools reddish while taking cefdinir.
items.a: Give the iron supplement at least 2 hours apart from the cefdinir
w: Give both together so the child takes fewer doses each day
Give the iron supplement with milk at the same time as cefdinir
Give the iron supplement only on days the child misses a cefdinir dose

items.q: A 9-year-old client with cellulitis has cephalexin ordered. The chart lists a penicillin allergy. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is low but not zero, and the type of reaction matters. A history of anaphylaxis needs to be reported before giving a cephalosporin.
items.a: Ask the parent what kind of reaction the child had to penicillin
w: Give the cephalexin because it is not a penicillin
Give the first dose with diphenhydramine as a precaution
Remove the allergy from the chart because the child is now older

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 2-month-old with oral thrush how to give nystatin suspension. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Nystatin works by contact, so it is placed in each side of the mouth after feeds and not rinsed away. Pacifiers and nipples should also be cleaned.
items.a: Put half the dose in each side of the mouth after feedings
w: Mix the dose into the bottle of formula at each feeding
Give the dose right before each feeding so it coats the nipple
Rinse the mouth with water right after each dose

items.q: The parent of a 10-year-old taking oseltamivir for influenza reports the child woke up confused and tried to leave the house. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Neuropsychiatric events, including confusion and self-injury, have been reported in children with influenza taking oseltamivir. The child needs supervision and provider evaluation.
items.a: Report the behavior to the provider and advise close supervision
w: Explain that confusion is caused by the fever and is not related
Tell the parent to give a double dose so the flu clears faster
Suggest giving an antihistamine at night to help the child sleep

items.q: An 8-year-old client takes methylphenidate for ADHD. Which data are most important for the nurse to track at each visit?
items.x: Stimulants can raise heart rate and blood pressure and can slow growth by suppressing appetite. Growth and cardiovascular vital signs are tracked over time.
items.a: Height, weight, blood pressure and heart rate
w: Serum potassium, blood glucose and urine ketones
Hearing screening, vision screening and head size
Temperature, respiratory rate and oxygen level

items.q: The parent of a child starting lisdexamfetamine says the child has trouble swallowing capsules and goes to bed at 9 p.m. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Morning dosing reduces insomnia, and the capsule contents can be mixed into yogurt, water or orange juice and taken right away.
items.a: Give it in the morning, and the capsule may be opened and mixed into yogurt or water
w: Give it at bedtime so the child is calm and focused for the next school day
Crush the beads inside the capsule and sprinkle them on food at the dinner meal
Give it in the evening with a snack, and the capsule should be swallowed whole

items.q: The parent of a 13-year-old who started atomoxetine 2 weeks ago says the child has been giving away belongings and talking about not wanting to be around. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Atomoxetine has a boxed warning for suicidal thinking in children and adolescents, most often early in therapy. Warning signs need immediate provider contact and supervision.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately and keep the child under close supervision
w: Reassure the parent that mood changes are expected during the first month
Recommend giving the daily dose with food to reduce mood-related side effects
Schedule a routine follow-up visit in 4 weeks to review the dose and the mood

items.q: A preterm infant receiving caffeine citrate for apnea of prematurity has a resting heart rate of 196 per minute before the scheduled dose. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Tachycardia is a common sign of caffeine toxicity, and many units hold the dose and notify for a heart rate above about 180. The provider may check a level or adjust the dose.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the heart rate in 4 hours
Give the dose with a feeding to slow absorption
Give half the dose and give the rest in 1 hour

items.q: A newborn with a ductal-dependent heart defect is started on an alprostadil infusion. Which adverse effect is the nurse's priority to monitor for?
items.x: Apnea is a common and serious adverse effect of alprostadil, especially in small infants in the first hours. Airway equipment and monitoring must be ready.
items.a: Apnea, so the infant needs continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
w: Hypertension, so the blood pressure needs checking every 4 hours
Hypoglycemia, so the glucose needs checking before each feeding
Bradycardia, so atropine must be kept at the bedside

items.q: A preterm infant is receiving IV indomethacin to close a patent ductus arteriosus. Which laboratory results should the nurse review before each dose?
items.x: Indomethacin can reduce renal blood flow and impair platelet function. Kidney function, urine output and platelets are checked before doses, and bleeding is watched for.
items.a: Serum creatinine and platelet count
w: Serum calcium and phosphorus level
Serum ammonia and liver enzymes
Serum glucose and urine ketones

items.q: The parent of a former 29-week preterm infant asks why the infant gets palivizumab injections. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Palivizumab is a monoclonal antibody that offers passive protection for about a month, so it is given monthly through RSV season. It does not treat active infection.
items.a: It gives the baby ready-made antibodies against RSV and is given monthly during RSV season
w: It is a vaccine that teaches the baby's body to make its own RSV antibodies for life
It treats an active RSV infection and shortens the time the baby stays in the hospital
It is a one-time shot at birth that protects against all winter respiratory viruses

items.q: A healthy newborn is due to receive nirsevimab before discharge during RSV season. Which information is most important for the nurse to confirm first?
items.x: Most infants do not need nirsevimab if the mother received the RSV vaccine at least 14 days before birth. Knowing the date avoids duplicate protection.
items.a: Whether the mother received an RSV vaccine during pregnancy and when
w: Whether the newborn has received the first hepatitis B vaccine dose
Whether the mother plans to breastfeed or formula feed
Whether any older siblings have had RSV in the past

items.q: The nurse is teaching the parent of a toddler with iron deficiency anemia about ferrous sulfate drops. Which instruction is most important for safety?
items.x: Accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of poisoning deaths in young children. Dark stools are expected, and milk reduces absorption.
items.a: Store the iron where the child cannot reach it, because an overdose can be fatal
w: Give the drops mixed in a bottle of milk so the child accepts the strong taste
Call the provider right away if the stools become dark green or black in color
Give an extra dose of the drops on any days when the child eats little red meat

items.q: A 3-year-old client is brought in after swallowing an unknown number of an adult's pills 30 minutes ago, and activated charcoal is ordered. What should the nurse assess first?
items.x: Activated charcoal is unsafe in a drowsy child without a protected airway because aspiration can cause severe lung injury.
items.a: Whether the child is alert and able to protect the airway
w: Whether the child has had a bowel movement yet today
Whether the child will drink it if it is mixed with juice
Whether the child has eaten a full meal in the last hour

items.q: A 6-year-old client is receiving a dopamine infusion through a peripheral IV. The nurse notes the skin around the site is cool, pale and swollen. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Dopamine extravasation can cause tissue necrosis, so the infusion at that site is stopped right away and the provider is notified. An antidote such as phentolamine may be ordered.
items.a: Stop the infusion at that site and notify the provider about the extravasation
w: Elevate the arm and apply a warm compress while the infusion continues
Slow the infusion rate and recheck the site in 1 hour
Flush the IV with saline and continue the infusion at the same site

items.q: Fifteen minutes into an IVIG infusion for Kawasaki disease, a 3-year-old client develops chills, flushing and a heart rate rising from 110 to 150. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Infusion reactions to IVIG are often rate related and occur early. The nurse pauses the infusion, assesses the child and notifies the provider for orders.
items.a: Slow the infusion per protocol, check vital signs and notify the provider
w: Increase the infusion rate so that the full dose is finished sooner
Give acetaminophen and continue the infusion at the same set rate
Cover the child with warm blankets and recheck the vitals in 30 min

items.q: A 2-year-old client who received high-dose IVIG for Kawasaki disease last week is due for the MMR and varicella vaccines. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Antibodies in IVIG can neutralize live measles and varicella vaccines, so these are typically delayed for about 11 months after high-dose IVIG.
items.a: Notify the provider, because these live vaccines are usually delayed for months after IVIG
w: Give both vaccines now, because IVIG strengthens the body's response to live vaccines
Give only the MMR vaccine today and then give the varicella vaccine at next week's visit
Give both vaccines today as scheduled, and then plan to repeat both of them in 1 month

items.q: A 4-month-old client is due for the rotavirus vaccine. The parent says the infant had intussusception at 3 months. What should the nurse do?
items.x: A history of intussusception is a contraindication to rotavirus vaccine. The nurse holds it and informs the provider.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the vaccine
w: Give the vaccine, because the intussusception has resolved
Give the vaccine by injection instead of by mouth
Give the vaccine and watch the infant for 15 minutes

items.q: A newborn is born to a mother who is positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. Which plan does the nurse expect?
items.x: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers need both the vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth, given at different injection sites, to prevent perinatal transmission.
items.a: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth at separate sites
w: Hepatitis B vaccine only, given at the 2-month checkup with other vaccines
HBIG only, given once before the newborn is discharged from the nursery
HBIG at birth and the first hepatitis B vaccine dose at 6 months of age

items.q: A 12-year-old client with cystic fibrosis is scheduled for albuterol, airway clearance, dornase alfa and inhaled tobramycin. Which medication should the nurse give last?
items.x: The usual order is bronchodilator, mucolytic, airway clearance, then the inhaled antibiotic, so the antibiotic reaches airways that have been cleared of mucus.
items.a: Inhaled tobramycin
w: Albuterol
Dornase alfa
The bronchodilator and the mucolytic together

items.q: A 10-year-old client with cystic fibrosis is starting lumacaftor-ivacaftor. Which laboratory results should the nurse expect to be checked before and during therapy?
items.x: CFTR modulators can raise liver enzymes, so liver tests are checked at baseline and periodically. Eye exams for cataracts are also advised in children.
items.a: Liver function tests such as ALT, AST and bilirubin
w: Serum amylase, lipase and fecal elastase level
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4 level
Hemoglobin A1C and a fasting lipid panel level

items.q: The nurse is preparing penicillin G benzathine for an adolescent client with strep pharyngitis. Which action is most important for safety?
items.x: Penicillin G benzathine is a suspension, and IV injection has caused cardiorespiratory arrest and death. It is only given deep IM.
items.a: Confirm it is given by deep IM injection only and never IV
w: Mix it with an equal volume of lidocaine to reduce injection pain
Warm the syringe in warm water before drawing up the dose
Give it through a running IV of normal saline to reduce pain

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing discharge teaching with the parent of a 3-year-old who receives acetaminophen for fever. Which statement by the parent shows a need for more teaching?
items.x: Many cough and cold products also contain acetaminophen, which risks a double dose. The other statements show safe use.
items.a: I will also give the cold medicine we have at home if the cough gets worse
w: I will use the syringe that came with this bottle to measure every single dose
I will write down the time of each dose so that I do not give it too often
I will call the provider if the fever lasts more than 3 days or gets higher

items.q: The LVN is collecting data before giving PRN ibuprofen to a 5-year-old with fever. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN before giving the dose?
items.x: Ibuprofen can harm the kidneys in a child who is dehydrated. Low urine output is reported before the dose is given.
items.a: The child has not urinated in 9 hours and has dry lips
w: The child's temperature is 38.9 C and rising
The child ate only half of breakfast this morning
The child says his head hurts and he feels warm

items.q: The LVN gives a 6-year-old an albuterol treatment ordered by the provider. Which finding after the treatment should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: Drowsiness and cyanosis point to worsening respiratory failure and need immediate reporting. Mild tachycardia and tremor are expected effects of albuterol.
items.a: The child is quiet, sleepy, and has blue-tinged lips
w: The child has a heart rate of 120 and a slight hand tremor
The child says he feels shaky and a little nervous
The child is talking in full sentences and coughing

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a child who uses an inhaled corticosteroid every day. Which statement by the parent shows understanding?
items.x: Rinsing after inhaled steroids helps prevent oral thrush. The inhaled steroid is a daily controller, not a rescue inhaler, and is continued as prescribed.
items.a: I will have my child rinse and spit after each dose
w: I will use this inhaler when my child starts to wheeze
I will give it only during the winter cold season
I will stop it as soon as my child feels better

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a 9-year-old who takes montelukast for asthma. Which report from the parent should the LVN share with the RN promptly?
items.x: Montelukast carries a boxed warning for mood changes, nightmares and suicidal thoughts. These changes need prompt reporting.
items.a: My child has been having bad dreams and seems very sad lately
w: My child takes the tablet every evening before bed
My child still uses the rescue inhaler before soccer practice
My child chews the tablet instead of swallowing it whole

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a child going home on a 5-day course of oral prednisolone for asthma. Which instruction should the LVN reinforce?
items.x: Giving prednisolone with food lowers stomach upset. Morning dosing is preferred because it can cause trouble sleeping.
items.a: Give each dose with food or milk to reduce stomach upset
w: Give each dose at bedtime so the child sleeps better
Give the doses only on days the child is wheezing
Give the doses on an empty stomach so they work faster

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a 2-year-old with an ear infection who is taking amoxicillin. Which statement by the parent shows correct understanding?
items.x: Finishing the full prescribed course helps clear the infection and reduces resistance. Leftover antibiotics should not be saved or used later.
items.a: I will give every dose until the bottle is finished even if he feels better
w: I will keep any leftover medicine in the fridge for the next time he gets sick
I will give the medicine until his fever has been gone for at least one day
I will give an extra dose of the medicine if he is still pulling at his ear

items.q: A 4-year-old taking amoxicillin-clavulanate has had 3 loose stools today. Which additional finding should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: Bloody or mucous diarrhea with fever can signal C. difficile infection and needs prompt reporting. Mild loose stools and diaper rash are common with this antibiotic.
items.a: Stools with blood or mucus and a new fever
w: Stools that are soft and slightly lighter in color
A mild decrease in appetite at lunch
A diaper rash that is red but not open

items.q: The parent of a child taking cefdinir says the child's stools have turned a reddish color. The child has no other symptoms. Which response by the LVN is most accurate?
items.x: Cefdinir can bind with iron in the gut and turn stools reddish, which is harmless. The LVN still reports the finding so the RN can assess.
items.a: This can happen with cefdinir, especially with iron, but I will let the nurse know
w: This is a sign of allergy to cefdinir, but I will let the nurse know about it
This means the infection has spread to the gut, but I will let the nurse know
This is common with any antibiotic, so there is no need for me to tell the nurse

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for a breastfeeding parent whose infant has oral thrush and is on nystatin suspension. Which instruction should the LVN reinforce?
items.x: Cleaning items that go in the infant's mouth helps prevent reinfection. Nystatin is given after feeds and left in the mouth, and breastfeeding can continue.
items.a: Boil or wash pacifiers and bottle nipples daily during treatment
w: Mix the nystatin into a bottle of formula or breast milk
Give the nystatin just before each breast or bottle feeding
Quit the nystatin once the white patches can no longer be seen

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching with the parent of a child who has started oseltamivir. Which instruction should the LVN reinforce?
items.x: Rare neuropsychiatric events have been reported in children with influenza who take oseltamivir. Parents watch for unusual behavior and report it.
items.a: Watch the child closely for confusion or unusual behavior and report it
w: Give the doses only on days when the child still has a fever
Give each dose on an empty stomach to help it absorb better
Expect the cough and fever to be gone after the first full day

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a 10-year-old taking methylphenidate for ADHD. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Stimulants can suppress appetite and slow growth, so weight loss is reported. The vital signs listed are normal for age.
items.a: The child has lost 3 kg since the last visit and skips lunch
w: The child's grades in school have improved
The child takes the dose with breakfast each morning
The child's heart rate is 88 and blood pressure is 102/66

items.q: The LVN gives ondansetron to a child with vomiting as ordered. Which follow-up data should the LVN collect and report?
items.x: The goal of the antiemetic is to allow oral rehydration, so the LVN checks whether the child tolerates small sips and reports the result.
items.a: Whether the child can keep down small sips of oral rehydration fluid
w: Whether the child will eat a full regular meal within the next hour
Whether the child has loose stools more often after the dose
Whether the child's temperature has come down since the dose

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a toddler with mild dehydration from gastroenteritis. Which statement shows the parent understands how to give oral rehydration solution?
items.x: Small frequent amounts are better tolerated and reduce vomiting. Mixing with juice changes the sugar and salt balance that makes the solution work.
items.a: I will give small amounts often, like a spoonful every few minutes
w: I will let him drink a full cup as fast as he wants whenever he is thirsty
I will mix it half and half with apple juice so that it tastes much better
I will only give it to him when he asks me for something else to drink

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for a parent whose 8-year-old has a peanut allergy and a new epinephrine auto-injector. Which statement shows the parent understands?
items.x: The auto-injector is given in the outer thigh at the first signs of anaphylaxis, followed by a call to 911. Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine, and heat in a car can damage it.
items.a: I will give it in the outer thigh and then call 911
w: I will give an antihistamine first and use the shot if that does not work
I will give it in the arm muscle and wait to see if it helps
I will keep it in the car glove box so it is always nearby

items.q: The LVN finds a postoperative 12-year-old who received an opioid difficult to wake, with a respiratory rate of 8 per minute. What should the LVN do first?
items.x: Slow breathing and difficulty waking are signs of opioid toxicity. The LVN gets help, stimulates the child and supports breathing so naloxone can be given per order.
items.a: Call for help, try to wake the child, and support breathing while the RN is notified
w: Raise the head of the bed, apply the pulse oximeter, and recheck the rate in 15 minutes
Leave to find the RN, then return with the naloxone and the emergency equipment
Check the pain score and the time of the last dose, then document the sedation level

items.q: The parent of a child on levetiracetam asks the LVN whether the medicine can be skipped on days the child feels fine. Which response is correct?
items.x: Antiseizure medicines keep a steady level only when taken daily as prescribed. Skipping or stopping suddenly raises the risk of seizures.
items.a: It needs to be given every day as prescribed, because missed doses can bring on a seizure
w: It can be skipped now and then, because this medicine stays in the body for several days
It needs to be given every day, but a missed dose should be doubled at the next dose time
It can be given every other day once the child has gone a full month without a seizure

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a toddler who is taking ferrous sulfate drops. Which statement by the parent shows understanding?
items.x: Vitamin C helps iron absorption, and brushing reduces tooth staining. Milk lowers absorption, dark stools are expected, and iron must be stored out of reach.
items.a: I will give it with orange juice and brush his teeth after
w: I will give it with his bottle of milk at bedtime
I will call right away if his stools turn dark
I will keep the bottle on the kitchen table so I remember it

items.q: A 4-year-old received diphenhydramine for itching. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN as a possible adverse effect?
items.x: Urinary retention is an anticholinergic adverse effect that needs reporting. Mild drowsiness and dry mouth are expected effects, and less itching is the goal.
items.a: The child has not urinated in 8 hours and the lower abdomen is firm
w: The child is slightly drowsy and wants to take a nap after the dose
The child's itching and hives have improved since the dose was given
The child asks for a drink because his mouth feels a little bit dry

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for an adolescent who uses fluticasone nasal spray for allergies. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?
items.x: Nasal steroids work best with regular daily use and can take days to reach full effect. Aiming away from the septum lowers irritation and nosebleeds.
items.a: I will use it only on days my nose feels stuffy
w: I will aim the spray away from the middle of my nose
I will use it every day during allergy season
I will call if I get nosebleeds that do not stop

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for the parent of a preterm infant who receives palivizumab. Which statement by the parent shows understanding?
items.x: Palivizumab gives short-term antibodies and is given monthly during RSV season. It does not treat RSV and does not replace routine vaccines.
items.a: My baby needs this shot every month during RSV season
w: My baby needs this shot once at the start of RSV season
My baby needs this shot only if she is exposed to RSV
My baby needs this shot every month all year round

items.q: During the preoperative interview, which finding in a client's history is most important for the nurse to report to the anesthesia provider before succinylcholine is used?
items.x: A family history of an unexplained intraoperative death or high fever suggests malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics are triggers.
items.a: A cousin died of a high fever during surgery
w: The client had nausea after a prior surgery
The client is allergic to adhesive tape
The client drinks two cups of coffee each morning

items.q: A client with extensive burns sustained 10 days ago is scheduled for wound excision. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to communicate if succinylcholine is planned?
items.x: Succinylcholine can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia in clients with burns, crush injuries or denervation after the first day or two. Potassium is the key value.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum sodium
Serum albumin
Hemoglobin

items.q: A client received succinylcholine for a short procedure. On the first postoperative day the client reports generalized muscle aches in the neck and shoulders. What should the nurse explain?
items.x: Postoperative myalgia from fasciculations is a common adverse effect of succinylcholine and typically resolves within a few days.
items.a: Muscle aches are a common effect of succinylcholine and usually resolve in a few days
w: Muscle aches mean the client is having a delayed allergic reaction to the drug given
Muscle aches mean the paralytic is still active and the client will need a reversal agent
Muscle aches are a sign of a deep blood clot in the neck and will need an ultrasound today

items.q: During general anesthesia with sevoflurane, the circulating nurse notes rising end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased ventilation, tachycardia and jaw rigidity. Which action should the nurse anticipate first?
items.x: Unexplained rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with rigidity and tachycardia are early signs of malignant hyperthermia. Triggers are stopped by anesthesia and dantrolene is the antidote.
items.a: Calling for the malignant hyperthermia cart and preparing dantrolene
w: Giving acetaminophen and applying a cooling blanket to the client
Increasing the sevoflurane concentration to deepen the anesthetic
Giving neostigmine and glycopyrrolate to reverse the jaw rigidity

items.q: The nurse is helping prepare dantrolene during a malignant hyperthermia crisis. Which action is correct?
items.x: Dantrolene is reconstituted with sterile water for injection without a bacteriostatic agent. Saline and dextrose solutions are not compatible for reconstitution.
items.a: Reconstitute each vial with preservative-free sterile water
w: Reconstitute each vial with 0.9 percent sodium chloride solution
Reconstitute each vial with dextrose 5 percent in water solution
Reconstitute each vial with bacteriostatic water for injection

items.q: A client is in the PACU after treatment for malignant hyperthermia with dantrolene. Which laboratory values should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Malignant hyperthermia causes muscle breakdown, so hyperkalemia, a rising CK and myoglobinuria with kidney injury are watched closely after the crisis.
items.a: Potassium, creatine kinase and urine myoglobin
w: Hemoglobin A1C, lipid panel and TSH level
Amylase, lipase and the serum albumin level
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free T4

items.q: A 4-year-old client is emerging from sevoflurane anesthesia in the PACU and is crying, thrashing and does not recognize the parent. Vital signs and SpO2 are stable. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Emergence delirium is common in young children after sevoflurane. The nurse protects the child, looks for causes such as pain or hypoxia, and notifies anesthesia if it persists.
items.a: Keep the child safe from injury and assess for pain and other causes
w: Apply soft restraints to all four limbs until the child is calm again
Give the child a cup of juice right away to help calm him back down
Tell the parent the child is having a reaction that needs an antidote

items.q: The nurse knows desflurane is not used for inhalation induction by mask. What is the reason?
items.x: Desflurane is pungent and irritating to the airway, causing coughing, breath holding and laryngospasm during mask induction.
items.a: It irritates the airway and can cause coughing and laryngospasm
w: It has a very slow onset and takes too long to produce sleep by mask
It causes severe bradycardia and heart block when breathed by mask
It is too weak on its own to produce a full loss of consciousness

items.q: A client is scheduled for surgery 5 days after a retinal repair in which an intraocular gas bubble was placed. Which information is most important for the nurse to communicate to the anesthesia team?
items.x: Nitrous oxide diffuses into gas-filled spaces and can expand an intraocular gas bubble, raising eye pressure and threatening vision. It is avoided while the bubble remains.
items.a: The gas bubble in the eye, because nitrous oxide can expand it
w: The eye patch, because it may interfere with the pulse oximeter
The eye drops, because they will interact with the induction drug
The eye surgery, because the client cannot lie flat

items.q: The nurse is managing a propofol infusion for sedation. Which practice is essential for infection prevention?
items.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that supports bacterial growth. Strict asepsis and timely discard of vials and tubing prevent sepsis.
items.a: Use strict aseptic technique and change the tubing and container within the time the label states
w: Mix the propofol with an antibiotic solution so the emulsion stays sterile for the whole day
Store opened vials in the refrigerator with the cap on so they can be used again the next day
Use one vial for several clients, as long as each new dose is drawn up with a new syringe

items.q: A client in the ICU has been on a propofol infusion for 3 days. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Propofol is delivered in a lipid emulsion, and prolonged infusions can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Triglycerides are checked regularly.
items.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum sodium
Serum magnesium
Thyroid-stimulating hormone

items.q: Right after a propofol bolus for a procedure, which finding should the nurse be most prepared to manage?
items.x: Propofol causes dose-related vasodilation and respiratory depression. Airway support and blood pressure management must be ready.
items.a: Hypotension and apnea
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Hyperthermia and rigidity
Hyperglycemia and polyuria

items.q: A 28-year-old client who takes an oral contraceptive received sugammadex at the end of surgery. What should the nurse teach before discharge?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind hormonal contraceptives and reduce their effect, equal to a missed dose. Clients use a backup nonhormonal method for 7 days.
items.a: Use a nonhormonal backup birth control method for the next 7 days
w: Stop the oral contraceptive for 1 week and restart it after
Take two contraceptive pills tomorrow to make up for the drug
No change is needed because sugammadex does not affect hormones

items.q: Shortly after receiving sugammadex in the operating room, a client develops a heart rate of 38 per minute. What should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Marked bradycardia, sometimes with cardiac arrest, has been reported within minutes of sugammadex. The heart rate is monitored and treated, for example with an anticholinergic.
items.a: Treatment of the bradycardia, because marked bradycardia can occur with sugammadex
w: Giving a second dose of sugammadex, because the reversal of the block was not complete
Giving neostigmine, because it reverses a slow heart rate that follows sugammadex use
No action, because this heart rate is an expected and harmless effect of the reversal

items.q: A client in the PACU received rocuronium during surgery. Which finding most strongly suggests residual neuromuscular blockade?
items.x: Inability to sustain a head lift suggests remaining muscle weakness from the paralytic, which can impair breathing and airway protection. Drowsiness and sore throat are common after anesthesia.
items.a: The client cannot lift the head off the pillow for 5 seconds
w: The client is drowsy but opens the eyes when spoken to by name
The client reports a scratchy sore throat after the extubation
The client is shivering and asks for a second warm blanket now

items.q: During a surgical case, the circulating nurse notes the client is receiving rocuronium. Which statement about the client's sedation is accurate?
items.x: Neuromuscular blockers have no sedative, amnestic or analgesic effect. Clients must receive adequate anesthesia to prevent awareness.
items.a: Rocuronium causes paralysis without sedation or pain relief
w: Rocuronium provides both muscle paralysis and deep sedation
Rocuronium provides pain relief but does not cause paralysis
Rocuronium makes the client forget the procedure afterward

items.q: A client who received vecuronium during surgery arrives in the PACU with shallow breaths, weak hand grip and SpO2 dropping to 89 percent. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Signs of residual blockade with hypoxemia need immediate airway and breathing support and reversal by anesthesia. Opioids would worsen breathing.
items.a: Support ventilation and notify the anesthesia provider right away
w: Encourage the client to cough and use the incentive spirometer
Raise the head of the bed and recheck the SpO2 in 15 minutes
Give the scheduled opioid to reduce splinting from pain

items.q: Glycopyrrolate is given together with neostigmine for reversal of rocuronium. What is the reason for the combination?
items.x: Neostigmine raises acetylcholine at muscarinic sites too, causing bradycardia and secretions. Glycopyrrolate blocks these muscarinic effects.
items.a: Glycopyrrolate blocks the bradycardia and secretions caused by neostigmine
w: Glycopyrrolate makes neostigmine reverse the block much faster
Glycopyrrolate prevents the nausea and vomiting caused by the paralytic
Glycopyrrolate keeps the client lightly sedated during the reversal

items.q: A client who received glycopyrrolate during surgery reports a very dry mouth in the PACU and has not voided for 7 hours. Which assessment is the priority?
items.x: Anticholinergics can cause urinary retention, which is common after anesthesia. Dry mouth is expected, and the bladder is checked for distention.
items.a: Check for bladder distention with a bladder scan
w: Check the blood glucose level with a fingerstick
Check the pupils for constriction with a penlight
Check the skin of the trunk for a spreading rash

items.q: A client received IV midazolam and fentanyl for a procedure. Which assessment is most important for the nurse during recovery?
items.x: Benzodiazepines and opioids together have additive respiratory depression. Breathing and oxygenation are the priority.
items.a: Respiratory rate, depth and oxygen saturation
w: Bowel sounds in all four abdominal quadrants
Capillary refill in the fingers and the toes
Pupil size and reaction to light every hour

items.q: A client who takes alprazolam daily for panic disorder is oversedated after procedural midazolam. Flumazenil is being considered. Which risk should the nurse communicate?
items.x: Flumazenil can precipitate benzodiazepine withdrawal and seizures in chronic users. Airway support is often preferred.
items.a: Flumazenil can trigger seizures in clients who use benzodiazepines long term
w: Flumazenil can cause severe opioid withdrawal symptoms in this client
Flumazenil will make the alprazolam last longer and deepen the sedation
Flumazenil will cause the client to bleed more easily for several hours

items.q: A client who received flumazenil for midazolam oversedation is now awake and talking. What is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Flumazenil has a shorter duration than many benzodiazepines, so sedation and respiratory depression can return. Monitoring continues.
items.a: Continue to monitor for resedation, because flumazenil may wear off first
w: Discharge the client to home now, because he is awake and talking clearly
Give the client a large meal right away to prevent a low blood sugar level
Remove the pulse oximeter, because the client is now alert and oriented

items.q: A client received remimazolam for procedural sedation and becomes oversedated. Which reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine, so flumazenil reverses it. Naloxone reverses opioids, and sugammadex and neostigmine reverse neuromuscular blockers.
items.a: Flumazenil
w: Naloxone
Sugammadex
Neostigmine

items.q: A PACU client is scheduled for IV hydromorphone for pain rated 8 out of 10, but is hard to keep awake and falls asleep mid-sentence. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Increasing sedation precedes opioid respiratory depression. A client who drifts off mid-conversation should not receive more opioid until reassessed.
items.a: Notify the provider about the sedation level before giving the opioid
w: Give the full opioid dose now, because the pain score of 8 is the priority
Give half of the opioid dose now and then recheck the client in 1 hour
Wake the client, give the opioid, and return to reassess at the next round

items.q: A postoperative client has a hydromorphone PCA. Which family behavior should the nurse correct?
items.x: PCA by proxy defeats the built-in safety, because a sedated client cannot press the button. Only the client should press it.
items.a: The spouse presses the PCA button while the client sleeps
w: The spouse reminds the client to press the button before walking
The spouse tells the nurse when the client seems more drowsy
The spouse helps the client use the incentive spirometer

items.q: A client who received IV fentanyl in the operating room is in the PACU with a respiratory rate of 7 per minute and SpO2 of 85 percent. What is the nurse's first action?
items.x: Airway and ventilation come first, then naloxone per order and notification. Waiting or charting first risks hypoxic injury.
items.a: Stimulate the client and support the airway and breathing
w: Raise the head of the bed and recheck the vitals in 10 minutes
Document the finding and lower the PCA settings for the next hour
Give an oral stimulant drink and recheck the SpO2 in 15 minutes

items.q: A client received a remifentanil infusion during surgery. The surgeon asks why the client is in severe pain on arrival to the PACU. What explanation is accurate?
items.x: Remifentanil is rapidly broken down, so its effect ends within minutes. A longer-acting analgesic plan is needed before emergence.
items.a: Remifentanil wears off within minutes, so longer-acting pain relief must be in place
w: Remifentanil itself causes pain as a side effect once the infusion ends
Remifentanil was given too slowly during surgery and did not reach full effect
Remifentanil blocks other opioids from working for several hours after surgery

items.q: A PACU client with opioid-induced respiratory depression has naloxone ordered. Which administration approach is best?
items.x: Titrating small doses restores breathing while avoiding abrupt reversal of pain, severe hypertension and pulmonary edema.
items.a: Give small diluted doses slowly and titrate to breathing
w: Give the full vial as a rapid push to reverse it fully
Give it orally so that it works slowly over several hours
Give it only after the SpO2 has fallen below 80 percent

items.q: Twenty minutes after naloxone reversed a client's opioid-induced respiratory depression, which finding should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so sedation and respiratory depression may return. Monitoring continues.
items.a: Return of sedation and slow breathing
w: A rise in the blood glucose level
A new raised rash on the chest and trunk
A drop in the urine output per hour

items.q: A client is recovering from ketamine anesthesia in the PACU. Which nursing action helps reduce emergence reactions?
items.x: Ketamine can cause vivid dreams and hallucinations on emergence, and a quiet, low-stimulation environment reduces them.
items.a: Keep the environment quiet and limit stimulation
w: Wake the client often by calling his name loudly
Turn on bright overhead lights to orient the client
Encourage the client to watch television to stay alert

items.q: A client in the PACU on a dexmedetomidine infusion has a heart rate of 44 per minute and a blood pressure of 84/50. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Bradycardia and hypotension are common adverse effects of dexmedetomidine and need prompt provider review.
items.a: Notify the provider right away about the bradycardia and hypotension
w: Increase the infusion rate to deepen the sedation and slow the heart
Give a fluid bolus without an order and keep the infusion at its rate
Document the vital signs as expected and recheck them again in 1 hour

items.q: A client with septic shock received etomidate for intubation. Which adverse effect should the nurse be aware of?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits adrenal steroid synthesis, which is a concern in sepsis. It is otherwise valued for hemodynamic stability.
items.a: Suppression of adrenal cortisol production
w: Severe hypertension and tachycardia
Increased intracranial pressure levels
Severe hyperkalemia and peaked T waves

items.q: After a nerve block with bupivacaine, a client reports a metallic taste, ringing in the ears and numbness around the mouth. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: These are early signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, which can progress to seizures and cardiac arrest. Lipid emulsion therapy may be needed.
items.a: Call for help and notify anesthesia for possible local anesthetic toxicity
w: Reassure the client that these effects are normal for a few hours after a block
Give the client sips of cold water to help clear the metallic taste in the mouth
Reposition the client on the other side and recheck the block level in an hour

items.q: A client with local anesthetic systemic toxicity from bupivacaine has a seizure followed by ventricular dysrhythmia. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Lipid emulsion 20 percent is the specific therapy for LAST, along with airway management and seizure control.
items.a: Lipid emulsion 20 percent
w: Sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous calcium gluconate
Flumazenil

items.q: A client received liposomal bupivacaine at the surgical site. The surgeon orders lidocaine for a bedside procedure the next day. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Liposomal bupivacaine releases drug for days, and other local anesthetics can add to toxicity risk and affect its release. The nurse checks with the provider.
items.a: Clarify the order with the provider because local anesthetic doses are cumulative
w: Give the lidocaine as ordered, because liposomal bupivacaine has worn off by now
Give the lidocaine into a vein instead, so that it stays away from the surgical site
Give the lidocaine as ordered and skip the client's next scheduled pain medicine

items.q: A client receiving IV lidocaine infusion for postoperative pain becomes confused and reports blurred vision. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Confusion and visual changes are signs of lidocaine toxicity. Stopping the infusion and notifying the provider is standard for this infusion reaction.
items.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider
w: Increase the infusion to control the pain
Give a dose of an antihistamine
Document the finding and recheck in 2 hours

items.q: A client with a ropivacaine epidural for pain after knee replacement has a blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg. Which action is most appropriate?
items.x: Epidural local anesthetics block sympathetic fibers and can cause hypotension. Anesthesia is notified and the client is kept supine and safe.
items.a: Notify the anesthesia provider and assess for hypotension from sympathetic block
w: Increase the epidural rate to improve comfort and lower the stress response
Help the client to stand at the bedside to improve circulation to the legs
Remove the epidural catheter and apply a dry dressing over the insertion site

items.q: A client has a continuous ropivacaine femoral nerve catheter after knee surgery. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Nerve blocks weaken the quadriceps and increase fall risk. Clients need assistance when walking.
items.a: Do not walk without help, because the leg may be weak and you could fall
w: Walk alone to the bathroom as soon as the numbness in the leg starts to fade
Put full weight on the leg right away to keep the catheter working properly
Apply a heating pad to the thigh over the catheter to keep the leg comfortable

items.q: Before an ester local anesthetic such as chloroprocaine is used, which history should the nurse report?
items.x: Ester local anesthetics are broken down to PABA and can cross-react with each other. A prior ester reaction needs to be reported.
items.a: A previous reaction to benzocaine or another ester local anesthetic
w: A previous allergy to latex gloves and to adhesive tape on the skin
A rash after a course of amoxicillin for an ear infection as a child
A history of motion sickness on boats and in cars on long road trips

items.q: After receiving prilocaine, a client has gray-blue skin, chocolate-brown blood and SpO2 of 85 percent that does not improve with oxygen. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Prilocaine can cause methemoglobinemia, which is treated with methylene blue. Supplemental oxygen alone does not correct it.
items.a: Methylene blue
w: Sodium bicarbonate
Naloxone
Vitamin K

items.q: The scrub nurse is preparing topical thrombin for use in surgery. Which action is essential for safety?
items.x: Topical thrombin can cause severe clotting if it enters circulation and must be used only on surfaces.
items.a: Label it clearly and make sure it is never injected into a vessel
w: Draw it into an unlabeled syringe on the field for quick access
Mix it into the client's IV fluids to help speed up the clotting
Inject it directly into a vein if bleeding at the site is heavy

items.q: The OR nurse is caring for a client with end-stage kidney disease and cirrhosis who needs a neuromuscular blocker. Why does the nurse expect cisatracurium to be chosen?
items.x: Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination in the plasma, so organ failure has little effect on its duration. It has no sedative effect.
items.a: It breaks down in the plasma and does not rely on the liver or kidneys
w: It lasts much longer than other paralytics, so fewer doses are needed
It provides sedation as well as paralysis, so less anesthetic is needed
It can be reversed only with sugammadex, which is safer in kidney failure

items.q: Shortly after atracurium is given during induction, the circulating nurse notes facial flushing and a drop in blood pressure. Which explanation is most likely?
items.x: Atracurium can release histamine, causing flushing, hypotension and sometimes bronchospasm. Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by succinylcholine and volatile agents, not atracurium.
items.a: Histamine release caused by the atracurium
w: Early malignant hyperthermia caused by the atracurium
Severe hyperkalemia caused by the atracurium
Residual paralysis caused by the atracurium

items.q: A client who takes dabigatran for atrial fibrillation needs emergency surgery for a perforated bowel. Which reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran. Protamine reverses heparin and vitamin K reverses warfarin.
items.a: Idarucizumab
w: Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione
Flumazenil

items.q: Protamine is ordered to reverse heparin at the end of a vascular surgery. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report before it is given?
items.x: Prior protamine exposure, such as through NPH insulin, and fish allergy raise the risk of severe hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions to protamine.
items.a: Daily use of NPH insulin and a known fish allergy
w: Daily use of acetaminophen for knee arthritis
Seasonal allergies treated with a nasal spray
A rash after a tetanus shot many years ago

items.q: While a protamine infusion is running after cardiac surgery, the client suddenly becomes hypotensive, flushed and short of breath. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Protamine can cause severe hypotension, bronchospasm and anaphylactoid reactions. Stopping the infusion during a reaction is standard nursing action, followed by notification.
items.a: Stop the infusion and notify the provider while supporting airway and blood pressure
w: Increase the infusion rate so the full dose is given sooner
Give a heparin bolus to counteract the protamine effect
Raise the head of the bed and continue the infusion

items.q: A client taking warfarin with an INR of 3.1 is scheduled for elective surgery tomorrow and receives oral phytonadione. The client asks when it will work. What should the nurse explain?
items.x: Vitamin K allows the liver to make new clotting factors, which takes many hours. The INR is rechecked before surgery, and faster reversal requires factor products.
items.a: It takes many hours, so the INR will be checked again before surgery
w: It works within minutes, so the client could go to surgery right now
It works by removing the warfarin from the blood right away by the kidneys
It only works if the client also stops eating leafy greens until surgery

items.q: The nurse is giving IV phytonadione to a client before urgent surgery. Which action is most important?
items.x: IV phytonadione carries a boxed warning for severe hypersensitivity reactions, including fatal ones. It is diluted and given slowly with monitoring.
items.a: Infuse it slowly and watch closely for signs of anaphylaxis
w: Give it as a rapid IV push over seconds so it works faster
Give it through the same IV line as the running heparin drip
Give it only after the client has eaten a full meal with fat

items.q: The preoperative nurse is reviewing the plan for a client having a hip replacement with cefazolin prophylaxis. Which timing is correct?
items.x: Surgical prophylaxis such as cefazolin is given within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are adequate when the skin is opened.
items.a: Finish giving it within 60 minutes before the skin incision
w: Give it at least 4 hours before the client goes to the OR
Give it in the PACU after the incision is closed
Give it at home the night before surgery

items.q: A client scheduled for surgery with cefazolin prophylaxis reports a past penicillin reaction. What should the nurse ask first?
items.x: The type of reaction guides whether cefazolin is safe. A history of anaphylaxis or a severe skin reaction is reported to the provider before the dose.
items.a: What happened during the reaction and how soon it started
w: Whether the client has ever taken cefazolin before
Whether the client has taken an antihistamine today
Whether anyone else in the family is allergic to penicillin

items.q: A PACU client with nausea has IV ondansetron ordered. The preoperative ECG showed a QTc of 520 ms and the potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval, and a long QTc with hypokalemia raises the risk of torsades de pointes. The nurse holds it and asks the provider for direction.
items.a: Clarify the order with the provider before giving the ondansetron
w: Give the ondansetron as ordered and recheck the nausea in 30 minutes
Give the ondansetron by IM injection to slow its absorption
Give the ondansetron with an extra dose of oral potassium

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client who will have a scopolamine patch placed before surgery to prevent nausea. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Scopolamine on the hands can dilate the pupil and blur vision if it reaches the eye. The patch is placed on hairless skin behind the ear.
