items.a: Wash your hands after touching the patch and keep them away from your eyes
w: Place the patch on your chest over the heart where you can check it easily
Cut the patch in half if you have only mild nausea after the surgery
Replace the patch with a new one every 4 hours while you are in the hospital

items.q: A 78-year-old client with a scopolamine patch placed before surgery is confused and agitated on the first postoperative day. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Scopolamine is anticholinergic and can cause confusion, agitation and hallucinations, especially in older adults. The nurse reports it so the provider can decide whether to remove the patch.
items.a: Report the confusion to the provider and ask about the scopolamine patch
w: Apply a second patch to help settle the nausea and agitation
Give a sleeping aid to help the client rest through the night
Document the confusion as expected after surgery and recheck tomorrow

items.q: IV promethazine is ordered for a PACU client with nausea. The client reports burning pain at the IV site during the injection. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Promethazine is a vesicant with a boxed warning for severe tissue injury. Pain during injection can mean extravasation or arterial injection, so the injection is stopped and the site assessed.
items.a: Stop injecting and assess the site for signs of extravasation
w: Finish the injection more quickly so the pain ends sooner
Flush the line rapidly with saline and complete the dose
Apply a warm pack and finish the injection slowly

items.q: A PACU client has scheduled IV ketorolac and a urine output of 15 mL per hour for the last 3 hours. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Ketorolac reduces renal blood flow and can cause acute kidney injury. Low urine output is a reason to hold the dose and report.
items.a: Notify the provider about the low urine output before giving the ketorolac
w: Give the ketorolac with a fluid bolus to help protect the kidneys from injury
Give the ketorolac by mouth instead of by vein to lower the effect on kidneys
Give half of the ketorolac dose now and reassess the urine output in 2 hours

items.q: A client going home after surgery asks how long ketorolac can be taken. What should the nurse teach?
items.x: Ketorolac is limited to 5 days of total use because of the risk of GI bleeding and kidney injury.
items.a: Total use, IV and oral combined, is limited to 5 days
w: It can be taken for as long as the pain lasts
It can be taken for up to 1 month with food
It can be taken for 2 weeks if the client drinks water

items.q: A PACU client has IV labetalol ordered for a blood pressure of 176/98. Which finding before the dose should make the nurse hold it and notify the provider?
items.x: Labetalol blocks beta receptors and slows the heart, so it is held for bradycardia. The high blood pressure is the reason it was ordered.
items.a: A heart rate of 48 per minute
w: A blood pressure of 178/100 mm Hg
A temperature of 37.4 C
A respiratory rate of 18 per minute

items.q: A postoperative client with moderate persistent asthma has IV labetalol ordered for hypertension. Which finding should the nurse watch for most closely?
items.x: Labetalol is a nonselective beta blocker that can cause bronchospasm in asthma.
items.a: New wheezing or chest tightness
w: A rise in blood glucose levels
A rise in the body temperature
A new red rash on both arms

items.q: A client received bupivacaine-meloxicam into the surgical site during a bunion repair. Which discharge teaching is most important?
items.x: This product contains meloxicam, an NSAID, so adding other NSAIDs raises the risk of kidney injury, GI bleeding and cardiovascular events.
items.a: Ask the provider before taking other NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen
w: Take ibuprofen every 4 hours to strengthen the effect
Take aspirin daily for a week to prevent blood clots
No drug limits are needed because it is placed in the wound

items.q: A client on the behavioral health unit takes lithium for bipolar I disorder. Which result should the nurse review before giving the morning dose?
items.x: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range, and the level is measured as a trough about 12 hours after the last dose to guide safe dosing.
items.a: Serum lithium level drawn about 12 hours after the last dose
w: Serum amylase level drawn on the morning of the day of admission
Fasting lipid panel drawn at the last outpatient clinic visit
Random serum magnesium level drawn an hour after breakfast today

items.q: A client taking lithium has vomiting, diarrhea, coarse hand tremor and new confusion. The lithium level is 2.1 mEq/L. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: These findings and level point to lithium toxicity, so the dose is held and the provider is notified at once. Restricting fluids would raise the level further.
items.a: Notify the provider now before giving the next lithium dose
w: Give the scheduled dose now with crackers to help ease the nausea
Restrict all oral fluids until the vomiting and diarrhea settle
Recheck the lithium level at the next routine morning lab draw

items.q: The nurse is reinforcing discharge teaching for a client starting lithium. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?
items.x: Sodium and fluid changes alter lithium clearance. Low sodium or dehydration raises lithium levels and can cause toxicity.
items.a: I will keep my salt and fluid intake about the same each day
w: I will cut out salt completely so the medicine protects my kidneys
I will limit myself to about four glasses of fluid a day while on it
I will take a double dose if I forget to take one the day before

items.q: A client stable on lithium reports back pain and has a new prescription for scheduled ibuprofen. What concern should the nurse raise with the provider?
items.x: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise the lithium level, so the order should be clarified and levels monitored.
items.a: NSAIDs can raise the lithium level toward toxicity
w: Ibuprofen lowers the lithium level and risks relapse
Ibuprofen blocks lithium absorption from the gut
The combination causes a hypertensive crisis

items.q: A client with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is prescribed clozapine. Which lab result must the nurse confirm before each dispensing?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so the absolute neutrophil count is monitored on a set schedule before dispensing.
items.a: Absolute neutrophil count
w: Serum potassium level
Prothrombin time
Thyroid-stimulating hormone

items.q: A client who started clozapine three weeks ago reports a sore throat and has a temperature of 38.6 C. What is the priority nursing action?
items.x: Fever and sore throat can signal severe neutropenia with clozapine. The dose is held and the provider is notified for an urgent ANC.
items.a: Report for an urgent neutrophil count before giving the dose
w: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours
Encourage warm salt water gargles every 2 hours
Document this as a likely viral illness

items.q: A client is in the first month of clozapine therapy. Which finding is most concerning for a serious adverse effect?
items.x: Persistent tachycardia with chest pain early in treatment can signal clozapine-induced myocarditis, which needs urgent evaluation.
items.a: Resting heart rate of 124 with chest pain and fatigue
w: Increased salivation that leaves the pillow wet at night
Weight gain of 1 kg since admission to the unit last week
Mild drowsiness for about an hour after each evening dose

items.q: Which data should the nurse assess every shift for a client taking clozapine to detect a potentially fatal adverse effect?
items.x: Clozapine slows gut motility and can cause severe constipation, ileus and bowel obstruction, so bowel function is monitored closely.
items.a: Bowel movement pattern and abdominal distention
w: Skin on sun-exposed areas for a photosensitivity rash
Breath for a fruity odor before each meal
Hearing acuity and ringing in both ears

items.q: Thirty minutes after IM haloperidol, a client has a twisted neck, eyes rolled upward and a frightened expression. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: This is acute dystonia, treated promptly with an anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine.
items.a: Give the prescribed PRN IM benztropine or diphenhydramine
w: Give a second dose of IM haloperidol for the agitation
Place the client in seclusion and observe through the window
Keep the client NPO for the next 24 hours to prevent choking

items.q: A client receiving haloperidol has a temperature of 40.1 C, lead-pipe rigidity, BP 182/104 and new confusion. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental status suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately before giving the antipsychotic
w: Give the PRN benztropine now and reassess the client in an hour
Encourage oral fluids and recheck all the vital signs in 4 hours
Apply a cooling blanket and chart the fever as a likely infection

items.q: A client with agitation and delirium is prescribed IV haloperidol. Which monitoring is most important?
items.x: Haloperidol, especially IV, can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes, so ECG monitoring is needed.
items.a: Continuous ECG monitoring of the QT interval
w: Hourly fingerstick blood glucose checks
Daily abdominal girth measurement at the umbilicus
Peak and trough serum haloperidol levels

items.q: A client has been taking olanzapine for 3 months. Which lab results should the nurse expect to monitor?
items.x: Olanzapine has a high risk of weight gain, hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia, so metabolic labs are monitored.
items.a: Fasting glucose and lipid panel
w: Serum ammonia level
Urine protein and specific gravity
Serum calcium and phosphorus

items.q: A client received IM olanzapine for acute agitation 20 minutes ago. The provider now orders IM lorazepam. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Combining IM olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine raises the risk of hypotension, bradycardia and respiratory depression, so the order is clarified.
items.a: Clarify the order because of the risk of cardiorespiratory depression
w: Give both injections at once in one syringe to limit needle sticks
Give the lorazepam by IV push instead because it acts faster
Give the lorazepam and let the client rest alone in a quiet room

items.q: A client receives a long-acting olanzapine pamoate injection. What is required after the injection?
items.x: Olanzapine pamoate can cause post-injection delirium and sedation syndrome, so the client is observed at least 3 hours under the REMS program.
items.a: Observe the client in the facility for at least 3 hours
w: Observe for 15 minutes and then discharge the client
Massage the site to speed absorption
Check blood glucose every 30 minutes for 2 hours

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client about oral ziprasidone. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Ziprasidone absorption is greatly increased when taken with food, so doses are taken with meals.
items.a: Take each dose with a meal
w: Take each dose on an empty stomach
Take each dose with grapefruit juice
Take each dose with an antacid

items.q: A client taking lurasidone has several new orders. Which order should the nurse question?
items.x: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole markedly raise lurasidone levels and are contraindicated with it.
items.a: Ketoconazole for a fungal infection
w: Acetaminophen for headache
Docusate for constipation
Polyethylene glycol for bowel care

items.q: A client started on quetiapine yesterday reports dizziness when getting out of bed. What should the nurse do first?
items.x: Quetiapine commonly causes orthostatic hypotension early in treatment. Orthostatic vital signs guide safety measures and reporting.
items.a: Measure lying and standing blood pressure
w: Give the next dose early to ease anxiety
Encourage the client to walk the hall quickly
Have the client drink a caffeinated beverage

items.q: A female client taking risperidone reports breast discharge and missed menstrual periods. Which lab result should the nurse expect to be ordered?
items.x: Risperidone commonly raises prolactin, which can cause galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
items.a: Serum prolactin level
w: Serum lipase level
Serum ammonia level
Serum cortisol level

items.q: A client with schizophrenia is discharged on monthly paliperidone palmitate injections. Which teaching point is most important?
items.x: Long-acting injections support adherence and prevent relapse only when given on schedule.
items.a: Keep every injection appointment even when feeling well
w: Skip the injection in any month when you are feeling well
Take an extra injection at the clinic if the symptoms return
Expect to need a blood drug level drawn before every injection

items.q: A client started on aripiprazole paces the hall, cannot sit still and says he feels jittery inside. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.x: Inner restlessness and pacing suggest akathisia, a common extrapyramidal effect of aripiprazole that should be reported.
items.a: Possible akathisia to report to the provider
w: Expected sign that the drug is working
Early tardive dyskinesia that is permanent
Return of psychosis needing seclusion

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client being discharged on chlorpromazine. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Chlorpromazine causes photosensitivity, so sun protection is needed.
items.a: Use sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors
w: Eat a high-tyramine diet to prevent fatigue
Take the dose with grapefruit juice daily
Avoid all dairy products while on the drug

items.q: An older client takes benztropine for drug-induced parkinsonism. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Benztropine is anticholinergic and can cause urinary retention, which needs prompt reporting, especially in older adults.
items.a: No urine output for 10 hours with a distended bladder
w: Mild dry mouth that is relieved by chewing sugar-free gum
Slight improvement in the hand tremor since the last week
Occasional blurry vision when reading small print up close

items.q: A client has received fluphenazine decanoate injections for several years. Which tool should the nurse use to screen for tardive dyskinesia?
items.x: The AIMS is a standard tool for detecting tardive dyskinesia during long-term antipsychotic therapy.
items.a: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale
w: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment
Braden Scale for pressure injury risk
Glasgow Coma Scale

items.q: A 19-year-old client started sertraline 10 days ago and seems more energetic. Which nursing action is most important?
items.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for suicidality in young adults, and risk can rise as energy returns, so suicide risk is assessed directly.
items.a: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans
w: Reduce safety checks because mood is improving
Teach that the full effect occurs within 2 days
Encourage the client to request discharge today

items.q: A client taking sertraline was started on linezolid. The client is now agitated and diaphoretic, with temperature 39 C, HR 128 and clonus. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
items.x: Linezolid has MAO-inhibitor activity. With an SSRI it can cause serotonin syndrome, which shows hyperthermia, tachycardia and clonus.
items.a: Possible serotonin syndrome needing immediate report
w: Expected adjustment during the first week
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needing benztropine
Alcohol withdrawal needing a CIWA score

items.q: A client took fluoxetine until 3 days ago. The provider now prescribes phenelzine to start tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Fluoxetine has a long half-life. At least 5 weeks must pass before starting an MAOI to prevent serotonin syndrome.
items.a: Question the order because a longer washout is needed
w: Give phenelzine as ordered tomorrow with the evening meal
Give phenelzine as ordered and monitor for weight gain
Ask the pharmacy to switch the phenelzine to a liquid form

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client starting phenelzine. Which foods should the client avoid?
items.x: MAOIs prevent tyramine breakdown. Tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheese and cured meats can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.a: Aged cheese, cured meats and tap beer
w: Fresh chicken, rice and steamed carrots
Fresh milk, eggs and white bread
Bananas, oatmeal and cottage cheese

items.q: A client taking phenelzine ate salami at a family visit. The client now has a severe occipital headache, stiff neck and BP 212/118. What should the nurse do?
items.x: These findings indicate a hypertensive crisis, which needs immediate treatment and close monitoring.
items.a: Notify the provider immediately and stay with the client
w: Give the PRN acetaminophen for the headache and recheck in one hour
Encourage the client to lie flat in a dark room and rest quietly
Document the reaction and teach the client about the tyramine diet

items.q: A client taking tranylcypromine asks about cold remedies. Which product should the nurse teach the client to avoid?
items.x: Sympathomimetic decongestants with an MAOI can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.a: Decongestants containing pseudoephedrine
w: Plain acetaminophen tablets for aches
Saline nasal spray used for congestion
Throat lozenges that have no medicine

items.q: The nurse is teaching a client who uses the selegiline transdermal patch. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: External heat can increase absorption from the patch. Patches are not cut, and the old patch is removed before applying a new one.
items.a: Avoid heating pads or direct heat over the patch
w: Cut the patch in half if any side effects occur
Apply a new patch directly on top of the old one
Keep the patch on during an MRI scan of the head

items.q: A client admitted with anorexia nervosa and purging has a new order for bupropion for depression. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Bupropion is contraindicated in eating disorders because of a higher seizure risk, so the order is clarified before giving it.
items.a: Clarify the order with the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose as ordered and weigh the client every day
Give the dose as ordered with a high-calorie snack
Give the dose at bedtime to help limit any insomnia

items.q: A client is admitted after an intentional overdose of amitriptyline. Which finding is the priority?
items.x: Tricyclic overdose causes sodium channel blockade. A widening QRS predicts dysrhythmias and seizures and needs urgent treatment.
items.a: Widened QRS complex on the cardiac monitor
w: Dry mouth and cracked, peeling lips
Dilated pupils with blurred near vision
Warm, flushed and dry skin over the face

items.q: An older client starting nortriptyline is at risk for falls. Which instruction should the nurse include?
items.x: Tricyclics cause orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic effects, so slow position changes reduce fall risk.
items.a: Rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing
w: Take the daily dose in the morning with coffee
Increase your activity level right after each dose
Drink less fluid in the day to reduce night voiding

items.q: A client with a history of hypertension is started on venlafaxine. Which assessment should the nurse do regularly?
items.x: Venlafaxine can cause a sustained, dose-related rise in blood pressure, so blood pressure is monitored.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Serum ammonia level
Peak expiratory flow
Visual acuity

items.q: A male client is prescribed trazodone for sleep. Which adverse effect must the nurse teach him to report as an emergency?
items.x: Trazodone can cause priapism, a urologic emergency.
items.a: An erection lasting more than 4 hours
w: Mild grogginess on waking in the morning
Dry mouth during the first week
Vivid dreams on the first few nights

items.q: A client self-administers esketamine nasal spray in the clinic. What monitoring is required?
items.x: Esketamine can raise blood pressure and cause sedation and dissociation, so BP is checked and the client is observed at least 2 hours under the REMS.
items.a: Blood pressure checks and observation for at least 2 hours
w: One blood pressure check and then discharge to drive home
Pulse oximetry for 15 minutes only, then discharge home
No monitoring at all as long as the client says he feels well

items.q: A client with postpartum depression is receiving a brexanolone infusion. Which monitoring is required during the infusion?
items.x: Brexanolone can cause excessive sedation and sudden loss of consciousness, so continuous pulse oximetry is required.
items.a: Continuous pulse oximetry
w: Hourly blood glucose
Continuous fetal monitoring
Hourly urine specific gravity

items.q: A postpartum client is prescribed zuranolone. Which instruction should the nurse include?
items.x: Zuranolone has a boxed warning for impaired ability to drive, so clients should not drive for at least 12 hours after each dose.
items.a: Do not drive for at least 12 hours after each dose
w: Take it in the morning on an empty stomach with water
Drink a glass of wine with it to help it work faster
It is safe to drive as soon as you feel fully awake

items.q: A client in alcohol withdrawal has PRN lorazepam ordered by symptom-triggered protocol. What should guide each dose?
items.x: Symptom-triggered dosing uses CIWA-Ar scores to give benzodiazepines when withdrawal symptoms reach the protocol threshold.
items.a: CIWA-Ar score per the protocol
w: The client's request for medicine
A fixed schedule every 2 hours
Blood alcohol level on admission

items.q: A client who received IV lorazepam for agitation is now difficult to arouse with a respiratory rate of 8. What should the nurse do after stimulating the client and supporting the airway?
items.x: Oversedation and respiratory depression require holding further sedatives and prompt notification. Flumazenil may be ordered.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving further doses
w: Give the next dose early to prevent agitation
Document the client as resting comfortably
Recheck in 1 hour during the next round

items.q: A client with bipolar disorder starts carbamazepine. Which lab results should the nurse expect to monitor?
items.x: Carbamazepine can cause blood dyscrasias and hyponatremia, so the CBC and sodium are monitored.
items.a: Complete blood count and serum sodium
w: Serum lithium level and thyroid panel
Serum amylase and lipase levels
Troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide

items.q: A client started lamotrigine two weeks ago for bipolar maintenance and now has a new rash. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Lamotrigine can cause life-threatening rashes such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Any new rash is reported promptly, usually with the dose held.
items.a: Report the rash right away before giving the next dose
w: Apply hydrocortisone cream to the rash and recheck it tomorrow
Give the dose as ordered and teach the client about sun protection
Document the rash as a likely contact dermatitis from new soap

items.q: A client on valproic acid is newly lethargic and confused without other changes. Which lab result should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Valproate can cause hyperammonemia with encephalopathy even with normal liver enzymes.
items.a: Serum ammonia level
w: Serum lithium level
Hemoglobin A1C
Serum ferritin

items.q: A client taking valproic acid reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Valproate carries a boxed warning for pancreatitis. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting needs urgent evaluation.
items.a: Notify the provider promptly about possible pancreatitis
w: Give the dose with food and reassess the pain in an hour
Give a PRN antacid and recheck the client's pain in 2 hours
Teach that this is a common early side effect that will pass

items.q: A client with alcohol use disorder has naltrexone ordered. The nurse learns the client also takes oxycodone daily for chronic pain. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Naltrexone blocks opioids and can precipitate acute withdrawal in clients taking opioids.
items.a: Clarify the order before giving the naltrexone
w: Give the naltrexone with the oxycodone
Give the naltrexone and monitor for sedation
Give half the oxycodone dose with naltrexone

items.q: The nurse is reinforcing teaching for a client starting disulfiram. Which client statement needs further teaching?
items.x: Hidden alcohol in mouthwash, sauces or cough syrup can trigger a disulfiram-alcohol reaction.
items.a: I can still use my regular alcohol-based mouthwash
w: I will read labels on sauces and cough syrups
A reaction can happen up to 2 weeks after my last dose
I will carry a card saying I take disulfiram

items.q: A client on methadone maintenance is admitted to the unit. Which baseline test is most important?
items.x: Methadone can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes, so baseline and follow-up ECGs are used.
items.a: 12-lead ECG for QTc interval
w: Chest x-ray for infiltrates
Serum lipase level
Bone density scan

items.q: A client on the unit starts varenicline for smoking cessation. Which teaching point is most important?
items.x: Varenicline labeling advises monitoring for neuropsychiatric changes. Clients should report mood or behavior changes promptly.
items.a: Report new depression, agitation or unusual behavior
w: Keep smoking as usual for the entire course of treatment
Take each dose on an empty stomach right at bedtime
Expect a severe peeling rash during the first week

items.q: A teen taking atomoxetine for ADHD has yellow sclera and dark urine. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Atomoxetine can cause severe liver injury. Jaundice and dark urine need prompt reporting.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose with food and reassess
Encourage more fluids and recheck tomorrow
Document an expected side effect

items.q: An older adult on citalopram has a QTc of 520 ms on today's ECG. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Citalopram causes dose-dependent QT prolongation. A markedly prolonged QTc warrants holding and reporting.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck the ECG next month
Give the dose with a potassium supplement
Give half the dose and document

items.q: The LVN is collecting data on a client taking lithium. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: Coarse tremor, vomiting and slurred speech suggest lithium toxicity, which needs prompt reporting. A fine tremor and thirst are common.
items.a: Vomiting, coarse tremor and slurred speech
w: Mild thirst and a fine tremor in both hands
Increased urination during the daytime
Mild nausea right after the morning dose

items.q: The LVN is reinforcing teaching for a client on lithium. Which client statement shows understanding?
items.x: Dehydration raises lithium levels, so fluid intake is kept up in heat and exercise. Low salt and NSAIDs also raise levels.
items.a: I will drink plenty of fluids when it is hot or I exercise
w: I will cut back on salt to keep my blood pressure down
I will use ibuprofen rather than acetaminophen for pain
I will need blood tests only for the first few weeks

items.q: A client taking clozapine tells the LVN he has a sore throat and feels feverish. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Fever and sore throat can signal neutropenia with clozapine, so the LVN collects data and reports promptly.
items.a: Measure his temperature and report findings to the RN
w: Give throat lozenges and recheck at the end of shift
Encourage him to rest and drink warm tea
Tell him this is a common cold and not a concern

items.q: Which finding should the LVN collect and report for a client taking clozapine?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe constipation and bowel obstruction, so missed bowel movements need reporting.
items.a: No bowel movement in 3 days
w: Drooling on the pillow at night
Feeling sleepy after the dose
Gaining 0.5 kg this week

items.q: A client received haloperidol and now has a stiff, twisted neck and eyes stuck looking upward. What should the LVN do first?
items.x: Acute dystonia is distressing and can affect the airway. The LVN stays with the client and alerts the RN, who can give the PRN anticholinergic.
items.a: Stay with the client and notify the RN at once
w: Reposition the client's neck and recheck in an hour
Reinforce that the stiffness will pass with rest
Offer fluids and document the client's posture

items.q: The LVN is collecting vital signs on a client taking haloperidol. Which finding should be reported immediately?
items.x: High fever with rigidity can signal neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency.
items.a: Temperature 39.8 C with muscle rigidity
w: Temperature 37.4 C with mild drowsiness
Temperature 37.0 C with a dry mouth
Blood pressure 118/72 with dry mouth

items.q: A client on olanzapine asks why the provider orders blood work. Which reinforcement by the LVN is correct?
items.x: Olanzapine can cause weight gain, high blood sugar and high lipids, so metabolic labs are monitored.
items.a: It checks blood sugar and cholesterol, which it can raise
w: It checks your white blood cell count, which it can lower
It checks the drug level in your blood, which must stay in range
It checks thyroid and kidney function, which it can reduce

items.q: The LVN notes a client on risperidone has a shuffling gait, stiff arms and a hand tremor at rest. What should the LVN do?
