items.x: Conjunctivitis is a common adverse effect of dupilumab and should be reported.
items.a: Report the eye symptoms to the RN
w: Reinforce that it is unrelated to the drug
Suggest allergy eye drops from the store
Document it as a seasonal allergy flare

items.q: Before a client's certolizumab pegol injection, which data should the LVN collect?
items.x: TNF inhibitors increase infection risk.
items.a: Signs of infection such as fever or cough
w: Blood pressure in both arms while seated
Fingerstick glucose before the injection
Apical pulse counted for one full minute

items.q: A client receiving hydrocortisone has a blood glucose of 260 mg/dL. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose.
items.a: Report the glucose result to the RN
w: Recheck the glucose before the next meal
Document it as expected with a steroid
Reinforce a low-sugar diet and recheck

items.q: A client on a medical-surgical unit has taken pantoprazole for two years and now reports muscle cramps and hand tremors. Which lab result is most important for the nurse to review?
items.x: Long-term proton pump inhibitor use can cause hypomagnesemia, which presents with cramps, tremors and dysrhythmias.
items.a: Serum magnesium level
w: Serum amylase level
Serum albumin level
Serum uric acid level

items.q: The LVN reinforces discharge teaching for a client prescribed pantoprazole delayed-release tablets. Which client statement should the LVN report to the RN as needing more teaching?
items.x: Delayed-release pantoprazole tablets must be swallowed whole; crushing destroys the protective coating.
items.a: I will crush the tablet and mix it in applesauce.
w: I will take it about 30 minutes before breakfast.
I will swallow the tablet whole with some water.
I will report black or tarry stools to my provider.

items.q: A client admitted with pneumonia has a new prescription for IV piperacillin-tazobactam. Before giving the first dose, which action is the priority?
items.x: Piperacillin is a penicillin, so a history of penicillin allergy must be identified before the first dose.
items.a: Ask about any past reaction to penicillin drugs
w: Ask whether the client has taken antacids today
Check the most recent fingerstick blood glucose
Ask whether the client prefers oral medicines

items.q: A client on day 6 of IV piperacillin-tazobactam has had five watery stools in 24 hours with abdominal cramping. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.x: Frequent watery stools during broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy suggest C. difficile; isolate the client and notify the provider for testing. Antidiarrheals can worsen C. difficile.
items.a: Place the client on contact precautions and notify the provider
w: Give loperamide from the PRN list and recheck the stools later
Encourage yogurt with meals and reassess the stools tomorrow
Document the stools as an expected effect of the antibiotic

items.q: A client is due for amlodipine. The blood pressure is 88/52 and the client reports dizziness when sitting up. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Hypotension with symptoms is a reason to notify the provider before giving an antihypertensive. The nurse does not change the dose independently.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and have the client sit on the bed edge
Give the dose with a full glass of water
Give half of the dose and recheck the pressure later

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client who started amlodipine two weeks ago. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN as a likely adverse effect?
items.x: Peripheral edema is the most common adverse effect of amlodipine. A dry cough is linked to ACE inhibitors, not calcium channel blockers.
items.a: New swelling of both ankles and feet
w: A dry cough that began after starting it
A heart rate of 78 with a regular rhythm
A potassium level of 4.2 on morning labs

items.q: The nurse teaches a postoperative client about docusate. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Docusate is a stool softener that draws water into the stool; adequate fluid intake helps it work. It should not be combined with mineral oil.
items.a: It softens stool and works best with plenty of fluids
w: It stimulates the bowel and works within about an hour
It should be taken with mineral oil for the best effect
It is safe to take daily for years without any review

items.q: A client receiving scheduled docusate and oxycodone has had no bowel movement for 4 days and now has abdominal distention, nausea and vomiting. Which action is most appropriate?
items.x: Distention with vomiting after several days without a stool may signal impaction or obstruction, which needs assessment and provider notification, not more stool softener.
items.a: Assess bowel sounds and notify the provider of the findings
w: Give an extra docusate dose now and reassess the client tomorrow
Encourage the client to eat a high-fiber meal at dinner tonight
Document the findings as an expected effect of opioid therapy

items.q: The LVN collects a medication history from a client with a new prescription for docusate. Which home medicine should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Docusate can increase absorption of mineral oil, so the combination is avoided.
items.a: Mineral oil taken nightly for constipation
w: A daily multivitamin taken with breakfast
Acetaminophen taken as needed for pain
Lisinopril taken each morning for blood pressure

items.q: The nurse teaches a client who will take senna at bedtime. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Oral senna is a stimulant laxative that usually acts in 6 to 12 hours, which is why it is often given at bedtime.
items.a: It usually produces a bowel movement in 6 to 12 hours
w: It usually works within 15 minutes of taking a tablet
It works by adding bulk with water over about 3 days
It must be taken with a full meal to work properly

items.q: A client taking senna says the urine looks reddish-brown. The client has no pain, and a urinalysis yesterday was normal. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.x: Senna can discolor urine yellow-brown or reddish, which is harmless. Persistent or painful changes would still be reported.
items.a: Explain that senna can harmlessly change urine color
w: Tell the client this is a sign of kidney injury from senna
Tell the client to double fluid intake to clear the color
Explain that senna causes bleeding in the urinary tract

items.q: The nurse prepares to give senna to a client on a medical-surgical unit. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before giving it?
items.x: Severe pain with absent bowel sounds suggests obstruction, where a stimulant laxative is contraindicated.
items.a: Severe abdominal pain with absent bowel sounds
w: Last bowel movement was two days ago
Taking an opioid every 6 hours for pain
Reports a mild feeling of fullness after meals

items.q: A client who has taken senna every day for months reports weakness and leg cramps. Which lab result should the LVN check and report to the RN?
items.x: Long-term stimulant laxative use causes potassium loss in the stool, and hypokalemia causes weakness and cramps.
items.a: Serum potassium level
w: Serum ammonia level
Serum lipase level
Serum bilirubin level

items.q: The nurse teaches a client about polyethylene glycol powder for constipation. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that must be dissolved in liquid. It usually takes 1 to 3 days to work.
items.a: Mix the powder fully in 4 to 8 ounces of liquid
w: Take the powder dry and follow it with some water
Mix the powder with mineral oil to speed the effect
Expect a bowel movement within about 30 minutes

items.q: A client receiving daily polyethylene glycol has had six watery stools today and reports dizziness when standing. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Diarrhea with orthostatic symptoms suggests fluid loss; the provider should be notified before more laxative is given.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the next dose
w: Give the dose and encourage more fluids today
Give the dose along with a stool softener now
Give the dose and offer the bedpan more often

items.q: An older adult on daily polyethylene glycol has had frequent loose stools for three days. Which lab results are most important for the nurse to review?
items.x: Ongoing diarrhea from an osmotic laxative can cause dehydration and sodium and potassium imbalances, especially in older adults.
items.a: Serum sodium and potassium levels
w: Serum lipase and amylase levels
Hemoglobin and hematocrit levels
Liver enzymes and bilirubin levels

items.q: The LVN reinforces teaching for a client starting polyethylene glycol. Which client statement shows understanding?
items.x: Polyethylene glycol usually produces a bowel movement in 1 to 3 days; fluids should be maintained and watery stools reported.
items.a: It may take one to three days to have a bowel movement.
w: I should have a bowel movement within an hour of a dose.
I can cut back on my fluids while I take this medicine.
I will take it every day even if my stools turn watery.

items.q: A client in septic shock is receiving norepinephrine and vasopressin infusions in the ICU. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?
items.x: Vasopressin causes strong vasoconstriction and can cause digital and peripheral ischemia, which must be reported promptly.
items.a: Cool, mottled fingers with delayed capillary refill
w: A mean arterial pressure of 68 on current infusions
Warm, dry skin over the trunk and both thighs
Urine output that matches the hourly goal

items.q: An ICU client is receiving a vasopressin infusion for vasodilatory shock. Which lab value should the nurse monitor closely because of the drug's antidiuretic effect?
items.x: Vasopressin is antidiuretic hormone; water retention can cause dilutional hyponatremia.
items.a: Serum sodium level
w: Serum lipase level
Serum ammonia level
Serum amylase level

items.q: An ICU client on a phenylephrine infusion has a MAP of 78. The heart rate has dropped from 88 to 46. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist; the rise in blood pressure can cause reflex bradycardia, which should be reported.
items.a: Notify the provider about the new bradycardia
w: Increase the infusion to raise the heart rate
Document the heart rate as the expected target
Give the scheduled metoprolol dose right now

items.q: Phenylephrine is infusing through a peripheral IV while a central line is placed. Which assessment is the priority?
items.x: Extravasation of a vasoconstrictor causes tissue ischemia and necrosis, so a peripheral site needs frequent checks.
items.a: Frequent checks of the site for blanching or swelling
w: Daily checks of the site for crusting or drainage
Hourly checks of the client's blood glucose level
Daily weights to track the client's fluid retention

items.q: An ED client with a sprained ankle will be discharged with hydrocodone-acetaminophen. Which question by the nurse is most important?
items.x: Many over-the-counter products contain acetaminophen; combining them can exceed the safe daily limit and cause liver injury.
items.a: Do you take any other products with acetaminophen?
w: Do you take any vitamins that contain vitamin C?
Do you prefer liquid or tablet forms of medicine?
Do you usually take your medicine with milk or juice?

items.q: Thirty minutes after hydrocodone-acetaminophen in the ED, a client has a respiratory rate of 8 and is difficult to arouse. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.x: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is treated by stimulating the client, supporting breathing and giving naloxone per protocol.
items.a: Stimulate the client and prepare naloxone per protocol
w: Let the client sleep and recheck the vital signs in an hour
Raise the head of the bed and offer the client oral fluids
Give the next dose early to keep the pain from returning

items.q: The ED nurse teaches a client being discharged with hydrocodone-acetaminophen. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Opioids cause sedation that is worsened by alcohol, and alcohol with acetaminophen raises the risk of liver injury.
items.a: Avoid alcohol and driving while taking this medicine
w: Take it with grapefruit juice to boost its pain relief
Take an extra tablet if pain is not gone in an hour
Expect diarrhea, which is its most common side effect

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client who has taken hydrocodone-acetaminophen for several days. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Jaundice and dark urine suggest liver injury, a serious adverse effect of acetaminophen.
items.a: Yellowing of the skin and dark amber urine
w: Mild drowsiness after the first few doses
Dry mouth that is relieved by sips of water
Mild nausea that improves with some food

items.q: Before giving oxycodone-acetaminophen to an ED client with a wrist fracture, what should the nurse assess first?
items.x: A baseline respiratory rate and sedation level are needed before any opioid so that respiratory depression can be recognized.
items.a: Respiratory rate and level of sedation
w: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Capillary refill in the toes of both feet
Date of the last tetanus immunization

items.q: An ED client will be discharged with oxycodone-acetaminophen. Which home medicine most increases the risk of respiratory depression?
items.x: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids cause additive CNS and respiratory depression.
items.a: Alprazolam taken at bedtime for anxiety
w: Amlodipine taken each morning for blood pressure
Levothyroxine taken before breakfast each day
Omeprazole taken once daily for heartburn

items.q: An ED client with a history of heavy alcohol use has a prescription for oxycodone-acetaminophen. Which lab result should the LVN report to the RN before the dose?
items.x: Elevated liver enzymes increase the risk of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity, so the RN and provider need to know before the dose.
items.a: Elevated ALT and AST on today's labs
w: Hemoglobin within normal limits today
Normal serum sodium on today's panel
Blood glucose slightly above normal

items.q: A client arrives in the ED with chest pain and suspected acute coronary syndrome. Aspirin is prescribed. What should the nurse ask before giving it?
items.x: Aspirin is given quickly in ACS unless the client has a true aspirin allergy or active bleeding.
items.a: Ask about aspirin allergy and any active bleeding
w: Ask when the client last ate a full meal
Ask whether the client had a flu vaccine this year
Ask about any family history of diabetes

items.q: The ED nurse gives aspirin to a client with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.x: Chewing aspirin speeds absorption and platelet inhibition in ACS. Dissolving under the tongue is the method for nitroglycerin.
items.a: Chew the tablet rather than swallowing it whole
w: Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water
Let the tablet dissolve slowly under your tongue
Take the tablet only after the chest pain resolves

items.q: An ED client took a large number of aspirin tablets and reports ringing in the ears and rapid breathing. Which lab results are most important for the nurse to follow?
items.x: Tinnitus and hyperventilation suggest salicylate toxicity; the salicylate level and ABG track severity and acid-base status.
items.a: Salicylate level and arterial blood gas
w: Ammonia level and serum lipase level
Troponin level and fasting lipid panel
Thyroid panel and serum cortisol level

items.q: The LVN collects a medication history from an ED client who will be started on daily aspirin. Which home medicine should the LVN report to the RN because it increases bleeding risk?
items.x: Aspirin with warfarin greatly increases bleeding risk, so the provider must be aware.
items.a: Warfarin taken each evening
w: Metformin taken with meals
Atorvastatin taken at bedtime
Levothyroxine taken each morning

items.q: An ED client with type 2 diabetes is treated for an asthma flare and receives prednisone. Which lab value should the nurse monitor most closely?
items.x: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose, which is especially important in clients with diabetes.
items.a: Blood glucose level
w: Serum ammonia level
Serum lipase level
Serum troponin level

items.q: The LVN reinforces teaching for an ED client discharged with a five-day course of prednisone. Which client statement shows understanding?
items.x: Prednisone is taken in the morning with food to limit stomach upset and insomnia, and the full course is completed.
items.a: I will take it with breakfast to protect my stomach.
w: I will take it at bedtime to sleep through side effects.
I will take it on an empty stomach for best absorption.
I can skip doses on days when my breathing feels fine.

items.q: A client is discharged from the cardiac unit on ticagrelor after a coronary stent. Which client statement shows understanding of the teaching?
items.x: Ticagrelor increases bleeding risk; signs of bleeding should be reported, and doses must not be missed because of stent thrombosis risk.
items.a: I will report black stools or blood in my urine.
w: I can take extra aspirin when I get headaches.
I only need to take this when I have chest pain.
I can skip doses before dental visits on my own.

items.q: A client on ticagrelor after a stent has a new prescription. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider?
items.x: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor that greatly raises ticagrelor levels and bleeding risk; the combination should be avoided.
items.a: Clarithromycin for a respiratory infection
w: Acetaminophen as needed for a tension headache
Docusate daily for opioid-related constipation
Nitroglycerin as needed for anginal chest pain

items.q: A client with heart failure is due for carvedilol. The heart rate is 50, the blood pressure is 86/50, and the client feels dizzy. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Symptomatic bradycardia and hypotension are reasons to notify the provider before giving a beta blocker.
items.a: Report the findings to the provider before giving it
w: Give the dose and recheck the apical pulse in one hour
Give the dose with food and have the client rest in bed
Give the dose and encourage extra oral fluids right now

items.q: The nurse teaches a client starting carvedilol for heart failure. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Taking carvedilol with food slows absorption and reduces orthostatic hypotension; rising slowly also helps.
items.a: Take it with food and rise slowly from sitting
w: Take it on an empty stomach at bedtime only
Take it with grapefruit juice for absorption
Skip it on days when your weight goes up

items.q: A cardiac client on carvedilol for heart failure is assessed in the morning. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Rapid weight gain with crackles signals worsening heart failure and fluid overload, which needs provider notification.
items.a: Weight gain of 3 pounds overnight with new crackles
w: Heart rate of 64 at rest before breakfast this morning
Blood pressure of 112/70 while sitting up in the chair
Mild tiredness during the first week after starting it

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client with type 1 diabetes who takes carvedilol and insulin. Which data is most important to collect because warning signs may be masked?
items.x: Beta blockers can mask the tachycardia and tremor of hypoglycemia, so glucose checks are essential.
items.a: Blood glucose, since a racing pulse may not occur with lows
w: Daily weight, since carvedilol often causes rapid weight loss
Urine color, since carvedilol tends to darken the client's urine
Temperature, since carvedilol often causes a sudden high fever

items.q: A laboring client who is group B strep positive asks why she needs IV penicillin G. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.x: Intrapartum penicillin for GBS-positive clients prevents early-onset GBS infection in the newborn.
items.a: It lowers the chance of passing GBS to your newborn
w: It treats a bladder infection found on admission
It helps the cervix soften and dilate more quickly
It prevents infection of a future cesarean incision

items.q: Minutes after IV penicillin G begins, a laboring client reports throat tightness and has hives and a falling blood pressure. The infusion has been disconnected. Which action is next?
items.x: Anaphylaxis is treated first with IM epinephrine; antihistamines alone are not enough.
items.a: Give IM epinephrine per the anaphylaxis protocol
w: Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in an hour
Restart the infusion later at a slower rate
Apply oxygen and document the reaction only

items.q: A laboring client with suspected chorioamnionitis has a new prescription for IV ampicillin. What should the nurse confirm before the first dose?
items.x: Ampicillin is a penicillin; a penicillin allergy history must be confirmed before the first dose.
items.a: Any past reaction to penicillin drugs
w: The time of the client's last full meal
The client's preferred pain plan in labor
Whether the client plans to breastfeed

items.q: The LVN collects data on a postpartum client on day 3 of IV ampicillin. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Watery stools with cramping during antibiotic therapy may indicate C. difficile. Lochia rubra on day 3 is expected.
items.a: Several watery stools with abdominal cramps
w: A moderate amount of lochia rubra on the pad
Mild fatigue after a night of breastfeeding
Mild perineal soreness when sitting upright

items.q: Which set of postpartum results indicates the nurse should expect to give Rho(D) immune globulin?
items.x: Rho(D) immune globulin is given to an unsensitized Rh-negative mother who delivers an Rh-positive newborn.
items.a: Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive newborn, negative Coombs
w: Rh-positive mother, Rh-negative newborn, negative Coombs
Rh-negative mother, Rh-negative newborn, negative Coombs
Rh-positive mother, Rh-positive newborn, positive Coombs

items.q: The nurse teaches an Rh-negative postpartum client about Rho(D) immune globulin. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Postpartum Rho(D) immune globulin is given to the mother within 72 hours of delivery.
items.a: It should be given within 72 hours after the birth
w: It can be given at any time within a month of birth
It is given only before the next pregnancy begins
It is given to the newborn right after the birth

items.q: Which client situation should prompt the nurse to confirm that Rho(D) immune globulin is planned?
items.x: Abdominal trauma with bleeding can cause fetal-maternal hemorrhage, so an Rh-negative client needs Rho(D) immune globulin. Rh-positive clients do not.
items.a: An Rh-negative client has vaginal bleeding after a car crash
w: An Rh-positive client has an amniocentesis at 16 weeks gestation
An Rh-positive client has a spontaneous miscarriage at 10 weeks
An Rh-positive client has an uncomplicated vaginal birth at term

items.q: The LVN reinforces teaching for an Rh-negative client receiving Rho(D) immune globulin after birth. Which client statement shows understanding?
items.x: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization, protecting future Rh-positive pregnancies. It is needed again with each qualifying event.
items.a: This keeps my body from making antibodies to Rh-positive blood.
w: This shot protects my newborn from jaundice over the next week.
This shot means I will not need it again in future pregnancies.
This shot is a vaccine that builds my own immunity to the Rh factor.

items.q: Shortly after poractant alfa is given to a preterm infant on a ventilator, the oxygen saturation rises from 88% to 99%. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Surfactant quickly improves lung compliance and oxygenation; oxygen and ventilator settings must be weaned to avoid hyperoxia and overdistension.
items.a: Wean oxygen per protocol and notify the provider
w: Increase the oxygen to keep the level near 100%
Document this as the goal and make no changes
Suction the tube to clear any leftover surfactant

items.q: During administration of poractant alfa, a preterm infant's heart rate falls to 80 and the oxygen saturation drops. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Bradycardia and desaturation during dosing are managed by interrupting dosing and supporting ventilation until the infant recovers.
items.a: Support ventilation with positive pressure until stable
w: Instill the rest of the dose faster to finish quickly
Suction the endotracheal tube to remove the surfactant
Turn the infant prone and observe for five minutes

items.q: The NICU nurse assists with beractant for a preterm infant with respiratory distress syndrome. What must be confirmed before it is given?
items.x: Surfactant is given through the endotracheal tube; incorrect tube position can send it to only one lung or the esophagus.
items.a: Endotracheal tube position in the trachea
w: A feeding was completed in the last hour
A stool has passed in the last 24 hours
A blood glucose was drawn in the last hour

items.q: Parents ask how beractant will help their preterm infant. Which explanation by the NICU nurse is accurate?
items.x: Surfactant lowers surface tension in the alveoli, keeping them open and improving gas exchange.
items.a: It coats the air sacs so they stay open more easily
w: It kills the bacteria that cause pneumonia in the lungs
It sedates the baby so the ventilator works better
It dries the lungs by pulling out the extra fluid

items.q: A preterm infant has just received beractant. Which nursing action is appropriate in the period right after dosing?
items.x: Suctioning soon after dosing removes the surfactant; it is avoided unless there are signs of airway obstruction.
items.a: Delay routine suctioning unless the airway is blocked
w: Suction the tube right away to clear any excess fluid
Turn the infant from side to side every five minutes
Raise the oxygen to keep the saturation close to 100%

items.q: The LVN collects data on a preterm infant one hour after beractant. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: A sudden desaturation with unequal chest movement suggests pneumothorax, a risk after surfactant as compliance improves.
items.a: A sudden drop in oxygen saturation with uneven chest rise
w: Oxygen saturation stable in the low 90s on current settings
Pink color with equal chest rise on both sides of the chest
A heart rate that stays steady between 140 and 150

items.q: A neonate receiving phenobarbital for seizures has become very sleepy and is feeding poorly. Which lab result is most important for the nurse to review?
items.x: Excess sedation and poor feeding suggest phenobarbital toxicity; the serum level guides the provider.
items.a: Serum phenobarbital level
w: Serum lipase level
Urine specific gravity
Serum triglyceride level

items.q: After an IV phenobarbital loading dose in the NICU, which monitoring is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Phenobarbital can cause respiratory depression and apnea in neonates, so breathing is the priority.
items.a: Respiratory rate and pattern with apnea monitoring
w: Daily head circumference and length measurements
Stool count and stool consistency for the shift
Skin color checks under the phototherapy lights

items.q: The LVN reinforces discharge teaching for parents of an infant who takes phenobarbital for seizures. Which parent statement shows understanding?
items.x: Consistent dosing keeps the level steady and prevents breakthrough seizures. Mixing in a full bottle risks an incomplete dose.
items.a: I will give it at the same times and not skip doses.
w: I can give it only on days the baby seems jittery.
I will mix it in a full bottle so it is easier to give.
I will give an extra dose if the baby seems sleepy.

items.q: A preterm infant is receiving fluconazole for a fungal infection. Which lab results should the nurse monitor?
items.x: Fluconazole can cause hepatotoxicity, so liver enzymes are monitored.
items.a: Liver enzymes such as ALT and AST
w: Thyroid stimulating hormone level
Serum lipase and amylase levels
Urine pH and urine specific gravity

items.q: A NICU infant on a midazolam infusion is started on fluconazole. What should the nurse monitor for?
items.x: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and raises midazolam levels, increasing sedation and respiratory depression.
items.a: Increased sedation and slower breathing
w: Less sedation and need for more boluses
Rising blood glucose needing insulin
A drop in urine output below the goal

items.q: The LVN collects data on an infant who has received fluconazole for two weeks. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Jaundice with pale stools and dark urine may indicate liver injury from fluconazole.
items.a: Yellow skin with pale stools and dark urine
w: Soft, seedy yellow stools after most feedings
Six or more wet diapers over the past day
Mild hiccups after each of the bottle feedings

items.q: Parents ask why erythromycin ointment was put in their newborn's eyes. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment is given at birth to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.
items.a: It prevents eye infection passed on during birth
w: It treats jaundice that appears in the first days
It keeps the eyes moist under the warming lights
It helps the baby focus on faces sooner

items.q: A young infant in the NICU is receiving oral erythromycin. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Oral erythromycin in young infants is linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which presents with projectile vomiting.
items.a: Projectile vomiting after feedings
w: A yellow, seedy stool after feedings
A wet diaper every three hours
Mild hiccups after most feedings

items.q: The pediatric nurse teaches a parent about oral prednisolone for a child's asthma flare. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Corticosteroids are given with food to reduce GI upset and the full course is completed.
items.a: Give it with food or milk to limit stomach upset
w: Give it at bedtime so the child sleeps through it
Mix it in a whole bottle of formula for the day
Skip it once the child seems better tomorrow

items.q: The LVN collects data on a child who has taken prednisolone daily for nephrotic syndrome for six weeks. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Long-term corticosteroids suppress immunity, so varicella exposure can lead to severe infection and must be reported. Increased appetite and a rounder face are expected.
items.a: Exposure to a classmate with chickenpox
w: Increased appetite at meals this week
Mild trouble falling asleep at night
A rounder face noted by the parent

items.q: The nurse teaches a parent about amoxicillin for a child's ear infection. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Completing the full antibiotic course helps clear the infection and limits resistance.
items.a: Give all doses for the full time prescribed
w: Give it until the fever has been gone a day
Save leftover medicine for the next ear infection
Give it only at bedtime in a full bottle

items.q: A child on the pediatric unit receives amoxicillin. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?
items.x: Hives with angioedema and stridor indicate anaphylaxis, an emergency.
items.a: Hives with lip swelling and noisy breathing
w: Mild loose stools once or twice during the day
A red diaper rash in the groin skin folds
Mild nausea after a dose taken on an empty stomach

items.q: The nurse teaches a parent about nebulized ipratropium for a child's asthma. Which instruction is correct?
items.x: Ipratropium mist in the eyes can cause pupil dilation and blurred vision, so a good mask fit matters.
items.a: Fit the mask well so the mist stays out of the eyes
w: Give it only after the albuterol has fully worn off
Rinse the mask with alcohol before every treatment
Expect the child's urine to turn bright orange

items.q: A child receives nebulized albuterol and ipratropium for an asthma flare. Which finding best shows the treatment is working?
items.x: Reduced wheezing and work of breathing show improved airflow.
items.a: Less wheezing and less work of breathing
w: A heart rate that rises over the baseline
A dry mouth right after the treatment
More frequent coughing after treatment

items.q: The LVN collects data on a child receiving ipratropium treatments. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Eye pain and blurred vision suggest the anticholinergic mist reached the eye and may raise eye pressure; dry mouth and bitter taste are minor.
items.a: Blurred vision and eye pain after a treatment
w: Mild dry mouth that is relieved by sips of water
A slight cough during the start of each treatment
A bitter taste in the mouth after each treatment

items.q: A 19-year-old client on the psychiatric unit is started on escitalopram for depression. Which assessment is most important in the first weeks?
items.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in young adults, especially early in treatment.
items.a: Ask directly about thoughts of suicide
w: Check the blood pressure twice daily
Weigh the client daily before breakfast
Check the client's lithium level weekly

items.q: A client taking escitalopram has a new prescription. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider?
items.x: An SSRI with an MAOI such as phenelzine can cause serotonin syndrome; the combination is contraindicated.
items.a: Phenelzine for resistant depression
w: Acetaminophen as needed for headache
Docusate daily for constipation
Calcium carbonate for heartburn

items.q: The nurse teaches a client starting escitalopram. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: SSRIs usually take several weeks for full effect and are taken daily as prescribed.
items.a: It may take a few weeks to feel the full benefit
w: It works within a day, so expect fast relief
Take it only on days you feel very sad
Double the dose if you feel no change in a week

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client on escitalopram who also started tramadol. Which findings should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: Agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and hyperthermia suggest serotonin syndrome, which tramadol with an SSRI can trigger.
items.a: Agitation, sweating, tremor and fever
w: Mild nausea during the first week
A mild headache that eases with rest
Some trouble sleeping the first nights

items.q: A client on the psychiatric unit is starting long-term risperidone. Which lab tests should the nurse expect to be monitored?
items.x: Second-generation antipsychotics can cause weight gain, hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia, so metabolic monitoring is required.
items.a: Fasting glucose and lipid panel
w: Serum lithium and sodium levels
Ammonia and serum lipase levels
Cortisol and thyroid hormone levels

items.q: A client who started risperidone yesterday suddenly has the neck twisted to one side and eyes rolled upward. Benztropine is prescribed PRN. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: This is acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal reaction treated with an anticholinergic such as benztropine.
items.a: Give the PRN benztropine and stay with the client
w: Give the next risperidone dose early to calm the client
Tell the client this will go away within a day
Place the client in seclusion to keep others safe

items.q: A client started on risperidone reports feeling dizzy when getting up. Which data should the LVN collect?
items.x: Risperidone can cause orthostatic hypotension; orthostatic vital signs confirm it.
items.a: Blood pressure lying, sitting and standing
w: Temperature by mouth and then by the ear
Pulse oximetry while the client is walking
Blood glucose before and after each meal

items.q: An older adult on the psychiatric unit receives PRN hydroxyzine for anxiety. Which assessment is the priority afterward?
items.x: Hydroxyzine is sedating and anticholinergic, raising fall risk, especially in older adults.
items.a: Level of sedation and risk for falls
w: Daily weight and intake and output
Skin turgor over the sternum
Blood glucose before the next meal

items.q: A client who takes PRN hydroxyzine is started on haloperidol. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.x: Hydroxyzine and haloperidol can both prolong the QT interval, so the ECG should be reviewed.
items.a: Review the latest ECG for QT prolongation
w: Check the client's serum lithium level
Check blood glucose before every meal
Review the chart for a sulfa allergy

items.q: The nurse teaches a client being discharged with hydroxyzine for anxiety. Which instruction is most important?
items.x: Alcohol adds to the CNS depression caused by hydroxyzine.
items.a: Avoid alcohol since it adds to drowsiness
w: Take it with grapefruit juice for absorption
Expect your urine to turn a dark color
Take it only with a high-protein meal

items.q: The LVN collects data on an older adult who has received hydroxyzine several times today. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Confusion and urinary retention are anticholinergic effects that older adults are prone to.
items.a: New confusion and trouble passing urine
w: Mild dry mouth relieved by sips of water
Calmer mood and less pacing in the hall
Falling asleep at the usual bedtime

items.q: A client on aripiprazole is assessed on the psychiatric unit. Which finding most suggests akathisia?
items.x: Akathisia is subjective inner restlessness with an inability to sit still; aripiprazole commonly causes it. The others describe tardive dyskinesia, dystonia and parkinsonism.
items.a: Constant pacing and an inner sense of restlessness
w: Rhythmic tongue movements and repeated lip smacking
Sustained twisting of the neck to one side
Shuffling gait with a fine resting tremor of the hand

items.q: The nurse teaches a client starting aripiprazole. Which instruction is important?
items.x: Aripiprazole carries a warning for impulse-control problems such as compulsive gambling, shopping and binge eating.
items.a: Report any new urges to gamble, shop or binge eat
w: Report any dry mouth that goes away with sips of water
Expect your urine to turn orange while you take it
Take it only on the days when your symptoms feel worse

items.q: A client with bipolar disorder started lamotrigine three weeks ago and now has a new rash with fever. Which action should the nurse take?
items.x: Lamotrigine can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, most often in the first weeks; any rash, especially with fever, must be reported at once.
items.a: Notify the provider right away about the rash
w: Apply hydrocortisone cream and recheck tomorrow
Give diphenhydramine and continue as ordered
Reassure the client that a rash is expected

items.q: A client is starting lamotrigine for bipolar disorder. Which home medicine most increases the risk of a serious rash?
items.x: Valproic acid roughly doubles lamotrigine levels and increases the risk of serious rash, so dosing must be adjusted.
items.a: Valproic acid taken for mood stability
w: Acetaminophen taken for headaches
Docusate taken daily for constipation
Melatonin taken at night for sleep

items.q: A client on the inpatient psychiatric unit is prescribed bupropion for major depression. Which history finding should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?
items.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated with a seizure disorder or a current or prior diagnosis of bulimia or anorexia. Sexual side effects on an SSRI are a common reason bupropion is chosen.
items.a: A history of seizures or a current eating disorder such as bulimia
w: A history of seasonal allergies treated with an oral antihistamine
Sexual side effects reported during a previous trial of an SSRI
A family history of high blood pressure managed with diet alone

items.q: The nurse is preparing a client on the psychiatric unit for discharge on bupropion. Which instruction is most important to include?
items.x: Seizure risk with bupropion is dose related, so doubling doses or heavy alcohol use or abrupt alcohol withdrawal increases it. Bupropion tends to cause weight loss, not gain, and takes weeks to work.
items.a: Avoid alcohol and never double a missed dose, because seizure risk rises
w: Take an extra dose on difficult days, since the effect begins within hours
Expect weight gain and a larger appetite as the main side effect of therapy
Do not use nicotine patches, because they cancel out the antidepressant effect

items.q: A client on the psychiatric unit is started on mirtazapine for depression with insomnia. Which instruction should the nurse give about timing?
items.x: Mirtazapine is strongly sedating, so it is given at bedtime, which also helps clients with insomnia. Antidepressants are taken daily, not as needed.
items.a: Take the dose at bedtime, since drowsiness is a common effect
w: Take the dose each morning to prevent insomnia later at night
Take the dose only on days when the mood is feeling especially low
Take the dose with grapefruit juice to improve how well it absorbs

items.q: A client taking mirtazapine on the psychiatric unit reports a sore throat and a temperature of 38.6 C. Which lab result should the nurse review first?
items.x: Mirtazapine can rarely cause agranulocytosis, so sore throat and fever call for a CBC with differential and a report to the provider.
items.a: Complete blood count with differential to check the neutrophil count
w: Serum lithium level to rule out an interaction with the antidepressant
Thyroid panel to look for an endocrine cause of the new fever and pain
Lipid panel to check for the cholesterol rise linked to this medicine

items.q: At a 4-week follow-up on the psychiatric unit, the nurse evaluates a client taking mirtazapine. Which finding is a common adverse effect the nurse should monitor?
items.x: Mirtazapine commonly increases appetite and weight and causes sedation. It has a low rate of sexual dysfunction compared with SSRIs.
items.a: Increased appetite with a weight gain of several pounds
w: Marked weight loss with a poor appetite at most meals
Persistent insomnia and restlessness through the night
Severe sexual dysfunction as the dominant complaint

items.q: The LVN collects data on a newly admitted client prescribed mirtazapine and learns the client took phenelzine until 5 days ago. What should the LVN do?
items.x: Mirtazapine must not be started within 14 days of an MAOI such as phenelzine because of serotonin syndrome risk, so the LVN reports it before the dose.
items.a: Report the recent phenelzine use to the RN before the dose is given
w: Give the mirtazapine as ordered and check for drowsiness in an hour
Give the dose with a full meal to lower the chance of an interaction
Tell the client the two medicines are safe to combine after 1 day

items.q: A client admitted for alcohol withdrawal has symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide prescribed. What should the nurse do before each dose?
items.x: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing is guided by a validated withdrawal score such as the CIWA-Ar.
items.a: Score the withdrawal symptoms using the CIWA-Ar scale
w: Measure a blood alcohol level using a breath analyzer
Check a capillary blood glucose with a bedside meter
Ask the client to rate alcohol cravings from 0 to 10

items.q: The nurse checks a client 2 hours after a dose of chlordiazepoxide for alcohol withdrawal. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
items.x: Oversedation with slow breathing signals benzodiazepine toxicity, especially as this long-acting drug accumulates. Mild tremor, anxiety and drowsiness with easy waking are expected.
items.a: Respiratory rate of 9 per minute and difficult to arouse
w: Heart rate of 96 per minute with a mild tremor of both hands
Blood pressure of 146/90 with mild ongoing anxiety
Reports feeling drowsy but wakes easily to voice

items.q: A client in alcohol withdrawal on the psychiatric unit has chlordiazepoxide prescribed. Which lab finding should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?
items.x: Chlordiazepoxide is metabolized by the liver to long-acting metabolites that accumulate in liver failure. A shorter-acting agent such as lorazepam is often preferred, so the provider needs this result.
items.a: AST and ALT markedly elevated with a prolonged INR
w: Serum sodium 138 with a normal potassium result
Hemoglobin 13.6 with a normal platelet count
Fasting glucose 104 with a normal creatinine

items.q: The LVN reinforces discharge teaching for a client who will finish a chlordiazepoxide taper at home. Which statement shows the client understands?
items.x: Chlordiazepoxide causes CNS depression that adds to alcohol and impairs driving. The taper must be followed as prescribed.
items.a: I will not drink alcohol or drive while I am taking this medicine.
w: I can have a beer at night because this medicine blocks the effects.
I will take extra capsules if I feel shaky so I can finish it sooner.
I can drive to work as usual since the drowsiness wears off quickly.

items.q: A client on the oncology unit finishes a chemotherapy infusion today and asks why the pegfilgrastim injection is not given right now. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.x: Pegfilgrastim is given at least 24 hours after chemotherapy and not within 14 days before the next cycle, because rapidly dividing myeloid cells are sensitive to chemotherapy.
items.a: It is given at least 24 hours after the chemotherapy has finished
w: It is given only if a fever develops in the days after chemotherapy
It must be given the day before the next chemotherapy cycle starts
It works only when it is given at the same time as the chemotherapy

items.q: The nurse on the oncology unit is teaching a client about pegfilgrastim. Which adverse effect is most common?
items.x: Bone pain from marrow expansion is the most common adverse effect and is usually managed with mild analgesics.
items.a: Aching bone pain in the back, hips and long bones
w: Severe constipation that lasts for several days
Darkening of the skin over the injection site
Ringing in the ears with gradual hearing loss

items.q: A client who received pegfilgrastim 4 days ago calls the oncology clinic. Which report should the nurse escalate to the provider right away?
items.x: Splenic rupture is a rare but serious risk with pegfilgrastim and presents as left upper quadrant or shoulder tip pain. Bone pain and mild site reactions are expected.
items.a: Left upper abdominal pain spreading to the left shoulder
w: Mild aching in the lower back and both thighs since the shot
Slight redness and tenderness at the injection site
Feeling more tired than usual after the last chemotherapy

items.q: The LVN reviews a complete blood count for a client receiving pegfilgrastim after chemotherapy. Which result shows the medicine is having its intended effect?
items.x: Pegfilgrastim stimulates neutrophil production, so a rising ANC shows it is working. It does not target red cells or platelets.
items.a: Absolute neutrophil count rising toward normal
w: Platelet count rising toward the normal range
Hemoglobin rising toward the normal range
Lymphocyte count falling below the normal range

items.q: A client on the oncology unit is due for cycle 3 of carboplatin. Which lab result should the nurse report to the provider before giving it?
items.x: Myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, is the dose-limiting toxicity of carboplatin, so low counts must be reported before the next cycle.
items.a: Platelet count of 58,000 with a low neutrophil count
w: Serum potassium of 4.1 and serum sodium of 139
Hemoglobin of 12.8 and a normal white blood cell count
Fasting glucose of 108 with a normal serum creatinine

items.q: The nurse on the oncology unit reviews the history of a client about to receive carboplatin. Which factor increases this client's risk of a hypersensitivity reaction?
items.x: The risk of carboplatin hypersensitivity rises with repeated exposure, especially after several cycles. The nurse watches closely and has emergency drugs ready.
items.a: Having received many prior cycles of platinum chemotherapy
w: Receiving an antiemetic before the infusion is started today
Having a normal creatinine clearance on the most recent labs
Being treated for ovarian cancer rather than for lung cancer

items.q: A client scheduled for carboplatin on the oncology unit has a serum creatinine that has doubled since the dose was calculated. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Carboplatin dosing is based on kidney function, so a major change in creatinine means the dose must be recalculated by the provider and pharmacy. The nurse does not adjust it alone.
items.a: Notify the provider so the dose can be recalculated
w: Give the dose and encourage extra oral fluids today
Give half of the dose and recheck the creatinine later
Give the dose as a slower infusion to protect the kidneys

items.q: The LVN reinforces home teaching for a client whose platelet count is low after carboplatin. Which instruction should the LVN reinforce?
items.x: Low platelets increase bleeding risk, so the client avoids trauma to gums and skin and avoids aspirin and NSAIDs.
items.a: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor at home
w: Floss firmly each day to prevent any gum infection
Take aspirin for aches that develop after the infusion
Use a straight razor for a closer and cleaner shave

items.q: Before starting paclitaxel on the oncology unit, the nurse confirms the client received the ordered premedications. Which group is expected?
items.x: Paclitaxel carries a risk of severe hypersensitivity, so clients are premedicated with dexamethasone, diphenhydramine and an H2 blocker.
items.a: A corticosteroid, an antihistamine and an H2 blocker
w: A loop diuretic, an antihistamine and a laxative
A corticosteroid, an opioid and a stool softener
An anticoagulant, an antiemetic and an H2 blocker

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client who has had four cycles of paclitaxel. Which finding is most important to report to the RN?
items.x: Peripheral neuropathy is a cumulative, dose-limiting effect of paclitaxel and may require a change in therapy. Hair loss and fatigue are expected.
items.a: Numbness and tingling in the hands and feet
w: Mild fatigue on the day after the infusion
Thinning hair that began after the first cycle
A metallic taste when eating some foods

items.q: A client who received pembrolizumab 3 weeks ago calls the oncology clinic reporting six watery stools a day and abdominal cramping. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Pembrolizumab can cause immune-mediated colitis, which may need corticosteroids and prompt evaluation. It should not be treated as routine chemotherapy diarrhea.
items.a: Report this to the oncology provider today as possible colitis
w: Suggest loperamide at home and ask the client to call in a week
Explain that diarrhea is expected and will pass without care
Advise clear liquids only and skip the next scheduled visit

items.q: The nurse on the oncology unit prepares a client for a pembrolizumab infusion. Which lab results are monitored routinely during this therapy?
items.x: Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause thyroiditis and hepatitis, so thyroid and liver function are checked at baseline and during therapy.
items.a: Thyroid function tests and liver function tests
w: Serum drug levels and coagulation study results
Lipid panel results and a urine drug screen result
Serum amylase results and repeat blood cultures

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client receiving pembrolizumab every 3 weeks. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: New cough and low oxygen saturation can signal immune-mediated pneumonitis, which needs prompt evaluation.
items.a: SpO2 of 89 percent with a new dry cough
w: Heart rate of 78 with a regular, steady rhythm
Temperature of 37 C with mild fatigue
Blood pressure of 124/76 while sitting

items.q: A client on the oncology unit is starting oxaliplatin. Which instruction should the nurse give to reduce a common neurologic effect?
items.x: Oxaliplatin causes acute neuropathy triggered or worsened by cold, so clients avoid cold exposure for several days. Ice chips are used with bolus fluorouracil, not oxaliplatin.
items.a: Avoid cold drinks and wear gloves when handling cold items
w: Suck on ice chips during the infusion to prevent mouth sores
Apply ice packs to the hands to prevent numbness and pain
Take a cold shower at home if a fever develops after therapy

items.q: During an oxaliplatin infusion, a client says the throat feels tight when drinking cold water. SpO2 is 98 percent, there is no stridor and no wheezing. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.x: Pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesia causes a sensation of difficulty breathing or swallowing without objective airway signs. The nurse still reports it and keeps the client warm.
items.a: Cold-triggered throat dysesthesia, a known oxaliplatin effect
w: Early anaphylaxis needing epinephrine right away at the bedside
An anxiety reaction that is not related to the chemotherapy
Fluid overload from the infusion causing laryngeal swelling

items.q: The nurse on the oncology unit is preparing to flush the IV line before and after oxaliplatin. Which fluid should the nurse use?
items.x: Oxaliplatin is incompatible with chloride-containing solutions, so the line is flushed with D5W.
items.a: Dextrose 5 percent in water
w: Normal saline, 0.9 percent
Lactated Ringer solution
Half-normal saline solution

items.q: The LVN reviews the morning labs of a client due for oxaliplatin today. Which result should the LVN report to the RN before therapy begins?
items.x: Oxaliplatin causes myelosuppression, and a low platelet count may require the provider to delay or change therapy.
items.a: Platelet count of 48,000 and falling
w: Serum sodium of 140 and stable today
Hemoglobin of 12.4 and stable today
Serum glucose of 112 and stable today

items.q: A client taking warfarin is starting fluorouracil on the oncology unit. Which lab should the nurse monitor more closely?
items.x: Fluorouracil can raise the INR and bleeding risk in clients on warfarin, so the INR is checked more often.
items.a: INR, because fluorouracil can increase the effect of warfarin
w: Serum potassium, because fluorouracil causes potassium losses
Serum glucose, because fluorouracil causes high blood sugars
Serum calcium, because fluorouracil binds calcium in the blood

items.q: A client is receiving bolus fluorouracil on the oncology unit. Which measure should the nurse teach to reduce mouth sores?
items.x: Oral cryotherapy with ice chips narrows mouth blood vessels during bolus fluorouracil and reduces mucositis. Alcohol rinses and firm brushes irritate the mucosa.
items.a: Suck on ice chips during the bolus to cool the mouth
w: Rinse with an alcohol-based mouthwash after each meal
Drink hot tea during the bolus to improve circulation
Brush with a firm toothbrush to remove mouth bacteria

items.q: The LVN collects data on a client receiving continuous fluorouracil. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Hand-foot syndrome is a known effect of fluorouracil and may need a change in therapy.
items.a: Red, tender, peeling skin on the palms and soles
w: Mild fatigue in the afternoon on infusion days
Slight thinning of the hair at the crown
Darker urine in the morning before drinking

items.q: A client on the oncology unit asks why dexamethasone tablets start the day before each docetaxel dose. Which explanation is accurate?
items.x: Oral corticosteroid premedication before docetaxel reduces the incidence and severity of fluid retention and hypersensitivity reactions.
items.a: To lower the risk of fluid retention and hypersensitivity
w: To prevent delayed nausea from the chemotherapy alone
To raise the white blood cell count before the infusion
To protect the kidneys from damage during the infusion

items.q: Before giving docetaxel on the oncology unit, the nurse reviews the client's labs. Which result should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Docetaxel is cleared by the liver, and an elevated bilirubin markedly increases the risk of severe toxicity, so the label advises against giving it.
items.a: Total bilirubin above the upper limit of normal
w: Serum potassium within the normal reference range
Neutrophil count within the normal reference range
Serum creatinine within the normal reference range

items.q: Five minutes into a docetaxel infusion on the oncology unit, which finding needs immediate action by the nurse?
items.x: Severe hypersensitivity to docetaxel can occur within minutes of starting the infusion. Flushing, chest tightness and hypotension need immediate action and a rapid response.
items.a: Flushing, chest tightness and a falling blood pressure
w: Mild fatigue and a regular heart rate of 82 per minute
Temperature of 37.1 C and a calm, relaxed appearance
SpO2 of 97 percent with clear and equal breath sounds

items.q: The LVN reinforces teaching for a client receiving docetaxel. Which finding should the client be told to report?
items.x: Docetaxel can cause cumulative fluid retention, so new edema and weight gain should be reported.
items.a: Swelling of the ankles with a rapid weight gain
w: Mild tiredness for a day or two after treatment
Thinning hair that began after the first dose
A slight change in taste when eating some foods

items.q: Before the first rituximab infusion on the oncology unit, which lab results must the nurse confirm are on the chart?
items.x: Rituximab can reactivate hepatitis B, sometimes fatally, so all clients are screened for HBsAg and anti-HBc before treatment.
items.a: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody results
w: Hepatitis A antibody and serum ammonia level results
Serum drug level and creatine kinase level results
Thyroid stimulating hormone and free T4 level results

items.q: The nurse is monitoring a client during a first rituximab infusion on the oncology unit. Which finding should the nurse act on immediately?
items.x: Infusion-related reactions are most common with the first rituximab infusion. Hypotension and bronchospasm signal a severe reaction needing immediate action.
items.a: Blood pressure falling from 128/76 to 90/50 with wheezing
w: Heart rate rising from 76 to 84 while the client talks
Temperature of 37.0 C with mild sleepiness from premeds
Respiratory rate of 18 with clear and equal breath sounds

items.q: A client on the oncology unit is starting trastuzumab. Which baseline test should the nurse confirm has been done?
items.x: Trastuzumab can cause cardiomyopathy, so LVEF is measured before and during therapy.
items.a: Left ventricular ejection fraction by echocardiogram
w: Pulmonary function testing with spirometry results
Audiogram to check for hearing loss before therapy
Renal ultrasound to measure the size of the kidneys

items.q: A client receiving trastuzumab every 3 weeks reports new shortness of breath when climbing stairs. Which additional finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Dyspnea, edema and weight gain suggest heart failure from trastuzumab cardiotoxicity and need prompt evaluation.
items.a: Ankle swelling and a weight gain of several pounds this week
w: Mild fatigue on the day after each infusion this month
A slight headache after the most recent infusion visit
Nail ridging and brittle nails that developed over the last few months

items.q: The LVN reinforces teaching for a client starting trastuzumab who previously received doxorubicin. Which statement shows the client understands the main risk?
items.x: Prior anthracycline therapy increases the risk of trastuzumab cardiotoxicity, so heart failure symptoms must be reported and heart monitoring continued.
items.a: I will report any swelling or new trouble breathing right away.
w: I will report any hair loss, since that means the drug is failing.
I will skip my heart scans, since my last chemo did not hurt my heart.
I will expect hearing loss and report it only if it becomes severe.

items.q: At the end of surgery, neostigmine is given to reverse neuromuscular blockade. Why is glycopyrrolate given with it?
items.x: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine at muscarinic as well as nicotinic sites, so an anticholinergic such as glycopyrrolate blocks bradycardia and secretions.
items.a: To prevent bradycardia and excess secretions
w: To speed the reversal of the muscle relaxant
To prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting
To reverse the sedation from the anesthetic

items.q: A client arrives in the PACU after neuromuscular blockade was reversed with neostigmine. Which finding should the nurse report to the anesthesia provider?
items.x: Symptomatic bradycardia is a cholinergic effect of neostigmine. A strong head lift and cough suggest adequate reversal.
items.a: Heart rate of 42 with dizziness and a falling blood pressure
w: Heart rate of 88 with a regular rhythm and warm, dry, pink skin
Respiratory rate of 16 with a strong cough and head lift
SpO2 of 96 percent on oxygen with clear breath sounds

items.q: A client in the PACU received glycopyrrolate during surgery. Which finding is an expected anticholinergic effect?
items.x: Glycopyrrolate blocks muscarinic receptors, causing dry mouth and tachycardia. The other options are cholinergic effects.
items.a: Dry mouth with a mildly faster heart rate
w: Heavy drooling with a noticeably slow heart rate
Pinpoint pupils with watery eyes
Frequent loose stools and cramping

items.q: During the preoperative interview, which history should the nurse report to the anesthesia provider before glycopyrrolate is given?
items.x: Anticholinergics can raise intraocular pressure and precipitate angle-closure glaucoma, so this history must be reported.
items.a: Untreated narrow-angle glaucoma in both eyes
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis every spring and fall
Mild osteoarthritis of both of the knees
Well-controlled hypothyroidism on therapy

items.q: The LVN collects data on a postoperative client who received glycopyrrolate in surgery. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Urinary retention is an anticholinergic effect, especially in older men, and needs a bladder scan and provider follow-up.
items.a: No urine voided in 8 hours with lower abdominal fullness
w: Mild thirst and a dry mouth that improves with ice chips
Pain rated 3 out of 10 at the incision after medication
Sleepiness that improves when the client is spoken to

items.q: After induction of general anesthesia, a client's blood pressure drops and IV ephedrine is given. Which response shows the drug is working as expected?
items.x: Ephedrine has direct and indirect alpha and beta effects, raising blood pressure and heart rate. A marked reflex drop in heart rate is more typical of phenylephrine.
items.a: Blood pressure rises with a modest rise in heart rate
w: Blood pressure rises with a marked drop in heart rate
Heart rate slows while the blood pressure stays low
Urine output falls and the skin becomes flushed

items.q: During the preoperative interview, which home medicine should the nurse report because of an interaction risk with ephedrine?
items.x: Ephedrine releases norepinephrine, and with an MAOI such as phenelzine it can cause a hypertensive crisis.
items.a: Phenelzine taken daily for depression
w: Acetaminophen taken for knee arthritis
Omeprazole taken for acid reflux symptoms
Atorvastatin taken for high cholesterol

items.q: In the operating room, a client's blood pressure responds less to each repeated dose of ephedrine. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.x: Ephedrine works partly by releasing stored norepinephrine, so repeated doses produce a smaller response as stores are depleted.
items.a: Tachyphylaxis from depleted norepinephrine stores
w: An allergic reaction developing to the medicine
Proof that the IV line has infiltrated the tissue
Expected reflex bradycardia caused by the drug

items.q: A client in the PACU received ephedrine for low blood pressure during surgery. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN right away?
items.x: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic that can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias and myocardial ischemia, so chest pain with tachycardia is reported immediately.
items.a: Chest pain with a heart rate of 128 per minute
w: Blood pressure of 118/72 and a pulse of 84
Mild nausea that settled after an antiemetic
Incision pain rated 4 out of 10 after an opioid

items.q: The nurse applies a scopolamine patch behind a client's ear before surgery. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.x: Touching the patch and then the eye can cause pupil dilation and blurred vision. Patches are not cut or heated.
items.a: Wash your hands well after touching the patch
w: Move the patch to the other ear every few hours
Cover the patch with a heating pad for comfort
Cut the patch in half if you feel too drowsy

items.q: An 82-year-old client has a scopolamine patch after surgery. Which finding should the LVN report to the RN?
items.x: Older adults are prone to anticholinergic delirium from scopolamine, and new confusion should be reported so the patch can be addressed by the provider.
items.a: New confusion, agitation and seeing things
w: Mild dry mouth relieved by sips of water
Sleepiness that improves with conversation
Incision pain that is relieved by an opioid

items.q: A client on hemodialysis receives darbepoetin alfa. The hemoglobin has risen from 9.6 to 11.4 over 2 weeks. What should the nurse do?

items.q: At an MCI using START triage, an adult is breathing 34 times per minute. How should this patient be triaged?
items.x: In START, a respiratory rate over 30 indicates immediate (red) priority.
items.a: Immediate
w: Delayed, because the patient is still breathing
Minor
Expectant

items.q: At an MCI, a 5-year-old is apneic but has a pulse. Using JumpSTART, what should you do?
items.x: JumpSTART calls for 5 rescue breaths for an apneic child with a pulse; if breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate.
items.a: Give 5 rescue breaths
w: Tag the child as expectant
Begin CPR
Move to the next patient

items.q: Using SALT triage, which lifesaving interventions may be done during individual assessment? Select all that apply.
items.x: SALT lifesaving interventions are quick actions such as hemorrhage control, airway opening, chest decompression, and antidote auto-injectors; CPR and splinting are not done during triage.
opts: Control major bleeding
Open the airway
Give an antidote auto-injector
Start CPR
Apply a traction splint
Obtain full vital signs
ok: Control major bleeding
Open the airway
Give an antidote auto-injector

items.q: When lifting a stretcher, what is the correct technique?
items.x: The power lift keeps the back straight and the weight close, using the legs to lift and reducing back injury.
items.a: Keep the weight close and lift with your legs
w: Bend at the waist and lift with your back
Twist your torso while lifting to face the ambulance
Hold the weight far from your body

items.q: A patient is in a car that is on fire. What type of move should you use?
items.x: An emergency move is used when there is immediate danger; pull along the long axis of the body to limit spinal movement.
items.a: An emergency move along the long axis of the body
w: A full spinal immobilization before moving
A standard stretcher move
A slow, careful extrication

items.q: A physician gives you an order over the radio. What should you do?
items.x: The echo technique confirms the order and prevents errors.
items.a: Repeat the order back to confirm it
w: Carry out the order immediately
Ask your partner to write it down for the report later
Ignore it if you disagree

items.q: You discover an error in a patient care report. How should you correct it?
items.x: Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date so the original remains readable; never erase or obliterate.
items.a: Draw a single line through it, initial, and date
w: Erase or white out the error
Rewrite the entire report and throw away the original copy
Ignore the error

items.q: An adult patient wants to refuse transport. Which elements are required for a valid refusal? Select all that apply.
items.x: A valid refusal requires capacity, informed understanding of the risks, and documentation; family agreement, age over 21, or police witness are not required.
opts: The patient has decision-making capacity
The patient is informed of the risks, including death
The refusal is documented and signed
A family member agrees
The patient is over 21
A police officer witnesses it
ok: The patient has decision-making capacity
The patient is informed of the risks, including death
The refusal is documented and signed

items.q: Which action would be considered abandonment?
items.x: Abandonment is terminating care without ensuring continued care at an equal or higher level.
items.a: Transferring care to a lower-level provider
w: Transferring care to a paramedic
Giving a report to a nurse
Waiting for ALS to arrive

items.q: A hospice patient with a valid DNR is short of breath but has a pulse. What should you do?
items.x: A DNR applies to resuscitation, not to comfort care; patients with a pulse should still receive appropriate treatment.
items.a: Give comfort care such as oxygen and positioning
w: Start CPR
Withhold all treatment
Call the police

items.q: You suspect a patient has tuberculosis. What PPE should you use?
items.x: Tuberculosis is airborne; responders should wear an N95 respirator and place a surgical mask on the patient if tolerated.
items.a: An N95 respirator
w: A surgical mask only
Gloves only
No PPE

items.q: You approach an overturned tanker with a hazmat placard. Where should you stage?
items.x: Stage upwind and uphill at a safe distance, identify the hazard with binoculars and the ERG, and wait for a hazmat team.
items.a: Upwind and uphill at a safe distance
w: Downwind and close
Downhill near the spill so you can see the product
Directly beside the truck

items.q: Where do most ambulance crashes occur?
items.x: Intersections are the most common location of ambulance crashes; slow down and ensure all lanes have stopped.
items.a: Intersections
w: Highways
Parking lots
Long straight rural roads

items.q: Which findings may indicate elder abuse? Select all that apply.
items.x: Multiple injuries in various stages, injuries inconsistent with the story, and a controlling caregiver suggest abuse; report suspected abuse per law.
opts: Bruises in different stages of healing
Injuries that do not match the explanation
A caregiver refuses to let the patient speak
Taking several medications
A single bruise consistent with a reported fall
ok: Bruises in different stages of healing
Injuries that do not match the explanation
A caregiver refuses to let the patient speak

items.q: You placed a supraglottic airway in a 55-year-old apneic man who still has a strong carotid pulse. How often should you deliver ventilations through the device?
items.x: An adult who is apneic but has a pulse receives about 10 breaths per minute, one every 6 seconds, whether ventilated by mask or advanced airway. Faster rates cause hyperventilation, raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous return.
items.a: One breath every 6 seconds
w: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds as fast as the bag refills
One breath every 12 to 15 seconds to limit gastric inflation
Two breaths after every 30 chest compressions

items.q: After inserting a supraglottic airway and making one attempt to reposition it, you see no chest rise, hear no lung sounds and get no capnography waveform. What should you do?
items.x: A device that still cannot ventilate after adjustment must be removed so oxygenation is not delayed. BVM ventilation with an oral or nasal airway is the fallback while you prepare a further attempt or transport.
items.a: Remove it and ventilate with a BVM and basic adjunct
w: Inflate the cuff with additional air and keep ventilating
Increase the ventilation rate until lung sounds become audible
Leave it in place and let the hospital team confirm placement

items.q: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for a supraglottic airway?
items.x: Supraglottic airways are for unresponsive patients without a gag reflex who need ventilation. An intact gag reflex, caustic ingestion and known esophageal disease are contraindications.
items.a: Adult in cardiac arrest with no gag reflex
w: Responsive overdose patient who gags when an oral airway is inserted
Adult who drank drain cleaner and is now drooling and anxious
Alert asthmatic who is tiring but still speaking in short phrases

items.q: A 30-year-old motorcyclist is unresponsive with snoring respirations after striking a guardrail. What is the best way to open the airway?
items.x: Snoring signals partial obstruction by the tongue, and the jaw-thrust opens the airway without moving the cervical spine. If the jaw-thrust fails to open the airway, a head-tilt chin-lift is still used because the airway takes priority.
items.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver with manual spinal stabilization
w: Head-tilt chin-lift maneuver with the head turned to the side
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway before any manual maneuver
Place the patient in the recovery position and observe

items.q: You hear gurgling while ventilating an unresponsive adult. What is the longest you should apply suction in a single attempt?
items.x: Adult suctioning is limited to 15 seconds per attempt because suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Shorter limits apply to children and infants, and the patient is reoxygenated between attempts.
items.a: 15 seconds
w: 5 seconds in adults and 15 seconds in infants
30 seconds or until the airway is clear
Until the oxygen saturation drops below 90 percent

items.q: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with a muffled voice, high fever and soft stridor. What is the most appropriate management?
items.x: This picture suggests epiglottitis, where agitation or throat manipulation can trigger complete obstruction. Give oxygen as tolerated, avoid examining the pharynx, keep the child with a caregiver and transport.
items.a: Keep her calm in a position of comfort and transport
w: Lay her supine and inspect the throat with a tongue depressor
Insert an oral airway to prevent the tongue from obstructing
Have her lie flat so you can start an IV before moving her

items.q: A firefighter removed a 40-year-old woman from a house fire. She has a headache and nausea, and her pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Which action is most appropriate?
items.x: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so readings stay falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. High-concentration oxygen shortens the half-life of carbon monoxide.
items.a: High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
w: Nasal cannula at 2 L/min because the saturation is normal
No oxygen, since a normal reading rules out poisoning
Room air with a repeat pulse oximetry reading in 15 minutes

items.q: A 70-year-old woman is breathing 6 times per minute with shallow breaths, and her waveform capnography reads 62 mmHg. What does this reading most likely indicate?
items.x: A normal ETCO2 is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg, and a high value with slow shallow breathing shows the patient is retaining carbon dioxide. She needs assisted ventilation.
items.a: Hypoventilation with carbon dioxide retention
w: Hyperventilation with excessive carbon dioxide loss
Normal ventilation for a patient of her age
Poor pulmonary blood flow from a large pulmonary embolism

items.q: A 19-year-old with a history of asthma has a capnography waveform with a slanted, shark-fin upstroke. What does this pattern suggest?
items.x: A sloped upstroke shows slow, obstructed exhalation from narrowed lower airways, as in asthma or COPD. The shape often improves as the bronchospasm is treated.
items.a: Bronchospasm
w: An esophageal placement of the sensor tubing
Cardiac arrest with absent pulmonary perfusion
Normal respiratory pattern in a young adult

items.q: A 68-year-old woman found on the floor next to opioid pills is breathing 6 times per minute with pinpoint pupils and an SpO2 of 82 percent. What should you do first?
items.x: Inadequate breathing is corrected right away with assisted ventilation, which treats the hypoxia while naloxone is being prepared. Naloxone is then titrated to restore adequate breathing.
items.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
w: Give naloxone and wait to see whether her breathing improves
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and reassess
Insert a supraglottic airway while she still has a gag reflex

items.q: You are considering CPAP for a patient in respiratory distress. Which finding is a contraindication?
items.x: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers venous return, so it can worsen hypotension. Other contraindications include an inability to protect the airway, unresponsiveness, suspected pneumothorax and vomiting.
items.a: Systolic blood pressure of 82 mmHg
w: Crackles in both lung bases with an SpO2 of 88 percent
Respiratory rate of 28 with accessory muscle use
An alert patient who can follow commands and hold the mask

items.q: While you ventilate a patient with a BVM, the abdomen becomes increasingly distended. Which change in technique best reduces this problem?
items.x: Gastric inflation happens when ventilation pressure exceeds esophageal opening pressure, usually from breaths that are too large or too fast. Slow, modest breaths lower the risk of regurgitation and aspiration.
items.a: Give each breath over 1 second with just enough volume to make the chest rise
w: Squeeze the bag faster and harder so the air reaches the lungs first
Stop ventilating and switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Push firmly on the upper abdomen during each ventilation

items.q: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 3-month-old infant on a flat surface. What helps keep the airway in a neutral position?
items.x: An infant's large occiput bends the neck forward when the infant lies flat, which can close off the airway. Padding under the shoulders aligns the airway in a neutral or sniffing position.
items.a: A folded towel under the shoulders
w: A pillow under the back of the head
Hyperextending the neck as far as possible
Placing the infant face down with the head turned

items.q: A 12-year-old with a tracheostomy has noisy breathing, retractions and a falling SpO2. His mother says the tube has not been cleaned today. What should you do first?
items.x: Mucus plugging is the most common cause of distress in a tracheostomy patient, and suctioning the tube often fixes it right away. If suctioning fails, the tube may need to be replaced or the patient ventilated through the stoma.
items.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
w: Apply a nonrebreather mask over the mouth and nose
Insert a supraglottic airway through the mouth
Start an IV and give a fluid bolus

items.q: A 9-year-old having an asthma attack has become drowsy, and her wheezing is getting quieter while her breath sounds fade. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Quieter wheezing with fading breath sounds and drowsiness means little air is moving and the child is tiring. Prepare to assist ventilation and transport urgently.
items.a: Impending respiratory failure
w: Improving bronchospasm because the wheezing is resolving
An anxiety reaction that is ending
A normal response to the albuterol she took at home

items.q: An adult is breathing but responds only to pain. Which findings indicate inadequate breathing that requires assisted ventilation? Select all that apply.
