items.x: Inadequate rate or depth, gasping and hypoxia despite oxygen all call for positive pressure ventilation. A normal rate with good chest rise and a normal ETCO2 shows adequate ventilation.
opts: Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow chest rise
Cyanosis with an SpO2 of 80 percent on oxygen
Irregular, gasping respirations
Rate of 16 with equal, full chest rise
Clear lung sounds with an ETCO2 of 38 mmHg
ok: Respiratory rate of 6 with shallow chest rise
Cyanosis with an SpO2 of 80 percent on oxygen
Irregular, gasping respirations

items.q: Which conditions are contraindications to inserting a supraglottic airway? Select all that apply.
items.x: Supraglottic airways sit in the esophagus or hypopharynx, so an intact gag reflex, caustic ingestion and esophageal disease make them unsafe. Unresponsive apneic patients without a gag reflex are typical candidates.
opts: Intact gag reflex
Recent ingestion of a caustic substance
Known esophageal disease such as varices
Cardiac arrest with no gag reflex
Apnea after an overdose with no gag reflex
ok: Intact gag reflex
Recent ingestion of a caustic substance
Known esophageal disease such as varices

items.q: After inserting a supraglottic airway, which findings help confirm proper placement? Select all that apply.
items.x: Placement is confirmed with chest rise, lung sounds and continuous waveform capnography together. Gagging means the patient has a gag reflex and does not tolerate the device, and epigastric sounds suggest air going into the stomach.
opts: Visible, equal chest rise with ventilation
Breath sounds over both lungs and none over the epigastrium
A consistent waveform on capnography
The patient begins to gag and cough on the device
Gurgling heard over the epigastrium with each breath
ok: Visible, equal chest rise with ventilation
Breath sounds over both lungs and none over the epigastrium
A consistent waveform on capnography

items.q: A 2-year-old has had increasing respiratory distress for several hours. Which findings suggest progression to respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Bradycardia, a decreased level of responsiveness and weakening respiratory effort show the child is tiring and hypoxic and needs ventilation. Flaring, retractions and tachypnea in an alert child indicate distress with compensation still intact.
opts: Heart rate falling from 170 to 80
Limp and responding only to painful stimuli
Slow, irregular respiratory effort
Nasal flaring while alert and crying
Tachypnea with intercostal retractions while watching you
ok: Heart rate falling from 170 to 80
Limp and responding only to painful stimuli
Slow, irregular respiratory effort

items.q: At what rate should chest compressions be performed on an adult in cardiac arrest?
items.x: Current AHA guidelines call for 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Slower rates decrease blood flow, and faster rates reduce depth and filling time.
items.a: 100 to 120 per minute
w: 80 to 100 per minute
At least 140 per minute
60 per minute with long pauses for recoil

items.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an average-sized adult?
items.x: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep and not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm). Compressions that are too shallow fail to circulate blood, and excessive depth increases injury.
items.a: At least 2 inches but no more than 2.4 inches
w: About 1 inch, or one-quarter of the chest depth
At least 3 inches, regardless of patient size
One-half the anterior-posterior chest diameter

items.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a pulseless 6-month-old infant without an advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
items.x: Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15 compressions to 2 breaths, with the two-thumb encircling-hands technique for infants. A single rescuer uses 30:2.

items.q: The AED has just delivered a shock to a 60-year-old man in cardiac arrest. What should you do next?
items.x: Compressions resume immediately after a shock and continue for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check. Even when defibrillation works, the heart usually needs perfusion support before a pulse can be felt.
items.a: Resume CPR, starting with compressions
w: Check for a carotid pulse for up to 30 seconds
Press analyze again to confirm the rhythm
Give two rescue breaths and then check for breathing

items.q: A supraglottic airway has been placed in an adult in cardiac arrest. How should compressions and ventilations now be coordinated?
items.x: With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilations are given asynchronously at 10 per minute. This keeps compressions going while avoiding hyperventilation.
items.a: Continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 seconds
w: Pauses after every 30 compressions to give 2 breaths
Continuous compressions with a breath every 2 seconds
Compressions paused for 1 breath every 15 compressions

items.q: You are about to use an AED on a pulseless 5-year-old, but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
items.x: If pediatric pads or an attenuator are unavailable, a standard AED with adult pads should be used. Pads must not touch or overlap, so anterior-posterior placement is used on a small chest.
items.a: Use the adult pads, placing them front and back if they would touch
w: Withhold defibrillation until pediatric pads arrive
Cut the adult pads in half to fit the small chest
Use one adult pad on the chest and skip the second pad

items.q: A 66-year-old diabetic woman complains of sudden fatigue, nausea and shortness of breath but denies chest pain. Her skin is cool and diaphoretic. What should you suspect?
items.x: Women, older adults and diabetics often have ACS without classic chest pain, presenting instead with dyspnea, weakness or nausea. Treat as a possible cardiac event and transport to an appropriate facility.
items.a: Atypical acute coronary syndrome
w: Gastroenteritis, because she has no chest pain
A panic attack brought on by the stress of the call
Hyperglycemia from missing her morning insulin

items.q: A 58-year-old man has substernal chest pressure and a BP of 146/90. He says he took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction about 12 hours ago. What is the correct approach to nitroglycerin?
items.x: Nitroglycerin given within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil) can cause profound hypotension. Continue other ACS care and tell the receiving facility.
items.a: Withhold it
w: Give half the usual dose and recheck the BP
Give it as normal since the BP is above 100
Give it only after a fluid bolus

items.q: A 71-year-old man with crushing chest pain is pale and cool with a BP of 78/50, HR of 112 and crackles throughout both lungs. Which action is most appropriate?
items.x: Hypotension with pulmonary edema after an MI suggests cardiogenic shock, where nitroglycerin and CPAP can worsen hypotension and large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema. Rapid transport for reperfusion is the priority.
items.a: Expedite transport to a PCI center without nitroglycerin
w: Infuse 2 liters of normal saline wide open to raise the BP
Give nitroglycerin to relieve the chest pain and pulmonary edema
Apply CPAP at high pressure to clear the crackles quickly

items.q: A 74-year-old woman has a new facial droop and slurred speech. Which piece of information is most important for the receiving stroke center?
items.x: Eligibility for clot-dissolving drugs and clot removal depends on the time since the patient was last known well. Get this time from witnesses and report it early.
items.a: Time she was last known to be well
w: Her blood pressure readings from last month
The name of her primary care physician
Whether she has had a flu vaccine this year

items.q: A 62-year-old man has sudden confusion and weakness on one side. Before you call a stroke alert, which assessment helps rule out a common stroke mimic?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can cause focal weakness and confusion that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check takes moments and changes management.
items.a: Blood glucose level
w: Pupil reaction to light
Capillary refill time
Temperature of the skin

items.q: An 80-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with severe dyspnea, crackles to the mid-lung fields, BP of 184/102 and an SpO2 of 86 percent. She is alert and following commands. Which intervention will most improve her oxygenation?
items.x: CPAP pushes fluid out of the alveoli, improves gas exchange and reduces the work of breathing in acute pulmonary edema. She is hypertensive and alert, so she is a good candidate.
items.a: Continuous positive airway pressure
w: A large isotonic fluid bolus
Oral glucose for possible hypoglycemia
Laying her flat to rest the heart

items.q: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension has sudden, tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. His BP is 190/100 in the right arm and 140/84 in the left. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back with a significant BP difference between the arms suggests aortic dissection. Transport rapidly and notify the receiving facility.
items.a: Aortic dissection
w: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Stable angina
Acute pericarditis

items.q: A 1-year-old has a heart rate of 50, mottled skin and poor responsiveness despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. What should you do next?
items.x: In children, a heart rate below 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation calls for CPR. Bradycardia in children is usually caused by hypoxia and is a sign of arrest about to happen.
items.a: Start chest compressions
w: Continue ventilating and recheck in 10 minutes
Give oral glucose
Apply the AED and deliver a shock

items.q: After defibrillation and 4 minutes of CPR, a 59-year-old man has a pulse. He remains unresponsive with a BP of 74/40 and clear lung sounds. Which intervention is appropriate?
items.x: After return of spontaneous circulation, hypotension is treated to keep systolic pressure at least 90 mmHg, and a crystalloid bolus is a first step when the lungs are clear. Keep the pads on in case of re-arrest.
items.a: An isotonic crystalloid bolus
w: Nitroglycerin to improve coronary flow
Ventilating at 30 breaths per minute
Removing the AED pads to prevent burns

items.q: An AED analyzes the rhythm of a pulseless, apneic 70-year-old woman and advises no shock. What should you do?
items.x: A no-shock message means the rhythm is not shockable, such as asystole or PEA, but the patient is still in arrest. Resume high-quality CPR and reanalyze every 2 minutes.
items.a: Resume CPR immediately
w: Turn off the AED and start transport without CPR
Check for a pulse for 1 full minute
Reposition the pads and analyze again right away

items.q: A bystander is doing CPR on a pulseless 25-year-old found with a syringe in his arm. What is your highest priority?
items.x: Once an opioid overdose patient is pulseless, CPR and defibrillation take priority. Naloxone may be given but must not delay or interrupt compressions.
items.a: High-quality CPR and early AED use
w: Naloxone before any other care
Placing an IV for drug administration
Searching the scene for the substance used

items.q: Which actions are components of high-quality adult CPR? Select all that apply.
items.x: Full recoil lets the heart refill, short pauses maintain coronary perfusion, and the correct rate maximizes blood flow. Leaning on the chest and overventilating both reduce venous return.
opts: Allowing full chest recoil after each compression
Keeping pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute
Leaning on the chest between compressions to keep pressure
Ventilating every 2 seconds once an advanced airway is placed
ok: Allowing full chest recoil after each compression
Keeping pauses in compressions under 10 seconds
Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute

items.q: Which findings are part of the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale? Select all that apply.
items.x: The Cincinnati scale assesses a facial smile, arm drift with eyes closed and repeating a simple sentence. Any one abnormal finding raises the chance of stroke.
opts: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech
Pupil size and reactivity
Blood pressure difference between arms
ok: Facial droop
Arm drift
Abnormal speech

items.q: Which actions are appropriate when using an AED? Select all that apply.
items.x: Clearing the patient, removing patches and drying the chest prevent injury and help the shock work. Pads go at least 1 inch away from an implanted device, and compressions stop during analysis so motion does not interfere.
opts: Ensuring no one touches the patient during analysis and shock
Removing a medication patch and wiping the skin before applying a pad
Moving the patient out of standing water and drying the chest
Placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Continuing compressions while the AED analyzes the rhythm
ok: Ensuring no one touches the patient during analysis and shock
Removing a medication patch and wiping the skin before applying a pad
Moving the patient out of standing water and drying the chest

items.q: A 76-year-old man reports worsening shortness of breath at night. Which findings support left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema? Select all that apply.
items.x: Left ventricular failure backs fluid into the lungs, causing crackles, orthopnea and frothy sputum. Pain relieved by leaning forward points to pericarditis, and clear lungs argue against pulmonary edema.
opts: Crackles in both lung bases
Needing to sleep sitting up in a recliner
Pink, frothy sputum
Clear and equal breath sounds throughout
Pain that improves when he leans forward
ok: Crackles in both lung bases
Needing to sleep sitting up in a recliner
Pink, frothy sputum

items.q: A 22-year-old has bright red blood spurting from a deep laceration on his upper thigh that continues despite firm direct pressure. What should you do next?
items.x: Life-threatening extremity bleeding that is not controlled by direct pressure requires a tourniquet placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound. Elevation and pressure points are not reliable for hemorrhage control.
items.a: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
w: Elevate the leg and add more gauze on top
Apply pressure to the femoral artery at the groin
Apply a cold pack and loosen the dressing

items.q: A 28-year-old man was stabbed in the abdomen. He is anxious with a weak radial pulse and a BP of 80/50, and there is no head injury. Transport will take 20 minutes. What is the best fluid strategy?
items.x: In penetrating torso trauma without head injury, permissive hypotension aims for a palpable radial pulse or a systolic pressure around 80 to 90 mmHg. Large volumes can raise pressure enough to disrupt clots and dilute clotting factors.
items.a: Small boluses to keep a radial pulse
w: Two liters wide open through two large-bore lines
No IV access until arrival at the trauma center
Dextrose infusion to provide energy to tissues

items.q: A 35-year-old has a severe head injury with a GCS of 7 and a BP of 84/50. What is the blood pressure goal for this patient?
items.x: Even one episode of hypotension worsens outcomes after a traumatic brain injury, so permissive hypotension is not used. Give fluids to keep the systolic pressure at or above 90 mmHg in adults.
items.a: Systolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg
w: Systolic pressure of 70 mmHg to limit brain swelling
The lowest pressure that keeps a radial pulse present
Systolic pressure above 200 mmHg to force perfusion

items.q: A patient with a head injury develops a BP of 196/110, a pulse of 48 and irregular breathing. What do these findings indicate?
items.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations make up Cushing's triad, a late sign of rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation. Manage the airway, avoid hypoxia and transport rapidly.
items.a: Increasing intracranial pressure
w: Hypovolemic shock that is still compensated
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
Pain-induced anxiety

items.q: You sealed a gunshot wound to the chest with an occlusive dressing. The patient now has worsening dyspnea, absent breath sounds on that side and a falling BP. What should you do?
items.x: These signs suggest a developing tension pneumothorax, and briefly unsealing the dressing lets trapped air escape. Reseal it afterward and transport rapidly to ALS or a trauma center.
items.a: Briefly lift the dressing to release trapped air
w: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Give a 2-liter fluid bolus
Place the patient supine with legs elevated

items.q: A 45-year-old was ejected from a vehicle. She has pelvic pain, instability and signs of shock. Which intervention is most appropriate?
items.x: A binder centered over the greater trochanters closes an open pelvic ring and reduces bleeding. Repeated manipulation can disrupt clots, and a binder placed too high is ineffective.
items.a: Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters
w: Rock the pelvis repeatedly to check for instability
Apply the binder around the waist at the iliac crests
Flex both hips and knees and tie the legs together

items.q: An 82-year-old who takes a blood thinner fell from standing and hit her head. She is alert with a small forehead bruise and wants to refuse transport. What is your main concern?
items.x: Anticoagulants and age-related brain atrophy raise the risk of a slowly expanding brain bleed after minor head trauma. These patients need hospital evaluation even when they appear well.
items.a: Delayed intracranial bleeding
w: Hip fracture from a minor fall
Dehydration from poor oral intake
Infection of the forehead abrasion

items.q: An adult has partial-thickness burns covering the entire anterior chest and abdomen and the entire right arm. Using the rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
items.x: In adults, the anterior trunk is 18 percent and each arm is 9 percent, giving 27 percent. Superficial burns are not counted in this total.
items.a: 27 percent
w: 18 percent
36 percent
45 percent

items.q: A 1-year-old has partial-thickness burns covering the entire head and the entire anterior trunk. Using the pediatric rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
items.x: In infants, the head is about 18 percent because it is larger in proportion, and the anterior trunk is 18 percent. Children lose heat and fluid quickly from burns, so prevent hypothermia.
items.a: 36 percent
w: 27 percent
18 percent
45 percent

items.q: A 24-year-old diver hit his head in shallow water. He cannot move his legs and has a BP of 78/48, pulse of 54, and warm, dry skin below the nipple line. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Spinal cord injury cuts off sympathetic tone, causing vasodilation, hypotension and a slow heart rate with warm, dry skin. Hemorrhagic shock usually produces tachycardia with cool, clammy skin.
items.a: Neurogenic shock
w: Hemorrhagic shock
Septic shock
Cardiogenic shock

items.q: You have made two unsuccessful IV attempts in a 30-year-old with hemorrhagic shock who has an altered mental status. What is the most appropriate next step for vascular access?
items.x: IO access is fast and reliable when peripheral IVs fail in a critically ill patient, and AEMTs can place it. An injured extremity should not be used for vascular access.
items.a: Intraosseous access
w: Keep attempting IVs in the hands until one succeeds
Abandon vascular access and give fluids orally
Place an IV in the foot of the injured leg

items.q: A 34-year-old fell from a ladder and has a femur fracture. Which findings suggest compensated shock? Select all that apply.
items.x: Tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and anxiety are early compensatory signs while blood pressure is still maintained. Hypotension marks decompensation, and bradycardia is a late, ominous finding.
opts: Heart rate of 122
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Restlessness and anxiety
Systolic BP of 70 mmHg
Heart rate of 46
ok: Heart rate of 122
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Restlessness and anxiety

items.q: Using national field triage guidelines, which injured adults meet high-risk criteria for transport to the highest level trauma center? Select all that apply.
items.x: Penetrating injuries to the torso, hypotension and amputations proximal to the wrist or ankle are high-risk criteria. Isolated minor injuries and ground-level falls in healthy young adults are not.
opts: Gunshot wound to the torso
Systolic BP of 84 mmHg after a crash
Amputation proximal to the wrist
Healthy 25-year-old who fell from standing
Isolated closed wrist fracture with good pulses
ok: Gunshot wound to the torso
Systolic BP of 84 mmHg after a crash
Amputation proximal to the wrist

items.q: Which actions are correct when applying a tourniquet for severe extremity bleeding? Select all that apply.
items.x: A tourniquet must be tight enough to stop arterial flow, placed above the wound and away from joints, and timed. Periodic loosening causes repeated blood loss and is not done in the field.
opts: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Tighten until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent
Record the time it was applied
Loosen it every 10 minutes to restore circulation
Place it directly over the knee for a lower leg wound
ok: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Tighten until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is absent
Record the time it was applied

items.q: A 54-year-old diabetic man is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 36 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.x: An unresponsive hypoglycemic patient cannot protect the airway, so oral glucose is unsafe. IV dextrose, such as D10 titrated to response, raises the glucose quickly.
items.a: Intravenous dextrose
w: Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
A rapid bolus of normal saline only
Waiting for him to wake up enough to drink juice

items.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has deep, rapid respirations, a fruity breath odor, a glucose reading of HI, a pulse of 124 and dry mucous membranes. Which intervention is most appropriate?
items.x: Diabetic ketoacidosis causes severe dehydration from osmotic diuresis, so isotonic fluid replacement is the key prehospital treatment. The deep, rapid breathing compensates for acidosis and should not be suppressed.
items.a: Isotonic crystalloid bolus
w: Oral glucose to correct the imbalance
Dextrose IV
Encouraging him to slow his breathing

items.q: A 70-year-old woman is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is a reasonable alternative within AEMT scope?
items.x: Glucagon given IM mobilizes stored glycogen when IV access cannot be obtained. It works more slowly than IV dextrose and depends on liver glycogen stores.
items.a: Glucagon IM
w: Oral glucose solution poured into the mouth
Nitroglycerin sublingually
Repeated IV attempts for 20 more minutes

items.q: An 18-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure that has stopped. He has a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and is becoming more alert. What is appropriate care?
items.x: Simple febrile seizures are common in this age group and are managed with airway support, passive cooling and transport. Ice baths and alcohol can cause shivering, hypothermia or toxicity.
items.a: Remove excess clothing and monitor during transport
w: Put the child in an ice water bath
Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol to cool the skin
Restrain the child to prevent another seizure

items.q: A 12-kg 2-year-old with vomiting and diarrhea is lethargic, with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 180. Protocol calls for a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. What volume should you give?
items.x: 20 mL/kg multiplied by 12 kg equals 240 mL. Reassess perfusion, mental status and lung sounds after each bolus.
items.a: 240 mL
w: 120 mL
480 mL

items.q: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying supine on a stretcher. What should you do?
items.x: In late pregnancy, the uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient lies supine, decreasing venous return. Left lateral positioning or manually moving the uterus to the left restores blood flow.
items.a: Position her on her left side
w: Elevate her legs and keep her supine
Place her in a seated position with her legs dangling
Start CPR

items.q: A woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, visual disturbances, swelling of the hands and face, and a BP of 172/112. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: Hypertension with headache and visual changes after 20 weeks of gestation suggests severe preeclampsia, which can progress to seizures (eclampsia). Keep the environment calm and transport.
items.a: Preeclampsia
w: Placenta previa
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Normal late pregnancy

items.q: A newborn was dried and stimulated and has received 30 seconds of effective ventilation, but the heart rate is 50. What should you do?
items.x: Newborn resuscitation calls for chest compressions when the heart rate remains below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. The ratio is 3 compressions to 1 breath.
items.a: Start compressions with ventilations at 3:1
w: Continue ventilations and recheck in 5 minutes
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen
Increase stimulation by flicking the feet

items.q: Ten minutes after delivering the placenta, a woman continues to bleed heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should you do first?
items.x: Fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction, the main way bleeding is controlled after delivery. Breastfeeding also helps, and signs of shock call for IV fluids and rapid transport.
items.a: Massage the fundus firmly
w: Pack the vagina with gauze
Have her sit upright
Pull gently on the umbilical cord

items.q: A 24-year-old woman has sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, a missed period and dizziness. Her pulse is 128 and BP is 86/56. What should you suspect?
items.x: A woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, a missed period and shock should be assumed to have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Treat for hemorrhagic shock and transport rapidly.
items.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
w: Gastroenteritis with mild dehydration
Urinary tract infection
Normal menstrual cramping

items.q: After a small dose of naloxone, a patient who overdosed on opioids is breathing 14 times per minute with good tidal volume but remains drowsy. What should you do?
items.x: Naloxone is titrated to adequate breathing, not to a full return of consciousness. Large doses can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
items.a: Continue to monitor without additional naloxone
w: Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Insert a supraglottic airway
Restrain him before giving another dose

items.q: A 21-year-old runner collapsed in a race on a hot day. She is confused with hot skin and a rectal temperature of 41.2 C (106.2 F). What is the priority?
items.x: Exertional heat stroke is a true emergency, and outcomes depend on how fast the core temperature drops. Cold water immersion or aggressive ice and water cooling should begin as soon as possible.
items.a: Rapid active cooling
w: Oral rehydration while monitoring her
Transport without cooling to avoid delay
Warming blankets to prevent shivering

items.q: A 7-year-old was pulled from a pool. She is unresponsive and apneic with a slow pulse. What is your first priority?
items.x: Drowning causes death by hypoxia, so ventilation is the priority. Abdominal thrusts delay ventilation and increase the risk of vomiting.
items.a: Rescue breaths
w: Abdominal thrusts to expel water
An AED
Rewarming before any other care

items.q: After a bee sting, a 40-year-old has widespread hives, wheezing, a swollen tongue and a BP of 76/44. Which medication is the first-line treatment?
items.x: Anaphylaxis with airway involvement and hypotension requires epinephrine IM in the lateral thigh. Albuterol can help with wheezing but does not reverse the systemic reaction.
items.a: Epinephrine 1 mg/mL IM
w: Albuterol by nebulizer
Oral glucose
Nitroglycerin SL

items.q: A 35-year-old man says he wants to kill himself and has a plan, but he refuses transport. He is calm and alert. What is the most appropriate action?
items.x: A patient with active suicidal intent and a plan lacks the capacity to refuse care for this condition and must not be left alone. Follow local protocols, which often require law enforcement assistance.
items.a: Stay with him and involve law enforcement as needed
w: Leave after he signs a refusal form
Agree to leave if he promises not to hurt himself
Leave him with a family member and depart

items.q: A 64-year-old dialysis patient with an AV fistula in his left arm needs IV access and a blood pressure reading. Which arm should you use?
items.x: Cuffs and IVs on the fistula arm can damage or clot the dialysis access. Use the opposite extremity.
items.a: The right arm
w: The left arm, above the fistula
The left arm, below the fistula
Either arm

items.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter is newly confused, with a temperature of 38.9 C (102 F), a pulse of 118, a respiratory rate of 26 and a BP of 84/50. Lung sounds are clear. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: This presentation suggests septic shock from a urinary source. Isotonic fluids are given while lung sounds are reassessed frequently, especially in older patients.
items.a: Isotonic crystalloid bolus
w: Nitroglycerin to support cardiac output
Oral glucose
Supine positioning with no IV

items.q: During a fluid bolus, a 79-year-old with a history of heart failure develops crackles, worsening dyspnea and a falling SpO2. What should you do?
items.x: New crackles and worsening oxygenation during fluid administration suggest fluid overload. Reduce the rate to keep the vein open, sit the patient up, give oxygen and notify medical direction.
items.a: Slow the infusion and raise the head
w: Increase the flow rate to finish the bolus
Lay the patient flat
Switch to a second large-bore IV

items.q: You notice cool, pale, swollen skin around an IV site, and the infusion has slowed. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: Infiltration occurs when fluid leaks into the surrounding tissue, causing swelling and coolness. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and restart in another site.
items.a: Infiltration
w: Air embolism
Pyrogenic reaction
Circulatory overload

items.q: You need to infuse 600 mL over 1 hour using a 10 gtt/mL set. What drip rate should you use?
items.x: 600 mL over 60 minutes is 10 mL/min, and 10 mL/min times 10 gtt/mL equals 100 gtt/min. Check the drip chamber against a watch and reassess.
items.a: 100 gtt/min
w: 60 gtt/min
10 gtt/min
600 gtt/min

items.q: Which findings are consistent with hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.
items.x: Low glucose triggers an adrenergic response and brain dysfunction. Deep rapid breathing and a fruity breath odor suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.
opts: Diaphoresis
Confusion
Tachycardia
Deep, rapid breathing
Fruity breath odor
ok: Diaphoresis
Confusion
Tachycardia

items.q: Which findings are consistent with anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Anaphylaxis involves multiple systems and can include skin, airway and circulatory findings. Unilateral leg swelling suggests DVT, and focal weakness suggests stroke.
opts: Hives
Stridor or wheezing
Hypotension
Unilateral leg swelling
Focal weakness
ok: Hives
Stridor or wheezing
Hypotension

items.q: Which findings distinguish heat stroke from heat exhaustion? Select all that apply.
items.x: Altered mental status and a core temperature above 40 C (104 F) define heat stroke. Sweating may persist in exertional heat stroke, so its presence does not rule it out.
opts: Altered mental status
Core temperature above 40 C (104 F)
Heavy sweating
Muscle cramps
Headache with normal mental status
ok: Altered mental status
Core temperature above 40 C (104 F)

items.q: Which findings suggest severe dehydration in an infant? Select all that apply.
items.x: Severe dehydration causes a sunken fontanelle, decreased tear production and poor perfusion. A bulging fontanelle suggests increased intracranial pressure.
opts: Sunken fontanelle
Absence of tears
Delayed capillary refill
Bulging fontanelle
Frequent wet diapers
ok: Sunken fontanelle
Absence of tears
Delayed capillary refill

items.q: Which findings suggest that delivery is imminent? Select all that apply.
items.x: Crowning, a strong urge to push and frequent, long contractions mean birth is near and you should prepare for delivery on scene. Early labor signs alone allow time for transport.
opts: Crowning
Urge to push or have a bowel movement
Contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 seconds
Contractions 15 minutes apart
Bloody show alone in a first pregnancy
ok: Crowning
Urge to push or have a bowel movement
Contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 seconds

items.q: You arrive at a tanker rollover with a placard on the truck. Where should you stage?
items.x: Staging upwind and uphill at a safe distance keeps responders away from vapors and runoff. Use the Emergency Response Guidebook to identify the hazard and set isolation distances.
items.a: Upwind and uphill
w: Downwind to monitor vapors
Close to the vehicle to start care quickly
Downhill so runoff is easy to see

items.q: Using START triage, how would you categorize an adult who cannot walk and has a respiratory rate of 36?
items.x: In START triage, a respiratory rate above 30 places the patient in the immediate category. No further assessment is needed for categorization.
items.a: Immediate
w: Delayed
Minor
Expectant

items.q: Which intervention is one of the lifesaving interventions allowed during SALT triage?
items.x: SALT allows only quick lifesaving interventions such as controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway, chest decompression, antidote autoinjectors, and 2 rescue breaths for children. Longer treatments wait until triage is complete.
items.a: Opening the airway
w: Splinting a fracture
Starting an IV
Applying a cervical collar

items.q: A diabetic man is alert and oriented after receiving IV dextrose, and he refuses transport. What must happen before you leave?
items.x: A competent adult may refuse care after being told the risks, benefits and alternatives. Recommend that he eat and have someone with him, and document thoroughly.
items.a: He makes an informed refusal and you document it
w: He must accept transport because he received medication
You must leave immediately when he refuses
You must call the police to force transport

items.q: You arrive to find a pulseless, apneic patient whose family shows you a valid, signed DNR order. What should you do?
items.x: A valid DNR order directs EMS not to start resuscitation. Follow local protocol for verifying the order and confirming death.
items.a: Withhold resuscitation per protocol
w: Start CPR until a physician arrives
Begin compressions but withhold ventilations
Ask the family to vote on care

items.q: While you treat a 3-year-old, you notice bruises in different stages of healing and an explanation that does not match the injuries. What is your obligation?
items.x: EMS providers are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse in most states. Document objective findings and report to the appropriate authority.
items.a: Report your concerns per mandatory reporting laws
w: Confront the parents about abuse
Ignore the bruises because they are old
Wait for the child to tell you what happened

items.q: Your service's written protocols allow you to give certain treatments without calling a physician. What type of medical direction is this?
items.x: Offline (indirect) medical direction includes protocols and standing orders written ahead of time. Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician.
items.a: Offline medical direction
w: Online medical direction
Direct medical control
Emergency medical dispatch

items.q: You discover an error on a patient care report you have already completed. How should you correct it?
items.x: A single line keeps the original entry readable and initialing it shows who made the correction. Follow agency policy for electronic reports.
items.a: Draw a single line through it and initial it
w: Use correction fluid to cover it
Erase it
Create a new report and destroy the old one

items.q: A patient has a chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum. What personal protection should you use?
items.x: These symptoms suggest tuberculosis, which spreads by airborne droplets. Wear an N95 respirator and put a surgical mask on the patient if possible.
items.a: An N95 respirator
w: A surgical mask only
Gloves only
No precautions

items.q: Which actions are appropriate for the first-arriving unit at a mass-casualty incident? Select all that apply.
items.x: The first unit establishes command, assesses the scene, requests resources and starts triage. Committing to one patient leaves no one to manage the incident.
opts: Establish command
Perform a size-up and request resources
Begin triage
Transport the first patient found
Treat the first critical patient until help arrives
ok: Establish command
Perform a size-up and request resources
Begin triage

items.q: Which are proper lifting techniques? Select all that apply.
items.x: Good body mechanics reduce injury by keeping the load near your center of gravity and using your leg muscles. Twisting and reaching increase strain on the back.
opts: Keep the load close to your body
Lift with your legs and keep your back straight
Communicate with your partner
Twist at the waist while lifting
Reach far out in front
ok: Keep the load close to your body
Lift with your legs and keep your back straight
Communicate with your partner

items.q: You are ventilating an intubated adult whose continuous capnography waveform has been normal at 38 mmHg. While moving him to the stretcher the waveform suddenly becomes a flat line at zero, although his SpO2 still reads 97 percent. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A sudden loss of the waveform after patient movement means the tube is out of the trachea (or the circuit is disconnected) until proven otherwise. SpO2 lags behind, so it cannot be used to rule out displacement.
items.a: Displacement of the endotracheal tube
w: Hypoventilation from a slow bagging rate
Developing bronchospasm
Return of spontaneous circulation

items.q: A 24-year-old with a severe asthma attack is being assisted with a bag-valve mask. The capnography waveform has a slanted, rounded upstroke with no flat plateau, giving a shark-fin shape. What does this pattern indicate?
items.x: A shark-fin waveform reflects slow, uneven emptying of narrowed lower airways, as in bronchospasm. Esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform at all.
items.a: Lower airway obstruction
w: Esophageal placement of the device
Hyperventilation with low CO2
Cardiogenic oscillations from the heartbeat

items.q: A 30-year-old with an isolated severe head injury is intubated. BP 138/82, HR 88, SpO2 99 percent, ETCO2 27 mmHg with no signs of herniation. What should you do?
items.x: Routine hyperventilation lowers cerebral blood flow and worsens outcomes in TBI. Ventilation should be slowed to bring ETCO2 back to 35 to 45 mmHg.
items.a: Slow the ventilation rate
w: Increase the tidal volume
Increase the rate to 20 breaths per minute
Add 15 cm H2O of PEEP

items.q: An adult in cardiac arrest now has an endotracheal tube in place and confirmed. How should ventilations be given during ongoing CPR?
items.x: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions are continuous and the adult is ventilated at about 10 breaths per minute. Faster rates raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce coronary perfusion.
items.a: One breath every 6 seconds
w: Two breaths after every 30 compressions
One breath every 3 seconds with compressions paused
One breath every 10 seconds timed to pauses in compressions

items.q: During an interfacility transfer, a ventilated 58-year-old abruptly becomes hypoxic with SpO2 dropping to 82 percent, and the high-pressure alarm sounds. What is your first step?
items.x: Taking the patient off the ventilator and bagging by hand removes the machine as a cause and lets you feel compliance while you work through tube displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure.
items.a: Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate by bag-valve device
w: Increase the FiO2 to 1.0 and continue to observe
Increase the PEEP setting to recruit alveoli
Give additional sedation and recheck in 5 minutes

items.q: You are setting up a transport ventilator for a 70-inch adult male with no lung injury. What tidal volume is generally recommended for lung-protective ventilation?
items.x: Lung-protective ventilation uses about 6 to 8 mL/kg based on ideal body weight, which depends on height and sex rather than actual weight. Larger volumes risk barotrauma and volutrauma.
items.a: 6 to 8 mL/kg of ideal body weight
w: 10 to 12 mL/kg of actual body weight
4 mL/kg of actual body weight
15 mL/kg of ideal body weight

items.q: A ventilated patient's blood pressure falls from 108/66 to 84/50 right after the PEEP is raised from 5 to 12 cm H2O. What best explains the change?
items.x: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and preload, so cardiac output and blood pressure can drop, especially in volume-depleted patients.
items.a: Higher chest pressure reducing venous return
w: Vasodilation caused by high oxygen concentration
Increased right ventricular preload
Hypercarbia from overventilation

items.q: Before rapid sequence intubation, a 64-year-old with pneumonia remains at SpO2 88 percent despite a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. He is breathing on his own. What is the best decision?
items.x: Starting RSI in a patient who is not preoxygenated leaves almost no safe apnea time. Improve oxygenation first, for example with a bag-valve mask and PEEP valve or noninvasive ventilation plus nasal cannula oxygen.
items.a: Delay induction and improve oxygenation first
w: Proceed with induction because the airway takes priority
Perform a surgical cricothyrotomy
Intubate quickly without further preoxygenation

items.q: After two failed intubation attempts and a failed supraglottic airway, you cannot keep an adult's SpO2 above 80 percent with a two-person bag-valve mask and adjuncts. What is the next step?
items.x: This is a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate situation. Once the less invasive rescue options have failed, a surgical airway is required without delay.
items.a: Surgical cricothyrotomy
w: A third intubation attempt with the same blade
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and wait
Give another dose of the paralytic

items.q: A 6-year-old with severe facial trauma cannot be intubated or oxygenated with any device. Which emergency airway is preferred for a child this age?
items.x: In young children the cricothyroid membrane is small and the larynx is funnel shaped, so needle cricothyrotomy is generally preferred over a surgical cricothyrotomy.
items.a: Needle cricothyrotomy
w: Open surgical cricothyrotomy
Blind nasotracheal intubation
Retrograde wire intubation

items.q: Which method is the most reliable way to confirm and continuously monitor endotracheal tube placement in the field?
items.x: Continuous waveform capnography is the standard for confirming and monitoring tube placement. Fogging, breath sounds and skin color can all be misleading.
items.a: Waveform capnography
w: Condensation fogging inside the tube
Bilateral breath sounds alone
Improvement in the patient's skin color

items.q: A 4-year-old with a tracheostomy is in respiratory distress with SpO2 82 percent, and you hear and feel little air moving through the tube. What should you do first?
items.x: Mucus plugging is the most common cause of tracheostomy obstruction. Suction is the first step, and the tube is changed if suction fails.
items.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
w: Begin chest compressions
Attempt orotracheal intubation
Give blow-by oxygen over the face

items.q: You are assessing a patient for a possible difficult laryngoscopy. Which finding predicts difficulty?
items.x: In the LEMON assessment, a thyromental distance under three fingerbreadths suggests a cramped mandibular space and a difficult view. The other findings are reassuring.
items.a: Thyromental distance under three fingerbreadths
w: Mouth opening of three fingerbreadths
Mallampati class I view
Neck flexion and extension without limit

items.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes is breathing deeply and rapidly. Blood glucose reads HI and ETCO2 is 18 mmHg with a normal square waveform. How should you interpret the ETCO2?
items.x: In DKA, deep rapid Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 to offset the metabolic acidosis, so a low ETCO2 is expected and is not a reason to slow the patient's breathing.
items.a: Compensation for metabolic acidosis
w: Hypoventilation with CO2 retention
A primary respiratory acidosis
A falsely low reading from equipment failure

items.q: While you ventilate a 3-month-old by bag-valve mask, the abdomen becomes distended and it is getting harder to squeeze the bag. What is the best correction?
items.x: Overventilation pushes air into the stomach, which splints the diaphragm and makes ventilation harder. Use proper positioning and the smallest volume that produces visible chest rise.
items.a: Reposition the airway and use only enough volume for chest rise
w: Increase the rate to 60 breaths per minute
Squeeze harder to overcome the resistance
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen

items.q: An arterial blood gas from a drowsy COPD patient shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mmHg and HCO3 26 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
items.x: A low pH with a high PaCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory acidosis with no metabolic compensation yet.
items.a: Acute respiratory acidosis
w: Metabolic acidosis with full compensation
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis

items.q: An intubated asthmatic is being bagged at 28 breaths per minute. BP falls to 72/40 and the bag gets stiffer with every breath. What should you do?
items.x: Rapid ventilation in obstructive disease traps air (auto-PEEP), which raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return. Allowing full exhalation and then using a slower rate with a long expiratory time reverses it.
items.a: Disconnect briefly to let the lungs empty, then ventilate slower
w: Raise the rate to clear the retained CO2
Increase the tidal volume
Add 15 cm H2O of PEEP

items.q: You have made two unsuccessful intubation attempts on an adult. SpO2 is falling to 85 percent and two-person bag-valve-mask ventilation is difficult. What is the next step?
items.x: A supraglottic airway is the rescue device after failed intubation when bag-mask ventilation is not working well. A surgical airway follows only if the SGA also fails to oxygenate.
items.a: Insert a supraglottic airway
w: A third attempt using the same technique
An immediate surgical cricothyrotomy
Stop ventilating and transport quickly

items.q: A 72-year-old with a long history of COPD and CO2 retention is mildly short of breath. What SpO2 target is generally appropriate?
items.x: In chronic CO2 retainers a target of about 88 to 92 percent avoids worsening hypercapnia while preventing hypoxia. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.
items.a: 88 to 92 percent
w: 100 percent
80 to 84 percent
96 to 100 percent

items.q: You find a 45-year-old after an overdose. Which findings indicate that ventilation is inadequate and needs assistance? Select all that apply.
items.x: A slow or shallow pattern, a high or rising ETCO2 and a falling level of consciousness all show inadequate ventilation that needs positive pressure. A normal rate with good chest rise and a normal ETCO2 does not.
opts: Respiratory rate of 6 with minimal chest rise
ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a rising trend
Respiratory rate of 16 with good chest rise
Responsive only to pain with shallow, irregular breathing
ETCO2 of 38 mmHg with a normal waveform
ok: Respiratory rate of 6 with minimal chest rise
ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a rising trend
Responsive only to pain with shallow, irregular breathing

items.q: An intubated patient suddenly deteriorates during transport. Which possible causes should you assess for? Select all that apply.
items.x: The DOPE mnemonic (displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment failure) guides troubleshooting. A steady waveform and equal breath sounds are reassuring, not causes.
opts: Displacement of the tube
Obstruction of the tube by secretions
A steady ETCO2 waveform at 38 mmHg
Tension pneumothorax
Equal breath sounds on both sides
ok: Displacement of the tube
Obstruction of the tube by secretions
Tension pneumothorax

items.q: You are planning an airway for a patient who may need RSI. Which findings predict difficult bag-valve-mask ventilation? Select all that apply.
items.x: The MOANS and BOOTS mnemonics list beards, obesity and missing teeth among the predictors of a poor mask seal or high airway resistance. Young age and normal neck mobility do not predict difficulty.
opts: Full beard
Morbid obesity
Age 25 years
No teeth
Normal neck mobility
ok: Full beard
Morbid obesity
No teeth

items.q: In a spontaneously breathing patient with a good waveform, which conditions can cause a low ETCO2? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hyperventilation removes CO2, while poor pulmonary blood flow from PE or shock delivers less CO2 to the lungs. Hypoventilation and fever raise ETCO2.
opts: Hyperventilation
Pulmonary embolism
Respiratory depression from an opioid overdose
Low cardiac output from shock
Rising body temperature with fever
ok: Hyperventilation
Pulmonary embolism
Low cardiac output from shock

items.q: You are considering CPAP for a patient in respiratory distress. Which findings are contraindications? Select all that apply.
items.x: CPAP needs an awake patient who can protect the airway and a blood pressure that can tolerate higher intrathoracic pressure, and it can worsen a pneumothorax. Pulmonary edema with tachypnea is a typical indication.
opts: Systolic BP of 80 mmHg
Unable to follow commands
Crackles from acute pulmonary edema
Suspected pneumothorax
Respiratory rate of 28
ok: Systolic BP of 80 mmHg
Unable to follow commands
Suspected pneumothorax

items.q: A 62-year-old has chest pain. The 12-lead shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in I and aVL. Which area of the heart is involved?
items.x: ST elevation in II, III and aVF points to the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery. Depression in I and aVL is the reciprocal change.
items.a: Inferior wall
w: Anterior wall
Lateral wall
Interventricular septum

items.q: A 66-year-old with an inferior STEMI has BP 82/50, clear lung sounds and distended neck veins. A right-sided lead V4R shows ST elevation. What is the most appropriate approach?
items.x: These findings point to right ventricular infarction, which depends on preload. Fluid supports cardiac output, while nitrates can cause severe hypotension.
items.a: Small fluid boluses and avoid nitrates
w: Nitroglycerin to relieve the chest pain
CPAP for the low blood pressure
Fluid restriction and diuresis

items.q: A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1 through V4. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
items.x: Anterior and septal leads V1 to V4 view tissue supplied by the left anterior descending artery. RCA lesions usually show inferior changes and circumflex lesions show lateral changes.
items.a: Left anterior descending artery
w: Right coronary artery
Circumflex artery
Posterior descending artery

items.q: A 58-year-old with crushing chest pain has ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and no ST elevation elsewhere. What is the best next step?
items.x: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves can be a mirror image of a posterior STEMI. Posterior leads V7 to V9 can confirm it.
items.a: Obtain posterior leads V7 to V9
w: Treat this as unstable angina only
Repeat the same 12-lead in an hour
Treat for a pulmonary embolism

items.q: A 28-year-old has palpitations. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186 with no visible P waves. BP 124/78, alert, no chest pain. What is the first treatment?
items.x: For a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal maneuvers such as the modified Valsalva are tried first. Electrical therapy is for patients who are unstable.
items.a: Vagal maneuvers
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation
Transcutaneous pacing

items.q: A 70-year-old is confused and pale. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 and BP 70/40. Which intervention is indicated?
items.x: A tachycardia with hypotension and altered mental status is unstable and needs immediate synchronized cardioversion. Vagal maneuvers should not delay it.
items.a: Synchronized cardioversion
w: Vagal maneuvers and reassessment
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Transcutaneous pacing

items.q: An unresponsive 55-year-old has a weak carotid pulse, BP 60 by palpation, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on the monitor. Which electrical therapy is appropriate?
items.x: The irregular, changing QRS shapes of polymorphic VT keep the defibrillator from syncing reliably. An unstable patient gets an unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy.
items.a: Unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy
w: Synchronized cardioversion at low energy
Transcutaneous pacing
No shock until the pulse is lost

items.q: A 78-year-old is diaphoretic with BP 72/40. The monitor shows third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape rhythm at 32. Atropine has had no effect. What is the next step?
items.x: An unstable bradycardia that does not respond to atropine needs pacing (or a chronotropic infusion). A wide escape rhythm from a third-degree block seldom responds to atropine.
items.a: Transcutaneous pacing
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation
Vagal maneuvers

items.q: A rhythm strip shows the PR interval getting longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, and then the pattern repeats. What is the rhythm?
items.x: A PR interval that lengthens until a beat is dropped, in a repeating cycle, is Mobitz I (Wenckebach). It is usually at the AV node and is often benign.
items.a: Second-degree AV block type I
w: Second-degree AV block type II
Third-degree AV block
First-degree AV block

items.q: A rhythm strip shows a constant PR interval with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS. The QRS is wide. What is the rhythm?
items.x: Dropped beats with a constant PR interval are Mobitz II. It arises below the AV node and can suddenly progress to complete heart block.
items.a: Second-degree AV block type II
w: Second-degree AV block type I
First-degree AV block
Sinus arrhythmia

items.q: The monitor shows sawtooth atrial waves at about 300 per minute and a regular ventricular rate of 150. What is the most likely rhythm?
items.x: Sawtooth flutter waves near 300 per minute with every second wave conducted give a regular ventricular rate of about 150, which is classic atrial flutter.
items.a: Atrial flutter with 2 to 1 conduction
w: Atrial fibrillation with rapid response
Sinus tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia

items.q: An unresponsive 60-year-old has sinus rhythm at 80 on the monitor but no palpable pulse. What should you do?
items.x: An organized rhythm without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity, which is not shockable. Good-quality CPR plus a search for the H's and T's is the priority.
items.a: Resume CPR and look for reversible causes
w: Defibrillate immediately
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Start transcutaneous pacing

items.q: You have just delivered a shock for ventricular fibrillation in an adult. What should happen next?
items.x: Compressions restart immediately after the shock without a pulse or rhythm check. Even if the shock worked, the heart usually needs perfusion support at first.
items.a: Resume compressions for 2 minutes
w: Check the carotid pulse right away
Analyze the rhythm again right away
Deliver two more stacked shocks

items.q: How deep should chest compressions be for an adult in cardiac arrest?
items.x: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm) deep, at 100 to 120 per minute with full recoil.
items.a: At least 2 inches but not over 2.4 inches
w: About 1 inch
About one-half the chest depth
At least 3 inches

items.q: During CPR on an intubated adult the ETCO2 stays at 8 mmHg. What does this most likely mean?
items.x: During CPR, ETCO2 mainly reflects the blood flow that compressions create. A value under 10 mmHg suggests poor compression quality, so check depth, rate and recoil and change compressors.
items.a: Compressions are not producing enough blood flow
w: Return of spontaneous circulation has occurred
The tube is definitely in the esophagus
The patient is being hyperventilated

items.q: After ROSC, a 64-year-old is intubated with SpO2 96 percent and BP 78/40. What is the priority?
items.x: Hypotension after cardiac arrest worsens brain and organ injury. Post-ROSC care targets a systolic BP of at least 90 mmHg and a MAP of at least 65 mmHg, using fluids and vasopressors.
items.a: Bring the systolic BP to at least 90 mmHg
w: Allow permissive hypotension
Increase ventilations to 30 per minute
Raise the head of the bed and observe

items.q: Two paramedics are doing CPR on a 5-year-old with no advanced airway. Which compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
items.x: Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15 compressions to 2 breaths. A lone rescuer uses 30 to 2, and newborns get 3 to 1.
items.a: 15 to 2
w: 30 to 2 as for adults
5 to 1
3 to 1

items.q: A 7-month-old is pale and mottled, with a heart rate of 52 despite effective ventilation with oxygen. What should you do next?
items.x: In pediatric bradycardia, a heart rate under 60 with poor perfusion despite good oxygenation and ventilation calls for CPR.
items.a: Begin chest compressions
w: Continue ventilations and reassess in 10 minutes
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Wait for a palpable pulse to disappear

items.q: A 4-year-old in cardiac arrest has been intubated. What ventilation rate is recommended during continuous compressions?
items.x: Current pediatric guidance recommends 20 to 30 breaths per minute (one every 2 to 3 seconds) once an advanced airway is in place, a faster rate than for adults.
items.a: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
w: One breath every 6 seconds
Two breaths after every 15 compressions
One breath every 10 seconds

items.q: A 71-year-old woman woke at 06:30 with right-sided weakness and slurred speech. She went to bed feeling normal at 22:00. What is her last known well time?
items.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at baseline. For wake-up strokes, that is when she went to sleep, not when the symptoms were found.
w: The time EMS arrived
The time of the 911 call

items.q: A 67-year-old with diabetes has new left-sided weakness and confusion. Before you call a stroke alert, which assessment is most important to rule out a common mimic?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check is required before stroke triage.
items.a: Blood glucose level
w: Pupil size
Skin temperature
Rhythm strip

items.q: A 59-year-old with hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. BP is 182/100 in the right arm and 140/80 in the left. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Sudden ripping pain that radiates to the back, with a large blood pressure difference between the arms, strongly suggests aortic dissection.
items.a: Aortic dissection
w: Inferior STEMI
Pulmonary embolism
Spontaneous pneumothorax

items.q: You achieve ROSC in a 58-year-old after a VF arrest. Which actions are part of post-arrest care? Select all that apply.
items.x: Post-ROSC care includes a 12-lead to look for STEMI, avoiding both hypoxia and hyperoxia, normal ventilation, and keeping systolic BP at 90 or higher. Hyperventilation and hypotension worsen outcomes.
opts: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98 percent
Hyperventilate at 30 per minute to protect the brain
Ventilate to ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg
Allow a systolic BP of 70 as permissive hypotension
ok: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 98 percent
Ventilate to ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg

items.q: Which of these are reversible causes of cardiac arrest included in the H's and T's? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins and thrombosis are the treatable causes to look for. Hypertension and tachycardia are not on the list.
opts: Hypovolemia
Tension pneumothorax
Hypertension
Hyperkalemia
Tachycardia
ok: Hypovolemia
Tension pneumothorax
Hyperkalemia

items.q: A patient has a heart rate of 160. Which findings would make this tachycardia unstable and call for immediate electrical therapy? Select all that apply.
items.x: Instability means the rhythm is causing hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure. Rate alone or palpitations with normal perfusion do not meet that standard.
opts: Hypotension with signs of shock
Acute change in mental status
Heart rate of 160 with no other findings
Ischemic chest discomfort
Palpitations with a normal blood pressure
ok: Hypotension with signs of shock
Acute change in mental status
Ischemic chest discomfort

items.q: A 60-year-old has ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which findings suggest the right ventricle is also involved? Select all that apply.
items.x: An RV infarct produces the triad of hypotension, distended neck veins and clear lungs, along with ST elevation in V4R. Crackles point to left ventricular failure.
opts: Hypotension with clear lung sounds
Jugular venous distention
Bilateral crackles in the lower lobes
ST elevation in lead V4R
ST depression in lead V4R
ok: Hypotension with clear lung sounds
Jugular venous distention
ST elevation in lead V4R

items.q: A 74-year-old has an acute stroke. Which findings suggest a large vessel occlusion? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cortical signs such as gaze deviation, aphasia and neglect suggest a large vessel occlusion that may need thrombectomy. Isolated dizziness or minor sensory changes do not.
opts: Gaze deviation toward one side
Aphasia
Isolated dizziness with a normal exam
Neglect of one side of the body
Tingling in one cheek only
ok: Gaze deviation toward one side
Aphasia
Neglect of one side of the body

items.q: You are about to defibrillate an adult in VF. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Patches can block current or cause burns, pads should not sit right on an implanted device, and pauses around the shock should be minimal. VF has no R wave to sync with, and compressions resume right after the shock.
opts: Remove a medication patch from the pad site
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Keep the pause in compressions under 10 seconds
Check for a pulse right after each shock
Synchronize the shock to the R wave
ok: Remove a medication patch from the pad site
Avoid placing a pad directly over an implanted pacemaker
Keep the pause in compressions under 10 seconds

items.q: You are about to perform needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax. Where should the needle enter in relation to the rib?
items.x: The intercostal artery, vein and nerve run along the inferior border of each rib, so the needle goes over the superior border of the rib below.
items.a: Just over the superior border of the rib
w: Just under the inferior border of the rib
Straight through the middle of the rib
Next to the sternum, medial to the nipple line

items.q: An intubated motorcycle crash victim is getting harder to bag. Breath sounds are absent on the right, the neck veins are distended and BP is 70/40. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Positive pressure can quickly turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax. One-sided absent breath sounds, rising airway resistance, JVD and hypotension call for immediate decompression.
items.a: Tension pneumothorax
w: Pericardial tamponade
Simple pneumothorax
Massive hemothorax

items.q: A 25-year-old has a stab wound to the left chest. He is hypotensive and has distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, with equal breath sounds on both sides. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart tones (Beck's triad) with equal breath sounds point to tamponade rather than tension pneumothorax.
items.a: Pericardial tamponade
w: Tension pneumothorax
Massive left hemothorax
Flail chest

items.q: A 34-year-old with a thigh laceration has bright red blood spurting from the wound. He is talking, with RR 24. What is the first intervention?
items.x: Severe external hemorrhage is controlled first (the X in XABCDE), because it can kill within minutes. The patient is talking, so his airway is open for now.
items.a: Control the bleeding with a tourniquet
w: Apply a cervical collar
Start two large-bore IVs
Apply high-flow oxygen

items.q: You applied a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above a forearm amputation, but bright red bleeding continues. What should you do?
items.x: A tourniquet is tightened until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. If one is not enough, a second is applied just above the first.
items.a: Tighten it more or add a second one above it
w: Loosen it to let some blood return
Remove it and use direct pressure instead
Elevate the arm and wait for a clot

items.q: A 22-year-old has a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He is alert with a radial pulse, BP 86/50 and HR 118. Your transport time is 12 minutes. What is the best fluid approach?
items.x: In penetrating torso trauma without a head injury, permissive hypotension (a palpable radial pulse, SBP around 80 to 90) limits clot disruption and dilution while you transport rapidly for surgery.
items.a: Limit fluids and transport rapidly
w: Infuse 3 liters of crystalloid to normalize BP
Withhold transport until BP reaches 120
Elevate the legs and start no IV

items.q: A 40-year-old has an isolated severe head injury after a fall, GCS 8, BP 84/50. What is the blood pressure goal?
items.x: Even one episode of hypotension doubles mortality in TBI. Keep systolic BP at 90 or higher (higher in some age groups) and avoid hypoxia, so permissive hypotension does not apply.
items.a: Systolic BP of at least 90 mmHg
w: Permissive hypotension near 70 systolic
No fluids, to avoid cerebral edema
Mean arterial pressure near 50 mmHg

items.q: A patient with a head injury now has BP 210/110, HR 48 and irregular respirations. What do these findings indicate?
items.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations (Cushing's triad) are late signs of rising ICP and possible herniation.
items.a: Rising intracranial pressure
w: Neurogenic shock
Compensated hypovolemic shock
Hypertensive emergency unrelated to the injury

items.q: An adult has partial-thickness burns covering the entire front of the torso and the whole right arm. Using the rule of nines, what is the burned body surface area?
items.x: For adults, the front of the torso is 18 percent and each whole arm is 9 percent, which totals 27 percent.
items.a: 27 percent
w: 18 percent, torso only
36 percent
45 percent

items.q: After a diving injury, a 30-year-old has BP 78/44, HR 52 and warm, dry skin below the nipple line. What type of shock is most likely?
items.x: Losing sympathetic tone after a cervical or high thoracic cord injury causes hypotension without the expected tachycardia, along with warm, dry skin, which is neurogenic shock. Hidden bleeding must still be ruled out.
items.a: Neurogenic shock
w: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock

items.q: Under the national field triage guidelines, which patient meets a high-risk injury criterion for transport to the highest-level trauma center?
items.x: Penetrating injuries to the head, neck, torso or extremities proximal to the elbow or knee are high-risk criteria. The other injuries do not meet triage criteria by themselves.
items.a: Penetrating wound to the upper thigh
w: Closed wrist fracture
Abrasions after a fall from standing
Neck soreness after a slow rear-end crash

items.q: You suspect an unstable pelvic fracture in a hypotensive patient. Where should the pelvic binder be centered?
items.x: Centering the binder over the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring most effectively. Placing it too high over the iliac crests can widen the fracture.
items.a: Over the greater trochanters
w: Over the iliac crests
At the level of the umbilicus
Over the middle of the thighs

items.q: An 82-year-old on an anticoagulant tripped and hit her head. She is alert with GCS 15 and a small forehead bruise. Why does her anticoagulant change the risk?
items.x: Anticoagulants do not cause the bleed, but they stop it from sealing. A patient can look well at first and worsen hours later, so she needs evaluation.
items.a: It lets a small bleed in the skull keep growing
w: It raises the pressure inside the skull directly
It masks pain so she cannot report a headache
It lowers her GCS even without any bleeding

items.q: A 4-year-old struck by a car has HR 160, cap refill of 4 seconds, cool hands and BP 98/60. How should you classify this?
items.x: Children keep a normal blood pressure until very late in shock. Tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion with a normal BP mean compensated shock that needs urgent care.
items.a: Compensated shock
w: Decompensated shock
Normal findings for age
Neurogenic shock

items.q: A firefighter was trapped in a burning room. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury? Select all that apply.
items.x: Singed hairs, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness or stridor, and facial burns suggest airway injury that can swell quickly and may need early advanced airway management.
opts: Singed nasal hairs
Soot in the sputum
Partial-thickness burns to both lower legs
A hoarse voice
Pain at the burn sites
ok: Singed nasal hairs
Soot in the sputum
A hoarse voice

items.q: After a fall, which findings indicate the need for spinal motion restriction? Select all that apply.
items.x: Midline tenderness, an unreliable exam from intoxication or altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits all call for spinal motion restriction. A reliable patient with a normal exam does not need it.
opts: Midline cervical spine tenderness
Intoxication with altered mental status
New numbness in both hands
Alert and sober with a normal exam and no neck pain
An isolated forearm laceration
ok: Midline cervical spine tenderness
Intoxication with altered mental status
New numbness in both hands

items.q: Under the national field triage guidelines, which findings meet high-risk criteria for the highest-level trauma center? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypotension, chest wall instability and an inability to follow commands are red criteria that call for transport to the highest-level trauma center. Isolated minor injuries do not.
opts: Systolic BP under 90 in an adult
Chest wall instability or deformity
Unable to follow commands after a head injury
An isolated ankle fracture
A scalp laceration with GCS 15
ok: Systolic BP under 90 in an adult
Chest wall instability or deformity
Unable to follow commands after a head injury

items.q: A patient with a severe head injury is deteriorating. Which findings suggest herniation? Select all that apply.
items.x: A blown pupil, posturing and Cushing's response are signs of herniation. Tachycardia with hypotension suggests blood loss, not raised ICP.
opts: One dilated, nonreactive pupil
Extensor posturing
Tachycardia with hypotension
Hypertension with bradycardia
Equal, briskly reactive pupils
ok: One dilated, nonreactive pupil
Extensor posturing
Hypertension with bradycardia

items.q: A term newborn is limp and apneic after you warm, dry, stimulate and position the airway. The heart rate is 80. What should you do next?
items.x: An apneic newborn or one with a heart rate under 100 after the initial steps needs PPV within the first minute. Ventilation is the most important part of neonatal resuscitation.
items.a: Begin positive pressure ventilation
w: Start chest compressions
Continue stimulation for another minute
Give blow-by oxygen only

items.q: After 30 seconds of effective PPV with corrective steps, a newborn's heart rate is 50. Chest compressions are started. What ratio should you use?
items.x: Neonatal compressions are coordinated with ventilation at 3 to 1, giving 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute, and oxygen is increased to 100 percent.
items.a: 3 compressions to 1 breath
w: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath

items.q: A term newborn is breathing and crying at 3 minutes of age with a heart rate of 150. A pulse oximeter on the right hand reads 72 percent. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Preductal saturation rises slowly after birth, with a target of about 70 to 75 percent at 3 minutes and 85 to 95 percent by 10 minutes. Giving oxygen to reach adult levels risks hyperoxia.
items.a: Normal for age, so oxygen need not be increased
w: Hypoxia requiring 100 percent oxygen
Hypoxia requiring intubation
A probe error because it should read 98 percent

items.q: During a delivery, the baby's head delivers but then retracts against the perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. What should you do first?
items.x: Shoulder dystocia is managed first with the McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure, which widen the pelvic outlet. Fundal pressure and strong traction on the head can cause injury.
items.a: Hyperflex the mother's thighs and apply suprapubic pressure
w: Pull firmly downward on the baby's head
Push on the top of the uterus
Have the mother stand and push

items.q: During active labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina before the baby. What should you do?
items.x: With a prolapsed cord, lifting the presenting part off the cord and placing the mother in knee-chest or Trendelenburg position keeps blood flowing to the baby during rapid transport.
items.a: Lift the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers
w: Push the cord back into the vagina
Have the mother bear down to speed delivery
Clamp and cut the exposed cord

items.q: A 26-year-old who is 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache and blurred vision. BP 168/112 and she has new swelling in her hands and face. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: New hypertension after 20 weeks with headache and visual changes is preeclampsia with severe features, which puts her at high risk of seizures (eclampsia).
items.a: Preeclampsia with severe features
w: Gestational diabetes
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Placenta previa

items.q: A 31-year-old at 36 weeks fell and now has constant abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. HR 118, BP 92/60. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Painful bleeding with a firm, tender uterus after trauma suggests abruption. Bleeding can be concealed, so shock may be worse than the visible blood suggests.
items.a: Placental abruption
w: Placenta previa
Braxton Hicks contractions
Ectopic pregnancy

items.q: A woman 35 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back. BP falls from 118/72 to 88/50. What should you do first?
items.x: The uterus can compress the inferior vena cava in the supine position. Left lateral positioning, or manually displacing the uterus to the left, restores venous return.
items.a: Turn her onto her left side
w: Elevate her legs while she stays supine
Have her sit upright and bear down
Begin fast fluid boluses while she stays supine

items.q: Ten minutes after a field delivery, the placenta has delivered but heavy vaginal bleeding continues and the uterus feels soft. What is the first intervention?
items.x: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Fundal massage, and breastfeeding if possible, helps the uterus contract.
items.a: Firm fundal massage
w: Pack the vagina with gauze
Pull on the remaining cord
Have the mother walk to the stretcher

items.q: A 24-year-old with a missed period seven weeks ago has sudden right lower abdominal pain, shoulder pain, HR 124 and BP 84/52. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain and shock should be treated as a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Shoulder pain suggests blood irritating the diaphragm.
items.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
w: Appendicitis
Kidney stone
Ovarian cyst without bleeding

items.q: A 5-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with a high fever, muffled voice and soft stridor. What is the best approach?
items.x: Epiglottitis can progress to complete obstruction if the child is upset or the throat is examined. Keep her calm and upright with the parent and be ready to manage the airway.
items.a: Leave her in a position of comfort and keep her calm
w: Look at the throat with a tongue blade
Lay her flat to examine the airway
Separate her from the parent to start an IV

items.q: What are the three components of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
items.x: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a quick visual check of appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin that identifies a sick child before any hands-on assessment.
items.a: Appearance, work of breathing, skin circulation
w: Pulse, blood pressure, temperature
Airway, breathing, blood glucose
Mental status, pupils, motor function

items.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 5-year-old?
items.x: For children aged 1 to 10, the lower limit of systolic BP is about 70 plus twice the age in years, so a 5-year-old's limit is 80 mmHg.
items.a: 80 mmHg
w: 70 mmHg
60 mmHg
90 mmHg, as for adults

items.q: An 84-year-old with type 2 diabetes has been confused for several days. Glucose is 1,100 mg/dL. She is profoundly dehydrated, breathing normally, and has no fruity odor. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: HHS develops over days in older type 2 diabetics, with extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration but little ketosis. That is why Kussmaul respirations and a fruity odor are absent.
items.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoglycemia
Adrenal crisis

items.q: A 78-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), HR 118, RR 26, BP 82/48 and new confusion. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: A likely source of infection plus hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea and altered mentation is septic shock, which needs early fluids and notification of the receiving hospital.
items.a: Septic shock
w: Hypovolemic shock from a GI bleed
Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylaxis

items.q: A farm worker has pinpoint pupils, drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing with heavy secretions and HR 44. Which exposure is most likely?
items.x: SLUDGE signs with bronchorrhea, bradycardia and miosis make up the cholinergic toxidrome typical of organophosphate poisoning.
items.a: Organophosphate pesticide
w: Anticholinergic plant
Opioid
Stimulant

items.q: A 17-year-old is agitated and picking at the air. He is hot, dry and flushed, with dilated pupils, HR 132 and a full bladder. Which toxidrome fits best?
items.x: Hot, dry, red skin, dilated pupils, delirium, tachycardia and urinary retention are the classic anticholinergic toxidrome, as seen with diphenhydramine overdose.
items.a: Anticholinergic
w: Cholinergic
Opioid
Sedative-hypnotic

items.q: A 45-year-old with a suspected overdose has a seizure. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS of 140 ms and BP 80/50. Which overdose is most likely?
items.x: Tricyclics block sodium channels, which widens the QRS and causes seizures, hypotension and dysrhythmias.
