items.a: Tricyclic antidepressant
w: Extended-release acetaminophen
Benzodiazepine
Opioid

items.q: Everyone in a family has had headaches and nausea since the furnace was turned on. The mother is confused with SpO2 99 percent on a standard pulse oximeter. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Several people with symptoms from an indoor heat source suggest CO poisoning. Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so the SpO2 is falsely reassuring.
items.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning
w: Viral gastroenteritis
Hypoglycemia
Migraine

items.q: You find a 30-year-old unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, RR 6, SpO2 84 percent and a pulse. What is the first action?
items.x: Ventilate and oxygenate first. Naloxone can follow, but supporting breathing is the immediate priority in opioid-induced respiratory depression.
items.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
w: Give naloxone before any other care
Place in recovery position and observe
Perform immediate intubation

items.q: A 40-year-old with epilepsy has been having continuous generalized seizure activity for 7 minutes on your arrival. What is this called?
items.x: A seizure lasting more than about 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between, is status epilepticus and needs prompt treatment.
items.a: Status epilepticus
w: Simple partial seizure
Postictal state
Psychogenic nonepileptic event

items.q: A 48-year-old had a sudden severe headache she calls the worst of her life while lifting weights. She is vomiting and has a stiff neck. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A sudden thunderclap headache that peaks within seconds, with vomiting and a stiff neck, is a classic sign of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
items.a: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
w: Tension headache
Migraine
Sinusitis

items.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions is weak, with HR 48. The ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Missed dialysis lets potassium build up. Peaked T waves, a widening QRS and bradycardia warn that hyperkalemia may lead to arrest.
items.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Hypokalemia
Hypomagnesemia
Hypoglycemia

items.q: Police have restrained a man with severe agitation, hyperthermia and extreme strength. How should he be positioned for transport?
items.x: Prone and hog-tie positions with weight on the back restrict breathing and are linked to sudden death. Keep restrained patients supine or on their side with continuous monitoring, including ETCO2.
items.a: On his side or back with continuous monitoring
w: Face down with his hands behind his back
Hobbled in a hog-tie position
Face down with an officer kneeling on his back

items.q: A 35-year-old tells you he plans to kill himself with a gun he keeps at home. He is calm and cooperative. What is the most important action?
items.x: A patient with a suicidal plan is at high risk. Scene safety and constant supervision come first, and he does not have capacity to refuse care.
items.a: Make sure the scene is safe and never leave him alone
w: Accept his refusal if he declines transport
Let him get his gun so police can secure it
Leave the room so he feels less pressured

items.q: A 19-year-old collapsed while running a race in hot, humid weather. He is confused with a core temperature of 41.4 C (106.5 F). What is the priority?
items.x: Exertional heat stroke is time-dependent. Rapid cooling, ideally by cold-water immersion, should start before or during transport.
items.a: Rapid whole-body cooling
w: Immediate transport with no cooling
Oral fluids and rest in the shade
Warm blankets to prevent shivering

items.q: A homeless man found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 30 C (86 F), HR 42 and BP 90/60, and he responds to pain. What is especially important in his care?
items.x: A cold myocardium is very irritable, and rough handling can trigger VF. Move him gently and horizontally, and use passive and active external rewarming.
items.a: Handle him gently and keep him horizontal
w: Rub his arms and legs to warm them
Have him walk to the ambulance
Give him hot drinks by mouth

items.q: An 80-year-old has become confused over the past day, with attention that comes and goes. Her family says she was sharp last week. How is this best described?
items.x: An abrupt, fluctuating change in attention and awareness is delirium. It usually has a treatable cause such as infection, medications or hypoxia, so it must be investigated.
items.a: Delirium
w: Dementia
Normal aging
Schizophrenia

items.q: A 72-year-old smoker has sudden severe back pain, a pulsating abdominal mass, HR 122 and BP 78/46. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Sudden back or abdominal pain with a pulsating mass and shock in an older smoker suggests a ruptured AAA, which needs rapid transport to a surgical center.
items.a: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
w: Kidney stone
Lumbar strain
Pancreatitis

items.q: Five days after knee surgery, a 52-year-old has sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing, HR 124 and SpO2 89 percent. Her lungs are clear. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Recent surgery and immobility raise the risk of clots. Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia with clear lungs suggest PE.
items.a: Pulmonary embolism
w: Pneumonia
Congestive heart failure
Asthma exacerbation

items.q: A term newborn is not crying. Which are part of the initial steps of newborn care? Select all that apply.
items.x: Warming, drying, positioning, clearing secretions only when needed, and stimulation are the first steps. Routine deep suctioning and routine tracheal suctioning for meconium are no longer recommended.
opts: Warm and dry the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Stimulate the baby
Deep suction every newborn
Routine tracheal suction for meconium-stained fluid
ok: Warm and dry the baby
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Stimulate the baby

items.q: You suspect sepsis in an adult. Which findings are qSOFA criteria? Select all that apply.
items.x: The qSOFA screen uses RR of 22 or more, altered mental status and SBP of 100 or less. Two or more positive criteria with suspected infection mean a higher risk of a poor outcome.
opts: Respiratory rate of 22 or more
Altered mentation
Systolic BP of 100 or less
Heart rate of 88
Temperature of 37.0 C (98.6 F)
ok: Respiratory rate of 22 or more
Altered mentation
Systolic BP of 100 or less

items.q: Which findings are part of the cholinergic toxidrome? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cholinergic excess causes secretions (SLUDGE), bronchorrhea and miosis. Dry, flushed skin and dilated pupils are anticholinergic signs.
opts: Heavy bronchial secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Excessive salivation
Hot, dry, flushed skin
Dilated pupils
ok: Heavy bronchial secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Excessive salivation

items.q: A 32-week pregnant patient is being assessed. Which findings suggest preeclampsia with severe features? Select all that apply.
items.x: Severe-range BP, neurologic symptoms and RUQ or epigastric pain are severe features of preeclampsia. Painless bright red bleeding points to placenta previa.
opts: Headache with visual changes
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Painless bright red vaginal bleeding
BP of 118/76
ok: Headache with visual changes
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain

items.q: A worker became ill in the heat. Which findings point to heat stroke rather than heat exhaustion? Select all that apply.
items.x: Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction with a core temperature usually above 40 C (104 F). A normal mental status with mild temperature elevation fits heat exhaustion or heat cramps.
opts: Altered mental status
Core temperature of 41 C (105.8 F)
Normal mentation with heavy sweating
Core temperature of 38 C (100.4 F)
Muscle cramps only
ok: Altered mental status
Core temperature of 41 C (105.8 F)

items.q: A 6-year-old is having an asthma attack. Which findings indicate impending respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Falling mental status, bradycardia and a quiet chest are ominous late signs that call for assisted ventilation. An alert, wheezing child who can talk is in distress but not yet in failure.
opts: Decreasing level of consciousness
Bradycardia
Diminished breath sounds with little air movement
Loud expiratory wheezing while alert
RR of 30 while talking in sentences
ok: Decreasing level of consciousness
Bradycardia
Diminished breath sounds with little air movement

items.q: During START triage at a bus crash, an adult who cannot walk is breathing at 34 per minute. What category is assigned?
items.x: In START, an adult with a respiratory rate above 30 is tagged immediate without further assessment.
items.a: Immediate (red)
w: Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

items.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 4-year-old is not breathing after you open the airway but has a palpable pulse. What should you do?
items.x: Children often stop breathing from respiratory causes, so JumpSTART calls for five rescue breaths when a pulse is present. If breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate.
items.a: Give five rescue breaths
w: Tag expectant and move on
Tag immediate without other action
Begin full CPR

items.q: An adult with decision-making capacity wants to refuse transport. Which is required for a valid informed refusal?
items.x: A valid refusal requires capacity and understanding of the risks, benefits and alternatives, including the possibility of death, and it should be documented.
items.a: He understands the risks, including possible death
w: A family member agrees with the decision
Medical direction signs the form at the scene
He has normal vital signs

items.q: Under HIPAA, which disclosure of patient information is permitted without the patient's written authorization?
items.x: Sharing protected health information with other providers for treatment is allowed. Disclosure to the public or the media is not.
items.a: Report to the receiving hospital staff
w: Description of the call on social media
Details to a curious neighbor
Account of the call to a news reporter

items.q: At a hazardous materials incident, in which zone should decontaminated patients receive full treatment?
items.x: The hot zone is for rescue only, decontamination happens in the warm zone, and full assessment and treatment take place in the cold zone.
items.a: Cold zone
w: Hot zone
Warm zone
Exclusion zone

items.q: You find an error in a paper patient care report you just completed. How should you correct it?
items.x: A single line keeps the original entry readable, and initialing and dating it show who changed it and when, which protects the record's integrity.
items.a: Draw one line through it, then initial and date it
w: Erase it and write over it
Black out the error completely
Rewrite the whole report and discard the original

items.q: While treating a 3-year-old, you notice burns in a stocking pattern on both feet and an explanation that does not fit the injury. What must you do?
items.x: Paramedics are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse in every state. You report suspicion, and proof is not required.
items.a: Report to the proper authority as required by law
w: Confront the caregivers about abuse
Do nothing unless the child confirms it
Report only if the hospital agrees

items.q: You are treating a gunshot victim at a crime scene. How should you remove his clothing?
items.x: Patient care comes first, but cutting around holes and limiting disturbance of the scene preserves evidence for law enforcement.
items.a: Cut around the bullet holes
w: Cut straight through the bullet holes
Pull it off and leave it at the scene
Shake it out and fold it for police

items.q: A hospice patient is found pulseless and apneic. The family shows you a valid DNR order that applies in your state. What should you do?
items.x: A valid out-of-hospital DNR order should be honored. Your role becomes confirming death per protocol and supporting the family.
items.a: Withhold resuscitation and support the family
w: Start CPR until medical direction is contacted
Do CPR but skip the advanced airway
Transport with lights and siren

items.q: While running lights and siren, you come to a red light at an intersection. What is the safest practice?
items.x: Intersections are where most ambulance crashes happen. Stop fully and check that each lane has yielded before crossing.
items.a: Stop and confirm every lane has yielded
w: Slow slightly and proceed through
Rely on the siren to clear traffic
Pass on the right of stopped cars

items.q: You leave a patient at the hospital entrance without handing off care to qualified staff. What legal problem have you created?
items.x: Ending care without transferring it to someone with equal or higher training is abandonment.
items.a: Abandonment
w: Assault
Libel
False imprisonment

items.q: A patient is suing a paramedic for negligence. Which elements must the patient prove? Select all that apply.
items.x: Negligence requires duty, breach of duty, damages and proximate cause. Intent to harm is not required, and a signed refusal does not prove negligence.
opts: The paramedic had a duty to act
The paramedic breached the standard of care
The patient signed a refusal form
The breach caused the injury
The paramedic intended to cause harm
ok: The paramedic had a duty to act
The paramedic breached the standard of care
The breach caused the injury

items.q: You are transporting a patient with suspected active tuberculosis. Which precautions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: TB spreads by the airborne route, so the crew needs N95 or higher respirators, source control on the patient and good ventilation. Surgical masks do not protect the wearer against airborne particles.
opts: A fit-tested N95 respirator for the crew
A surgical mask on the patient if tolerated
The patient compartment exhaust fan on
A surgical mask on the crew alone is enough
No precautions if the patient is not coughing
ok: A fit-tested N95 respirator for the crew
A surgical mask on the patient if tolerated
The patient compartment exhaust fan on

items.q: Under the Incident Command System, which positions belong to the command staff? Select all that apply.
items.x: The command staff are the safety, public information and liaison officers. Triage and treatment unit leaders sit under the operations section in the general staff.
opts: Safety officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer
Triage unit leader
Treatment unit leader
ok: Safety officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer

items.q: You are preparing to ventilate an unresponsive 8-month-old lying flat on a firm surface. His head is bent forward, chin toward the chest. What simple step will best help open his airway?
items.x: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine; padding under the shoulders brings the head to a neutral position, while hyperextension can kink the soft trachea.
items.a: Place a thin folded towel under his shoulders
w: Place a thick pillow under the back of his head
Hyperextend his neck as far as it will go
Turn his head fully to one side

items.q: Which structure closes over the glottic opening during swallowing to keep food out of the trachea?
items.x: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap that folds over the larynx during swallowing; when it fails or is bypassed, aspiration can occur.
items.a: Epiglottis
w: Uvula
Cricoid cartilage
Vallecula

items.q: A 2-month-old with a runny nose and low-grade fever is breathing 64 times per minute with nasal flaring and audible nasal congestion. SpO2 is 92%. What should you do first?
items.x: Young infants breathe mainly through the nose, so clearing nasal secretions can significantly improve their breathing; this child is still breathing on his own and does not yet need ventilation.
items.a: Gently suction the nose with a bulb syringe
w: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway
Begin BVM ventilation at 40 breaths per minute
Have the parent feed the infant a bottle

items.q: How is a nasopharyngeal airway measured for an adult patient?
items.x: An NPA is sized from the tip of the nose to the earlobe, and its diameter should fit comfortably in the nostril without blanching.
items.a: From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
w: From the corner of the mouth to the chin
From the earlobe to the sternal notch
From the nostril to the corner of the eye

items.q: You are inserting a nasopharyngeal airway into the right nostril. How should the bevel be oriented?
items.x: The bevel should face the septum (the midline) so the tip slides along it rather than catching on the turbinates; lubricate with a water-soluble gel first.
items.a: Toward the nasal septum
w: Toward the outside of the nose
Pointing up toward the eye
It does not matter in the right nostril

items.q: You are placing an oropharyngeal airway in an unresponsive 4-year-old. Which insertion method is recommended?
items.x: In children, use a tongue depressor and insert the OPA in its anatomic position; rotating it can injure the soft palate.
items.a: Depress the tongue and insert it right side up
w: Insert it upside down and rotate it 180 degrees
Insert it sideways and turn it 90 degrees
Push it straight in without moving the tongue

items.q: Shortly after you insert an OPA, a 40-year-old seizure patient begins gagging and coughing. What should you do?
items.x: A gag reflex means the patient cannot tolerate an OPA and may vomit; remove it and use an NPA if an adjunct is still needed.
items.a: Remove the OPA and consider an NPA
w: Push the OPA in farther to stop the gag
Tape the OPA in place and continue
Suction around the OPA and leave it in

items.q: While you suction the mouth of a 6-week-old infant, her heart rate drops from 150 to 84/min. What should you do?
items.x: Stimulating the back of the throat can trigger a vagal response and bradycardia in infants; stop, oxygenate or ventilate, and limit suction time.
items.a: Stop suctioning and oxygenate her
w: Insert the catheter deeper to finish
Switch to a larger rigid catheter
Continue suctioning but at lower pressure

items.q: You hear gurgling while ventilating an unresponsive 50-year-old woman with a BVM. What should you do?
items.x: Gurgling means fluid is in the upper airway; ventilating through it pushes fluid into the lungs, so suction first.
items.a: Suction the airway, then resume ventilating
w: Increase the force of each ventilation to push past it
Increase the oxygen flow rate
Switch to a nonrebreather mask

items.q: An unresponsive man with no suspected spinal injury vomits a large volume, more than your suction unit can keep up with. What should you do?
items.x: Turning the patient lets gravity clear large amounts of vomit quickly; then finish clearing with suction and resume ventilation.
items.a: Roll him onto his side to drain the airway
w: Keep suctioning while ventilating over it
Insert an OPA to hold the airway open
Give abdominal thrusts to empty the stomach

items.q: Two EMTs are available to ventilate an apneic adult with a BVM. What is the most effective division of tasks?
items.x: Two-rescuer BVM ventilation gives a much better mask seal, the most common reason single-rescuer BVM fails.
items.a: One seals the mask with both hands while the other squeezes the bag
w: One squeezes the bag while the other does chest compressions
Each EMT alternates mouth-to-mask and BVM every few breaths
One holds the bag and mask while the other only watches

items.q: When a BVM with a reservoir is attached to oxygen for ventilating an adult, what flow rate should be used?
items.x: A flow of 15 L/min keeps the reservoir full so each ventilation delivers oxygen concentrations near 100 percent.
items.a: 15 L/min
w: 4 L/min
6 L/min to conserve the cylinder
8 L/min

items.q: An apneic 62-year-old man with a pulse has a laryngectomy stoma in his neck. How should you ventilate him?
items.x: A patient with a total laryngectomy breathes only through the stoma, so seal a small round mask over it and ventilate there.
items.a: Through the stoma using an infant or child mask
w: Through the mouth with the stoma left uncovered
With a nonrebreather placed over his face
By mouth only after closing the stoma with gauze

items.q: A 55-year-old woman with mild dyspnea and an SpO2 of 92% says she feels smothered by a face mask. What is an appropriate alternative?
items.x: A nasal cannula is well tolerated and suits mild hypoxia; a nonrebreather needs 10-15 L/min or the patient will rebreathe exhaled air.
items.a: A nasal cannula at 1 to 6 L/min
w: A nonrebreather at 4 L/min
A BVM held over her face
No oxygen at all

items.q: Which device delivers the highest oxygen concentration to a patient who is breathing adequately on his own?
items.x: A nonrebreather at 10-15 L/min with a full reservoir delivers the highest concentration available to a spontaneously breathing patient.
items.a: Nonrebreather mask
w: Nasal cannula
Simple face mask
Venturi mask set at 28 percent

items.q: You arrive at a home where a 78-year-old man on home oxygen is lighting a cigarette. What should you do first?
items.x: Oxygen strongly supports combustion, so an open flame near a flowing oxygen source is a fire and burn hazard; stop the hazard before patient care.
items.a: Have him put out the cigarette and turn off the oxygen
w: Increase his oxygen flow so he stays oxygenated
Move the oxygen tank to the next room and continue your exam
Ask him to finish quickly before you begin

items.q: An unresponsive 30-year-old man who took an unknown amount of heroin has an SpO2 of 97% on a nonrebreather. His respirations are 6 per minute and shallow. What does this reading tell you?
items.x: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not ventilation; high-flow oxygen can keep saturation up while carbon dioxide builds, so a rate of 6 still needs BVM ventilation.
items.a: It does not show that he is ventilating adequately
w: His breathing is adequate and needs no help
He has carbon monoxide poisoning
The probe is faulty and should be ignored

items.q: Your paramedic partner points to the capnography display on a breathing adult. In a healthy person, what range of end-tidal CO2 is considered normal?
items.x: Normal ETCO2 is about 35-45 mmHg; a low value can mean hyperventilation or poor perfusion and a high value can mean hypoventilation.
items.a: 35 to 45 mmHg
w: 10 to 20 mmHg
60 to 80 mmHg
94 to 99 mmHg, matching the SpO2 target

items.q: You are helping a 19-year-old with mild wheezing use her own metered-dose inhaler, which has no spacer. What should you coach her to do?
items.x: Exhaling first and then inhaling deeply as the canister is pressed, followed by a breath hold, carries the medication deep into the lungs.
items.a: Exhale fully, then breathe in deeply while pressing the inhaler
w: Breathe in and out rapidly while spraying several puffs
Hold the inhaler at arm's length and inhale slowly
Inhale through the nose while spraying into the mouth

items.q: A thin 71-year-old man with a 50-year smoking history has a barrel-shaped chest and breathes out through pursed lips. Which chronic condition do these findings most suggest?
items.x: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and traps air, causing a barrel chest; pursed-lip breathing helps keep the small airways open during exhalation.
items.a: Emphysema
w: Asthma
Pneumonia
Pulmonary edema

items.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has had a fever and cough with yellow sputum for 2 days. You hear crackles over the right lower lung only. Which condition is most likely?
items.x: Fever, productive cough, and crackles localized to one area point to pneumonia; CHF usually causes crackles in both bases without fever.
items.a: Pneumonia
w: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Asthma attack
Congestive heart failure

items.q: A 31-year-old woman who gave birth 2 weeks ago has sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing. HR is 124, lungs are clear, SpO2 is 89%. Which condition should you suspect?
items.x: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and hypoxia with clear lungs in a postpartum patient strongly suggest PE; give oxygen and transport promptly.
items.a: Pulmonary embolism
w: Asthma attack
Pneumonia
Anxiety attack

items.q: A tall, thin 20-year-old man felt sudden sharp left chest pain and shortness of breath while sitting in class. Breath sounds are diminished on the left. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall, thin young men when a small weak area of lung ruptures, causing sudden pain and unilateral decreased breath sounds.
items.a: Spontaneous pneumothorax
w: Acute myocardial infarction
Pulmonary edema
Croup

items.q: A 24-year-old with a known spontaneous pneumothorax becomes more short of breath during transport. His neck veins are now distended, BP has fallen to 82/50, and breath sounds are absent on the right. What should you do?
items.x: These are signs of a developing tension pneumothorax, which needs needle decompression beyond EMT scope; CPAP can make it worse.
items.a: Request ALS for decompression and expedite transport
w: Begin CPAP to re-expand the lung
Have him lie flat on his right side
Slow down so the ride is smoother

items.q: A 2-year-old has had a cold for 2 days and tonight developed a seal-like barking cough and noisy breathing on inspiration. She has a low-grade fever and is not drooling. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: A barking cough and inspiratory stridor after a viral illness, typically worse at night, is classic croup, a swelling of the larynx and trachea.
items.a: Croup
w: Epiglottitis
Asthma
Bronchiolitis

items.q: A 3-year-old was eating peanuts when he suddenly began coughing. He is now coughing forcefully, crying, and has pink skin. What should you do?
items.x: A child who can cough forcefully and cry has a mild obstruction; do not interfere with an effective cough, but be ready to act if it becomes ineffective.
items.a: Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
w: Give 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts
Perform abdominal thrusts until the coughing stops
Sweep his mouth with your finger to find the nut

items.q: A 45-year-old woman clutches her throat at a restaurant. She has a weak, ineffective cough, a high-pitched noise when inhaling, and is becoming dusky. What should you do?
items.x: A weak cough with high-pitched sounds and cyanosis means poor air exchange and should be treated as a severe obstruction with abdominal thrusts.
items.a: Perform abdominal thrusts
w: Encourage her to keep coughing
Give her water to wash it down
Have her lie down and wait for ALS

items.q: A 6-year-old is sitting calmly watching television and breathing 40 times per minute. How should you interpret this rate?
items.x: A resting rate of about 18-30 is typical for a school-age child, so 40 at rest is tachypnea and warrants a search for a cause.
items.a: It is faster than normal for her age
w: It is normal for a school-age child
It is slower than normal for her age
Rate alone cannot be interpreted in children

items.q: You hear a high-pitched sound mainly on inspiration from a patient's neck. What does this most likely indicate?
items.x: Inspiratory stridor comes from narrowing of the upper airway, such as from swelling or a foreign body, and is a warning sign of possible complete obstruction.
items.a: Partial upper airway obstruction
w: Fluid in the alveoli
Narrowing of the small lower airways
Normal breath sounds

items.q: You hear fine crackles at the bases of both lungs in a 76-year-old woman. What do crackles generally indicate?
items.x: Crackles (rales) are popping sounds made as fluid-filled alveoli and small airways open, as in pulmonary edema or pneumonia.
items.a: Fluid in the small airways and alveoli
w: Narrowing of the bronchioles from spasm
An object lodged in the upper airway
A collapsed lung

items.q: A 23-year-old with type 1 diabetes is breathing very deeply and rapidly, and her breath has a fruity odor. What breathing pattern is this?
items.x: Deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing is the body's attempt to blow off acid in diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.a: Kussmaul respirations
w: Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Agonal respirations
Biot respirations

items.q: A 7-year-old with a tracheostomy tube is in respiratory distress, and you hear gurgling from the tube. What should you do first?
items.x: Secretions commonly obstruct tracheostomy tubes, so suctioning the tube is the first step; prepare to ventilate through it with a BVM.
items.a: Suction the tracheostomy tube
w: Cover the tube and ventilate by mouth
Place a nonrebreather over the face
Remove the tube and wait for ALS

items.q: A ventilator-dependent 9-year-old's home ventilator is alarming, and the child is pale and struggling to breathe. What should you do first?
items.x: When a ventilated patient is in distress, take the machine out of the equation and ventilate manually with a BVM while looking for the cause.
items.a: Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate through the tube with a BVM
w: Increase the ventilator settings
Wait for the parents to reset the machine
Place a nasal cannula under the ventilator tubing

items.q: Your partner wants to press on the cricoid cartilage throughout BVM ventilation of every unresponsive patient to prevent vomiting. What is the current recommendation?
items.x: Routine cricoid pressure can impede ventilation and does not reliably prevent aspiration, so it is no longer routinely recommended.
items.a: Routine cricoid pressure is not recommended
w: It should be used on every patient during BVM ventilation
It should only be used in infants
It is required before suctioning

items.q: A 35-year-old found unresponsive after drinking heavily is breathing 14 times per minute with good chest rise. There is no sign of trauma. How should you position her?
items.x: An unresponsive patient who is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal injury should be placed on the side to keep the airway clear if she vomits.
items.a: Recovery position on her side
w: Supine with her head flat and arms at her sides
Sitting fully upright
Prone with her face down

items.q: An alert 68-year-old man with COPD is leaning forward with his hands on his knees and refuses to lie down. How should he be transported?
items.x: A patient in respiratory distress who can protect his airway should stay upright, which eases the work of the breathing muscles.
items.a: Sitting upright in his position of comfort
w: Supine with his legs raised to improve blood return
Flat on his left side
Supine with his head lowered

items.q: Twenty minutes after a bee sting, a 33-year-old woman's voice has become hoarse and she has a tight feeling in her throat. What do these findings most suggest?
items.x: Hoarseness and throat tightness after an allergen exposure mean the larynx is swelling, a life-threatening sign of anaphylaxis requiring immediate treatment and transport.
items.a: Swelling of the upper airway
w: Normal anxiety after a sting
A lower airway infection
Pulmonary edema from heart failure

items.q: A 52-year-old man was in a house fire. He has soot around his mouth, singed nasal hairs, and a hoarse voice, but no distress yet. What is the main concern?
items.x: Signs of inhalation injury mean the airway may swell rapidly over minutes to hours; give high-flow oxygen and transport promptly, with early ALS.
items.a: Airway swelling that may progress quickly
w: A minor burn that needs no oxygen
Hypoglycemia from the stress of the fire
Dehydration from sweating

items.q: A 14-year-old was pulled from a pool. He has a pulse but is breathing 4 times per minute. What should you do first?
items.x: Drowning causes hypoxia, so ventilation is the priority; abdominal thrusts to remove water delay care and risk vomiting.
items.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
w: Give abdominal thrusts to remove water
Place him on a nonrebreather
Tilt his head down to drain the lungs

items.q: An alert 2-year-old with croup has mild retractions and cries when you bring an oxygen mask near her face. She is in her mother's lap. What is the best approach?
items.x: Upsetting a child with upper airway swelling can worsen the obstruction, so keep her calm with her parent and give oxygen by the least distressing method.
items.a: Have her mother hold blow-by oxygen near her face
w: Restrain her and secure the mask tightly
Lay her flat on the stretcher with a nasal cannula
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway

items.q: An alert 46-year-old man without lung disease has an SpO2 of 88% on room air. How should this be interpreted?
items.x: A healthy adult normally saturates about 95 percent or higher, so 88 percent indicates hypoxia that needs oxygen and a search for the cause.
items.a: He is hypoxic and should receive oxygen
w: This is normal for an adult at rest
The reading is high and oxygen should be avoided
It is only significant if he is cyanotic

items.q: In a healthy person, what is the main stimulus that triggers the urge to breathe?
items.x: Chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond mainly to rising carbon dioxide; low oxygen is a backup drive.
items.a: A rising level of carbon dioxide in the blood
w: A falling level of oxygen in the blood
A falling level of carbon dioxide in the blood
A rising level of glucose in the blood

items.q: You are ventilating a 3-year-old with a BVM. How should you judge how much volume to give with each squeeze?
items.x: Volume is guided by visible chest rise; more than that causes gastric distention and can injure the lungs.
items.a: Squeeze only until you see the chest begin to rise
w: Squeeze the bag fully every time
Give as much volume as you would to an adult
Squeeze about halfway regardless of chest rise

items.q: A term newborn is limp and not breathing after warming, drying, and stimulation. What should you do next?
items.x: Under NRP, a newborn who is apneic or gasping, or has a heart rate under 100, after initial steps needs positive-pressure ventilation at 40-60 breaths per minute.
items.a: Begin positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
w: Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Continue rubbing the back for 2 more minutes
Give blow-by oxygen and observe

items.q: You need to ventilate a severely obese, unresponsive 39-year-old man who is breathing inadequately. How can you position him to make ventilation easier?
items.x: A ramped position, with the ear level with the sternal notch, improves airway alignment and lowers the weight of the chest and abdomen on the lungs.
items.a: Elevate his head and shoulders so his ear lines up with his sternum
w: Lay him completely flat with no padding
Place him in the Trendelenburg position
Roll him onto his stomach

items.q: An unresponsive 80-year-old woman with snug-fitting dentures needs BVM ventilation. What should you do about the dentures?
items.x: Well-fitting dentures help maintain facial shape and mask seal; remove them only if they are loose or obstructing the airway.
items.a: Leave them in to support a better mask seal
w: Always remove them before ventilating
Push them farther back in the mouth
Remove only the lower denture and leave the upper one

items.q: A 47-year-old man with pneumonia is anxious and breathing 34 times per minute with shallow breaths. His SpO2 is 85% on a nonrebreather. You decide to assist his ventilations with a BVM. How should you time the breaths?
items.x: Assisted ventilation should match the patient's own inhalations, then gradually adjust to a more effective rate and depth.
items.a: Squeeze as he begins each inhalation and gradually slow his rate
w: Squeeze as hard as possible when he exhales
Ignore his own breaths and ventilate at 30 per minute
Squeeze only every other time he exhales

items.q: An alert 64-year-old man with CHF has been on CPAP for 5 minutes and is improving, but he suddenly becomes confused and can no longer follow commands. What should you do?
items.x: CPAP requires an alert patient who can protect his airway; declining mental status signals failure, so switch to BVM ventilation.
items.a: Remove the CPAP and assist ventilations with a BVM
w: Increase the oxygen and leave the CPAP on
Tighten the mask straps for a better seal
Sit him up and wait 10 minutes

items.q: A 4-year-old has a sudden high fever and respiratory distress. Which findings suggest epiglottitis rather than croup? Select all that apply.
items.x: Epiglottitis develops rapidly with high fever, drooling, and tripod positioning; a barking cough after a few days of cold symptoms is typical of croup.
opts: Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Rapid onset over a few hours
Sitting forward in a tripod position
A barking, seal-like cough
Several days of runny nose before the noisy breathing
ok: Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Rapid onset over a few hours
Sitting forward in a tripod position

items.q: Which findings are consistent with a spontaneous pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
items.x: Spontaneous pneumothorax causes sudden sharp pain, dyspnea, and diminished breath sounds on the affected side; bilateral crackles and fever suggest other conditions.
opts: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain
Decreased breath sounds on one side
Crackles in both lung bases
Fever and productive cough for 3 days
A barking cough at night
ok: Sudden onset of sharp chest pain
Decreased breath sounds on one side

items.q: Which steps are correct when inserting a nasopharyngeal airway? Select all that apply.
items.x: An NPA is sized from nose tip to earlobe, lubricated with water-soluble gel, and inserted gently; if resistance is met, try the other nostril rather than forcing it.
opts: Lubricate it with a water-soluble gel
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Insert it gently along the floor of the nostril
Lubricate it with petroleum jelly
Insert it upside down and rotate it 180 degrees
Force it past resistance to secure the airway
ok: Lubricate it with a water-soluble gel
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Insert it gently along the floor of the nostril

items.q: A 38-year-old woman has sudden shortness of breath. Which history findings increase your suspicion of a pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
items.x: Recent surgery, prolonged immobility, and estrogen use with smoking all increase clot risk; allergies and regular exercise do not.
opts: Knee surgery 10 days ago
A recent 14-hour flight
Taking oral contraceptives and smoking
A history of seasonal allergies
Running 3 miles a day
ok: Knee surgery 10 days ago
A recent 14-hour flight
Taking oral contraceptives and smoking

items.q: A patient is receiving CPAP for respiratory distress. Which changes mean you should stop CPAP and prepare to ventilate with a BVM? Select all that apply.
items.x: Unresponsiveness or vomiting means the patient can no longer protect his airway under a sealed mask; rising saturation, a slowing rate, and patient relief show CPAP is working.
opts: He becomes unresponsive
He begins vomiting
His SpO2 rises from 86% to 93%
His respiratory rate falls from 32 to 24
He says his breathing feels easier
ok: He becomes unresponsive
He begins vomiting

items.q: Which features of a child's airway differ from an adult's? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children have relatively large tongues and heads and soft, narrow tracheas; young infants breathe mainly through the nose.
opts: The tongue is larger in proportion to the mouth
The occiput is larger, flexing the neck when supine
The trachea is softer and more easily kinked
The airway is wider and less affected by swelling
Infants breathe mainly through the mouth
ok: The tongue is larger in proportion to the mouth
The occiput is larger, flexing the neck when supine
The trachea is softer and more easily kinked

items.q: Which practices are appropriate for oxygen cylinder safety? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cylinders must be secured and kept from heat and flame; oil, grease, and adhesive near high-pressure oxygen can ignite.
opts: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall or roll
Keep cylinders away from open flames and smoking
Lubricate a sticking regulator with oil or grease
Store cylinders in a hot vehicle trunk
Use adhesive tape to mark the cylinder valve
ok: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall or roll
Keep cylinders away from open flames and smoking

items.q: A 22-year-old with asthma calls for help. Which findings indicate a severe attack? Select all that apply.
items.x: Short phrases, tripod positioning, and hypoxia show a severe attack; mild wheezes with a normal rate and full sentences indicate a mild one.
opts: Speaking only 2 or 3 words between breaths
Sitting forward braced on her arms
SpO2 of 88% on room air
Mild end-expiratory wheezes with RR of 18
Talking in full sentences while you assess her
ok: Speaking only 2 or 3 words between breaths
Sitting forward braced on her arms
SpO2 of 88% on room air

items.q: Which techniques are appropriate when suctioning an adult's oropharynx with a rigid tip? Select all that apply.
items.x: Suction under direct vision, apply it on withdrawal, keep attempts brief, and oxygenate around each attempt to limit hypoxia.
opts: Insert the tip only as far as you can see
Oxygenate the patient before and after suctioning
Apply suction while withdrawing the tip
Apply suction while advancing the tip
Suction for as long as secretions remain
ok: Insert the tip only as far as you can see
Oxygenate the patient before and after suctioning
Apply suction while withdrawing the tip

items.q: Which findings are EARLY signs of hypoxia in an adult? Select all that apply.
items.x: Early hypoxia causes restlessness, tachycardia, and tachypnea; cyanosis, bradycardia, and unresponsiveness are late, ominous signs.
opts: Restlessness or anxiety
Increased heart rate
Increased respiratory rate
Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds
Slowing heart rate
Unresponsiveness
ok: Restlessness or anxiety
Increased heart rate
Increased respiratory rate

items.q: A patient was in an enclosed-space fire. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury to the airway? Select all that apply.
items.x: Singed facial hair, soot in the airway, and hoarseness indicate heat or smoke injury that may lead to rapid airway swelling.
opts: Singed eyebrows or nasal hairs
Soot in the mouth or sputum
Hoarseness or a change in voice
A first-degree burn on the forearm
A heart rate of 88/min
ok: Singed eyebrows or nasal hairs
Soot in the mouth or sputum
Hoarseness or a change in voice

items.q: Which actions are part of correct BVM technique for an unresponsive adult with inadequate breathing? Select all that apply.
items.x: An E-C clamp seal, an airway adjunct, and 1-second breaths with visible chest rise give effective ventilation without gastric inflation; flexing the neck closes the airway.
opts: Use an E-C clamp to seal the mask
Insert an OPA or NPA if one is tolerated
Deliver each breath over about 1 second
Squeeze the bag as fast and hard as possible
Hold the head in full flexion to protect the airway
ok: Use an E-C clamp to seal the mask
Insert an OPA or NPA if one is tolerated
Deliver each breath over about 1 second

items.q: A 58-year-old man has substernal chest pressure. He is alert, and his SpO2 is 98% on room air with no shortness of breath. What is the best approach to oxygen?
items.x: Current guidance gives oxygen in suspected ACS for hypoxia or respiratory distress, not routinely when saturation is normal.
items.a: Monitor; extra oxygen is not routinely needed with normal saturation
w: Give 15 L/min by nonrebreather to all chest pain patients
Ventilate with a BVM to protect the heart muscle
Withhold oxygen even if his saturation later drops

items.q: A 52-year-old woman has had indigestion-like upper abdominal discomfort, sweating, and nausea for an hour. She has no chest pain and thinks it is something she ate. What is the most appropriate EMT action?
items.x: Women frequently have ACS without classic chest pain; epigastric discomfort with diaphoresis and nausea should be treated as a possible heart attack.
items.a: Treat this as possible ACS and transport
w: Give her an antacid and transport non-emergent
Assume food poisoning and offer a sip of water
Give nitroglycerin before checking her blood pressure

items.q: Why might a patient with long-standing diabetes have a heart attack without significant chest pain?
items.x: Diabetic neuropathy can dull the warning pain of ischemia, so these patients may present only with weakness, dyspnea, or nausea.
items.a: Nerve damage can blunt the sensation of pain
w: High blood sugar protects the heart muscle
Insulin blocks pain signals from the heart
Diabetes prevents coronary artery blockage

items.q: A 67-year-old man had a heart attack 2 days ago. He is now confused, with cool clammy skin, crackles in both lungs, HR 118, and BP 76/50. What type of shock is most likely?
items.x: A damaged heart that cannot pump effectively causes low blood pressure with fluid backing into the lungs, the hallmark of cardiogenic shock.
items.a: Cardiogenic
w: Hypovolemic
Anaphylactic
Neurogenic

items.q: An 8-year-old who has been vomiting for 2 days has a heart rate of 140, cool hands and feet, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Her blood pressure is normal for her age. How should you interpret these findings?
items.x: Children maintain their blood pressure until late in shock; tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion with a normal BP indicate compensated shock.
items.a: Compensated shock
w: Normal findings for a sick child
Irreversible shock
Decompensated shock

items.q: In a child developing shock, which finding is a late sign that suggests decompensation?
items.x: Hypotension in a child is a late sign that compensatory mechanisms are failing and cardiac arrest may be near.
items.a: Falling blood pressure
w: Increased heart rate
Delayed capillary refill
Anxiety or restlessness

items.q: An 81-year-old woman with a 2-day history of fever and urinary symptoms is confused. Her skin is flushed, HR is 122, RR is 28, and BP is 84/48. Which condition should you suspect?
items.x: Fever, confusion, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension with a likely infection source point to sepsis with shock, which needs early hospital notification.
items.a: Septic shock
w: Cardiogenic shock
Hypertensive emergency
Stable angina

items.q: A 74-year-old man has had black tarry stools for 2 days and feels dizzy when standing. He is pale, HR 118, BP 92/60. After giving oxygen as needed, how should you position him?
items.x: Signs of GI bleeding with tachycardia and dizziness suggest hypovolemic shock; keep him supine, prevent heat loss, and transport rapidly.
items.a: Supine and kept warm
w: Sitting fully upright
Standing to recheck his vital signs
Head-down Trendelenburg

items.q: A 79-year-old who takes a beta-blocker fell and has a large thigh bruise. She is pale and anxious with a BP of 88/54, but her heart rate is 70. What should you conclude about the heart rate?
items.x: Beta-blockers can prevent the compensatory rise in heart rate, so older patients on these medications may be in shock without tachycardia.
items.a: A normal heart rate does not rule out shock in this patient
w: It proves she is not bleeding significantly
It means the blood pressure reading is wrong
It means she is in cardiogenic shock

items.q: Where should you place your hands to perform chest compressions on an adult?
items.x: Compressions are delivered on the lower half of the breastbone in the center of the chest; pressing on the xiphoid can injure the liver.
items.a: On the lower half of the sternum
w: On the xiphoid process
On the upper third of the sternum
Over the left nipple

items.q: You are performing CPR on a 7-year-old child. What compression depth should you target?
items.x: For children, compress at least one-third of the chest depth, which is about 2 inches (5 cm).
items.a: About 2 inches
w: About 1 inch
About 3 inches
About one-half inch

items.q: You are alone with a 4-month-old infant in cardiac arrest until your partner returns from the ambulance. Which compression technique should you use?
items.x: Current guidance for infant CPR uses the two-thumb encircling hands technique or, if the rescuer cannot encircle the chest, the heel of one hand.
items.a: Two-thumb encircling hands or the heel of one hand
w: Two fingers placed just below the nipple line
The heel of both hands stacked on the sternum
One thumb pressing on the xiphoid process

items.q: You are the only rescuer performing CPR on an 18-month-old. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
items.x: A single rescuer uses 30:2 for all ages beyond the newborn period; 15:2 is used when two rescuers perform infant or child CPR.
w: 5 compressions to 1 breath

items.q: A term newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min despite 30 seconds of positive-pressure ventilation that moves the chest well. What should you do?
items.x: Under NRP, a heart rate below 60 despite effective ventilation calls for compressions with a 3:1 ratio (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute).
items.a: Begin chest compressions coordinated with ventilations at 3:1
w: Continue ventilations alone and recheck in 5 minutes
Stop ventilating and dry the baby again
Begin compressions at a ratio of 15:2

items.q: Where should you place AED pads on an adult in the standard anterolateral position?
items.x: Anterolateral placement puts one pad below the right clavicle and the other on the left lateral chest, so current travels through the heart.
items.a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side below the armpit
w: Both pads side by side on the center of the chest
On the left shoulder and the right hip
On the upper back and the right shoulder

items.q: The AED analyzes the rhythm of a 63-year-old man in cardiac arrest and advises no shock. What should you do?
items.x: No shock advised does not mean the patient has a pulse; resume CPR for about 2 minutes before the next analysis.
items.a: Resume CPR immediately, starting with compressions
w: Turn off the AED and remove the pads
Check for a pulse for 30 seconds
Reanalyze right away to confirm

items.q: You are transporting a patient in cardiac arrest, and it is time for the AED to analyze. What should be done?
items.x: Vehicle motion can interfere with rhythm analysis, so the ambulance should be stopped during analysis and shock delivery.
items.a: Stop the ambulance for analysis and any shock
w: Analyze while the vehicle is moving
Skip the analysis until arrival at the hospital
Analyze only if the road is smooth

items.q: A 54-year-old man in cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of rainwater on a sidewalk. What should you do before using the AED?
items.x: Standing water can conduct current to rescuers and divert it from the heart; move the patient to a dry surface and dry the chest quickly.
items.a: Move him to a dry area and dry his chest
w: Apply the pads and shock immediately where he lies
Skip the AED and perform CPR only
Place the pads on his back instead

items.q: You place AED pads on a man with a very hairy chest, and the AED prompts that the pads are not making good contact. What should you do?
items.x: Quickly removing the first pads, or shaving the area, removes hair so a second set can make good contact; do not delay defibrillation longer than necessary.
items.a: Pull off the pads to remove hair and apply a new set
w: Push harder on the pads during the shock
Place the pads over his clothing
Continue CPR without the AED

items.q: You are treating an alert 60-year-old man with an implanted defibrillator when it delivers a shock while your hand is on his chest. What is true?
items.x: Implanted defibrillators deliver low-energy shocks that a rescuer may feel but that do not harm rescuers.
items.a: You may feel a tingle, but it is not dangerous to you
w: You will likely receive a dangerous shock
The device will stop working permanently
You should immediately apply AED pads over the device

items.q: A 26-year-old was pulled from a lake after being submerged and is pulseless and apneic. What is especially important in this arrest?
items.x: Drowning arrests are caused by hypoxia, so effective ventilations are a key part of CPR along with compressions and the AED.
items.a: Early effective ventilation along with compressions
w: Abdominal thrusts to remove water from the lungs
Delaying CPR until the patient is fully warmed
Compressions only, with no breaths

items.q: A 22-year-old is found pulseless in the snow after a night outdoors, with a core temperature that feels very cold. There are no obvious signs of death. What should you do?
items.x: Severely hypothermic patients may survive prolonged arrest, so begin resuscitation, protect from further cooling, and transport.
items.a: Start CPR and apply the AED while preventing further heat loss
w: Pronounce death because he is too cold to resuscitate
Rewarm him for 30 minutes before starting CPR
Rub his arms and legs vigorously to warm him

items.q: What is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children?
items.x: Pediatric arrest is usually the end result of hypoxia from respiratory failure or shock, so supporting airway and breathing early can prevent it.
items.a: Respiratory failure or shock
w: A sudden ventricular dysrhythmia
A heart attack
Pulmonary embolism

items.q: During a cardiac arrest, the paramedic team leader says to you, Take over compressions at the next switch. Which response reflects good closed-loop communication?
items.x: Closed-loop communication means repeating the order back so the leader knows it was heard and understood.
items.a: Taking over compressions at the next switch
w: Okay
Nodding silently and moving toward the chest
Asking someone else to do it

items.q: During a resuscitation you notice the person doing compressions is allowing the chest to recoil only partway. What should you do?
items.x: Effective teams encourage members to speak up about quality problems during the event so they can be corrected immediately.
items.a: Tell the compressor and team leader clearly and respectfully
w: Say nothing so as not to disrupt the team
Stop compressions yourself and take over without speaking
Report it only after the call is over

items.q: You arrive at a home where an 89-year-old man is pulseless and apneic. His wife hands you a valid, signed out-of-hospital DNR order. What should you do?
items.x: A valid out-of-hospital DNR or POLST order should be honored; confirm it belongs to the patient and follow local protocol.
items.a: Verify the document and withhold resuscitation
w: Start CPR anyway until medical control arrives
Apply the AED and shock only once
Begin CPR because DNR orders are only valid in hospitals

items.q: A 76-year-old woman with a valid DNR order has severe shortness of breath and a strong pulse. What care should you provide?
items.x: A DNR order addresses resuscitation from arrest, not other care; patients with DNR orders should still receive oxygen, comfort, and appropriate treatment.
items.a: Oxygen and comfort measures
w: No treatment of any kind
Only transport, with no assessment
Full CPR if she becomes worse

items.q: A 70-year-old man is pulseless and apneic in his bed. His adult son says his father never wanted CPR, but there is no written order. There are no signs of obvious death. What should you do?
items.x: Without a valid written order or obvious signs of death, resuscitation should be started; verbal wishes from family generally are not sufficient.
items.a: Begin resuscitation
w: Withhold CPR based on the son's request
Wait for the family to find the paperwork
Call the patient's doctor before doing anything

items.q: Under the widely used BLS termination of resuscitation rule, which finding means resuscitation should continue and the patient should be transported?
items.x: The BLS rule allows considering termination only if the arrest was not witnessed by EMS, no shock was given, and there was no ROSC; a delivered shock means continue.
items.a: The AED delivered a shock
w: The arrest was not witnessed by EMS
There was no return of pulse on scene
The patient is over 65 years old

items.q: A 64-year-old man regained a pulse after AED shocks. During transport, he again becomes pulseless. What should you do?
items.x: Rearrest is common after ROSC; restart compressions immediately and follow AED prompts.
items.a: Resume CPR and use the AED
w: Continue ventilations only
Check his blood pressure first
Wait 2 minutes to see if the pulse returns

items.q: A 15-year-old baseball catcher collapses after a pitch strikes him in the chest. He is unresponsive and pulseless. What should you do?
items.x: A blow to the chest at the wrong moment can trigger ventricular fibrillation (commotio cordis); early CPR and defibrillation are lifesaving.
items.a: Begin CPR and apply the AED immediately
w: Splint his chest and transport
Give oxygen and observe for 5 minutes
Stabilize the spine before any other care

items.q: An adult in cardiac arrest is lying in a soft hospital-style bed at home. What should you do before starting compressions?
items.x: Compressions on a soft mattress lose depth; move the patient to a firm surface quickly or place a backboard beneath him.
items.a: Move him to the floor or a firm surface
w: Do compressions on the bed with extra force
Sit him up against the headboard
Place a pillow under his back

items.q: Where should you check for a pulse in an unresponsive 5-month-old?
items.x: The brachial pulse on the inside of the upper arm is the most reliable location in infants, whose short necks make carotid checks difficult.
items.a: Brachial artery
w: Carotid artery
Radial artery
Dorsalis pedis artery

items.q: You arrive to find a bystander performing good CPR on a 60-year-old man. What should you do first?
items.x: Keep compressions going while the AED is applied, minimizing interruptions, then take over CPR.
items.a: Have the bystander continue while you apply the AED
w: Stop the bystander and recheck for breathing for 30 seconds
Take over compressions and delay the AED until ALS arrives
Ask the bystander how long he has been doing CPR

items.q: Which of these is added in BE-FAST that the basic FAST stroke screen does not include?
items.x: BE-FAST adds sudden loss of balance and vision changes to face, arm, and speech findings, catching posterior strokes that FAST can miss.
items.a: Balance and eyes
w: Face and arms
Speech and time
Blood pressure and glucose

items.q: A 66-year-old woman went to bed at 10 p.m. feeling fine and woke at 6 a.m. unable to move her left arm. When was she last known well?
items.x: For symptoms discovered on waking, the last known well time is when the patient was last seen normal, here at bedtime.
w: 6 a.m.
The time EMS was called
Midnight, the start of the new day

items.q: You are treating a 73-year-old man with sudden facial droop, arm weakness, and slurred speech that began 30 minutes ago. Which action will most shorten his time to definitive treatment?
items.x: Early prehospital notification lets the hospital prepare its stroke team and imaging before the patient arrives.
items.a: Notify the receiving stroke-capable hospital early
w: Delay transport until his symptoms stabilize
Transport without lights and sirens to the closest clinic
Wait to see if his symptoms resolve

items.q: A 69-year-old man had 20 minutes of slurred speech and right-hand weakness that completely resolved before you arrived. He feels fine and wants to refuse transport. What should you advise?
items.x: A TIA is a warning that a stroke may follow soon, so the patient should be transported for urgent evaluation.
items.a: He needs evaluation because this may be a TIA with high stroke risk
w: He is fine because his symptoms resolved
Transport non-emergent, since TIAs never progress
Give oral glucose in case it was hypoglycemia

items.q: A 48-year-old woman has a sudden, explosive headache she calls the worst of her life, followed by vomiting and a stiff neck. What should you suspect?
items.x: A sudden severe headache with vomiting suggests a hemorrhagic stroke such as a subarachnoid hemorrhage; monitor the airway and transport rapidly.
items.a: Bleeding in or around the brain
w: A tension headache
A sinus infection
Migraine with aura

items.q: A 57-year-old man has a severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion. His BP is 232/138. What condition is most likely?
items.x: Severely elevated blood pressure with signs of organ damage such as confusion or vision changes is a hypertensive emergency requiring prompt transport.
items.a: Hypertensive emergency
w: Stable angina
Hypovolemic shock
Vasovagal syncope

items.q: A 28-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, spots in her vision, and swollen hands and face. BP is 166/112. What should you do?
items.x: These are signs of severe preeclampsia with a high risk of seizures; minimize stimulation, use left-side positioning, and transport while being ready to manage a seizure.
items.a: Keep her calm in a quiet setting, position her on her left side, and transport
w: Have her walk to the ambulance to improve circulation
Turn on lights and sirens and keep the cabin bright so you can watch her
Lay her supine and elevate her legs

items.q: A 77-year-old man has distended neck veins, swelling in both ankles, and an enlarged abdomen, but his lungs are clear. Which condition do these findings suggest?
items.x: Right-sided failure causes blood to back up into the body, producing JVD, peripheral edema, and abdominal swelling; left-sided failure causes pulmonary edema.
items.a: Right-sided heart failure
w: Left-sided heart failure
Asthma
Spontaneous pneumothorax

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with CHF says she now has to sleep on three pillows and wakes up at night gasping for air. What does this history suggest?
items.x: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occur when lying flat lets fluid shift into the lungs, a sign of worsening heart failure.
items.a: Worsening fluid in the lungs when lying flat
w: Improving heart function
An upper airway obstruction
A normal sign of aging

items.q: A 61-year-old man with high blood pressure has sudden severe chest pain he describes as tearing, radiating to his back. BP is 182/104 in the right arm and 140/82 in the left. What should you suspect?
items.x: Sudden tearing pain to the back with a blood pressure difference between arms is classic for aortic dissection; keep him calm and transport rapidly.
items.a: Aortic dissection
w: Stable angina
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Pericarditis

items.q: A 20-year-old woman fainted after seeing blood at a clinic. She is now awake, lying supine, and reports feeling nauseated and warm. What should you do?
items.x: Vasovagal syncope usually follows a trigger, but sitting or standing too soon can cause another faint; keep her supine while you assess.
items.a: Keep her lying down while you assess her
w: Have her stand quickly to check her balance
Give her a large glass of water
Place her in a sitting position immediately

items.q: A 16-year-old basketball player suddenly fainted while sprinting and recovered within a minute. He feels fine now. What is the most important concern?
items.x: Syncope during exertion in a young athlete may indicate a structural or electrical heart problem that can cause sudden death; he needs evaluation.
items.a: A possible underlying heart condition
w: Simple dehydration that needs no care
An anxiety reaction to the game
Low blood sugar from skipping breakfast

items.q: A 30-year-old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back for your assessment. What should you do?
items.x: The heavy uterus can compress the vena cava when she lies supine, reducing blood return to the heart; left lateral positioning relieves it.
items.a: Position her on her left side
w: Elevate her legs while she stays supine
Have her sit up and drink water
Place her face down

items.q: You are called for a 58-year-old man with an LVAD who feels weak. He is alert and talking, but you cannot feel a radial pulse or obtain a BP with your cuff. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Continuous-flow LVADs may produce little or no palpable pulse; assess perfusion by mental status, skin color, and capillary refill rather than pulse alone.
items.a: His continuous-flow pump often makes the pulse hard to feel
w: He is in cardiac arrest and needs compressions
Your equipment must be malfunctioning
He is in severe hypovolemic shock

items.q: Which findings may be the presenting symptoms of ACS, even without chest pain? Select all that apply.
items.x: Jaw or arm discomfort, sudden dyspnea, and sweating with nausea can all be ACS, especially in women, older adults, and diabetics; cold symptoms and rashes are not.
opts: Jaw or arm discomfort
Sudden unexplained shortness of breath
Sweating with nausea
A sore throat with runny nose
An itchy rash on both arms
ok: Jaw or arm discomfort
Sudden unexplained shortness of breath
Sweating with nausea

items.q: You are about to deliver an AED shock. Which actions promote safety? Select all that apply.
items.x: Announcing and confirming clear and moving oxygen away prevents injury and fire; touching the patient during analysis or shock is unsafe and interferes with the device.
opts: State loudly that everyone is clear
Visually confirm no one is touching the patient
Move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest
Continue compressions while the AED analyzes
Hold the patient's hand to feel for a pulse during the shock
ok: State loudly that everyone is clear
Visually confirm no one is touching the patient
Move free-flowing oxygen away from the chest

items.q: Which findings are typical of hypovolemic shock in an adult? Select all that apply.
items.x: Volume loss causes tachycardia, pale cool clammy skin, and anxiety; flat, not distended, neck veins and rapid shallow breathing are expected.
opts: Rapid heart rate
Cool, pale, clammy skin
Anxiety or restlessness
Warm, flushed, dry skin
Distended neck veins
Slow, deep respirations
ok: Rapid heart rate
Cool, pale, clammy skin
Anxiety or restlessness

items.q: An adult has ROSC after defibrillation. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: After ROSC, keep the AED attached because rearrest is common, avoid hyperventilation, monitor vital signs, and transport to an appropriate facility.
opts: Leave the AED pads attached
Ventilate if needed without hyperventilating
Check blood pressure and prepare for rearrest
Remove the AED to prevent accidental shocks
Ventilate at 30 breaths per minute to remove CO2
ok: Leave the AED pads attached
Ventilate if needed without hyperventilating
Check blood pressure and prepare for rearrest

items.q: Which conditions can mimic a stroke in the field? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypoglycemia and postictal weakness can produce stroke-like deficits; atrial fibrillation and high cholesterol are stroke risk factors, not mimics.
opts: Hypoglycemia
A postictal state after a seizure
High cholesterol
A history of atrial fibrillation
A sprained ankle
ok: Hypoglycemia
A postictal state after a seizure

items.q: Which findings suggest an aortic dissection? Select all that apply.
items.x: Dissection causes abrupt tearing pain and can block branch arteries, producing unequal arm pressures or pulses.
opts: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back
A large blood pressure difference between arms
A weak or absent pulse in one arm
Pain that developed gradually over a week with fever
Pain only when swallowing
ok: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back
A large blood pressure difference between arms
A weak or absent pulse in one arm

items.q: Which findings are consistent with congestive heart failure? Select all that apply.
items.x: CHF causes bilateral edema, orthopnea, and JVD; a barking cough suggests croup and one-sided calf swelling suggests a DVT.
opts: Swelling in both ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Jugular vein distention
A barking cough
Pain and swelling in one calf only
ok: Swelling in both ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Jugular vein distention

items.q: Which practices reflect effective teamwork during a resuscitation? Select all that apply.
items.x: Clear roles, closed-loop communication, and speaking up improve resuscitation; multiple leaders and long pauses in compressions harm it.
opts: Repeating orders back to the leader
Having a leader assign clear roles
Speaking up when you see an error
Several people giving orders at once
Stopping compressions so everyone can check a pulse
ok: Repeating orders back to the leader
Having a leader assign clear roles
Speaking up when you see an error

items.q: A patient with a valid DNR order is breathing and has a pulse. Which care can still be given? Select all that apply.
items.x: A DNR order limits resuscitation after arrest, but patients still receive oxygen, suctioning, comfort, and other supportive care.
opts: Oxygen
Suctioning of the airway
Comfort positioning
Chest compressions if he arrests
Defibrillation if he arrests
ok: Oxygen
Suctioning of the airway
Comfort positioning

items.q: You are caring for a patient with an LVAD. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: LVAD patients need their equipment and the VAD team's guidance; perfusion is judged by mental status and skin, and a missing pulse alone does not mean arrest.
opts: Call the VAD coordinator listed on the device
Bring the controller and spare batteries
Judge perfusion by mental status and skin
Disconnect the pump to check for a pulse
Assume no palpable pulse means cardiac arrest
ok: Call the VAD coordinator listed on the device
Bring the controller and spare batteries
Judge perfusion by mental status and skin

items.q: A 59-year-old man has a BP of 224/132. Which findings indicate a hypertensive emergency rather than just high blood pressure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Severe hypertension becomes an emergency when it causes organ damage, shown by neurologic changes, vision problems, or chest pain.
opts: New confusion
Blurred vision
Chest pain
No symptoms at all
He missed one dose of his medication
ok: New confusion
Blurred vision
Chest pain

items.q: Which features of a fainting episode suggest a dangerous cardiac cause? Select all that apply.
items.x: Exertional syncope, syncope without warning, and palpitations suggest a dysrhythmia or structural heart problem; triggered faints with warning signs are usually vasovagal.
opts: It occurred during exercise
It happened without any warning
Palpitations just before fainting
It followed the sight of a needle
It followed prolonged standing in the heat with nausea
ok: It occurred during exercise
It happened without any warning
Palpitations just before fainting

items.q: A 30-year-old man fell 15 feet from a roof and is unresponsive. You hear gurgling with each breath, his right wrist is deformed, and there is no visible bleeding. After manually stabilizing his head, what should you do first?
items.x: Gurgling means fluid in the airway, an immediate threat found in the primary survey; splinting, vital signs, and history all wait until airway, breathing, and circulation are managed.
items.a: Suction the airway
w: Splint the deformed wrist before moving him onto the stretcher
Apply a cervical collar and secure him to a long backboard
Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs and a SAMPLE history

items.q: During the assessment of a multisystem trauma patient, when should you perform a detailed secondary assessment and obtain a full SAMPLE history?
items.x: The primary survey finds and treats immediate life threats first; the secondary assessment and history follow, and in a critical patient they are often done en route.
items.a: After life threats from the primary survey are treated
w: Before any treatment, so care is based on complete information
Only after arrival at the receiving hospital
During scene size-up, before touching the patient

items.q: A 22-year-old woman was thrown from a horse and is unresponsive with snoring respirations. You suspect a cervical spine injury. How should you open her airway?
items.x: The jaw-thrust opens the airway while keeping the head and neck in line; if it fails to open the airway, a head-tilt may be needed because the airway takes priority.
items.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver
w: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway before any manual maneuver
Turn her head to the side and sweep the mouth

items.q: A 19-year-old cut his palm on broken glass while washing dishes. He is alert, the bleeding is controlled, and he has no other complaints. After the primary survey, what type of physical exam is most appropriate?
items.x: With no significant mechanism and an isolated injury, a focused exam of the affected area, including distal circulation, sensation, and movement, is appropriate.
items.a: A focused exam of the injured hand
w: A rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment with spinal motion restriction
A full detailed exam of every body region before transport
No physical exam, since the bleeding has stopped

items.q: A 34-year-old man has heavy, life-threatening bleeding from a laceration in the middle of his lower leg. Where should the tourniquet be placed?
items.x: When the wound location is clear, a tourniquet goes 2-3 inches above the wound and not over a joint; if the wound cannot be seen or located, place it high and tight on the limb.
items.a: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over the knee
w: Directly over the wound so it compresses the bleeding vessel
Over the knee joint to anchor it securely
On the upper thigh only, regardless of where the leg wound is

items.q: A bystander applied a commercial tourniquet to a patient's arm 25 minutes before you arrived. The bleeding is controlled, but the patient complains of severe pain from the tourniquet. What should you do?
items.x: A properly applied tourniquet that controls bleeding should not be loosened or removed in the field; tourniquet pain is expected, and the application time must be recorded.
items.a: Leave it in place and document the time it was applied
w: Loosen it briefly to restore circulation and then retighten it
Remove it and replace it with a pressure dressing
Loosen it until the pain is tolerable to the patient

items.q: A 26-year-old man has a deep laceration to the side of his neck with dark blood flowing from it. What is the most important dressing for this wound?
items.x: An open neck vein can draw in air and cause an air embolism, so cover it with an occlusive dressing and hold pressure; never wrap a bandage around the neck.
items.a: An occlusive dressing held with direct pressure
w: A circumferential pressure bandage wrapped snugly around the neck
A loose, moist sterile dressing taped on all sides
A tourniquet placed just below the wound

items.q: A 28-year-old woman fell from a ladder and cannot move or feel her legs. Her blood pressure is 82/50, pulse 54, and her skin is warm, dry, and pink below the nipple line. What type of shock is most likely?
items.x: A spinal cord injury can cause loss of sympathetic tone, producing hypotension with a normal or slow heart rate and warm, dry skin, unlike the tachycardia and pale, cool skin of hemorrhagic shock.
items.a: Neurogenic shock
w: Hemorrhagic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylactic shock

items.q: A 78-year-old man who takes a beta blocker fell down several stairs and complains of left upper abdominal pain. His pulse is 74, blood pressure 98/62, and his skin is pale and moist. How should you interpret his heart rate?
items.x: Beta blockers and aging blunt the normal tachycardia of shock, so an older adult can be bleeding significantly with a normal pulse; his pale, moist skin and low pressure point to shock.
items.a: It may not rise in shock because of his medication
w: It proves his blood loss is minimal
It indicates a heart attack rather than an injury
It is too slow and he needs CPR

items.q: A 24-year-old man was stabbed in the left chest. He has distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds, and a blood pressure of 76/58. What is the most appropriate EMT action?
items.x: Hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds with equal breath sounds suggest cardiac tamponade, which requires hospital treatment; EMTs treat it with rapid transport.
items.a: Rapid transport to a trauma center with ALS intercept if available
w: Seal the wound and wait on scene for a paramedic unit
Position him flat with legs raised and complete a full secondary exam on scene
Have him sit upright and breathe into a paper bag

items.q: An unrestrained driver hit a tree head-on. The steering wheel is bent and the windshield has a starred spider-web break. Which injuries should you suspect? Select all that apply.
items.x: A frontal impact can send an unrestrained occupant up and over into the windshield (head and neck) and into the steering wheel (chest), or down and under into the dash (knees, femurs, hips); airbags do not rule out serious injury.
opts: Head and cervical spine injury
Blunt chest injury such as rib fractures or cardiac contusion
Knee, femur, or hip injury from striking the dash
No serious injury because the airbag deployed
Injuries limited to the side opposite the impact
ok: Head and cervical spine injury
Blunt chest injury such as rib fractures or cardiac contusion
Knee, femur, or hip injury from striking the dash

items.q: A car was struck on the driver's door in a T-bone collision with significant intrusion. Which abdominal organ of the driver is most at risk?
items.x: In a lateral impact, injuries occur on the side struck; for the driver in a left-side impact, the spleen, left ribs, and left pelvis are at highest risk.
items.a: The spleen
w: The liver
The appendix
The bladder

items.q: Under the 2021 National Guideline for Field Triage, which mechanisms of injury are considered high risk for serious injury? Select all that apply.
items.x: The 2021 guideline lists falls over 10 feet, ejection, and pedestrians or cyclists thrown, run over, or with significant impact as high-risk mechanisms that warrant trauma center transport.
opts: Fall from a height greater than 10 feet
Partial or complete ejection from a vehicle
Pedestrian thrown or run over by a vehicle
Fall from standing in an alert, healthy 30-year-old
Low-speed crash with a seat belt and no intrusion
ok: Fall from a height greater than 10 feet
Partial or complete ejection from a vehicle
Pedestrian thrown or run over by a vehicle

items.q: A 35-year-old man with a head injury is becoming less responsive. Which findings suggest brain herniation? Select all that apply.
items.x: A unilateral fixed, dilated pupil, posturing, and a declining GCS indicate rising pressure forcing the brain downward; bruising behind the ears and nasal fluid suggest a skull fracture but are not herniation signs.
opts: One pupil dilated and not reactive to light
Extension posturing of the arms and legs
A falling Glasgow Coma Scale score
Bruising behind the ears
Equal pupils that react briskly to light
Clear fluid draining from the nose
ok: One pupil dilated and not reactive to light
Extension posturing of the arms and legs
A falling Glasgow Coma Scale score

items.q: A 40-year-old woman has a serious head injury after a fall. Which priority does the most to prevent further damage to her brain during your care?
items.x: Even brief episodes of low oxygen or low blood pressure worsen outcomes after a brain injury; routine hyperventilation is harmful because it reduces blood flow to the brain.
items.a: Preventing hypoxia and hypotension
w: Hyperventilating her at 30 breaths per minute as soon as possible
Keeping her flat with her legs elevated
Checking her blood glucose every 2 minutes

items.q: Two hours after being struck in the head with a baseball bat, a 20-year-old man has bruising behind both ears. What does this finding suggest?
