items.x: Bruising over the mastoid process behind the ear (Battle sign) is a delayed sign of a basilar skull fracture, often appearing hours after the injury.
items.a: A basilar skull fracture
w: An epidural hematoma
A cervical spine fracture
A fractured mandible

items.q: A 17-year-old was hit in the side of the head by a baseball, briefly lost consciousness, then woke up talking normally. Twenty minutes later he becomes confused and drowsy. What injury does this pattern suggest?
items.x: A brief loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval and then rapid decline is the classic pattern of an epidural hematoma, an arterial bleed that needs rapid transport.
items.a: Epidural hematoma
w: Simple concussion with full recovery
Basilar skull fracture
Spinal cord injury

items.q: After a crash, a 33-year-old man opens his eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws his hand from a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
items.x: Eye opening to pain is 2, incomprehensible sounds are 2, and withdrawal from pain is 4, for a total of 8.

items.q: A 26-year-old was struck in the face with a nail gun. A nail passes completely through his cheek, and blood is draining into his mouth and threatening his airway. What should you do?
items.x: An object impaled in the cheek may be removed if it threatens the airway; then dress the outside and pack the inside of the cheek while managing the airway.
items.a: Remove the nail and pack the inside of the cheek with gauze
w: Stabilize the nail in place with bulky dressings on the outside only
Push the nail through into the mouth to clear the outside wound
Place him supine and suction only when he starts choking

items.q: A 41-year-old carpenter has a small metal shard impaled in his right eye. How should you care for the eye?
items.x: Impaled objects in the eye are stabilized, not removed; covering both eyes reduces sympathetic eye movement that could worsen the injury.
items.a: Stabilize the object with a cup and cover both eyes
w: Remove the object gently and flush the eye with saline
Cover only the injured eye tightly with a pressure patch
Leave both eyes uncovered so he can see during transport

items.q: A 36-year-old worker splashed a cleaning chemical into his left eye. How should you irrigate it?
items.x: Irrigate immediately and continuously, directing the flow from the inner corner outward so contaminated fluid does not wash into the other eye; do not delay to identify the chemical.
items.a: With water flowing from the inner corner outward
w: With water flowing from the outer corner toward the nose
With a few drops of saline every few minutes
Only after you identify the exact chemical

items.q: A 23-year-old was struck across the front of the neck by a wire while riding a motorcycle. He is hoarse, and you feel a crackling sensation under the skin of his neck. What does this suggest?
items.x: Hoarseness and subcutaneous air after a blow to the neck suggest injury to the larynx or trachea, which can rapidly obstruct the airway.
items.a: Possible laryngeal or tracheal injury that may compromise the airway
w: A minor abrasion that needs only a dressing
A cervical spine injury with spinal cord damage
Normal swelling expected after any neck trauma

items.q: A 31-year-old man was in a low-speed crash. He is alert, sober, has no neck pain or midline tenderness, no numbness or weakness, and no other painful injuries. Based on current national guidance, what is the most appropriate approach to spinal motion restriction?
items.x: Current joint guidance supports selective spinal motion restriction; an alert, sober patient with no spinal pain, tenderness, neurologic deficit, or distracting injury does not need it.
items.a: It is not needed for this patient
w: Apply a cervical collar and long backboard because he was in a crash
Apply a cervical collar only, since the mechanism alone requires it
Have him lie on the floor while you call for a backboard

items.q: You are placing a 2-year-old on a firm, flat device for spinal motion restriction. What should you do to keep the spine in a neutral position?
items.x: A young child's large head flexes the neck forward when lying flat, so padding under the shoulders and torso keeps the airway open and the spine neutral.
items.a: Pad beneath the shoulders and torso
w: Place a folded towel under the back of the head
Tilt the head forward with the chin on the chest
Leave the child flat on the device with no padding

items.q: A 29-year-old motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet is vomiting and you cannot clear his airway with the helmet on. What should you do?
items.x: A helmet must be removed if it prevents airway management; two rescuers work together, one stabilizing the head and neck while the other removes the helmet.
items.a: Remove the helmet with two rescuers while keeping the head stable
w: Leave the helmet on and suction through the face opening only
Cut the chin strap and tilt the head back to drain the vomit
Have him remove the helmet himself while you hold suction ready

items.q: An 86-year-old woman with a severely curved upper spine (kyphosis) needs spinal motion restriction after a fall. How should you position her?
items.x: Older adults with kyphosis cannot lie flat without forcing the spine out of its normal position, so padding fills the gaps and keeps them in a neutral, comfortable position.
items.a: Pad behind her head and shoulders to support her natural curve
w: Force her head back against the board so it lies flat
Place her prone on the stretcher to protect her airway
Secure her flat without padding to keep the spine straight

items.q: A 21-year-old man dove into a shallow pool. His chest wall does not move as he breathes, but his abdomen rises and falls with each breath. What should you be prepared to do?
items.x: Abdominal breathing without chest movement suggests a cervical spinal cord injury that paralyzes the intercostal muscles; breathing may quickly become inadequate.
items.a: Assist his ventilations
w: Apply a pelvic binder
Place him in the recovery position
Give oral glucose

items.q: A 64-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A section of his right chest moves inward when he inhales and outward when he exhales. His breathing is shallow at 32 per minute with an SpO2 of 86 percent. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Paradoxical movement means a flail segment, and the underlying lung injury causes poor oxygenation; positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM supports breathing and stabilizes the segment from inside.
items.a: Assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen
w: Tape a heavy sandbag over the moving segment
Wrap a bandage tightly around the entire chest
Place him on his left side and give oxygen by nasal cannula

items.q: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the right chest. Air bubbles from the wound each time he breathes. What should you do first?
items.x: An open chest wound should be sealed immediately, first with a gloved hand and then with an occlusive dressing, to stop air from entering the chest.
items.a: Cover the wound with a gloved hand
w: Look for an exit wound on his back
Place him supine and elevate his legs
Apply a bulky gauze dressing with tape

items.q: A 55-year-old man fell onto a railing and has no open wounds. He is increasingly short of breath with absent breath sounds on the left, distended neck veins, and falling blood pressure. What is the most appropriate EMT care?
items.x: These findings suggest a tension pneumothorax; needle decompression is outside EMT scope, so EMTs support oxygenation and ventilation and get the patient to definitive care quickly.
items.a: High-flow oxygen, assisted ventilations as needed, and rapid transport with ALS intercept
w: Insert a needle into the second intercostal space on the left side
Seal the left chest with an occlusive dressing
Keep him on scene until his breath sounds return

items.q: After a fall, a 42-year-old man has diminished breath sounds on the right and signs of shock. Which finding suggests massive hemothorax rather than tension pneumothorax?
items.x: Both can cause decreased breath sounds and shock, but blood loss into the chest usually leaves the neck veins flat, while tension pneumothorax often distends them.
items.a: Flat neck veins
w: Absent breath sounds on the injured side
Rapid heart rate
Shortness of breath

items.q: A 14-year-old baseball catcher is struck in the chest by a pitch and immediately collapses. He is unresponsive, not breathing, and pulseless. What should you do?
items.x: A blow directly over the heart at a vulnerable moment can trigger ventricular fibrillation (commotio cordis); immediate CPR and early defibrillation are lifesaving.
items.a: Start CPR and apply an AED as soon as possible
w: Apply high-flow oxygen and check for rib fractures
Assess for a tension pneumothorax and transport
Place him in the recovery position and monitor

items.q: A 38-year-old man was pinned under a car for several minutes with heavy pressure on his chest. His face and neck are purple and swollen, with small red spots on the skin and bloodshot eyes. What injury does this suggest?
items.x: Sudden severe chest compression forces blood back into the head and neck, producing the purple face, petechiae, and bloodshot eyes of traumatic asphyxia; associated chest injuries are common.
items.a: Traumatic asphyxia
w: Smoke inhalation
An allergic reaction
A simple facial contusion

items.q: A 33-year-old restrained driver has a red, bruised band across her lower abdomen from the lap belt. Her vital signs are normal and she says she feels fine. How should you interpret this?
items.x: A seat belt sign is associated with injuries to the bowel, other abdominal organs, and the lumbar spine; patients can look stable early before shock develops.
items.a: Suspect an internal abdominal injury despite normal vital signs
w: A seat belt mark is expected and not concerning in a stable patient
Normal vital signs rule out internal bleeding
The injury is limited to the skin and needs only a cold pack

items.q: Where should a pelvic binder be positioned to stabilize a suspected unstable pelvic fracture?
items.x: A pelvic binder centered over the greater trochanters (the bony points of the hips) best closes the pelvic ring; placing it too high is a common error.
items.a: Over the greater trochanters
w: Around the waist at the level of the navel
Just below the ribs
Around the upper thighs above the knees

items.q: A 13-year-old fell off a skateboard and has a painful, deformed midshaft forearm. When splinting, which joints must be immobilized?
items.x: For a long bone fracture, splint the joint above and the joint below; for a midforearm fracture, that is the wrist and elbow.
items.a: The wrist and the elbow
w: The elbow and the shoulder
Only the wrist
Only the elbow

items.q: A 25-year-old basketball player has a deformed, painful elbow after a fall. He has a strong radial pulse and normal sensation in his fingers. How should you splint it?
items.x: Joint injuries with intact distal circulation are splinted in the position found because manipulation could injure nearby nerves and vessels.
items.a: In the position found
w: Straighten the arm fully before splinting
Pull firmly on the forearm to reduce the joint
Apply a traction splint to the arm

items.q: A 47-year-old man has a severely angulated midshaft fracture of the lower leg. His foot is cool and pale with no pulse. What should you do?
items.x: A long bone with absent distal circulation should be gently realigned to restore blood flow; stop if resistance or a large increase in pain occurs, then splint and reassess pulses.
items.a: Apply gentle manual traction to align the limb, then splint
w: Splint in the angulated position and transport immediately
Wrap the foot in a heat pack and recheck in 15 minutes
Elevate the leg and apply a tourniquet above the fracture

items.q: A 24-year-old has a crushed lower leg from a motorcycle crash. Which findings suggest compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.
items.x: Compartment syndrome is rising pressure within a muscle compartment; early signs are pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and tense swelling, while pulses may stay present until late.
opts: Pain far greater than expected for the injury
Severe pain when the toes are passively stretched
A tense, firm swelling of the lower leg
Crepitus at the fracture site
Bright red blood spurting from the wound
ok: Pain far greater than expected for the injury
Severe pain when the toes are passively stretched
A tense, firm swelling of the lower leg

items.q: A 22-year-old fell on his outstretched arm. He holds his arm away from his body and will not let it move; the shoulder looks squared off. How should you splint it?
items.x: An anterior shoulder dislocation is splinted in the position of comfort, often with a pillow filling the gap between arm and chest, then a sling and swathe.
items.a: Place a pillow between the arm and chest and secure with a sling and swathe
w: Pull the arm down and in until it pops back into place
Straighten the arm against his side and tape it there
Apply a rigid splint from wrist to shoulder with the arm extended overhead

items.q: You have applied a splint to a fractured forearm. Which steps are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Assess distal function before and after, pad the splint, and remove jewelry before swelling worsens; leave the fingertips exposed to monitor circulation.
opts: Check circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting
Pad the splint to fill gaps and protect the skin
Remove rings or watches from the injured limb
Apply the splint tightly enough to stop all finger movement
Leave the fingertips covered so they stay warm
ok: Check circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting
Pad the splint to fill gaps and protect the skin
Remove rings or watches from the injured limb

items.q: A 10-month-old infant was scalded over the entire head and the entire front of the torso. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area is burned?
items.x: In infants the head is about 18 percent and the front of the torso is 18 percent, totaling 36 percent; the infant head is proportionally larger than an adult head.
items.a: 36 percent
w: 27 percent
18 percent
About 45 percent

items.q: A 45-year-old man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 40 percent of his body. The burning process has been stopped. Which dressing is most appropriate?
items.x: Large burns destroy the skin's ability to hold heat, so after cooling briefly, cover with dry sterile dressings and prevent hypothermia; ice and prolonged wet dressings over large areas cause harm.
items.a: Dry, sterile dressings and blankets to keep him warm
w: Wet, cold towels over all burned areas for the entire transport
Burn ointment applied under occlusive plastic wrap
Ice packs placed directly on the burned skin

items.q: A 52-year-old woman was rescued from a house fire. Which finding is most concerning for an airway burn that could rapidly obstruct her airway?
items.x: Hoarseness, along with soot in the mouth, singed nasal hair, and stridor, signals swelling of the upper airway that can progress quickly; early ALS and rapid transport are needed.
items.a: Hoarse voice
w: Burns to the backs of both hands
Pain in her lower legs
Smoke odor on her clothing

items.q: A utility worker is still in contact with a downed power line and appears unresponsive. What should you do?
items.x: Never approach a patient in contact with an electrical source until trained personnel have confirmed it is safe; improvised tools and standard gloves do not protect from high voltage.
items.a: Stay clear until the power company confirms the line is de-energized
w: Use a dry wooden broom handle to push the wire away
Grab him by his clothing and pull him away quickly
Approach with rubber gloves and boots to assess his pulse

items.q: A 30-year-old electrician received a high-voltage shock. He has small burns on his hand and foot and says he feels fine. What is your main concern?
items.x: Electrical current can damage deep tissues and the heart even when surface burns are small, so these patients need transport and monitoring for dysrhythmias.
items.a: Hidden internal injury and abnormal heart rhythms
w: Infection of the small skin burns
Dehydration from sweating
A sprained wrist from the fall

items.q: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are injured; one is pulseless and apneic while others are awake and moving. How should triage differ from a typical MCI?
items.x: Lightning victims in arrest often have a good chance of recovery with prompt CPR and ventilation, and those still conscious are likely to survive, so lightning triage reverses the usual priority.
items.a: Treat the patient in cardiac arrest first
w: Tag the pulseless patient as deceased and move on
Treat the awake and moving patients first
Wait for police before treating anyone

items.q: A combative patient must be restrained per protocol for safe transport. Which practice is correct?
items.x: Prone hobble restraint and chest compression can cause positional asphyxia and death; restrain supine or on the side, avoid chest compression, and continuously monitor the airway and breathing.
items.a: Restrain the patient face up and continually monitor breathing
w: Restrain the patient face down with hands and feet tied together
Tighten restraints across the chest to prevent all movement
Leave the patient unattended once restraints are secure

items.q: An 80-year-old woman is lying supine on a narrow bathroom floor after a fall and needs to be lifted with minimal body movement. Which device separates into two halves that slide beneath her from each side?
items.x: A scoop (orthopedic) stretcher splits lengthwise so each half slides under the patient from the sides, lifting her with very little rolling or movement.
items.a: Scoop stretcher
w: Stair chair
Wheeled stretcher
Vest-type extrication device

items.q: You arrive at a house where a man has been shot. Police tell you the scene is secure. As you enter, you notice a firearm on the floor near the patient. What should you do?
items.x: Notify law enforcement of any weapon and leave it alone if possible; if it must be moved for safety, tell police exactly what you did.
items.a: Tell police about it and avoid touching it unless needed for safety
w: Pick it up and unload it before treating the patient
Kick it under a couch so no one can reach it
Place it in the ambulance for safekeeping

items.q: Which single action is most effective at preventing the spread of infection between patients and EMS providers?
items.x: Cleaning hands before and after patient contact and after removing gloves is the most effective way to prevent infection transmission.
items.a: Hand hygiene
w: Wearing a surgical mask on every call
Giving every patient antibiotics
Keeping the ambulance windows open

items.q: A 30-week pregnant woman was injured in a car crash. Which statements about her care are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Caring well for the mother protects the fetus; pregnant patients can compensate for substantial blood loss, and a left tilt keeps the uterus off the vena cava. Even minor crashes can injure the placenta.
opts: The best care for the fetus is aggressive care of the mother
She may lose a significant amount of blood before her vital signs change
If she is secured to a board, tilt it to her left
The fetus is well protected, so minor crashes need no evaluation
Keep her flat on her back to protect the spine
ok: The best care for the fetus is aggressive care of the mother
She may lose a significant amount of blood before her vital signs change
If she is secured to a board, tilt it to her left

items.q: A 40-year-old worker has a liquid industrial chemical splashed across his chest and arms. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Protect yourself, remove contaminated clothing, and flush with large volumes of water for a prolonged time; neutralizing agents can cause heat-producing reactions, and ointments trap the chemical.
opts: Wear appropriate protective equipment before contact
Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry
Flush the skin with large amounts of water
Neutralize the chemical with vinegar or baking soda
Apply burn ointment before flushing
ok: Wear appropriate protective equipment before contact
Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry
Flush the skin with large amounts of water

items.q: Which disclosures of patient information are permitted under HIPAA without the patient's written authorization? Select all that apply.
items.x: HIPAA permits sharing information for treatment, payment, and health care operations and for legally required reports such as abuse; disclosures to media or employers need authorization.
opts: Report to the receiving hospital staff for treatment
Information sent to your agency's billing office for payment
A required report of suspected child abuse to authorities
Details given to a reporter at the scene
Information shared with the patient's employer
ok: Report to the receiving hospital staff for treatment
Information sent to your agency's billing office for payment
A required report of suspected child abuse to authorities

items.q: Which are correct radio communication practices? Select all that apply.
items.x: Good radio practice includes listening before transmitting, brief plain-language messages, and echoing orders; patient names should not be broadcast, and speaking before keying the microphone cuts off words.
opts: Listen to make sure the channel is clear before transmitting
Use plain English and keep transmissions brief
Repeat back orders received from medical control
Broadcast the patient's full name for accuracy
Begin speaking before pressing the transmit button
ok: Listen to make sure the channel is clear before transmitting
Use plain English and keep transmissions brief
Repeat back orders received from medical control

items.q: A 41-year-old man has upper abdominal pain. You ask him, "Does the pain move or spread anywhere else?" Which part of OPQRST are you assessing?
items.x: The R in OPQRST covers where the pain is located and whether it radiates to another area.
items.a: Region and radiation
w: Provocation or palliation
Quality of the pain
Time and duration of the pain

items.q: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes tells you she took her usual morning insulin but skipped lunch because she was busy. In the SAMPLE history, this information falls under which component?
items.x: The L in SAMPLE is last oral intake, which is especially relevant for diabetic patients because missed meals after insulin can cause hypoglycemia.
items.a: Last oral intake
w: Past pertinent history
Medications currently taken
Signs and symptoms

items.q: A 73-year-old man lying in bed does not respond when you speak loudly to him but moans and opens his eyes when you squeeze his trapezius muscle. How should you document his mental status on the AVPU scale?
items.x: A patient who reacts only to a painful stimulus, not to voice, is documented as P on the AVPU scale.
items.a: Responsive to painful stimulus
w: Alert but disoriented to time and place
Responsive to verbal stimulus
Unresponsive to all forms of stimulus

items.q: A 56-year-old woman opens her eyes when you speak to her, answers questions but is confused about where she is, and follows your commands to squeeze your hand. What is her Glasgow Coma Scale score?
items.x: Eye opening to voice scores 3, confused speech scores 4, and obeying commands scores 6, for a total of 13.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman has vomited for 3 days. Lying down, her BP is 116/74 and pulse 86. When she sits up, she becomes lightheaded and her pulse rises to 118. How should you interpret this?
items.x: A marked rise in heart rate with dizziness on sitting or standing suggests a low circulating volume, as seen with prolonged vomiting or bleeding.
items.a: She likely has significant volume loss
w: This is a normal response to changing position
It shows that she is having an allergic reaction
It confirms that her dizziness is from an inner ear disorder

items.q: From the doorway you see a 3-year-old boy who is limp and not interacting with his mother. His breathing appears quiet and unlabored, but his skin is pale and mottled. What does this general impression suggest?
items.x: Abnormal appearance combined with abnormal circulation to the skin on the Pediatric Assessment Triangle indicates shock and a critically ill child.
items.a: He is critically ill, likely in shock
w: He has respiratory distress that is well compensated
He has an isolated breathing problem from a partial airway obstruction
He is stable, so a slower, detailed assessment is acceptable

items.q: A 4-year-old girl is drowsy and not tracking your movements. Her breathing is quiet and unlabored, and her skin color is normal. Using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, which problem is most likely?
items.x: Abnormal appearance with normal work of breathing and normal circulation points to a primary brain or metabolic problem, such as hypoglycemia, poisoning, or head injury.
items.a: A brain dysfunction such as a toxin, low glucose, or head injury
w: Compensated shock from fluid loss
Upper airway obstruction from a foreign body
Lower airway disease such as asthma or bronchiolitis

items.q: You are forming a general impression of a 2-year-old using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle. Which findings indicate increased work of breathing? Select all that apply.
items.x: Nasal flaring, retractions, and head bobbing are signs of increased work of breathing; skin color reflects circulation and playfulness reflects normal appearance.
opts: Nasal flaring
Retractions between the ribs
Head bobbing with each breath
Pink skin with brisk capillary refill
Playing with a toy while sitting on a parent's lap
ok: Nasal flaring
Retractions between the ribs
Head bobbing with each breath

items.q: A calm, content 6-month-old has a resting heart rate of 140/min and a respiratory rate of 40/min. How should you interpret these vital signs?
items.x: Normal infant heart rates are roughly 100-160/min and respiratory rates roughly 30-60/min, so these values are expected.
items.a: They are within normal limits for an infant
w: Both indicate early compensated shock
The heart rate is normal but the respiratory rate shows distress
Both are too slow and suggest hypoxia

items.q: A 47-year-old woman with a medical complaint is awake and able to answer questions. After the primary assessment, what is usually the next step?
items.x: For a responsive medical patient, the history guides the exam, so the history of present illness and SAMPLE history come before the focused secondary assessment.
items.a: Obtain the history of the present illness and SAMPLE history
w: Perform a rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment before speaking with her
Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs before asking any questions
Transport immediately and defer all history to the hospital staff

items.q: You find a 60-year-old man unresponsive on his kitchen floor with no signs of trauma. His airway is open and breathing is adequate. What is the most appropriate approach to the secondary assessment?
items.x: An unresponsive medical patient cannot give a history, so a rapid full-body exam is done first, followed by information from family, bystanders, and the scene.
items.a: Rapid full-body exam, then history from bystanders
w: Focused exam of only the chest and abdomen, guided by his chief complaint
Wait until he wakes up, then obtain a SAMPLE history from him directly
Skip the physical exam and transport, since unresponsive patients cannot be assessed

items.q: In which patient is capillary refill time most useful as an indicator of perfusion?
items.x: Capillary refill is most reliable in young children; cold exposure, age, smoking, and some medications reduce its accuracy in adults.
items.a: A 3-year-old in a warm room
w: An 82-year-old found on a cold porch
A 45-year-old smoker in freezing weather
A 70-year-old taking blood pressure medication

items.q: A 71-year-old woman with dementia is more confused than usual, has a temperature of 100.9 F, and her caregiver reports new incontinence and foul-smelling urine. What should you suspect?
items.x: Acute worsening of mental status with fever and urinary symptoms in an older adult suggests infection, such as a urinary tract infection, which can lead to sepsis.
items.a: An infection that may be developing into sepsis
w: Normal progression of her dementia over time
A psychiatric emergency requiring restraint
Simple dehydration from not drinking enough fluids

items.q: A 52-year-old man smelling strongly of alcohol is confused, has slurred speech, and is staggering. What is the main danger of assuming he is simply intoxicated?
items.x: Alcohol odor does not explain all altered mental status; hypoglycemia, head injury, stroke, infection, and other poisonings can coexist and must be considered.
items.a: Missing low glucose, head injury, or other serious causes
w: Embarrassing him in front of bystanders and family
Delaying the police response to the scene
Failing to document the odor of alcohol on the report

items.q: A 34-year-old man with epilepsy has two generalized seizures in a row without regaining consciousness between them. What is this condition called?
items.x: Continuous seizure activity, or repeated seizures without return to consciousness between them, is status epilepticus, a life-threatening emergency.
items.a: Status epilepticus
w: A postictal state
An absence seizure
A simple partial seizure

items.q: A 38-year-old woman has been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. She is cyanotic and her mouth is full of secretions. What should you do?
items.x: Prolonged seizures need airway clearance, oxygenation, ventilation as needed, ALS support for medications, and prompt transport; restraint and objects in the mouth cause injury.
items.a: Suction, give high-flow oxygen, request ALS, and transport
w: Insert a bite block between her teeth to protect her tongue
Hold her arms and legs down firmly to stop the movements
Wait until the seizure stops before beginning any care

items.q: A 25-year-old man is drowsy and confused after a witnessed seizure that has stopped. He is breathing adequately with gurgling sounds. How should you position him?
items.x: The recovery position lets secretions drain and protects the airway of a postictal patient who is breathing adequately; suction should be ready.
items.a: On his side in the recovery position
w: Supine with his legs elevated
Prone with his face turned to one side
Sitting upright with his head tilted back

items.q: A 31-year-old was found on the floor after a brief loss of consciousness. Which findings suggest a seizure rather than a simple faint? Select all that apply.
items.x: Lateral tongue biting, prolonged rhythmic activity, and a postictal period favor seizure, while warning symptoms and rapid recovery suggest syncope.
opts: Bitten side of the tongue
Confusion lasting 20 minutes after the event
Rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 2 minutes
Lightheadedness and tunnel vision just before collapse
Full alertness within seconds of lying flat
ok: Bitten side of the tongue
Confusion lasting 20 minutes after the event
Rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 2 minutes

items.q: A 79-year-old man suddenly passed out while seated at dinner, with no warning symptoms. He is now alert with normal vital signs. Why is transport important?
items.x: Syncope without a warning period, especially while seated or in an older adult, raises concern for a cardiac rhythm problem that may recur.
items.a: Sudden syncope in an older adult may indicate a dysrhythmia
w: Syncope while seated is always caused by low blood sugar
He needs observation for a likely postictal period
Fainting in an older adult always means he has had a stroke

items.q: A 22-year-old fainted when she saw blood during a lab draw. She is now alert, with normal vital signs. What is the most likely mechanism?
items.x: Vasovagal syncope occurs when a trigger such as fear or pain stimulates the vagus nerve, slowing the heart rate and dilating blood vessels so that brain blood flow briefly falls.
items.a: A vagal response that slowed her heart and dilated vessels
w: A seizure triggered by a sudden emotional shock
A sudden drop in her blood glucose level
An allergic reaction to the needle or skin cleanser

items.q: Which features of a fainting episode raise concern for a serious underlying cause? Select all that apply.
items.x: Exertional syncope, associated chest pain or palpitations, and sudden collapse without warning in older adults suggest a cardiac cause; brief faints with a clear trigger are usually benign.
opts: Fainting during exercise
Chest pain or palpitations before the event
No warning symptoms in an older adult
Lightheadedness after standing for a long time in a hot room
Fainting after seeing an injury, with quick recovery
ok: Fainting during exercise
Chest pain or palpitations before the event
No warning symptoms in an older adult

items.q: Which findings suggest hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypoglycemia typically develops quickly with sympathetic signs such as diaphoresis and agitation, while hyperglycemia develops slowly with thirst, Kussmaul respirations, and fruity breath.
opts: Cool, pale, sweaty skin
Onset over minutes
Anxiety or combativeness
Deep, rapid respirations
Fruity odor on the breath
Increased thirst over several days
ok: Cool, pale, sweaty skin
Onset over minutes
Anxiety or combativeness

items.q: A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes has had flu symptoms and vomiting for 2 days. She now has abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing. Why is she breathing this way?
items.x: In diabetic ketoacidosis, deep rapid respirations blow off carbon dioxide to offset the metabolic acidosis caused by ketones.
items.a: Her body is compensating for acid buildup
w: She is anxious and having a panic attack
She has inhaled vomit into her lungs
Her blood sugar has dropped dangerously low

items.q: A 67-year-old man was hypoglycemic, received oral glucose, and is now alert. He takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication and wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
items.x: Some diabetes medications last many hours, so hypoglycemia can recur after a temporary improvement; this should be explained during any refusal discussion.
items.a: His glucose may drop again
w: Oral glucose may cause high blood sugar later
He may have an allergic reaction to the glucose
He will need insulin within the next hour

items.q: A 68-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Her blood glucose is 38 mg/dL. What should you keep in mind?
items.x: Low blood glucose can cause focal weakness and speech changes that look like a stroke, so it must be identified and treated, with reassessment of the neurologic findings.
items.a: Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke
w: The low glucose confirms she has had a stroke
Glucose readings are unreliable in stroke patients
She should be given nothing and reassessed in an hour

items.q: An 81-year-old with type 2 diabetes has become confused over the past week. She is very dehydrated, has no fruity breath odor, and breathes normally. Her glucose meter reads "HI." What condition is most likely?
items.x: Older type 2 diabetics can develop extremely high glucose and severe dehydration over days without significant ketone production, so Kussmaul breathing and fruity odor are often absent.
items.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Insulin shock
Acute alcohol intoxication

items.q: A 30-year-old man has itchy hives on his arms after eating shrimp. He has no history of severe reactions, no breathing difficulty, no swelling of the face or throat, and normal vital signs. What is appropriate?
items.x: Isolated skin findings without respiratory, circulatory, or other systemic signs indicate a mild allergic reaction, but it can progress, so close monitoring is essential.
items.a: Monitor closely for progression during transport
w: Administer an epinephrine auto-injector right away
Insert an oral airway to prevent swelling
Place him supine with legs elevated and give nothing else

items.q: A 10-year-old with a peanut allergy ate a cookie at a party. She has stridor, a hoarse voice, and hives, and has her prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. What is the most important action?
items.x: Airway involvement with known allergen exposure is anaphylaxis, and early epinephrine is the treatment that reverses airway swelling and shock.
items.a: Administer her epinephrine auto-injector
w: Have her drink water to rinse the allergen down
Give high-flow oxygen and wait to see if it resolves
Transport first and let the hospital decide on treatment

items.q: A 26-year-old's breathing and blood pressure improved after his epinephrine auto-injector. He now feels fine and wants to refuse transport. Why should he be transported?
items.x: Epinephrine acts for a short time, and anaphylaxis can recur or a second phase can develop hours later, so observation at a hospital is needed.
items.a: Symptoms can return as the epinephrine wears off
w: The epinephrine will cause a dangerously high blood sugar
He needs a second injection given at the hospital
He is at risk for low blood pressure from the injection itself

items.q: A 45-year-old woman stung by a wasp has wheezing, facial swelling, and a BP of 78/50. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Anaphylaxis requires epinephrine, oxygen, ALS support, and rapid transport; tourniquets are not used for stings and exertion worsens shock.
opts: Administer epinephrine by auto-injector per protocol
Provide high-flow oxygen
Request ALS and transport promptly
Apply a tight tourniquet above the sting site
Have her walk to the ambulance to save time
ok: Administer epinephrine by auto-injector per protocol
Provide high-flow oxygen
Request ALS and transport promptly

items.q: A 2-year-old swallowed liquid drain cleaner. There are burns around his mouth and he is drooling. What should you do?
items.x: Vomiting re-exposes the esophagus and airway to a corrosive, so it is never induced; giving anything by mouth should be guided by medical direction or poison control.
items.a: Do not induce vomiting; transport and contact poison control
w: Make him vomit to empty the stomach quickly
Give him milk to neutralize the chemical
Give him a large glass of water to dilute the chemical

items.q: A 50-year-old man is removed from a closed garage where a car was running. He has a headache and nausea, and his SpO2 reads 99%. How should you interpret the SpO2?
items.x: Standard pulse oximeters read carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin as oxygenated, so the reading can be falsely high; treat suspected CO exposure with high-flow oxygen.
items.a: It may be falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen
w: It confirms that he has no carbon monoxide exposure
It shows that he needs no supplemental oxygen
It means his headache must have another cause

items.q: A family of three has headaches and confusion after running a generator indoors. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: CO patients need removal from the source, high-flow oxygen, and evaluation; symptoms improving in fresh air does not rule out significant poisoning, and routine pulse oximetry is unreliable.
opts: Remove them from the environment if it is safe to do so
Give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Transport for evaluation even if they feel better
Use pulse oximetry to decide who needs oxygen
Skip oxygen once the windows are opened
ok: Remove them from the environment if it is safe to do so
Give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Transport for evaluation even if they feel better

items.q: You arrive at a farm where two workers have collapsed inside a manure storage tank. A third worker climbed in to help and also collapsed. What should you do?
items.x: Multiple collapses in a confined space suggest a toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere; only rescuers with proper training and supplied-air equipment should enter.
items.a: Stay out and request specialized rescue
w: Enter quickly while holding your breath
Lower a rope into the tank and climb in after it
Enter wearing a surgical mask over your face

items.q: A landscaper has a dry chemical powder on his arms and clothing. The label says it reacts with water. What should you do first?
items.x: Dry chemicals should be brushed off and contaminated clothing removed before any flushing, especially when the product reacts with water.
items.a: Brush off the powder and remove contaminated clothing
w: Flush the area immediately with large amounts of water
Wipe the skin with an alcohol pad to remove it
Cover the area with a dressing and leave it in place

items.q: A worker got a liquid industrial chemical splashed in both eyes. Which action is most important?
items.x: Prolonged irrigation is the key treatment for chemical eye exposure and should continue during transport when possible.
items.a: Flush the eyes with clean water for at least 20 minutes
w: Patch both eyes and transport without flushing them
Rinse briefly with saline and stop when the pain eases
Have the patient rub his eyes to clear the chemical

items.q: A 28-year-old is found unresponsive in a public restroom with drug paraphernalia nearby. Which findings are consistent with an opioid overdose? Select all that apply.
items.x: The opioid toxidrome is respiratory depression, constricted pupils, and depressed mental status; dilated pupils and hot, dry skin suggest other toxidromes.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Respiratory rate of 6/min
Decreased level of responsiveness
Widely dilated pupils
Hot, flushed, dry skin
Respiratory rate of 32/min
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Respiratory rate of 6/min
Decreased level of responsiveness

items.q: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who overdosed on an opioid is awake and breathing well. He wants to leave. What is the main risk of refusal?
items.x: Many opioids act longer than naloxone, so respiratory depression can return after the antidote wears off.
items.a: The naloxone may wear off before the opioid
w: He will become hypoglycemic within minutes
The naloxone will cause delayed anaphylaxis
He is likely to develop dangerously high blood pressure

items.q: A 24-year-old who used cocaine is agitated and sweating heavily, with a heart rate of 142, a temperature of 104 F, and dilated pupils. Which toxidrome does this represent?
items.x: Stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and dilated pupils.
items.a: Sympathomimetic
w: Opioid
Cholinergic
Sedative-hypnotic

items.q: A 15-year-old took a large amount of an over-the-counter antihistamine. Which findings would you expect?
items.x: Anticholinergic poisoning causes dry, hot, red skin, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate, and confusion, the opposite of the wet cholinergic picture.
items.a: Hot, dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils
w: Cool, sweaty skin with pinpoint pupils
Heavy drooling, tearing, and frequent urination
Slow breathing with pinpoint pupils and no agitation

items.q: A 55-year-old who drinks heavily every day stopped 2 days ago. He is tremulous, sweating, and seeing insects on the wall. Why is this serious?
items.x: Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which carries significant mortality and needs medical care.
items.a: Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and death
w: Withdrawal symptoms are mild and fade within an hour
It shows that he is intoxicated again and needs only rest
Hallucinations confirm a primary psychiatric illness

items.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden, severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. You feel a pulsating mass above his navel. His BP is 90/58. What should you do?
items.x: These findings suggest a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm; avoid vigorous palpation, treat for shock, and transport rapidly to an appropriate facility.
items.a: Treat for shock and transport promptly
w: Palpate the mass firmly to estimate its size
Have him walk to the stretcher to save time
Give him water to ease his discomfort

items.q: A 44-year-old woman has right upper quadrant abdominal pain that began after a fatty meal and spreads to her right shoulder. Which organ is most likely involved?
items.x: Gallbladder inflammation often follows fatty meals and refers pain to the right shoulder or scapula.
items.a: Gallbladder
w: Appendix
Spleen
Left kidney

items.q: A 19-year-old has pain that began around his navel and over several hours moved to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and a low-grade fever. What should you suspect?
items.x: Pain that starts near the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and fever, is classic for appendicitis.
items.a: Appendicitis
w: Gallbladder disease
Pancreatitis
Kidney stone

items.q: A 61-year-old has had black, tarry, foul-smelling stools for 2 days and feels dizzy when standing. What does this suggest?
items.x: Black, tarry stool (melena) is digested blood, usually from the stomach or upper intestine, and dizziness on standing suggests significant blood loss.
items.a: Bleeding in the upper digestive tract
w: Bleeding from hemorrhoids
A bladder infection
Food poisoning from undercooked meat

items.q: A 37-year-old has severe abdominal pain with nausea. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Abdominal pain care is supportive: position of comfort, nothing by mouth, monitoring for shock, and airway protection if vomiting occurs.

Give nothing by mouth
Watch for signs of shock
Be ready to suction or position for vomiting
Give a small meal to settle the stomach
Apply a heating pad to the abdomen
ok: Allow a position of comfort
Give nothing by mouth
Watch for signs of shock
Be ready to suction or position for vomiting

items.q: A 58-year-old man with a long history of heavy drinking is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. What is your first priority?
items.x: Massive upper GI bleeding, such as from esophageal varices, threatens the airway first; position and suction to prevent aspiration while treating for shock.
items.a: Keep the airway clear with suction and positioning
w: Give him water to rinse his mouth between episodes
Lay him flat on his back and elevate his legs
Collect the vomit to measure its volume

items.q: Which findings suggest gastrointestinal bleeding? Select all that apply.
items.x: Coffee-ground emesis, melena, and orthostatic symptoms indicate GI blood loss; a stiff neck with fever and flank-to-groin pain suggest other conditions.
opts: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Black, tarry stools
Dizziness or fainting on standing
Fever with a stiff neck
Pain radiating from the flank to the groin
ok: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Black, tarry stools
Dizziness or fainting on standing

items.q: A 66-year-old dialysis patient missed his last two treatments. He is weak, and his pulse is 46 and irregular. What is the greatest concern?
items.x: Missed dialysis allows potassium to build up, which can slow the heart and cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
items.a: A high potassium level causing a dangerous rhythm
w: Low blood sugar from skipping meals
Dehydration from too much fluid removal
Infection of his dialysis access site

items.q: A 59-year-old just left her dialysis center and is bleeding steadily from her AV fistula needle site. What should you do first?
items.x: Direct pressure controls most fistula bleeding; escalate per bleeding control guidelines if pressure fails, but avoid clamping the fistula.
items.a: Apply firm direct pressure to the site
w: Apply a tourniquet before trying anything else
Clamp the fistula shut with a hemostat
Elevate the arm and wait for clotting

items.q: A 70-year-old dialysis patient who missed treatment is short of breath, with crackles in both lungs and swollen ankles. What should you do?
items.x: Missed dialysis can cause fluid overload and pulmonary edema; an upright position, oxygen, ventilatory support as needed, and transport are appropriate.
items.a: Sit him upright and support his breathing
w: Lay him flat with his legs raised
Give him fluids by mouth to restore volume
Apply cold packs to his chest and legs

items.q: A 35-year-old man is pacing and cannot get comfortable. He has severe left flank pain radiating to his groin and blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with restlessness and hematuria is typical of a kidney stone.
items.a: Kidney stone
w: Appendicitis
Abdominal aortic aneurysm
Testicular infection

items.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has a temperature of 96.2 F, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, BP 94/58, and new confusion. What should you suspect?
items.x: Older adults with serious infections may have low or normal temperatures; tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and altered mentation point to sepsis.
items.a: Sepsis, even without a fever
w: Normal aging changes in vital signs
Mild dehydration only
Hypothermia from a cold room

items.q: A 62-year-old with a cough and fever is being assessed. Which findings raise concern for sepsis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Altered mentation, a respiratory rate of 22 or more, and a systolic BP of 100 or less in a patient with infection suggest sepsis and the need for early notification.
opts: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26/min
Systolic BP of 92 mmHg
Respiratory rate of 14/min
Clear speech and normal orientation
ok: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26/min
Systolic BP of 92 mmHg

items.q: You suspect sepsis in a 58-year-old woman who is hypotensive and confused. Which action most improves her care?
items.x: Sepsis outcomes depend on early antibiotics and fluids, so prompt transport and early hospital notification matter, along with oxygen and warmth as needed.
items.a: Notify the hospital early of possible sepsis
w: Delay transport to obtain repeated vital signs
Allow her to walk to the ambulance
Give her large amounts of water by mouth

items.q: A 30-year-old man was extremely agitated, sweating, and fighting with police. He is now physically restrained and suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
items.x: Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, restrained patient can signal respiratory or cardiac arrest, so assess breathing and circulation immediately.
items.a: Immediately check his breathing and pulse
w: Assume he has calmed down and continue transport
Tighten the restraints to prevent further struggle
Leave him alone so he does not become agitated again

items.q: A violent patient must be restrained for transport. Which practices promote safety? Select all that apply.
items.x: Restraint must never compress the chest or use prone hobble positions; adequate personnel, a safe position, and continuous monitoring reduce the risk of sudden death.
opts: Have enough trained personnel to control each limb
Keep him supine or on his side
Monitor his airway and breathing continuously
Check circulation beyond each restraint
Place him prone with wrists tied to ankles
Kneel on his back until he stops resisting
ok: Have enough trained personnel to control each limb
Keep him supine or on his side
Monitor his airway and breathing continuously
Check circulation beyond each restraint

items.q: You are called for a 40-year-old man who is anxious and agitated but not violent. How should you position yourself while talking with him?
items.x: Keeping your exit route clear lets you leave if the situation escalates; do not let the patient come between you and the door.
items.a: With a clear path to the exit
w: Between him and the only door in the room
Directly face to face within arm's reach
Behind him, out of his line of sight

items.q: A 27-year-old woman is breathing rapidly after an argument and has tingling around her mouth and in her hands. What should you do?
items.x: Coaching slower breathing and reassurance help anxiety-related hyperventilation; paper bag rebreathing is unsafe because serious medical causes of rapid breathing may be missed.
items.a: Reassure her and coach her breathing
w: Have her breathe into a paper bag
Tell her the symptoms are all in her head
Restrain her until her breathing slows

items.q: A 64-year-old man says he is "tired of living." Which findings increase his risk of suicide? Select all that apply.
items.x: Prior attempts, a specific plan with access to lethal means, and recent loss with isolation increase risk; social support and future plans are protective.
opts: A previous suicide attempt
A detailed plan with access to a firearm
Recently widowed and living alone
Strong support from friends and family
Plans for an upcoming family trip
ok: A previous suicide attempt
A detailed plan with access to a firearm
Recently widowed and living alone

items.q: A 17-year-old is withdrawn and tearful after a breakup. What is the best approach?
items.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to find out whether she is in danger.
items.a: Ask her directly if she is thinking of suicide
w: Avoid the topic because asking may put the idea in her head
Tell her she will feel better soon and change the subject
Ask her parents but not her about suicidal thoughts

items.q: A 36-year-old man says he took a bottle of pills to end his life. He is alert and refuses transport. What should you do?
items.x: A patient with a suicide attempt and possible overdose lacks capacity to refuse; do not leave him, and use law enforcement and medical direction per local protocol.
items.a: Stay with him and involve law enforcement and medical direction
w: Have him sign a refusal form and leave
Leave a crisis hotline number and clear the scene
Wait outside until he changes his mind

items.q: A 32-year-old hiker is shivering, alert, and talking clearly after falling into a cold stream. What is the best care?
items.x: Mild hypothermia is treated by removing wet clothing, insulating, and passive or external rewarming in a warm environment.
items.a: Remove wet clothing and warm her in a heated area
w: Rub her arms and legs briskly to restore circulation
Give her a drink of alcohol to warm her up
Have her walk quickly to generate body heat

items.q: A 74-year-old was found in an unheated house. He is unresponsive, with very cold skin. How should you check his pulse?
items.x: In severe hypothermia, the pulse may be very slow and faint, so it should be checked for longer than usual before deciding on CPR.
items.a: Feel for a pulse longer than usual
w: Check briefly and start CPR if none is felt immediately
Skip the pulse check and begin CPR at once
Check only the radial pulse

items.q: A 68-year-old is moderately hypothermic after a night outdoors. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Gentle handling, removal of wet clothing, and warming of the trunk are recommended; rubbing extremities and exertion can cause tissue injury or dysrhythmias.
opts: Handle him gently
Remove wet clothing
Apply heat packs to the armpits and groin
Massage his arms and legs
Have him walk to the ambulance
ok: Handle him gently
Remove wet clothing
Apply heat packs to the armpits and groin

items.q: A skier's cheeks are pale and numb, but the skin is soft and regains color when warmed. What condition is this?
items.x: Frostnip is superficial cold injury with blanched, numb skin that remains soft and recovers with warming.
items.a: Frostnip
w: Deep frostbite
Trench foot
Heat exhaustion

items.q: A 46-year-old roofer working in the heat has painful cramps in his legs. He is alert and sweating. What should you do?
items.x: Heat cramps from salt and fluid loss respond to rest, cooling, and oral electrolyte replacement in an alert patient.
items.a: Move him to a cool place and give electrolyte fluid by mouth
w: Apply a tourniquet to his legs to relieve cramping
Immerse him immediately in an ice water bath
Have him continue working to stretch the muscles

items.q: A 38-year-old is dizzy and nauseated after working in the heat. Her skin is pale and sweaty, her heart rate is 110, and she is fully alert and oriented. What is most likely?
items.x: Heat exhaustion causes weakness, dizziness, sweating, and tachycardia with normal mental status; altered mental status indicates heat stroke.
items.a: Heat exhaustion
w: Heat stroke
Heat cramps
Hypoglycemia

items.q: A 21-year-old soldier collapses during a march. He is confused and his skin is hot. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Exertional heat stroke needs rapid cooling on scene, with cold-water immersion being the most effective method when available.
opts: Remove excess clothing
Cool rapidly, ideally with cold-water immersion
Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits, and groin
Rub his skin with alcohol
Delay cooling until arrival at the hospital
ok: Remove excess clothing
Cool rapidly, ideally with cold-water immersion
Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits, and groin

items.q: An 11-year-old was pulled from a pool. She coughed up water and is now alert and breathing normally. Her parents want no transport. What is your concern?
items.x: Aspiration of water can cause delayed respiratory compromise, so evaluation after a submersion event is important even when the patient looks well.
items.a: Breathing problems can develop hours later
w: She has a high risk of hypothermia from the warm pool
She may have swallowed too much chlorine
She may become dehydrated from swallowing water

items.q: A 16-year-old dove into the shallow end of a lake and is floating face down. What should you suspect?
items.x: Diving into shallow water causes cervical spine injuries; remove the patient from the water with in-line stabilization while maintaining the airway.
items.a: A spinal injury
w: Hyperthermia
Decompression sickness
Anaphylaxis from lake water

items.q: A 9-year-old is pulled from a lake. She is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. What should you do?
items.x: Drowning arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilations are especially important; attempts to drain water delay care.
items.a: Begin CPR with emphasis on effective ventilations
w: Drain water from her lungs before starting CPR
Perform abdominal thrusts to remove water
Do not attempt CPR because she was submerged

items.q: Lightning struck a group of hikers. One is screaming in pain, one is confused, and one is apneic and pulseless. Whom should you treat first?
items.x: In lightning strikes, those in respiratory or cardiac arrest often survive with prompt care, so reverse triage puts them first.
items.a: The apneic, pulseless hiker
w: The hiker who is screaming in pain
The confused hiker
All are equal, so treat whoever is closest

items.q: A 39-year-old was bitten while moving wood. She now has severe abdominal cramping and a rigid abdomen. Which bite is most likely?
items.x: Black widow venom acts on nerves and causes muscle cramping and abdominal rigidity, while brown recluse bites cause local tissue damage.
items.a: Black widow spider
w: Brown recluse spider
Non-venomous snake
Domestic cat

items.q: A 23-year-old was stung by a bee and the stinger is still in his skin. What should you do?
items.x: Prompt removal limits venom delivery; the method matters less than speed, and scraping is a common technique.
items.a: Remove it quickly, such as by scraping with a card
w: Leave it in place for removal at the hospital
Squeeze it out between your fingers slowly
Cover it with a tight dressing to trap the venom

items.q: A 30-year-old stepped on a stingray. She has severe foot pain and a small wound. What is appropriate?
items.x: Hot water immersion, without causing burns, helps relieve pain from many marine venoms.
items.a: Immerse the foot in hot water as tolerated
w: Apply ice to the wound
Apply a tight tourniquet above the ankle
Rub sand into the wound to remove venom

items.q: A 42-year-old scuba diver has joint pain and tingling in his arms 2 hours after surfacing. What should you suspect?
items.x: Nitrogen bubbles forming after a dive cause joint pain, skin changes, and neurologic symptoms; high-flow oxygen and transport to a facility able to provide hyperbaric care are needed.
items.a: Decompression sickness
w: Heat exhaustion
Arterial gas embolism
Carbon monoxide poisoning

items.q: A 28-year-old diver ascended quickly and, within a minute of surfacing, became unresponsive with one-sided weakness. What is most likely?
items.x: Rapid ascent can force air into the arterial circulation, causing stroke-like signs immediately after surfacing.
items.a: Arterial gas embolism
w: Decompression sickness
Hypoglycemia
Heat stroke

items.q: During a delivery, the baby's head has delivered and you have checked for a cord. What is the next step?
items.x: Gentle downward guidance helps the upper shoulder deliver, then upward guidance for the lower shoulder; never pull hard on the head.
items.a: Support the head and guide it gently downward to deliver the upper shoulder
w: Pull firmly on the head to deliver the body quickly
Push the head back up to slow down the delivery
Wait until the next day for the mother to deliver the shoulders

items.q: When should you suction a newborn's mouth and nose after delivery?
items.x: Routine suctioning is not recommended for newborns; suction the mouth before the nose only when secretions obstruct breathing or ventilation is needed.
items.a: Only if secretions block the airway
w: Always, immediately after delivery
Only after the placenta delivers
Never, under any circumstances

items.q: A healthy term newborn is crying with good tone. When should the umbilical cord be clamped?
items.x: Delayed cord clamping for at least 30 to 60 seconds is recommended for vigorous newborns.
items.a: After at least 30 to 60 seconds
w: Immediately before the baby breathes
Only after the placenta delivers
Within 5 seconds of delivery

items.q: After delivery of the baby, the placenta has not yet delivered. What should you do?
items.x: Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus; the placenta should deliver naturally and be bagged for examination.
items.a: Allow it to deliver naturally and bring it to the hospital
w: Pull firmly on the cord to speed it up
Push on the uterus forcefully to expel it
Cut the cord close to the vagina and leave the placenta

items.q: During delivery, the umbilical cord is wrapped tightly around the baby's neck and cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
items.x: A tight nuchal cord that cannot be loosened must be clamped and cut so delivery can continue safely.
items.a: Clamp the cord in two places and cut between them
w: Pull the baby out quickly to loosen the cord
Push the baby's head back in
Leave it and continue the delivery

items.q: During a breech delivery, the body has delivered but the head has not after 3 minutes. What should you do?
items.x: Creating an airway by placing fingers alongside the baby's face allows breathing while transport continues.
items.a: Place gloved fingers to form an airway for the baby
w: Pull firmly on the legs to deliver the head
Push the body back into the vagina
Wait until the mother can be transported

items.q: After the baby's head delivers, it pulls back tightly against the mother's perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. What should you do?
items.x: This is shoulder dystocia; flexing the mother's hips by drawing her knees to her chest widens the pelvis and can free the shoulder.
items.a: Have her pull her knees back toward her chest
w: Pull hard on the baby's head
Push on the top of the uterus
Push the head back into the vagina

items.q: A 37-weeks-pregnant woman is having a seizure. Her BP is 172/112. What is appropriate?
items.x: Eclampsia is life-threatening; protect the airway, position on the left side, give oxygen, minimize stimulation, and transport rapidly.
items.a: Place her on her left side, give oxygen, and transport rapidly
w: Give her oral glucose and wait
Put her flat on her back and elevate her legs
Place a bite block in her mouth

items.q: A woman who gave birth 10 days ago has a seizure. Her BP is 170/110. What should you suspect?
items.x: Preeclampsia and eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, so new seizures and hypertension postpartum are concerning.
items.a: Eclampsia after delivery
w: Epilepsy that she has always had
A simple faint
Normal changes after childbirth

items.q: A woman 33 weeks pregnant has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
items.x: Placenta previa causes painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy; never perform a vaginal exam.
items.a: Placenta previa
w: Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Normal labor

items.q: A 35-weeks-pregnant woman has sudden abdominal pain. Which findings suggest placental abruption? Select all that apply.
items.x: Abruption causes painful, rigid uterus and concealed bleeding that leads to shock, while painless bleeding suggests previa.
opts: Painful, rigid abdomen
Shock signs out of proportion to visible bleeding
Dark red vaginal bleeding
Painless bright red bleeding
Normal soft uterus
ok: Painful, rigid abdomen
Shock signs out of proportion to visible bleeding
Dark red vaginal bleeding

items.q: A 27-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding with cramping and has passed clots and tissue. Her pulse is 116. What should you do?
items.x: A likely miscarriage with tachycardia needs shock care and transport; place a pad over the vaginal opening, never pack it, and bring tissue for examination.
items.a: Treat for shock and bring the passed tissue to the hospital
w: Discard the tissue in a biohazard bag to reduce infection risk
Pack gauze into the vagina to stop the bleeding
Reassure her that early pregnancy bleeding is normal and suggest she follow up with her doctor

items.q: A 30-year-old woman is in labor with her second child. Which findings indicate that delivery is imminent? Select all that apply.
items.x: Crowning, the urge to bear down, and strong contractions about 2 minutes apart signal imminent delivery; ruptured membranes or bloody show alone do not.
opts: Crowning during contractions
A strong urge to push or move her bowels
Contractions about 2 minutes apart and lasting about a minute
Her water broke 6 hours ago, with contractions 10 minutes apart
A small amount of blood-tinged mucus with no contractions
ok: Crowning during contractions
A strong urge to push or move her bowels
Contractions about 2 minutes apart and lasting about a minute

items.q: You have just delivered a baby at home. The mother's abdomen remains about as large as before, and strong contractions begin again a few minutes later. What should you suspect?
items.x: A uterus that stays large with renewed contractions after the first birth suggests multiple gestation; prepare for a second delivery and additional newborn care.
items.a: A second baby is about to deliver
w: The placenta is delivering and nothing else is expected
She has a uterine rupture and needs immediate surgery
This is normal and she can be transported without further preparation

items.q: A term baby is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid. He is crying vigorously with good muscle tone. What should you do?
items.x: A vigorous newborn needs routine care (warm, dry, stimulate, clear the airway only if needed) whether or not meconium is present.
items.a: Provide routine newborn care
w: Suction deeply below the vocal cords before stimulating him
Begin positive pressure ventilation at once
Withhold drying until the meconium is suctioned

items.q: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110/min, a grimace to stimulation, some flexion of the arms and legs, and a weak, slow cry. What is the APGAR score?
items.x: Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1, and respiration 1 total 6.

items.q: A newborn is limp and not breathing immediately after birth. How should the APGAR score affect your initial care?
items.x: The APGAR score describes the newborn's condition at 1 and 5 minutes but is not used to decide whether to start resuscitation; breathing and heart rate guide care.
items.a: Do not wait for it to begin resuscitation
w: Wait for the 1-minute score to decide whether to ventilate
Begin compressions only if the 1-minute score is below 7
Delay ventilation until both the 1-minute and 5-minute scores are known

items.q: Despite effective ventilation, a newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min and you begin chest compressions. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
items.x: Neonatal resuscitation uses a 3:1 ratio, giving about 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute.

items.q: Two minutes after birth, a crying newborn has a pink trunk and lips but bluish hands and feet. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Acrocyanosis, bluish extremities with a pink central body, is common in the first minutes of life and does not require treatment.
items.a: It is a normal finding
w: It indicates severe hypoxia that requires chest compressions
It is a sign of shock that requires immediate fluid replacement
It suggests a heart defect and requires high-flow oxygen by mask

items.q: Which method gives the most accurate heart rate in a newborn who needs resuscitation in the field?
items.x: Auscultation of the chest is more reliable than palpation in newborns, whose peripheral pulses are difficult to feel.
items.a: Listening over the chest
w: Palpating the radial pulse at the wrist
Palpating the carotid pulse in the neck
Estimating from capillary refill time

items.q: You have dried and stimulated a newborn. Which findings indicate a need for positive pressure ventilation? Select all that apply.
items.x: Apnea, gasping, or a heart rate below 100/min after initial steps calls for positive pressure ventilation; a crying newborn with a normal heart rate and acrocyanosis does not.
opts: Apnea
Gasping respirations
A heart rate of 80/min
Crying with a heart rate of 150/min
Bluish hands and feet with a pink trunk
ok: Apnea
Gasping respirations
A heart rate of 80/min

items.q: You are providing positive pressure ventilation to an apneic newborn with a heart rate of 90/min. At what rate should you ventilate?
items.x: Newborn positive pressure ventilation is given at 40 to 60 breaths per minute, watching for chest rise and a rising heart rate.
items.a: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
w: 10 to 12 breaths per minute
20 to 30 breaths per minute
100 to 120 breaths per minute

items.q: A 20-month-old with a fever of 103 F has had a seizure. Which findings suggest something more serious than a simple febrile seizure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalized, and do not recur within 24 hours; focal seizures, recurrence, or signs of meningitis suggest a more serious cause, while a quick fever rise and brief drowsiness are typical.
opts: A stiff neck with a purple, non-blanching rash
Jerking limited to one side of the body
A second seizure later the same day
A rapid rise in temperature before the seizure
Drowsiness for a few minutes afterward
ok: A stiff neck with a purple, non-blanching rash
Jerking limited to one side of the body
A second seizure later the same day

items.q: An 8-month-old has had diarrhea for 3 days. She is lethargic, with a heart rate of 190/min, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and cool, mottled extremities. What does this indicate?
items.x: Lethargy, marked tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and cool, mottled skin indicate shock; give oxygen, keep her warm, and transport rapidly.
items.a: Shock from severe dehydration
w: Mild dehydration that only needs oral fluids
Normal findings for an infant who has been sleeping
A fever that has broken and is resolving

items.q: A 2-month-old is found unresponsive in his crib. He is warm, has no lividity or rigor mortis, and has no pulse. What should you do?
items.x: Without obvious signs of death, an infant in cardiac arrest should receive immediate resuscitation; questions about the cause come later.
items.a: Begin CPR and transport
w: Pronounce death on scene and call the medical examiner
Interview the parents in detail before touching the infant
Wait for law enforcement to photograph the scene first

items.q: A 3-month-old briefly stopped breathing, turned blue, and went limp, then recovered within a minute. She now looks well. The parents ask whether transport is needed. What should you advise?
items.x: A brief resolved unexplained event can be caused by serious problems such as infection, seizures, heart rhythm problems, or abuse, so evaluation is recommended even when the infant appears well.
items.a: Transport for evaluation
w: No care is needed because she looks normal now
Transport only if it happens again in front of you
Give her a bottle and recheck her in an hour

items.q: You are caring for an injured 2-year-old. Which findings suggest possible abuse? Select all that apply.
items.x: Inconsistent histories, multiple healing stages, immersion burn patterns, and delays in seeking care are red flags; shin bruises and forehead bumps are common accidental toddler injuries.
opts: An explanation that does not fit the injury
Bruises in many different stages of healing
Burns on both feet with sharp lines like a sock
A long delay before calling for help
Bruises on the shins of an active toddler
A single bump on the forehead from a fall while walking
ok: An explanation that does not fit the injury
Bruises in many different stages of healing
Burns on both feet with sharp lines like a sock
A long delay before calling for help

items.q: You suspect that a 5-year-old's injuries were caused by abuse. The caregiver is present. What should you do?
items.x: Suspected abuse must be reported according to state law and agency policy; avoid confrontation, care for the child, and document objectively.
items.a: Report your concerns as required by law
w: Confront the caregiver about your suspicions
Avoid transporting the child to prevent conflict
Ask the child repeatedly until he admits what happened

items.q: A 4-month-old is lethargic and has been vomiting, with no visible injuries. The caregiver says the baby was "fine an hour ago" and gives a vague story. What should you suspect?
items.x: Unexplained lethargy and vomiting in an infant, with an inconsistent history, can be signs of abusive head trauma even without external injury.
items.a: Abusive head trauma
w: Normal teething discomfort
Colic that will resolve on its own
Normal infant sleepiness after a feeding

items.q: An 82-year-old takes nine medications. Her family says she became confused and fell twice since a new medication was added last week. What should you consider?
items.x: Polypharmacy is a common cause of new confusion and falls in older adults; bring the medications or a list to the hospital.
items.a: An adverse drug effect or interaction
w: Normal aging that requires no further evaluation
Long-standing dementia that has not changed
Too little sleep, with no other cause to consider

items.q: A 78-year-old woman fell in her bathroom and has hip pain. Why is it important to ask what happened just before the fall?
items.x: Falls in older adults are often caused by syncope, dysrhythmias, stroke, hypoglycemia, or medications, and these must be identified along with the injury.
items.a: A medical problem may have caused it
w: To decide who is legally responsible
To determine which hospital she prefers
To confirm whether she needs a walker

items.q: You respond to an 86-year-old woman who lives with her son. Which findings suggest possible elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
items.x: Unexplained injuries, a controlling caregiver, and signs of neglect are red flags; a well-kept home and hearing loss are not.
opts: Unexplained bruises in different stages of healing
A son who answers every question and will not leave her alone
Poor hygiene with untreated pressure ulcers
A tidy home with medications organized in a pillbox
Mild hearing loss
ok: Unexplained bruises in different stages of healing
A son who answers every question and will not leave her alone
Poor hygiene with untreated pressure ulcers

items.q: An 85-year-old has mild abdominal discomfort, normal vital signs, and no fever. Why is transport still recommended?
items.x: Older adults often have blunted pain, fever, and heart rate responses, so serious conditions can present with mild symptoms and normal vital signs.
items.a: Serious problems may present subtly in older adults
w: Older adults usually exaggerate their pain
Abdominal pain in older adults is almost always minor
Normal vital signs rule out serious illness in older adults

items.q: A 76-year-old with known dementia has become much more confused and agitated over the past day. What does this suggest?
items.x: A sudden change in mental status is delirium, which often signals infection, dehydration, medication effects, or another acute medical problem.
items.a: Delirium from an acute medical problem
w: Expected progression of dementia
A new psychiatric illness only
A normal change in older adults

items.q: A 54-year-old on a home ventilator is in respiratory distress and the ventilator alarm is sounding. What should you do?
items.x: When a ventilator-dependent patient is in distress, remove the ventilator from the equation and ventilate manually while looking for the cause.
items.a: Disconnect and ventilate with a BVM
w: Silence the alarm and continue to watch him
Increase the ventilator rate and wait
Call the equipment company before any care

items.q: A 10-year-old with a tracheostomy who uses a home ventilator is in respiratory distress. Which problems should you consider? Select all that apply.
items.x: Displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, and equipment failure are common causes of distress in patients with a tracheostomy and ventilator.
opts: The tube has come out of position
The tube is blocked with mucus
The ventilator or tubing is malfunctioning
The child is breathing too deeply
The oxygen tank is too full
ok: The tube has come out of position
The tube is blocked with mucus
The ventilator or tubing is malfunctioning

items.q: A 64-year-old with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is alert and talking. You cannot feel a radial pulse or hear a blood pressure. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Many LVADs produce continuous flow with little or no pulse; assess mental status and skin perfusion, and contact the device coordinator listed on the equipment.
items.a: It may be normal with this device
w: He is in cardiac arrest
He needs immediate CPR
The device has failed

items.q: A 70-year-old with a gastrostomy feeding tube develops coughing and difficulty breathing right after a feeding. What should you suspect?
items.x: Patients with feeding tubes can aspirate stomach contents; position them upright, suction as needed, and support breathing.
items.a: Aspiration of the feeding
w: An allergic reaction to the formula
Hypoglycemia from the feeding
Dehydration from the feeding

items.q: A 45-year-old receiving long-term treatment through a central venous catheter has a fever, chills, and a heart rate of 118. What should you suspect?
items.x: Central lines provide a direct route for infection into the blood, so fever and tachycardia in these patients raise concern for sepsis.
items.a: A serious bloodstream infection
w: A normal reaction to the catheter
A blood clot in the leg
Low blood sugar

items.q: A 7-year-old with a shunt for hydrocephalus has a headache, vomiting, and increasing sleepiness. What should you suspect?
