Minor (green)
Expectant (black)

items.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 5-year-old is not breathing after you position the airway but has a palpable pulse. What should you do?
items.x: Children often arrest from respiratory causes, so JumpSTART calls for five rescue breaths in an apneic child with a pulse. A child who resumes breathing is tagged immediate, and one who does not is tagged expectant.
items.a: Give five rescue breaths
w: Tag the child expectant and move on
Tag the child immediate and move on without intervening
Begin chest compressions

items.q: During SALT triage at a mass casualty incident, which intervention may be performed before assigning a category?
items.x: SALT allows quick lifesaving interventions, such as controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway and giving autoinjector antidotes, because they take little time and change survival. Time-consuming care is deferred until resources allow.
items.a: Applying a tourniquet for major hemorrhage
w: Starting an IV for fluid resuscitation
Splinting a closed forearm fracture
Starting an IV and running a fluid bolus for shock

items.q: A 27-year-old has a knife wound to the abdomen with a loop of bowel protruding. What is the correct care?
items.x: An evisceration is covered with a sterile dressing moistened with saline and then an occlusive layer to keep it moist and warm. Replacing the organs can introduce contamination and cause further injury.
items.a: Moist sterile dressing covered by an occlusive layer
w: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen
Cover it with a dry gauze pad that adheres to the bowel
Rinse the bowel with tap water and leave it uncovered

items.q: A 20-year-old has a wooden object impaled through his cheek. Blood is pooling in his mouth faster than you can suction it, and he is struggling to breathe. What should you do?
items.x: Impaled objects are normally stabilized, but one in the cheek that compromises the airway may be removed. Dressing material is placed between the cheek and teeth, and the airway is suctioned and protected.
items.a: Remove the object and pack the inside of the cheek
w: Stabilize the object in place with bulky dressings
Cut the object flush with the skin
Insert a supraglottic airway alongside the object and ventilate

items.q: A 34-year-old's thumb was amputated by a saw. Bleeding is controlled. How should you care for the amputated part?
items.x: The part is wrapped in sterile gauze moistened with saline, sealed in a plastic bag and kept cool on a separate layer of ice or cold packs. Direct contact with ice or water damages the tissue.
items.a: Wrap it in moist sterile gauze, seal it in a bag and keep it cool
w: Place it directly on ice to preserve the tissue
Submerge it in a cup of saline or tap water to keep it hydrated
Leave it on scene so it does not delay transport

items.q: Why is preventing heat loss a priority in a patient with severe hemorrhage?
items.x: Hypothermia, acidosis and impaired clotting reinforce one another in trauma patients. Covering the patient, warming the ambulance and using warmed fluids help prevent this cycle.
items.a: Hypothermia impairs blood clotting
w: Warming the patient raises the BP to a normal level
Cold blood is more likely to clot excessively
Shivering stops bleeding

items.q: A 23-year-old has a deep stab wound in the groin with heavy bleeding. A tourniquet cannot be placed above the wound. What should you do?
items.x: Junctional wounds such as the groin and axilla cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing hemostatic or plain gauze deep into the wound and holding firm pressure for several minutes is the recommended technique.
items.a: Pack the wound tightly and hold firm direct pressure
w: Place a tourniquet below the wound on the thigh
Elevate the leg and apply a light dressing
Apply cold packs and elevate the leg until arrival at the hospital

items.q: After a fall onto his left side, a 16-year-old has left upper abdominal pain and pain in his left shoulder, which was not injured. What does the shoulder pain suggest?
items.x: Blood under the diaphragm from a splenic injury can refer pain to the left shoulder, a finding known as Kehr sign. It should raise concern for internal bleeding and shock.
items.a: Irritation of the diaphragm from splenic bleeding
w: A separate shoulder dislocation
Referred pain from a fractured left femur or pelvis
Anxiety rather than injury

items.q: Which factors worsen secondary brain injury in a patient with traumatic brain injury? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypotension and hypoxia each markedly increase death and disability after TBI, and hyperventilation lowers brain blood flow. Neutral alignment and normothermia are part of good care.
opts: A single episode of hypotension
Hypoxia with an SpO2 below 90 percent
Routine hyperventilation
Keeping the head in line with the body
Maintaining a normal body temperature
ok: A single episode of hypotension
Hypoxia with an SpO2 below 90 percent
Routine hyperventilation

items.q: Which actions are appropriate when managing a suspected unstable pelvic fracture? Select all that apply.
items.x: A binder reduces pelvic volume and helps tamponade bleeding, and binding the legs adds stability. Repeated manipulation can disrupt clots, and the binder stays on until hospital staff remove it.
opts: Apply a pelvic binder when signs of shock are present
Pad the knees and ankles and bind the legs together
Rock the pelvis repeatedly to confirm instability
Remove the binder once the BP improves
Wait for hospital imaging before applying a binder
ok: Apply a pelvic binder when signs of shock are present
Pad the knees and ankles and bind the legs together

items.q: Which findings suggest a developing tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
items.x: Trapped air under pressure collapses the lung and impairs venous return, producing unilateral absent breath sounds, JVD and falling BP. A slow pulse with widening pulse pressure suggests increased intracranial pressure instead.
opts: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Worsening hypotension
Equal breath sounds bilaterally
Slow pulse with a widening pulse pressure
ok: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Worsening hypotension

items.q: A 42-year-old was rescued from a burning apartment. Which findings suggest an inhalation injury? Select all that apply.
items.x: Facial burns, singed hair, hoarseness and soot in the mouth or sputum indicate heat or smoke injury to the airway, which can swell quickly. These patients need close airway monitoring and early ALS involvement.
opts: Singed nasal hairs
Hoarse voice
Soot in the sputum
Blistering burn to the forearm only
Pain in the ankle
ok: Singed nasal hairs
Hoarse voice
Soot in the sputum

items.q: Which findings indicate that a blunt trauma patient needs spinal motion restriction? Select all that apply.
items.x: Altered mentation, midline spinal tenderness and focal neurological deficits all suggest possible spinal injury. An alert, sober patient with no spinal pain, tenderness or deficit does not need SMR solely because of an extremity injury.
opts: Intoxication or altered mental status
Midline neck or back tenderness
New numbness or weakness in the extremities
Pain isolated to an ankle after a ground-level fall in an alert, sober patient
Anxiety about the crash
ok: Intoxication or altered mental status
Midline neck or back tenderness
New numbness or weakness in the extremities

items.q: Which physiologic changes make older adults more vulnerable after trauma? Select all that apply.
items.x: Older adults have less reserve, fragile bones and medications such as beta-blockers and anticoagulants that hide or worsen shock. National triage guidance treats a systolic below 110 in those over 65 as a concerning finding.
opts: Medications may blunt the heart rate response to blood loss
Bones fracture with less force
A systolic BP below 110 may represent shock
They lose blood volume more slowly than younger adults
Their pain response is always exaggerated
ok: Medications may blunt the heart rate response to blood loss
Bones fracture with less force
A systolic BP below 110 may represent shock

items.q: Which statements about children involved in trauma are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children have proportionally large heads, pliable ribs and strong compensation that keeps BP normal until late. Their large surface area relative to mass makes them lose heat quickly.
opts: The head is large relative to the body, increasing head injury risk
Flexible ribs allow internal injury without rib fractures
Hypotension is a late sign of shock
They lose body heat more slowly than adults
Their BP drops early in blood loss
ok: The head is large relative to the body, increasing head injury risk
Flexible ribs allow internal injury without rib fractures
Hypotension is a late sign of shock

items.q: Which are concerns specific to the injured pregnant patient in the third trimester? Select all that apply.
items.x: Late pregnancy brings caval compression, abruption risk and an expanded blood volume that hides early shock. Heart rate normally rises in pregnancy, and the fetus may be in distress while the mother still appears stable.
opts: Supine positioning can compress the vena cava and lower BP
Placental abruption may follow even minor trauma
A resting heart rate slower than before pregnancy is expected
The fetus is safe as long as the mother is talking
Signs of shock may appear only after large blood loss
ok: Supine positioning can compress the vena cava and lower BP
Placental abruption may follow even minor trauma
Signs of shock may appear only after large blood loss

items.q: A man has been trapped under machinery for 3 hours. Which complications are associated with crush syndrome? Select all that apply.
items.x: Releasing a prolonged crush sends potassium, acids and myoglobin into the circulation, causing dysrhythmias, kidney injury and shock. Patients may deteriorate suddenly after appearing stable while trapped.
opts: Hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias after release
Kidney failure from muscle breakdown products
Hypoglycemia as the main life threat
Immediate improvement once the weight is removed
Hypotension from fluid shifting into injured tissue
ok: Hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias after release
Kidney failure from muscle breakdown products
Hypotension from fluid shifting into injured tissue

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic woman is confused and sweaty with a blood glucose of 48 mg/dL. She follows commands, swallows normally and protects her own airway. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
items.x: A hypoglycemic patient who is awake enough to swallow safely can be treated quickly with oral glucose. IV dextrose or glucagon is reserved for patients who cannot swallow or protect the airway.
items.a: Oral glucose, watching her airway closely
w: An isotonic fluid bolus to dilute the insulin in her blood
Start an IV for dextrose before giving anything by mouth
High-flow oxygen and repeat glucose check in 15 minutes

items.q: A 74-year-old who takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication was hypoglycemic. After IV dextrose his glucose is 118 mg/dL and he wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
items.x: Some oral agents keep lowering glucose for many hours, so hypoglycemia can recur once a single dextrose dose is used up. He should be strongly encouraged to accept transport, and if he still refuses, he must eat and have someone stay with him.
items.a: His glucose may fall again over the next several hours
w: The dextrose will push him into diabetic ketoacidosis within the hour
A glucose of 118 mg/dL is dangerously high for an older adult
He is likely to have a delayed allergic reaction to the dextrose

items.q: A 68-year-old has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. Which assessment should you perform early because its result could change your field impression?
items.x: Hypoglycemia can produce focal weakness and speech changes that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check is part of every stroke assessment and takes only seconds.
items.a: Blood glucose
w: Oral temperature
Capillary refill in the fingers
Orthostatic vital signs before moving her

items.q: A 30-year-old diabetic is pale, sweaty and confused. Her glucose reads 420 mg/dL from a fingertip that is sticky because she was just eating candy. What should you do next?
items.x: Sugar on the skin can produce a falsely high reading, and her signs fit hypoglycemia. The site is cleaned and the test repeated before making treatment decisions.
items.a: Clean the skin, then recheck with a new sample
w: Treat her for DKA with large fluid boluses
Accept the reading and withhold all sugar
Repeat the test immediately on the same fingertip

items.q: An 80-year-old with type 2 diabetes has become more confused over several days. Her glucose reads HI and she is profoundly dehydrated, with no fruity odor and no rapid deep breathing. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state develops slowly in older type 2 diabetics, with extreme glucose levels and severe dehydration but little ketone production. It requires careful fluid replacement and hospital care.
items.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis from missed insulin
Hypoglycemia with a meter error
Insulin shock

items.q: A 55-year-old malnourished alcoholic with a glucose of 34 mg/dL received IM glucagon 15 minutes ago and has not improved. What is the most likely reason?
items.x: Glucagon raises glucose by releasing glycogen stored in the liver, so it often fails in malnourished or alcoholic patients. IV or IO dextrose is needed when glucagon does not work.
items.a: His liver has little stored glycogen
w: Glucagon is effective only in children
Glucagon must be given by mouth to be absorbed
The meter always reads falsely low in alcoholics

items.q: A 16-year-old with an insulin pump is unresponsive with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. Along with treating the hypoglycemia, what should be done with the pump?
items.x: An insulin pump keeps delivering insulin and will keep driving the glucose down. Suspending or disconnecting it stops further insulin while the hypoglycemia is treated, and the device goes to the hospital with the patient.
items.a: Suspend or disconnect it so insulin delivery stops
w: Leave it running because stopping it will cause immediate DKA
Increase its infusion rate to stabilize the glucose level
Pull out the infusion catheter and discard the entire device

items.q: A 40-year-old is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, respirations of 6 per minute and an SpO2 of 82 percent. What should you do first?
items.x: Inadequate breathing is corrected immediately with BVM ventilation and oxygen. Naloxone may follow, but ventilation is never delayed while waiting for a drug to work.
items.a: Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
w: Give naloxone and wait for the breathing to improve
Apply a nonrebreather
Check a blood glucose level before any airway care

items.q: A 58-year-old smells strongly of alcohol, is confused and was found at the bottom of a short staircase. What is the best approach?
items.x: Alcohol odor does not explain an altered mental status. Intoxicated patients frequently have hypoglycemia, head injuries or other illness that must be looked for before attributing the confusion to alcohol.
items.a: Check glucose and assess for head injury
w: Assume he is intoxicated and let him sleep it off in a quiet place
Request police custody
Give oral glucose without testing because alcoholics are often hypoglycemic

items.q: A 35-year-old with a seizure disorder has been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. Which care is most appropriate within AEMT scope?
items.x: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is status epilepticus and needs anticonvulsant medications beyond AEMT scope. AEMT care is protecting the patient, supporting the airway and oxygenation, treating hypoglycemia and getting ALS or rapid transport.
items.a: Protect him, give oxygen, check glucose and request ALS
w: Place a bite block between his teeth to protect his tongue
Hold his arms and legs firmly to stop the movements
Wait until the seizure stops before requesting any help

items.q: A 27-year-old has just stopped seizing. She is breathing adequately with gurgling sounds and is not yet responsive. How should you position her?
items.x: The recovery position lets secretions drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway during the postictal period. Suction and oxygen are provided as she recovers.
items.a: On her side with suction ready
w: Supine with her legs elevated 12 inches
Sitting upright with her head supported
Prone, face turned aside

items.q: A woman who is 33 weeks pregnant and has no seizure history has a generalized seizure. Her BP is 182/112 and her face and hands are swollen. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A seizure in a pregnant woman with hypertension and edema is eclampsia until proven otherwise. She needs ALS for anticonvulsant medication, a dim and quiet environment and rapid transport.
items.a: Eclampsia
w: New-onset epilepsy
Hypoglycemia caused by the pregnancy
Supine hypotensive syndrome

items.q: A 20-year-old fainted while standing in a long line, had a few seconds of jerking and was alert within a minute. Which finding would most suggest a seizure rather than syncope?
items.x: A prolonged postictal period of confusion favors a seizure. Brief jerking with a rapid return to alertness is common in ordinary fainting.
items.a: Prolonged confusion afterward
w: A brief feeling of lightheadedness before falling
Pale, sweaty skin just before the event
A few seconds of jerking movements during the faint

items.q: A 72-year-old woman woke at 6 a.m. unable to speak clearly. She went to bed feeling normal at 10 p.m. When was she last known well?
items.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at her baseline. For symptoms present on waking, that is when she went to sleep, which affects eligibility for time-sensitive stroke treatments.
items.a: 10 p.m., when she was last seen normal
w: 6 a.m., when she woke with the symptoms
The time EMS arrived and began the assessment
The time her husband called 911

items.q: A 66-year-old with a suspected stroke has a BP of 188/104 and a normal glucose. What should you do about the BP?
items.x: Elevated BP is common in acute stroke and helps perfuse the brain tissue around the injury. Lowering it in the field can enlarge the stroke, so BP management is left to the receiving hospital.
items.a: Monitor it without trying to lower it
w: Give nitroglycerin to bring the systolic below 140
Run a fluid bolus to protect the brain from the high pressure
Coach slow breathing until the BP falls below 160

items.q: A 70-year-old with a suspected stroke has a facial droop and slurred speech and asks for a drink of water. Why should you withhold anything by mouth?
items.x: Stroke often weakens the muscles of swallowing, so liquids and pills can be aspirated into the lungs. Patients are kept NPO until a formal swallow screen is done.
items.a: Her ability to swallow safely may be impaired
w: Water will raise the BP and extend the stroke
Fluids by mouth will dilute the blood glucose
Stroke patients cannot absorb water from the stomach

items.q: A 24-year-old took a large amount of an over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aid. He is agitated and confused with hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils and a pulse of 136. Which toxidrome does this fit?
items.x: Anticholinergic toxicity causes hot, dry, red skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, delirium and urinary retention. Many antihistamines produce this pattern in overdose.
items.a: Anticholinergic
w: Cholinergic
Opioid
Sedative-hypnotic

items.q: A 29-year-old is agitated after using a stimulant. He is tachycardic, hypertensive and hyperthermic with dilated pupils. Which finding best distinguishes this from an anticholinergic toxidrome?
items.x: Sympathomimetic toxicity causes heavy sweating, while anticholinergic toxicity produces dry skin. Both can cause dilated pupils, tachycardia and agitation.
items.a: Sweaty skin
w: Dilated pupils
Fast heart rate
Agitation

items.q: A 19-year-old took about 40 acetaminophen tablets an hour ago. She feels fine and wants to refuse transport. What should you explain?
items.x: Acetaminophen overdose often causes few early symptoms while liver damage develops over the next day or two. An antidote works best when started early, so prompt hospital evaluation is critical.
items.a: Early symptoms can be mild even after a lethal dose
w: The overdose is harmless because she has no symptoms
Inducing vomiting now is enough to remove the tablets
She will have seizures within minutes

items.q: A family of four all have headaches and nausea that started after they began using a fuel-burning space heater. One adult has an SpO2 of 99 percent. How should you interpret this reading?
items.x: Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin from oxygen, so readings may look normal. Remove everyone from the source and give high-concentration oxygen.
items.a: It can read normal despite significant poisoning
w: It rules out carbon monoxide poisoning in that adult
It shows the headaches are most likely from a viral illness
It means none of the family needs supplemental oxygen

items.q: A 32-year-old allergic to peanuts received epinephrine for wheezing, hives and hypotension and improved. Ten minutes later her wheezing and hypotension return. What should you do?
items.x: Epinephrine acts briefly, and symptoms of anaphylaxis commonly return. A repeat dose is given for persistent or recurring signs, along with oxygen and IV fluid.
items.a: Repeat the epinephrine and support breathing and BP
w: Give oral glucose for the stress response
Wait another 20 minutes for the first dose to take full effect
Give nitroglycerin to relieve the chest tightness

items.q: A 28-year-old has a few itchy hives on one arm after eating shellfish. She has no breathing difficulty, no facial swelling, no GI symptoms and normal vital signs. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: Localized hives without involvement of breathing, circulation or another body system are a mild allergic reaction. She is watched closely during transport for signs of progression to anaphylaxis.
items.a: Monitor closely during transport
w: Give epinephrine immediately to prevent progression
Start a fluid bolus
Place a supraglottic airway as a precaution against swelling

items.q: A 50-year-old in anaphylaxis remains hypotensive at 78/48 after epinephrine. Breath sounds are clear. What should you add?
items.x: Anaphylaxis causes vasodilation and capillary leak, so persistent hypotension is treated with isotonic fluid boluses along with repeat epinephrine. Lung sounds and BP are reassessed during the infusion.
items.a: An isotonic fluid bolus
w: Dextrose 10 percent infusion
Sublingual nitroglycerin
Oral fluids to replace lost volume

items.q: A 70-year-old has a productive cough, a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F), respirations of 28, a pulse of 112, a BP of 108/64 and new confusion. What should you suspect?
items.x: Infection with rapid breathing, tachycardia and new confusion indicates sepsis. Early recognition, oxygen, fluids when hypotensive and hospital notification improve survival.
items.a: Sepsis from pneumonia
w: Simple dehydration from poor oral intake
An asthma exacerbation
Acute stroke with aspiration

items.q: You are giving fluid to a septic 65-year-old with a BP of 82/50. After 500 mL, which finding best shows the fluid is helping and being tolerated?
items.x: Fluid in sepsis is given in boluses with reassessment between them. Improved mentation and BP with clear lung sounds show better perfusion without fluid overload.
items.a: Better mentation and BP with clear lungs
w: New crackles in both bases with a rising BP
A rising heart rate and increasing confusion
A faster respiratory rate with a falling SpO2

items.q: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.3 C (101 F) but is feeding normally and alert. What should you advise the parents?
items.x: Young infants can have serious bacterial infections with fever as the only sign. Any fever in an infant younger than about 2 to 3 months warrants prompt medical evaluation.
items.a: Transport for prompt evaluation of a possible serious infection
w: Treat it as a minor cold, since she is feeding normally
Give a cool bath and wait to see if the fever breaks
Wait until the fever is above 40 C (104 F) before seeking care

items.q: A 19-year-old college student has a fever, stiff neck and a purple rash that does not blanch. Which infection control precaution is most important?
items.x: Fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal infection, which spreads by respiratory droplets. A surgical mask on the patient and providers plus gloves and eye protection is appropriate.
items.a: Droplet precautions with masks for the patient and crew
w: Contact precautions with gloves and gown only
No precautions beyond standard handwashing
A respirator only after arrival at the hospital

items.q: A 60-year-old has vomited coffee-ground material and has black, tarry stools. His BP is 88/56 and pulse is 124. Where is the bleeding most likely coming from?
items.x: Coffee-ground vomit and black, tarry stool indicate bleeding from the upper GI tract, such as an ulcer. With signs of shock he needs rapid transport and IV access.
items.a: Upper GI tract
w: Lower colon or rectum
Lungs, with swallowed blood
Urinary bladder

items.q: A 52-year-old with liver disease is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood and is drowsy. What should you do first?
items.x: Massive upper GI bleeding in an altered patient creates a high aspiration risk. Side positioning and suction protect the airway before shock is addressed.
items.a: Turn him on his side and suction the airway
w: Give oral fluids to replace the lost volume
Lay him flat on his back with legs elevated
Apply a nasal cannula and start an IV

items.q: A 72-year-old man has sudden tearing back pain, a pulsating abdominal mass and a BP of 84/50. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: A leaking or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs immediate surgery. The abdomen is handled gently, and IV fluids are limited to maintaining minimal perfusion during rapid transport.
items.a: Rapid transport with limited fluids
w: Deep palpation to estimate the size of the mass
Large fluid boluses until the systolic BP exceeds 120
Have him walk out

items.q: A 64-year-old dialysis patient missed two treatments. He is weak with a pulse of 44, and the monitor shows tall, peaked T waves. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Missed dialysis lets potassium build up, causing weakness, bradycardia, peaked T waves and possible cardiac arrest. Rapid transport and ALS are needed.
items.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Hypoglycemia
Hypothermia
Dehydration from fluid removal

items.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient missed treatments. She is breathing 30 times per minute with crackles throughout, an SpO2 of 88 percent and a BP of 178/98. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: A dialysis patient who misses treatments accumulates fluid in the lungs. She needs upright positioning, oxygen or assisted ventilation and rapid transport, not more fluid.
items.a: Sit her up, give oxygen and avoid fluid boluses
w: Lay her flat and give a fluid bolus to support her kidneys
Give a fluid bolus first, then place her upright if she tolerates it
Insert a supraglottic airway

items.q: In an 88-year-old, which finding is least reliable for judging dehydration?
items.x: Skin loses elasticity with age, so tenting does not reliably indicate dehydration in older adults. History, mucous membranes, mental status and vital signs are more useful.
items.a: Skin turgor on the back of the hand
w: Dry mucous membranes
Dizziness when standing
A rapid heart rate

items.q: A 4-year-old is moderately dehydrated from vomiting and needs an IV fluid bolus. Which fluid is appropriate?
items.x: Isotonic fluids such as normal saline restore intravascular volume in pediatric dehydration. D5W and sterile water are hypotonic, and concentrated dextrose is for hypoglycemia, not volume.
items.a: Normal saline
w: 5 percent dextrose in water
Dextrose 50 percent
Sterile water for injection

items.q: After placing an IO needle in a 2-year-old, which finding best confirms correct placement?
items.x: A properly placed IO needle stands firmly in the bone and allows fluid to flow without swelling of the surrounding tissue. Swelling indicates infiltration, and the needle should be removed.
items.a: Fluid flows freely without swelling
w: The needle wobbles when gently touched
Swelling develops in the calf as you flush
The child's BP drops slightly during the flush

items.q: An 82-year-old with heart failure who takes a diuretic has had vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days. She is dizzy when sitting up, with a pulse of 112 and a BP of 96/60. How should you give IV fluids?
items.x: Older adults with heart disease may need fluid for dehydration but are prone to pulmonary edema. Small boluses with reassessment of lung sounds and breathing balance these risks.
items.a: Small boluses with frequent lung checks
w: A rapid 2-liter bolus through two large-bore lines
No fluids at all
By mouth only, regardless of her vomiting

items.q: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
items.x: Painless bright red bleeding in late pregnancy is typical of placenta previa, a placenta lying over the cervix. Do not examine inside the vagina; treat for shock and transport.
items.a: Placenta previa
w: Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Normal bloody show of early labor

items.q: During labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina ahead of the baby. What should you do?
items.x: The presenting part compresses a prolapsed cord and cuts off fetal oxygen. A gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord, the mother is positioned with hips elevated, and transport is rapid.
items.a: Lift the presenting part off the cord
w: Push the cord back into the vagina
Pull gently on the cord to speed delivery
Clamp and cut the cord immediately

items.q: During a breech delivery, the body delivers but the head does not after 3 minutes. What should you do?
items.x: Placing gloved fingers in a V on either side of the baby's nose holds the vaginal wall off the face so the baby can breathe. Keep the airway open and transport rapidly.
items.a: Make an airway with a V of your fingers
w: Pull on the legs
Push the baby back into the birth canal
Wait for several more contractions without intervening

items.q: After the head delivers, the baby's shoulders become stuck. What is the first maneuver?
items.x: Shoulder dystocia is managed first by flexing the mother's thighs sharply toward her abdomen, the McRoberts maneuver, which widens the pelvic outlet. Pulling on the head or pushing on the fundus can injure the baby.
items.a: Sharply flex the mother's thighs
w: Pull the head firmly downward
Press hard on the top of the uterus
Tell the mother to stop pushing and wait

items.q: A term newborn is not breathing after being warmed, dried and stimulated. What should you do next?
items.x: A newborn who stays apneic after initial steps needs positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute, at 40 to 60 breaths per minute. Term newborns start with room air.
items.a: Begin positive-pressure ventilation
w: Begin chest compressions
Give blow-by oxygen and observe
Continue stimulating for 2 more minutes

items.q: You are giving PPV to a newborn whose heart rate is 80, but the chest is not rising. What should you do?
items.x: Ineffective ventilation is corrected first by checking mask seal and head position, then suctioning, opening the mouth and increasing pressure. Chest rise is the key sign that ventilation is working.
items.a: Reposition the head and reseal the mask
w: Begin chest compressions at a 3-to-1 ratio
Increase the ventilation rate to 80 per minute
Give blow-by oxygen

items.q: A baby is born at about 30 weeks. How should you prevent heat loss?
items.x: Very preterm newborns lose heat rapidly. Placing the body in plastic wrap or a bag without drying it, plus a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
items.a: Plastic wrap without drying the body
w: Dry the baby and leave it uncovered on the mother's abdomen
Turn down the heat in the ambulance
Give a warm water bath

items.q: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110, grimaces when stimulated, some flexion of the arms and legs and a weak cry. What is the APGAR score?
items.x: Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1 and respiration 1 total 6.

items.q: A woman about 10 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping. Her pulse is 118. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: Early pregnancy loss can cause heavy bleeding and shock. Treat for shock, bring passed tissue to the hospital and provide emotional support.
items.a: Treat for shock and bring any passed tissue
w: Pack the vagina with gauze to stop the bleeding
Have her walk to the ambulance
Wait on scene until the bleeding stops

items.q: After delivering a healthy baby, the placenta has not delivered after 30 minutes. What should you do?
items.x: Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus. The mother is transported with monitoring for bleeding.
items.a: Transport without pulling on the cord
w: Pull firmly on the cord
Reach inside the uterus to remove the placenta
Cut the cord at the vagina and push it back in

items.q: A 67-year-old found outdoors in winter is confused and no longer shivering, with a core temperature of 29 C (84 F) and a pulse of 42. Why should you move him gently and keep him horizontal?
items.x: A severely cold heart is irritable, and jarring movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Remove wet clothing, insulate him and keep him horizontal during transport.
items.a: Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
w: Gentle handling allows his muscles to resume shivering
Moving him upright helps blood return to the brain faster
Rough handling causes the skin to rewarm too quickly

items.q: A hiker has frozen, waxy toes and must walk out through deep snow for several more hours before reaching transport. What should you do about the toes?
items.x: Thawing followed by refreezing causes much worse tissue damage than leaving the part frozen until definitive rewarming. Protect the area, pad it and never rub frostbitten tissue.
items.a: Leave them frozen until refreezing can be prevented
w: Rub them vigorously with snow to restore circulation
Rewarm them beside the campfire before the hike out
Thaw them in warm water, then continue the walk out

items.q: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are down. Which patients should receive care first?
items.x: Unlike standard triage, lightning patients in cardiac or respiratory arrest are treated first because they often recover with prompt CPR and ventilation. Conscious patients usually survive, so this is called reverse triage.
items.a: Those who are pulseless and apneic
w: Those who are awake and talking with burns
Those with confusion and ringing in the ears
Those who are walking with minor injuries

items.q: A 35-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She is confused with a headache and vomiting, a normal temperature and a glucose of 94 mg/dL. What should you suspect?
items.x: Drinking excess water during endurance events dilutes blood sodium, causing headache, confusion, vomiting and seizures. Giving large volumes of fluid can make it worse, so she needs prompt hospital evaluation.
items.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
w: Heat stroke from exertion
Hypoglycemia from glycogen depletion
Dehydration from sweat loss

items.q: A scuba diver made a rapid ascent and within 2 minutes of surfacing developed chest pain and weakness of one arm. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Gas forced into the arterial circulation during rapid ascent causes stroke-like and cardiac symptoms within minutes of surfacing. Give high-concentration oxygen, keep the patient supine and transport toward recompression.
items.a: Arterial gas embolism
w: Nitrogen narcosis from deep diving
Hypothermia from cold water
Delayed decompression sickness from long bottom time

items.q: A 40-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake 10 minutes ago. Swelling is spreading. What is appropriate care?
items.x: Pit viper bites are managed by keeping the patient calm, immobilizing the limb, removing rings or tight items and marking the advancing swelling. Tourniquets, ice, cutting and suction cause harm.
items.a: Immobilize the leg and mark the swelling edge
w: Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite to trap the venom
Pack the bite in ice
Make a small incision and suction out the venom

items.q: A 31-year-old with suspected hyperactive delirium, sometimes called excited delirium, was hot, sweaty and fighting restraints. He suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
items.x: Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, hyperthermic patient may mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check immediately and start resuscitation if needed.
items.a: Check breathing and pulse at once
w: Let him rest since he has finally calmed down
Tighten the restraints before he becomes agitated again
Turn him prone so he cannot strike the crew

items.q: How should a combative patient be positioned once physical restraint is required?
items.x: Prone and hobble positions, and any weight on the back, can cause positional asphyxia and death. Restrained patients are placed supine or on their side with continuous monitoring of breathing and mental status.
items.a: Supine or on the side, continuously monitored
w: Prone with wrists and ankles tied together behind him
Prone with a long backboard strapped over his back
Seated with a blanket held over his face to calm him

items.q: You are dispatched to a man who is waving a knife and threatening his neighbors. What should you do?
items.x: Responder safety comes first. EMS stages at a safe distance and enters only after police have secured the scene, then provides care.
items.a: Stage until law enforcement secures the scene
w: Approach calmly and try to talk him into putting it down
Enter with your partner and restrain him together
Cancel the call because it is a law enforcement matter

items.q: A 74-year-old with COPD is newly combative and confused. Her SpO2 is 82 percent and her glucose is 110 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause of the behavior?
items.x: Hypoxia commonly causes confusion, restlessness and combativeness. Medical causes of behavior change are identified and treated before assuming a psychiatric cause.
items.a: Hypoxia from her lung disease
w: A new psychiatric illness
Alcohol intoxication
Normal age-related dementia

items.q: A 40-year-old says he feels hopeless and has been giving away his belongings. What is the best way to assess suicide risk?
items.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and plans does not increase risk and is the best way to identify patients who need emergency evaluation. Giving away belongings is a warning sign.
items.a: Ask directly whether he is thinking of suicide
w: Avoid the topic because asking may plant the idea
Change the subject to something more positive
Reassure him that things will get better soon

items.q: A 23-year-old has right lower abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus, with fever, nausea and pain when the ambulance hits bumps. What should you suspect?
items.x: Appendicitis classically begins with pain around the umbilicus that moves to the right lower quadrant, often with fever, nausea and pain on movement. Transport in a position of comfort and give nothing by mouth.
items.a: Appendicitis
w: Kidney stone
Gastroenteritis
Gallbladder disease

items.q: Which findings are consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis? Select all that apply.
items.x: DKA develops over hours to days with Kussmaul breathing, a ketone odor and polyuria from high glucose. Cool, clammy skin and sudden onset point to hypoglycemia.
opts: Rapid, deep respirations
Fruity breath odor
Excessive thirst and urination
Cool, clammy, sweaty skin
Onset over a few minutes
ok: Rapid, deep respirations
Fruity breath odor
Excessive thirst and urination

items.q: Which conditions can mimic an acute stroke? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypoglycemia, postictal weakness and complex migraine can all produce focal deficits. Atrial fibrillation is a cause of stroke and elevated BP often accompanies stroke, so neither explains away the deficits.
opts: Hypoglycemia
Weakness after a seizure
Complex migraine
Atrial fibrillation
A BP of 170/90
ok: Hypoglycemia
Weakness after a seizure
Complex migraine

items.q: A 2-year-old with vomiting received a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. He is still listless with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 170, and his lungs are clear. What should you do next?
items.x: Persistent signs of poor perfusion after one bolus in a child without signs of fluid overload call for another isotonic bolus with reassessment after each one.
items.a: Repeat the isotonic bolus and reassess perfusion
w: Stop fluids because one bolus is the limit for children
Switch to oral fluids now that one bolus is in
Give dextrose 50 percent for the poor perfusion

items.q: A 38-year-old man has sudden severe left flank pain that radiates to his groin. He is restless and cannot find a comfortable position, and he has blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Kidney stones cause colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, restlessness and blood in the urine. In an older patient, an abdominal aortic aneurysm must also be considered.
items.a: Kidney stone
w: Appendicitis
Pancreatitis
Small bowel obstruction

items.q: Which findings are consistent with opioid toxicity? Select all that apply.
items.x: The opioid toxidrome is pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and depressed consciousness. Agitation with sweating and dilated pupils suggests a stimulant.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Slow, shallow breathing
Decreased level of consciousness
Hot, sweaty skin with agitation
Widely dilated pupils
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Slow, shallow breathing
Decreased level of consciousness

items.q: An 84-year-old has an infection. Which findings suggest sepsis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Older adults often do not mount a fever and may even be hypothermic, while new confusion and tachypnea are early signs of sepsis.
opts: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26
A temperature below normal
A high fever is always present
Hives on the trunk
ok: New confusion
Respiratory rate of 26
A temperature below normal

items.q: Which patients are at increased risk for hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
items.x: Kidney failure and crush injuries raise serum potassium, which causes weakness, bradycardia and lethal dysrhythmias.
opts: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
A man released after a prolonged crush
A young adult hyperventilating from anxiety
A runner who has been sweating heavily
A patient with kidney failure and new muscle weakness
ok: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
A man released after a prolonged crush
A patient with kidney failure and new muscle weakness

items.q: At which sites should IO placement be avoided? Select all that apply.
items.x: Fluid leaks out of a fractured or previously punctured bone, and placing a needle through infected tissue can seed the bone. Shock and cardiac arrest are indications for IO access.
opts: A bone with a fracture
An area with signs of infection
A bone with a failed IO attempt earlier that day
The proximal tibia of a hypotensive child
The humerus of an adult in cardiac arrest
ok: A bone with a fracture
An area with signs of infection
A bone with a failed IO attempt earlier that day

items.q: A woman who is 36 weeks pregnant has vaginal bleeding. Which findings suggest placental abruption? Select all that apply.
items.x: Abruption causes painful bleeding, a firm uterus and concealed hemorrhage behind the placenta. Painless bleeding with a soft uterus suggests placenta previa.
opts: Constant abdominal pain
A rigid, tender uterus
Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding
Painless bright red bleeding
A soft, nontender uterus
ok: Constant abdominal pain
A rigid, tender uterus
Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding

items.q: Which are initial steps for a term newborn who is not vigorous at birth? Select all that apply.
items.x: NRP initial steps are to warm, dry, stimulate and position the airway, clearing secretions only if needed. Term newborns start with room air, and routine deep suctioning can cause bradycardia.
opts: Warm the baby
Dry and stimulate
Position the airway
Routine deep suctioning
Hold the baby upside down
Give 100 percent oxygen
ok: Warm the baby
Dry and stimulate
Position the airway

items.q: Which findings are consistent with severe hypothermia? Select all that apply.
items.x: As the core temperature falls, shivering stops, the pulse slows and mental status declines. Rapid breathing and hot skin point elsewhere.
opts: Shivering has stopped
Bradycardia
Altered mental status
Hot, dry skin
Rapid breathing with agitation
ok: Shivering has stopped
Bradycardia
Altered mental status

items.q: Which findings are associated with hyperactive delirium with severe agitation? Select all that apply.
items.x: These patients are hyperthermic, tachycardic, sweaty and violent with unusual strength. They are at high risk of sudden cardiac arrest, especially during struggle and restraint.
opts: High body temperature
Extreme strength with insensitivity to pain
Tachycardia
Bradycardia and hypothermia
Calm, cooperative behavior
ok: High body temperature
Extreme strength with insensitivity to pain
Tachycardia

items.q: Which actions are appropriate during and after a generalized seizure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Protection from injury, timing the event and checking glucose are core seizure care. Restraint causes injury, and objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway.
opts: Move objects away to protect the patient
Note how long the seizure lasts
Check the glucose once the seizure ends
Restrain the arms and legs
Place a bite block between the teeth
ok: Move objects away to protect the patient
Note how long the seizure lasts
Check the glucose once the seizure ends

items.q: A farm worker collapsed after spraying a field. Which findings suggest organophosphate poisoning? Select all that apply.
items.x: Organophosphates cause cholinergic toxicity with excess secretions, bronchospasm and small pupils. Decontaminate the patient before care in the ambulance to protect the crew.
opts: Drooling and heavy secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Wheezing
Hot, dry, flushed skin
Dilated pupils
ok: Drooling and heavy secretions
Pinpoint pupils
Wheezing

items.q: Which findings suggest carbon monoxide poisoning? Select all that apply.
items.x: Carbon monoxide causes headache, nausea and confusion in people sharing the same space, with relief after leaving it. Pulse oximetry often reads normal, and cherry red skin is a rare, late finding.
opts: Headache and nausea
Several people in the home are ill
Symptoms improve after leaving the home
A reliably low SpO2 reading
Cherry red skin in most patients
ok: Headache and nausea
Several people in the home are ill
Symptoms improve after leaving the home

items.q: An adult has signs of septic shock. Which actions are appropriate within AEMT scope? Select all that apply.
items.x: Early fluids with frequent reassessment and hospital prealert are key in sepsis. Oxygen is given for hypoxia, and dextrose does not treat hypotension.
opts: Give an isotonic fluid bolus
Reassess lung sounds after each bolus
Notify the hospital early of suspected sepsis
Withhold oxygen to avoid hiding hypoxia
Give dextrose to raise the BP
ok: Give an isotonic fluid bolus
Reassess lung sounds after each bolus
Notify the hospital early of suspected sepsis

items.q: Which findings in an older adult with dehydration suggest the need for IV fluids rather than oral rehydration? Select all that apply.
items.x: Patients who are confused, cannot keep fluids down or are hypotensive need IV or IO fluids. Mild thirst alone can usually be managed orally.
opts: Altered mental status
Persistent vomiting
Hypotension
Mild thirst
Dry lips after a long walk
ok: Altered mental status
Persistent vomiting
Hypotension

items.q: You are assessing a 48-year-old man before intubation. Using the 3-3-2 approach, you find only one fingerbreadth between the hyoid bone and the top of the thyroid cartilage. What does this suggest?
items.x: Fewer than two fingerbreadths from hyoid to thyroid cartilage means the larynx sits high and anterior, so the glottis is harder to bring into the line of sight.
items.a: A high, anterior larynx that is hard to visualize
w: Mouth opening too narrow to insert a laryngoscope blade
Probable difficulty obtaining a bag-valve-mask seal
Restricted neck extension from cervical arthritis

items.q: A 55-year-old woman sitting upright opens her mouth and protrudes her tongue. You can see only her hard palate; the soft palate and uvula are hidden. What does this predict?
items.x: Seeing only the hard palate (Mallampati class IV) predicts a poor laryngoscopic view, so a bougie, video laryngoscope, supraglottic airway and surgical backup should be ready.
items.a: Difficult laryngoscopy
w: An easy view with a curved blade
A high risk of aspiration during bag-valve-mask ventilation
A normal airway needing no special preparation

items.q: A 62-year-old alert man needs rapid sequence intubation for worsening pneumonia. SpO2 is 95 percent on a nonrebreather mask. Which preoxygenation approach best fills his lungs with oxygen before induction?
items.x: Several minutes of tidal breathing on high-flow oxygen washes nitrogen out of the lungs, creating an oxygen reservoir that lengthens safe apnea time.
items.a: At least 3 minutes of high-flow oxygen with tidal breathing
w: One minute of nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min
Rapid bag-valve-mask ventilation at 30 breaths/min for 1 minute
Room air until induction so the oximeter shows his true baseline

items.q: A 160-kg woman needs to be intubated. How should she be positioned to improve both preoxygenation and the laryngoscopic view?
items.x: Ramping an obese patient so the external ear canal lines up with the sternal notch improves the glottic view and reduces the abdominal pressure that speeds desaturation.
items.a: Ramped, ear canal level with the sternal notch
w: Flat supine with a rolled towel under her shoulders
Head-down tilt to improve venous return to the heart
Left lateral recumbent with the neck flexed forward

items.q: During your first intubation attempt on a 50-year-old man, his SpO2 falls from 99 to 89 percent and you still cannot see the vocal cords. What should you do?
items.x: Falling saturation means the attempt should end; reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask and change something (position, device or operator) before the next attempt.
items.a: Stop and reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask
w: Keep going until the cords are seen, since the oximeter reading lags
Pass the tube blindly and check it with capnography
Have your partner apply cricoid pressure and continue looking

items.q: A 67-year-old septic patient needs intubation for a worsening mental status. BP is 74/40 and HR is 128. What should be addressed before induction drugs are given?
items.x: Induction drugs and positive pressure ventilation commonly drop blood pressure further, so resuscitating the hypotension first reduces the risk of peri-intubation cardiac arrest.
items.a: Hypotension, with fluids or vasopressors per protocol
w: Hypothermia, by warming the patient compartment first
Hyperventilation, by bagging at a slower rate beforehand
Agitation, by applying soft restraints to both arms and legs

items.q: A 24-year-old in severe diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 34/min with an ETCO2 of 16 mmHg. After he is intubated, how should his ventilation be managed?
items.x: His low CO2 is compensation for a severe metabolic acidosis; ventilating at a normal rate lets CO2 rise, the pH falls sharply and cardiac arrest can follow.
items.a: Match his high pre-intubation minute ventilation
w: Ventilate at 10 breaths/min to prevent barotrauma
Let the ETCO2 rise to 40 mmHg so it is normal
Ventilate only when the SpO2 falls below 90 percent

items.q: On laryngoscopy of a 44-year-old man you can see the epiglottis but none of the glottic opening. Which device is most helpful for passing the tube?
items.x: With an epiglottis-only view a bougie can be steered under the epiglottis; clicks against the tracheal rings or hold-up in a small airway confirm placement before the tube is passed over it.
items.a: A tracheal tube introducer (bougie)
w: A larger endotracheal tube
An oropharyngeal airway placed first
A nasopharyngeal airway placed first

items.q: During laryngoscopy you can see only the posterior part of the vocal cords. Which maneuver may improve your view?
items.x: External laryngeal manipulation, such as backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage, moves the larynx into view; cricoid pressure can actually worsen the view.
items.a: Backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage
w: Firm pressure on the cricoid cartilage throughout the attempt
Turning the patient's head toward the left shoulder
Pressing downward on the forehead while lifting the patient's chin

items.q: After intubating an adult you check the endotracheal tube cuff with a manometer. Which cuff pressure range is generally recommended?
items.x: A cuff pressure of about 20 to 30 cm H2O seals the airway while limiting injury to the tracheal lining; cuffs inflated by feel are often far too tight.
items.a: 20 to 30 cm H2O
w: 5 to 10 cm H2O
40 to 50 cm H2O
60 to 80 cm H2O

items.q: After intubating a 5-foot-2-inch woman, you hear breath sounds only on the right. The tube is at 27 cm at the teeth and the ETCO2 waveform is normal. What should you do?
items.x: A normal waveform with right-only breath sounds and a deep tube suggests a right mainstem intubation; withdrawing the tube a short distance usually restores left-sided ventilation.
items.a: Deflate the cuff and pull back slightly while listening
w: Remove the tube completely and reintubate with a smaller size
Perform needle decompression of the left side of the chest
Advance the tube 2 cm further and then reassess breath sounds

items.q: A ventilated 30-year-old after a fall from height has rising airway pressures, absent breath sounds on the left, BP 70/40 and distended neck veins. What should you do?
items.x: Positive pressure ventilation can rapidly turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax; hypotension with distended neck veins and absent breath sounds needs immediate decompression.
items.a: Perform needle decompression on the left
w: Increase the PEEP to reinflate the left lung
Withdraw the tube 2 cm and recheck
Increase the tidal volume to improve oxygenation

items.q: The transport ventilator on an intubated patient sounds a low-pressure alarm and the exhaled tidal volumes have dropped sharply. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Low pressure with loss of returned volume points to a leak, such as a disconnected circuit, a deflated cuff or a tube pulled above the cords; obstruction, bronchospasm and pneumothorax raise pressures.
items.a: A leak or disconnection in the circuit
w: A mucus plug in the tube
Worsening bronchospasm
A tension pneumothorax

items.q: You hear air escaping from the mouth of an intubated patient with each breath, and the pilot balloon is flat. Tube depth is unchanged and the ETCO2 waveform persists but is smaller. What is the first step?
items.x: A deflated cuff with the tube still in place is first managed by reinflating it; if the cuff will not hold air, the tube needs to be exchanged.
items.a: Reinflate the cuff and see if it holds
w: Remove the tube immediately and insert a supraglottic airway instead
Increase the tidal volume to make up for the lost volume
Advance the tube 3 cm so the cuff sits deeper in the trachea

items.q: An intubated, sedated 52-year-old has a normal square ETCO2 waveform, but over 20 minutes his ETCO2 has risen from 38 to 56 mmHg. SpO2 is 97 percent and BP is stable. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
items.x: A rising ETCO2 with a normal waveform means CO2 is not being removed fast enough; increasing the rate or tidal volume increases CO2 elimination.
items.a: Increase minute ventilation
w: Decrease the respiratory rate
Lower the oxygen concentration
Increase the PEEP

items.q: The capnography waveform of a patient being bagged no longer returns to zero between breaths; the baseline now sits at 8 mmHg. What does this indicate?
items.x: An elevated baseline means the inhaled gas contains CO2, as with a faulty exhalation valve, inadequate fresh gas flow or a contaminated sensor, so the equipment should be checked.
items.a: Rebreathing of exhaled CO2
w: Esophageal intubation
Bronchospasm
Cardiac arrest

items.q: You intubate a 40-year-old with a pulse who had been drinking soda shortly before he became unresponsive. Capnography shows small waveforms for 4 breaths that steadily fade to zero. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: CO2 from stomach contents can produce a few waveforms after an esophageal intubation, but they fade within several breaths; a sustained waveform is required to confirm tracheal placement.
items.a: The tube is in the esophagus
w: The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
He has severe bronchospasm
His cardiac output has suddenly improved

items.q: An intubated patient's capnogram shows a regular plateau with a small notch dipping into it on each breath. What does this notch most likely mean?
items.x: A cleft in the plateau appears when the patient makes spontaneous respiratory efforts, often as paralysis or sedation wears off, and may signal the need for more sedation.
items.a: The patient is starting to breathe on his own
w: The tube has migrated into the esophagus
CO2 is being rebreathed from the circuit
The patient has gone into cardiac arrest

items.q: A ventilated 58-year-old who had hip surgery 3 days ago suddenly has his ETCO2 drop from 36 to 18 mmHg with an unchanged waveform shape. SpO2 falls to 85 percent and BP to 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: An abrupt ETCO2 drop with a preserved waveform plus hypotension and hypoxia suggests a sudden loss of pulmonary blood flow, such as a massive PE; extubation gives a flat line and a kink raises pressures.
items.a: A large pulmonary embolism
w: Accidental extubation
Hyperventilation by the ventilator
A kinked endotracheal tube

items.q: During CPR on an intubated 63-year-old, ETCO2 has been 14 mmHg. It suddenly jumps to 42 mmHg with no change in ventilation. What does this most likely indicate?
items.x: An abrupt, sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR is an early sign of ROSC because restored blood flow delivers more CO2 to the lungs; confirm with a pulse check.
items.a: Return of spontaneous circulation
w: Displacement of the tube into the esophagus
Fatigue of the person doing compressions
Hypoventilation by the person bagging

items.q: During CPR you intubate an adult. Capnography shows a consistent waveform with every breath and a value of 12 mmHg. How should you interpret this?
items.x: A persistent waveform confirms the tube is in the trachea even during arrest; the low number reflects limited pulmonary blood flow, not misplacement.
items.a: Tracheal placement with low blood flow
w: The tube is in the esophagus and must be removed now
The tube has entered the right mainstem bronchus
The capnography sensor is faulty and should be replaced

items.q: A 66-year-old on a transport ventilator for acute pulmonary edema has an SpO2 of 86 percent on 100 percent oxygen with PEEP of 5 cm H2O. BP is 148/90 and tube position is confirmed. Which change is most likely to improve oxygenation?
items.x: PEEP holds fluid-filled alveoli open and improves oxygenation; with an adequate blood pressure, raising PEEP is the usual next step when oxygen is already at 100 percent.
items.a: Increase the PEEP
w: Reduce the PEEP to zero
Increase the respiratory rate
Lower the tidal volume to 4 mL/kg

items.q: An intubated 26-year-old asthmatic on a ventilator has high peak pressures, and the expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath starts. Which change best reduces air trapping?
items.x: In severe asthma the lungs need a long time to empty; a slower rate lengthens exhalation, reducing trapped air (auto-PEEP), even if CO2 rises somewhat.
items.a: Slow the rate to allow longer exhalation
w: Raise the respiratory rate to clear CO2 faster
Increase the PEEP to 15 cm H2O
Increase the tidal volume

items.q: During a critical care transfer of a patient with ARDS, which ventilator goal reflects a lung-protective strategy?
items.x: Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS uses small tidal volumes and limits plateau pressure to about 30 cm H2O or less to reduce further lung injury.
items.a: Plateau pressure at or below 30 cm H2O
w: Tidal volumes of 12 mL/kg to recruit alveoli
PEEP of zero to avoid barotrauma
A PaO2 above 300 mmHg

items.q: A 45-year-old admitted 2 days ago with severe pancreatitis is being transferred. He has worsening hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, flat neck veins and no cardiac history. What condition is most likely?
items.x: ARDS is an inflammatory, noncardiogenic lung injury triggered by conditions such as sepsis, pancreatitis or major trauma, causing refractory hypoxia with bilateral infiltrates.
items.a: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
w: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Acute asthma exacerbation
Spontaneous pneumothorax

items.q: How does CPAP improve oxygenation in a patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
items.x: CPAP splints alveoli open to improve gas exchange and raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return (preload) to the failing heart.
items.a: It keeps alveoli open and reduces preload
w: It increases heart rate and contractility
It removes fluid from the alveoli by suction
It raises systemic vascular resistance

items.q: Compared with CPAP, what does BiPAP add for a patient with a COPD exacerbation and CO2 retention?
items.x: BiPAP delivers a higher inspiratory pressure above the expiratory pressure, increasing tidal volume and helping clear CO2, whereas CPAP holds one constant pressure.
items.a: Higher pressure during inspiration
w: A guaranteed higher delivered oxygen concentration
Built-in protection of the airway from aspiration
A lower risk of hypotension because chest pressure is lower

items.q: A 71-year-old with COPD has been on CPAP for 15 minutes. He is now hard to arouse, respirations are shallow at 8/min and ETCO2 has climbed to 74 mmHg. What should you do?
items.x: A falling mental status with rising CO2 means noninvasive ventilation is failing; he needs assisted ventilation and likely an advanced airway.
items.a: Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask
w: Increase the CPAP pressure
Change to a nonrebreather mask
Continue CPAP and recheck in 10 minutes

items.q: You must perform a surgical cricothyrotomy on a 40-year-old. Where is the incision through the membrane made?
items.x: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid ring below; it is superficial and relatively avascular.
items.a: Between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages
w: Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Just above the suprasternal notch
Between the first and second tracheal rings

items.q: A 6-year-old with an obstructed upper airway is being oxygenated through a needle cricothyrotomy. Which problem limits how long this technique can be relied on?
items.x: A needle cricothyrotomy can oxygenate but allows poor exhalation, so CO2 accumulates; it is only a temporary bridge to a definitive airway.
items.a: Carbon dioxide builds up
w: Oxygen cannot reach the alveoli
The catheter needs constant suctioning
It cannot deliver high-concentration oxygen

items.q: A 68-year-old who had a total laryngectomy is apneic. A stoma is visible at the base of his neck. How should you ventilate him?
items.x: After a total laryngectomy the trachea no longer connects to the mouth or nose, so ventilation must be delivered through the stoma, often with an infant or pediatric mask.
items.a: Through the stoma with a small mask
w: With a standard adult mask sealed over the mouth and nose
Through the mouth after placing an oropharyngeal airway
With a nasal cannula running at 15 L/min

items.q: A 3-year-old's tracheostomy tube came out at home and the parents could not replace it. The child is cyanotic. You have a same-size tube and one a half size smaller. What should you do first?
items.x: Reinserting a tube into the existing stoma, trying the smaller size if needed, is the fastest way to restore the airway; if that fails, ventilate through the stoma or by mouth with the stoma covered.
items.a: Insert a replacement tube into the stoma
w: Ventilate with a mask over the mouth and nose only
Perform a needle cricothyrotomy
Intubate orally with a tube two sizes larger

items.q: A 50-year-old choked on steak and became unresponsive. You cannot ventilate him despite several cycles of CPR. Which advanced technique should you use?
items.x: Paramedics can look directly into the upper airway with a laryngoscope and remove a visible obstruction with Magill forceps; blind sweeps can push the object deeper.
items.a: Laryngoscopy and Magill forceps
w: Repeated blind finger sweeps of the posterior pharynx
Abdominal thrusts with the patient supine
Insert a supraglottic airway and ventilate through it

items.q: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 4-month-old lying supine on the stretcher. His head flexes forward. What should you do?
items.x: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine; padding under the shoulders brings the airway into a neutral position.
items.a: Place a folded towel under the shoulders
w: Hyperextend the neck as for an adult
Place a pillow under the head
Turn the head to one side

items.q: Using the age-based formula for cuffed tubes, which endotracheal tube size is appropriate for a 6-year-old?
items.x: For cuffed tubes the size is about age divided by 4 plus 3.5, so a 6-year-old needs roughly 5.0 mm; a half size larger and smaller should be ready.
items.a: 5.0 mm cuffed
w: 6.5 mm cuffed
4.0 mm cuffed
7.0 mm cuffed

items.q: During intubation of a 2-year-old, the heart rate falls from 140 to 70/min and the SpO2 to 80 percent. What should you do?
items.x: Bradycardia during pediatric intubation is usually caused by hypoxia; stopping to oxygenate usually reverses it.
items.a: Stop and ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
w: Give atropine and continue the attempt
Begin chest compressions immediately
Pass the tube as quickly as possible

items.q: An unvaccinated 5-year-old is sitting upright and drooling, with a muffled voice, a temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F) and soft inspiratory stridor. What is the best approach?
items.x: These signs suggest epiglottitis; agitating the child or instrumenting the throat can cause complete obstruction, so keep him calm, give oxygen as tolerated and transport with airway equipment ready.
items.a: Keep him calm in a position of comfort
w: Examine the throat with a tongue blade to confirm the cause
Place him supine and insert an oropharyngeal airway
Attempt intubation now before he gets worse

items.q: A 15-year-old with asthma has been wheezing for hours. Now he is drowsy, his chest is nearly silent and SpO2 is 86 percent. What does the silent chest indicate?
items.x: A silent chest in a tiring asthmatic means too little air is moving to produce a wheeze; with drowsiness it signals impending respiratory arrest and the need for assisted ventilation.
items.a: Minimal air movement and impending arrest
w: The bronchospasm is resolving and airflow is improving
Pneumonia has developed and replaced the wheezing
Hyperventilation from anxiety that will settle with coaching

items.q: A 34-year-old rescued from a house fire has singed nasal hair, soot in his sputum and a hoarse voice that is getting worse. SpO2 is 96 percent. What is the key airway concern?
items.x: Progressive hoarseness after inhalation injury signals upper airway edema; early definitive airway management may be needed before swelling makes intubation impossible.
items.a: Swelling that may close the airway
w: Carbon monoxide causing a falsely low SpO2 reading
Bronchospasm that should be managed with CPAP
Aspiration of gastric contents during transport

items.q: What is an advantage of a second-generation supraglottic airway with a gastric channel?
items.x: The gastric channel lets air and fluid vent from the stomach or a gastric tube be passed, reducing the risk of regurgitation, although it does not fully protect against aspiration.
items.a: It allows the stomach to be decompressed
w: It completely protects the lungs from aspiration
It can be inserted in patients with an intact gag reflex
It provides confirmation that the tube is in the trachea

items.q: A 58-year-old has rapidly progressing tongue and lip swelling with a muffled voice, and you decide he needs an advanced airway. How should you prepare?
items.x: With upper airway swelling, intubation can fail and supraglottic devices may not seal, so a double setup with the neck prepared for cricothyrotomy is essential.
items.a: Be ready for a surgical airway if intubation fails
w: Plan blind nasal intubation as the only option
Use a supraglottic airway as the primary device
Wait until he becomes apneic before intervening

items.q: A septic 70-year-old has an ABG of pH 7.24, PaCO2 26 mmHg and HCO3 11 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
items.x: A low pH with a low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 reflects the lungs blowing off CO2 to compensate.
items.a: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
w: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis together

items.q: A 22-year-old with severe anxiety, tingling fingers and carpopedal spasm has an ABG of pH 7.53, PaCO2 27 mmHg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
items.x: A high pH with a low PaCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory alkalosis; serious causes such as pulmonary embolism should still be considered before blaming anxiety.
items.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis
w: Metabolic acidosis
Compensated metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory acidosis

items.q: A 40-year-old has vomited repeatedly for 4 days. His ABG shows pH 7.51, PaCO2 47 mmHg and HCO3 35 mEq/L. Which disorder is present?
items.x: Losing stomach acid raises bicarbonate; a high pH and high HCO3 identify metabolic alkalosis, and the slightly raised PaCO2 is compensatory hypoventilation.
items.a: Metabolic alkalosis
w: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis

items.q: A 74-year-old with long-standing COPD who is at his baseline has an ABG of pH 7.36, PaCO2 62 mmHg and HCO3 34 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
items.x: A near-normal pH with high PaCO2 and high bicarbonate shows the kidneys have retained bicarbonate over time to offset chronic CO2 retention.
items.a: Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis
w: Acute respiratory acidosis requiring immediate intubation
Primary metabolic alkalosis
A completely normal blood gas

items.q: You are assessing a 52-year-old for intubation. Which findings predict a difficult laryngoscopy? Select all that apply.
items.x: Limited mouth opening, restricted neck movement and obstruction such as a hematoma all make laryngoscopy harder; missing teeth make bag-mask sealing harder but usually make laryngoscopy easier.
opts: Mouth opening of less than two fingerbreadths
A rigid cervical collar limiting neck extension
An expanding hematoma in the neck
Missing upper front teeth
A thin patient with a long neck
ok: Mouth opening of less than two fingerbreadths
A rigid cervical collar limiting neck extension
An expanding hematoma in the neck

items.q: Which measures lengthen the safe apnea time before rapid sequence intubation? Select all that apply.
items.x: Upright positioning, apneic oxygenation and PEEP all improve the oxygen reserve; aggressive bagging inflates the stomach and lying flat or removing oxygen speeds desaturation.
opts: Head-up or ramped positioning
Nasal cannula oxygen at high flow left on during laryngoscopy
A PEEP valve on the bag-valve mask for a patient who stays hypoxic
Bagging at 30 breaths/min before induction
Removing oxygen briefly to check the room air saturation
Laying an obese patient completely flat
ok: Head-up or ramped positioning
Nasal cannula oxygen at high flow left on during laryngoscopy
A PEEP valve on the bag-valve mask for a patient who stays hypoxic

items.q: You have just intubated an adult with a pulse. Which findings support tracheal placement? Select all that apply.
items.x: Continuous waveform capnography, direct visualization and auscultation support placement; fogging can occur with an esophageal tube, and SpO2 can stay normal for minutes after misplacement.
opts: A sustained ETCO2 waveform over several breaths
Seeing the tube pass between the vocal cords
Equal breath sounds with no sounds over the epigastrium
Fogging inside the tube
A normal SpO2 immediately after the tube is placed
ok: A sustained ETCO2 waveform over several breaths
Seeing the tube pass between the vocal cords
Equal breath sounds with no sounds over the epigastrium

items.q: An intubated patient's peak airway pressure suddenly rises on the ventilator. Which problems could explain this? Select all that apply.
items.x: Obstruction, bronchospasm and biting all raise resistance to airflow; leaks and disconnections cause low pressure alarms.
opts: A mucus plug in the tube
Bronchospasm
The patient biting down on the tube
A leak in the cuff
Disconnection of the circuit
ok: A mucus plug in the tube
Bronchospasm
The patient biting down on the tube

items.q: Which situations can produce an elevated ETCO2 with a normal waveform shape? Select all that apply.
items.x: ETCO2 rises when CO2 production or delivery to the lungs increases, or when ventilation falls; hyperventilation, PE and hypothermia lower it.
opts: Hypoventilation from an opioid
Return of spontaneous circulation during CPR
Fever with increased metabolism
Hyperventilation
A massive pulmonary embolism
Hypothermia
ok: Hypoventilation from an opioid
Return of spontaneous circulation during CPR
Fever with increased metabolism

items.q: Which patients are good candidates for CPAP? Select all that apply.
items.x: CPAP needs an alert patient who can protect the airway and is breathing spontaneously; unresponsiveness, vomiting and pneumothorax are contraindications.
opts: An alert 70-year-old with acute pulmonary edema and BP 170/100
An alert 66-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and accessory muscle use
An alert near-drowning victim with crackles and SpO2 88 percent
An unresponsive patient with agonal respirations
A patient who is actively vomiting
A patient with a suspected pneumothorax
ok: An alert 70-year-old with acute pulmonary edema and BP 170/100
An alert 66-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and accessory muscle use
An alert near-drowning victim with crackles and SpO2 88 percent

items.q: You cannot intubate or oxygenate a patient and need an emergency front-of-neck airway. In which patients is needle cricothyrotomy preferred over a surgical cricothyrotomy? Select all that apply.
items.x: Young children have a small, pliable cricothyroid membrane, so needle cricothyrotomy is preferred; adults generally receive a surgical cricothyrotomy.
opts: A 4-year-old with severe facial burns
An 18-month-old with an obstructing foreign body that cannot be removed
A 35-year-old with massive facial trauma
A 60-year-old with severe angioedema
A 28-year-old with an expanding neck hematoma
ok: A 4-year-old with severe facial burns
An 18-month-old with an obstructing foreign body that cannot be removed

items.q: Which anatomic features of a young child's airway differ from an adult's? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children have a large tongue and occiput and a higher larynx; their trachea is short and soft, and their oxygen consumption per kilogram is higher, so they desaturate quickly.
opts: A tongue that is large relative to the mouth
A large occiput
A larynx positioned higher and more anterior
A longer, more rigid trachea
Lower oxygen use per kilogram
ok: A tongue that is large relative to the mouth
A large occiput
A larynx positioned higher and more anterior

items.q: You are ventilating an intubated patient during a severe asthma attack. Which findings suggest dangerous air trapping? Select all that apply.
items.x: Incomplete exhalation causes stacked breaths, rising pressures and reduced venous return; complete exhalation with matching volumes indicates the lungs are emptying.
opts: Blood pressure falling with each breath series
Steadily rising peak airway pressures
Exhalation still occurring when the next breath begins
Exhaled volumes matching delivered volumes
A long pause after exhalation before the next breath
ok: Blood pressure falling with each breath series
Steadily rising peak airway pressures
Exhalation still occurring when the next breath begins

items.q: Which arterial blood gas values fall within normal adult ranges? Select all that apply.
items.x: Normal values are about pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg and HCO3 22 to 26 mEq/L; a PaO2 of 55 mmHg is hypoxemia and pH 7.30 is acidemia.
opts: PaCO2 40 mmHg
HCO3 24 mEq/L
PaO2 55 mmHg on room air
ok: PaCO2 40 mmHg
HCO3 24 mEq/L

items.q: A 69-year-old is dizzy. The rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 84/min, with every other P wave followed by a narrow QRS. The PR interval of the conducted beats is constant. What is the rhythm?
items.x: When every second P wave is blocked, the block cannot be firmly classified as type I or type II; it is described as 2 to 1 second-degree AV block, and a wide QRS makes an infranodal (more dangerous) block more likely.
items.a: Second-degree AV block with 2 to 1 conduction
w: First-degree AV block
Third-degree AV block
Atrial flutter with 2 to 1 conduction

items.q: A rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular narrow QRS complexes at 44/min, with no consistent relationship between them; the P waves march through the QRS complexes. What is the rhythm?
items.x: Atria and ventricles beating independently is complete heart block; a narrow escape rhythm in the 40s to 50s arises from the AV junction and is usually more stable than a wide ventricular escape.
items.a: Third-degree AV block with a junctional escape
w: Second-degree AV block type I
Sinus bradycardia
Atrial fibrillation with slow response

items.q: A 54-year-old on methadone collapses. The monitor shows a wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude repeatedly grows and shrinks, appearing to twist around the baseline. What is this rhythm?
items.x: Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic VT with twisting amplitude linked to a prolonged QT interval, which methadone and many other drugs can cause.
items.a: Torsades de pointes
w: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy
Coarse ventricular fibrillation
