items.q: A 73-year-old has had palpitations for an unknown number of days. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 128/min. He is alert with BP 132/80. Why is elective cardioversion avoided in the field?
items.x: Atrial fibrillation lasting more than about 48 hours, or of unknown duration, may have formed atrial clots that can embolize when sinus rhythm returns, causing a stroke.
items.a: It may dislodge a clot from the atria
w: It will convert the rhythm into asystole
It is ineffective for atrial rhythms
It requires general anesthesia in all patients

items.q: A 22-year-old with palpitations has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240/min with QRS complexes that vary in width. He has a history of an accessory pathway. BP is 118/72. Which treatment approach must be avoided?
items.x: In atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (pre-excitation), blocking the AV node can push more impulses down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation.
items.a: AV nodal blocking medications
w: Obtaining a 12-lead ECG
Preparing for synchronized cardioversion
Consulting medical direction

items.q: During CPR on a 66-year-old, the rhythm check shows a flat line in lead II. What should you do?
items.x: Before treating as asystole, confirm the leads are connected, the gain is adequate and the flat line persists in another lead, so fine VF is not missed; CPR continues meanwhile.
items.a: Confirm in another lead and check the gain
w: Defibrillate in case it is fine VF
Stop CPR, since asystole is not survivable
Synchronize and cardiovert

items.q: A 67-year-old on a ventilator for COPD loses his pulse. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 130/min. Breath sounds are absent on the right and his neck veins are distended. Which cause of PEA is most likely?
items.x: A fast, narrow PEA suggests a mechanical problem; absent breath sounds and distended neck veins in a ventilated COPD patient point to tension pneumothorax, which needs decompression.
items.a: Tension pneumothorax
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypothermia
Acidosis

items.q: A 58-year-old dialysis patient who has missed two treatments is pulseless. The monitor shows slow, very wide, bizarre complexes at 30/min. Which reversible cause is most likely?
items.x: Slow, wide PEA in a patient who has missed dialysis strongly suggests hyperkalemia, which needs specific treatment along with high-quality CPR.
items.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Tension pneumothorax
Cardiac tamponade
Hypovolemia

items.q: A 77-year-old with several days of black, tarry stools becomes pulseless. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 120/min. Which treatment addresses the most likely cause?
items.x: A fast, narrow PEA after GI bleeding points to hypovolemia; restoring volume, ideally with blood where available, treats the cause while CPR continues.
items.a: Rapid volume replacement
w: Needle decompression of the chest
Synchronized cardioversion
Transcutaneous pacing

items.q: A 61-year-old has chest pain with ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 and ST depression in III. Which coronary artery is most likely involved?
items.x: ST elevation limited to the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) usually reflects occlusion of the circumflex artery or one of its branches.
items.a: Left circumflex artery
w: Right coronary artery
Posterior descending artery
Proximal left anterior descending artery

items.q: A 64-year-old has chest pain. His 12-lead shows ST depression in III and aVF and subtle ST elevation in I and aVL. How should this be interpreted?
items.x: ST depression in the inferior leads can be the mirror image of a high lateral infarction; subtle elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal inferior depression should be treated as STEMI.
items.a: High lateral STEMI with inferior reciprocal changes
w: Inferior ischemia only, not a STEMI
Pericarditis affecting the inferior wall
A normal variant in an older adult

items.q: A 59-year-old with an inferior STEMI has more ST elevation in lead III than in lead II, with ST depression in lead I. Which artery is most likely occluded?
items.x: In an inferior STEMI, ST elevation greater in III than II with depression in lead I points to the right coronary artery, which also raises concern for right ventricular involvement.
items.a: Right coronary artery
w: Left circumflex artery
Left anterior descending artery
Left main coronary artery

items.q: A 70-year-old with crushing chest pain and BP 92/60 has ST elevation in aVR and widespread ST depression in most other leads. What does this pattern suggest?
items.x: ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggests severe ischemia from left main or three-vessel disease, a high-risk pattern needing rapid transport to a PCI-capable center.
items.a: Left main or multivessel ischemia
w: Benign early repolarization
Isolated right ventricular infarction
Acute pericarditis

items.q: A 51-year-old had chest pain yesterday that has now resolved. His 12-lead shows deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in V2 and V3 with no ST elevation. What is the concern?
items.x: This Wellens pattern indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis with a high risk of a large anterior MI in the coming days, so the patient needs cardiology evaluation even though pain-free.
items.a: Critical narrowing of the proximal LAD
w: A healed old infarction needing no action
Normal T waves for a middle-aged adult
Pericarditis in its late stage

items.q: A 48-year-old with ongoing chest pain has upsloping ST depression at the J point with tall, symmetric T waves across V1 to V6 and no ST elevation. How should this be handled?
items.x: This de Winter pattern signals acute proximal LAD occlusion without classic ST elevation and should prompt activation of the STEMI system per protocol.
items.a: As a STEMI equivalent from LAD occlusion
w: As nonspecific changes needing no special action
As benign early repolarization
As typical findings of hyperventilation

items.q: A 75-year-old with a known left bundle branch block has chest pain. Which finding on his 12-lead most strongly suggests an acute MI?
items.x: In LBBB, ST segments normally go opposite the QRS; ST elevation of at least 1 mm in the same direction as the QRS (concordant) is a specific sign of acute infarction.
items.a: ST elevation in the same direction as the QRS
w: ST elevation opposite to a deep negative QRS in V1
A QRS width of 0.14 seconds
T waves opposite to the main QRS direction

items.q: A healthy 23-year-old athlete has a 12-lead done after a minor injury. It shows concave ST elevation in V2 to V4 with a notched J point, no reciprocal depression, and no symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Concave ST elevation with J-point notching and no reciprocal changes in a young, asymptomatic person is typical of early repolarization, a common STEMI mimic.
items.a: Benign early repolarization
w: Acute anterior STEMI
Brugada pattern
Hyperkalemia

items.q: A 31-year-old has sharp chest pain and diffuse ST elevation. Which additional ECG finding favors pericarditis over STEMI?
items.x: Pericarditis typically causes widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR; localized elevation with reciprocal depression favors STEMI.
items.a: PR depression in many leads
w: ST depression in leads opposite to the elevation
ST elevation confined to II, III and aVF
New Q waves in the anterior leads

items.q: A 33-year-old fainted at rest. His ECG shows a right bundle branch-like pattern with coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Why is this important?
items.x: Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 with syncope suggests Brugada syndrome, which predisposes to ventricular fibrillation and requires hospital evaluation.
items.a: It indicates a risk of sudden cardiac death
w: It is a normal finding in young men
It indicates an old septal infarction
It shows that the faint was vasovagal

items.q: A 25-year-old marathon runner has a heart rate of 42/min in sinus rhythm during a screening exam. He is alert, BP is 118/70 and he has no complaints. What is the appropriate treatment?
items.x: Bradycardia is treated only when it causes symptoms or poor perfusion; well-conditioned athletes often have resting rates in the 40s.
items.a: No treatment for the slow rate
w: Atropine to raise the rate
Transcutaneous pacing on standby at 60/min
An immediate fluid bolus

items.q: You are pacing a 74-year-old with complete heart block. Each pacer spike is followed by a wide QRS on the monitor. How should you confirm mechanical capture?
items.x: Electrical capture on the monitor does not prove the heart is pumping; a femoral pulse matching the paced rate confirms mechanical capture, and carotid checks are confused by muscle twitching.
items.a: Palpate a femoral pulse that matches the paced rate
w: Palpate a carotid pulse during pacing
See that the pacer spikes appear on the screen
Watch for chest wall muscle twitching

items.q: A 72-year-old has second-degree AV block type II with a wide QRS at 54/min. He is alert, BP 118/70, with no chest pain or dizziness. What is the most appropriate action?
items.x: Type II block can suddenly progress to complete heart block, so pads should be on and ready for pacing even in a stable patient.
items.a: Apply pacing pads and monitor closely
w: Begin pacing immediately at 80/min
Perform synchronized cardioversion
No monitoring is needed since he is stable

items.q: A 60-year-old who had a heart transplant 5 years ago has symptomatic bradycardia at 38/min with BP 78/44. Why is atropine unlikely to help?
items.x: A transplanted heart is denervated, so blocking vagal tone has little effect; pacing or an adrenergic infusion is usually needed.
items.a: The transplanted heart lacks vagal innervation
w: Transplant patients are allergic to atropine
Atropine only works for wide-complex rhythms
Atropine is used only in children

items.q: A 34-year-old with 2 days of fever and vomiting has a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 142/min with visible P waves before each QRS. The rate varies slightly with movement. BP is 104/66. What is the best management?
items.x: Sinus tachycardia is a response to an underlying problem, such as fever, pain or hypovolemia; treating the cause is correct, and cardioversion or vagal maneuvers are not.
items.a: Treat the dehydration and fever
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers to break the rhythm
Transcutaneous pacing

items.q: You deliver a synchronized shock to a hypotensive 66-year-old in atrial fibrillation with rapid response, but the rhythm does not change. Before delivering the next synchronized shock, what must you check?
items.x: Many monitors return to unsynchronized mode after each shock, so sync must be confirmed before every shock to avoid delivering it on the T wave.
items.a: That the sync mode is still selected
w: That the pads have been moved to the back
That the monitor is in pacing mode
That the patient's pulse is absent

items.q: A 29-year-old with stable SVT at 188/min is alert and normotensive. Which vagal technique is most likely to convert the rhythm?
items.x: The modified Valsalva maneuver, a strain against resistance followed immediately by lying flat with legs raised, converts SVT more often than a standard Valsalva; eyeball pressure and bilateral carotid massage are dangerous.
items.a: Modified Valsalva with leg raise
w: Carotid massage on both sides at once
Pressing firmly on both eyeballs
Holding the breath for 5 seconds

items.q: A 48-year-old had a witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR. He remains in VF after three shocks. A mechanical CPR device is in place and your system has an ECPR center 15 minutes away. What is the most appropriate step?
items.x: Refractory VF in a young patient with a witnessed arrest and good bystander CPR is the classic ECPR candidate; early transport with mechanical CPR is needed because outcomes depend on the time to bypass.
items.a: Early transport to the ECPR center per protocol
w: Continue on scene for 60 minutes before moving
Stop resuscitation after the third failed shock
Transport to the nearest non-ECPR hospital

items.q: You are ventilating an intubated 59-year-old after ROSC. Which ETCO2 range is generally targeted?
items.x: Post-arrest ventilation aims for normal CO2 levels; hyperventilation lowers CO2 and reduces cerebral blood flow, while hypoventilation worsens acidosis.
items.a: 35 to 45 mmHg
w: 15 to 20 mmHg
20 to 25 mmHg
55 to 65 mmHg

items.q: A 57-year-old has ROSC after a VF arrest. His post-ROSC 12-lead shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. Where should he be transported?
items.x: Post-arrest patients with STEMI benefit from emergency coronary angiography, so they should go to a PCI-capable center, ideally a designated cardiac arrest center.
items.a: A PCI-capable center
w: The closest emergency department regardless of capability
A stroke center
A trauma center

items.q: A comatose 62-year-old has ROSC after a cardiac arrest. Which temperature-related practice is not recommended in the prehospital setting?
items.x: Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold IV fluid infusion has not improved outcomes and has caused pulmonary edema and re-arrest; preventing fever remains part of post-arrest care.
items.a: Rapid infusion of cold IV fluids
w: Avoiding fever
Monitoring temperature when possible
Preventing hyperthermia from heavy blankets

items.q: A 3-month-old has a heart rate of 270/min with a narrow QRS, no visible P waves and no beat-to-beat variation. The parents say he was feeding normally an hour ago. What is the most likely rhythm?
items.x: In infants, SVT is usually above 220/min with absent P waves, a fixed rate and abrupt onset; sinus tachycardia is usually lower, varies with activity and follows a cause such as fever or dehydration.
items.a: Supraventricular tachycardia
w: Sinus tachycardia from fever
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation

items.q: A 6-month-old has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 280/min. He is lethargic and mottled with weak pulses. No vascular access has been obtained yet. What is the appropriate treatment?
items.x: Unstable SVT with poor perfusion needs immediate synchronized cardioversion when vascular access is not available; delaying for access worsens shock.
items.a: Synchronized cardioversion
w: Unsynchronized defibrillation
Wait for IO access before any treatment
Begin chest compressions

items.q: A 20-kg child is in ventricular fibrillation. What energy should be used for the first defibrillation?
items.x: The initial pediatric defibrillation dose is 2 J/kg, so 40 J for a 20-kg child; later shocks are increased to 4 J/kg or more.

items.q: You are preparing to defibrillate a 5-month-old in VF, but the adult-size pads would touch each other on the front of the chest. What should you do?
items.x: Pads must not touch; when the chest is too small, anterior-posterior placement allows the current to pass through the heart without arcing between pads.
items.a: Place one pad on the front and one on the back
w: Overlap the pads slightly on the front of the chest
Cut the pads to a smaller size
Place both pads on the back

items.q: A 10-month-old with bronchiolitis is limp, with a heart rate of 58/min, SpO2 of 70 percent and poor perfusion. No ventilation has been given yet. What is the first priority?
items.x: Bradycardia in children is most often caused by hypoxia; oxygenation and ventilation come first, and compressions start if the rate stays below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
items.a: Ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
w: Begin transcutaneous pacing
Give atropine
Synchronized cardioversion

items.q: A 66-year-old dialysis patient has weakness. The 12-lead shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves with otherwise normal intervals. What do these findings suggest?
items.x: Peaked T waves are usually the first ECG sign of rising potassium; with further rises the P wave flattens, the QRS widens and a sine-wave pattern can precede arrest.
items.a: Early hyperkalemia
w: Hypokalemia
Acute pericarditis
Digoxin effect

items.q: A 79-year-old found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 30 C (86 F). The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a distinct hump at the end of each QRS complex. What is this finding?
items.x: Osborn waves, an extra deflection at the J point, are characteristic of hypothermia and tend to grow as the temperature falls.
items.a: Osborn (J) waves from hypothermia
w: Delta waves from pre-excitation
U waves from hypokalemia
Epsilon waves from cardiomyopathy

items.q: A 68-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with pink, frothy sputum, crackles throughout, BP 222/124 and SpO2 84 percent. She is alert and follows commands. Which intervention should be started first?
items.x: Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema responds rapidly to CPAP, usually combined with nitrates per protocol; fluids and lying flat worsen the congestion.
items.a: CPAP
w: A 1-liter fluid bolus
Supine positioning with legs raised
Nebulized bronchodilator alone

items.q: A 64-year-old with an anterior STEMI is cool and clammy, with BP 76/48, crackles to the mid-lung fields and SpO2 89 percent. What should be avoided?
items.x: This is cardiogenic shock; nitrates worsen hypotension and large fluid volumes worsen pulmonary edema, so management focuses on careful hemodynamic support and rapid reperfusion.
items.a: Nitroglycerin and large fluid boluses
w: Rapid transport to a PCI-capable center
Oxygen to keep SpO2 above 90 percent
A repeat 12-lead ECG during transport

items.q: A 71-year-old with severe COPD has distended neck veins, swollen ankles and an enlarged, tender liver. His lungs have scattered wheezes but no crackles. Which condition do these findings suggest?
items.x: Right heart failure, often from chronic lung disease, causes systemic venous congestion such as JVD, edema and liver enlargement, without the pulmonary crackles of left-sided failure.
items.a: Right-sided heart failure
w: Left-sided heart failure
Hypovolemic shock
Acute pericarditis

items.q: A 63-year-old has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back, a weak left radial pulse and ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What is the key concern?
items.x: An aortic dissection can involve a coronary artery and cause STEMI; recognizing it matters because antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy can be catastrophic, so the receiving center must be told.
items.a: A dissection extending into the right coronary artery
w: A routine inferior STEMI needing standard treatment only
Acute pericarditis from a viral illness
Gastroesophageal reflux with a nonspecific ECG

items.q: A 72-year-old man suddenly developed severe low back and flank pain, then fainted. He has a pulsatile abdominal mass and BP 84/50. What is the most appropriate approach?
items.x: A suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs surgery; limit scene time, avoid raising the BP to normal, and transport to a facility that can repair it.
items.a: Rapid transport to a center with vascular surgery
w: Large fluid boluses to bring the systolic BP to 140 mmHg
Prolonged scene stabilization before transport
Transport to the nearest clinic for imaging

items.q: A 69-year-old has left arm weakness, right gaze deviation and neglect starting 50 minutes ago. Your regional plan allows bypassing a primary stroke center 10 minutes away for a thrombectomy-capable center 25 minutes away when an LVO is suspected. Where should she go?
items.x: With a positive LVO screen and modest added time, direct transport to a thrombectomy-capable center speeds clot retrieval, as regional stroke plans allow.
items.a: The thrombectomy-capable center
w: The primary stroke center 10 minutes away
The nearest urgent care clinic
Her primary care physician's office

items.q: A 58-year-old suddenly develops right-sided weakness. Which feature most suggests a hemorrhagic rather than an ischemic stroke?
items.x: Sudden severe headache with vomiting and a declining level of consciousness suggests raised intracranial pressure from bleeding, although only imaging can confirm the stroke type.
items.a: Severe headache, vomiting and falling LOC
w: Slurred speech that began on waking
Facial droop that is resolving
A history of atrial fibrillation

items.q: A 35-year-old with epilepsy had a witnessed generalized seizure 20 minutes ago and now has right arm weakness. Glucose is 112 mg/dL. Which condition can mimic a stroke in this patient?
items.x: Temporary weakness after a seizure (Todd paralysis) is a common stroke mimic, though a stroke cannot be ruled out in the field and the history should be clearly reported.
items.a: Postictal (Todd) paralysis
w: Bell palsy
Hypoglycemia
Transient global amnesia

items.q: A 74-year-old with an acute ischemic stroke 1 hour ago has BP 196/104. She is alert with stable vital signs otherwise. What is the appropriate field management of her blood pressure?
items.x: Elevated blood pressure helps perfuse threatened brain tissue, so it is not lowered in the field unless directed by medical control; the hospital manages it according to treatment plans.
items.a: Monitor it without trying to lower it
w: Lower it to 120/80 within 15 minutes
Give a large fluid bolus to protect the brain
Lay her flat with legs raised

items.q: A 61-year-old has sudden vertigo, vomiting, double vision and cannot walk without falling. His face, arm drift and speech are normal. What should you suspect?
items.x: Posterior circulation strokes often spare the face, arms and speech, so screening tools that include balance and eye findings help detect them.
items.a: Posterior circulation stroke
w: Benign inner ear vertigo
Migraine with aura
Simple dehydration

items.q: A 57-year-old with lung cancer is short of breath and hypotensive. The 12-lead shows low voltage, and the QRS height alternates from beat to beat. What does this suggest?
items.x: Low voltage with electrical alternans, the heart swinging within a large fluid-filled pericardium, suggests a large effusion and possible tamponade.
items.a: A large pericardial effusion
w: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hyperkalemia
Acute anterior STEMI

items.q: A 63-year-old with a left ventricular assist device is alert and talking. You cannot palpate a radial pulse and the automatic BP cuff gives no reading. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: Continuous-flow LVADs often produce no palpable pulse or measurable cuff pressure; perfusion is judged by mental status, skin signs and device alarms, and an alert patient is not in arrest.
items.a: This can be normal with a continuous-flow device
w: He is in cardiac arrest and needs compressions
The device has failed and must be switched off
He is in hypovolemic shock and needs fluids

items.q: A rhythm strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 50/min. In lead II the P waves are inverted and appear just before each QRS with a very short PR interval. What is the rhythm?
items.x: Impulses from the AV junction spread backward through the atria, producing inverted P waves just before, during or after the QRS, at a rate of about 40 to 60.
items.a: Junctional rhythm
w: Sinus bradycardia
First-degree AV block
Atrial flutter

items.q: A 76-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and SpO2 of 84 percent has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 118/min with at least three different P wave shapes. What is the best approach to this rhythm?
items.x: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is driven by underlying illness, especially lung disease and hypoxia; it does not respond to cardioversion and improves when the cause is treated.
items.a: Treat the hypoxia and lung disease
w: Synchronized cardioversion
Transcutaneous pacing
Unsynchronized defibrillation

items.q: After reperfusion of an inferior STEMI, a 62-year-old's monitor shows a regular wide-complex rhythm at 72/min. He has a strong pulse and BP 124/76. What is this rhythm most likely to be?
items.x: A wide ventricular rhythm at 40 to 100 after reperfusion is usually accelerated idioventricular rhythm; it is generally benign and should not be suppressed with antiarrhythmics.
items.a: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm
w: Ventricular tachycardia needing cardioversion
Ventricular fibrillation
Third-degree AV block with slow escape

items.q: A newborn's heart rate remains 50/min after 30 seconds of positive pressure ventilation that moves the chest. What is the next step?
items.x: NRP calls for chest compressions coordinated with ventilations at 3 to 1, with increased oxygen, when the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation.
items.a: Start compressions at a 3 to 1 ratio
w: Continue ventilation alone for 2 more minutes
Start compressions at a 15 to 2 ratio
Stop resuscitation

items.q: Which conditions can cause ST elevation without an acute coronary occlusion? Select all that apply.
items.x: LVH, LBBB and early repolarization are common STEMI mimics; reciprocal depression actually makes a true STEMI more likely.
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left bundle branch block
Benign early repolarization
Reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads
A ventricular rate of 72 in sinus rhythm
ok: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left bundle branch block
Benign early repolarization

items.q: A 29-year-old had a flu-like illness last week and now has chest pain. Which findings support acute pericarditis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Pericarditis causes sharp, pleuritic, positional pain and sometimes a friction rub, often after a viral illness; exertional crushing pain and localized elevation with reciprocal changes suggest ischemia.
opts: Pain that is worse lying flat and better leaning forward
A scratchy friction rub heard over the chest
Pain that is sharp and worse with deep breaths
Crushing pain relieved by rest
ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior depression
ok: Pain that is worse lying flat and better leaning forward
A scratchy friction rub heard over the chest
Pain that is sharp and worse with deep breaths

items.q: Which patients are at increased risk of hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
items.x: Kidney failure and muscle breakdown from crush injury raise serum potassium; vomiting and loop diuretics typically lower it.
opts: A dialysis patient who missed two treatments
A worker freed after hours trapped under heavy debris
A patient with acute kidney failure
A patient with several days of vomiting
A patient taking a high-dose loop diuretic
ok: A dialysis patient who missed two treatments
A worker freed after hours trapped under heavy debris
A patient with acute kidney failure

items.q: A 58-year-old has a sudden tearing chest pain. Which findings support aortic dissection? Select all that apply.
items.x: Dissection can block branch arteries, causing pulse deficits or stroke symptoms, and can disrupt the aortic valve, causing a new diastolic murmur.
opts: A pulse deficit in one arm
New weakness on one side of the body
A new diastolic heart murmur
Pain that built up slowly over several days and eases with rest
Sharp pain that changes with position and improves leaning forward
ok: A pulse deficit in one arm
New weakness on one side of the body
A new diastolic heart murmur

items.q: Which factors make a cardiac arrest patient a better candidate for ECPR? Select all that apply.
items.x: ECPR works best with short no-flow times, shockable rhythms and patients without severe comorbidities; long no-flow periods and terminal illness predict poor outcomes.
opts: Witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR
Refractory ventricular fibrillation
Younger age without major chronic illness
Age 89 with metastatic cancer
Unwitnessed arrest found after at least 45 minutes
Asystole after a long period without CPR
ok: Witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR
Refractory ventricular fibrillation
Younger age without major chronic illness

items.q: You are starting transcutaneous pacing on a conscious 79-year-old with complete heart block and BP 70/40. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Output is raised until capture, comfort measures are considered for the conscious patient, and demand mode needs the ECG leads; twitching is expected and carotid checks are unreliable.
opts: Increase the output until each spike is followed by a wide QRS
Consider analgesia or sedation per protocol
Keep the monitoring leads attached for demand pacing
Confirm capture by feeling the carotid pulse
Stop pacing when chest muscle twitching appears
ok: Increase the output until each spike is followed by a wide QRS
Consider analgesia or sedation per protocol
Keep the monitoring leads attached for demand pacing

items.q: Which findings suggest cardiogenic shock in a patient with an acute MI? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cardiogenic shock combines poor perfusion and hypotension with congestion; warm skin suggests distributive shock and flat veins with clear lungs suggest hypovolemia.
opts: Cool, clammy skin
Crackles in both lungs
Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with altered mental status
Warm, flushed skin with bounding pulses
Flat neck veins with clear lungs after vomiting
ok: Cool, clammy skin
Crackles in both lungs
Systolic BP below 90 mmHg with altered mental status

items.q: A patient in PEA has a narrow QRS at a fast rate, suggesting a mechanical cause. Which conditions fit this pattern? Select all that apply.
items.x: Narrow, fast PEA usually means the heart is electrically intact but cannot fill or eject, as in tamponade, tension pneumothorax or PE; hyperkalemia and sodium channel toxins widen the QRS.
opts: Cardiac tamponade
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism
Severe hyperkalemia
Overdose of a sodium channel blocking drug
ok: Cardiac tamponade
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism

items.q: You are transporting a suspected stroke patient. Which information is most important to give the receiving stroke team? Select all that apply.
items.x: Last known well, anticoagulant use and glucose directly affect treatment eligibility and mimic exclusion; the 911 call time is not the onset time.
opts: The last known well time
Whether the patient takes an anticoagulant
The blood glucose result
The exact time the 911 call was placed
Results of a cholesterol test from last year
ok: The last known well time
Whether the patient takes an anticoagulant
The blood glucose result

items.q: A 45-year-old fainted while sitting at his desk. Which ECG findings make a dangerous cause of syncope more likely? Select all that apply.
items.x: Conduction blocks, long QT and pre-excitation can cause sudden arrhythmic syncope; a normal ECG and respiratory sinus arrhythmia are reassuring.
opts: Second-degree AV block type II
A markedly prolonged QT interval
A delta wave with a short PR interval
Normal sinus rhythm at 72/min with normal intervals
Sinus arrhythmia that varies with breathing
ok: Second-degree AV block type II
A markedly prolonged QT interval
A delta wave with a short PR interval

items.q: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Displacing the uterus relieves aortocaval compression; standard defibrillation is safe in pregnancy, and early notification allows rapid delivery if ROSC is not achieved.
opts: Manual left uterine displacement during CPR
Defibrillation at standard adult energy
Early notification for possible resuscitative delivery
Compressions placed lower on the abdomen
Withholding defibrillation to protect the fetus
ok: Manual left uterine displacement during CPR
Defibrillation at standard adult energy
Early notification for possible resuscitative delivery

items.q: A 2-year-old has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which findings indicate compensated shock? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children maintain blood pressure until late, so tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion signal compensated shock; hypotension and bradycardia are late signs of decompensation.
opts: Tachycardia
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Cool hands and feet
Systolic hypotension
Bradycardia
ok: Tachycardia
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Cool hands and feet

items.q: A 29-year-old construction worker has a near-amputation of the left lower leg with massive bleeding. He has snoring respirations and a GCS of 10. Using the MARCH sequence, what do you address first?
items.x: MARCH puts massive hemorrhage before the airway because a person can bleed to death from a severed leg artery within minutes. The airway is managed right after the bleeding is controlled.
items.a: Apply a tourniquet high and tight on the leg
w: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway to relieve the snoring
Expose the chest and look for an open pneumothorax
Obtain a blood glucose and a full set of vital signs

items.q: You have controlled bleeding, managed the airway, sealed a chest wound and started an IV on a 40-year-old gunshot victim lying on wet pavement on a cold night. Under MARCH, what should you do next?
items.x: The H in MARCH covers hypothermia and head injury. Even mild hypothermia worsens bleeding by impairing clotting, so heat loss must be prevented early.
items.a: Remove wet clothing and cover him to prevent heat loss
w: Start a second IV and give a large crystalloid bolus
Complete a detailed secondary exam before covering him
Splint his minor finger fractures

items.q: A 25-year-old has a gunshot wound to the right groin with steady bright red bleeding. There is no room above the wound for a limb tourniquet. What should you do?
items.x: Groin wounds are junctional and cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing the wound cavity onto the bleeding vessel and holding direct pressure, or using a junctional device, is the correct approach.
items.a: Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic gauze and hold firm pressure
w: Apply a limb tourniquet just below the wound
Elevate the leg and place a bulky dressing over the wound surface
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters

items.q: A 32-year-old with a tourniquet on his thigh for an arterial bleed asks you to loosen it because the pain is severe. Bleeding is controlled and transport time is 25 minutes. What should you do?
items.x: A properly applied tourniquet is painful, and loosening it can restart life-threatening bleeding. It should stay in place, the time should be noted, and pain should be managed per protocol.
items.a: Leave it in place and treat his pain
w: Loosen it briefly every 10 minutes to reduce pain
Remove it and replace it with a pressure dressing
Move it lower on the leg to a less painful spot

items.q: A 70-kg man was crushed between two vehicles. He is confused and anxious, HR 128, BP 84/58, RR 32, with pale cool skin. Which class of hemorrhagic shock best fits these findings?
items.x: Class III blood loss is the point where systolic pressure falls, with marked tachycardia and confusion. Class II usually keeps a normal systolic pressure, and class IV brings profound hypotension and lethargy.
items.a: Class III, about 30 to 40 percent blood loss
w: Class I, under 15 percent blood loss
Class II, about 15 to 30 percent blood loss
Class IV, more than 40 percent with lethargy and no measurable pressure

items.q: A 30-year-old fell from a ladder and is anxious, with HR 112, BP 124/100, RR 22 and capillary refill of 3 seconds. What does his blood pressure reading most likely reflect?
items.x: A rising diastolic pressure with a normal systolic gives a narrow pulse pressure, an early sign that the body is compensating for blood loss with vasoconstriction. A normal systolic pressure does not rule out shock.
items.a: Vasoconstriction narrowing the pulse pressure
w: Normal perfusion with no blood loss
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
A rising intracranial pressure

items.q: A 34-year-old with a severe head injury has a GCS of 5, a fixed dilated right pupil and new extensor posturing. He is intubated and the BP is 142/80. What ETCO2 should you target while signs of herniation persist?
items.x: With active signs of herniation, brief controlled hyperventilation to an ETCO2 of about 30 to 35 mmHg is recommended. Driving it lower causes cerebral vasoconstriction severe enough to cause ischemia.
items.a: 30 to 35 mmHg
w: 20 to 25 mmHg
35 to 45 mmHg
45 to 50 mmHg

items.q: You have been mildly hyperventilating an intubated head-injured adult with a blown pupil. After 10 minutes the pupil begins to react and his posturing stops. What should you do now?
items.x: Hyperventilation is a temporary bridge only while signs of herniation are present. Once they resolve, ventilation returns to normal to avoid the cerebral ischemia caused by prolonged low CO2.
items.a: Return to a normal rate targeting an ETCO2 of 35 to 40
w: Continue hyperventilating until arrival at the hospital
Increase the rate further to keep improving the pupil
Stop ventilating briefly to let the ETCO2 rise above 50

items.q: In a patient with a severe traumatic brain injury, which pair of secondary insults most strongly worsens outcome and must be prevented in the field?
items.x: Even a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension is linked to markedly higher death rates after TBI. Field care focuses on keeping SpO2 at least 90 percent and avoiding low blood pressure.
items.a: Hypoxia and hypotension
w: Hyperthermia and hyperglycemia
Hypertension and tachycardia
Hypocarbia and hypernatremia

items.q: A 19-year-old was hit in the temple with a baseball and was knocked out briefly. He then talked normally for 30 minutes but is now vomiting, with a GCS of 10 and a dilated right pupil. What is the most likely injury?
items.x: A brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid decline after a blow to the temple is the classic picture of an arterial epidural hematoma. This needs rapid transport for surgery.
items.a: Epidural hematoma
w: Concussion
Chronic subdural hematoma
Diffuse axonal injury

items.q: After a fall, a 50-year-old has bruising around both eyes and clear fluid draining from the nose. Which airway adjunct should you avoid?
items.x: Raccoon eyes and CSF rhinorrhea suggest a basilar skull fracture, and a nasal airway could pass through the fractured cribriform plate into the cranial vault. Oral routes are preferred.
items.a: Nasopharyngeal airway
w: Oropharyngeal airway
Bag-valve mask with oxygen
Nonrebreather mask

items.q: A head-injured patient opens his eyes only to pain, says inappropriate words and withdraws from a painful stimulus. What is his GCS?
items.x: Eye opening to pain scores 2, inappropriate words score 3, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, for a total of 9.

items.q: A 22-year-old with a stab wound to the right chest had a vented chest seal placed. He is now more short of breath, SpO2 has dropped to 86 percent, HR is 132 and BP 84/52. What should you do first?
items.x: A chest seal can clog or fail and allow a tension pneumothorax to build. Burping or briefly removing the dressing is the first step, followed by needle decompression if signs persist.
items.a: Lift a corner of the seal to release trapped air
w: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first one
Increase oxygen and reassess in 5 minutes
Place him on his left side and start a fluid bolus

items.q: You need to perform needle decompression on an adult with a tension pneumothorax but cannot use the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Which alternate site is accepted?
items.x: The lateral site at the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line often has a thinner chest wall. Sites next to the sternum risk the internal mammary vessels, and low anterior sites risk the heart, liver or spleen.
items.a: Fourth or fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
w: Second intercostal space right beside the sternum
Sixth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
Third intercostal space just medial to the nipple

items.q: A 40-year-old crushed under a vehicle has absent breath sounds on the right, dullness to percussion on that side, flat neck veins and BP 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Dullness with absent breath sounds and flat neck veins point to a chest filling with blood. Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and usually distended neck veins.
items.a: Massive hemothorax
w: Tension pneumothorax
Pericardial tamponade
Simple pneumothorax

items.q: A patient has a suspected massive hemothorax with hypotension, dullness on the left and flat neck veins. What is the best prehospital management?
items.x: Needle decompression does not drain blood and will not help a hemothorax. Care is focused on oxygenation, hemorrhage-focused resuscitation that avoids overloading with fluids, and fast transport to surgery.
items.a: Oxygen, rapid transport and fluids to a radial pulse
w: Needle decompression of the left chest
Supine position with legs raised and a 2-liter bolus
An occlusive dressing over the left chest wall

items.q: A 28-year-old with a stab wound to the left chest is hypotensive. On the monitor the QRS amplitude alternates from tall to short with every beat. What does this suggest?
items.x: Electrical alternans comes from the heart swinging within a fluid-filled pericardial sac. In a penetrating chest injury with hypotension, it strongly suggests tamponade.
items.a: Pericardial tamponade
w: Tension pneumothorax
Blunt aortic injury
Ventricular tachycardia

items.q: A 68-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A segment of his right chest moves inward when he inhales. RR 30 and shallow, SpO2 88 percent. What is the most serious underlying problem?
items.x: The paradoxical movement is dramatic, but the main cause of hypoxia is the pulmonary contusion beneath the flail segment. Pain also limits ventilation and adds to the problem.
items.a: The bruised lung under the flail segment
w: The flail segment collapsing the lung completely
Rib ends lacerating the heart muscle
Loss of the cough reflex

items.q: A patient with a flail chest has RR 36 with very shallow breaths and SpO2 84 percent on a nonrebreather. What should you do?
items.x: Positive pressure ventilation supports gas exchange and splints the flail segment from the inside. Sandbags and tight wrapping restrict chest movement and worsen ventilation.
items.a: Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
w: Splint the segment with a sandbag
Wrap the chest tightly with tape
Continue the nonrebreather and recheck in 10 minutes

items.q: An unrestrained driver's chest struck the steering wheel. He has sternal bruising, HR 118 with frequent PVCs and BP 128/80. What injury should you suspect?
items.x: Blunt cardiac injury commonly presents with unexplained tachycardia and dysrhythmias after a blow to the sternum. Cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG are indicated.
items.a: Blunt cardiac injury
w: Commotio cordis
Traumatic aortic rupture
Simple rib contusion

items.q: After a high-speed frontal crash, a 45-year-old has pain between the shoulder blades and a BP of 150/90 in the right arm but 112/70 in the left. What injury is most likely?
items.x: Sudden deceleration can tear the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum. Interscapular pain and a blood pressure difference between the arms are warning signs.
items.a: Traumatic aortic disruption
w: Blunt cardiac injury
Cervical spine fracture
Tension pneumothorax

items.q: A 24-year-old snowboarder fell onto his left side. He now has left upper quadrant tenderness, left shoulder pain without shoulder injury, HR 118 and BP 104/70. Which organ is most likely injured?
items.x: Pain referred to the left shoulder, called Kehr's sign, comes from blood irritating the diaphragm. With left upper quadrant tenderness it suggests a splenic injury.
items.a: Spleen
w: Liver
Pancreas
Left kidney

items.q: A 9-year-old restrained only by a lap belt has a band of bruising across the lower abdomen after a crash. Which injuries should you suspect?
items.x: A seatbelt sign raises concern for hollow organ injury and a flexion-distraction fracture of the lumbar spine. Children riding in lap belts without proper boosters are at particular risk.
items.a: Bowel and lumbar spine injuries
w: Splenic and left rib injuries
Femur and hip fractures
Cervical spine and facial injuries

items.q: A 30-year-old with a knife wound to the abdomen has a loop of bowel protruding from the wound. What is the correct care?
items.x: An evisceration is covered with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive or dry layer to keep it moist and warm. Replacing the organs risks contamination and further injury.
items.a: Cover it with a moist sterile dressing
w: Gently push the bowel back inside
Tape a dry gauze pad tightly over it
Irrigate and leave it uncovered for inspection

items.q: A motorcyclist has pelvic pain, leg length discrepancy and BP 86/50. How should you assess and handle his pelvis?
items.x: Repeated pelvic compression or rocking can disrupt clots and worsen bleeding. When a fracture is suspected, a binder is applied and movement of the pelvis is kept to a minimum.
items.a: Avoid rocking it and apply a binder
w: Rock the iliac crests firmly to confirm instability
Log roll him fully to inspect the back first
Flex his hips to relieve the pelvic pain

items.q: Why is a pelvic binder applied to a hypotensive patient with a suspected open-book pelvic fracture?
items.x: Closing the widened pelvic ring decreases the space for blood to collect and limits fragment movement. This mostly slows venous and bone bleeding while the patient is moved to surgery.
items.a: It reduces pelvic volume and stabilizes fragments
w: It raises the blood pressure by compressing the aorta
It prevents spinal cord injury in the lumbar spine
It allows the legs to be elevated safely

items.q: A 74-year-old fell forward and struck her chin. She has burning pain in her hands and much more weakness in her arms than in her legs. What spinal cord syndrome is most likely?
items.x: Hyperextension of an arthritic neck in older adults damages the center of the cord, where the arm fibers lie. Weakness is greater in the arms than the legs.
items.a: Central cord syndrome
w: Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome
Complete cord transection

items.q: A 26-year-old was stabbed in the back. His right leg is weak with poor position sense, and he cannot feel pain or temperature in his left leg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Damage to one side of the cord causes loss of motor function and position sense on the same side, and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.
items.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome
w: Central cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Neurogenic shock

items.q: A 31-year-old ejected from a vehicle has a suspected cervical cord injury with no movement below the shoulders. He is pale, cool and clammy with HR 128 and BP 82/50. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Neurogenic shock typically causes warm dry skin and a normal or slow heart rate. Tachycardia with cool, clammy skin suggests blood loss, which must be found and treated.
items.a: Assume hemorrhage until proven otherwise
w: Neurogenic shock alone fully explains these findings
This is spinal shock and no treatment is needed
These are signs of a normal stress response

items.q: After a diving injury, a 20-year-old is quadriplegic with abdominal breathing, RR 28 and shallow, and a falling SpO2. Why is he at high risk for respiratory failure?
items.x: Cervical cord injuries paralyze the intercostal muscles, leaving the diaphragm, supplied by C3 to C5, to do all the work. Injuries at or above that level can stop breathing entirely.
items.a: Intercostal paralysis leaves only the diaphragm
w: The phrenic nerve is unaffected by neck injuries
Cord injuries cause bronchospasm
His airway is blocked by the tongue

items.q: A 40-year-old was burned at 1400 hours and you reach the hospital at 1530. When does the first 8-hour period of the Parkland formula begin?
items.x: Half of the 24-hour Parkland volume is given in the first 8 hours counted from the time of injury. Delays in starting fluids mean the remaining volume must be given faster.
items.a: At the time of the burn
w: At hospital arrival
When the first IV is started
When the burn size is calculated

items.q: An 80-kg man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 25 percent of his body. Using the Parkland formula of 4 mL x kg x percent TBSA, how much fluid is planned for the first 8 hours?
items.x: The 24-hour total is 4 x 80 x 25, or 8,000 mL, and half of it, 4,000 mL, is planned for the first 8 hours from the burn. Many systems now start with a lower rate and adjust to urine output.

items.q: A 30-year-old has superficial, red, unblistered burns on 20 percent of his body and partial-thickness blistered burns on 10 percent. What burn size is used for fluid calculations?
items.x: Superficial burns are not counted in the TBSA used for fluid resuscitation. Only partial- and full-thickness burns are included.
items.a: 10 percent
w: 20 percent
30 percent
15 percent

items.q: A 2-year-old has partial-thickness burns to the entire head and both entire arms. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what is the burned surface area?
items.x: In young children the head is about 18 percent and each arm about 9 percent, giving 36 percent. The larger head proportion is the key difference from the adult chart.
items.a: 36 percent
w: 27 percent
18 percent
45 percent

items.q: A 45-year-old has full-thickness circumferential burns around the chest. He is becoming harder to ventilate with a bag-valve mask despite a patent airway. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Leathery eschar does not stretch, so a circumferential chest burn can restrict ventilation. It may need surgical escharotomy at the hospital.
items.a: Stiff eschar restricting chest wall movement
w: Bronchospasm from the oxygen
A misplaced oral airway
Fluid overload from the IV

items.q: A lineman contacted a 10,000-volt line. He has a small burn on his hand and another on his foot and is alert with stable vital signs. What is the most important concern?
items.x: High-voltage current travels through deep tissue, so small skin wounds hide extensive muscle damage and the risk of dysrhythmias. Cardiac monitoring and transport to a burn center are needed.
items.a: Hidden deep tissue and cardiac injury
w: The burns are minor and need only dressings
A normal ECG on scene rules out cardiac injury
Treat only the visible surface burns

items.q: A 35-year-old has partial- and full-thickness burns over 45 percent of his body. The fire was put out 10 minutes ago. How should you dress the burns?
items.x: Large burns lose heat rapidly, and prolonged cooling causes hypothermia. After the burning process is stopped, cover with clean dry dressings and prevent heat loss.
items.a: Clean dry dressings or sheets, keeping him warm
w: Wet sheets for the whole transport
Ice packs on the deepest burns
Ointment over all burned areas

items.q: A family of four has headaches, nausea and confusion after running a generator in the garage. The father's SpO2 reads 99 percent. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, giving falsely normal values. High-flow oxygen is needed, and CO oximetry should be used if available.
items.a: Standard pulse oximetry can't detect carbon monoxide
w: His oxygenation is normal, so oxygen is not needed
The reading proves this is a viral illness
The reading rules out poisoning

items.q: A man pulled from a house fire is unresponsive with seizures, BP 72/40 and a normal SpO2. Cyanide toxicity is suspected along with carbon monoxide. Which antidote approach is preferred?
items.x: Nitrites work by creating methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen delivery in a patient already poisoned with CO. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide without that harm.
items.a: Hydroxocobalamin
w: Amyl and sodium nitrites
Naloxone and observation
Glucagon infusion

items.q: A 38-year-old pulled from a burning building has singed nasal hair and soot in his mouth. Over 15 minutes his voice becomes hoarse and soft stridor develops. What is the priority?
items.x: Progressive hoarseness and stridor signal airway swelling that can close the airway within minutes. Early definitive airway management is safer than waiting.
items.a: Secure the airway early
w: Wait until stridor becomes severe before acting
Give oral fluids to soothe the throat
Place a nasal cannula at 2 L/min

items.q: A 50-year-old's legs have been pinned under a concrete slab for 4 hours. Rescuers are ready to lift it. What should you do before the slab is lifted?
items.x: Release of a prolonged crush sends potassium, acid and myoglobin into the circulation. Fluids before release and cardiac monitoring help prevent sudden dysrhythmias and kidney injury.
items.a: Start IV fluids and apply the cardiac monitor
w: Apply tourniquets to both legs and leave them for transport
Lift the slab right away and assess afterward
Elevate his head and apply ice to his legs

items.q: Minutes after a crushed leg is freed, the patient's ECG shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Potassium released from damaged muscle causes peaked T waves and QRS widening and can lead to cardiac arrest. Treatment follows protocol for hyperkalemia.
items.a: Hyperkalemia
w: Hypokalemia
Hypothermia
Hypocalcemia alone

items.q: A 28-year-old with a splinted tibia fracture has worsening leg pain out of proportion to the injury and severe pain when you gently move his toes. Pedal pulses are present. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses are often present until very late, so a pulse does not rule it out.
items.a: Compartment syndrome
w: Arterial transection
Fat embolism
Deep vein thrombosis

items.q: After a bomb blast, a woman has multiple penetrating wounds from flying glass. What category of blast injury is this?
items.x: Secondary blast injuries come from debris and fragments driven by the explosion. Primary is the pressure wave, tertiary is the body being thrown, and quaternary includes burns and other effects.
items.a: Secondary
w: Primary
Tertiary
Quaternary

items.q: A woman 34 weeks pregnant was in a car crash. She is supine on a long board and complains of dizziness, BP 88/50, HR 110. What should you do first?
items.x: In late pregnancy the uterus compresses the vena cava when the patient is supine. Moving the uterus to the left or tilting the board improves venous return.
items.a: Manually displace the uterus to the left
w: Raise her legs and start a large fluid bolus
Place her in Trendelenburg
Sit her upright at 90 degrees

items.q: A pregnant trauma patient seems stable, but her fetus may be in danger. What is the most effective way to protect the fetus in the field?
items.x: The body diverts blood away from the uterus to protect the mother, so the fetus may be in shock before maternal vital signs change. Supporting the mother's oxygenation and circulation is the best fetal care.
items.a: Aggressively resuscitate the mother
w: Focus on fetal heart tones before maternal care
Keep the mother supine for close monitoring
Withhold fluids to avoid placental swelling

items.q: A woman 30 weeks pregnant had a car crash. She has steady abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus and only slight vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
items.x: A painful, rigid uterus after trauma suggests the placenta has separated. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the amount seen does not reflect blood loss.
items.a: Placental abruption
w: Placenta previa
Normal labor
Ectopic pregnancy

items.q: An 8-year-old was run over by a car. You feel no rib fractures, but she has crackles, RR 34 and SpO2 89 percent. Why is lung injury likely despite intact ribs?
items.x: A child's flexible chest wall bends without breaking and transfers energy to the lungs. Pulmonary contusion without rib fractures is common.
items.a: Pliable ribs pass the force to the lungs
w: Children's lungs are larger than adults'
Rib fractures in children are always hidden
Hypoxia in children is normal after trauma

items.q: You place a 3-year-old supine on a firm surface for spinal motion restriction. His neck flexes forward because of his large head. What should you do?
items.x: A young child's large occiput flexes the neck when lying flat. Padding under the torso brings the spine into a neutral position.
items.a: Pad under the shoulders and torso
w: Place a folded towel under the head
Tape the forehead down more tightly
Elevate the head of the board 30 degrees

items.q: What systolic blood pressure indicates hypotension in a 5-year-old trauma patient?
items.x: Hypotension in children 1 to 10 years is a systolic pressure below 70 plus twice the age in years, so below 80 for a 5-year-old. Hypotension is a late sign in children.
items.a: Below 80 mmHg
w: Below 70 mmHg
Below 90 mmHg
Below 100 mmHg

items.q: Under the 2021 National Guideline for Field Triage, which systolic pressure meets a red criterion in a trauma patient 65 or older?
items.x: The 2021 guideline uses a systolic pressure below 110 in patients 65 and older because older adults may be in shock at pressures that look normal. A heart rate greater than the systolic pressure is also a criterion.
items.a: Below 110 mmHg
w: Below 90 mmHg
Below 80 mmHg
Below 100 mmHg

items.q: A 30-year-old fell 14 feet from scaffolding. He is alert with normal vital signs and only a sprained wrist. Under the 2021 field triage guideline, what is the right destination?
items.x: A fall from more than 10 feet is a yellow mechanism criterion that calls for a trauma center. Without red criteria, it need not be the highest level.
items.a: A trauma center, not necessarily the highest level
w: The highest-level trauma center only
The closest emergency department regardless of level
No transport is needed

items.q: A 26-year-old shot in the left chest has just lost his pulse in front of you, with PEA on the monitor. Which intervention is most likely to help?
items.x: In traumatic arrest, outcomes depend on correcting the cause, such as tension pneumothorax, bleeding or hypoxia. Decompressing the chest addresses a reversible cause quickly.
items.a: Bilateral needle decompression
w: Repeated epinephrine with CPR on scene
Synchronized cardioversion
A prolonged search for medical causes

items.q: A 36-year-old has a laceration on the side of the neck with dark blood flowing and sucking sounds from the wound. What should you apply?
items.x: An open neck vein can draw in air and cause a fatal air embolism. An occlusive dressing with careful pressure seals the wound without obstructing the airway.
items.a: An occlusive dressing
w: A tourniquet around the neck
A dry, loosely taped gauze pad
A circumferential pressure bandage

items.q: A 79-year-old on metoprolol fell down stairs. He is pale with a firm, distended abdomen. HR 74, BP 112/70. How should you interpret his heart rate?
items.x: Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to blood loss, and older adults may be in shock with pressures that look normal. Rely on other findings such as the abdomen and skin.
items.a: Beta blockers may mask tachycardia from bleeding
w: A normal heart rate rules out significant bleeding
He is in neurogenic shock
His blood pressure proves he is stable

items.q: An 84-year-old on an anticoagulant fell yesterday and hit her head. Today she is more confused and has a headache. What injury is most likely?
items.x: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins in older adults, and anticoagulants make them bleed more. Subdural bleeding often causes delayed decline hours to days later.
items.a: Subdural hematoma
w: Epidural hematoma
Concussion with no bleeding
Basilar skull fracture

items.q: Which components make up the lethal triad of trauma? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed one another and worsen bleeding. Field care aims to prevent heat loss and avoid diluting clotting factors with large fluid volumes.
opts: Hypothermia
Acidosis
Coagulopathy
Hyperglycemia
Hypertension
ok: Hypothermia
Acidosis
Coagulopathy

items.q: Which findings make up Beck's triad? Select all that apply.
items.x: Beck's triad of muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension and hypotension suggests pericardial tamponade. Tracheal deviation points to tension pneumothorax, and Cushing's response suggests raised ICP.
opts: Muffled heart sounds
Distended neck veins
Hypotension
Tracheal deviation
Bradycardia with hypertension
ok: Muffled heart sounds
Distended neck veins
Hypotension

items.q: Which findings support a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
items.x: Unilateral absent breath sounds, JVD and shock with increasing distress suggest tension pneumothorax. Dullness suggests blood, and bradycardia with warm skin suggests neurogenic shock.
opts: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Hypotension with worsening respiratory distress
Dullness to percussion on the affected side
Bradycardia with warm, dry skin
ok: Absent breath sounds on one side
Distended neck veins
Hypotension with worsening respiratory distress

items.q: Which findings are consistent with compartment syndrome? Select all that apply.
items.x: Severe pain, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment are the important early findings. Pulses usually remain until late, so their presence does not rule it out.
opts: Pain out of proportion to the injury
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles
A tense, firm compartment
Absent distal pulses are required to make the diagnosis
Pain relieved completely by splinting
ok: Pain out of proportion to the injury
Pain on passive stretch of the muscles
A tense, firm compartment

items.q: Which findings are typical of neurogenic shock? Select all that apply.
items.x: Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation and an unopposed vagal effect on the heart. Cool clammy skin and tachycardia suggest hemorrhagic shock instead.
opts: Hypotension
Bradycardia or a normal heart rate
Warm, dry skin below the injury
Pale, cool, clammy skin
Marked tachycardia
ok: Hypotension
Bradycardia or a normal heart rate
Warm, dry skin below the injury

items.q: After a prolonged crush injury is released, which complications should you anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Damaged muscle releases potassium and myoglobin, and fluid moves into injured tissue. Calcium usually falls rather than rises.
opts: Hyperkalemia
Kidney injury from myoglobin
Hypovolemia from fluid shifting into tissues
Hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia
ok: Hyperkalemia
Kidney injury from myoglobin
Hypovolemia from fluid shifting into tissues

items.q: Which injuries result from the primary blast wave? Select all that apply.
items.x: The pressure wave injures air-filled organs. Shrapnel wounds are secondary, and injuries from being thrown are tertiary.
opts: Ruptured eardrums
Blast lung
Bowel perforation
Wounds from flying shrapnel
A fracture from being thrown into a wall
ok: Ruptured eardrums
Blast lung
Bowel perforation

items.q: Which normal changes of late pregnancy affect trauma assessment? Select all that apply.
items.x: Increased blood volume can hide early blood loss, and a higher heart rate is normal. Blood pressure tends to drop slightly, and reduced functional residual capacity makes pregnant patients desaturate quickly.
opts: Blood volume increases by up to about 50 percent
Resting heart rate is higher than usual
The uterus can compress the vena cava when supine
Blood pressure is usually higher than before pregnancy
Lung reserve volume is larger, so hypoxia develops slowly
ok: Blood volume increases by up to about 50 percent
Resting heart rate is higher than usual
The uterus can compress the vena cava when supine

items.q: Which features make children more prone to certain injury patterns? Select all that apply.
items.x: A large head leads to more head injuries, the solid organs extend below a pliable rib cage, and force passes to the lungs. Children have thinner abdominal walls and relatively large tongues.
opts: A proportionally larger and heavier head
Liver and spleen less protected by the ribs
A flexible chest wall
Thicker abdominal wall muscles
A proportionally smaller tongue
ok: A proportionally larger and heavier head
Liver and spleen less protected by the ribs
A flexible chest wall

items.q: Which factors increase the risk of serious injury in older trauma patients? Select all that apply.
items.x: Anticoagulants increase bleeding, beta blockers hide signs of shock, and brain atrophy raises the risk of subdural bleeding. Bones become more brittle with age.
opts: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Beta blockers masking tachycardia
Brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins
A stronger and more elastic rib cage
An exaggerated fever response to injury
ok: Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Beta blockers masking tachycardia
Brain atrophy that stretches bridging veins

items.q: Under the 2021 field triage guideline, which findings are EMS judgment factors that should prompt consideration of a trauma center? Select all that apply.
items.x: The guideline lists anticoagulant use, pregnancy over 20 weeks and low-level falls with head impact in older adults or young children as factors to weigh. Patient preference alone is not a triage criterion.
opts: Anticoagulant use
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
A fall from standing with head impact in an older adult
A minor finger laceration in a healthy adult
A patient request to go to a specific hospital
ok: Anticoagulant use
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
A fall from standing with head impact in an older adult

items.q: Which wound locations are junctional areas where a limb tourniquet usually cannot control bleeding? Select all that apply.
items.x: Junctional areas lie where the limbs or head join the torso. Wounds there need packing, direct pressure or junctional devices, while mid-limb wounds can take a tourniquet.
opts: Groin
Axilla
Neck
Mid-thigh
Mid-forearm
ok: Groin
Axilla
Neck

items.q: Which findings suggest carbon monoxide poisoning? Select all that apply.
items.x: Grouped symptoms that improve away from the source and falsely normal pulse oximetry point to CO. Cherry red skin is a late and unreliable finding.
opts: Headache and nausea in several people from the same home
Symptoms that improve after leaving the building
Confusion with a normal standard SpO2 reading
A low SpO2 that improves with oxygen proves it is not CO
Cherry red skin is required for the diagnosis
ok: Headache and nausea in several people from the same home
Symptoms that improve after leaving the building
Confusion with a normal standard SpO2 reading

items.q: Which findings suggest a basilar skull fracture? Select all that apply.
items.x: Battle's sign, raccoon eyes and CSF leakage suggest a basilar skull fracture. Periumbilical and flank bruising suggest intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding.
opts: Bruising behind the ear
Bruising around both eyes
Clear fluid draining from the ear
Bruising around the umbilicus
Bruising along the flank
ok: Bruising behind the ear
Bruising around both eyes
Clear fluid draining from the ear

items.q: You call a physician by radio for permission to give a treatment not covered by your standing orders. What type of medical direction is this?
items.x: Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician. Offline direction includes protocols, standing orders, training and quality review.
items.a: Online medical direction
w: Offline medical direction
Retrospective medical direction
Prospective protocol direction

items.q: Online medical direction orders a medication dose that you believe is ten times too high. What should you do?
items.x: Repeating orders back is a safety step. If an order seems wrong, ask for clarification, and do not carry out an order you believe would harm the patient; document the exchange.
items.a: Repeat the order back and question it
w: Give it as ordered because the physician is responsible
Give half the dose without telling anyone
Give the dose you think is correct

items.q: A 45-year-old diabetic has a glucose of 38 mg/dL. He is confused and refuses care. What is true about his refusal?
items.x: Hypoglycemia with confusion impairs the ability to understand and weigh choices. Without capacity, emergency treatment proceeds under implied consent per protocol.
items.a: He lacks capacity, so treat under implied consent
w: His refusal must be honored because he is an adult
You must wait for police before giving any care
You must get written consent from his spouse first

items.q: A married 17-year-old with a minor ankle injury declines transport. She is alert and understands the risks. How should you proceed?
items.x: Minors who are married or otherwise emancipated can usually consent to or refuse their own care. Local law defines emancipation, so follow protocol.
items.a: Treat her as an adult who may refuse
w: Transport her against her will because she is a minor
Call her parents to consent for her
Have police place her in custody

items.q: A 70-year-old with a POLST marked do not resuscitate and selective treatment is in respiratory distress from pneumonia with a pulse. Which care fits his orders?
items.x: Selective treatment allows noninvasive care such as CPAP, IV fluids and hospital transport, but not intubation. A DNR applies to cardiac arrest, while the POLST guides care when a pulse is present.
items.a: CPAP, IV fluids and transport
w: Intubation and mechanical ventilation
No treatment because a DNR is in place
Comfort care only, with no transport

items.q: A patient with a valid DNR order develops a narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 with chest pain and is still awake. How should you proceed?
items.x: A DNR applies to resuscitation after cardiac arrest. Conditions with a pulse are treated normally unless another order limits care.
items.a: Treat the dysrhythmia per protocol
w: Withhold all treatment because of the DNR
Wait until he becomes pulseless
Ask the family to decide

items.q: An 88-year-old is found in cardiac arrest. The family says she has a DNR, but no one can find the document. What should you do?
items.x: Without valid documentation, most protocols require resuscitation. Medical direction can help while the family searches.
items.a: Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction
w: Withhold resuscitation based on the family's word
Wait until the document is found
Pronounce death without assessment

items.q: Which statement is an example of a pertinent negative in a chest pain report?
items.x: A pertinent negative documents an important finding that is absent, such as no shortness of breath with chest pain. It shows the finding was checked.
items.a: Denies shortness of breath
w: Patient is a 54-year-old male
Patient was found sitting in a recliner

items.q: You smell alcohol on a patient's breath. Which narrative entry is most appropriate?
items.x: Documentation should be objective and describe what you observed. Labels and opinions can be used against you and may be libelous.
items.a: Odor of an alcoholic beverage on the breath
w: Patient was drunk
Patient was intoxicated and belligerent
Typical drunk patient, uncooperative

items.q: Your partner asks you to record a medication on the report that was never given, to match the narcotic count. What should you do?
items.x: Falsifying a medical record is illegal and dishonest. Accurate records and reporting a narcotic discrepancy through proper channels are required.
items.a: Refuse, document accurately and report it
w: Record it as given to keep things simple
Leave the medication off the report
Record it with a note that you are unsure

items.q: An alert adult with capacity refuses care, but a paramedic threatens to restrain her if she does not comply. What has the paramedic committed?
items.x: Assault is causing a person to fear immediate bodily harm. Battery is unlawful touching without consent.
items.a: Assault
w: Battery
Libel
Abandonment

items.q: You arrive at a hospital emergency department with a patient. The charge nurse asks you to take her to another hospital without being seen. What applies?
items.x: Once a patient arrives on hospital property seeking emergency care, EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilization. Hospitals cannot turn patients away for financial or capacity reasons alone.
items.a: EMTALA requires a medical screening exam
w: The hospital may refuse any patient it chooses
You must leave right away for the other hospital
Only HIPAA applies to this situation

items.q: An 85-year-old who depends on her son has pressure sores, soiled bedding and unexplained bruises. What must you do?
items.x: EMS providers are mandated reporters of suspected elder abuse and neglect in most states. Report as required and document objective findings.
items.a: Report suspected elder abuse per state law
w: Leave it to the family to manage
Confront the son on scene
Report it only if the patient asks you to

items.q: You honor an alert, capable patient's decision to decline a treatment you recommend. Which ethical principle are you following?
items.x: Autonomy is the right of capable people to make their own decisions. Beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, and justice is fairness.
items.a: Autonomy
w: Beneficence
Justice
Nonmaleficence

items.q: You are asked to transfer a patient with an infusion outside your scope of practice. What should you do?
items.x: Paramedics cannot manage care beyond their scope. A qualified provider can accompany the patient, or the sending physician can change the treatment.
items.a: Request a qualified provider to accompany the patient
w: Transport and manage the infusion yourself
Transport after a brief lesson on the pump from the nurse
Refuse the transfer without discussion

items.q: A large incident involves fire, police and EMS from several jurisdictions. What ICS structure should be used?
items.x: Unified command lets agencies with responsibility share decisions and set common objectives. Separate commands lead to conflicts.
items.a: Unified command
w: Single command
A separate command for each agency
Area command for each department

items.q: What is the recommended span of control for a supervisor in ICS?
items.x: A span of control of three to seven, with five ideal, keeps supervisors effective. Larger groups should be divided into more units.
items.a: Three to seven, ideally five
w: One to two
Ten to fifteen
As many as the situation demands

items.q: At a mass casualty incident, which officer manages arriving ambulances and assigns them when needed?
items.x: The staging officer tracks and releases resources as requested. This prevents vehicle congestion at the scene.
items.a: Staging officer
w: Treatment officer
Triage officer
Safety officer

items.q: At a mass casualty incident, who coordinates patient destinations so the nearest hospital is not overwhelmed?
items.x: The transport officer works with hospitals to distribute patients. This prevents a single facility from being overloaded.
items.a: Transport officer
w: Staging officer
Public information officer
Liaison officer

items.q: In SALT triage, which patients are assessed first after the global sort?
items.x: SALT asks walking patients to move and others to wave. Patients who do neither are assessed first.
items.a: Those who are still or have an obvious life threat
w: Those who walk to the designated area
Those who wave or move purposefully
Those who are crying loudly

items.q: Under START triage, an adult who cannot walk has RR 22 and a radial pulse but cannot follow simple commands. What category is assigned?
items.x: START checks respirations, perfusion and mental status. Failure to follow simple commands puts the patient in the immediate category.
items.a: Immediate
w: Delayed
Minor
Expectant

items.q: During JumpSTART triage, a 6-year-old who cannot walk has a respiratory rate of 48. What category is assigned?
items.x: In JumpSTART, a respiratory rate below 15 or above 45 is immediate. The child's range differs from the adult threshold.
items.a: Immediate
w: Delayed
Minor
Deceased

items.q: At an MCI, a 7-month-old cannot walk because of her age. How is she triaged with JumpSTART?
items.x: Infants who cannot walk because of development are evaluated with the rest of the algorithm. They are not automatically assigned minor.
items.a: Continue through the full algorithm
w: Assign minor because she cannot walk
Assign immediate due to her age
Leave her for last

items.q: You are approaching a tanker rollover with a placard on the tank. What is the safest approach?
items.x: Staying uphill and upwind keeps vapors and runoff away. Placards and the ERG can be read from a distance.
items.a: Approach from uphill and upwind, using binoculars
w: Approach downwind for a closer look
Approach from downhill to stay low
Approach directly to read the placard up close

items.q: Patients from a chemical release are arriving at your location. Which single action removes the largest share of contamination?
items.x: Removing clothing removes much of the contaminant. Washing with water follows for liquid exposures.
items.a: Removing their clothing
w: Washing their hair first
Spraying them with bleach
Covering them in blankets

items.q: After a subway vapor release, several commuters have runny noses and pinpoint pupils but no breathing problems. What exposure should you suspect?
items.x: Miosis is the most consistent sign of nerve agent vapor exposure, often with rhinorrhea. More severe exposures add secretions, bronchospasm and seizures.
items.a: Mild nerve agent vapor exposure
w: Cyanide poisoning
Opioid overdose
Chlorine gas exposure

items.q: Several patients have a fever and a rash, with all lesions at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. What should you suspect?
items.x: Smallpox lesions are at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. Chickenpox lesions vary in stage and appear mostly on the trunk.
items.a: Smallpox
w: Chickenpox
Measles
Anthrax

items.q: At an active shooter incident, you reach a victim with severe leg bleeding while the shooter is still active nearby. What should you do?
items.x: In direct threat care, only massive bleeding is treated with a tourniquet before moving to cover. Other care waits for a safer zone.
items.a: Apply a tourniquet and move to cover
w: Perform a full primary survey on the spot
Insert an airway and start an IV
Leave the victim because it is unsafe

items.q: At an active shooter incident, where does a rescue task force operate?
items.x: Rescue task forces work in areas that have been cleared but are not fully secured. Police provide protection while EMS treats and removes victims.
items.a: The warm zone, with police protection
w: The hot zone, before police arrive
Only the cold zone
Inside the command post

items.q: A helicopter has landed at your scene. How should you approach it?
items.x: Approach in view of the pilot and only after signaling. Tail rotors and uphill approaches risk serious injury.
items.a: From the front, only when signaled by the crew
w: From the tail to stay out of the pilot's sight
From uphill so you are close to the rotor
As soon as it lands to save time

items.q: During air transport, what happens to an untreated pneumothorax as altitude increases?
items.x: Gas expands as pressure decreases, by Boyle's law. Air in the chest or a tube cuff expands with altitude.
items.a: It expands
w: It shrinks
It does not change
It resolves on its own

items.q: You stick yourself with a used needle. What should you do first?
items.x: Wash the area immediately and report so testing and prophylaxis can start quickly. Prophylaxis works best when started within hours.
items.a: Wash with soap and water and report right away
w: Wait until the end of your shift to report
Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Ignore it if the patient seems healthy

items.q: After caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhea, how should you clean your hands?
