items.x: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores. Washing with soap and water removes them.
items.a: Soap and water
w: Alcohol gel only
A dry towel
Gloves alone without hand cleaning

items.q: When removing PPE after caring for a patient on airborne precautions, which item is removed last?
items.x: The respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, and then hands are cleaned.
items.a: The respirator
w: The gloves
The gown
The eye protection

items.q: Your partner says "give 1 mg of epinephrine," and you reply "giving 1 mg of epinephrine" before giving it, then confirm "1 mg given." What practice is this?
items.x: Closed-loop communication confirms the order and its completion, reducing errors.
items.a: Closed-loop communication
w: Situational awareness
Task fixation
Implied consent

items.q: You are working on a highway crash. How should the fire apparatus be positioned?
items.x: Positioning apparatus upstream protects workers from oncoming traffic. Responders should also wear high-visibility vests.
items.a: Upstream, to block traffic
w: Downstream, beyond the scene
On the opposite side of the road
Parked as close to the patient as possible

items.q: A colleague says he feels hopeless and has been thinking about not being here after a series of bad calls. What should you do?
items.x: Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and allows you to connect the person with help.
items.a: Ask directly about suicide and connect him to help
w: Tell him to take a few days off and see
Avoid the topic so it does not upset him
Report him for disciplinary action

items.q: Which type of study provides the strongest evidence for a treatment?
items.x: Systematic reviews of well-designed randomized trials give the highest level of evidence.
items.a: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
w: Single case report
Expert opinion
Retrospective chart review

items.q: What does high sensitivity in a diagnostic test mean?
items.x: Sensitivity is the ability to detect people who have the condition. Specificity is the ability to identify those who do not.
items.a: It correctly identifies most people with the condition
w: It correctly identifies most people without the condition
It never gives false positives
It works only in large populations

items.q: Why are patients randomized in a clinical trial?
items.x: Randomization balances known and unknown factors so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
items.a: To reduce bias between groups
w: To make sure patients choose their treatment
To speed up enrollment
To avoid the need for consent

items.q: Which elements show that a patient has decision-making capacity? Select all that apply.
items.x: Capacity means understanding, appreciating consequences, reasoning and communicating a choice. Disagreement or a mental health history alone does not remove capacity.
opts: Understands information about his condition
Appreciates the consequences of his choice
Can communicate a clear choice
Agrees with the paramedic's advice
Has no history of mental illness
ok: Understands information about his condition
Appreciates the consequences of his choice
Can communicate a clear choice

items.q: Under EMTALA, which conditions should be met before an unstable patient is transferred? Select all that apply.
items.x: EMTALA requires an accepting facility, records and appropriate transport. Payment cannot be a factor.
opts: The receiving facility has accepted the patient
Copies of medical records go with the patient
Transfer uses qualified staff and equipment
The patient has paid in advance
The sending hospital has run out of beds for any patient
ok: The receiving facility has accepted the patient
Copies of medical records go with the patient
Transfer uses qualified staff and equipment

items.q: Which life-saving interventions are allowed during SALT triage? Select all that apply.
items.x: SALT permits fast interventions such as bleeding control, airway opening, chest decompression and antidote autoinjectors. Time-consuming care waits.
opts: Controlling major hemorrhage
Opening the airway
Needle chest decompression
Placing an endotracheal tube
Starting IV fluids
ok: Controlling major hemorrhage
Opening the airway
Needle chest decompression

items.q: Which findings suggest severe nerve agent poisoning? Select all that apply.
items.x: Nerve agents cause excess secretions, miosis and muscle twitching. Dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils suggests an anticholinergic syndrome.
opts: Pinpoint pupils
Copious secretions
Muscle twitching
Dilated pupils with dry skin
Warm, flushed skin
ok: Pinpoint pupils
Copious secretions
Muscle twitching

items.q: Which actions are appropriate in the hot zone during an active threat? Select all that apply.
items.x: Care in the hot zone is limited to bleeding control and moving to cover. Other care waits for safer zones.
opts: Apply a tourniquet for severe bleeding
Move the patient to cover
Insert an advanced airway
Start an IV
Perform a full secondary assessment
ok: Apply a tourniquet for severe bleeding
Move the patient to cover

items.q: Which practices are part of crew resource management? Select all that apply.
items.x: CRM relies on clear communication, speaking up and checklists. Silent deference leads to errors.
opts: Closed-loop communication
Encouraging any crew member to speak up about safety concerns
Using checklists for high-risk procedures
Deferring to the most senior person without question
Keeping concerns to yourself to avoid conflict
ok: Closed-loop communication
Encouraging any crew member to speak up about safety concerns
Using checklists for high-risk procedures

items.q: Which items should be included when documenting a refusal? Select all that apply.
items.x: Documentation should show capacity, the information given and the patient's decision. Opinions and false assurances are inappropriate.
opts: An assessment of the patient's capacity
The risks explained to the patient
The patient's signature or a witness
Your opinion that the patient is foolish
A promise that nothing bad will happen
ok: An assessment of the patient's capacity
The risks explained to the patient
The patient's signature or a witness

items.q: Which practices help protect a restrained, combative patient? Select all that apply.
items.x: Prone restraint and pressure on the back can cause positional asphyxia. Continuous monitoring and adequate staff improve safety.
opts: Placing him supine or on his side
Monitoring breathing and SpO2 continuously
Using enough personnel to restrain safely
Hog-tying him in the prone position
Placing a backboard on top of him
ok: Placing him supine or on his side
Monitoring breathing and SpO2 continuously
Using enough personnel to restrain safely

items.q: Which practices make a helicopter landing zone safer? Select all that apply.
items.x: Debris, wires and bystanders are major hazards. Lights should not blind the pilot, and level ground is preferred.
opts: Clearing loose debris
Identifying overhead wires
Keeping bystanders well away
Shining lights into the pilot's eyes
Choosing a steep slope
ok: Clearing loose debris
Identifying overhead wires
Keeping bystanders well away

items.q: Which ethical principles are shown in the following actions? Select all that apply.
items.x: Nonmaleficence, justice and beneficence are core principles. Hiding errors violates honesty, and overriding capable refusals violates autonomy.
opts: Avoiding unnecessary harm reflects nonmaleficence
Allocating scarce resources fairly reflects justice
Acting in the patient's best interest reflects beneficence
Hiding errors from patients reflects honesty
Overriding capable refusals reflects autonomy
ok: Avoiding unnecessary harm reflects nonmaleficence
Allocating scarce resources fairly reflects justice
Acting in the patient's best interest reflects beneficence

items.q: A 29-year-old in status epilepticus stops seizing after a benzodiazepine. He remains unresponsive with snoring respirations at 6 per minute and SpO2 86 percent. What should you do next?
items.x: Benzodiazepines and the postictal state can both depress breathing. A rate of 6 with snoring and hypoxia is inadequate, so the airway must be opened and ventilations assisted with a bag-valve mask.
items.a: Open the airway and assist ventilations
w: Give a second benzodiazepine dose to prevent a recurrence
Place him in the recovery position and observe him
Give naloxone to reverse the respiratory depression

items.q: A 52-year-old's generalized seizure stopped 20 minutes ago, but she is still unresponsive, with rhythmic twitching of the right eyelid and fingers and her eyes deviated to the right. What should you suspect?
items.x: Failure to wake combined with subtle rhythmic movements or gaze deviation suggests nonconvulsive status epilepticus, which needs treatment just like a visible convulsion.
items.a: Ongoing subtle seizure activity
w: A normal postictal recovery period
A psychogenic nonepileptic event
Expected sedation from the seizure

items.q: A 67-year-old with diabetes is found with new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which assessment is most important to complete before activating a stroke alert?
items.x: Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible stroke mimic that can produce focal deficits. A glucose check should precede stroke activation and destination decisions.
items.a: A blood glucose measurement
w: A 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation
Orthostatic blood pressure measurements
A check of the deep tendon reflexes

items.q: A 74-year-old developed symptoms 40 minutes ago. She has dense left-sided weakness, her eyes are deviated to the right, and she ignores people standing on her left. What do these findings suggest?
items.x: Cortical signs such as gaze deviation, neglect and aphasia with dense hemiparesis suggest a large vessel occlusion, which may benefit from transport to a thrombectomy-capable center under local destination protocols.
items.a: A large vessel occlusion stroke
w: A small lacunar stroke deep in the brain
A transient ischemic attack that will resolve
Hypertensive encephalopathy

items.q: A 62-year-old went to bed at 22:00 acting normally. His wife found him unable to speak when he woke at 06:30. What is his last known well time?
items.x: Last known well is the last time the patient was confirmed to be at baseline. For wake-up strokes that is the time he went to sleep, not the time the deficit was discovered.
items.a: 22:00 the previous night
w: 06:30, when his wife found him
The time the 911 call was placed
Midnight, at the start of the new day

items.q: A 40-year-old has a new facial droop. Which finding most suggests Bell palsy rather than a stroke?
items.x: The forehead has nerve supply from both sides of the brain, so a central (stroke) lesion usually spares it. Inability to raise the brow on the affected side points to a peripheral facial nerve palsy.
items.a: Loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side
w: Slurred speech with drift of the arm on the same side
Sudden onset of the droop within the last hour
Drooping at the corner of the mouth on smiling

items.q: Which conditions are recognized mimics of an acute stroke? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypoglycemia, postictal (Todd) paralysis and complicated migraine can all cause focal neurologic deficits. Stroke still cannot be excluded in the field until a glucose check and full assessment are done.
opts: Hypoglycemia
Postictal weakness after a seizure
Complicated migraine
Renal colic
Acute otitis externa
Plantar fasciitis
ok: Hypoglycemia
Postictal weakness after a seizure
Complicated migraine

items.q: A 19-year-old college student has fever, severe headache, a stiff neck and a purple rash on her legs that does not blanch. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Fever, meningismus and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal infection, which spreads by droplets and can progress rapidly to shock. Early notification speeds antibiotics and isolation.
opts: Use droplet precautions with masks for the crew and the patient
Assess closely for signs of septic shock
Notify the receiving facility early
Treat the rash as a drug reaction with an antihistamine alone
Skip masks because meningitis spreads only through blood
ok: Use droplet precautions with masks for the crew and the patient
Assess closely for signs of septic shock
Notify the receiving facility early

items.q: A 2-month-old has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F), poor feeding and irritability that worsens when his mother picks him up. His anterior fontanelle is bulging. What is the most concerning possibility?
items.x: Young infants with meningitis rarely show a stiff neck. Fever with paradoxical irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle should be treated as meningitis until proven otherwise.
items.a: Meningitis
w: Infant colic
Acute otitis media
Teething pain

items.q: A 38-year-old has weakness that began in his feet two weeks after a diarrheal illness and has climbed to his hands. His reflexes are absent. Which findings suggest he is heading toward respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
items.x: Ascending weakness with areflexia suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can paralyze the respiratory muscles. A weak cough, short breath counts and rising CO2 signal failing ventilation, while a normal SpO2 can be falsely reassuring.
opts: He cannot count to 20 in a single breath
His cough is weak and secretions are pooling
His ETCO2 is rising
His SpO2 is 98 percent on room air
His voice is loud and strong
ok: He cannot count to 20 in a single breath
His cough is weak and secretions are pooling
His ETCO2 is rising

items.q: A 58-year-old with myasthenia gravis has worsening ptosis, double vision, a nasal voice and trouble clearing secretions. RR 28 and shallow, SpO2 95 percent on room air, ETCO2 56 mmHg. How should you interpret these findings?
items.x: Myasthenic crisis weakens the breathing muscles, so CO2 builds up while SpO2 may stay normal, especially early. Rising ETCO2 with shallow breathing and pooled secretions means she may soon need ventilatory support.
items.a: Impending ventilatory failure
w: She is stable, because her oxygen saturation is normal
Hyperventilation from anxiety about her illness
Compensation for a metabolic acidosis

items.q: A 30-year-old with a complete T4 spinal cord injury has a pounding headache, BP 210/118, HR 52, and flushing and sweating above the level of injury. What should you do first?
items.x: Autonomic dysreflexia is a dangerous hypertensive response to a stimulus below the injury, most often a full bladder or kinked catheter. Sitting upright lowers pressure, and removing the trigger usually resolves it.
items.a: Sit him up and look for a trigger such as a blocked catheter
w: Lay him flat, raise his legs and recheck the pressure in 15 minutes
Apply a cooling blanket to his trunk
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the bradycardia

items.q: A 7-year-old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has had worsening headache, vomiting and sleepiness over the day. She has no fever. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Headache, vomiting and decreasing level of consciousness in a child with a shunt suggest obstruction and rising intracranial pressure, which needs prompt evaluation.
items.a: Shunt malfunction
w: Viral gastroenteritis
Migraine headache
Dehydration from vomiting

items.q: A 22-year-old in DKA has been breathing deeply at 34 per minute with an ETCO2 of 18 mmHg. He becomes obtunded and is intubated. How should he be ventilated?
items.x: His rapid deep breathing was blowing off CO2 to offset a severe metabolic acidosis. Slowing ventilation after intubation lets CO2 rise and can cause a dangerous fall in pH and cardiac arrest.
items.a: Keep a high rate that matches his own compensation
w: Ventilate at 10 per minute as for any adult patient
Ventilate to bring ETCO2 up to 35 to 45 mmHg as quickly as possible
Ventilate at 6 per minute to rest his respiratory muscles

items.q: A 9-year-old in DKA is receiving IV fluids. During transport he develops a headache, becomes confused, and his HR falls from 130 to 64 while his BP rises. What should you suspect?
items.x: Cerebral edema is a leading cause of death in pediatric DKA. Headache, declining mental status, bradycardia and rising BP are warning signs of rising intracranial pressure.
items.a: Cerebral edema
w: Hypoglycemia from his insulin
Heart failure from fluid overload
Worsening dehydration

items.q: Which features are more typical of DKA than of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)? Select all that apply.
items.x: DKA produces ketoacidosis, causing Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath, and it develops relatively quickly. HHS develops slowly in older type 2 patients and usually has higher glucose with little or no ketosis.
opts: Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations
A fruity odor on the breath
Onset over hours to a day or two
Glucose often above 1,000 mg/dL
Most common in older adults with type 2 diabetes
Onset over many days to weeks
ok: Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations
A fruity odor on the breath
Onset over hours to a day or two

items.q: A 76-year-old taking glipizide was found with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. After IV dextrose he is alert with a glucose of 112 and wants to refuse transport. What should you advise?
items.x: Sulfonylureas act for many hours, so hypoglycemia often recurs after dextrose wears off. These patients usually need observation and should be strongly encouraged to accept transport.
items.a: Transport, because hypoglycemia is likely to recur
w: Give a second dose of glucagon before transport
Stop monitoring his glucose since it is now normal
Take a second dose of dextrose before you leave the scene

items.q: A malnourished 50-year-old with chronic heavy alcohol use has a glucose of 32 mg/dL. No IV could be started, and IM glucagon 15 minutes ago has not helped. What is the most likely reason?
items.x: Glucagon raises glucose by releasing liver glycogen. Malnourished and chronically alcoholic patients have little glycogen, so they need dextrose by IV or IO access.
items.a: Depleted glycogen stores in the liver
w: IM absorption takes at least an hour
Alcohol binds and inactivates glucagon
Glucagon works only when given by the IV route

items.q: A 45-year-old has taken prednisone daily for years but stopped 3 days ago because of vomiting. He is lethargic with BP 74/40 despite 2 liters of fluid and a glucose of 58 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, and stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension and hypoglycemia. Treatment requires stress-dose steroids in addition to fluids.
items.a: Acute adrenal insufficiency
w: Hypovolemic shock from vomiting alone
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Thyroid storm

items.q: Which findings are typical of adrenal crisis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Loss of cortisol and aldosterone causes refractory hypotension, low glucose, low sodium and high potassium.
opts: Hypotension that does not respond well to fluids
Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Marked hypertension
ok: Hypotension that does not respond well to fluids
Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia

items.q: A 34-year-old with Graves disease stopped her medication a month ago. Which findings would suggest thyroid storm? Select all that apply.
items.x: Thyroid storm causes high fever, tachydysrhythmias and altered mental status. Bradycardia, hypothermia and facial puffiness point the other way, toward severe hypothyroidism.
opts: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F)
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Agitation and delirium
Sinus bradycardia
Hypothermia with puffy facial swelling
ok: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F)
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
Agitation and delirium

items.q: An 81-year-old is found in a cold house in winter with a temperature of 33.8 C (92.8 F), HR 44, RR 8, a puffy face and coarse dry skin. She has not taken her levothyroxine in months. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and altered mental status, often triggered by cold or illness. Expect hypoglycemia and support ventilation.
items.a: Myxedema coma
w: Primary environmental hypothermia alone
Opioid overdose
Adrenal crisis

items.q: A 38-year-old took an overdose of amitriptyline. QRS is 150 ms, HR 128, BP 82/50. Which intervention most directly treats the wide QRS?
items.x: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels. Sodium bicarbonate supplies sodium and alkalinizes the blood, narrowing the QRS; class IA and IC antidysrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade.
items.a: Sodium bicarbonate
w: Amiodarone
Procainamide
Synchronized cardioversion

items.q: A 60-year-old took an overdose of his blood pressure medicine. HR 38, BP 70/40, glucose 290 mg/dL. Which drug class is most likely?
items.x: Both beta blockers and calcium channel blockers cause bradycardia and hypotension. Calcium channel blockers also impair insulin release and cause hyperglycemia, while beta blocker overdose tends to cause hypoglycemia.
items.a: Calcium channel blocker
w: Beta blocker
Digoxin
Tricyclic antidepressant

items.q: A 2-year-old may have swallowed one of his grandmother's extended-release verapamil tablets an hour ago. He is alert with normal vital signs. What is the best plan?
items.x: A single tablet of some cardiac drugs can be dangerous to a toddler, and extended-release forms may not cause symptoms for many hours. The child needs transport and observation.
items.a: Transport, since toxicity from extended-release tablets can be delayed
w: Give activated charcoal and atropine on scene before moving him
Give syrup of ipecac and transport
Induce vomiting before leaving the scene

items.q: A farm worker was sprayed with an organophosphate pesticide and has heavy secretions and vomiting. What is the priority before you provide care?
items.x: Organophosphates are absorbed through skin, so responders must protect themselves and remove the patient's contaminated clothing and decontaminate before or alongside treatment.
items.a: Proper PPE and decontamination
w: Immediate intubation in the field
Starting an IV in the contaminated arm
Giving atropine through his wet clothing

items.q: You are giving repeated doses of atropine to a patient with organophosphate poisoning. Which finding is the main endpoint for atropine?
items.x: Atropine is titrated to dry the bronchial secretions and ease breathing. Pupil size and heart rate are unreliable endpoints and may lag behind or mislead.
items.a: Drying of respiratory secretions
w: Dilation of the pupils to normal size or larger
A heart rate that rises above 120 per minute
Return to a normal level of consciousness

items.q: A 41-year-old swallowed a large quantity of an over-the-counter pain reliever 6 hours ago. Which findings suggest salicylate toxicity? Select all that apply.
items.x: Salicylates cause tinnitus, stimulate breathing (respiratory alkalosis) and cause metabolic acidosis and hyperthermia. If intubation is needed, a high minute ventilation must be maintained.
opts: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Elevated temperature
Pinpoint pupils
Marked bradycardia
ok: Ringing in the ears
Rapid, deep breathing
Elevated temperature

items.q: A 17-year-old says she swallowed 30 acetaminophen tablets 2 hours ago. She feels fine and her vital signs are normal. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Acetaminophen toxicity often causes no symptoms for the first day, while liver injury silently develops. The antidote is most effective when started within about 8 hours, so early transport matters.
items.a: Liver injury may still develop, and the antidote works best early
w: Normal vitals 2 hours after ingestion show the dose was not toxic
Liver damage occurs only if she vomits blood within 4 hours
A single dose of charcoal now makes the overdose harmless

items.q: A 48-year-old drank windshield washer fluid yesterday. He now has blurred vision he describes as like a snowstorm, and deep rapid respirations. Which substance most likely caused this?
items.x: Methanol is metabolized to formic acid, which damages the optic nerve and causes a severe metabolic acidosis. Visual changes after a delay are a hallmark.
items.a: Methanol
w: Isopropyl alcohol
Ethanol
Propylene glycol

items.q: A 55-year-old heavy daily drinker stopped drinking 3 days ago. He is confused and hallucinating, tremulous and sweating, with HR 138 and a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Delirium tremens typically starts 2 to 4 days after the last drink, with autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations and confusion. It is life-threatening and needs aggressive treatment.
items.a: Delirium tremens
w: Acute alcohol intoxication
Anticholinergic toxidrome
Wernicke encephalopathy alone

items.q: A man pulled from an enclosed house fire is unresponsive with BP 78/40, SpO2 98 percent and SpCO 8 percent. Which treatment targets the most likely additional poison?
items.x: Smoke from burning plastics contains cyanide. Coma and hypotension that are out of proportion to a modest carboxyhemoglobin level suggest cyanide toxicity, treated with hydroxocobalamin.
items.a: Hydroxocobalamin
w: Naloxone
Atropine
Methylene blue

items.q: A 32-year-old taking sertraline started tramadol 2 days ago. He is agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 39.0 C (102.2 F), HR 124, diarrhea, and sustained clonus and brisk reflexes in his legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Combining serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome, which comes on quickly and features clonus and hyperreflexia, most marked in the legs.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: A 44-year-old started haloperidol a week ago. He is confused, with a temperature of 40.2 C (104.4 F), rigid lead-pipe muscles, slow reflexes and a fluctuating blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after starting antipsychotics, with hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, decreased reflexes and autonomic instability.
items.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome
Bacterial meningitis
Exertional heat stroke

items.q: Which features favor serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply.
items.x: Serotonin syndrome is rapid and causes neuromuscular hyperactivity and GI hyperactivity. NMS is slower, with rigidity and sluggish reflexes.
opts: Onset within hours of a medication change
Clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs
Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds
Lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes
Gradual onset over days after starting an antipsychotic
ok: Onset within hours of a medication change
Clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in the legs
Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds

items.q: A 24-year-old used a stimulant at a party. He is agitated with HR 140, BP 176/100, temperature 38.8 C (101.8 F) and dilated pupils. Which finding best separates a sympathomimetic toxidrome from an anticholinergic one?
items.x: Both toxidromes cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia and mydriasis. Sympathomimetics cause diaphoresis, while anticholinergics cause hot, dry skin.
items.a: Moist, sweaty skin
w: Dilated pupils
A fast heart rate
An elevated temperature

items.q: You are ventilating a 40-year-old with an opioid overdose and a respiratory rate of 4. What is the goal of naloxone?
items.x: Naloxone is titrated to restore adequate breathing. Pushing for full arousal can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
items.a: Adequate spontaneous breathing
w: Full wakefulness so he can refuse care
Pupils that return to normal size
A heart rate above 100 per minute

items.q: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who injected fentanyl now breathes 14 times a minute with SpO2 96 percent but remains deeply sedated, with HR 52 and chronic wounds on his forearms. What is the best approach?
items.x: Xylazine is a common adulterant that causes sedation, bradycardia and chronic wounds and does not respond to naloxone. Once breathing is adequate, support the airway and monitor rather than giving more naloxone.
items.a: Supportive care, as a non-opioid sedative such as xylazine may be present
w: Keep repeating naloxone doses until he is fully awake
Give flumazenil to reverse the remaining sedation
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the heart rate

items.q: You find a person unresponsive in a closed car with a note on the window warning of toxic gas, and you notice a rotten egg odor. What should you do?
items.x: Chemical suicide with hydrogen sulfide can kill rescuers quickly. Scene safety comes first, and rescue requires proper respiratory protection.
items.a: Back away, isolate the area and request hazmat
w: Open the doors and rapidly remove the patient
Hold your breath and reach in to check a pulse
Break a window to air out the car, then enter

items.q: A 70-year-old in septic shock has received 30 mL/kg of IV fluid. Her lungs remain clear, HR 118, MAP 56 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step under sepsis guidelines?
items.x: When hypotension persists after initial fluid resuscitation, a vasopressor such as norepinephrine is started to reach a MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
items.a: Begin a vasopressor infusion
w: Give a diuretic to mobilize the fluid
Accept the pressure, since a MAP above 50 is adequate
Give a steroid in place of a vasopressor

items.q: A 66-year-old with pneumonia has HR 122, RR 30, BP 100/62 and an ETCO2 of 22 mmHg by nasal cannula. How should you interpret the low ETCO2?
items.x: In sepsis, a low ETCO2 reflects compensatory hyperventilation for metabolic acidosis and correlates with elevated lactate and poor perfusion.
items.a: A sign of metabolic acidosis with likely high lactate
w: Hypoventilation with CO2 retention that needs a bag-valve mask
A faulty sensor, since sick patients always have high CO2
A normal value for a patient with pneumonia

items.q: A 57-year-old received chemotherapy 9 days ago. She has a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F), HR 112 and BP 104/66 but says she feels okay. What is the best approach?
items.x: Chemotherapy can lower the white cell count around 7 to 14 days after treatment. Fever in that window can signal sepsis that progresses quickly, and rectal procedures should be avoided.
items.a: Treat it as possible sepsis and transport promptly
w: Take a rectal temperature to confirm the fever
Advise acetaminophen and a call to her oncologist in the morning
Delay transport unless her fever rises above 39 C (102.2 F)

items.q: An 88-year-old with dementia is more confused than usual. Temperature 35.6 C (96.1 F), HR 104, RR 24, BP 96/58, and her urine is cloudy. How should you interpret these findings?
items.x: Older adults often have no fever with sepsis and may even become hypothermic. New confusion, tachycardia and tachypnea with a likely source should be treated as sepsis.
items.a: Sepsis is still likely despite the low temperature
w: Infection is unlikely because she has no fever
She is simply having a bad day with her dementia
Her findings are explained by a cool room

items.q: A 3-year-old has a fever and is lethargic. Which findings indicate compensated shock? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children maintain blood pressure until late, so tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion signal shock before hypotension appears. Hypotension or bradycardia means decompensation.
opts: Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Heart rate of 168
Cool, mottled hands and feet
Systolic blood pressure of 60 mmHg
Heart rate of 58
ok: Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Heart rate of 168
Cool, mottled hands and feet

items.q: A 74-year-old dialysis patient with suspected sepsis has BP 84/50 and clear lungs. How should IV fluid be given?
items.x: Patients with kidney failure or heart failure still need fluid for septic hypotension, but they are prone to pulmonary edema, so fluid is given in smaller amounts with frequent reassessment.
items.a: Small boluses with frequent lung reassessment
w: Start a vasopressor with no fluid because he receives dialysis
Give the full sepsis bolus as fast as possible without reassessing
Give oral fluids only and avoid IV access

items.q: A dialysis patient with hyperkalemia has a wide QRS. What is the main purpose of giving IV calcium?
items.x: Calcium protects the heart from dysrhythmias within minutes but does not lower potassium. Other treatments are needed to shift or remove potassium.
items.a: Stabilize the heart muscle cell membranes
w: Move potassium out of the blood into the cells
Remove potassium through the kidneys
Bind potassium in the gut

items.q: Which ECG changes are associated with worsening hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hyperkalemia progresses from peaked T waves to loss of P waves and QRS widening, then to a sine wave and arrest. U waves suggest hypokalemia.
opts: Peaked T waves
Widening of the QRS complex
Flattened or absent P waves
Prominent U waves
Osborn J waves
Delta waves
ok: Peaked T waves
Widening of the QRS complex
Flattened or absent P waves

items.q: A 34-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She has nausea, headache and confusion, then has a seizure. Her glucose is normal and she has gained weight. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Drinking more water than is lost can dilute the blood sodium, causing brain swelling with confusion and seizures. Giving more hypotonic fluid makes it worse.
items.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
w: Heat exhaustion
Hypoglycemia
Dehydration

items.q: A 66-year-old is bleeding briskly from the puncture site of his dialysis fistula at home. What should you do first?
items.x: Fistula bleeding usually stops with steady direct pressure. A tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening bleeding that pressure cannot control.
items.a: Firm direct pressure over the bleeding site
w: Apply a tourniquet above the fistula before anything else
Elevate the arm and apply an ice pack without pressure
Clamp the fistula with a hemostat

items.q: A 61-year-old missed two dialysis sessions. She is in severe respiratory distress with crackles throughout, BP 196/104 and SpO2 84 percent. Which intervention is most helpful prehospital?
items.x: Fluid overload from missed dialysis causes pulmonary edema. CPAP and upright positioning improve oxygenation and reduce the work of breathing while she is transported for dialysis.
items.a: CPAP with the patient sitting upright
w: A 1-liter fluid bolus
Lying her flat to rest
Nebulized albuterol alone

items.q: A 46-year-old had thyroid surgery 2 days ago. She has tingling around her mouth and fingers, spasm of her hands and a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: The parathyroid glands can be injured during thyroid surgery, causing low calcium with paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and QT prolongation.
items.a: Hypocalcemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypoglycemia
Hypermagnesemia

items.q: An 81-year-old was found on the floor after about 2 days. His urine is dark brown. What is the most immediately dangerous complication?
items.x: Prolonged immobility can cause rhabdomyolysis, releasing potassium from damaged muscle. Hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmias, and myoglobin can injure the kidneys.
items.a: Hyperkalemia with dysrhythmias
w: Hypercalcemia with seizures
Hypernatremia from overhydration
Hypertension from fluid overload

items.q: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. GCS 10, HR 132, BP 78/44. What is the first priority?
items.x: Massive hematemesis with a depressed level of consciousness puts the patient at high risk of aspiration. Airway protection comes first, then vascular access and resuscitation.
items.a: Suction and position to protect the airway
w: Start bilateral large-bore IVs before anything else
Insert an orogastric tube to empty the stomach
Obtain a 12-lead ECG

items.q: Which findings suggest bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract? Select all that apply.
items.x: Upper GI bleeding shows as hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit or melena from digested blood. Small amounts of bright red blood with stool usually come from the lower tract.
opts: Coffee-ground vomit
Black, tarry, sticky stools
Bright red blood on the toilet paper only
Painless blood after a hard stool
Vomiting bright red blood
ok: Coffee-ground vomit
Black, tarry, sticky stools
Vomiting bright red blood

items.q: A 74-year-old taking metoprolol and an anticoagulant has had black stools for 2 days. He is pale and dizzy when standing. HR 76, BP 96/58. How should you interpret his heart rate?
items.x: Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to hemorrhage, so a normal rate does not rule out significant blood loss in an anticoagulated patient with orthostatic symptoms.
items.a: His medication may hide the tachycardia of blood loss
w: A normal heart rate proves the blood loss is minor
His low pressure is from his BP medicine, not bleeding
His heart rate shows he is fully compensating

items.q: A 70-year-old with several prior abdominal surgeries has crampy diffuse pain, a distended abdomen, foul brown vomit and no stool or gas for 2 days. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Adhesions from earlier surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, which causes crampy pain, distension, vomiting and absent stool or flatus.
items.a: Small bowel obstruction
w: Appendicitis
Gastroenteritis
Diverticulitis

items.q: A 42-year-old heavy drinker has severe constant upper abdominal pain boring through to his back, with vomiting. HR 118, BP 100/64. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and can cause large fluid shifts and shock. Alcohol and gallstones are the main causes.
items.a: Acute pancreatitis
w: Cholecystitis
Appendicitis
Kidney stone

items.q: A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated has sudden severe abdominal pain, yet his abdomen is soft and barely tender. What should you be most concerned about?
items.x: Pain out of proportion to the exam in an older patient with atrial fibrillation suggests an embolus to the mesenteric arteries, a time-critical emergency.
items.a: Mesenteric ischemia
w: Constipation
Gastroenteritis
Anxiety

items.q: A 30-year-old was stung by a bee 10 minutes ago. She is dizzy with BP 76/42 and HR 128. She has no hives. How should you interpret this?
items.x: Hypotension soon after exposure to a known or likely allergen meets the criteria for anaphylaxis even without skin involvement. Give IM epinephrine promptly.
items.a: Anaphylaxis, even without skin findings
w: Not anaphylaxis, because hives are required
A vasovagal reaction to the pain of the sting
A local reaction that needs only ice

items.q: A 22-year-old's food-related anaphylaxis resolved completely after one IM epinephrine dose. She wants to refuse transport. What should you tell her?
items.x: A biphasic reaction can recur hours later without re-exposure, and epinephrine wears off within minutes to hours. Patients should be observed after anaphylaxis.
items.a: Symptoms can return hours later
w: Resolution after epinephrine means the reaction is over for good
An oral antihistamine taken now fully prevents any recurrence
A recurrence is only possible if she eats the food again

items.q: A 64-year-old who has taken lisinopril for years has had swelling of the tongue and lips over 2 hours, without hives, itching or wheezing. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin levels and can cause angioedema at any time, even after years of use. It often responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines.
items.a: ACE inhibitor angioedema
w: Food anaphylaxis
Ludwig angina
Peritonsillar abscess

items.q: The same patient now has drooling, stridor and cannot swallow. What is the most important airway consideration?
items.x: Angioedema distorts the upper airway. Plan for a difficult intubation by the most experienced provider and prepare for a surgical airway. A supraglottic device does not bypass the swelling.
items.a: Expect a difficult airway with a surgical backup ready
w: Insert a supraglottic airway as the first choice
Lay him flat to improve airway alignment
Wait for the swelling to respond to antihistamines

items.q: Minutes after eating shrimp, which findings support anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Anaphylaxis involves two or more body systems after exposure, or hypotension after a known allergen. Isolated mild local or eye and nose symptoms do not meet the criteria.
opts: Hives with wheezing
Hives with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting
Hypotension
Itchy eyes and sneezing only
Mild swelling limited to the lips without other signs
A single hive on the forearm
ok: Hives with wheezing
Hives with crampy abdominal pain and vomiting
Hypotension

items.q: A 16-year-old with sickle cell disease has chest pain, a temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F), cough, RR 30 and SpO2 89 percent. What is the most concerning diagnosis?
items.x: Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, with chest pain, fever, respiratory symptoms and hypoxia. It needs oxygen and prompt transport.
items.a: Acute chest syndrome
w: A simple pain crisis
An asthma exacerbation
Anxiety

items.q: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease is pale and lethargic, with HR 180, capillary refill of 4 seconds and an enlarging mass in the left upper abdomen. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: In young children, sickled cells can pool in the spleen, enlarging it rapidly and causing anemia and hypovolemic shock.
items.a: Splenic sequestration crisis
w: Acute appendicitis
A simple pain crisis
Intussusception

items.q: A 24-year-old is in a sickle cell pain crisis with severe leg and back pain. SpO2 97 percent and vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate care?
items.x: Vaso-occlusive crisis needs early, adequate pain control and fluids if dehydrated. Oxygen is given for hypoxia, and cold can worsen sickling.
items.a: Prompt pain relief and transport
w: Give pain medication only after the hospital confirms the crisis
High-flow oxygen for everyone with sickle cell, whatever the SpO2
Cold packs on the painful areas

items.q: A 12-year-old with hemophilia A hit his head on a door 2 hours ago. He has a mild headache and GCS 15. What is the best plan?
items.x: Patients with clotting disorders can develop delayed intracranial bleeding after minor trauma and need evaluation and often factor replacement.
items.a: Transport, as bleeding inside the skull is a real risk
w: Transport non-emergent, since a normal neuro exam rules out a bleed
Apply ice and recheck GCS on scene in 30 minutes
Wait on scene for 1 hour to see if he gets worse

items.q: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient on immunosuppressants has fatigue, a cough and a temperature of 37.9 C (100.2 F). How should you interpret this?
items.x: Immunosuppression blunts fever and inflammation, so serious infections can look mild. These patients should be evaluated promptly.
items.a: Serious infection may be present despite mild signs
w: A low-grade fever means only a minor infection
He should stop his immunosuppressants on scene
His new kidney protects him from infection

items.q: An agitated 28-year-old with hyperactive delirium has been chemically sedated after physical restraint. What monitoring is required?
items.x: Sedated patients with hyperactive delirium are at risk of respiratory depression and sudden cardiac arrest. Continuous capnography and cardiac monitoring detect deterioration early.
items.a: Continuous ETCO2, SpO2 and ECG monitoring
w: A single set of vital signs before transport
Visual checks only, to avoid agitating him
Hourly vital signs as with any stable patient

items.q: A restrained, combative, hyperthermic man suddenly becomes quiet and still during transport. What does this most likely mean?
items.x: Sudden calm after severe agitation can mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check breathing and pulse immediately.
items.a: A possible arrest that needs immediate assessment
w: He has calmed down and no longer needs monitoring
His sedation is working as expected
He is tired from the struggle and is sleeping

items.q: A 42-year-old is tearful after a breakup and says she feels hopeless. How should you ask about suicide?
items.x: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to assess it accurately.
items.a: Ask directly if she is thinking about killing herself
w: Avoid the topic, since asking may plant the idea
Ask her family privately instead, so as not to upset her
Wait for her to bring up the subject herself

items.q: Which factors increase a patient's risk of suicide? Select all that apply.
items.x: A prior attempt, a plan with access to lethal means and substance use raise risk. Social connection and future plans are protective, and asking does not increase risk.
opts: A previous suicide attempt
A specific plan with access to the means
Alcohol or drug use
Strong family ties and plans for the future
Being asked directly about suicidal thoughts
ok: A previous suicide attempt
A specific plan with access to the means
Alcohol or drug use

items.q: A 30-year-old took a handful of pills to end his life and now refuses transport. He is alert and oriented. What is the correct approach?
items.x: A patient at immediate risk of self-harm lacks the capacity to refuse care. Follow local law and protocol, which may involve law enforcement.
items.a: He cannot make a valid refusal
w: He may refuse because he is alert and oriented
He may refuse if he signs in front of a witness
He may refuse if a family member stays with him

items.q: Which practices are appropriate for a physically restrained, agitated patient? Select all that apply.
items.x: Restraint can cause positional asphyxia and sudden death. Patients should never be placed prone or hobbled, and they need ongoing monitoring and documentation.
opts: Continuous monitoring of breathing and circulation
Frequent checks of circulation in the restrained limbs
Prone positioning with weight on the back
Restraining the hands and feet together behind the back
Documenting the reason for restraint and each reassessment
ok: Continuous monitoring of breathing and circulation
Frequent checks of circulation in the restrained limbs
Documenting the reason for restraint and each reassessment

items.q: You are cooling a patient with exertional heat stroke by cold water immersion. At about what core temperature should active cooling stop?
items.x: Cooling is usually stopped at about 38.5 to 39 C (101.3-102.2 F) to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.
items.a: About 39 C (102.2 F)
w: About 37 C (98.6 F)
About 36 C (96.8 F)

items.q: Which cooling methods are effective for exertional heat stroke? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cold water immersion is the fastest method, and towels or evaporative cooling are used when immersion is not possible. Fever reducers do not work for heat stroke.
opts: Cold water immersion
Rotating ice-water-soaked towels over the body
Misting with water and fanning
Waiting until arrival at the hospital to start cooling
An oral fever reducer as the main treatment
ok: Cold water immersion
Rotating ice-water-soaked towels over the body
Misting with water and fanning

items.q: A 35-year-old was pulled from an icy lake after 25 minutes. He is pulseless and in asystole with a core temperature of 26 C (78.8 F) and no lethal injuries. What is the best approach?
items.x: Hypothermia protects the brain, and people have survived long arrests after rewarming. Continue CPR and transport to a center capable of extracorporeal rewarming.
items.a: Begin CPR and transport for active internal rewarming
w: Pronounce death because asystole at 26 C (78.8 F) is unsurvivable
Delay CPR until he has been rewarmed above 30 C (86 F)
Give rescue breaths only, since compressions cause VF

items.q: A hiker has frostbitten feet and must walk 3 hours to reach the trailhead. What should you do about rewarming?
items.x: Thawing and refreezing causes more tissue damage than delaying rewarming. Walking on frozen feet is preferable to thawing them before a long walk out.
items.a: Do not thaw the feet if they could refreeze
w: Rub the feet with snow to restore circulation
Thaw the feet with dry heat from a campfire
Thaw the feet in hot water before walking out

items.q: For a drowning victim in cardiac arrest, what is emphasized compared with a typical adult cardiac arrest?
items.x: Drowning causes a hypoxic arrest, so early ventilation is key. Spinal precautions are not routine unless there is a diving or trauma mechanism.
items.a: Early effective ventilation
w: Hands-only CPR so compressions are not delayed
Defibrillation before any breaths are given
Full spinal motion restriction before CPR

items.q: A climber at 4,200 meters has a headache, confusion and cannot walk heel to toe. What is the most important treatment?
items.x: Ataxia and altered mental status at altitude suggest high-altitude cerebral edema, which can be fatal. Immediate descent is the definitive treatment.
items.a: Descent to a lower altitude
w: Rest at the same altitude for 24 hours
Fluids and sleep, deciding in the morning
Continued ascent to finish the climb quickly

items.q: After 2 days at 3,800 meters, a hiker has shortness of breath at rest, a cough with pink frothy sputum, crackles and SpO2 70 percent. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: High-altitude pulmonary edema causes dyspnea at rest, cough and hypoxia. It is treated with oxygen and descent.
items.a: High-altitude pulmonary edema
w: Bacterial pneumonia
Asthma exacerbation
Spontaneous pneumothorax

items.q: A diver ran out of air and ascended rapidly. Within 3 minutes of surfacing, he became confused with weakness on one side. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Rapid ascent can rupture alveoli and send gas bubbles into the arteries, causing stroke-like signs within minutes. Treat with 100 percent oxygen and arrange hyperbaric therapy.
items.a: Arterial gas embolism
w: Type I decompression sickness
Nitrogen narcosis
Hypoglycemia

items.q: Six hours after a deep dive, a diver has deep aching pain in his shoulder and fatigue. He plans to fly home tonight. What is the best advice?
items.x: Joint pain hours after diving suggests decompression sickness. Flying lowers ambient pressure and worsens bubbles, so he needs oxygen and evaluation for hyperbaric treatment.
items.a: 100 percent oxygen and evaluation for recompression
w: Fly home and see a doctor afterward
Massage and heat for the sore shoulder
Return to depth to recompress in the water

items.q: A 30-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake and swelling is spreading up his leg. Which treatment is appropriate?
items.x: Pit viper bites are managed by immobilizing the limb, marking swelling progression and rapid transport for antivenom. Tourniquets, incisions and ice cause harm.
items.a: Keep the limb still and mark the edge of the swelling
w: Apply a tight arterial tourniquet above the bite to stop the venom
Cut over the fang marks and suction out the venom
Pack the leg in ice to slow venom absorption

items.q: A 22-year-old at 37 weeks has a generalized seizure. BP 172/110. What is the first-line medication to stop and prevent eclamptic seizures?
items.x: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for eclampsia. A benzodiazepine may be used if magnesium is not available.
items.a: Magnesium sulfate
w: Phenytoin
Labetalol
Diphenhydramine

items.q: A pregnant patient is receiving magnesium sulfate for severe preeclampsia. Which findings suggest magnesium toxicity? Select all that apply.
items.x: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity, followed by respiratory depression and decreased consciousness. Stop the infusion, support breathing and consider calcium.
opts: Loss of the patellar reflexes
Respiratory rate of 8
Increasing drowsiness
Brisk reflexes with clonus
Respiratory rate of 26
ok: Loss of the patellar reflexes
Respiratory rate of 8
Increasing drowsiness

items.q: A 29-year-old delivered a baby 10 days ago. She has a severe headache, BP 166/104 and is seeing spots. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: Preeclampsia can develop up to 6 weeks after delivery and carries the same risk of seizures and stroke.
items.a: Postpartum preeclampsia
w: Tension headache
Postpartum depression
Migraine

items.q: A 32-year-old at 33 weeks has vaginal bleeding. Which findings favor placenta previa over placental abruption? Select all that apply.
items.x: Placenta previa causes painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus. Abruption is painful with a tender, rigid uterus. Never perform a digital vaginal exam with third-trimester bleeding.
opts: Painless bleeding
Bright red blood
A soft, nontender uterus
A rigid, tender uterus
Dark blood with constant abdominal pain
ok: Painless bleeding
Bright red blood
A soft, nontender uterus

items.q: A 30-year-old in active labor who had a prior cesarean section has sudden tearing abdominal pain, her contractions stop, and fetal parts are easily felt through the abdomen. HR 130, BP 84/50. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A previous uterine scar increases the risk of rupture, which causes sudden pain, loss of contractions, palpable fetal parts and maternal shock.
items.a: Uterine rupture
w: Placenta previa
Braxton Hicks contractions
Normal transition stage of labor

items.q: Which are recognized causes of postpartum hemorrhage? Select all that apply.
items.x: The main causes are tone (atony), tissue (retained placenta), trauma (lacerations) and thrombin (clotting disorders). Breastfeeding helps the uterus contract.
opts: Uterine atony
Retained placental tissue
Lacerations of the birth canal
Rh incompatibility
Breastfeeding the newborn
ok: Uterine atony
Retained placental tissue
Lacerations of the birth canal

items.q: During a breech delivery the body and arms have delivered, but the head has not delivered after 3 minutes. What should you do?
items.x: If the head does not deliver, place gloved fingers to hold the vaginal wall away from the baby's face to create an airway, and transport rapidly.
items.a: Make an airway with a gloved hand and transport
w: Pull firmly on the baby's legs to deliver the head
Push the baby's body back into the vagina
Apply firm pressure to the top of the uterus

items.q: You have placed the mother in the McRoberts position for a shoulder dystocia, but the shoulders still do not deliver. What should you do next?
items.x: Suprapubic pressure helps dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone. Fundal pressure worsens impaction.
items.a: Firm suprapubic pressure
w: Firm pressure on the top of the uterus
Strong downward traction on the head
Push the head back into the vagina

items.q: The baby's head delivers with the cord wrapped tightly around the neck twice, and it cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
items.x: A cord too tight to slip over the head must be clamped and cut to allow delivery.
items.a: Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps
w: Pull firmly on the head so the shoulders deliver more quickly
Push the head back and wait for the next contraction
Leave the cord in place and continue the delivery

items.q: During labor, a 35-year-old suddenly becomes severely short of breath and hypoxic, then hypotensive, then has a seizure and arrests. After resuscitation she bleeds from her IV sites. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden hypoxia, shock and arrest during labor or just after delivery, often followed by a bleeding disorder.
items.a: Amniotic fluid embolism
w: Eclampsia
Pulmonary embolism
Anaphylaxis

items.q: At what rate should positive-pressure ventilation be given to a newborn?

items.x: The MR SOPA steps correct ineffective ventilation: mask, reposition, suction, open mouth, pressure increase, alternative airway. Compressions begin only after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

Reposition the head in the sniffing position
Gradually increase the ventilation pressure

50 percent
60 to 70 percent

items.q: A newborn delivered through thick meconium-stained fluid is limp and not breathing. What should you do?

items.a: Initial steps, then PPV if still apneic
w: Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
Suction the stomach before drying and warming
Wait for the 1-minute Apgar score

items.q: A baby born at 28 weeks is delivered in the ambulance. How should you keep the baby warm?
items.x: Very premature newborns lose heat rapidly. Covering them up to the neck in plastic wrap without drying, along with a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
items.a: Place the body in plastic wrap without drying first
w: Dry vigorously and leave the skin uncovered for assessment
Bathe the baby with warm water to remove the vernix
Place the baby on a cool surface to prevent overheating

items.q: During newborn resuscitation with chest compressions, which method gives the most accurate heart rate?
items.x: NRP recommends an electronic cardiac monitor during compressions, since palpation and pulse oximetry can be inaccurate.
items.a: A cardiac monitor with ECG leads
w: Palpating the umbilical cord
Palpating the brachial pulse
The pulse oximeter reading

items.q: A newborn is apneic at birth. When should you calculate the 1-minute Apgar score before starting resuscitation?
items.x: Apgar scores describe the newborn's condition but are not used to decide whether to resuscitate.
items.a: Do not wait for the Apgar score
w: After the 1-minute score is done
After the 5-minute score is done
After both scores are averaged

items.q: A 3-month-old has had a runny nose for 3 days and now has wheezing, retractions, poor feeding and SpO2 91 percent. What is the most helpful first step?
items.x: Infants breathe mainly through the nose, and secretions from bronchiolitis can block the airway. Suctioning improves breathing and feeding, while bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely helpful.
items.a: Gentle nasal suctioning
w: A routine albuterol nebulizer for the wheezing
An oral steroid dose for the inflammation
Chest physiotherapy with back percussion

items.q: A 2-year-old has croup. Which finding indicates severe croup?
items.x: Stridor at rest, especially with retractions or agitation, means significant airway narrowing that needs treatment.
items.a: Stridor at rest
w: A loud barking cough that is worse at night
Low-grade fever with a runny nose
A hoarse voice while crying

items.q: Which features favor croup rather than epiglottitis? Select all that apply.
items.x: Croup is a viral illness with a gradual onset and a barking cough. Epiglottitis is sudden, with high fever, drooling and tripod positioning.

Gradual onset after cold symptoms
Drooling and difficulty swallowing
Sitting in a tripod position
Sudden high fever with a toxic appearance
ok: A barking, seal-like cough
Gradual onset after cold symptoms

items.q: Which findings indicate significant dehydration in a 9-month-old? Select all that apply.

No wet diaper in 8 hours
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
A bulging fontanelle
Tears when crying
ok: A sunken anterior fontanelle
No wet diaper in 8 hours
Capillary refill of 4 seconds

items.q: Which feature makes a febrile seizure complex rather than simple?
items.x: Complex febrile seizures last longer than 15 minutes, are focal or recur within 24 hours. Simple seizures are brief and generalized.
items.a: Lasting longer than 15 minutes
w: Occurring in a 2-year-old
A generalized tonic-clonic seizure
A temperature of 39.5 C (103.1 F)

items.q: A 20-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure with a temperature of 39.4 C (102.9 F). He is now drowsy but improving, with a patent airway. What is the best plan?
items.x: Simple febrile seizures are usually harmless, but children need evaluation. Cold baths, alcohol and objects in the mouth are dangerous.

Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol
Place a bite block to protect the tongue

items.q: Which findings should raise suspicion of child abuse? Select all that apply.
items.x: Delays, inconsistent histories and injuries that do not fit the child's development are red flags. Crying and common toddler injuries are expected.
opts: A delay in seeking care for an injury
A history that changes between caregivers
An injury that does not fit the child's developmental stage
A child who cries when examined
A forehead bruise on a toddler learning to walk
ok: A delay in seeking care for an injury
A history that changes between caregivers
An injury that does not fit the child's developmental stage

items.q: Which bruising pattern in a 2-year-old is most concerning for abuse?
items.x: Bruises on protected areas such as the ears, neck and torso are rarely accidental in young children. Shins, forehead and knees are common sites for accidental injuries.
items.a: Bruising on the ears, neck or torso
w: Bruises over the shins
A bump on the forehead
Scrapes on the knees and elbows

items.q: A 4-month-old has irritability, vomiting, lethargy and an episode of apnea, without fever or visible injury. What should you suspect?
items.x: Shaken infants may have no external injury. Unexplained lethargy, vomiting and apnea in an infant should raise concern for abusive head trauma.
items.a: Abusive head trauma
w: Gastroenteritis
Infant colic
Reflux

items.q: You suspect a child has been abused. What is your responsibility?
items.x: EMS providers are mandated reporters in most states. Reasonable suspicion is enough, and the report should be objective without accusations.
items.a: Document objectively and report as required by law
w: Confront the caregivers about your suspicion on scene
Report only if you are certain abuse occurred
Leave reporting to the hospital without telling staff

items.q: A 10-month-old has bouts of inconsolable crying with his knees drawn up every 15 to 20 minutes, is lethargic between episodes and has passed red jelly-like stool. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: In intussusception the bowel telescopes into itself, causing intermittent severe pain, lethargy and currant jelly stool.
items.a: Intussusception
w: Colic
Gastroenteritis
Constipation

items.q: A 6-week-old briefly turned pale and limp for 20 seconds, then recovered. She now looks normal. What is the best plan?
items.x: A brief resolved unexplained event can signal serious illness, such as infection, abuse or a cardiac problem, and needs medical evaluation.
items.a: Transport for evaluation despite the normal exam
w: Transport without monitoring since she looks normal
Begin back blows and chest thrusts now
Transport only if her pulse oximetry is low

items.q: An 82-year-old has new confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention after starting an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Older adults are very sensitive to anticholinergic drugs, which can cause delirium, urinary retention and constipation.
items.a: Anticholinergic side effects
w: Normal progression of dementia
Alzheimer disease starting suddenly
Hyperthyroidism

items.q: Which findings suggest elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
items.x: Patterned or multiple bruises, controlling caregivers and signs of neglect are red flags. A single injury with a consistent history is not.
opts: Bruises of different ages on protected areas
A caregiver who answers for the patient and will not leave
Severe pressure ulcers and soiled bedding
A single bruised shin after a witnessed fall
A diagnosis of dementia
ok: Bruises of different ages on protected areas
A caregiver who answers for the patient and will not leave
Severe pressure ulcers and soiled bedding

items.q: A 79-year-old hospice patient with a POLST for comfort measures only has new pauses in breathing and gurgling. She appears comfortable. What is the best approach?
items.x: These are normal changes near death. Follow the patient's wishes and support the family.
items.a: Follow the comfort-care plan and contact hospice
w: Begin aggressive suctioning and assist with a BVM
Start CPR if her breathing stops for 20 seconds
Transport emergently for intubation

items.q: What is the best way to manage noisy upper airway secretions in a dying patient receiving comfort care?
items.x: Repositioning helps secretions drain. Deep suction is uncomfortable and usually ineffective at this stage.
items.a: Turn the patient onto the side
w: Deep nasotracheal suctioning every few minutes
A large IV fluid bolus to thin secretions
Intubation to clear the airway

items.q: An 85-year-old with a valid do-not-resuscitate order has a pulse and acute respiratory distress. What should you do?
items.x: A DNR order does not mean no treatment. Provide oxygen, positioning and other care allowed by her orders and local protocol.
items.a: Treat her distress within the limits of her orders
w: Provide no treatment because she has a DNR
Intubate, since a DNR applies only to cardiac arrest
Call her family before any care is given

items.q: A 24-year-old has a partial leg amputation with bright red spurting blood, snoring respirations and a GCS of 9. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Massive external bleeding can cause death within minutes, so it comes first in modern trauma care (often taught as X-ABCDE or MARCH). The airway follows, then breathing, then circulation and shock care, and finally a quick neurologic check.
opts: Control the massive bleeding with a tourniquet
Open the airway with a jaw thrust
Assess breathing and assist ventilations if inadequate
Assess circulation and treat for shock
Check disability: GCS and pupils
ok: Control the massive bleeding with a tourniquet
Open the airway with a jaw thrust
Assess breathing and assist ventilations if inadequate
Assess circulation and treat for shock
Check disability: GCS and pupils

items.q: A 58-year-old collapses in front of you and is pulseless and apneic. Your monitor is at the patient's side. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: For a witnessed arrest, compressions begin right away and continue while the pads go on. A shockable rhythm gets one shock, followed immediately by 2 minutes of CPR. In AHA adult guidance for VF or pulseless VT, epinephrine is given after the second shock.
opts: Start high-quality chest compressions
Apply defibrillation pads while compressions continue
Deliver one shock for ventricular fibrillation
Resume compressions immediately for 2 minutes
Give epinephrine after the second shock
ok: Start high-quality chest compressions
Apply defibrillation pads while compressions continue
Deliver one shock for ventricular fibrillation
Resume compressions immediately for 2 minutes
Give epinephrine after the second shock

items.q: A 31-year-old stung by a bee has hives, stridor and a blood pressure of 78/40. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and treats both the airway swelling and the low blood pressure. Oxygen and IV fluids support it. Antihistamines ease hives and itching but do not treat the airway or shock, so they are add-on care. Epinephrine can be repeated per protocol if there is no response.
opts: Give intramuscular epinephrine
Apply high-flow oxygen
Start an IV fluid bolus for the hypotension
Give an antihistamine as an add-on treatment
Reassess and repeat epinephrine per protocol if no improvement
ok: Give intramuscular epinephrine
Apply high-flow oxygen
Start an IV fluid bolus for the hypotension
Give an antihistamine as an add-on treatment
Reassess and repeat epinephrine per protocol if no improvement

items.q: An unresponsive 60-year-old with no trauma has gurgling respirations at 6 per minute. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: An airway cannot be cleared or ventilated until it is opened. Gurgling means fluid, so suction comes before the oral airway. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen treats the slow breathing, and an advanced airway is considered once basic ventilation is under way.
opts: Open the airway with a head tilt-chin lift
Suction the airway
Insert an oropharyngeal airway
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Consider an advanced airway
ok: Open the airway with a head tilt-chin lift
Suction the airway
Insert an oropharyngeal airway
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Consider an advanced airway

items.q: A term newborn is limp and not breathing after delivery. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: NRP begins with warming, drying and stimulating, then positioning and clearing the airway. Ventilation is the single most important step in newborn resuscitation. Compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 after effective ventilation, and epinephrine follows if it still stays below 60.
opts: Warm, dry and stimulate the newborn
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Start positive-pressure ventilation if apneic or heart rate below 100
Start chest compressions if heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation
Give epinephrine if heart rate stays below 60 with compressions and ventilation
ok: Warm, dry and stimulate the newborn
Position the airway and clear secretions if needed
Start positive-pressure ventilation if apneic or heart rate below 100
Start chest compressions if heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation
Give epinephrine if heart rate stays below 60 with compressions and ventilation

items.q: A 71-year-old has a heart rate of 34, confusion and a blood pressure of 72/40. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Unstable bradycardia care in the AHA algorithm starts with the airway, breathing and oxygen if hypoxic, along with the monitor and IV access. Atropine is the first drug. If atropine does not work, transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion is the next step.
opts: Support the airway and breathing, with oxygen if hypoxic
Attach the monitor and obtain IV access
Give atropine
Start transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion if atropine is not effective
ok: Support the airway and breathing, with oxygen if hypoxic
Attach the monitor and obtain IV access
Give atropine
Start transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion if atropine is not effective

items.q: A worker's clothing caught fire. The flames are out but the fabric is still smoldering, and his voice is hoarse. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Smoldering clothing keeps burning tissue, so stopping the burning process is first. The airway is next, because soot or hoarseness can mean swelling that closes the airway. Jewelry comes off before swelling traps it, the burns are covered dry and the patient kept warm, and the size of the burn is estimated for fluid and destination decisions.
opts: Stop the burning process
Assess the airway for signs of inhalation injury
Remove jewelry and constricting clothing
Cover the burns with dry sterile dressings and keep him warm
Estimate the burned body surface area
ok: Stop the burning process
Assess the airway for signs of inhalation injury
Remove jewelry and constricting clothing
Cover the burns with dry sterile dressings and keep him warm
Estimate the burned body surface area

items.q: A 27-year-old with a suspected opioid overdose is apneic with a carotid pulse. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: For an apneic patient with a pulse, AHA guidance puts ventilation first: opening the airway and breathing for the patient fixes the low oxygen right away. Naloxone treats the cause but takes time to work, and the patient is reassessed afterward.
opts: Open the airway
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Give naloxone
Reassess breathing and responsiveness
ok: Open the airway
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
Give naloxone
Reassess breathing and responsiveness

items.q: A 52-year-old with diabetes is unresponsive with snoring respirations at 14 per minute. Her family says she took insulin and skipped lunch. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: The snoring airway is the immediate threat, so it is opened first. A glucose check confirms the cause before treatment. IV dextrose corrects the low sugar, and the patient is reassessed with a repeat glucose because long-acting insulin can cause the level to fall again.
opts: Open the airway
Check the blood glucose
Give IV dextrose for a low reading
Reassess mental status and recheck the glucose
ok: Open the airway
Check the blood glucose
Give IV dextrose for a low reading
Reassess mental status and recheck the glucose

items.q: A 19-year-old runner collapses at the finish line. He is confused, his skin is hot, and his core temperature is 41 C (105.8 F). What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Exertional heat stroke damages organs the longer the temperature stays high, so the patient is removed from the heat and cooled as fast as possible; cold-water immersion is the fastest method. Glucose is checked because low sugar can also cause confusion. Temperature and mental status are tracked to avoid overcooling.
opts: Move him out of the heat
Start rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion or ice and wet sheets
Check the blood glucose
Monitor his temperature and mental status during transport
ok: Move him out of the heat
Start rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion or ice and wet sheets
Check the blood glucose
Monitor his temperature and mental status during transport

items.q: A 30-year-old has heavy vaginal bleeding 10 minutes after delivering her baby. Her uterus feels soft and boggy and her blood pressure is 84/50. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: A soft, boggy uterus is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, and fundal massage helps it contract and slow the bleeding. IV access and fluids treat the shock, warmth helps blood clot, and transport brings her to definitive obstetric care.
opts: Massage the uterine fundus
Start large-bore IV access and fluids for shock
Keep her warm
Transport to a facility with obstetric care
ok: Massage the uterine fundus
Start large-bore IV access and fluids for shock
Keep her warm
Transport to a facility with obstetric care

items.q: You walk up to a 64-year-old sitting on a porch who called for shortness of breath. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: The NREMT patient assessment (medical) sheet moves from a general impression to the level of responsiveness, then airway, breathing and circulation. The transport priority decision comes at the end of the primary assessment, once life threats are found and treated.

Check responsiveness with AVPU
Assess the airway
Assess breathing
Assess circulation
Decide the transport priority
ok: Form a general impression
Check responsiveness with AVPU
Assess the airway
Assess breathing
Assess circulation
Decide the transport priority

items.q: A 33-year-old stabbed in the right chest is talking, with labored breathing and a wound that bubbles with each breath. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: An open chest wound lets air enter the chest, so sealing it comes first; a vented seal lets air escape. Oxygen treats the hypoxia. Sealing the wound can let pressure build, so the patient is watched for tension signs (worsening distress, falling blood pressure, absent breath sounds), and needle decompression treats it if it develops.
opts: Seal the wound with an occlusive (vented) chest seal
Apply high-flow oxygen
Watch for signs of a tension pneumothorax
Perform needle decompression if tension signs develop
ok: Seal the wound with an occlusive (vented) chest seal
Apply high-flow oxygen
Watch for signs of a tension pneumothorax
Perform needle decompression if tension signs develop

items.q: A 22-year-old with asthma is sitting bolt upright, can say only one word at a time, and has an SpO2 of 86 percent. What is most important to do for this patient? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: Hypoxia is treated first, with the patient kept upright. Inhaled bronchodilators open the airways fastest. Corticosteroids reduce the inflammation but take hours to work. Magnesium or epinephrine are added for a severe attack that does not respond to the first treatments.
opts: Apply oxygen with the patient sitting upright
Give an inhaled bronchodilator such as albuterol with ipratropium
Start IV access and give a corticosteroid
Consider magnesium or epinephrine per protocol if not improving
ok: Apply oxygen with the patient sitting upright
Give an inhaled bronchodilator such as albuterol with ipratropium
Start IV access and give a corticosteroid
Consider magnesium or epinephrine per protocol if not improving

items.q: At a multiple-casualty incident triaged with START, which patients are most important to move first? Put these categories in order of transport priority, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: In START, immediate (red) patients have life threats that can be helped by fast care, so they go first. Delayed (yellow) patients are serious but stable for now, minor (green) patients can wait, and expectant or deceased (black) patients come last.
opts: Immediate (red)
Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant or deceased (black)
ok: Immediate (red)
Delayed (yellow)
Minor (green)
Expectant or deceased (black)

items.q: You arrive first at a tanker crash with an unknown leaking liquid and two people down near the tanker. What is most important to do? Put these actions in order, from most important (first) to least important (last).
items.x: The Emergency Response Guidebook teaches RAIN: Recognize, Avoid, Isolate, Notify. Rescuers who rush in become patients themselves, so spotting the hazard and staying clear of it come before anything else; then others are kept out and the hazmat team is called to reach the patients safely.
opts: Recognize the hazard from placards and the scene
Avoid contact by staying upwind and uphill at a distance
Isolate the area and deny entry
Notify the hazmat team

Avoid contact by staying upwind and uphill at a distance
Isolate the area and deny entry
Notify the hazmat team

items.q: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
items.x: Sudden dyspnea and confusion after a long-bone fracture suggest fat or pulmonary embolism, an emergency. A saturation of 89% can be the target range for a client with COPD.

A client 1 day after abdominal surgery who rates incisional pain 6 of 10
