Clean surfaces with a product labeled to kill norovirus

items.q: Which findings in a client's room are safety hazards that the practical nurse should correct? Select all that apply.

The bed wheels are locked
A night light is on near the bathroom door

items.q: The practical nurse is cleaning hands with an alcohol-based hand rub. Place the steps in order. Put in order.

Rub the palms together

items.q: The parent of a 1-year-old asks the practical nurse which way the car seat should face. Which reinforcement is accurate?
items.x: Children ride rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the top height or weight allowed by the seat.
items.a: Keep it rear-facing until the child outgrows the seat's limits
w: Turn it forward-facing now that the child is walking on their own
Turn it forward-facing once the child can sit up without help
Use a booster seat with the adult seat belt from this age on

items.q: A 15-year-old client comes to the clinic with a parent for a sports physical. Which action by the practical nurse best supports the teen's development?
items.x: Teens are developing identity and independence. Private time lets them ask questions and share risk behaviors.
items.a: Give the teen some time to talk with staff without the parent

Talk only with the parent, since the teen is still a minor
Tell the teen that anything said will be shared with the parent

items.q: A 67-year-old client with no chronic illness asks which vaccine is recommended at this age. Which vaccine should the practical nurse reinforce?
items.x: Pneumococcal vaccine is recommended for older adults. HPV and rotavirus vaccines are for younger ages, and BCG is not routinely used in the United States.
items.a: Pneumococcal vaccine to protect against pneumonia
w: Human papillomavirus vaccine to prevent cervical cancer

BCG vaccine to prevent tuberculosis infection in adults

items.q: A client at 32 weeks of pregnancy asks how to count fetal movements. Which reinforcement is accurate?
items.x: A common guide is to feel ten movements within two hours. Fewer movements may mean the fetus is in trouble and should be reported promptly.

w: Fewer movements late in pregnancy are normal and need no call
Count movements only once a week, at the same time of day
Call only if the baby has not moved at all for a full day

items.q: A client who gave birth two days ago asks what to expect with vaginal bleeding. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
items.x: Lochia changes from rubra (red) to serosa (pinkish brown) to alba (yellowish white). Bright red bleeding that returns or large clots should be reported.
items.a: 'It will go from red to pinkish brown and then yellowish white.'
w: 'It should stay bright red with large clots for about six weeks.'
'It should stop completely before I go home from the hospital.'
'It will turn bright red again once the first week has passed.'

items.q: The practical nurse is reinforcing testicular self-examination with a 19-year-old client. Which statement shows understanding?
items.x: Monthly checks after a warm shower, when the scrotum is relaxed, help find lumps early. Testicular cancer is most common in young men.
items.a: 'I will check once a month after a warm shower or bath.'
w: 'I will check once a year at my annual physical exam.'
'I only need to start checking after I turn forty years old.'
'I will check right after exercise when I am still cold.'

items.q: A client asks how to lower the risk of skin cancer. Which instruction should the practical nurse reinforce?
items.x: Broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or more, reapplied about every two hours and after swimming, lowers risk. Tanning beds increase risk.
items.a: Use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher and reapply it often
w: Use sunscreen only on cloudy days when burns are less obvious
Use a tanning bed first to build a protective base tan
Apply sunscreen once in the morning; it lasts the whole day

items.q: The parent of a 2-year-old asks how to know when the child is ready for toilet training. Which sign of readiness should the practical nurse reinforce?

items.a: The child stays dry for about two hours at a time
w: The child can count to ten and say the alphabet
The child has started sleeping through the night
The child has turned two, so training should begin

items.q: The parent of an 11-year-old asks when the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine should be given. Which reinforcement is accurate?

items.a: At age 11 or 12, well before any exposure to the virus
w: Only after the child becomes sexually active as a teen
Only for girls, once they begin their monthly periods
At age 26, after the immune system is fully mature

items.q: A postmenopausal client asks how to keep her bones strong. Which statement shows understanding?
items.x: Weight-bearing exercise such as walking, plus enough calcium and vitamin D, helps keep bone density. Swimming is not weight-bearing.

w: 'I will swim every day, since swimming builds the most bone.'

items.q: The parent of a 2-year-old says they rent an older home with peeling paint on the windowsills. Which action should the practical nurse reinforce?

Sand off the old paint indoors with the windows shut
Give the child a daily multivitamin to block lead

items.q: Which changes are expected with normal aging? Select all that apply.

Slower reaction time
Smaller bladder capacity
Sudden confusion over one day
New loss of bladder control
Inability to learn new things

Slower reaction time
Smaller bladder capacity

items.q: The practical nurse is reinforcing umbilical cord care with new parents. Which statements show understanding? Select all that apply.

ok: 'I will keep the cord clean and dry.'

items.q: A client planning a pregnancy asks which foods are good sources of folic acid. Which foods should the practical nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.

items.q: Place Erikson's stages of psychosocial development in order from infancy to adolescence. Put in order.

items.q: A client with paranoid thinking refuses meals and says staff are poisoning the food. Which action should the practical nurse take?

w: Tell the client the food is safe and must be eaten now

Remove the tray and wait until the client asks to eat

items.q: A client in the clinic has bruises on both arms. The client's partner stays in the room and answers every question. What should the practical nurse do?

w: Ask the client in front of the partner if they are being hurt

items.q: A client with severe depression has been withdrawn for two weeks. Today the client is suddenly cheerful and calm. What should the practical nurse do?

items.a: Report the sudden change to the RN as a possible suicide risk
w: Tell the client how good it is to see the depression lifting

Encourage the client to plan a weekend pass with family

items.q: A client with borderline personality disorder says, 'You are the only nurse here who understands me. The others are terrible.' Which response is best?
items.x: This is splitting. The nurse avoids taking sides, responds consistently and lets the team know so everyone sets the same limits.
items.a: 'All the nurses here work together to help you with your care.'
w: 'Thank you. I will try to be your nurse every day from now on.'
'Tell me which nurses are terrible so I can talk to them.'
'You are right, some of the staff do not listen very well.'

items.q: A client with schizophrenia says, 'The voices are telling me to hurt the man in the next room.' What should the practical nurse do first?
items.x: Command hallucinations to harm others are an emergency. The nurse acts to keep everyone safe and reports right away.
items.a: Report it to the RN at once and keep the client and others safe
w: Tell the client the voices are not real and to ignore them

Document the statement and check on the client again in an hour

items.q: A client who had a mastectomy two days ago will not look at the incision during dressing changes. What should the practical nurse do?
items.x: Body image changes take time. The nurse accepts the client's feelings and lets her set the pace.
items.a: Acknowledge her feelings and let her look when she is ready
w: Tell her she must look today so she can care for it at home
Cover the mirror and avoid talking about the incision at all
Tell her many women feel fine about the change after surgery

items.q: An 80-year-old client who was alert before hip surgery is now confused, picking at the sheets and seeing bugs on the wall. What should the practical nurse do?

items.a: Report the sudden change, since it may be delirium
w: Document it as dementia that is part of normal aging
Tell the family this confusion is expected after surgery
Turn off all lights so the client can rest without stimulation

items.q: A client admitted for alcohol use disorder says, 'I only drink on weekends. I don't have a problem.' Which defense mechanism is the client using?

w: Projection
Sublimation
Displacement

items.q: An older client tells the practical nurse that she wants her eldest son to receive her health information and help make decisions. What should the nurse do?
items.x: Respecting cultural and personal preferences is part of client-centered care. The client's wishes are confirmed and documented with proper consent.
items.a: Confirm the client's wishes and report them to the RN to document
w: Explain that only the client may be told about her health
Give the son all information without asking the client about it again
Tell the client that she must make all decisions on her own

items.q: A veteran with post-traumatic stress disorder wakes from a nightmare shaking and confused about where he is. What should the practical nurse do?
items.x: Calm orientation to the present helps a client with PTSD feel safe. Sudden touch or pushing for details can increase distress.
items.a: Speak calmly, say who you are and help him see where he is
w: Turn on all of the room's bright lights and leave him alone
Shake his shoulder firmly and tell him to calm down now
Ask him to describe the details of the nightmare right away

items.q: The parent of a hospitalized 4-year-old is upset that the child has begun wetting the bed again. Which reinforcement is best?

Suggest the parent scold the child so the habit does not last

items.q: A client has severe anxiety and is pacing. Which actions by the practical nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.

Speak in short, simple sentences

Sitting quietly with the client for a few moments

items.q: A client is learning to use a standard walker. Which instruction should the practical nurse reinforce?

Place it directly on bare skin so the heat goes in deeper

items.q: A client with chronic kidney disease has a high potassium level and asks for a snack. Which choice should the practical nurse offer?

Orange juice
A baked potato

items.q: A client in long-term care is starting a bladder training program for urge incontinence. Which action supports the program?

items.q: A client with a hearing aid is getting ready for bed. Which action by the practical nurse is correct?

w: Leave the hearing aid in so the client can hear the call light
Rinse the hearing aid under running water before storing it
Store the hearing aid in a tissue on the client's meal tray

items.q: A client has a new plaster cast on the arm that is still damp. How should the practical nurse handle it?

Rest the cast on the hard edge of the bed side rail

Only when the client says it feels heavy

items.q: A client is prescribed an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma. Which instruction should the practical nurse reinforce?

items.q: A pulseless combat casualty with torso trauma is found during TACEVAC. What does TCCC list before considering CPR?
items.x: In traumatic arrest, TCCC lists bilateral needle decompression. CPR may be attempted only if there are no obviously fatal wounds and surgical care is close.
items.a: Bilateral needle decompression
w: An immediate shock with an AED
Hypertonic saline
Ondansetron

items.q: A diver who breathed compressed gas surfaces and becomes unconscious within minutes. What does the U.S. Navy Diving Manual say to assume?
items.x: Any diver who breathed compressed gas and surfaces unconscious or with neurological symptoms within 10 minutes is assumed to have arterial gas embolism.
items.a: Arterial gas embolism
w: Type I decompression sickness
Simple fatigue
Nitrogen narcosis

items.q: A diver has a deep, dull shoulder ache a few hours after a dive, with a normal full neurological exam. Which category fits?
items.x: Joint pain with a dull, aching quality and no neurological findings is the classic Type I picture. Without a complete neurological exam, it is treated as Type II.
items.a: Type I (pain-only) decompression sickness
w: Type II decompression sickness
Arterial gas embolism
Inner ear barotrauma

items.q: After a dive, a diver has a band of pain wrapping around the trunk. How does the Navy Diving Manual classify it?
items.x: Pain in the chest, abdomen or hips, and girdle pain wrapping around the body, suggest spinal cord involvement and are treated as Type II.
items.a: As Type II DCS, a sign of spinal cord involvement
w: As Type I pain-only DCS
As a muscle strain
As normal post-dive fatigue

items.q: Why does the Navy Diving Manual advise against giving pain medicine to make a DCS patient comfortable?
items.x: The pain marks where bubbles are and shows whether recompression is working, so masking it can hide the response.
items.a: Pain may be the only way to localize the problem and track the treatment
w: Pain medicine causes more bubbles
Divers cannot take pain medicine for 24 hours
It is not allowed in a chamber

items.q: A casualty needs prolonged sedation during a long hold. Put these steps for a ketamine-based drip in order, from first to last.
items.x: Prolonged casualty care guidance builds sedation on a ketamine drip with adjuncts only as needed, one drug per bag, and close monitoring.
opts: Set up airway equipment, pulse oximetry and end-tidal CO2

Add small pushes of an adjunct only if needed
Trend the RASS score and vital signs
ok: Set up airway equipment, pulse oximetry and end-tidal CO2
Start the ketamine drip in its own bag
Add small pushes of an adjunct only if needed
Trend the RASS score and vital signs

items.q: Why does prolonged care guidance run each sedation drug in its own bag?
items.x: Each medicine runs separately so it can be adjusted or stopped on its own and to avoid untested mixtures.
items.a: Mixing drugs in one bag is untested and can form unsafe compounds
w: It saves IV fluid
It makes the drip run faster
One bag cannot hold two drugs

items.q: During a long hold, what does hourly urine output from a Foley mainly show?
items.x: Urine output is one of the most useful trends in prolonged care, because it reflects blood flow to the kidneys.
items.a: Whether the kidneys are being perfused, a sign of adequate resuscitation
w: How much pain the casualty has
Whether antibiotics are working
The depth of sedation

items.q: Why might famotidine be given during prolonged casualty care?
items.x: Critically ill casualties are at risk of stomach bleeding from stress ulcers. Acid reducers like famotidine help prevent them.
items.a: To help prevent stress ulcers in a critically ill casualty
w: To treat nausea from ketamine
To raise blood pressure
To prevent seizures

items.q: After several units of stored blood, which i-STAT change is expected?
items.x: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, so ionized calcium falls. Potassium often rises.
items.a: Low ionized calcium
w: Low potassium
High hemoglobin
Low sodium

items.q: A casualty with a high above-knee amputation is in hemorrhagic shock 40 minutes after injury. The tourniquet is controlling the bleeding. Which medication is the priority now?
items.x: TCCC gives TXA as early as possible, within 3 hours of injury, to casualties expected to need significant transfusion. Ketorolac impairs platelets, enoxaparin is an anticoagulant, and hetastarch worsens coagulopathy.
items.a: Tranexamic acid as soon as possible
w: Ketorolac for pain and inflammation
Enoxaparin to prevent clots in the limb
Hetastarch to restore blood pressure

items.q: You reach a casualty with ongoing hemorrhagic shock 4 hours after his injury. No TXA has been given. What is the correct approach to TXA?
items.x: In CRASH-2, TXA started more than 3 hours after injury was linked to higher death from bleeding, so TCCC limits it to the first 3 hours. Late dosing is not a catch-up step.
items.a: Withhold it, as the 3-hour window has passed
w: Give it now, then repeat it after an hour
Give it now, since late doses still reduce bleeding
Give it only after the second unit of blood

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of tranexamic acid?
items.x: TXA is a lysine analog that blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, inhibiting fibrinolysis. It adds no factors or platelets and does not affect citrate.
items.a: It blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, slowing clot breakdown
w: It activates platelets directly at the site of vessel injury
It replaces fibrinogen consumed during massive bleeding
It reverses the anticoagulant effect of citrate in stored blood

items.q: A medic pushes tranexamic acid rapidly through an IO line. Which adverse effect is the FDA label warning most associated with rapid IV injection?
items.x: The TXA label notes hypotension with rapid intravenous injection, which is why TCCC directs a slow IV or IO push. Seizures and thrombosis are other labeled risks.
items.a: Hypotension
w: Hyperkalemia
Bronchospasm
Bradycardia with heart block

items.q: A casualty with a blunt head injury from a blast has a GCS of 10, no major external bleeding, and was injured 1 hour ago. Per current TCCC, which statement about TXA is correct?
items.x: TCCC includes signs of significant TBI or altered mental status after blast or blunt trauma as an indication for TXA within 3 hours, supported by CRASH-3. Imaging is not required first.
items.a: Significant TBI is an indication for TXA within 3 hours
w: TXA is reserved for casualties with a tourniquet in place
TXA is contraindicated in any casualty with a head injury
TXA is given only after a CT scan excludes brain bleeding

items.q: A casualty is about to receive his first unit of cold-stored low-titer O whole blood. Per TCCC, when is calcium given?
items.x: TCCC gives calcium during or right after the first blood product because citrate binds calcium and many casualties are hypocalcemic on arrival. Waiting for labs or symptoms delays care.
items.a: During or immediately after the first unit
w: Only after the fourth unit has been given
Only if ionized calcium is measured as low
Only when the casualty develops tetany

items.q: Why do transfused blood products lower the recipient's ionized calcium?
items.x: Citrate prevents clotting in the bag by chelating calcium, and it does the same in the casualty until the liver metabolizes it. Shock, hypothermia, and liver injury slow that clearance.
items.a: Citrate anticoagulant in the bag binds calcium
w: Stored red cells absorb calcium from the plasma
Cold blood drives calcium into skeletal muscle
Plasma proteins in the unit excrete calcium

items.q: Compared with calcium gluconate, what is the key practical difference of calcium chloride?
items.x: Calcium chloride delivers roughly three times as much elemental calcium per volume but is caustic, so a large vein, central line, or IO is preferred. Extravasation of either can injure tissue.
items.a: About three times the elemental calcium and more vein irritation
w: Less elemental calcium per volume and safer in small fragile veins
No risk of tissue injury if it leaks out of the vein
It requires refrigeration and cannot be carried in the aid bag

items.q: After several units of blood, a casualty becomes more hypotensive despite ongoing transfusion, and the monitor shows a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Citrate-induced low ionized calcium reduces cardiac contractility and vascular tone and prolongs the QT interval. It is treated with calcium.
items.a: Ionized hypocalcemia from citrate
w: Hypermagnesemia from stored plasma
Hyperglycemia from additive solution
Hypernatremia from anticoagulant

items.q: Which group of findings makes up the lethal diamond of trauma?
items.x: The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy was expanded to a diamond by adding hypocalcemia, which worsens clotting and cardiac function. Each component feeds the others.
items.a: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypocalcemia
w: Hypothermia, hypoxia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia
Acidosis, hypernatremia, coagulopathy, and fever
Hypotension, bradycardia, hypoxia, and hypocalcemia

items.q: Per current TCCC, what is the preferred fluid for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: TCCC lists cold-stored low-titer O whole blood first because it replaces red cells, plasma, and platelets together. Crystalloid and colloid dilute clotting factors, and red cells alone lack them.
items.a: Cold-stored low-titer O whole blood
w: Lactated Ringer's in warmed boluses
Hetastarch as a volume expander
Packed red cells given alone

items.q: Cold-stored whole blood is not available. Per the TCCC resuscitation order, what comes next?
items.x: After cold-stored low-titer O whole blood, TCCC lists prescreened low-titer O fresh whole blood, then plasma, red cells, and platelets 1:1:1, then plasma and red cells 1:1, then plasma or red cells alone.
items.a: Prescreened low-titer O fresh whole blood
w: Plasma and red cells given in a 1:1 ratio
Red blood cells given alone
Plasma-Lyte A until evacuation

items.q: No whole blood of any kind is available, but components are. Which combination best follows the TCCC order?
items.x: Balanced component therapy approximates whole blood. Plasma and red cells 1:1 is the next step down, and single components are the last blood option.
items.a: Plasma, red cells, and platelets 1:1:1
w: Red cells alone until whole blood arrives
Plasma alone followed by crystalloid
Red cells with lactated Ringer's 1:2

items.q: A casualty in hemorrhagic shock without a head injury is receiving whole blood. Which finding is a TCCC endpoint for slowing resuscitation?
items.x: TCCC resuscitates until a palpable radial pulse, improved mental status, or a systolic pressure of 100 mmHg. Pushing pressure higher risks disrupting clot and wasting scarce blood.
items.a: A palpable radial pulse with improved mentation
w: Heart rate below 60 beats per minute on the monitor
Systolic pressure above 140 mmHg
Return of normal urine color

items.q: A casualty with suspected moderate TBI is in hemorrhagic shock. Which blood pressure target does TCCC set when monitoring is available?
items.x: Hypotension worsens secondary brain injury, so TCCC sets a systolic target of 100 to 110 mmHg in TBI rather than the permissive targets used for torso hemorrhage.
items.a: Systolic pressure of 100 to 110 mmHg
w: Systolic pressure of 70 to 80 mmHg
Mean arterial pressure of 50 mmHg
Systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher

items.q: Why is permissive hypotension used for a casualty with uncontrolled torso hemorrhage and no head injury?
items.x: Raising pressure before surgical control can blow off fragile clot and, if achieved with crystalloid, dilutes clotting factors. TBI is the main exception because the brain needs perfusion pressure.
items.a: Higher pressures can dislodge clot and dilute factors
w: Low pressure lowers the need for calcium replacement
Low pressure prevents transfusion reactions
Higher pressures cause hypothermia directly

items.q: Why is large-volume crystalloid avoided in hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: Crystalloid carries no oxygen or clotting factors, dilutes what remains, adds cold fluid, and can cause edema and hyperchloremic acidosis. Blood products are the resuscitation fluid for bleeding.
items.a: It dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis and cooling
w: It contains citrate that binds the casualty's calcium
It carries a high risk of acute hemolytic reaction
It raises hemoglobin too quickly and makes the blood too thick

items.q: Which adverse effect carries an FDA boxed warning for hetastarch in critically ill patients?
items.x: Hydroxyethyl starch products carry a boxed warning for mortality, kidney injury, and coagulopathy in critically ill adults, including sepsis. They also interfere with platelet function and factor VIII.
items.a: Kidney injury, along with bleeding risk
w: Hyperkalemia, along with peaked T waves
Severe hypoglycemia in septic patients
Profound bradycardia in head injury

items.q: Which crystalloid is compatible with blood products in the same IV line according to standard transfusion practice and its labeling?
items.x: LR contains calcium that can overcome citrate and clot the line, dextrose solutions can cause red cell clumping or hemolysis, and sterile water lyses red cells. Normal saline is the standard compatible fluid.
items.a: 0.9% sodium chloride
w: Lactated Ringer's
5% dextrose in water
Sterile water for injection

items.q: Why can low-titer group O whole blood be given before the recipient's blood type is known?
items.x: Group O red cells cannot be attacked by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B. The plasma does contain anti-A and anti-B, so donors are screened for low titers to limit hemolysis of a non-O recipient's cells.
items.a: O cells lack A and B antigens and low titers limit plasma risk
w: Group O plasma contains no antibodies at all against A or B cells
Low-titer units have had all white cells and plasma removed
Group O blood binds antibodies already in the recipient

items.q: Which ABO group is the universal donor for plasma?
items.x: AB plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so it can be given to any ABO group. Group O is the universal red cell donor, the reverse of plasma.
items.a: Group AB
w: Group O
Group A
Group B

items.q: A female casualty of childbearing potential needs emergency whole blood. Only Rh-positive low-titer O is on hand. What is the best course?
items.x: Rh-negative product is preferred for females of childbearing potential, but the JTS whole blood CPG accepts Rh-positive product when it is all that exists and the bleeding is life-threatening. Delaying blood carries the greater risk.
items.a: Transfuse it; Rh-negative is preferred but not worth a delay
w: Give crystalloid alone until Rh-negative blood arrives
Give only plasma, which carries no risk of sensitization
Transfuse only after typing her own Rh status in the field

items.q: What is the chief clinical advantage of fresh whole blood over cold-stored components?
items.x: Fresh whole blood gives warm red cells, plasma, and functional platelets together with less anticoagulant and additive dilution. It still carries infectious and immune risks, which is why donors are prescreened.
items.a: Functional platelets and factors in one warm unit
w: No need to screen the donor for infectious disease
No risk of any immune-mediated transfusion reaction
Longer shelf life than any refrigerated product

items.q: Which complication is a particular concern with fresh whole blood because it contains viable donor lymphocytes?
items.x: Fresh, non-irradiated whole blood contains living donor T cells that can attack recipient tissue, especially from a closely related or HLA-similar donor. Irradiation prevents it but is not available in the field.
items.a: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease
w: Transfusion-related circulatory overload
Febrile reaction from bacterial endotoxin
Delayed hyperkalemia from red cell leakage

items.q: What is the purpose of drawing retained samples from a walking blood bank donor at the time of an emergency donation?
items.x: Rapid field tests at donation do not cover every agent or window period, so samples are sent for retrospective testing and recipients can be followed if a result returns positive.
items.a: Later confirmatory infectious disease testing
w: Measuring the donor's hemoglobin after donation
Cross-matching against every future recipient
Proving the donor consented to the donation

items.q: During a walking blood bank activation, which volunteer is the best reason to defer as a donor?
items.x: Acute illness risks bacteremia in the unit and harms the donor. A documented low titer and group O status are what make a donor useful, and a recent meal is not a deferral.
items.a: A soldier with fever and diarrhea today
w: A soldier with a documented low anti-A titer
A soldier who ate a meal an hour ago
A soldier who is type O-positive

items.q: Before fresh whole blood from a non-O, type-specific donor is transfused, what is essential?
items.x: Type-specific transfusion depends on a correct match, so both ABO types are confirmed, typically with prior records plus a field typing card. Mistyping is the main cause of acute hemolytic reactions.
items.a: Confirming the ABO type of both donor and recipient
w: Checking the donor's blood pressure only
Confirming the recipient's Rh status by verbal history alone
Warming the unit above 42 C (107.6 F) to kill pathogens

items.q: Which casualty is most likely to need massive transfusion?
items.x: Penetrating mechanism, tachycardia, and hypotension are core predictors of massive transfusion in scores such as ABC. Controlled extremity or scalp wounds with good perfusion rarely need it.
items.a: Penetrating torso wound, HR 130, SBP 84
w: Isolated forearm laceration with bleeding controlled
Ankle fracture with a strong radial pulse
Scalp laceration with a dressing in place, HR 96

items.q: A casualty has a heart rate of 132 and a systolic blood pressure of 88 mmHg. What is the shock index and its meaning?
items.x: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure; 132 divided by 88 is 1.5. Values above about 1.0 predict transfusion need and significant hemorrhage.
items.a: About 1.5, suggesting significant blood loss
w: About 0.7, which is within normal adult limits
About 1.0, consistent only with anxiety
About 0.4, suggesting fluid overload

items.q: After transfusion of several older stored red cell units, a casualty develops peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the first drug to give?
items.x: Potassium leaks from red cells during storage and can cause hyperkalemia with large transfusions. Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes; insulin, albuterol, and bicarbonate shift potassium but act more slowly.
items.a: Calcium chloride or calcium gluconate
w: Regular insulin with dextrose
Sodium bicarbonate
Albuterol by nebulizer

items.q: Regular insulin with dextrose is given to shift potassium into cells. Which adverse effect needs the closest monitoring afterward?
items.x: Insulin lowers glucose as it drives potassium into cells, and hypoglycemia can appear an hour or more later even with dextrose given. Glucose is rechecked on a schedule.
items.a: Hypoglycemia
w: Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia
Hypermagnesemia

items.q: Why are blood products warmed during resuscitation in the field?
items.x: Refrigerated blood rapidly cools a casualty, and hypothermia slows clotting enzymes and platelet function. Inline warmers and the hypothermia prevention kit are part of resuscitation.
items.a: Cold blood worsens hypothermia, which impairs clotting
w: Warming activates the platelets inside the bag
Warm blood carries no citrate into the casualty
Warming prevents febrile transfusion reactions

items.q: Minutes after starting type-specific fresh whole blood, a casualty develops fever, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine. What is the first action?
items.x: These signs indicate acute hemolysis from ABO mismatch. Stop the unit, keep IV access, support perfusion and urine output, and recheck donor and recipient identification.
items.a: Stop the transfusion and support blood pressure
w: Slow the transfusion rate and give acetaminophen
Give diphenhydramine and continue the unit
Finish the unit and then reassess the casualty

items.q: During a transfusion, a casualty's temperature rises by 1 C (33.8 F) with chills. Blood pressure, breathing, and urine color are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction from cytokines or anti-leukocyte antibodies causes fever and chills without hemodynamic or respiratory change. Stop the unit, exclude hemolysis and sepsis, and treat with acetaminophen.
items.a: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction
w: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload

items.q: A casualty develops a few hives during a plasma transfusion. Vital signs and breathing are normal. What is the best management?
items.x: Isolated urticaria is a mild allergic reaction to plasma proteins. Pausing and giving an antihistamine is standard, and the unit may be resumed if hives resolve with no other signs.
items.a: Pause the unit and give diphenhydramine
w: Give epinephrine and stop all blood products
Give methylprednisolone and speed the rate
Continue the unit without any treatment

items.q: Within minutes of starting plasma, a casualty develops stridor, diffuse hives, and a systolic pressure of 70 mmHg. What is the most important drug?
items.x: This is anaphylaxis, so stop the unit and give epinephrine. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts that do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
items.a: Intramuscular epinephrine
w: Oral diphenhydramine
Intravenous famotidine
Intravenous methylprednisolone

items.q: Severe anaphylaxis to plasma-containing products is classically linked to which recipient condition?
items.x: Patients lacking IgA can form anti-IgA antibodies and react severely to the IgA in donor plasma. Future transfusions use IgA-deficient or washed products.
items.a: IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
w: Group O blood type with high titers
Rh-negative status in a male recipient
Recent treatment with tranexamic acid

items.q: Two hours after a transfusion, a casualty becomes hypoxic with bilateral crackles, fever, and hypotension. Neck veins are flat. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: TRALI causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours, often with fever and hypotension and no sign of volume overload. TACO features hypertension, distended neck veins, and response to diuresis.
items.a: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
w: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction
Simple allergic transfusion reaction

items.q: A 62-year-old contractor with heart failure develops dyspnea, crackles, distended neck veins, and a blood pressure of 178/100 during a slow red cell transfusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Hypertension and distended neck veins point to volume overload, common in older or cardiac patients. Treatment is stopping or slowing the transfusion, sitting upright, oxygen, and a diuretic.
items.a: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
w: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
Septic transfusion reaction

items.q: What is the main mechanism of TRALI?
items.x: Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies, often from plasma of previously pregnant donors, trigger neutrophils to injure pulmonary capillaries. Management is supportive oxygen and ventilation.
items.a: Donor antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the lung
w: Recipient antibodies destroy the transfused red cells
Bacteria in the unit release endotoxin into the blood
Excess volume raises pressure in the pulmonary veins

items.q: Which blood product carries the highest risk of bacterial contamination and septic transfusion reaction?
items.x: Platelets are stored at room temperature, which allows bacteria to grow. Refrigerated red cells and frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate carry much lower risk.
items.a: Platelets
w: Red blood cells
Cryoprecipitate
Frozen plasma

items.q: What is the main logistical advantage of dried plasma in the prehospital setting?
items.x: Dried plasma avoids freezers and thawing, weighs little, and is reconstituted with sterile water in minutes. It contains no red cells and is still a donor-derived product.
items.a: Room-temperature storage with fast reconstitution
w: No need for any IV or IO access to give it
It contains red cells as well as plasma proteins
It can be given without regard to infection risk

items.q: A PCC casualty has ongoing oozing despite balanced transfusion, and testing shows low fibrinogen. Which product best corrects this?
items.x: Cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and factor XIII. Fibrinogen concentrate is an alternative where carried.
items.a: Cryoprecipitate
w: Platelets
Red blood cells
Lactated Ringer's

items.q: Which blood product is stored at room temperature with constant gentle agitation?
items.x: Platelets are kept at 20 to 24 C (68-75.2 F) with agitation to preserve function. Whole blood and red cells are refrigerated at 1 to 6 C (33.8-42.8 F), and plasma and cryoprecipitate are frozen.
items.a: Platelets
w: Cold-stored whole blood
Red blood cells
Cryoprecipitate

items.q: A casualty with a gunshot wound to the thigh is in shock and has severe pain. Per TCCC, which analgesic is preferred?
items.x: TCCC uses ketamine for moderate to severe pain when the casualty is in shock or respiratory distress, or at significant risk of either, because it preserves blood pressure and airway reflexes. Opioids can worsen both.
items.a: Ketamine
w: Morphine
Ketorolac
Fentanyl lozenge

items.q: A casualty has a minor fragment wound, mild pain, and is still able to fight. Which TCCC option fits best?
items.x: Mild to moderate pain in a casualty who can still fight is treated with the oral non-opioid combination in the combat wound medication pack. Opioids and ketamine impair function on the battlefield.
items.a: Oral acetaminophen and meloxicam
w: Intravenous ketamine infusion
Intramuscular morphine injection
Intranasal fentanyl spray

items.q: Why is meloxicam the NSAID chosen for casualties instead of ketorolac or aspirin?
items.x: Meloxicam is COX-2 preferential and has little antiplatelet effect at usual doses. Aspirin and ketorolac impair platelets and are avoided in casualties who may bleed.
items.a: It has little effect on platelet function at usual doses
w: It is the only NSAID that is completely free of kidney effects
It works through opioid receptors rather than COX
It reverses the effects of citrate in stored blood

items.q: During ketamine analgesia, a casualty becomes agitated and frightened by vivid hallucinations. Which drug best treats this?
items.x: Emergence reactions are treated with a benzodiazepine such as midazolam. Naloxone and flumazenil reverse opioids and benzodiazepines, and ondansetron treats nausea.
items.a: Midazolam
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Ondansetron

items.q: A casualty receiving ketamine develops heavy salivation that is pooling in the mouth. Which drug reduces this secretion?
items.x: Ketamine increases salivary and bronchial secretions. Glycopyrrolate, an anticholinergic, dries secretions without crossing into the brain; atropine is an alternative.
items.a: Glycopyrrolate
w: Ondansetron
Naloxone
Dexmedetomidine

items.q: Which statement about ketamine in a casualty with TBI reflects current TCCC guidance?
items.x: Older concerns that ketamine raises intracranial pressure are not supported by current evidence. Its support of blood pressure helps prevent secondary brain injury, and TCCC does not exclude TBI.
items.a: It is acceptable and helps preserve blood pressure
w: It is contraindicated because it raises brain pressure
It is given only with a paralytic already on board
It is reserved for TBI casualties with a GCS of 15

items.q: Thirty minutes after transmucosal fentanyl, a casualty has a respiratory rate of 6 and pinpoint pupils. After ventilating with a BVM, what is the next step?
items.x: Naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression and is titrated to adequate breathing rather than full wakefulness. Remove the lozenge if it is still in the mouth.
items.a: Give naloxone titrated to breathing
w: Give flumazenil to reverse sedation
Give ketamine to stimulate breathing
Give midazolam to prevent seizures

items.q: A casualty wakes after naloxone for an opioid overdose. Why is continued monitoring the priority?
items.x: Naloxone's effect is often shorter than that of many opioids, so respiratory depression can return. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
items.a: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does
w: Naloxone causes delayed hypoglycemia
Naloxone slowly converts into an opioid
Naloxone raises the risk of hemolysis

items.q: After a rapid large IV push of fentanyl, a casualty cannot be ventilated because the chest feels rigid. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Rapid high-dose fentanyl can cause chest wall muscle rigidity. It is treated with naloxone or a neuromuscular blocker with ventilation, and slow administration helps prevent it.
items.a: Chest wall rigidity from fentanyl
w: Tension pneumothorax from bagging
Bronchospasm from histamine release
Laryngospasm from ketamine use

items.q: What is the mechanism of suzetrigine, an FDA-approved non-opioid for moderate to severe acute pain?
items.x: Suzetrigine blocks the NaV1.8 channel in peripheral pain-sensing neurons, reducing pain signals without opioid effects. Strong CYP3A inhibitors are contraindicated with it.
items.a: Selective blockade of NaV1.8 sodium channels
w: Partial agonism at the mu-opioid receptor
NMDA receptor antagonism in the spinal cord
Selective COX-2 enzyme inhibition

items.q: What is esketamine nasal spray FDA-approved for?
items.x: Esketamine nasal spray is approved for treatment-resistant depression and depressive symptoms with suicidal thoughts, given under supervision in a REMS program. It is not a field analgesic.
items.a: Treatment-resistant depression under a REMS program
w: First-line analgesia for battlefield trauma and burn pain
Induction of anesthesia before intubation
Treatment of opioid overdose in the field

items.q: A casualty receiving ondansetron for nausea is also given haloperidol for agitation. Which combined risk is the main concern?
items.x: Both ondansetron and haloperidol prolong the QT interval, and together they raise the risk of torsades de pointes. ECG monitoring and correcting low potassium and magnesium reduce the risk.
items.a: QT prolongation and torsades
w: Severe hypertension
Serotonin-related hypoglycemia
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: Hours after haloperidol, a casualty has a sustained upward eye deviation and neck twisting. Which drug treats this?
items.x: This is an acute dystonic reaction from dopamine blockade. An anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine relieves it quickly.
items.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Ondansetron
Flumazenil
Naloxone

items.q: Why is flumazenil avoided in a casualty with an unknown overdose?
items.x: Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users or after co-ingestion of seizure-causing drugs such as tricyclics. Supportive airway care is usually safer.
items.a: It can trigger seizures that resist benzodiazepines
w: It causes severe respiratory depression in most adults
It produces dangerous hyperkalemia
It prolongs opioid effects for hours

items.q: Which of these drugs requires refrigeration for routine storage per its label?
items.x: Lorazepam injection is labeled for refrigerated storage and degrades in heat, a problem in field kits. Midazolam, diazepam, and ketamine are stored at room temperature.
items.a: Lorazepam
w: Midazolam
