Normal saline

items.q: If whole blood is unavailable, what does TCCC list next for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: Component therapy in a balanced 1:1:1 ratio approximates whole blood; plasma or red cells alone come next, and crystalloid is a last resort.
items.a: Plasma, red cells and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio
w: Hetastarch followed by red cells
Lactated Ringer's solution until the radial pulse returns
Red cells alone without plasma

items.q: What is the end point for blood product resuscitation in a casualty with hemorrhagic shock and no head injury?
items.x: TCCC uses permissive hypotension until surgical control: restore mentation and a radial pulse without driving pressure high enough to dislodge clots.
items.a: Improved mental status and a palpable radial pulse
w: A systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg
A heart rate below 60 beats per minute
Clear urine output of at least 200 mL per hour

items.q: Why does TCCC recommend giving calcium with the first blood product in hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: Hypocalcemia is common on arrival in severe trauma and worsens with citrated products; calcium supports clotting and myocardial function.
items.a: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and low calcium impairs clotting and contraction
w: Calcium prevents febrile and allergic transfusion reactions to low-titer O whole blood
Calcium raises the core temperature of a hypothermic casualty
Calcium neutralizes the potassium released from burned tissue

items.q: Why is permissive hypotension avoided in a casualty who has a traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: A single episode of hypotension is linked to markedly worse outcomes in TBI, so resuscitation targets a normal radial pulse and an adequate systolic pressure instead of permissive hypotension.
items.a: Low blood pressure reduces cerebral perfusion and worsens secondary brain injury
w: Low blood pressure raises intracranial pressure directly by compressing the brainstem
Blood products cannot be used in casualties with TBI
Permissive hypotension causes hyperkalemia in brain injury

items.q: Which factors form the lethal triad of trauma?
items.x: Cold, acid and clotting failure each worsen the others; prevention of heat loss and early blood products interrupt the cycle.
items.a: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy
w: Hypoxia, hypertension and bradycardia
Hyperthermia, alkalosis and anemia
Hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia and tachycardia

items.q: A casualty has a heart rate of 130 and a systolic blood pressure of 100. What is the shock index, and what does it suggest?
items.x: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure; values above about 1.0 suggest substantial blood loss even when the blood pressure still appears acceptable.
items.a: 1.3, suggesting significant hemorrhage
w: 0.8, which is within the normal range for a fit adult
2.3, suggesting cardiogenic shock
0.3, suggesting overhydration

items.q: In which casualty does TCCC recommend tranexamic acid?
items.x: TXA reduces bleeding death when given early; benefit is greatest in the first hour, and use after 3 hours was associated with harm in CRASH-2.
items.a: Hemorrhagic shock or signs of significant TBI, within 3 hours of injury
w: Any casualty with a minor laceration to reduce dressing changes
A casualty with significant bleeding more than 6 hours after injury
Only casualties who have already received a massive transfusion of blood products

items.q: Before transfusing fresh whole blood from a walking blood bank, which donor issue is a key safety concern?
items.x: Fresh whole blood is collected under field conditions, so correct ABO matching and prescreened, tested donors are central to avoiding hemolytic reactions and infections.
items.a: ABO compatibility and screening for transfusion-transmitted infection
w: The donor's caffeine and energy drink intake during the past day
The donor's rank and duty position
Whether the donor has eaten in the past 2 hours

items.q: Why is crystalloid avoided as the primary fluid for hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: Large crystalloid volumes cause dilutional coagulopathy, edema and acidosis; blood products restore oxygen delivery and clotting.
items.a: It dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis and hypothermia
w: It contains too much potassium for most casualties with kidney injury
It is too viscous to run through an IO needle
It cannot be warmed before infusion

items.q: During a whole blood transfusion, a casualty develops sudden fever, hypotension and dark urine. What is the best next step?
items.x: Fever, hypotension and hemoglobinuria during transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the product and supporting circulation are the first actions.
items.a: Stop the transfusion and treat a suspected hemolytic reaction
w: Speed up the transfusion to correct the hypotension and recheck in 15 minutes
Add calcium and continue the same bag of blood
Give antibiotics and continue the transfusion

items.q: Which device is used to warm blood products in the field to help prevent hypothermia?
items.x: Inline warmers deliver blood at body temperature; cold products are a major source of heat loss in casualties already at risk of the lethal triad.
items.a: A portable inline fluid warmer
w: A chemical heat pack placed directly on the IV bag
A heated blanket wrapped around the IO site
A vacuum mattress

items.q: A casualty with a head injury has a GCS that drops from 13 to 9, a dilated right pupil and left-sided weakness. What does this suggest?
items.x: A falling GCS with a unilateral dilated pupil and opposite-side weakness are signs of brain herniation requiring urgent measures to lower intracranial pressure and rapid evacuation.
items.a: Impending transtentorial herniation
w: A simple concussion that will resolve
A spinal cord injury in the neck
Alcohol intoxication

items.q: A casualty shows signs of herniation after head trauma. Which temporary measures are used in the field?
items.x: Hypertonic saline and head elevation lower ICP; mild hyperventilation is used only briefly for herniation because deep hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia.
items.a: Hypertonic saline, head up 30 degrees, brief hyperventilation to EtCO2 30 to 35 mmHg
w: Lay flat, restrict fluids and hold ventilations
Hyperventilate to an EtCO2 below 20 mmHg for the whole evacuation and lay flat
Place in Trendelenburg position and give hypotonic fluids

items.q: For a casualty with TBI and no signs of herniation, what EtCO2 target is maintained during ventilation?
items.x: Normocapnia preserves cerebral blood flow; hyperventilation is reserved for active herniation, and hypoventilation raises ICP through vasodilation.
items.a: 35 to 40 mmHg
w: 20 to 25 mmHg
45 to 55 mmHg
10 to 15 mmHg

items.q: Which oxygen saturation target is maintained in a casualty with a traumatic brain injury?
items.x: Hypoxia below 90 percent is strongly linked to worse outcome after TBI, so oxygen and airway support aim to keep saturation at or above 90 percent.
items.a: At least 90 percent
w: At least 75 percent
Between 80 and 85 percent
Any value as long as he is breathing

items.q: A casualty with a closed head injury has a blood pressure of 190/100, a heart rate of 48 and irregular respirations. What is this pattern called?
items.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing form the Cushing triad, a late sign of rising intracranial pressure; Beck triad describes cardiac tamponade.
items.a: Cushing triad
w: Beck triad
Neurogenic shock
Virchow triad

items.q: A casualty was shot in the neck and is awake, breathing well and moving all limbs. What is the TCCC approach to spinal immobilization?
items.x: Spinal injury after penetrating trauma is rarely unstable, and immobilization can hide neck wounds and delay airway care; it is reserved for blunt mechanisms with suspected spinal injury.
items.a: Spinal immobilization is not used for isolated penetrating injury
w: Full spinal immobilization on a long board before moving
A cervical collar and head blocks for all neck wounds
Keep the casualty sitting upright without moving his neck for transport

items.q: A casualty fell from a vehicle rollover and has neck pain and numbness in his hands. What is the appropriate approach?
items.x: Blunt mechanisms with neck pain or neurologic signs call for spinal motion restriction; penetrating injury alone is where TCCC drops routine immobilization.
items.a: Spinal motion restriction during movement and evacuation
w: No spinal precautions because the injury is blunt
Have him walk to the evacuation point to assess function
Apply traction to the neck to relieve pressure

items.q: A casualty with a suspected cervical spinal cord injury has a blood pressure of 78/40, a heart rate of 54 and warm, dry skin below the injury. What is the likely cause?
items.x: High cord injury removes sympathetic outflow, causing hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin; hemorrhage usually causes tachycardia and cool skin, and hemorrhage is excluded before attributing shock to the cord.
items.a: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone
w: Hemorrhagic shock from internal bleeding
Septic shock from wound infection
Cardiogenic shock from a cardiac contusion

items.q: Using the rule of nines, what is the TBSA of partial- and full-thickness burns covering the entire front of the torso and the whole of one arm?
items.x: In the adult rule of nines the anterior trunk is 18 percent and each arm is 9 percent, for a total of 27 percent.
items.a: 27 percent
w: 18 percent
36 percent
45 percent

items.q: When estimating burn size, which burn depth is excluded from the TBSA calculation?
items.x: Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted; superficial burns resembling sunburn do not cause the fluid shifts that drive resuscitation.
items.a: Superficial (first-degree) burns
w: Superficial partial-thickness burns with blisters
Deep partial-thickness burns
Full-thickness burns

items.q: For small or scattered burns, what is the approximate TBSA of the casualty's own palm including the fingers?
items.x: The palm including the fingers approximates 1 percent of body surface area, which helps estimate irregular burns that do not fit the rule of nines.
items.a: 1 percent
w: 5 percent
9 percent
0.1 percent

items.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what is the initial fluid rate for a 70 kg casualty with 40 percent TBSA burns?
items.x: The Rule of Ten multiplies TBSA by 10 to give mL per hour for adults 40 to 80 kg: 40 x 10 = 400 mL per hour, adjusted later to urine output.
items.a: 400 mL per hour
w: 40 mL per hour
700 mL per hour
2800 mL per hour

items.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what is the initial fluid rate for a 100 kg casualty with 30 percent TBSA burns?
items.x: The rate is TBSA x 10 (300 mL per hour) plus 100 mL per hour for every 10 kg above 80 kg (200 mL per hour), giving 500 mL per hour.
items.a: 500 mL per hour
w: 300 mL per hour
1000 mL per hour
3000 mL per hour

items.q: In TCCC, above what burn size is fluid resuscitation started in the field?
items.x: TCCC starts burn fluid resuscitation when partial- and full-thickness burns exceed 20 percent TBSA; hemorrhagic shock in a burned casualty is treated with blood first.
items.a: Greater than 20 percent TBSA
w: Greater than 5 percent TBSA
Greater than 50 percent TBSA
Any burn regardless of size

items.q: Which urine output target is used to adjust fluid resuscitation in an adult burn casualty?
items.x: Adult burn fluids are titrated to 30 to 50 mL per hour of urine; less suggests under-resuscitation and much more suggests fluid creep, which causes edema and compartment syndromes.
items.a: 30 to 50 mL per hour
w: 5 to 10 mL per hour
150 to 200 mL per hour
Urine output is not used to guide burn fluids

items.q: A casualty pulled from a burning vehicle has singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth and a hoarse voice. What is the main concern?
items.x: Facial burns with soot, hoarseness or stridor signal inhalation injury; swelling can close the airway over hours, so early definitive airway control is considered before evacuation.
items.a: Inhalation injury with risk of rapid airway swelling
w: A simple superficial facial burn
Anxiety-related hyperventilation
Isolated carbon monoxide exposure with no airway risk

items.q: A casualty from an enclosed-space fire has a headache and confusion, and the pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Why is the reading misleading?
items.x: Carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin reads as saturated on standard oximeters, so a normal SpO2 does not exclude CO poisoning; high-flow oxygen is given.
items.a: Standard oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin
w: Pulse oximeters read falsely low in all burn casualties because of skin damage
Fire smoke speeds the pulse oximeter's light signal
Confusion alters the sensor's detection of saturation

items.q: A casualty has circumferential full-thickness burns of the chest, and ventilation is becoming difficult with rising airway pressures. What procedure addresses this?
items.x: Rigid circumferential eschar restricts chest expansion; escharotomy through the burned tissue releases it. Extra fluids worsen edema and do not relieve the constriction.
items.a: Escharotomy of the chest wall
w: Needle decompression on both sides
Tighter chest bandaging
Increase the fluid rate

items.q: Which finding in a limb with a circumferential full-thickness burn suggests the need for escharotomy?
items.x: As edema builds under inelastic eschar, distal perfusion fails; loss of pulses or delayed capillary refill indicates escharotomy is needed to restore circulation.
items.a: Progressive loss of distal pulses and capillary refill
w: Blisters forming on the unburned skin surrounding the circumferential burn
Pain at the edges of the burn
Mild redness above the burn

items.q: A casualty with 45 percent TBSA burns from 4 days ago needs rapid sequence intubation. Which paralytic is avoided?
items.x: Upregulated acetylcholine receptors after burns cause a dangerous potassium surge with succinylcholine beginning roughly 24 to 48 hours after injury; rocuronium is the usual alternative.
items.a: Succinylcholine
w: Rocuronium
Both paralytics are equally safe
Neither paralytic can be used after burns

items.q: Which other conditions share the same succinylcholine risk as major burns?
items.x: Denervation, massive muscle injury and prolonged immobility upregulate receptors and can cause life-threatening hyperkalemia with succinylcholine.
items.a: Crush injury and prolonged immobilization
w: Simple fractures treated within 1 hour
Isolated eye injuries
Mild dehydration

items.q: What is the correct way to cool a fresh burn in the field?
items.x: Burned casualties lose heat rapidly through damaged skin; ice, prolonged wet dressings and open exposure drive hypothermia, which worsens coagulopathy and mortality, while ointments and butter trap heat and contaminate the wound.
items.a: Stop the burning, cover with dry sterile dressings and prevent hypothermia
w: Apply butter or a thick ointment and leave the burn open to the air
Apply butter or ointment and leave open to air
Keep the burn wet with soaked dressings during evacuation

items.q: A casualty has an open tibia fracture with bone visible. What is part of field management?
items.x: Open fractures are dressed, splinted in position and treated early with antibiotics; reducing contaminated bone back into the wound and tourniquets for non-severe bleeding add harm.
items.a: Cover with a dressing, splint, and give TCCC open-wound antibiotics
w: Push the bone back under the skin before splinting
Push the exposed bone back under the skin before applying the splint
Apply a tourniquet routinely for all open fractures

items.q: What is checked before and after applying a splint to an injured limb?
items.x: Splints can compress vessels and nerves, so distal circulation, movement and sensation are checked before and after, and the splint is loosened if they worsen.
items.a: Distal pulse, motor function and sensation
w: Blood pressure on the injured limb
Core temperature
Pupil response

items.q: Which finding is an early sign of acute compartment syndrome in an injured leg?
items.x: Pain with passive stretch and disproportionate pain occur early; loss of pulses and paralysis are late findings once damage is advanced.
items.a: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain with passive stretch
w: Loss of the distal pulse in the foot compared with the uninjured side
Complete paralysis of the foot
Pale, cold toes

items.q: Which compartment pressure finding supports the diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome?
items.x: A delta pressure (diastolic minus compartment) below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate perfusion and supports fasciotomy; low compartment pressures are normal.
items.a: A diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure of less than 30 mmHg
w: A compartment pressure below 10 mmHg
A mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg
A difference of more than 60 mmHg between systolic and compartment pressure

items.q: During prolonged care, a casualty with a crush injury of the leg is suspected of compartment syndrome. What is avoided while awaiting surgical care?
items.x: Elevation above the heart lowers arterial inflow and worsens compartment perfusion; the limb is kept at heart level and constricting dressings are loosened.
items.a: Elevating the limb well above the level of the heart
w: Removing tight dressings, casts or circumferential wraps from the limb
Frequent reassessment of the limb
Documenting the time symptoms started

items.q: A casualty's legs were trapped under rubble for 6 hours. Just after release, he develops weakness and peaked T waves on the monitor. What is the likely cause?
items.x: Reperfusion of crushed muscle releases potassium, acid and myoglobin; peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia, which can cause sudden cardiac arrest.
items.a: Hyperkalemia from potassium released by damaged muscle
w: Hypoglycemia from prolonged fasting while he was trapped under the rubble
Hypothermia from exposure
A tension pneumothorax

items.q: Before releasing a casualty from prolonged entrapment of a limb, what is the priority when possible?
items.x: Fluids before release help dilute the potassium and myoglobin surge; cardiac monitoring and medications for hyperkalemia are ready for release.
items.a: Start IV fluids and prepare to treat hyperkalemia
w: Give oral water only after release
Withhold fluids to avoid swelling
Apply ice to the limb

items.q: Which medication class is given first to stabilize the heart during hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
items.x: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes; insulin with dextrose, albuterol and sodium bicarbonate shift potassium into cells afterward.
items.a: IV calcium
w: IV potassium chloride
IV succinylcholine
Oral famotidine

items.q: A crush casualty has dark, tea-colored urine. What does this suggest?
items.x: Myoglobin from broken-down muscle colors the urine and can injure the kidneys; aggressive fluids to maintain high urine output are the main field treatment.
items.a: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis
w: Normal concentrated urine
Dehydration only
Urinary tract infection

items.q: A casualty has a penetrating eye injury with a fragment embedded in the globe. What is the best field treatment?
items.x: Pressure on an open globe can extrude eye contents, so a rigid shield is used; TCCC lists moxifloxacin for penetrating eye injuries.
items.a: A rigid eye shield without pressure, plus oral antibiotics
w: Remove the fragment carefully and apply a tight gauze pressure patch
Irrigate forcefully to wash the fragment out
Apply a tight gauze pressure dressing

items.q: A casualty has a chemical splash to the eye. What is the first step?
items.x: Chemical injuries are the exception where immediate, prolonged irrigation is the priority, since damage continues while the chemical remains on the eye.
items.a: Immediate copious irrigation with clean water
w: Rigid eye shield and wait for evacuation
Instill a neutralizing acid or base
Pressure patch the eye closed

items.q: A casualty has an abdominal wound with loops of bowel protruding. What is the best field management?
items.x: Eviscerated bowel is kept moist and covered; reducing it in the field risks contamination and injury, while dry gauze sticks and damages tissue.
items.a: Cover with a moist sterile dressing and do not push the bowel back in
w: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen and close the wound with tape
Leave uncovered to allow inspection
Cover with a dry, adherent gauze dressing

items.q: Which blast injury mechanism causes most wounds in combat casualties?
items.x: Fragments propelled by the explosion (secondary blast injury) cause most combat wounds; primary blast injury affects air-filled organs.
items.a: Secondary blast injury from fragments and debris
w: Primary blast injury from the pressure wave
Quaternary blast injury from burns and toxins
Tertiary blast injury from being thrown

items.q: Which organs are most vulnerable to primary blast injury from the pressure wave?
items.x: The blast wave damages tissue at air-fluid interfaces, causing blast lung, eardrum rupture and bowel injury.
items.a: Air-filled organs such as the lungs, ears and bowel
w: Solid organs such as the liver and spleen
Long bones of the legs
The skin and fat layers only

items.q: After a close blast, a casualty without visible chest wounds develops shortness of breath, hemoptysis and falling oxygen saturation. What is the likely cause?
items.x: Blast lung presents with dyspnea, hemoptysis and hypoxia, sometimes hours after exposure; aggressive fluid use is avoided because it worsens pulmonary edema.
items.a: Blast lung from primary blast injury
w: Heat exhaustion
Anxiety hyperventilation
Isolated eardrum rupture

items.q: Which item is part of the hypothermia prevention kit used in TCCC?
items.x: Hypothermia prevention uses active heating and an insulating, heat-reflective barrier; wet materials and exposure increase heat loss.
items.a: An active heating blanket and heat-reflective shell
w: An ice pack and a fan
A wet blanket to reduce burns
An open-sided litter cover

items.q: When is hypothermia prevention started for a casualty in TCCC?
items.x: Trauma casualties lose heat even in warm climates; hypothermia worsens clotting, so prevention starts early in all environments.
items.a: As early as possible, regardless of the environment or ambient temperature
w: Only after the core temperature has fallen below 32 degrees C
Only after the core temperature falls below 32 degrees C
Only after arrival at surgical care

items.q: A soldier collapses during a ruck march in the heat. He is confused and combative with a core temperature of 41.2 degrees C. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Exertional heat stroke is treated with rapid cooling on site, since survival depends on time above 40 degrees C; antipyretics do not work on heat stroke.
items.a: Immediate whole-body cold water immersion, cooling before evacuation
w: Oral fluids and shade, then reassess core temperature in 30 minutes
Transport first, then cool at the hospital
Give acetaminophen to lower the temperature

items.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
items.x: Heat stroke involves altered mental status with high core temperature, while heat exhaustion has normal mental status; sweating may persist in exertional heat stroke.
items.a: Altered mental status with a core temperature above 40 degrees C
w: Heavy sweating with pale, moist skin and a rapid, weak pulse
Painful muscle cramps in the legs and abdomen after exertion
Feeling tired and thirsty

items.q: A soldier who drank large volumes of water during a long training event is confused and vomiting with a normal core temperature. What is the likely cause?
items.x: Excess water intake with salt loss dilutes serum sodium, causing confusion and seizures; giving more water worsens it, and hypertonic saline treats severe cases.
items.a: Exertional hyponatremia
w: Heat stroke
Hypoglycemia
Dehydration

items.q: A soldier has a frostbitten foot during a mountain operation, and evacuation will require walking through snow. What is the best approach?
items.x: Thaw-refreeze cycles cause far more tissue damage than delayed thawing; rubbing and high heat also injure tissue.
items.a: Avoid rewarming until there is no risk of refreezing
w: Rewarm by rubbing the foot vigorously
Rewarm in hot water above 45 degrees C
Rewarm with a fire and then walk

items.q: Which water temperature is used for rapid rewarming of frostbite?
items.x: Warm water at about 37 to 39 degrees C rewarms frozen tissue quickly without burning it; hotter water causes injury in numb tissue.
items.a: 37 to 39 degrees C
w: 20 to 25 degrees C
45 to 50 degrees C
Ice water

items.q: A soldier has cold, swollen, numb feet after days in wet, non-freezing conditions. What is the diagnosis?
items.x: Prolonged cold, wet exposure above freezing causes nerve and vessel injury known as trench foot; it is prevented by dry socks and foot care.
items.a: Non-freezing cold injury (trench foot)
w: Frostbite
Cellulitis
Compartment syndrome

items.q: A severely hypothermic casualty with a core temperature of 27 degrees C is being moved. Why is gentle handling important?
items.x: The cold heart is irritable, and rough movement can precipitate ventricular fibrillation; casualties are kept horizontal and handled gently.
items.a: Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
w: Rough handling causes frostbite
Rough handling increases shivering
Rough handling lowers blood sugar

items.q: At 4,000 meters, a soldier develops confusion and ataxia after a headache for 2 days. What is the best treatment?
items.x: Confusion and ataxia indicate high-altitude cerebral edema; descent is the most important treatment, with oxygen and medications as adjuncts.
items.a: Immediate descent
w: Continue ascent
Rest at the same altitude
Increase exertion to acclimatize

items.q: At high altitude, a soldier has worsening breathlessness at rest, a cough with frothy sputum and crackles. What is the likely diagnosis?
items.x: HAPE causes dyspnea at rest, cough and crackles from fluid in the lungs; descent and oxygen are the main treatment.
items.a: High-altitude pulmonary edema
w: Acute mountain sickness only
Asthma
Pneumothorax

items.q: A diver surfaces rapidly and within minutes develops one-sided weakness and confusion. What is the likely cause?
items.x: Neurologic deficits within minutes of surfacing suggest arterial gas embolism from lung overpressure; treatment is oxygen and urgent recompression.
items.a: Arterial gas embolism
w: Decompression sickness type I
Nitrogen narcosis
Hypothermia

items.q: A diver has joint pain several hours after a dive. What is the most important treatment?
items.x: Decompression sickness is treated with high-flow oxygen and recompression; returning to the water without a chamber is dangerous.
items.a: 100 percent oxygen and recompression in a hyperbaric chamber
w: Return to depth on the remaining air supply to recompress in the water
Hot shower and rest
Analgesics only

items.q: A casualty with decompression sickness needs air evacuation. What is a key consideration?
items.x: Reduced pressure at altitude enlarges nitrogen bubbles and worsens DCS, so evacuation is low altitude or with a pressurized cabin.
items.a: Fly at the lowest safe altitude or with cabin pressure near sea level
w: Fly as high as possible to shorten the trip and the time to the chamber
Delay evacuation for 24 hours
Altitude does not matter

items.q: A soldier exposed to a vapor develops pinpoint pupils, runny nose, drooling, wheezing and muscle twitching. What is the likely agent class?
items.x: Pinpoint pupils, secretions, bronchospasm and fasciculations are cholinergic signs of nerve agent exposure.
items.a: Nerve agent (organophosphate)
w: Cyanide
Lung agent
Blister agent

items.q: In nerve agent poisoning, what is the main end point for atropine treatment?
items.x: Atropine is titrated to drying of airway secretions and improved ventilation; pupils and heart rate are unreliable end points.
items.a: Drying of bronchial secretions and easier breathing
w: Return of normal pupil size in both eyes after each dose
A heart rate above 140
Complete absence of muscle twitching

items.q: A casualty exposed to a nerve agent begins seizing. Which medication class is used to treat the seizures?
items.x: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam or midazolam treat nerve agent seizures; atropine does not control them.
items.a: Benzodiazepines
w: Opioids
Beta blockers
Antibiotics

items.q: A soldier in an enclosed space collapses suddenly with seizures, hypotension and bright red skin. What is the likely toxin?
items.x: Cyanide blocks cellular use of oxygen, producing sudden collapse, seizures and cherry-red skin without cyanosis; nerve agents cause miosis and secretions, and phosgene injury is delayed for hours.
items.a: Cyanide
w: Nerve agent
Phosgene
Chlorine

items.q: Which antidote is used for cyanide poisoning in a casualty from a smoke-filled enclosed space?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted; it causes red discoloration of skin and urine.
items.a: Hydroxocobalamin
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Atropine

items.q: Several hours after exposure to a gas that smelled like fresh-mown hay, a soldier develops severe shortness of breath and frothy sputum. What is the likely agent?
items.x: Phosgene smells like fresh-mown hay and causes noncardiogenic pulmonary edema hours after a quiet exposure; exertion accelerates it, so exposed soldiers rest and are observed, unlike chlorine, which irritates immediately.
items.a: Phosgene
w: Nerve agent
Cyanide
Tear gas

items.q: What is the first step in decontaminating a casualty exposed to a chemical agent?
items.x: Removing clothing removes most of the contaminating agent and is the single most effective early decontamination step; washing the skin follows, and covering a contaminated casualty traps vapor against the skin.
items.a: Remove clothing
w: Apply ointment
Give antibiotics
Cover with a blanket

items.q: In military mass casualty triage, which category is used for a casualty with injuries so severe that survival is unlikely given available resources?
items.x: Expectant casualties have wounds unlikely to be survivable with current resources; they receive comfort care and are reassessed, since the category can change as resources arrive.
items.a: Expectant
w: Immediate
Delayed
Minimal

items.q: In military triage, which category is used for a casualty who needs life-saving intervention immediately?
items.x: Immediate casualties need life-saving intervention now and are likely to survive with it; Delayed casualties need care but can wait, and Minimal casualties have minor wounds.
items.a: Immediate
w: Delayed
Minimal
Expectant

items.q: Which information is on line 3 of the 9-line MEDEVAC request?
items.x: Line 3 gives the number of patients by precedence (urgent, urgent-surgical, priority, routine, convenience); location is line 1, special equipment line 4 and marking method line 7.
items.a: Number of patients by precedence
w: Location of the pickup site
Special equipment required
Method of marking the pickup site

items.q: What does a MIST report contain?
items.x: MIST (Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment) is a short structured handoff that gives the receiving team the key facts in a predictable order during evacuation.
items.a: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment
w: Medication, Injury, Status, Time
Mental status, Injuries, Signs, Triage
Mechanism, Intervention, Status, Transport

items.q: Which form is used to document casualty care in TCCC?
items.x: The DD Form 1380 TCCC Card travels with the casualty and records injuries, vital signs, tourniquet times and medications so the next level of care can act on them.
items.a: DD Form 1380 (TCCC Card)
w: DD Form 214
SF 600
DA Form 31

items.q: A male casualty who is 71 inches (180 cm) tall is intubated for prolonged care. Using lung-protective ventilation, what is the target tidal volume range?
items.x: Predicted body weight for a male is 50 + 2.3 x (height in inches - 60), about 75 kg here, and 6-8 mL/kg PBW gives roughly 450-600 mL; dosing tidal volume by actual weight or a fixed large volume over-distends the lungs.
items.a: About 450 to 600 mL
w: About 750 to 900 mL
About 300 to 350 mL
About 900 to 1,050 mL

items.q: On volume assist-control, a ventilated casualty has a plateau pressure of 34 cmH2O. What is the best adjustment?
items.x: Plateau pressure reflects alveolar distending pressure and is kept under 30 cmH2O, so tidal volume is reduced (raising the rate to protect minute ventilation); faster flow changes peak, not plateau, and removing PEEP causes derecruitment.
items.a: Lower the tidal volume toward 6 mL/kg PBW
w: Raise the tidal volume to improve CO2 clearance
Increase the inspiratory flow rate only
Remove PEEP entirely to drop the pressure

items.q: On a volume-control mode, what happens to airway pressures if the casualty's lung compliance falls?
items.x: Volume control guarantees the set volume, so stiffer lungs show up as higher pressures; a falling tidal volume at fixed pressure describes pressure control instead.
items.a: Peak and plateau pressures rise at the same set volume
w: Delivered tidal volume falls while pressures stay fixed
The rate automatically drops to compensate
Pressures fall because less air enters the lungs

items.q: On pressure control ventilation, a casualty develops worsening abdominal distension and stiffer lungs. What change is expected?
items.x: In pressure control the inspiratory pressure is fixed, so lower compliance means less volume per breath and possible hypoventilation; monitoring exhaled tidal volume and EtCO2 catches it.
items.a: Delivered tidal volume decreases
w: Peak pressure climbs well above the set level
Delivered tidal volume increases
The respiratory rate doubles on its own

items.q: Which ventilator mode delivers a set number of mandatory breaths and lets the casualty take additional spontaneous breaths that are not full machine breaths?
items.x: SIMV synchronizes mandatory breaths with effort and allows unassisted or pressure-supported spontaneous breaths between them; in assist-control every triggered breath is a full set breath.
items.a: SIMV
w: Assist-control volume
CPAP alone
Pressure control assist-control

items.q: A casualty on assist-control volume is agitated and triggering at 34 breaths per minute, with rising measured PEEP. What is the main hazard of this mode here?
items.x: Every triggered breath in AC receives the full set volume, so rapid triggering shortens exhalation and traps air; the fix is treating pain, agitation and the cause of tachypnea.
items.a: Breath stacking and auto-PEEP from full breaths each trigger
w: Apnea because the mode has no backup rate
Hypercapnia because spontaneous breaths are unsupported
Barotrauma only from the PEEP valve itself

items.q: Pressure support ventilation is best suited for which casualty?
items.x: PSV augments only patient-triggered breaths and has no guaranteed rate, so it depends on a reliable drive; paralyzed, deeply sedated or apneic casualties need a mandatory mode.
items.a: One with an intact respiratory drive being weaned
w: One paralyzed for transport with no drive
One in deep sedation with frequent apnea
One with fresh herniation signs after a TBI

items.q: On a ventilator, which two settings mainly determine oxygenation?
items.x: Oxygenation depends on FiO2 and mean airway pressure, which PEEP drives; rate and tidal volume set minute ventilation and so control CO2.
items.a: FiO2 and PEEP
w: Respiratory rate and tidal volume
Inspiratory flow and trigger sensitivity
Rate and inspiratory time

items.q: A ventilated casualty's EtCO2 has risen from 38 to 52 mmHg with stable vital signs and a good waveform. Which change most directly lowers CO2?
items.x: CO2 removal follows minute ventilation (rate x tidal volume), and raising rate keeps tidal volume lung-protective; FiO2 and PEEP improve oxygenation, not ventilation.
items.a: Increase the respiratory rate
w: Increase the FiO2
Increase the PEEP
Decrease the inspiratory flow

items.q: A conscious casualty with pulmonary edema after a blast has SpO2 87% on a mask, protects his airway and follows commands. Which noninvasive support adds both inspiratory and expiratory pressure?
items.x: BiPAP gives a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) and a lower expiratory pressure (EPAP), assisting ventilation as well as oxygenation; CPAP holds one continuous pressure throughout the cycle.
items.a: BiPAP
w: CPAP
High-flow nasal cannula
Simple face mask

items.q: Which finding makes CPAP or BiPAP unsuitable for a casualty in respiratory distress?
items.x: Noninvasive ventilation needs a casualty who can protect the airway and cooperate, so vomiting and decreasing mental status point to intubation; hypoxia and tachypnea are the reasons to try it.
items.a: Vomiting with a falling level of consciousness
w: SpO2 of 89% on supplemental oxygen
Respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute
Bilateral crackles after smoke exposure

items.q: In the Berlin definition, what PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines severe ARDS?
items.x: Berlin grades ARDS on PEEP of at least 5 as mild (P/F 201-300), moderate (101-200) and severe (100 or less); 400 is near normal lung function.
items.a: 100 or less
w: 200 or less
300 or less
400 or less

items.q: A casualty on 50% FiO2 has a PaO2 of 75 mmHg on an i-STAT blood gas. What is the P/F ratio?
items.x: P/F = PaO2 divided by FiO2 as a decimal, so 75 / 0.5 = 150, which is moderate ARDS range if the other criteria are met; dividing by the percent or multiplying gives meaningless numbers.

items.q: In a casualty with ARDS on lung-protective settings, which oxygen saturation target is standard in ARDSNet practice?
items.x: ARDSNet targets SpO2 88-95% (PaO2 55-80 mmHg) to limit oxygen toxicity and the high FiO2 and PEEP needed to chase 100%; persistent saturations in the low 80s risk hypoxic injury.
w: Any level above 75%

items.q: A casualty with severe ARDS remains hypoxic with a P/F under 150 despite optimized PEEP and FiO2. Which intervention has shown a mortality benefit?
items.x: The PROSEVA trial showed lower mortality with prolonged prone sessions in severe ARDS; large tidal volumes raise mortality and removing PEEP worsens derecruitment.
items.a: Prone positioning for prolonged sessions
w: Increasing tidal volume to 12 mL/kg PBW
Routine high-dose steroids on day one
Removing PEEP to lower intrathoracic pressure

items.q: When lung-protective ventilation causes the PaCO2 to rise to 55 mmHg with a pH of 7.28 in a casualty without head injury, what is the usual approach?
items.x: Modest respiratory acidosis is tolerated to keep volumes and pressures protective; it is avoided in TBI, where CO2 raises intracranial pressure.
items.a: Accept it as permissive hypercapnia
w: Raise tidal volume to 10 mL/kg PBW
Give bicarbonate to normalize the pH
Stop PEEP to improve CO2 clearance

items.q: How is plateau pressure measured on a ventilated casualty?
items.x: An inspiratory pause removes flow so the reading reflects alveolar pressure; the peak includes airway resistance, and an expiratory hold measures auto-PEEP instead.
items.a: An inspiratory hold at end inspiration
w: An expiratory hold at end exhalation
Reading the highest pressure during each breath
Subtracting PEEP from the peak pressure

items.q: A ventilated casualty suddenly desaturates and the EtCO2 waveform drops to a flat line. What is the first step?
items.x: Sudden deterioration is approached with DOPE (Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment); bagging off the vent separates the casualty from the equipment while tube position and breath sounds are checked.
items.a: Disconnect from the vent and hand-bag with oxygen
w: Increase PEEP and FiO2 on the ventilator
Push additional sedation and reassess
Order a chest X-ray before acting

items.q: A ventilated casualty has a high peak pressure alarm. Peak is 45 cmH2O and plateau is 22 cmH2O. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A wide gap between peak and plateau means high airway resistance, such as secretions, kinking, biting or bronchospasm; pneumothorax, mainstem intubation and ARDS lower compliance and raise both pressures.
items.a: Mucus plug or kinked tube
w: Tension pneumothorax
Right mainstem intubation
Worsening ARDS

items.q: A ventilated blast casualty becomes hypotensive with both peak and plateau pressures rising sharply and absent breath sounds on the left. What is the best next step?
items.x: Rising peak and plateau with unilateral absent breath sounds and shock indicate tension pneumothorax, which positive pressure worsens quickly; suctioning treats resistance problems, not this.
items.a: Needle decompression of the left chest
w: Suction the tube and give a bronchodilator
Deflate and reinflate the tube cuff
Lower the alarm limits and observe

items.q: A ventilated casualty has a low-pressure alarm and the exhaled tidal volume is far below the set volume. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Low pressure with lost exhaled volume means gas is escaping, so check connections, the cuff and the tube depth; obstruction and pneumothorax set off high-pressure alarms.
items.a: A circuit disconnection or cuff leak
w: Bronchospasm with air trapping
Mucus plug in the tube
A tension pneumothorax

items.q: During transport, an intubated casualty's EtCO2 waveform shows a shark-fin shape with an upsloping plateau. What does this suggest?
items.x: The shark-fin shape reflects slow, uneven emptying of narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD; esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform.
items.a: Bronchospasm or expiratory obstruction
w: Esophageal intubation
Return of spontaneous circulation
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: What is the usual target endotracheal tube cuff pressure measured with a manometer?
items.x: A cuff pressure of 20-30 cmH2O seals the airway while staying below tracheal mucosal perfusion pressure; low pressure allows leaks and aspiration, high pressure causes ischemic injury.
items.a: 20 to 30 cmH2O
w: 5 to 10 cmH2O
40 to 50 cmH2O
60 to 80 cmH2O

items.q: When setting the ventilator for an intubated casualty with severe asthma, which strategy is preferred?
items.x: Air trapping is the danger in asthma, so a low rate, short inspiratory time and prolonged exhalation reduce auto-PEEP, with permissive hypercapnia accepted; high rates worsen trapping.
items.a: Low rate with long expiratory time
w: High rate to wash out CO2 quickly
Large tidal volumes to open airways
High PEEP to splint the bronchi

items.q: Minutes after intubation, a casualty with status asthmaticus becomes hypotensive and pressures climb. Breath sounds are equal and quiet. What is the best immediate action?
items.x: Dynamic hyperinflation compresses venous return; disconnecting and gently pressing the chest lets trapped air out, then lower rate and longer exhalation prevent recurrence. Higher rate or PEEP worsens it.
items.a: Disconnect the vent to let trapped air escape
w: Increase the rate to improve ventilation
Raise PEEP to recruit collapsed alveoli
Give a fluid bolus and leave settings unchanged

items.q: How is intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP) measured on a ventilated casualty?
items.x: An expiratory hold lets alveolar and circuit pressure equilibrate, and the total minus set PEEP is auto-PEEP; an inspiratory hold measures plateau pressure.
items.a: An end-expiratory hold maneuver
w: An end-inspiratory hold maneuver
The peak inspiratory pressure reading
The set PEEP shown on the display

items.q: An intubated casualty with a moderate TBI and no signs of herniation is being ventilated. What EtCO2 range is the target?
items.x: TCCC and JTS guidance targets normocapnia at 35-40 mmHg; hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia, and hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure.
items.a: 35 to 40 mmHg
w: 25 to 30 mmHg
45 to 50 mmHg
50 to 55 mmHg

items.q: A ventilated TBI casualty develops a unilateral dilated pupil and extensor posturing. Along with hyperosmolar therapy, which ventilation change is a reasonable brief temporizing step?
items.x: Brief, monitored hyperventilation lowers intracranial pressure as a bridge for impending herniation; prolonged or deep hypocapnia under 30 risks cerebral ischemia, and hypercapnia raises ICP.
items.a: Mild hyperventilation keeping EtCO2 near 30-35
w: Lower the rate to raise EtCO2 above 45
Remove PEEP and cut FiO2 to room air
Aggressive hyperventilation to EtCO2 of 20

items.q: Which positioning measure helps lower intracranial pressure in an intubated TBI casualty without spinal concerns?
items.x: Elevating the head about 30 degrees with the neck midline improves venous drainage; head-down positions and neck flexion or tight collars raise ICP.
items.a: Head of the litter raised about 30 degrees
w: Flat supine with legs elevated
Trendelenburg to support blood pressure
Lateral position with the neck flexed

items.q: In a TBI casualty, which pair of secondary insults most worsens outcome and is the focus of prolonged care?
items.x: Even single episodes of hypotension or hypoxia markedly raise TBI mortality, so oxygenation and perfusion are the priorities; an EtCO2 of 38 is within target.
items.a: Hypotension and hypoxia
w: Mild fever and anemia
Tachycardia and hypocapnia of 38
Hyperglycemia and bradycardia

items.q: On the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), what score describes a casualty who is alert and calm?
items.x: RASS runs from +4 (combative) to -5 (unarousable), with 0 meaning alert and calm; -3 is moderate sedation with movement to voice but no eye contact.

items.q: A ventilated casualty opens his eyes and makes eye contact for more than 10 seconds to voice, then drifts off. What is his RASS score?
items.x: Sustained awakening to voice with eye contact over 10 seconds is -1 (drowsy); -2 is under 10 seconds, -3 is movement without eye contact, and -4 needs physical stimulation.

items.q: For most ventilated casualties without severe ARDS or paralysis, what sedation target is preferred?
items.x: Light sedation reduces ventilator days, delirium and hypotension; deep sedation is reserved for specific needs such as neuromuscular blockade or severe dyssynchrony.
items.a: Light sedation around RASS 0 to -2
w: Deep sedation around RASS -4 to -5
Agitation around RASS +2 to +3
No sedation goal, titrated to vital signs

items.q: What is the analgesia-first approach to sedation in ventilated casualties?
items.x: Pain drives much of the agitation and ventilator dyssynchrony in trauma, so analgesia comes first and lowers sedative needs; paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
items.a: Treat pain first, then add sedatives only as needed
w: Give sedatives first and pain medication later
Avoid analgesics to allow neurologic exams
Use a paralytic in place of sedation

items.q: A ventilated casualty receives rocuronium for transport. What is the key safety requirement?
items.x: Neuromuscular blockers provide no sedation or pain relief, so a paralyzed casualty without them is awake and in pain; paralysis also hides seizures and agitation, making monitoring more important.
items.a: Adequate sedation and analgesia before and during paralysis
w: Stopping all sedation so the exam is reliable
Turning off the high-pressure alarm
Removing the EtCO2 monitor to save battery

items.q: A hypotensive, intubated casualty in hemorrhagic shock needs ongoing sedation. Which agent best preserves blood pressure?
items.x: Ketamine supports sympathetic tone and is favored for sedation and analgesia in shock; propofol and dexmedetomidine commonly cause hypotension and benzodiazepines add hypotension in shock states.
items.a: Ketamine
w: Propofol
Dexmedetomidine
Midazolam infusion

items.q: Which feature makes dexmedetomidine useful in a ventilated casualty being prepared for extubation?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist, gives cooperative sedation without much respiratory depression; its common effects are bradycardia and hypotension, and it is not suited to deep sedation.
items.a: Arousable sedation with little respiratory depression
w: Strong analgesia that replaces all opioids
Rapid blood pressure support in shock
Deep sedation for neuromuscular blockade

items.q: A ventilated casualty has received prolonged high-rate propofol and develops unexplained metabolic acidosis, rising potassium and dark urine. What is suspected?
items.x: Propofol infusion syndrome brings metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and cardiac failure with prolonged or high-rate use; stopping the infusion is the key step.
items.a: Propofol infusion syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Hypoglycemic reaction

items.q: A casualty on a fentanyl infusion has worsening sedation, pinpoint pupils and a falling respiratory rate after extubation. Which medication reverses this effect?
items.x: Naloxone reverses opioid effects, titrated to breathing rather than full wakefulness; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures.
items.a: Naloxone
w: Flumazenil
Glycopyrrolate
Ondansetron

items.q: A casualty on day 3 of prolonged care has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), heart rate 124, respiratory rate 26, confusion and SBP 92. Which qSOFA criteria are met?
items.x: qSOFA uses respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation and SBP of 100 or less; temperature and heart rate are not part of it, and two or more criteria flag high risk.
items.a: All three: RR 22 or higher, altered mentation, SBP 100 or lower
w: Only the fever and the heart rate
Only the respiratory rate
None, because the SBP is above 90

items.q: In suspected septic shock, when are antibiotics given relative to recognition?
items.x: Each hour of delay in septic shock is linked to higher mortality, so broad-spectrum antibiotics are given within 1 hour; cultures are drawn first only if that causes no delay.
items.a: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour
w: After culture results return in 48 hours
Only after fluids fail to correct the BP
Once the fever has lasted 24 hours

items.q: A wounded casualty becomes septic on day 2 with a contaminated open fracture. Which TCCC/JTS-supported IV option covers broad gram-negative and anaerobic organisms?
items.x: Ertapenem covers gram-negative, gram-positive and anaerobic organisms and is a TCCC wound antibiotic; oral first-generation cephalosporins and metronidazole alone are too narrow for this.
items.a: Ertapenem
w: Cephalexin
Cefadroxil
Metronidazole alone

items.q: A septic casualty remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is first-line?
items.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock; dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and vasopressin is usually added rather than used alone.
items.a: Norepinephrine
w: Phenylephrine
Dopamine
Vasopressin alone

items.q: A casualty in prolonged care has a red, warm, tender wound with purulent drainage and fever on day 3. What is the most important step besides antibiotics?
items.x: Antibiotics penetrate pus poorly, so drainage, debridement and irrigation are the definitive source control; closing an infected wound traps the infection.
items.a: Source control by opening and draining the wound
w: Closing the wound tightly to keep bacteria out
Applying a tourniquet above the wound
Covering it with an occlusive dressing for a week

items.q: A casualty with spreading skin discoloration, crepitus and pain out of proportion around a wound on day 2 is suspected of having which condition?
items.x: Crepitus, rapid spread and pain out of proportion suggest necrotizing infection, a surgical emergency needing early teleconsult, broad antibiotics and urgent evacuation.
items.a: Necrotizing soft tissue infection
w: Simple cellulitis
Contact dermatitis
Superficial abrasion

items.q: For a casualty in hemorrhagic shock, which resuscitation fluid does TCCC prefer?
items.x: TCCC prefers whole blood, then blood components; crystalloids and colloids dilute clotting factors and worsen coagulopathy, so they are not the fluids for bleeding.
items.a: Low-titer O whole blood
w: Lactated Ringer's
Hetastarch
Normal saline

items.q: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what initial fluid rate is calculated for a 70 kg casualty with a 40% TBSA burn?
items.x: The Rule of Ten multiplies %TBSA by 10 for casualties 40-80 kg, so 40 x 10 = 400 mL/hr; 100 mL/hr is added for every 10 kg above 80 kg.
items.a: 400 mL/hr
w: 280 mL/hr
700 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr

items.q: Using the Rule of Ten, what initial burn fluid rate is calculated for a 100 kg casualty with a 30% TBSA burn?
items.x: 30 x 10 = 300 mL/hr, plus 100 mL/hr for each 10 kg above 80 kg (2 x 100), totaling 500 mL/hr.
items.a: 500 mL/hr
w: 300 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr
400 mL/hr

items.q: Using the rule of nines, what TBSA percentage is burned in an adult with full-thickness burns of the entire front of the torso and the entire left arm?
items.x: The anterior trunk is 18% and one entire arm is 9%, totaling 27%; superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.

items.q: In an adult burn casualty, what urine output target guides adjustment of burn resuscitation fluids?
items.x: JTS burn guidance titrates fluids to 30-50 mL/hr of urine in adults; low output signals under-resuscitation, and far higher output signals over-resuscitation and edema.
items.a: 30 to 50 mL/hr
w: 5 to 10 mL/hr
100 to 150 mL/hr
200 mL/hr or more

items.q: In a casualty with suspected rhabdomyolysis from crush injury, which finding supports the diagnosis?
items.x: Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin (dark urine), potassium and CK; treatment centers on early, generous fluids and watching for hyperkalemia.
items.a: Dark tea-colored urine with high potassium
w: Clear dilute urine with low potassium
Low creatine kinase with normal urine
Pinpoint pupils and slow breathing

items.q: An i-STAT shows Na 140, Cl 104 and HCO3 12. What is the anion gap?
items.x: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 140 - 116 = 24, which is elevated (normal about 8-12) and points to causes such as lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis.

items.q: An i-STAT shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 28 and HCO3 11. What is the primary disorder?
items.x: A low pH with low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis, and the low PaCO2 is the expected compensation; Winter's formula (1.5 x 11 + 8, about 24-26) checks whether it is adequate.
items.a: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
w: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis

items.q: Using Winter's formula, a casualty with HCO3 of 14 has an expected PaCO2 of about 27-31. The measured PaCO2 is 45. What does this indicate?
items.x: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29 (plus or minus 2); a PaCO2 well above that means ventilation is failing to compensate, a warning sign of fatigue or oversedation.
items.a: A concurrent respiratory acidosis
w: Appropriate respiratory compensation
A concurrent respiratory alkalosis
A primary metabolic alkalosis

items.q: An i-STAT on a ventilated casualty shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 and HCO3 26. What is the disorder?
items.x: Low pH with high PaCO2 and a near-normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, which suggests inadequate minute ventilation; increasing the rate is the usual correction.
items.a: Acute respiratory acidosis
w: Metabolic acidosis
Chronic metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis

items.q: After several whole blood transfusions, a casualty's i-STAT ionized calcium is 0.88 mmol/L. What is the cause and response?
items.x: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and low ionized calcium (normal about 1.12-1.32) weakens clotting and cardiac contraction; TCCC calls for calcium with transfusion.
items.a: Citrate binding; give calcium
w: Kidney failure; give bicarbonate
Dilution; give normal saline
Lab error; repeat in 24 hours

items.q: A crush casualty's i-STAT shows potassium 7.1 and the ECG shows peaked T waves and widening QRS. What is the first priority?
items.x: Calcium does not lower potassium but protects the heart within minutes; insulin with dextrose, albuterol and bicarbonate then shift potassium into cells.
items.a: Calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane
w: Furosemide to remove potassium
Repeat the i-STAT in an hour
Potassium chloride to balance levels

items.q: A casualty has an i-STAT sodium of 118 that developed over several days. What is the key risk of correcting it too quickly?
items.x: Chronic hyponatremia corrected faster than about 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours can cause osmotic demyelination; severe symptoms such as seizures still warrant prompt partial correction.
items.a: Osmotic demyelination
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Acute kidney stones
Tension pneumothorax

items.q: Which i-STAT finding is expected in a casualty with prolonged nasogastric suction?
items.x: Loss of gastric acid raises bicarbonate and causes potassium and chloride depletion; acidosis with high potassium fits renal failure or tissue breakdown instead.
items.a: Metabolic alkalosis with low potassium
w: Metabolic acidosis with high potassium
Respiratory acidosis with high sodium
Normal gas with high calcium

items.q: On day 4 a casualty starts tube feeds after several days without nutrition and develops weakness and arrhythmias. Which lab pattern is most likely?
items.x: Refeeding syndrome drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells when feeding restarts; feeds are started slowly and electrolytes checked and replaced.
items.a: Low phosphate, potassium and magnesium
w: High phosphate, potassium and magnesium
High sodium and calcium only
Normal electrolytes with high lactate

items.q: A casualty is on a litter in prolonged care for 48 hours. How often is repositioning done to prevent pressure injury?
items.x: Pressure injuries on the sacrum, heels and occiput can develop within hours on a hard litter; turning about every 2 hours plus padding bony prominences prevents them.
items.a: About every 2 hours
w: Once every 12 hours
Only when skin breakdown appears
Only at each evacuation leg

items.q: A sedated, ventilated casualty has eyes that do not fully close. What eye care is indicated?
items.x: Sedated casualties lose blink and lid closure, causing exposure keratopathy and corneal ulcers; lubricant and gentle closure protect the cornea. Pressure patches are avoided if globe injury is possible.
items.a: Lubricate and keep the lids closed with tape or film
w: Leave the eyes open to allow pupil checks
Apply firm pressure patches over both eyes
Irrigate the eyes hourly with tap water

items.q: Which measure is part of a ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle?
items.x: Head elevation, oral care, suctioning secretions and daily sedation review reduce aspiration and VAP; flat positioning increases aspiration, and frequent circuit changes add risk.
items.a: Head of litter at 30 to 45 degrees
w: Keeping the casualty flat
Changing the circuit every 4 hours
Deflating the cuff between suctioning

items.q: What urine output target is used for an adult non-burn casualty in prolonged care to judge perfusion?
items.x: Urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr reflects adequate kidney perfusion; trending it hourly with a Foley guides resuscitation.
items.a: At least 0.5 mL/kg/hr
w: At least 5 mL/kg/hr
About 10 mL/hr total
Any amount above zero

items.q: Which Foley catheter practice reduces catheter-associated urinary tract infection?
items.x: A closed system kept below the bladder prevents backflow and contamination; breaking the system or raising the bag pushes contaminated urine back.
items.a: A closed system with the bag below the bladder
w: Opening the system to empty the bag
Hanging the bag on the litter above the bladder
Routine catheter change every 12 hours

items.q: A ventilated casualty has controlled hemorrhage and stable hemoglobin on day 2. Which DVT prophylaxis approach fits?
items.x: Trauma casualties are at high VTE risk; once bleeding is controlled, a low molecular weight heparin such as enoxaparin is started, with mechanical compression added or used alone if bleeding risk remains.
items.a: Enoxaparin with mechanical compression if possible
w: No prophylaxis until evacuation
Aspirin only after discharge
Tourniquet placement to limit venous flow

items.q: Which situation makes chemical DVT prophylaxis with enoxaparin inappropriate at this time?
items.x: Anticoagulant prophylaxis is held while bleeding is active; immobility, ventilation and major trauma are risk factors that call for prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled.
items.a: Ongoing active hemorrhage
w: Immobility from a femur fracture
Mechanical ventilation for 2 days
Major abdominal injury that is now stable

items.q: A casualty ventilated for more than 48 hours with coagulopathy is in prolonged care. Which medication provides stress ulcer prophylaxis?
items.x: Mechanical ventilation over 48 hours and coagulopathy are major risks for stress-related GI bleeding; acid suppression with an H2 blocker or PPI lowers it. Ketorolac raises bleeding risk.
items.a: Famotidine or pantoprazole
w: Ondansetron
Ketorolac
Diphenhydramine

items.q: When is enteral nutrition started for a stable casualty in prolonged care who cannot eat?
items.x: Early enteral feeding supports gut integrity and immunity and lowers infection; it is delayed in unresolved shock with escalating vasopressors.
items.a: Early, within about 24 to 48 hours
w: Only after 7 days of fasting
Only once evacuated to a hospital
Only if the casualty asks for food

items.q: What is the purpose of a daily sedation interruption or lightening in a ventilated casualty?
items.x: Daily sedation lightening, paired with a breathing trial, shortens ventilation time and allows a neurologic exam; it is not done during paralysis or uncontrolled intracranial hypertension.
items.a: To assess neurologic status and readiness to wean
w: To allow the ventilator battery to recharge
To lower the FiO2 requirement
To raise the plateau pressure

items.q: A ventilated casualty on day 3 becomes inattentive, fluctuates between agitation and drowsiness, and pulls at lines. What is the likely diagnosis?
items.x: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered awareness is delirium, linked to worse outcomes; causes such as hypoxia, infection, pain and benzodiazepines are sought and treated.
items.a: Delirium
w: Expected recovery from sedation
Simple anxiety
Ventilator alarm fatigue

items.q: A contaminated blast wound is being managed in prolonged care. Which approach to closure is preferred?
items.x: Combat wounds are heavily contaminated, so they are irrigated, debrided and left open for delayed closure; early closure traps bacteria and leads to abscess.
items.a: Leave open with delayed primary closure
w: Close tightly with sutures in the field
Glue the skin edges after irrigation
Apply staples once the bleeding stops

items.q: For wound irrigation in an austere setting when sterile saline is unavailable, what is an acceptable alternative?
items.x: Potable water is as effective as sterile saline for wound irrigation; peroxide and bleach damage tissue, and seawater adds contamination.
items.a: Clean drinkable water
w: Diluted bleach solution
Undiluted hydrogen peroxide
Seawater from nearby

items.q: On day 2, a casualty with a tibial fracture has pain out of proportion, pain on passive toe stretch and a tense calf. Distal pulses are present. What is suspected?
items.x: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome; pulses are often present until late, so their presence does not exclude it.
items.a: Compartment syndrome
w: Simple muscle cramp
