items.q: How long is post-exposure prophylaxis for anthrax, and why?
items.x: Spores can germinate long after exposure, so a 60-day antibiotic course with vaccination is used; shortened courses have been followed by late cases.
items.a: 60 days, because spores can persist in the lungs
w: 7 days, matching plague
10 days, as for most bacterial infections
Until the fever settles

items.q: An alert, afebrile casualty has double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech and trouble swallowing, with symmetric weakness spreading downward. Sensation is normal. What fits best?
items.x: Botulism produces a descending symmetric flaccid paralysis starting with bulbar muscles, with a clear mind, normal sensation and no fever.
items.a: Botulism
w: Guillain-Barre syndrome
Nerve agent exposure
Brainstem stroke

items.q: What distinguishes nerve agent poisoning from botulism at the bedside?
items.x: The cholinergic picture of wet secretions, pinpoint pupils and fasciculations is absent in botulism, which produces dry mouth and dilated pupils.
items.a: Nerve agents cause tiny pupils, heavy secretions and twitching
w: Nerve agents cause descending paralysis and botulism causes ascending
Botulism causes fever and nerve agents do not
Botulism causes loss of sensation

items.q: Botulinum antitoxin is given as early as possible because it
items.x: Antitoxin halts further binding of toxin. Nerve endings that are already blocked recover only as they regrow, which takes weeks to months.
items.a: Neutralizes circulating toxin but does not reverse paralysis already present
w: Reverses paralysis within hours
Prevents person-to-person spread
Replaces the need for ventilation

items.q: Which feature separates smallpox from chickenpox?
items.x: Smallpox lesions progress together, are deep-seated and involve palms and soles; varicella shows mixed stages, is trunk-heavy and spares palms and soles.
items.a: Lesions on one area are all at the same stage, and palms and soles are involved
w: Lesions appear in several stages at once
The rash is heaviest on the trunk
There is no prodrome

items.q: A rash illness with fever also has prominently swollen lymph nodes. Which possibility does that favor?
items.x: Marked lymphadenopathy is a recognized feature of mpox and is not typical of smallpox, which helps separate the two.
items.a: Mpox
w: Smallpox
Ricin exposure
Staphylococcal enterotoxin B

items.q: Which precautions fit suspected smallpox?
items.x: Smallpox spreads by droplets, by airborne routes in some settings and by contact with lesion material, so airborne and contact precautions are used together.
items.a: Airborne and contact precautions together
w: Droplet precautions only
Standard precautions only
Contact precautions only

items.q: Roughly 4 hours after a shared exposure, many people develop fever, chills, headache and a dry cough. Almost none become critically ill and none infect anyone else. What fits best?
items.x: A short incubation measured in hours, a large number of similar casualties, low mortality and no person-to-person spread is the SEB pattern.
items.a: Staphylococcal enterotoxin B
w: Pneumonic plague
Inhalational anthrax
Smallpox

items.q: Why do antibiotics not change the course of SEB illness?
items.x: SEB is a toxin-mediated illness. Antibiotics have no target, although they are often started before the cause is known.
items.a: It is caused by a preformed toxin rather than an infection
w: The organism is resistant to all antibiotics
The toxin inactivates antibiotics
Antibiotics are only withheld because of supply

items.q: About 12 hours after an inhalational exposure, casualties develop cough and worsening low oxygen with widespread pulmonary infiltrates. There is no spread to caregivers and no response to antibiotics. What fits best?
items.x: Inhaled ricin produces a progressive chemical-type pneumonitis over 12 to 24 hours with no transmission and no antibiotic response.
items.a: Ricin
w: Tularemia
Q fever
Brucellosis

items.q: What treatment exists for ricin poisoning?
items.x: There is no licensed antidote or vaccine for ricin; care centers on decontamination, oxygen and lung-protective ventilation when needed.
items.a: Supportive care only, with no antidote or vaccine
w: A monoclonal antitoxin
Hydroxocobalamin
Doxycycline

items.q: Which agent on these lists causes burning skin and blistering within minutes of contact?
items.x: Trichothecenes injure skin, eyes and airways on contact, which is unlike the bacteria and viruses on these lists, where exposure causes no sensation.
items.a: T-2 mycotoxin
w: Anthrax
Botulinum toxin
Q fever

items.q: Why is immediate decontamination especially important after T-2 exposure?
items.x: T-2 continues to damage tissue on contact, so washing early limits injury. It does not pass between people.
items.a: The toxin keeps injuring tissue while it remains on the skin
w: It prevents person-to-person spread
It stops the marrow suppression entirely
Soap and water inactivate the toxin in the bloodstream

items.q: A casualty who recovered from a T-2 exposure develops bleeding and infection two weeks later. What explains this?
items.x: Trichothecenes suppress rapidly dividing cells, so low white cells and platelets appear days to weeks after the exposure looks resolved.
items.a: Bone marrow suppression, as in radiation injury
w: A secondary bacterial pneumonia
Delayed toxin release from fat
An allergic reaction to decontamination

items.q: Which statement about alcohol-based hand gel and anthrax spores is correct?
items.x: Alcohol does not kill anthrax spores. Removing clothing and washing with soap and water physically removes them.
items.a: It does not kill spores, so soap, water and friction are used
w: It kills spores faster than soap and water
It is adequate when no water is available
It is preferred for decontaminating clothing

items.q: Which first-line options does CDC treatment guidance give for pneumonic plague?
items.x: Streptomycin or gentamicin, or a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, are placed first for pneumonic and septicemic plague.
items.a: An aminoglycoside or a fluoroquinolone
w: A beta-lactam alone
Azithromycin alone
No antibiotics, as care is supportive

items.q: A cluster develops severe febrile illness with cough, the chest films look worse than the lungs sound, and nobody transmits it to anyone else. Mortality is low with treatment. What fits best?
items.x: Tularemia produces severe constitutional illness with modest examination findings, is not spread person to person, and has much lower mortality than plague or anthrax.
items.a: Tularemia
w: Pneumonic plague
Smallpox
Botulism

items.q: Why are two drugs used over several weeks for brucellosis?
items.x: Brucella survives inside cells, so combination therapy for at least six weeks is used; single agents and short courses relapse.
items.a: Single short courses are followed by relapse
w: It is resistant to every single agent
To cover a possible coinfection
To reduce the cost of treatment

items.q: Which incubation period fits Q fever after a shared exposure?
items.x: Q fever typically incubates 10 to 40 days, most often two to three weeks, which separates it from the agents that strike within days.
items.a: About 2 to 3 weeks
w: 4 to 8 hours
1 to 2 days
Several months

items.q: A pneumonia with abscesses and skin nodules fails standard antibiotics in a patient with heavy soil and water exposure. Which group fits?
items.x: These organisms form abscesses and resist many common antibiotics; ceftazidime or a carbapenem is used, followed by months of oral therapy.
items.a: Burkholderia (melioidosis or glanders)
w: Francisella tularensis
Coxiella burnetii
Variola virus

items.q: Early in viral hemorrhagic fever, which finding is most common?
items.x: Bleeding is a late and inconsistent finding. The early illness looks like a severe febrile gastrointestinal illness, and that is when transmission risk is already present.
items.a: Fever with heavy vomiting and diarrhea
w: Visible bleeding
A vesicular rash
Descending paralysis

items.q: Which measure has lowered mortality most in viral hemorrhagic fever?
items.x: Supportive care, especially careful replacement of large gastrointestinal losses, has done more for survival than any single specific agent.
items.a: Aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement
w: Early antibiotics
Corticosteroids
Antitoxin

items.q: Where are caregivers most often infected during care of a filovirus patient?
items.x: Doffing is the recognized high-risk step, which is why trained doffing with an observer is part of the protocol.
items.a: While removing personal protective equipment
w: While donning equipment
Through intact skin contact with the patient's clothing
By airborne spread across the ward

items.q: An explosive outbreak of fever and severe headache occurs where horses are dying of neurologic illness. A few patients develop seizures. What fits best?
items.x: Venezuelan, eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses cause disease in horses and people, and sick or dying horses are a classic clue.
items.a: An equine encephalitis virus
w: Plague
Q fever
SEB

items.q: What treatment exists for the equine encephalitis viruses?
items.x: No specific antiviral exists. Care is supportive, with seizure control and airway protection for patients who progress to encephalitis.
items.a: Supportive care, with no specific antiviral
w: Ribavirin
Tecovirimat
Doxycycline

items.q: Which pattern most strongly suggests a toxin rather than an infection?
items.x: Toxins act in hours, do not spread between people and do not respond to antibiotics; infections incubate for days and several of them transmit.
items.a: Symptoms within hours and no spread between people
w: Symptoms after several days with spread to caregivers
A rash appearing on day three
Response to antibiotics

items.q: When is a suspected biological agent reported?
items.x: Early reporting is what starts prophylaxis, protective measures and specimen handling for everyone else; waiting for confirmation costs that time.
items.a: Immediately on suspicion, before confirmation
w: After laboratory confirmation
At the end of the shift
Only if more than ten casualties are involved

items.q: Why is the laboratory warned when one of these agents is suspected?
items.x: Brucella, Francisella and Yersinia pestis in particular have caused laboratory-acquired infections, so advance notice lets staff handle specimens at the right containment level.
items.a: Several have infected laboratory workers handling routine cultures
w: Specimens are otherwise discarded
It is needed to release antibiotics
It speeds billing

items.q: A cluster of acute liver failure is traced to a shared grain supply with no viral cause found. Which agent fits?
items.x: Aflatoxins are fungal toxins of grain and nuts, weaponized by Iraq in the 1980s. A large dose causes acute liver failure; the characteristic harm, liver cancer, takes years.
items.a: Aflatoxin
w: Ricin
Botulinum toxin
Epsilon toxin

items.q: A casualty with tetrodotoxin poisoning appears unresponsive with fixed dilated pupils. What is the key point?
items.x: Tetrodotoxin blocks sodium channels without affecting consciousness. People have been declared dead while awake. Survivors recover completely if ventilated through it, usually over 24 to 72 hours.
items.a: They are conscious and aware, and sedation is part of the care
w: They are brain dead and care can be withdrawn
The pupils rule out tetrodotoxin
Paralysis here is permanent

items.q: What is the earliest warning of a Rift Valley fever outbreak in people?
items.x: The veterinary picture precedes the human outbreak. Most human cases come from handling infected animal blood and tissue, so the slaughtering and animal-contact history is the question that separates it from other deployment fevers.
items.a: Livestock abortion storms and an animal die-off
w: A rash in the first cases
A rise in mosquito trap counts alone
Vision loss in the index case

items.q: What distinguishes pandemic influenza from most of the classic biological warfare agents?
items.x: Anthrax, ricin and most agents on these lists affect only those exposed to the release. Influenza keeps going, so the first few cases change the posture of the whole unit rather than just the treatment of those casualties.
items.a: It spreads efficiently from the casualty to the team and onward
w: It has no treatment
It only affects the people present at the release
It is a toxin rather than an organism

items.q: Why is a neuraminidase inhibitor started before test confirmation in suspected pandemic influenza?
items.x: Oseltamivir works best within 48 hours of symptoms. Waiting for confirmation commonly spends that window, so treatment is started on clinical suspicion in a suspected outbreak.
items.a: Its benefit falls off sharply after 48 hours from symptom onset
w: Testing is never available
It is harmless so the threshold does not matter
It also treats bacterial pneumonia

items.q: A soldier has fever, severe calf pain and red eyes without discharge, a week after a river crossing. What fits best?
items.x: Conjunctival suffusion without discharge plus severe calf pain after fresh-water exposure is close to specific for leptospirosis. It responds to doxycycline, so presumptive treatment is low-cost and the untreated severe form kills.
items.a: Leptospirosis
w: Dengue
Scrub typhus
Typhoid fever

items.q: What is the most useful physical finding in suspected scrub typhus, and why is it missed?
items.x: The eschar is painless and typically in the groin, axilla, waistband or under a breast, so it is only found if someone deliberately looks. Doxycycline usually breaks the fever within 48 hours.
items.a: A painless black eschar at the mite bite, usually hidden in a skin fold
w: A petechial rash on the palms
Splinter hemorrhages
Neck stiffness

items.q: How does typhoid fever differ from ordinary foodborne gastroenteritis?
items.x: Typhoid is a systemic illness, not a gut infection. Constipation is as common as diarrhea, the pulse is slower than the fever predicts, and the lethal complication is intestinal perforation in the third week.
items.a: Fever climbs stepwise over a week and the bowel can perforate in the third week
w: It resolves within 24 hours
It causes profuse watery diarrhea immediately
It is not treatable with antibiotics

items.q: Why does a hepatitis A cluster point to an exposure about a month earlier?
items.x: The long incubation hides the cause, so several people jaundiced in the same week shared an exposure weeks ago. Shedding also peaks before symptoms, so cases found late were infectious earlier.
items.a: The incubation period is 15 to 50 days
w: The virus takes a month to become infectious
Testing lags by four weeks
Jaundice is always a late sign of any illness

items.q: A soldier has had three weeks of pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics after working in desert dust, with red tender nodules on the shins. What fits?
items.x: Coccidioides lives in desert soil, and disturbing it aerosolizes spores. Erythema nodosum with a respiratory illness in that setting is close to diagnostic, and it points away from more antibacterials rather than toward them.
items.a: Coccidioidomycosis
w: Tuberculosis
Q fever
Psittacosis

items.q: In dengue, when does the dangerous phase begin?
items.x: Defervescence marks the start of the critical phase. A casualty who looks better as the fever settles but has abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or a rising hematocrit with falling platelets is entering plasma leak.
items.a: As the fever falls, when plasma leak starts
w: In the first 24 hours of fever
Only after the rash fades completely
Two weeks after recovery

items.q: Which analgesic is used in suspected dengue, and why?
items.x: Dengue causes thrombocytopenia and bleeding, which NSAIDs and salicylates worsen. Acetaminophen is the analgesic and antipyretic used throughout.
items.a: Acetaminophen, because NSAIDs and aspirin worsen the bleeding risk
w: Ibuprofen, because it also reduces plasma leak
Aspirin, because it prevents thrombosis
Ketorolac, because it is the most effective

items.q: How is dengue distinguished from a viral hemorrhagic fever in posture terms?
items.x: Dengue is mosquito-borne and not transmitted person to person, while Ebola, Marburg, Lassa and CCHF spread through fluids. A travel, mosquito and contact history is what separates them and determines the isolation posture.
items.a: Dengue does not spread between people, so isolation precautions differ
w: Dengue has a higher mortality
Dengue causes no bleeding
They are managed identically

items.q: A casualty pulled from a bunker is drooling, tearing, wheezing and twitching, with pinpoint pupils. Which endpoint guides atropine dosing?
items.x: Pupils can stay small for hours after secretions clear, so they are a poor endpoint. Atropine is titrated to dry secretions and improved ventilation; large cumulative doses may be needed.
items.a: Drying of airway secretions and easier ventilation
w: Return of pupils to normal size
A heart rate above 100
A fixed total dose of 6 mg

items.q: What does the oxime component of a nerve-agent auto-injector add that atropine does not?
items.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does nothing at the neuromuscular junction. An oxime such as pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme before it ages, which is where nicotinic weakness improves.
items.a: It reactivates acetylcholinesterase, which can help the muscle weakness
w: It blocks muscarinic receptors more completely
It stops seizures
It speeds skin decontamination

items.q: Which benzodiazepine role is specific to nerve-agent exposure?
items.x: Nerve-agent seizures respond poorly to most anticonvulsants and cause ongoing brain injury. A benzodiazepine is given for seizures and, in doctrine, alongside multiple auto-injectors in severe exposure.
items.a: Seizure control, which also limits nerve-agent brain injury
w: Reversing bradycardia
Reactivating cholinesterase
Drying secretions

items.q: A casualty has painless skin redness after a reported chemical attack, with blisters appearing hours later. Which agent fits?
items.x: Mustard exposure is typically painless at the time, with erythema in 2 to 24 hours and blistering later. Lewisite and phosgene oxime hurt immediately.
items.a: Sulfur mustard
w: Lewisite
Phosgene oxime
Hydrofluoric acid

items.q: How does fluid resuscitation for a large mustard blister injury differ from a thermal burn of the same size?
items.x: Mustard lesions are more superficial than they look and leak less. Applying a thermal burn formula unchanged tends to over-resuscitate, so fluids are titrated to perfusion and urine output.
items.a: Mustard injuries generally need less fluid than a thermal burn formula predicts
w: They need roughly twice the Parkland volume
They need no fluid at all
They need colloid only

items.q: Which vesicant has a specific chelating antidote?
items.x: Lewisite is an arsenical, and dimercaprol chelates arsenic. There is no antidote for sulfur or nitrogen mustard or for phosgene oxime; care is decontamination and wound care.
items.a: Lewisite, with dimercaprol
w: Sulfur mustard, with dimercaprol
Phosgene oxime, with pralidoxime
Nitrogen mustard, with hydroxocobalamin

items.q: A casualty from a fire in an enclosed space is comatose with a lactate of 14, normal-looking skin and no cyanosis. Which antidote is generally preferred?
items.x: In smoke inhalation, nitrites induce methemoglobinemia on top of possible carbon monoxide, further cutting oxygen carriage. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide without that problem.
items.a: Hydroxocobalamin
w: Sodium nitrite
Methylene blue
Dimercaprol

items.q: Why is the quiet interval after phosgene exposure a trap?
items.x: Phosgene injures the alveolar membrane slowly. A latent period of hours is common, exertion shortens and worsens it, so exposed casualties are kept at rest and observed even while well.
items.a: A casualty can look well for hours and then develop pulmonary edema, and exertion makes it worse
w: Symptoms always appear within minutes
The quiet interval means the dose was trivial
Phosgene has an antidote that must be given during it

items.q: What is the main difference in where chlorine and ammonia injure the airway?
items.x: Water solubility drives the level of injury. Ammonia dissolves in the upper airway, causing immediate pain and potential obstruction; chlorine is intermediate and reaches the lower airway as well.
items.a: Ammonia is highly water-soluble and hits the upper airway early, while chlorine reaches deeper
w: Chlorine hits the upper airway and ammonia the alveoli
Both injure only the alveoli
Neither affects the airway

items.q: Why can a small hydrofluoric acid burn be dangerous?
items.x: Burn size predicts systemic risk poorly with hydrofluoric acid. Absorbed fluoride chelates calcium and magnesium, so monitoring and calcium are considerations even with a modest-looking burn.
items.a: Fluoride is absorbed and binds calcium and magnesium, causing dysrhythmias
w: It converts to hydrochloric acid in the blood
It causes methemoglobinemia
It blocks cholinesterase

items.q: A worker collapses instantly in a sewer, and the first responder to approach also collapses. Which agent fits best?
items.x: Hydrogen sulfide at high concentration causes immediate knockdown, and rescuers are classic secondary casualties. Its rotten-egg smell is lost at dangerous concentrations.
items.a: Hydrogen sulfide
w: Carbon monoxide
Chlorine
Sulfur mustard

items.q: A casualty is hot, dry, flushed, confused and hallucinating, with dilated pupils and no sweating after a reported chemical release. Which picture is this?
items.x: This is the anticholinergic toxidrome, the opposite of the wet nerve-agent picture. Care is cooling, protection from injury and supportive sedation; physostigmine use is a medical direction decision.
items.a: An anticholinergic incapacitating agent
w: A nerve agent
Cyanide
Phosgene

items.q: Why are white phosphorus wounds kept wet during care?
items.x: Retained particles can reignite when they dry and contact air. Dressings are kept wet while particles are removed, and the dressings themselves are handled as a hazard.
items.a: Drying lets retained particles reignite in air
w: Water neutralizes phosphorus chemically
Wet dressings reduce pain only
It prevents absorption of phosphate

items.q: A casualty exposed to arsine develops dark urine, jaundice and anemia over hours. What is the main threat?
items.x: Arsine is a hemolytic gas. The danger is hemolysis and the pigment load on the kidneys, so care centers on supportive measures and renal protection, not blister care.
items.a: Massive hemolysis with kidney failure
w: Blistering of the skin
Cholinergic crisis
Pulmonary edema from the gas itself

items.q: Does dimercaprol treat arsine-induced hemolysis?
items.x: Although arsine is an arsenic compound, chelation does not address the hemolysis that causes the harm. Supportive care, transfusion as needed and renal protection are the mainstays.
items.a: No, chelation does not reverse the hemolysis
w: Yes, it is the first-line treatment
Yes, but only within one hour
Only when combined with an oxime

items.q: How does an organophosphate pesticide poisoning differ in course from a military nerve agent?
items.x: Lipophilic pesticides redistribute slowly, so cholinergic crisis can persist or relapse over days and infusions of antidote may be needed, while nerve-agent exposure tends to be shorter.
items.a: Pesticide effects can last days and may relapse, so prolonged treatment is common
w: It causes no cholinergic signs
Atropine is contraindicated
Oximes are never used

items.q: Which decontamination step matters most for a liquid nerve-agent or mustard exposure?
items.x: Removing clothing takes away most of the agent, and physical removal from skin limits both the casualty's dose and the risk to the team. Antidote and decontamination proceed together in severe exposure.
items.a: Removing clothing and physically removing the agent from skin early
w: Giving the antidote before any decontamination
Flushing the eyes only
Waiting for a decontamination line at the hospital

items.q: Why is pyridostigmine a pretreatment rather than a treatment?
items.x: Pyridostigmine bromide is taken before anticipated soman exposure to protect a reserve of enzyme. It is not a treatment, it does not replace antidotes, and it is stopped once exposure occurs and antidotes are given.
items.a: It reversibly occupies some cholinesterase so antidotes work better afterward, and it is stopped at exposure
w: It is an antidote given after exposure
It reactivates aged enzyme
It blocks mustard absorption

items.q: A crowd-control agent exposure leaves a casualty with burning eyes and coughing that improves within 30 minutes outdoors. What is the usual care?
items.x: Riot-control agents are irritants with short-lived effects. Care is removal from exposure, air, decontamination and eye irrigation; persisting or severe symptoms suggest a confined space, a different agent or asthma.
items.a: Fresh air, removing contaminated clothing and eye irrigation
w: Atropine and an oxime
Hydroxocobalamin
Dimercaprol

items.q: What makes the Novichok class a particular field problem?
items.x: These agents are persistent and have caused prolonged environmental contamination and secondary casualties. Care remains cholinergic management with high-dose atropine, oxime and benzodiazepine under medical direction.
items.a: Very low volatility and persistence, so contamination and secondary exposure last
w: They are not cholinesterase inhibitors
They cause blistering rather than cholinergic signs
Standard antidotes have no role at all

items.q: A casualty exposed to aircraft hydrazine fuel is seizing despite repeated benzodiazepines. What is specifically indicated?
items.x: Hydrazines interfere with pyridoxine-dependent enzymes, the same mechanism as isoniazid overdose. High-dose vitamin B6 is the specific treatment, given with benzodiazepines rather than instead of them.
items.a: High-dose pyridoxine
w: A second oxime dose
Hydroxocobalamin
Dimercaprol

items.q: Which poisoning is made worse by routine supplemental oxygen?
items.x: Paraquat concentrates in the lung and kills by oxidative damage, so oxygen feeds the mechanism. It is withheld unless hypoxia is severe, which inverts the usual reflex.
items.a: Paraquat ingestion
w: Carbon monoxide
Cyanide
Phosgene

items.q: Workers opening a fumigated shipping container collapse with refractory shock and a garlic odor. Which agent fits?
items.x: Aluminum and zinc phosphide release phosphine on contact with moisture. It blocks mitochondrial energy production, and the characteristic death is refractory cardiogenic shock within the first day.
items.a: Phosphine from metal phosphide fumigant
w: Chlorine
Sulfur mustard
Carbon monoxide

items.q: Why is gastric lavage with water avoided after metal phosphide ingestion?
items.x: The tablet releases phosphine gas on contact with moisture, so adding water to the stomach generates more of the toxic gas. Decontamination decisions here are made with poison center input.
items.a: Water releases more phosphine from the remaining tablet
w: It causes aspiration more than other lavage fluids
It neutralizes the antidote
It raises the risk of seizures

items.q: What makes nitrogen dioxide exposure different from chlorine?
items.x: Nitrogen dioxide has a two-phase course: delayed pulmonary edema, apparent recovery, then bronchiolitis obliterans weeks later. Discharging a well-looking casualty without a return instruction misses it.
items.a: A second illness, bronchiolitis obliterans, appears two to six weeks later
w: It causes no pulmonary edema
Effects are always immediate
It has a specific antidote

items.q: A casualty exposed to a tear-gas-like agent has eyes that settle in fresh air, but the exposure was heavy. What is the concern with chloropicrin specifically?
items.x: Chloropicrin combines immediate irritant effects with the delayed deep-lung injury of a choking agent. Treating it as a simple riot-control exposure and releasing the casualty misses the second part.
items.a: Delayed pulmonary edema hours later
w: Permanent corneal scarring within minutes
Cholinergic crisis
Hemolysis

items.q: How does diphosgene differ practically from phosgene?
items.x: Diphosgene is a liquid that breaks down into phosgene. The clinical course is the same, but it persists on clothing and equipment, so decontamination matters here in a way it does not for the pure gas.
items.a: It is a liquid, so it contaminates clothing and gear and keeps releasing phosgene
w: It has no latent period
It causes blistering rather than lung injury
It responds to an antidote

items.q: A casualty exposed to a vomiting agent such as adamsite reports that symptoms got worse after leaving the cloud. What does this mean?
items.x: The delayed onset and continued worsening after leaving the area is the characteristic feature, and it is what makes people remove their masks. Keeping the mask on through that window prevents a further dose.
items.a: This is expected; effects continue to worsen for 20 to 30 minutes after exposure ends
w: The mask failed and they took a second dose
They have been exposed to a nerve agent instead
They are having an allergic reaction

items.q: Several people in a building have headache and nausea, and a pulse oximeter reads 98 percent on all of them. What should be considered?
items.x: A pulse oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it reads normal in significant poisoning. A co-oximeter or blood gas is what answers the question, and oxygen is started on suspicion.
items.a: Carbon monoxide, which a pulse oximeter cannot distinguish from oxygen
w: Dehydration
Food poisoning
Nothing further; the saturation is reassuring

items.q: A casualty from an enclosed-space fire has a severe lactic acidosis and did not improve on high-flow oxygen. What else is likely present?
items.x: Burning synthetics release cyanide alongside carbon monoxide. Hydroxocobalamin treats the part oxygen cannot, and it is preferred over nitrites here because nitrites would add methemoglobinemia on top of the carbon monoxide.
items.a: Cyanide from burning synthetic materials
w: Methemoglobinemia from the smoke
Organophosphate exposure
Nothing; carbon monoxide explains it

items.q: What finding typically prompts the diagnosis of thallium poisoning, and why is that a problem?
items.x: The painful ascending neuropathy comes first and is often read as Guillain-Barre. The hair loss that names it arrives around two weeks, so waiting for it loses the window when Prussian blue works best.
items.a: Hair loss at around two weeks, by which point the treatment window has largely passed
w: Immediate blistering, which is easily confused with mustard
Pinpoint pupils on arrival
A positive bedside screening test

items.q: Several people become ill with seizures and severe acidosis after sharing a meal, and two arrest. What does the pattern suggest?
items.x: Multiple casualties from a shared source means the source is still active. Agents like sodium fluoroacetate are odorless, tasteless and water-soluble, and there is no antidote, so recognizing the pattern is what protects everyone else.
items.a: A deliberately contaminated food or water source that is still in use
w: An outbreak of viral gastroenteritis
Carbon monoxide in the building
Heat illness

items.q: A casualty has whole-body extensor spasms triggered by noise and touch, and is fully conscious throughout. What does that consciousness change?
items.x: Strychnine blocks spinal inhibition without affecting consciousness, so the casualty experiences all of it. A dark, quiet space with minimal handling is an active treatment, and paralysis without sedation would leave an aware, paralyzed casualty.
items.a: Sedation becomes part of the treatment, and stimulation is minimized
w: It confirms a seizure disorder rather than a poisoning
It means paralysis alone is sufficient
It rules out strychnine

items.q: A casualty received a significant whole-body dose from an external source and is not contaminated. What hazard do they pose to the team?
items.x: Irradiation and contamination are different things. A casualty exposed to external penetrating radiation is not a source, and delaying their care on that belief is the most common error in radiation events.
items.a: None. External irradiation does not make a person radioactive

items.a: Ongoing hemorrhagic shock with lactic acidosis and breathing compensation
w: Primary respiratory alkalosis from pain
Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation
Low blood oxygen from a chest injury

items.q: Fifteen minutes after a thigh gunshot wound, a tourniquet is in place. Heart rate is 128 and the casualty is pale. A sample is run before any fluid or blood. i-STAT (CG8+): Hematocrit 42%, Hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, pH 7.31, PCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 16.5 mmol/L, Base excess -10 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, Glucose 142 mg/dL. How is the normal hemoglobin best interpreted here?
items.x: Hemoglobin falls only after dilution. Base deficit and lactate rise sooner and track hemorrhage severity better. In the first hour after injury, hemoglobin and hematocrit can look normal even after large blood loss. Base deficit, lactate and the clinical exam are the earlier markers. Hematocrit is trended, and a falling value later can reflect both ongoing bleeding and dilution.
items.a: It reflects the lag of hemoglobin after acute bleeding; the base deficit is the earlier warning
w: It shows the blood loss was minor
It suggests the acidosis is a lab error
It means the tourniquet has fully stopped the shock process

items.q: A casualty with an abdominal wound had a lactate of 6.1 mmol/L and base excess of -12 an hour ago. After two units of whole blood and calcium, a repeat arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.36, PCO2 37 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L, Base excess -5 mmol/L, Lactate 2.8 mmol/L, PO2 98 mmHg, sO2 97%. What does the trend suggest?
items.x: Lactate fell by more than half and the base deficit narrowed from -12 to -5, a strong sign that shock is reversing. Lactate clearance (the percent fall over time) and an improving base deficit are among the best signs that resuscitation is working. A single high lactate means less than the trend. Ongoing values guide whether more blood or surgical control is needed.
items.a: Resuscitation is restoring perfusion and acid is clearing
w: The casualty is getting worse because lactate is still high
A new respiratory problem has appeared
The results are normal, so no more trending is needed

items.q: A casualty has a fragment wound to the forearm with minimal bleeding, now dressed. Heart rate is 96 and the casualty is anxious. An arterial sample is run as part of a routine work-up. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.41, PCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 1.3 mmol/L, PO2 96 mmHg, sO2 98%. What do these results show?
items.x: Every value is within range. The mild tachycardia fits anxiety and pain, and the exam and vital signs remain the main tools going forward. Most results in a minor injury are normal, and reading them as normal is a skill. A normal lactate and base excess make significant hidden hemorrhage unlikely at the time of the sample. A change in vital signs or exam is a reason to repeat the panel.
items.a: No lab evidence of shock at this time
w: Compensated shock hidden by a normal pH
Respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
Early metabolic acidosis

items.q: A casualty has received four units of cold-stored whole blood and tranexamic acid (TXA) during a long hold. Calcium has not yet been given. i-STAT (CG8+): pH 7.29, Ionized calcium 0.91 mmol/L, Potassium 5.6 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L, Glucose 128 mg/dL, Hematocrit 33%, Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL. Which finding is most directly caused by the transfusion and most urgent?
items.x: Citrate binds calcium. Low ionized calcium weakens clotting and heart contraction, which is why TCCC pairs calcium with the first unit of blood. Low ionized calcium is one of the most common and most treatable findings after transfusion. Citrate in each unit binds calcium, and hypocalcemia worsens bleeding and blood pressure. Ionized calcium is trended with each few units, alongside potassium.
items.a: Low ionized calcium from citrate in the stored blood
w: The glucose of 128 mg/dL
Low calcium caused by the TXA
The hematocrit, which proves the transfusion failed

items.q: During a massive transfusion of stored red cells and plasma, the cardiac monitor shows taller, peaked T waves. A sample is run. i-STAT (EG7+): Potassium 6.6 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 0.88 mmol/L, pH 7.22, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Hematocrit 30%. Which combination raises the most concern for a dangerous heart rhythm?
items.x: Each one adds to cardiac risk, and calcium stabilizes the heart muscle against potassium. The peaked T waves fit this combination. Massive transfusion can raise potassium (from stored red cells and acidosis) while lowering calcium (from citrate). The pair is especially dangerous for the heart. Calcium, correction of acidosis and fresher products are part of the response, and potassium and calcium are trended together.
items.a: High potassium together with low ionized calcium and acidosis
w: Normal sodium with normal PCO2
Low hematocrit alone
Low bicarbonate alone

items.q: Blood is being given rapidly through a fluid warmer. The casualty reports tingling around the mouth and fingers, and blood pressure has dropped despite the blood. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Ionized calcium 0.78 mmol/L, Potassium 4.6 mmol/L, Sodium 142 mmol/L, Chloride 104 mmol/L, Glucose 140 mg/dL, Hematocrit 35%, Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL. What best explains the tingling and low blood pressure?
items.x: Perioral and finger tingling with low blood pressure during rapid transfusion fits a very low ionized calcium. Calcium supports blood vessel tone and heart contraction. Rapid transfusion, liver injury and hypothermia slow citrate clearance, so ionized calcium can fall quickly. Numbness, tingling, muscle cramps, low blood pressure and a long QT interval are clues. Calcium replacement and ionized calcium trends are standard parts of transfusion care.
items.a: Citrate toxicity causing very low ionized calcium
w: High potassium from stored blood
Low blood sugar
Anemia alone

items.q: A casualty received two units of fresh whole blood collected from screened unit members. A blood gas and a clotting test are run together. i-STAT (CG8+ and PT/INR): Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 1.08 mmol/L, Hematocrit 37%, Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, pH 7.34, INR 1.2, PT 13.0 sec. Which statement fits these results?
items.x: Normal potassium and a near-normal INR fit fresh product; the mildly low ionized calcium reflects citrate. Fresh whole blood replaces red cells, plasma and platelets in one product with little stored-cell potassium. It is still anticoagulated with citrate, so ionized calcium is still trended. A stable INR and potassium after transfusion are reassuring signs.
items.a: Fresh whole blood supplies working clotting factors with little potassium load, but calcium can still fall
w: Fresh whole blood has no effect on calcium
The INR shows a worsening coagulopathy
The potassium shows a transfusion reaction

items.q: Midway through a unit of blood, a casualty develops fever, chills, low back pain and dark red urine. Hematocrit was 35% before this unit. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 5.9 mmol/L, Hematocrit 29%, Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 24 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.15 mmol/L, Sodium 139 mmol/L, Glucose 118 mg/dL. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Fever, back pain and dark urine during a unit, with rising potassium, falling hematocrit and rising creatinine, point to destruction of incompatible red cells. An acute hemolytic reaction is usually from blood group incompatibility. Stopping the transfusion and supporting blood pressure and kidney function are the core of care. Potassium, hematocrit and creatinine are trended, and the unit and labels are kept for review.
items.a: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
w: Citrate toxicity
Ongoing hemorrhage only
Stored-blood potassium load

items.q: Three hours after a blast, a casualty has a GCS of 14, headache and repeated vomiting. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Elevated, UCH-L1 Elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Glucose 98 mg/dL, Hematocrit 43%, Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL. What does an elevated TBI result mean here?
items.x: The i-STAT TBI test is cleared to help decide on CT in mild head injury (GCS 13 to 15) within 24 hours of injury. The TBI cartridge reports GFAP and UCH-L1 against set cutoffs. An elevated result means CT imaging is more likely to show an injury, which affects evacuation priority. It does not replace the neurologic exam, which is trended for any decline.
items.a: It indicates a higher chance of a CT-visible brain injury, supporting the need for CT imaging
w: It confirms a severe brain injury requiring surgery
It is explained by the vomiting and dehydration
It rules out concussion

items.q: Six hours after a nearby blast, a casualty has a GCS of 15, a mild headache and a normal neurologic exam. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Not elevated, UCH-L1 Not elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Glucose 94 mg/dL, Hematocrit 44%. How is this result best interpreted?
items.x: A negative TBI test has a high negative predictive value for CT findings. Concussion is a clinical diagnosis that the test does not exclude. A not-elevated TBI result can help show that a CT scan, and the evacuation needed to get one, may not be needed. It does not rule out concussion, so symptom tracking, rest and repeat neurologic checks continue. A worsening exam overrides a reassuring test.
items.a: A CT-visible brain injury is unlikely, but concussion is still possible and symptoms are followed
w: Concussion is ruled out and the casualty is cleared
The test is invalid because the chemistry is normal
A CT scan is urgent because of the headache

items.q: A head-injured casualty has received hypertonic saline twice for signs of rising brain pressure. Sodium was 141 mmol/L before the first dose. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 156 mmol/L, Chloride 121 mmol/L, TCO2 20 mmol/L, Anion gap 19 mmol/L, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, Glucose 182 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. How is the sodium of 156 mmol/L best read?
items.x: Head injury protocols accept a raised sodium to pull fluid out of the brain, and many treat values above about 160 mmol/L as a ceiling. Hypertonic saline raises sodium and chloride by design. Each dose is guided by the sodium trend, with many protocols treating about 160 mmol/L as an upper limit. High chloride can add a mild normal-gap acidosis, and glucose is kept out of the high range.
items.a: It reflects the intended effect of hypertonic saline, with limited room left before about 160 mmol/L
w: It shows dehydration and the need for more free water
It is a lab error because sodium cannot rise this fast
It explains the brain swelling

items.q: An intubated head-injured casualty is being bagged quickly during a bumpy ground transport. End-tidal CO2 reads low. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.53, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -2 mmol/L, PO2 112 mmHg, Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What is the main problem?
items.x: Fast bagging drives PCO2 down. In TBI, a PCO2 well below about 35 mmHg can worsen brain ischemia. In traumatic brain injury, ventilation is usually targeted to a PCO2 of about 35 to 40 mmHg. Over-ventilation is common during hand bagging and transport, and it narrows brain blood vessels. End-tidal CO2 is trended and matched against blood gas PCO2.
items.a: Over-ventilation causing respiratory alkalosis, which can reduce blood flow to the injured brain
w: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting
Low oxygen in the blood
Hemorrhagic shock

items.q: A casualty was pinned under a collapsed wall for several hours before extrication. The legs are swollen and tense. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 6.4 mmol/L, Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 31 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.02 mmol/L, TCO2 18 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L, Sodium 139 mmol/L, Glucose 112 mg/dL. What is the greatest immediate threat?
items.x: A potassium of 6.4 mmol/L, made worse by low calcium and acidosis, can cause sudden cardiac arrest. Crush syndrome releases potassium, acid, myoglobin and phosphate from damaged muscle. Potassium is the most immediate danger, followed by kidney injury. Large-volume fluid resuscitation, cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium values are core features of care.
items.a: High potassium and its effect on heart rhythm
w: The creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL
The sodium
The mild glucose rise

items.q: A casualty has been pinned at the thigh for about one hour and is still trapped. IV access is in place and a sample is run before release. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 4.6 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, BUN 18 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.16 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Glucose 132 mg/dL. What do these pre-release results tell you?
items.x: Reperfusion washes potassium and acid from the crushed muscle into circulation, so the post-release sample matters most. Before release, a crushed limb can hold its potassium and acid. Release restores flow and can cause a sudden potassium spike and cardiac arrest. A baseline panel helps, but post-release values and cardiac monitoring show the real risk.
items.a: Values are normal now, but potassium and acid can surge after release, so repeat values matter
w: Crush syndrome will not develop
The casualty has hidden hyperkalemia
The glucose shows diabetic ketoacidosis

items.q: After a long ruck march and heavy exercise in the heat, a soldier has severe thigh pain and cola-colored urine. Core temperature is 37.8 C (100 F) and mental status is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, BUN 28 mg/dL, Potassium 5.3 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 1.08 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L, Hematocrit 50%, Glucose 96 mg/dL. Which pattern fits best?
items.x: Muscle pain, dark urine, rising creatinine and potassium, and low calcium after heavy exertion fit muscle breakdown. Exertional rhabdomyolysis is common in training. The i-STAT does not measure CK (creatine kinase), so the diagnosis rests on the story, dark urine and lab clues such as rising potassium and creatinine. Fluid resuscitation and trends in potassium and kidney function guide care.
items.a: Exertional rhabdomyolysis with early kidney injury
w: Simple dehydration only
Heat stroke
Exercise-associated hyponatremia

items.q: Twenty minutes after a crushed leg was freed, the casualty's monitor shows widening QRS complexes. A sample is run. i-STAT (CG8+): Potassium 7.1 mmol/L, pH 7.24, HCO3 15 mmol/L, Base excess -12 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 0.98 mmol/L, Sodium 138 mmol/L, Hematocrit 47%. What best explains the sudden potassium rise?
items.x: Restored blood flow washes potassium and acid out of dead and injured muscle, and the ECG change matches. The minutes after release are the highest-risk period in crush injury. Potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes is an emergency, and calcium, measures that shift potassium into cells and fluid are part of hospital protocols. A hemolyzed sample can mislead, so the ECG and clinical picture are read alongside the number.
items.a: Reperfusion of the crushed limb releasing potassium and acid
w: Sample hemolysis, which fully explains the result
Kidney failure developing in twenty minutes
Stored blood transfusion

items.q: Six hours after a 45% body surface area burn, urine output has been low. Lactate was 2.4 mmol/L at the first draw. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.29, PCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Base excess -11 mmol/L, Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, PO2 88 mmHg. What does the rising lactate most likely reflect?
items.x: Large burns leak plasma into tissue. Rising lactate, a deepening base deficit and low urine output point to too little circulating volume. Burn shock develops over hours as plasma leaks into burned and unburned tissue. Urine output is the main guide to burn fluids, and rising lactate or base deficit add warning that resuscitation is falling behind. In an enclosed-space burn, carbon monoxide or cyanide are also considered when lactate is high.
items.a: Burn shock from under-resuscitation
w: Normal healing response
Respiratory failure from smoke
Fluid overload

items.q: Four hours after a large flame burn, the casualty has had limited fluid during a delayed evacuation. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Hematocrit 56%, Hemoglobin 19.0 g/dL, Sodium 147 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, Potassium 4.8 mmol/L, Glucose 168 mg/dL. What does the high hematocrit mean here?
items.x: Burns leak plasma, concentrating red cells. Rising BUN, creatinine and sodium add to the picture of low volume. A rising hematocrit early after a large burn reflects plasma loss, not more red cells. It falls as resuscitation restores volume. Kidney values and urine output show whether perfusion is improving.
items.a: Loss of plasma volume with hemoconcentration, a marker of a fluid deficit
w: The casualty has too many red cells and needs no fluid
It is a lab error
It rules out internal bleeding

items.q: A casualty was pulled from a burning vehicle after several minutes inside. There is a headache, confusion and soot around the nose. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): PO2 96 mmHg, sO2 98%, pH 7.30, PCO2 35 mmHg, HCO3 17 mmol/L, Base excess -9 mmol/L, Lactate 5.2 mmol/L. Why is the sO2 of 98% misleading here?
items.x: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin tightly, but PO2 stays normal. Only co-oximetry measures the true fraction of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. In carbon monoxide poisoning, PO2, calculated sO2 and standard pulse oximetry can all look normal. Headache, confusion, enclosed-space exposure and a high lactate are the clues, and high-concentration oxygen is the core treatment. Cyanide often coexists in smoke, especially when lactate is very high.
items.a: It is calculated from PO2 and cannot detect carboxyhemoglobin; co-oximetry is needed
w: It is not misleading; oxygen delivery is normal
Smoke raises the PO2 falsely
Pulse oximetry and the i-STAT both measure carbon monoxide directly

items.q: A casualty touched a high-voltage line. There are small entry and exit burns on the hand and foot, and the forearm is swollen and firm. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL, BUN 22 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.05 mmol/L, Glucose 120 mg/dL, Hematocrit 45%. What do these results suggest?
items.x: High potassium, rising creatinine and low calcium after high-voltage injury point to deep muscle breakdown. High-voltage electrical injury damages muscle along the current path, often with little skin injury. Labs often look like crush syndrome: high potassium, falling calcium and kidney injury. Burn formulas based on skin area underestimate the fluid needs, and urine output and potassium trends guide care.
items.a: Deep muscle injury with rhabdomyolysis, similar to crush injury
w: The injury is minor because the skin burns are small
Simple dehydration
Hemorrhagic shock

items.q: After several doses of an opioid for a leg fracture, a casualty is difficult to wake, breathing 6 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. An arterial sample is drawn on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.24, PCO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 62 mmHg, sO2 88%, Lactate 1.2 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
items.x: A high PCO2 with low pH and near-normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, matching the slow breathing and pinpoint pupils. Opioid oversedation suppresses breathing, raising PCO2 and lowering PO2. A normal bicarbonate shows the change is acute. Airway support, ventilation and opioid reversal are the core of care, and capnography (end-tidal CO2) is the field trend to follow.
items.a: Acute respiratory acidosis from opioid-related hypoventilation
w: Metabolic acidosis from shock
Mixed metabolic and respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis from pain

items.q: An intubated casualty on a transport ventilator has a set rate of 8 with a small tidal volume. End-tidal CO2 has been climbing. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.27, PCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 145 mmHg, Lactate 1.1 mmol/L. What does this pattern point to?
items.x: High PCO2 with normal bicarbonate on a low set rate and small volume points to under-ventilation. Oxygenation and ventilation are separate problems. PO2 mainly reflects oxygen settings and lung function, while PCO2 reflects minute ventilation. A high PCO2 on a ventilator usually means rate or tidal volume is set too low for the casualty. End-tidal CO2 is trended after each change and compared with blood gas PCO2.
items.a: Ventilator minute ventilation is too low to clear CO2
w: The ventilator is delivering too little oxygen
Shock is causing metabolic acidosis
The casualty is over-ventilated

items.q: A casualty with a painful ankle fracture is breathing fast, reports tingling hands and is very anxious. There is no fever, and the chest exam is normal. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.51, PCO2 29 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 104 mmHg, sO2 98%, Lactate 1.2 mmol/L. What is the most likely disturbance?
items.x: High pH, low PCO2 and normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory alkalosis. Normal PO2 and lactate make low oxygen or sepsis less likely. Pain and anxiety commonly cause respiratory alkalosis, and the low CO2 can cause tingling and cramps. Before settling on that explanation, low oxygen, early sepsis, pulmonary embolism and chest injury are considered. A normal PO2 and lactate help narrow the cause.
items.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis from pain and anxiety
w: Metabolic alkalosis
Compensated metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis

items.q: A team has been operating at about 10,000 feet for two days. One member reports mild headache and breathlessness on exertion. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.47, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -3 mmol/L, PO2 60 mmHg, sO2 91%, Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What best describes these results?
items.x: Low PO2 drives hyperventilation, and the mildly low bicarbonate shows the kidneys adjusting over days. At altitude, low PO2 and respiratory alkalosis are expected, and the kidneys lower bicarbonate over days. Values that move outside this pattern, such as worsening PO2 or rising lactate, can signal altitude illness such as high-altitude pulmonary edema. Symptoms and trends matter more than one sample.
items.a: An expected altitude pattern: hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis and early kidney compensation
w: Severe lactic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis from altitude
Carbon monoxide poisoning

items.q: The casualty from an earlier under-ventilation case had the ventilator rate increased. A repeat arterial sample is run twenty minutes later. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.39, PCO2 41 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, PO2 118 mmHg, Lactate 1.0 mmol/L. What do the repeat results show?
items.x: pH and PCO2 are normal. The only value out of range is a high PO2 from supplemental oxygen. After a ventilator change, a repeat gas confirms the effect. Normal pH and PCO2 show ventilation now matches the casualty's needs. A PO2 well above range on oxygen is not harmful in the short term but often allows oxygen to be reduced, which conserves supply in the field.
items.a: The ventilator change corrected the CO2, and oxygenation is more than adequate
w: A new metabolic acidosis
Ongoing hypoventilation
Dangerous hypoxemia

items.q: During a long training day in the heat, a trainee drank large amounts of water. The trainee is now confused and vomiting, with swollen hands. Core temperature is 38.0 C (100.4 F). i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 124 mmol/L, Chloride 91 mmol/L, Potassium 3.7 mmol/L, BUN 7 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, Glucose 92 mg/dL, Anion gap 14 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of the confusion?
items.x: A sodium of 124 mmol/L with low BUN after heavy drinking fits dilution. Low sodium causes brain swelling and confusion. Exercise-associated hyponatremia and heat stroke can look alike in the field, with confusion after exertion in the heat. Sodium separates them: low in overhydration, normal or high in heat stroke. Giving more plain water worsens hyponatremia, and treatment centers on restricting water and, for severe symptoms, hypertonic saline.
items.a: Exercise-associated hyponatremia from excess water intake
w: Heat stroke with dehydration
Hypoglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis

items.q: A soldier collapsed near the end of a timed run. Core temperature is 41.5 C (106.7 F) and the soldier is combative and confused. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 148 mmol/L, BUN 32 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, Potassium 5.2 mmol/L, Glucose 64 mg/dL, Hematocrit 52%, Hemoglobin 17.7 g/dL, TCO2 19 mmol/L. Which pattern fits best?
items.x: Very high core temperature with altered mental status is heat stroke. High sodium, BUN and hematocrit show dehydration, and creatinine shows organ injury. Heat stroke is defined by high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction. Rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion, is the most important treatment and comes first. Labs show the organ damage: kidney injury, muscle breakdown, low glucose and, later, clotting problems.
items.a: Heat stroke with dehydration, early kidney injury and low glucose
w: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Simple heat exhaustion
Diabetic ketoacidosis

items.q: A casualty with a leg wound was pulled from a cold river after 40 minutes. Core temperature is 31 C (87.8 F). The analyzer and cartridges were kept warm in a chest pocket. Results are reported at 37 C (98.6 F). i-STAT (CG8+): pH 7.28, PCO2 47 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -5 mmol/L, Potassium 3.2 mmol/L, Glucose 185 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.10 mmol/L, Hematocrit 49%. Which statement best fits these results?
items.x: Hypothermia slows breathing, impairs perfusion, suppresses insulin and moves potassium into cells. Rewarming changes all of these, so values are trended. Hypothermia, acidosis and bleeding form the trauma lethal triad. Blood gases are analyzed at 37 C (98.6 F), and many clinicians read them uncorrected. The i-STAT has an ambient operating range, so cartridges and the device are kept within it in cold environments.
items.a: Cold is contributing to the acidosis, glucose rise and potassium shift, and these change during rewarming
w: The low potassium means potassium is low in the whole body
The high glucose means diabetes
The results are invalid because the patient is cold

items.q: After a long patrol in the heat, a soldier is tired, nauseated and dizzy on standing. Core temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F) and mental status is normal. The soldier has been drinking a mix of water and electrolyte drinks. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 141 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, BUN 20 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, Glucose 98 mg/dL, Hematocrit 47%. What do these results suggest?
items.x: Symptoms with normal mental status and normal labs fit heat exhaustion. Cooling, rest and oral fluids are typical care, with reassessment for any change. Heat exhaustion causes fatigue, dizziness and nausea without central nervous system dysfunction or organ injury. Normal sodium, potassium, BUN and creatinine help rule out the dangerous look-alikes. Any confusion or a rising core temperature changes the picture to possible heat stroke.
items.a: Heat exhaustion without electrolyte or kidney problems
w: Heat stroke
Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Exertional rhabdomyolysis

items.q: A casualty was rescued from a burning building filled with smoke from burning plastics. Breathing is labored, blood pressure is low, and the casualty is on high-flow oxygen. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.12, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 9 mmol/L, Base excess -21 mmol/L, Lactate 11.8 mmol/L, PO2 210 mmHg. Which cause best explains a very high lactate with a high PO2?
items.x: Cyanide stops cells from using oxygen. A lactate above about 8 to 10 mmol/L after smoke exposure strongly suggests cyanide, even with good PO2. Burning plastics, foam and wool release hydrogen cyanide. A very high lactate with good oxygenation, low blood pressure and altered mental status after smoke exposure is the classic clue. Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) is the antidote used in this setting, and carbon monoxide often coexists.
items.a: Cyanide poisoning from burning plastics
w: Respiratory acidosis from smoke in the airway
Low oxygen in the blood
Mild heat exhaustion

items.q: After a suspected nerve agent exposure, a casualty has heavy secretions, wheezing, pinpoint pupils and muscle twitching. An arterial sample is drawn on room air. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.22, PCO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 24.5 mmol/L, Base excess -3 mmol/L, PO2 58 mmHg, sO2 86%, Lactate 3.4 mmol/L. What is the dominant problem?
items.x: The high PCO2 with normal bicarbonate and low PO2 show the lungs and breathing muscles are failing, the main cause of death in nerve agent poisoning. Nerve agents cause excess secretions, bronchospasm and breathing muscle weakness, leading to combined respiratory failure. Lab values show severity but do not make the diagnosis, which is clinical. Drying secretions and supporting ventilation are central to care.
items.a: Respiratory failure: high PCO2 and low PO2 from secretions and weak breathing
w: Pure metabolic acidosis from shock
Respiratory alkalosis
Carbon monoxide poisoning

items.q: A service member found confused in the motor pool admits drinking from an unmarked bottle several hours ago. There is no injury, no history of diabetes, and blood pressure is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): TCO2 10 mmol/L, Anion gap 32 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Chloride 102 mmol/L, Potassium 4.5 mmol/L, Glucose 101 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 15 mg/dL. What best explains this high anion gap acidosis?
items.x: A large gap with normal glucose, normal blood pressure and a history of drinking an unknown liquid fits a toxic alcohol. A high anion gap acidosis has a short list of causes: lactate, ketones, kidney failure and toxins such as toxic alcohols and salicylates. Lactate measurement helps rule out shock, and some lab methods can read glycolate from ethylene glycol as lactate. Antifreeze and windshield fluid are found in motor pools, and specific antidotes and dialysis are used in hospital care.
items.a: Toxic alcohol poisoning such as ethylene glycol (antifreeze)
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Uremia from kidney failure
Hyperchloremic acidosis from saline

items.q: A service member took most of a bottle of aspirin after a personal crisis. There is ringing in the ears, vomiting and fast, deep breathing. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.44, PCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Base excess -8 mmol/L, Lactate 2.6 mmol/L, PO2 104 mmHg. What does the normal pH hide?
items.x: Salicylate stimulates breathing and also creates metabolic acid. The two offset each other, leaving a deceptively normal pH. When pH is normal but PCO2 and bicarbonate are both abnormal, two disorders are present. Salicylate poisoning classically causes this mix. Losing the breathing compensation, for example from sedation or a ventilator set too low, lets the pH drop sharply, which is why ventilation is managed carefully in these patients. Behavioral health care is part of the full response.
items.a: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, typical of salicylate poisoning
w: Nothing; the acid-base status is normal
Simple respiratory alkalosis from anxiety
Compensated respiratory acidosis

items.q: Three days after a fragment wound to the calf during a prolonged hold, a casualty has fever, a heart rate of 112 and a breathing rate of 26. The wound is red and draining. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.48, PCO2 31 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 2.6 mmol/L, PO2 88 mmHg, sO2 97%. What do these results most likely represent?
items.x: Fast breathing with a low PCO2 is often one of the earliest sepsis signs, and a lactate above 2 mmol/L adds concern. Respiratory alkalosis is a common early sign of sepsis, before acidosis develops. A lactate above 2 mmol/L in suspected infection marks higher risk. Source control of the wound, antibiotics and fluids are core sepsis care, and a repeat lactate shows the direction.
items.a: Early sepsis with respiratory alkalosis and a rising lactate
w: Anxiety only
Hemorrhagic shock
Acute respiratory acidosis

items.q: A casualty with a known abdominal wound infection now has low blood pressure despite fluids, cool mottled skin and confusion. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.27, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 13 mmol/L, Base excess -14 mmol/L, Lactate 5.4 mmol/L, PO2 76 mmHg. What is the main problem?
items.x: Low blood pressure despite fluids, with a lactate over 4 mmol/L and a deep base deficit, fits septic shock. Septic shock combines infection, low blood pressure needing support and a raised lactate. Fluids, antibiotics, source control and blood pressure support are central, and the lactate trend over hours shows whether perfusion is improving. In prolonged casualty care, early evacuation or telemedicine consultation is part of planning.
items.a: Septic shock with lactic acidosis
w: Primary respiratory failure
Metabolic alkalosis
Mild infection without organ dysfunction

items.q: Five days into a prolonged hold, a casualty with an infected burn has had little urine output over the last 12 hours. The casualty has no history of diabetes. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, Potassium 5.4 mmol/L, Sodium 135 mmol/L, Glucose 182 mg/dL, TCO2 17 mmol/L, Chloride 99 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L. What best fits these results?
items.x: Low urine output with rising creatinine, BUN and potassium in an infected casualty points to sepsis-related kidney injury. Acute kidney injury is a common organ failure in sepsis. Rising creatinine and BUN with falling urine output are the markers, and potassium becomes a growing danger. Kidney injury also changes how fluids and many medications are handled, which is part of prolonged care planning.
items.a: Sepsis with acute kidney injury and rising potassium
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Simple dehydration
Hyperchloremic acidosis

items.q: A casualty has a mildly red, warm wound edge and a temperature of 38.2 C (100.8 F). Heart rate is 92 and blood pressure is normal. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 1.1 mmol/L, PO2 95 mmHg. How are these results best interpreted?
items.x: Normal lactate and acid-base values are reassuring, but a local infection can still progress. A normal lactate and blood gas in a local infection is a good sign but not a final answer. Infections can progress over hours, especially in prolonged care. Vital signs, wound appearance and a repeat lactate if things change are the key trends.
items.a: No lab sign of sepsis-related hypoperfusion now; the wound and vital signs are trended
w: They rule out infection
They show early septic shock
They show hidden respiratory alkalosis

items.q: A service member with type 1 diabetes ran out of insulin during a long mission. There is vomiting, abdominal pain, deep fast breathing and a fruity breath odor. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Glucose 486 mg/dL, TCO2 8 mmol/L, Anion gap 32 mmol/L, Potassium 4.8 mmol/L, Sodium 131 mmol/L, Chloride 96 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. How is the potassium of 4.8 mmol/L best interpreted?
items.x: Insulin drives potassium back into cells. In DKA, a normal starting value often drops into a dangerous low range during treatment. DKA shows high glucose, low bicarbonate and a high anion gap. Potassium may look normal or even high at first, yet total body potassium is low. DKA protocols track potassium closely, often every one to two hours, because insulin moves it into cells.
items.a: The blood value looks normal, but the body is depleted, and potassium will fall when insulin is started
w: Potassium is normal and needs no attention
Potassium is high and dangerous
Potassium does not change in DKA

items.q: The DKA casualty from the earlier case has had four hours of IV fluids and an insulin infusion. The casualty now reports muscle weakness and the monitor shows flattened T waves. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 3.1 mmol/L, Glucose 238 mg/dL, TCO2 15 mmol/L, Anion gap 21 mmol/L, Sodium 137 mmol/L, Chloride 104 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Why has the potassium fallen?
items.x: Insulin moves potassium into cells. DKA protocols typically pause insulin when potassium falls below about 3.3 mmol/L until it is replaced. Low potassium is a major cause of preventable harm during DKA treatment. As insulin works, potassium drops, often fast. Weakness and ECG changes such as flattened T waves or U waves are warning signs, and potassium replacement is part of every DKA protocol.
items.a: Insulin is driving potassium into cells, exposing the total-body deficit
w: The lab has made an error
Potassium is being lost in vomit only
The kidneys have failed

items.q: After a long patrol with little food, a soldier who uses insulin is sweating, shaky and confused. There is no head injury and core temperature is normal. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Glucose 38 mg/dL, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, BUN 14 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, Hematocrit 45%. What explains the confusion?
items.x: A glucose of 38 mg/dL explains sweating, shaking and confusion. All other values are normal. Hypoglycemia is quick to identify and correct, and it can mimic head injury, intoxication or heat illness. A glucose check belongs early in any altered mental status work-up. The other normal values here help rule out the look-alikes.
items.a: Hypoglycemia from insulin use with little food intake
w: Exercise-associated hyponatremia
Heat stroke
Kidney failure

items.q: A service member has had several days of vomiting from a stomach illness with little intake. A blood gas and chemistry panel are run together. i-STAT (CG4+ and CHEM8+): pH 7.52, HCO3 37 mmol/L, PCO2 47 mmHg, Potassium 3.0 mmol/L, Chloride 88 mmol/L, TCO2 38 mmol/L, BUN 30 mg/dL. What is the primary disturbance?
items.x: High pH and bicarbonate after vomiting, with low chloride and potassium, is a classic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. Vomiting removes acid and chloride, raising bicarbonate. The kidneys then hold sodium and lose potassium, which worsens the alkalosis. Fluid and electrolyte replacement, especially chloride and potassium, corrects this pattern.
items.a: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting with low chloride and potassium
w: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis

items.q: A casualty received large volumes of normal saline during a long delay before blood was available. Bleeding is controlled and blood pressure is now normal. i-STAT (CG4+ and CHEM8+): Chloride 116 mmol/L, TCO2 18 mmol/L, Sodium 144 mmol/L, Anion gap 14 mmol/L, pH 7.31, Lactate 1.3 mmol/L, Potassium 4.2 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. What is the cause of the acidosis?
items.x: High chloride, low bicarbonate and a normal gap with normal lactate point to the saline itself. Large volumes of normal saline cause a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis. It can be mistaken for ongoing shock, but a normal lactate and gap tell them apart. TCCC favors blood products for hemorrhagic shock, and balanced crystalloids such as lactated Ringer's carry less chloride than saline.
items.a: Hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) acidosis from large-volume saline
w: Lactic acidosis from ongoing shock
Ketoacidosis
Kidney failure

items.q: A casualty had hours of low blood pressure before reaching a surgical team. Two days later in a prolonged care setting, urine output has fallen. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, BUN 54 mg/dL, Potassium 5.8 mmol/L, TCO2 17 mmol/L, Anion gap 24 mmol/L, Sodium 137 mmol/L, Hematocrit 32%, Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL. What best explains these results?
items.x: Rising creatinine, BUN and potassium with low urine output after hours of low blood pressure fit kidney injury from poor perfusion. Shock-related kidney injury shows rising creatinine and BUN, falling urine output, high potassium and high anion gap acidosis. Fluid balance becomes delicate because the kidneys cannot clear excess. Potassium, creatinine and urine output are the key trends, and severe cases need dialysis.
items.a: Acute kidney injury from prolonged shock
w: Normal recovery after surgery
Simple dehydration
Hyperchloremic acidosis

items.q: A soldier has had diarrhea for two days during a field exercise and has been drinking little. The soldier is dizzy on standing but alert. i-STAT (CHEM8+): BUN 38 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, Sodium 147 mmol/L, Hematocrit 50%, Potassium 4.4 mmol/L, Glucose 102 mg/dL. What does the BUN to creatinine ratio suggest?
items.x: A ratio above 20 with high sodium after fluid loss points to low volume. This often reverses with fluids. A high BUN to creatinine ratio with signs of dehydration suggests a prerenal problem that usually reverses with fluid. Creatinine returning toward normal after fluids confirms it. A rising creatinine despite fluids suggests the kidney itself is injured.
items.a: Prerenal kidney stress from dehydration
w: Intrinsic kidney damage
Rhabdomyolysis
Exercise-associated hyponatremia

items.q: A casualty had a sodium of 118 mmol/L that had fallen slowly over several days. Twelve hours after treatment began, a repeat sample is run. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 130 mmol/L, Chloride 96 mmol/L, Potassium 3.8 mmol/L, Glucose 96 mg/dL, BUN 9 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. What is the main concern?
items.x: With slowly developing hyponatremia, the brain adapts. A rise faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours can damage brain cells. In hyponatremia that developed over more than about 48 hours, rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination, a severe and sometimes permanent brain injury. Many guidelines limit the rise to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Frequent sodium checks are how the rate is tracked.
items.a: Sodium has risen too fast, raising the risk of osmotic demyelination
w: Sodium is still low, so correction is too slow
No concern because the casualty is improving
Potassium is the problem

items.q: Before blood was available, a casualty received large volumes of crystalloid and then red cells only, with no plasma or whole blood. The casualty is now oozing from IV sites. i-STAT (PT/INR and CHEM8+): INR 1.9, PT 21.5 sec, Hematocrit 28%, Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, Ionized calcium 0.95 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L. What explains the rising INR?
items.x: Fluids and red cells without plasma replace volume but not clotting factors, so the INR rises. Dilutional coagulopathy develops when volume is replaced without clotting factors. Whole blood or balanced plasma, platelets and red cells limit it, which is why TCCC prefers whole blood. INR and calcium trends help track it.
items.a: Dilution of clotting factors by crystalloid and plasma-free red cells
w: Warfarin use
Lab error from the low hematocrit
Normal response to injury that needs no attention

items.q: A hypothermic trauma casualty (core temperature 33 C (91.4 F)) is oozing from every wound. A clotting test and a blood gas are run. i-STAT (PT/INR and CG8+): INR 1.1, PT 12.0 sec, pH 7.25, Ionized calcium 1.05 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, Hematocrit 36%. Why is the casualty bleeding despite a normal INR?
items.x: Clotting enzymes slow down in the cold. The INR test warms the blood, hiding this, and it does not assess platelets. Hypothermia, acidosis and low calcium all impair clotting, and none of them show up fully in a standard INR run at 37 C (98.6 F). Warming, correcting calcium and acidosis and using whole blood address this. A normal INR in a cold, bleeding casualty is not reassuring.
items.a: The INR is measured at 37 C (98.6 F), so it misses cold-related clotting failure; acidosis and low calcium add to it
w: The INR proves clotting is normal
The oozing is from high potassium
The low hematocrit alone explains the bleeding

items.q: Within an hour of a severe blast injury, before any fluid or blood has been given, a clotting test and blood gas are run. The casualty is in shock. i-STAT (PT/INR and CG4+): INR 1.5, PT 17.4 sec, pH 7.26, PCO2 33 mmHg, HCO3 14 mmol/L, Base excess -13 mmol/L, Lactate 5.9 mmol/L. What best explains the INR rise?
items.x: Severe injury and shock trigger clotting failure within minutes, before any dilution. It is linked to higher mortality. Acute traumatic coagulopathy appears early in severe injury with shock. It is a reason that TCCC emphasizes early whole blood, TXA and calcium. Shock severity markers such as base deficit and lactate often move with it.
items.a: Acute traumatic coagulopathy from shock and tissue injury
w: Dilution from fluids
Warfarin use
Lab error from acidosis

items.q: An older civilian casualty fell and struck the head. Family members report the casualty takes warfarin. The neurologic exam is normal so far. i-STAT (PT/INR and CHEM8+): INR 3.4, PT 36 sec, Hematocrit 40%, Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Why does this INR matter for a head injury?
items.x: An INR of 3.4 means slower clotting, and head injury in anticoagulated patients carries a high risk of delayed intracranial bleeding. The i-STAT PT/INR test is designed for monitoring warfarin. It is not reliable for heparin or the newer direct oral anticoagulants. In head injury, a raised INR from warfarin raises the priority for CT and reversal at a higher level of care.
items.a: Anticoagulation raises the risk of delayed brain bleeding, which raises evacuation and imaging priority
w: It does not matter if the exam is normal
It shows dilutional coagulopathy
It shows acute traumatic coagulopathy from shock

items.x: Non-compressible bleeding needs blood, TXA and a surgeon. Hypotensive resuscitation limits clot disruption until surgery. Non-compressible torso hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable combat death. TCCC: resuscitate to a palpable radial pulse, normal mentation or a systolic pressure near 100, with whole blood and TXA, while pushing for surgical care.

Ertapenem is the TCCC parenteral choice. Keeping the casualty without food or drink protects the airway and a later surgery, and a damp gauze eases thirst.

items.x: Fresh whole blood supplies red cells, plasma and working platelets. Calcium corrects the citrate effect seen on the i-STAT. The walking blood bank uses prescreened donors whose type is confirmed in the field with a rapid typing card. Ionized calcium falls with every citrated unit, and repeat i-STAT checks guide replacement.
items.a: Walking blood bank activated with ABO confirmation on donors and recipient, and calcium replacement
w: Hetastarch to stretch the remaining resources
Vasopressin to support blood pressure until surgery
No more blood because systolic pressure is above 80

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+3 (Patrol base): After a unit of fresh whole blood, his radial pulse is stronger and he answers questions clearly. The team plans the night. Which monitoring plan fits best?
items.x: Frequent, structured reassessment catches re-bleeding early and creates the trend record for teleconsult and handoff. The PCC flowsheet records vitals, intake, urine output, medications and products over time. Trends drive decisions during a long hold and give the receiving surgeon the story.
items.a: A Foley with hourly urine output, vitals every 15 to 30 minutes, serial abdominal exams and a PCC flowsheet
w: Vital signs every 4 hours to let him sleep
Blood pressure alone as the trigger for action
