A nasogastric tube passed blind to check for blood in the stomach

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+6 (Patrol base): His pain is 9 out of 10 and he is guarding his abdomen. A teammate worries that pain medication will hide a worsening exam. Which analgesic approach fits best?
items.x: Both work quickly with IV or IO access and are TCCC options for severe pain. Ketamine is favored if pressure drops again. Pain control is part of care, not a threat to diagnosis. TCCC and the JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG favor titrated fentanyl or ketamine for severe pain and avoid NSAIDs other than meloxicam in casualties who may bleed.
items.a: Titrated IV fentanyl or ketamine, with pain and sedation scores recorded
w: Ketorolac, since it avoids opioid side effects
Analgesia withheld to keep the abdominal exam reliable
IM morphine for its longer effect

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+12 (Patrol base): He is stable through the night. Hemoglobin is holding. A teammate suggests raising his pressure further with fluid and starting clot prevention. What fits best now?
items.x: With bleeding controlled for now, the goal is steady perfusion without over-resuscitation while surgery is awaited. After the shock phase, prolonged care shifts to careful maintenance and watching for re-bleeding. DVT prophylaxis waits until bleeding is surgically controlled, a decision made with a teleconsult.
items.a: Measured maintenance fluid with ongoing reassessment, nothing by mouth, and a teleconsult update
w: Enoxaparin started to prevent DVT during the long hold
Large crystalloid boluses to push systolic pressure higher
A regular meal to support healing

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He is confused and breathing fast. His abdomen is rigid and tender everywhere. His skin is warm and flushed. What is happening, and what fits best?
items.x: Fever, confusion, fast breathing, low pressure and high lactate after bowel injury add up to septic shock that needs source control. The JTS Sepsis in PFC CPG uses early recognition, fluid boluses with reassessment, broad antibiotics and vasopressors when needed. Source control means surgery here, so the casualty's evacuation priority rises.
items.a: Septic shock from peritonitis; fluid bolus with reassessment, antibiotic coverage reviewed by teleconsult, lactate repeated, evacuation priority raised
w: Re-bleeding; more whole blood
Fever only; acetaminophen and recheck in 4 hours
Fluids withheld to avoid abdominal swelling

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+32 (Long hold, day 2): After two fluid boluses his lungs are still clear, but his mean arterial pressure stays low and his urine output is falling. What is the best next step?
items.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock once initial fluid has been given. Septic shock: MAP target of 65 or more, norepinephrine first, vasopressin as a second agent. Infusions in the field need a secure line, a pump or careful drip counting, and close blood pressure checks.
items.a: Norepinephrine titrated to a MAP of at least 65 through secure access
w: Dopamine as the first vasopressor
Repeated boluses until crackles appear
A MAP of 58 accepted since he is still mentating

items.q: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): A helicopter is inbound. He is on norepinephrine with improving lactate. The team prepares for handoff. Which handoff fits best?
items.x: Complete documentation lets the surgical team act right away and avoid repeating or missing treatments. The DD1380 and PCC flowsheet travel with the casualty. They include tourniquet and product times, walking blood bank donor information, medications with times, and trends in vitals, urine output and labs.
items.a: DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with trends, all products and donor IDs, antibiotic and infusion times, plus a MIST verbal report
w: A quick verbal summary to the flight medic
A blank DD1380 sent with a promise to email details later
Only the most recent set of vital signs

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:10 (Point of injury): He has snoring respirations and does not open his eyes to pain. External bleeding is controlled. What fits best for his airway?
items.x: With a GCS of 7 and hypoxia, he needs a definitive airway. Ketamine or etomidate with rocuronium keeps blood pressure stable. In TBI, a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension raises mortality. TCCC and the JTS TBI in PFC CPG aim for SpO2 above 90% and avoid hypotension during airway management. Ketamine is acceptable in TBI.
items.a: Rapid sequence intubation with a hemodynamically stable induction agent and a paralytic, with preoxygenation and waveform capnography
w: A nasopharyngeal airway and observation
Hyperventilation by bag right away to reduce brain swelling
Midazolam alone to facilitate intubation

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated and on the ventilator. A teammate set a high rate to protect his brain. How is ventilation best adjusted?
items.x: Normal CO2 keeps cerebral blood flow steady. Hyperventilation is a short bridge only for active herniation. JTS TBI in PFC targets: SpO2 above 90%, normal EtCO2 near 35 to 40 mmHg, systolic pressure above 110 mmHg, head of bed raised about 30 degrees, and normal temperature and glucose.
items.a: Rate reduced to bring EtCO2 to 35 to 40 mmHg
w: EtCO2 kept at 28 to protect the brain
EtCO2 allowed to rise to 50 for lung protection
Only FiO2 adjusted, since EtCO2 is not relevant in TBI

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): His right pupil is now 6 mm and sluggish, the left is 3 mm. His blood pressure is rising and his heart rate is falling. What fits best now?
items.x: A blown pupil with the Cushing triad signals herniation. Hypertonic saline draws water from the brain and supports pressure. Herniation signs: a dilated or sluggish pupil, posturing, falling GCS, or the Cushing triad of high blood pressure, slow heart rate and irregular breathing. JTS favors hypertonic saline. Mannitol is an alternative but can lower blood pressure through diuresis.
items.a: Hypertonic saline bolus, head of bed at 30 degrees with the neck straight, brief hyperventilation to EtCO2 near 30 to 35 as a bridge, and an urgent teleconsult
w: Metoprolol to bring blood pressure down
Atropine for the bradycardia
Observation until both pupils are fixed

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+2 (Casualty collection point): He has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting more than 2 minutes. The ventilator alarms. What fits best?
items.x: Midazolam or lorazepam stops the seizure quickly, and levetiracetam covers the early post-injury period. The JTS TBI in PFC CPG recommends seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam for severe TBI for about 7 days. Active seizures are stopped first with a benzodiazepine while watching blood pressure.
items.a: A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, then levetiracetam for ongoing prophylaxis
w: A paralytic to stop the movement
Levetiracetam alone, then waiting for it to work
Observation, since seizures stop on their own

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+4 (Patrol base): He is settled after the seizure. Labs come back. A teammate wants to start a dextrose-containing maintenance fluid. Which fluid plan fits best?
items.x: Isotonic fluid avoids pulling water into the brain, and repeat checks catch dangerous sodium or glucose shifts. In TBI, sodium is kept normal to mildly high with a target set by teleconsult, and swings are avoided. Glucose is kept roughly in the 80 to 180 mg/dL range because both low and high glucose harm the injured brain.
items.a: Isotonic fluid such as Plasma-Lyte or normal saline, with sodium and glucose rechecked every 4 to 6 hours
w: Dextrose-containing maintenance fluid
Large volumes of Lactated Ringer's to keep the kidneys perfused
Fluids stopped to keep the brain dry

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+8 (Patrol base): He coughs and bucks against the ventilator during suctioning. His heart rate and blood pressure spike. What fits best?
items.x: Coughing and agitation raise intracranial pressure. Analgesia first, then sedation, protects the brain while keeping pressure up. Analgesia-first sedation reduces intracranial pressure spikes. Ketamine does not raise intracranial pressure in ventilated patients when CO2 is controlled. Propofol lowers intracranial pressure but often drops blood pressure.
items.a: Analgesia and sedation deepened with ketamine and fentanyl, propofol only if blood pressure allows
w: Rocuronium alone to stop the bucking
Restraints only, since medications cloud the neuro exam
Suctioning stopped completely

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+14 (Patrol base): After propofol was increased, his blood pressure dropped. A teammate says a systolic of 92 is fine under TCCC. What fits best?
items.x: Removing the cause and supporting pressure maintains brain perfusion. TBI blood pressure target: systolic above 110 mmHg in the JTS TBI in PFC CPG. When sedation lowers pressure, the sedative is adjusted first and a vasopressor is added as needed.
items.a: Propofol reduced, volume status checked, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine or phenylephrine to keep systolic above 110
w: A systolic of 92 accepted as within TCCC targets
Head of bed lowered flat to raise blood pressure
More hypertonic saline only

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has jumped to about 300 mL per hour of pale, watery urine. No hypertonic saline has been given in 10 hours. What is most likely, and what fits best?
items.x: Large volumes of dilute urine with rising sodium after severe TBI point to diabetes insipidus. Central diabetes insipidus can follow severe TBI. Clues are high urine output, dilute urine and rising sodium. Treatment needs teleconsult guidance, and sodium is lowered slowly.
items.a: Diabetes insipidus from pituitary injury; teleconsult, hypertonic saline held, and water replacement guided by frequent sodium checks
w: Response to earlier hypertonic saline; more hypertonic saline
Normal diuresis; no change
Fluid restriction to slow urine output

items.q: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His temperature is climbing. His eyes are not fully closed, and his skin over the sacrum is pink. Which care fits best?
items.x: Fever control, eye protection and pressure injury prevention are core nursing tasks in prolonged TBI care. Prolonged TBI nursing includes normal temperature, eye care, oral care, head of bed at 30 degrees, repositioning every 2 hours, and recording GCS and pupil checks on the flowsheet.
items.a: Cooling and acetaminophen, a search for infection, eye lubrication and taping, and repositioning every 2 hours
w: Fever left alone as a normal response
Ice packs to the head only
Turning stopped to avoid raising intracranial pressure

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:10 (Point of injury): His nasal hair is singed, his voice is hoarse and he is coughing up black sputum. Mild stridor has started. What fits best for his airway?
items.x: Hoarseness, stridor and carbonaceous sputum predict airway swelling. Intubating early is easier and safer. Signs of inhalation injury: facial burns, singed hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness and stridor. The JTS Burn CPG supports early intubation when these are present and transport will be prolonged.
items.a: Early rapid sequence intubation by the most experienced provider, with a cricothyroidotomy kit ready
w: Observation until stridor worsens
Nebulized racemic epinephrine as the main airway treatment
A nasopharyngeal airway

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated. He was confused before intubation and the fire was in an enclosed space. The pulse oximeter reads high, but the i-STAT lactate is very high. What fits best?
items.x: An enclosed-space fire, altered mental status, hypotension and very high lactate suggest cyanide, and hydroxocobalamin is the preferred antidote. Smoke from burning plastics and furnishings contains carbon monoxide and cyanide. High-flow oxygen treats CO, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin turns skin and urine red and can interfere with some lab tests.
items.a: 100% oxygen and hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide poisoning
w: SpO2 of 99% taken as proof of good oxygenation
Sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Amyl nitrite for cyanide

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+1 (Casualty collection point): His burns are mapped and estimated at 40% TBSA, not counting superficial redness. A teammate wants a large fluid bolus based on the Parkland formula. Which fluid approach fits best?
items.x: The Rule of Ten gives a quick starting rate from TBSA and weight, and urine output guides changes from there. TCCC and the JTS Burn CPG use the Rule of Ten for adults 40 to 80 kg: TBSA rounded to the nearest 10, times 10, gives the starting hourly rate. Superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.
items.a: Lactated Ringer's started at the Rule of Ten rate, then titrated hourly to urine output
w: The full first 8-hour Parkland volume given as a bolus
Hetastarch to reduce the total volume
Fluids withheld until 2 hours after the burn

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+3 (Patrol base): A Foley catheter is in. Urine output over the last hour is low and dark. Heart rate is climbing. What is the best adjustment?
items.x: Hourly titration to urine output is the standard way to adjust burn fluid. In burns, urine output is the main resuscitation gauge: about 30 to 50 mL per hour for adults. The fluid rate is raised or lowered in steps, and every hour is recorded on the burn flowsheet.
items.a: Lactated Ringer's rate increased stepwise, with urine output rechecked each hour toward a target of about 30 to 50 mL per hour
w: A large bolus to catch up
Mannitol to increase urine output
Low urine output accepted as expected in burns

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+6 (Patrol base): Ventilator peak pressures have risen and his chest barely moves. The circumferential chest burn is leathery and tight. After a quick DOPE check is normal, what fits best?
items.x: A tight chest eschar can restrict ventilation, and releasing it restores chest wall movement. Circumferential burns of the chest or limbs can restrict breathing or circulation. Escharotomy is a high-risk procedure in the field, usually done with teleconsult guidance when ventilation or limb perfusion is failing.
items.a: Chest escharotomy with teleconsult guidance
w: Sedation increased
A paralytic to improve compliance
PEEP increased alone

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+10 (Patrol base): The burns are exposed while being checked. The room is cool and his temperature is dropping. Which wound and temperature plan fits best?
items.x: Burned skin cannot hold heat, so covering, warming the room and warming fluids prevent hypothermia. Burn casualties lose heat quickly through damaged skin. The JTS Burn CPG emphasizes dry dressings, active warming and a warm environment. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for burns alone.
items.a: Clean, dry burn dressings, an active warming blanket, a warm room, and warmed fluids
w: Cool, wet dressings over all the burns for comfort
Burns left open to air to let them dry
Prophylactic systemic antibiotics for the burns

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+16 (Patrol base): He grimaces during dressing changes and his heart rate jumps. He is ventilated. Which analgesia and sedation approach fits best?
items.x: Burn pain is severe and spikes with dressing changes, so analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and fentanyl fits. Burns are among the most painful injuries. Analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and opioids is common. Burn patients often need more than expected, and pain and sedation scores are recorded on the flowsheet.
items.a: Ketamine and fentanyl titrated to pain and sedation scores, with extra analgesia before dressing changes
w: Ketorolac for analgesia
Midazolam alone for sedation
Dressing changes stopped to avoid pain

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His endotracheal tube cuff fails and he needs re-intubation. A teammate grabs succinylcholine. Which paralytic fits best?
items.x: Rocuronium avoids the burn-related hyperkalemia risk and still allows rapid sequence intubation. After about 24 hours, burns increase muscle acetylcholine receptors, and succinylcholine can cause a life-threatening rise in potassium. The same risk applies to crush injury, prolonged immobility and denervation injuries.
items.a: Rocuronium
w: Succinylcholine for its fast onset and short duration
No paralytic, sedation only
Succinylcholine with calcium given ahead of time

items.q: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has been 80 to 100 mL per hour for several hours. His face, arms and abdomen are very swollen. What fits best?
items.x: Over-resuscitation causes abdominal compartment syndrome, worsening lung function and limb compartment problems. Fluid creep is a major cause of burn complications. When urine output exceeds the target, the rate is lowered stepwise. A tense abdomen with rising airway pressures can signal abdominal compartment syndrome.
items.a: Lactated Ringer's rate reduced stepwise, with abdominal pressure and airway pressures checked
w: The fluid rate kept the same
An extra bolus to protect the kidneys
Hetastarch to pull fluid back into the vessels

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0 (Point of injury): He is awake and talking. Engineers are ready to lift the slab in about 10 minutes. What fits best before release?
items.x: Fluid before release dilutes the potassium, acid and myoglobin that flood in when blood returns to the crushed muscle. Crush syndrome develops after compression of large muscle groups, often more than an hour. Preparation before release includes access, fluid, a cardiac monitor and medications for hyperkalemia ready to give.
items.a: IV or IO access with isotonic fluid running before the slab is lifted, and the cardiac monitor attached
w: Immediate lift, with fluids started once he is out
Oral water only
Lift delayed several hours to plan the evacuation

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): Minutes after release, the monitor shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS. His heart rate is slowing. What comes first?
items.x: Calcium protects the heart within minutes and buys time for the potassium-lowering treatments. Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: calcium first to stabilize the heart, then shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose, albuterol, and bicarbonate if acidotic. Only dialysis or the kidneys remove potassium from the body.
items.a: Calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane
w: Insulin with dextrose to lower potassium
Sodium bicarbonate alone
Potassium recheck in 2 hours

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:50 (Casualty collection point): After calcium, the QRS narrows. A teammate says the problem is fixed. What fits best next?
items.x: These shift potassium into cells and lower the serum level while the kidneys recover. Calcium stabilizes but does not lower potassium. The JTS Hyperkalemia CPG lists insulin and dextrose, albuterol and bicarbonate as shift therapies, with potassium and glucose rechecked often.
items.a: Regular insulin with dextrose, nebulized albuterol, and sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis
w: No further treatment since the ECG improved
Potassium-containing maintenance fluid
Repeated calcium alone every 30 minutes

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+2 (Patrol base): He is sweaty and confused. The i-STAT is rechecked. What fits best?
items.x: Hypoglycemia is a common complication of insulin for hyperkalemia and is quickly reversed with dextrose. Insulin for hyperkalemia commonly causes hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours later. Hourly glucose checks for several hours are part of the treatment.
items.a: Dextrose, with glucose checked every hour while insulin effects last
w: More insulin to keep potassium falling
Observation since potassium is improving
Albuterol for the confusion

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+4 (Patrol base): His urine is dark brown like tea. A Foley is in, and output is low. Which plan fits best?
items.x: High urine flow flushes myoglobin through the kidneys and lowers the risk of kidney failure. Rhabdomyolysis from crush injury releases myoglobin that damages the kidneys. The goal is high urine output with isotonic fluid, while watching for lung crackles and edema.
items.a: Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target of about 200 to 300 mL per hour, with lung and edema checks
w: Fluids restricted to protect the lungs
Mannitol as first-line treatment
Dark urine accepted as expected

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+8 (Patrol base): His left calf is tense and shiny. He has severe pain when his toes are moved and numbness on top of his foot. Pulses are present. What fits best?
items.x: Pain with passive stretch and numbness suggest compartment syndrome. Present pulses do not rule it out. Compartment syndrome signs: severe pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling and numbness. In crush injury, the fasciotomy decision is complex and is made with expert teleconsult input.
items.a: Leg kept at heart level, tight dressings loosened, hourly compartment checks, and a teleconsult about fasciotomy
w: Leg elevated high to reduce swelling
Ice packs and more opioid
Waiting until pulses are lost

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+14 (Patrol base): Potassium is rising again. Urine output has dropped despite fluids, and there are new crackles in both lungs. What fits best?
items.x: Kidney failure with rising potassium needs dialysis, which only a hospital can provide. Oliguric kidney failure after crush injury needs dialysis. In the field, potassium is managed with repeated shift therapy and the evacuation priority rises.
items.a: Repeat shift therapy, fluids reduced, oxygen, and an urgent teleconsult to raise evacuation priority for dialysis
w: More fluid boluses to restart urine flow
Potassium chloride in the IV fluid
Atropine for prevention

items.q: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and in severe pain from his legs. Kidney function is poor. Which analgesic approach fits best?
items.x: Neither relies on the kidneys for clearance as much as morphine, so they are better choices in kidney failure. In kidney failure, NSAIDs are avoided and morphine is used with caution. Fentanyl and ketamine are preferred. Pain and sedation scores are recorded with each dose.
items.a: Fentanyl or ketamine titrated to pain, with sedation and breathing watched
w: Ketorolac or meloxicam for non-opioid pain control
Morphine repeated as needed
Pain medication withheld because of kidney failure

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:05 (Point of injury): The wound bubbles with each breath. He is short of breath but talking in full sentences. Breath sounds are present on both sides. What fits best for the wound?
items.x: A vented seal stops air entry through the wound while letting pleural air escape, and tension can still develop later. TCCC: open or sucking chest wounds receive a vented or non-vented chest seal, then the casualty is monitored for tension pneumothorax. Placing the casualty in the sitting or recovery position, injured side down, can ease breathing when the casualty is conscious.
items.a: A vented chest seal applied, then close watch for progressive respiratory distress
w: Wound left open to air so tension cannot build
Needle decompression before the seal goes on
Hemostatic gauze packed into the chest wound

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is gasping and anxious. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The chest seal was burped and briefly removed without improvement. What fits best?
items.x: Suspected tension pneumothorax with shock and hypoxia is decompressed right away, and TCCC lists both sites. TCCC: suspected tension pneumothorax with progressive respiratory distress on the injured side is decompressed with a needle, and repeated if signs return. Simple thoracostomy is an option for providers trained in it.
items.a: Needle decompression at the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line or the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
w: Observation until tracheal deviation confirms tension
A fluid bolus to treat the falling blood pressure
Intubation and positive pressure ventilation first

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): He improved, then tired and was intubated with ketamine and rocuronium. On the ventilator, his oxygen and pressure fall again and peak pressure climbs. What fits best?
items.x: Positive pressure keeps refilling the pleural space, and an open finger thoracostomy decompresses it reliably in a ventilated casualty. In a ventilated casualty, recurrent tension after needle decompression is an indication for simple thoracostomy by a trained provider. A chest tube follows when the hold is long and a kit and teleconsult are available.
items.a: Finger (simple) thoracostomy at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
w: More needle decompressions, one every few minutes
Tidal volume increased to improve oxygen
Sedation deepened for ventilator dyssynchrony

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+3 (Patrol base): A chest tube placed with teleconsult guidance drains about 900 mL of blood at once and then keeps dripping. His pressure is still low. What fits best?
items.x: Hemorrhagic shock from a hemothorax needs blood, and hourly output tells whether surgery is urgent. Surgical bleeding is suggested by about 1,500 mL drained at once, or about 200 mL per hour for 2 to 4 hours. Chest tube output is recorded hourly on the PCC flowsheet alongside vitals and products.
items.a: Whole blood, TXA because he is within 3 hours of injury, calcium, warming, and hourly chest tube output tracking
w: Chest tube clamped to tamponade the bleeding
Crystalloid bolus to bring pressure up
Output ignored now that the lung has re-expanded

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+6 (Patrol base): His SpO2 drops suddenly and the ventilator alarms high pressure. The EtCO2 waveform is still present but smaller. The chest tube has stopped draining. What fits best?
items.x: DOPE finds the cause in a structured way; a kinked or clotted tube with a new pneumothorax fits these findings. DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment. Bagging off the ventilator separates a patient problem from a machine problem, and a chest tube that suddenly stops draining is checked for kinks, clots and position.
items.a: Disconnection from the ventilator, bag ventilation, and a DOPE check that includes chest tube patency
w: FiO2 and PEEP raised and the alarm silenced
More sedation for coughing
Paralysis to lower airway pressure

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+10 (Patrol base): Chest tube output has been about 150 to 200 mL per hour for 3 hours. All stored units are used. What fits best?
items.x: This bleeding likely needs a thoracotomy, so the team raises priority and replaces blood until then. Ongoing hemothorax output is one of the clearest field signals that surgery is needed. The teleconsult report includes hourly output, products given, and vital sign and lab trends.
items.a: Teleconsult reporting the trend, evacuation priority raised to urgent surgical, and fresh whole blood from the walking blood bank
w: A second chest tube to drain faster
Output accepted as normal after a chest wound
Chest tube clamped to slow the loss

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+18 (Patrol base): Bleeding has slowed. An arterial i-STAT is run on FiO2 0.6. He has a large pulmonary contusion. Which ventilator adjustment fits best?
items.x: Rate clears CO2 and PEEP recruits lung without the overstretch of larger breaths. Lung-protective ventilation uses tidal volume based on ideal body weight, a plateau pressure under 30, and PEEP and FiO2 adjusted together. Mild permissive hypercapnia is acceptable when there is no brain injury.
items.a: Lung-protective tidal volume kept, PEEP titrated for oxygenation, and rate increased for CO2
w: Sodium bicarbonate for the low pH
Tidal volume increased well above the lung-protective range to clear CO2
FiO2 at 1.0 for the rest of the hold

items.q: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He has a new fever and thick yellow secretions on suctioning. The head of the litter has been flat most of the night. What fits best?
items.x: Fever with purulent secretions in a ventilated casualty suggests pneumonia, and the bundle limits further aspiration. Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention includes head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning and daily sedation checks. New fever in prolonged care prompts a source search and antibiotic choice guided by teleconsult.
items.a: Pneumonia bundle with head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning, and an antibiotic chosen with teleconsult
w: Chest tube removed as the likely source
Acetaminophen and recheck later
Suctioning reduced to rest the airway

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0 (Point of injury): He is confused and combative. His skin is hot and still sweaty. A rectal thermometer is in the aid bag. What fits best?
items.x: Time above about 40 C (104 F) drives organ injury, and rapid cooling within 30 minutes gives the best outcomes. Exertional heat stroke is a high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction. Sweaty skin does not rule it out. Cold water immersion is the fastest method, with tarp-assisted cooling or ice sheets as field alternatives.
items.a: Immediate whole-body cooling with cold water immersion or tarp-assisted cooling with ice water
w: Shade, loosened gear and oral water
Evacuation first, with cooling at the aid station
Acetaminophen for the high temperature

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:20 (Point of injury): His rectal temperature is falling quickly. A teammate wants to keep cooling until it reaches 37 C (98.6 F). When is active cooling stopped?
items.x: Stopping near 39 C (102.2 F) avoids overshoot, and ongoing checks catch rebound. Active cooling stops near 39 C (about 102 F) measured rectally. Oral, ear and forehead readings are unreliable in heat stroke, and rebound hyperthermia is common in the first hours.
items.a: At about 39 C (102.2 F), with continued rectal temperature checks
w: When shivering starts
Only once mental status is fully normal

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:30 (Point of injury): During cooling he has a generalized seizure and fights the tarp. What fits best?
items.x: Midazolam or diazepam stops seizures and shivering, both of which generate heat. Benzodiazepines are the agents of choice for seizures, agitation and shivering during heat stroke cooling. Antipsychotics are avoided.
items.a: A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, with cooling continued and the airway protected
w: Haloperidol for the agitation
Cooling paused until the seizure ends
Restraints to keep him on the tarp

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:45 (Casualty collection point): Cooling is done but he is still slow to answer. An i-STAT CHEM8+ is run. What fits best?
items.x: Hypoglycemia after prolonged exertion adds to his confusion and corrects quickly. Glucose is checked in every casualty with altered mental status. Exertional illness can also cause hyponatremia, so sodium guides fluid choice. Both are trended on the PCC flowsheet.
items.a: Dextrose, then repeat glucose checks
w: Free water by mouth for the low sodium
Insulin with dextrose for the potassium
Observation, since confusion is expected after heat stroke

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+2 (Patrol base): A Foley drains a small amount of cola-colored urine. His legs ache. What fits best?
items.x: Brisk urine flow protects the kidneys from myoglobin, and potassium is watched as muscle breaks down. Exertional heat stroke often causes rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. Isotonic fluid is titrated to a high urine output, watching for crackles, edema and falling sodium.
items.a: Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target, with lung checks and potassium trends
w: Fluids restricted to avoid swelling
A diuretic to increase urine flow
Cola-colored urine accepted as dehydration that will clear

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+8 (Patrol base): There is new oozing from IV sites and his gums, and petechiae on his chest. What fits best?
items.x: Heat stroke can trigger DIC, which needs factor replacement and hospital care. DIC is a late, ominous complication of heat stroke, often with liver injury. Field care is supportive: blood products when available, avoidance of drugs that worsen bleeding, and urgent evacuation.
items.a: Teleconsult, whole blood or plasma if available, and a higher evacuation priority
w: TXA to stop the oozing
Enoxaparin to treat microclots
Aspirin for the petechiae

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+16 (Patrol base): His temperature rebounds. His right upper abdomen is tender. A teammate reaches for fever medication. What fits best?
items.x: Rebound hyperthermia is treated the same way as the first episode: physical cooling. Rebound hyperthermia is common after heat stroke. External cooling is the treatment, and liver injury from heat stroke is another reason to avoid acetaminophen.
items.a: External cooling restarted with ice water and fanning, with rectal temperature monitored
w: Ketorolac to bring the temperature down
Acetaminophen to bring the temperature down
Observation, since the peak has passed

items.q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and oriented and says he feels fine. Evacuation is inbound. What fits best?
items.x: This record lets the hospital judge kidney, liver and clotting injury and plan follow-up. Feeling well does not mean organ recovery. Kidney, liver and clotting injury evolve over days, and the record of cooling start time, peak temperature and lab trends guides care and return-to-duty decisions.
items.a: DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with cooling times, temperatures, glucose, labs and urine output, plus a MIST report
w: Return to duty since he feels better
A verbal handoff only
The last set of vital signs only

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+2 (Patrol base): He is bucking the ventilator, grimacing and reaching for the tube. What fits best?
items.x: Pain is the most common driver of agitation in a fresh trauma casualty. The JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG uses analgesia-first sedation. Pain is scored with a tool such as CPOT or a behavioral scale when the casualty cannot talk, and RASS is recorded with every check.
items.a: Analgesia first with ketamine or fentanyl, then sedation titrated to a RASS goal of 0 to -2
w: Rocuronium to stop him fighting the ventilator
Midazolam alone to calm him
Soft restraints and observation

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+6 (Patrol base): A teammate added propofol for better sedation, and his pressure dropped. What fits best?
items.x: Ketamine supports blood pressure and breathing, which fits a recently bled trauma casualty. Propofol is short acting but causes vasodilation and hypotension. In prolonged casualty care with limited monitoring, ketamine is often the backbone agent, with fentanyl for analgesia.
items.a: Propofol reduced or stopped, with ketamine as the main agent and volume status checked
w: Propofol continued and a vasopressor added to cover it
A switch to dexmedetomidine
Midazolam in place of propofol

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+10 (Patrol base): While turning him, the team hears gurgling at the mouth. The EtCO2 waveform disappears and his SpO2 falls. What fits best?
items.x: A lost waveform after moving a casualty is displacement until proven otherwise. Waveform capnography is the fastest monitor for displacement. DOPE starts with D, and tube depth at the teeth is recorded on the flowsheet and checked after every move.
items.a: Tube displacement recognized, bag-mask ventilation, and re-intubation confirmed by waveform capnography
w: FiO2 increased to 100%
Needle decompression on both sides
Suctioning through the tube

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+18 (Patrol base): He does not open his eyes to voice or move to shoulder shaking. His sedation has not been lightened since H+6. What fits best?
items.x: Light sedation is the goal, and reassessing pain avoids swinging into agitation. Daily sedation lightening and a set RASS target reduce ventilator days and delirium. Reversal agents are for overdose emergencies, not routine sedation adjustment.
items.a: Sedation lightened toward a RASS of 0 to -2, with pain reassessed as he wakes
w: Deep sedation kept for comfort
Flumazenil to wake him
Naloxone for full opioid reversal

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Skin checks show a patch of non-blanching redness over the sacrum and red heels. He has been on a litter for a day. What fits best?
items.x: Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury, and offloading prevents progression. Litters and ventilated immobility cause pressure injuries fast. JTS PCC guidance includes turns every 2 hours, padding, skin checks, and keeping skin dry, all recorded on the PCC flowsheet.
items.a: Repositioning every 2 hours, padding over bony areas, heels floated off the litter, and skin documented
w: Massage of the red area to restore blood flow
Turns every 6 hours to let him rest
A donut-shaped cushion under the sacrum

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): Hemoglobin has been stable on three checks, the leg wound is dry, and he has no brain or spinal cord injury. A teammate asks about clot prevention. What fits best?
items.x: With hemorrhage controlled and no brain injury, the benefit of prophylaxis outweighs the bleeding risk. Trauma casualties are hypercoagulable after the first day. Enoxaparin prophylaxis begins once bleeding is controlled, often around 24 to 36 hours, with teleconsult input. Intermittent compression devices can be used earlier when carried.
items.a: Enoxaparin started now that bleeding is controlled, after a teleconsult
w: Aspirin for DVT prevention
No prophylaxis until he reaches a hospital
Enoxaparin given at H+1, right after the wound was packed

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+36 (Long hold, day 2): He has been ventilated with nothing by mouth for 36 hours. There is a small amount of coffee-ground fluid in the mouth during suctioning. What fits best?
items.x: Acid suppression protects the stomach, and gastric access allows decompression and early nutrition. Ventilated trauma casualties are at high risk for stress ulcers. Pantoprazole or famotidine and early enteral nutrition through a gastric tube are standard in prolonged care, and nutrition is planned with teleconsult guidance.
items.a: Stress ulcer prophylaxis, an orogastric tube to decompress the stomach, and a teleconsult about starting enteral feeding
w: No action, since the amount is small
An oral diet once he is lighter
IV fluids alone for nutrition

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+48 (Long hold, day 3): Dexmedetomidine was added to ease agitation as sedation was lightened. His heart rate falls and he looks pale. What fits best?
items.x: Bradycardia and hypotension are expected effects of dexmedetomidine and usually improve when it is reduced. Dexmedetomidine allows light, rousable sedation but causes bradycardia and hypotension. It is reduced or stopped first. Atropine or glycopyrrolate treats symptomatic bradycardia.
items.a: Dexmedetomidine reduced or stopped, with atropine or glycopyrrolate ready if he becomes unstable
w: Dexmedetomidine increased because he is still restless
Haloperidol added for agitation
Observation only, since heart rate often drops with sedation

items.q: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+72 (Long hold, day 3): The evacuation aircraft is inbound. He is on ketamine and fentanyl at a RASS of -1. Which handoff fits best?
items.x: A complete record supports safe continuity of care and avoids missed or repeated treatments. In a 72-hour hold, the PCC flowsheet is the medical record. It includes sedation and pain scores, ventilator settings, devices with placement times, medications with times, skin and wound checks, and intake and output.
items.a: PCC flowsheet with RASS and pain scores, ventilator settings, tube depth, line and drain times, medications with times, skin checks and intake and output
w: A verbal report to the flight crew
A blank DD1380 with a note to call later
The last set of vital signs only

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1 (Casualty collection point): Stored blood is gone and he is still in shock. Several soldiers volunteer to donate. Which donor approach fits best?
items.x: Pre-deployment screening plus field confirmation and labeling lower the risk of mismatch and clerical error. The JTS Whole Blood Transfusion CPG relies on prescreened donors, low titer O when the recipient type is unknown, field ABO confirmation, and careful labeling. Most severe reactions come from identification errors.
items.a: Prescreened donors from the roster, with ABO confirmed by rapid typing on both donor and recipient and each unit labeled
w: Any volunteer whose ID tag says type O
The first available volunteer, to save time
No transfusion until evacuation

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:40 (Casualty collection point): Fifteen minutes into the first fresh unit he develops a high fever, back and flank pain, oozing around the IV, and dark red urine in the Foley bag. What fits best?
items.x: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, oozing and dark urine early in a unit point to an acute hemolytic reaction. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: fever, chills, flank or back pain, hypotension, red or dark urine and oozing from DIC, usually early in the unit. The first step for any suspected reaction is stopping the transfusion.
items.a: Transfusion stopped at once, the line kept open with saline through new tubing, and donor and recipient identity and typing rechecked
w: Transfusion slowed and the casualty watched closely
Acetaminophen for the fever and the unit continued
Diphenhydramine and the unit continued

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:50 (Casualty collection point): The transfusion is stopped. He remains hypotensive and urine output is low and dark. What fits best?
items.x: Hemolysis causes shock, kidney injury, high potassium and DIC, so support focuses on each. Hemolytic reactions release potassium and free hemoglobin. Support includes blood pressure, urine output to protect the kidneys, treatment of hyperkalemia, and watching for DIC.
items.a: Blood pressure supported with fluid and norepinephrine, high urine output maintained, potassium and calcium treated, and a teleconsult
w: The same unit restarted once his pressure improves
Sodium bicarbonate as the main treatment
Observation until the fever breaks

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+2:30 (Casualty collection point): Retyping shows the recipient is type A. The donor recorded as O retypes as B. The tube labels were swapped during collection. Which donor fits best for the next unit?
items.x: These are compatible with a type A recipient, and one-at-a-time labeling prevents another swap. Fresh whole blood is type-specific or low titer O. Collecting and labeling one donor at a time, with two-person checks, prevents most clerical errors.
items.a: Type A or low titer O donor, both confirmed by rapid typing, with one collection labeled at a time
w: Another type B donor
Any type O donor without a known titer
No more blood after a reaction

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+4 (Casualty collection point): During a type A unit his temperature rises and he shivers. Blood pressure is stable, urine is clear, and there is no pain or rash. What fits best?
items.x: Isolated fever and chills with stable vitals fit a febrile non-hemolytic reaction once worse causes are excluded. Febrile non-hemolytic reactions are common, especially with fresh whole blood. Hemolysis and bacterial contamination are excluded before deciding to resume or use another unit.
items.a: Transfusion paused, hemolysis and contamination looked for, acetaminophen for fever, and a teleconsult decision on resuming or using a new unit
w: Transfusion continued without a pause
Epinephrine for the reaction
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+5 (Casualty collection point): During the next unit, hives appear on his chest and he itches. Breathing, voice and blood pressure are normal. What fits best?
items.x: Isolated hives are a mild allergic reaction, which is the one reaction where the same unit is often resumed. Mild allergic reactions cause hives and itching only. Wheezing, throat tightness, swelling or hypotension change the picture to anaphylaxis, which is treated with epinephrine and the transfusion is not resumed.
items.a: Transfusion paused, diphenhydramine, and the unit resumed if hives resolve and nothing else develops
w: Epinephrine for possible anaphylaxis
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold
Methylprednisolone and the unit continued without a pause

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+6:30 (Casualty collection point): About 90 minutes after the last unit he becomes acutely short of breath with frothy secretions and crackles in both lungs. His neck veins are flat. What fits best?
items.x: Hypoxia within 6 hours of transfusion with fever, hypotension and flat neck veins points to TRALI, which is treated with supportive care. TRALI: hypoxia within 6 hours, fever, hypotension and normal or flat neck veins. TACO: hypoxia with high blood pressure, distended neck veins and a positive fluid balance, and it responds to diuresis.
items.a: Oxygen and ventilatory support with PEEP, any running blood stopped, and a teleconsult, treated as TRALI
w: A diuretic for fluid overload
Another unit of blood for the low pressure
Observation, since the transfusion is already finished

items.q: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+12 (Patrol base): His oxygen requirement is falling and his pressure is stable. The team prepares records for the morning evacuation. Which documentation fits best?
items.x: This record supports donor follow-up for infection testing, reaction investigation and safe care at the next level. Walking blood bank records link every unit to a donor for later infection testing and reaction review. The mismatched unit and samples are kept when possible.
items.a: Each unit's donor ID, ABO results, start and stop times, reactions with vitals, treatments, and the set-aside unit, recorded on the DD1380 and PCC flowsheet
w: A verbal handoff only
Records of the mismatched unit discarded to avoid confusion
The last set of vital signs only

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:20 (Casualty collection point): The tourniquet has been on for 20 minutes. He is alert with a strong radial pulse. The team can watch him closely. What fits best for the tourniquet?
items.x: He is not in shock, the wound is not an amputation, and he can be monitored, which fits TCCC conversion criteria. TCCC: tourniquets are reassessed and converted when possible within 2 hours if the casualty is not in shock, can be monitored, and does not have an amputation. A loosened tourniquet stays in place for quick re-tightening.
items.a: Conversion to a hemostatic or pressure dressing, with the loosened tourniquet left in place and the wound watched
w: Tourniquet left in place until evacuation
Tourniquet loosened every 30 minutes
Tourniquet removed and the leg elevated without a dressing

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): The bleeding is controlled. The thigh is shortened and deformed, and bone is visible. What fits best?
items.x: Traction stabilizes the fracture, reduces bleeding and pain, and limits fat embolism risk. Traction splints are used for midshaft femur fractures without contraindications such as pelvic or knee injury. Distal pulse, motor and sensory checks are recorded before and after.
items.a: Wound dressed, then a traction splint applied, with distal pulses and sensation checked before and after
w: No splint, to avoid disturbing the wound
Exposed bone pushed back into the wound before splinting
Tight elastic wrap around the whole thigh

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+1 (Casualty collection point): No antibiotics have been given. He is not vomiting and has IV access. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
items.x: Early IV antibiotics reduce infection after open fractures, and the JTS favors cefazolin for open extremity fractures. The JTS Prevention of Combat-Related Infections CPG recommends cefazolin for open extremity fractures, ideally within the first hour. TCCC lists moxifloxacin by mouth or ertapenem or ceftriaxone for open combat wounds.
items.a: IV cefazolin, or ertapenem or ceftriaxone if that is what the kit carries, now
w: Antibiotics deferred until fever appears
Topical antiseptic only
The wound sutured closed to keep bacteria out

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+3 (Patrol base): His pain is 9 out of 10 despite the splint. He is not in shock and is breathing comfortably. Which analgesic approach fits best?
items.x: Combining agents improves pain control while limiting the side effects of any one drug. Multimodal analgesia is standard in prolonged care. The JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG includes acetaminophen, ketamine and opioids, and newer non-opioids such as suzetrigine may be used for moderate pain.
items.a: Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen plus titrated ketamine or fentanyl, with pain and sedation scores recorded and an antiemetic as needed
w: Midazolam to help him relax
Frequent IM morphine
Analgesia withheld to avoid masking compartment syndrome

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+8 (Patrol base): His lower leg is tense and shiny. Moving his toes causes severe pain, and he reports numbness between the first and second toes. Pedal pulses are present. What fits best?
items.x: Pain with passive stretch and numbness suggest compartment syndrome even with pulses present. Compartment syndrome signs: severe pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling and numbness. Fasciotomy in the field is a high-risk procedure usually performed with teleconsult guidance.
items.a: Splint straps and dressings loosened, leg at heart level, hourly checks, and an urgent teleconsult about fasciotomy
w: The leg elevated well above the heart
More opioid until the pain settles
Observation until pulses are lost

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+20 (Patrol base): After a fasciotomy under telementoring, he is alert and asking for food. Urine output has been adequate. What fits best?
items.x: Early oral nutrition supports healing, and tracking intake and output catches dehydration or kidney injury. Nutrition and hydration are part of prolonged casualty care. Oral intake is preferred when the gut works, and intake and output are recorded on the PCC flowsheet.
items.a: Oral fluids and calorie-dense rations, with intake and output tracked and fasciotomy wounds checked
w: Nothing by mouth until evacuation
IV crystalloid alone for hydration
Food only after he is evacuated

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+36 (Long hold, day 2): He becomes confused and short of breath. There are pinpoint petechiae on his chest, armpits and inside his eyelids. What fits best?
items.x: Hypoxia, confusion and petechiae 24 to 72 hours after a long bone fracture are classic fat embolism syndrome. Fat embolism syndrome: hypoxia, confusion and petechiae, typically 24 to 72 hours after long bone fracture. Care is supportive with oxygen, ventilation if needed, and fracture stabilization.
items.a: Fat embolism syndrome recognized: oxygen and ventilatory support, the femur kept immobilized, a teleconsult, and a higher evacuation priority
w: Sepsis alone assumed, with broader antibiotics
A benzodiazepine for the confusion
Methylprednisolone for the emboli

items.q: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+60 (Long hold, day 3): His oxygen has improved, but the thigh wound and fasciotomy sites now have purulent drainage and spreading redness. What fits best?
items.x: This is sepsis from a wound source, which needs source control and antibiotics. Sepsis from wound infection is common in prolonged care. Field source control means opening, irrigating and cleaning the wound, and the JTS Sepsis in PFC CPG guides fluids, antibiotics and vasopressors.
items.a: Wounds opened, irrigated and cleaned, antibiotics broadened with teleconsult, fluid bolus with reassessment, lactate repeated, and evacuation priority raised
w: Acetaminophen and observation
More dressing layers to contain the drainage
Antibiotics stopped because they failed

items.q: On a 1:2 IABP arterial tracing, the dicrotic notch is lost and inflation begins on the downslope of the systolic upstroke, before the aortic valve closes. What is the main harm of this timing?
items.x: Inflating before the dicrotic notch means the balloon expands while the ventricle is still ejecting. The aortic valve closes prematurely, stroke volume falls and LV wall stress rises. The fix is to move inflation later until it starts at the dicrotic notch.
items.a: Early inflation forces the aortic valve closed early, cutting stroke volume and raising afterload
w: Early inflation lowers coronary perfusion because diastolic augmentation is shortened
Early inflation is harmless as long as the augmented diastolic pressure exceeds the patient's systolic pressure
Early inflation mainly raises the risk of balloon rupture and helium embolism

items.q: On a 1:2 IABP tracing, the assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure equals the unassisted end-diastolic pressure, and the assisted systole is lower than the unassisted systole only slightly. The augmented diastolic wave rises well after the dicrotic notch. What timing error is present?
items.x: When inflation starts after the dicrotic notch, part of diastole passes before augmentation, so diastolic augmentation is suboptimal and coronary perfusion gains are reduced. A clearly visible dicrotic notch before the augmentation upstroke is the clue.
items.a: Late inflation
w: Early deflation
Late deflation
Early inflation

items.q: An IABP tracing at 1:2 shows a sharp drop after diastolic augmentation, the assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure is equal to the unassisted end-diastolic pressure, and the assisted systolic pressure rises above the unassisted systolic pressure. What is the timing error and its consequence?
items.x: Deflating too early lets aortic pressure rebound to baseline before systole, so there is no afterload reduction (assisted systole is not lower). The sharp U-shaped dip can pull blood backward from the coronary and carotid arteries.
items.a: Early deflation, which loses afterload reduction and can cause retrograde coronary and carotid flow
w: Late deflation, which makes the ventricle eject against a still-inflated balloon
Early inflation, which closes the aortic valve prematurely
Late inflation, which shortens diastolic augmentation only

items.q: On a 1:2 IABP tracing, the assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure is HIGHER than the unassisted end-diastolic pressure and the rate of rise of the next (assisted) systole is prolonged. Which timing error is most dangerous here and why?
items.x: Late deflation is the most harmful timing error: the balloon is still occupying the aorta when the aortic valve opens, so it impedes ejection. The tell is assisted end-diastolic pressure equal to or higher than unassisted.
items.a: Late deflation: the LV ejects against a balloon still partly inflated, raising afterload
w: Early deflation: aortic pressure falls too soon, so coronary flow reverses before systole
Late inflation: augmentation starts after diastole is half over, losing coronary benefit
Early inflation: the balloon fills before the valve closes, cutting stroke volume short

items.q: During transport, a patient on an IABP set to ECG trigger develops atrial fibrillation with a rapid, irregular ventricular response and the pump begins alarming and assisting poorly. What is the most appropriate trigger change?
items.x: In irregular rhythms, ECG-based timing can mistime deflation. Most consoles offer an AF mode (deflation on the R-wave) or pressure trigger. Internal trigger is used only when there is no cardiac output, such as during CPR without a usable ECG or pressure.
items.a: Switch to arterial pressure trigger or the AF mode so deflation tracks each real systole
w: Change the assist ratio to 1:3 so fewer beats are mistimed while keeping ECG trigger
Switch to internal trigger at a fixed rate so the console ignores the irregular rhythm
Increase balloon volume so the beats that are assisted make up for the ones missed

items.q: An IABP patient goes into cardiac arrest and CPR is started. The ECG shows only CPR artifact. Which IABP setting best supports perfusion during compressions?
items.x: During CPR the compressions create a pressure waveform the console can follow, so pressure trigger synchronizes the balloon with compressions. Internal trigger is used when there is no pressure signal; standby risks clot forming on the idle balloon.
items.a: Arterial pressure trigger so the balloon times off the compression-generated pressure
w: Internal trigger at a fixed rate of 120 per minute, independent of compressions
ECG trigger at 1:1 so the balloon follows the CPR artifact on the monitor
Standby mode until ROSC, to avoid inflating against chest compressions

items.q: Brownish flecks appear in the helium tubing of an IABP shortly after a flight medic notes a loss of augmentation and a gas leak alarm. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: Blood in the gas tubing means the balloon membrane has torn. The risks are helium embolism and the balloon clotting in place, so the pump is stopped and the team prepares to remove the catheter promptly.
items.a: Balloon membrane rupture with blood entering the gas line
w: Kinked catheter causing hemolysis inside the shuttle line
Condensation from altitude-related humidity changes
Helium tank contamination from the aircraft cabin

items.q: A patient on an IABP has a cool, pale left leg with weak pedal pulses one hour after insertion through the left femoral artery. Which finding would most strongly suggest the catheter is too high rather than causing limb ischemia?
items.x: A balloon placed too high (proximal) can occlude the left subclavian artery, reducing the left radial pulse. Placed too low, it can block the renal arteries and cut urine output. Leg ischemia is from the sheath itself.
items.a: A new drop in left radial pulse and urine output staying normal
w: A new fall in urine output with normal radial pulses
Worsening chest pain with ST elevation
A rising PA occlusion pressure

items.q: Why is helium, rather than air or carbon dioxide, the usual driving gas in an IABP?
items.x: Helium's low density allows rapid shuttling. Its drawback is poor solubility in blood, so a rupture carries a gas embolism risk; CO2 is more soluble but slower.
items.a: Its low density lets the balloon fill and empty fast enough to match each beat
w: It is more soluble in blood than CO2, so a membrane rupture causes less embolism
It expands less with altitude than other gases, so volume stays steady in flight
It coats the balloon membrane and keeps clot from forming during long support

items.q: At altitude in an unpressurized aircraft, what happens to the IABP balloon volume if the console does not automatically compensate?
items.x: Boyle's law: lower ambient pressure lets the gas expand. Modern transport consoles auto-vent or refill as altitude changes, but crews monitor for over- or under-inflation alarms during climb and descent.
items.a: The helium expands as cabin pressure falls, which can over-distend the balloon
w: The helium contracts and the balloon under-fills
The helium dissolves into the blood faster
Nothing changes because the system is a closed, rigid circuit

items.q: Which hemodynamic change best shows that an IABP is helping a patient in cardiogenic shock?
items.x: An effective IABP lowers afterload (assisted systole and end-diastolic pressure fall) and raises diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion. Clinically, filling pressures fall and end-organ perfusion improves.
items.a: Lower assisted systolic and end-diastolic pressures, higher augmentation, better urine output
w: Assisted systolic pressure higher than unassisted, showing the LV is ejecting harder
A rising heart rate as the balloon raises cardiac output and coronary blood flow
A higher PA occlusion pressure because the balloon is supporting left-sided preload

items.q: Which condition is an absolute contraindication to an intra-aortic balloon pump?
items.x: Diastolic inflation would push more blood backward through an incompetent aortic valve. Acute MR and post-MI VSD are classic indications, because afterload reduction improves forward flow.
items.a: Significant aortic regurgitation
w: Mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
Ventricular septal rupture after myocardial infarction
Refractory angina awaiting catheterization

items.q: An IABP patient has a new platelet count of 68,000 on day 3. What is the most likely cause linked to the device?
items.x: Balloon pumping damages platelets, and the heparin given with it adds the possibility of HIT. Platelet counts are followed daily.
items.a: Mechanical platelet destruction by the balloon, made worse by heparin exposure
w: Dilution from fluids and helium leaking slowly across the balloon membrane
Marrow suppression from the aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitor given after the MI
Splenic sequestration from the low cardiac output state before balloon placement

items.q: A patient on an Impella CP has a sudden fall in device flow with a 'suction' alarm and a falling CVP. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Suction events happen when the LV is underfilled, so the inlet pulls against tissue. A low CVP suggests volume depletion; a high CVP with low LV filling suggests RV failure. Treat the cause and reduce the P-level if needed.
items.a: Low LV filling (hypovolemia or RV failure) letting the inlet suck against the ventricular wall
w: Pump thrombosis raising motor current and lowering the delivered flow
The pump migrating fully into the aorta so both ends sit above the valve
New aortic regurgitation from the cannula holding the valve leaflets open

items.q: On an Impella console, the placement signal (aortic pressure waveform) changes to a ventricular-looking waveform. What does this indicate?
items.x: The Impella's pressure sensor sits near the outlet. A ventricular waveform means the outlet is in the LV (too deep). An aortic waveform on the motor current with flat pulsatility suggests the inlet is in the aorta (pulled back).
items.a: The pump has slid too far into the ventricle, so the outlet now sits in the LV
w: The pump has backed out into the aorta, so both openings now sit above the valve
The pressure line is damped by a clot and needs flushing before any change
The patient has new severe aortic stenosis narrowing flow around the cannula

items.q: An Impella motor current waveform becomes flat (non-pulsatile) while the placement signal shows an aortic waveform. What is the most likely position problem?
items.x: When both the inlet and outlet are in the aorta, there is no pressure difference across the pump, so the motor current loses its pulsatility and the placement signal reads aortic. The pump needs repositioning under imaging.
items.a: The whole pump has backed out into the aorta
w: The pump is too deep in the left ventricle
The pump is correctly placed with very poor native contractility
There is a purge pressure failure

items.q: Why does an Impella need a continuous purge solution?
items.x: The purge fluid flows opposite to blood across the motor seal, creating a pressure barrier. It usually contains heparin or bicarbonate, but its main job is to protect the motor.
items.a: To keep blood out of the motor housing and prevent the bearings from clotting
w: To cool the pump motor during high P-levels
To deliver the patient's anticoagulant systemically as the main dose
To flush air bubbles out of the aortic pressure line

items.q: A patient on an Impella has dark red-brown urine and a rising plasma free hemoglobin. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Red cell shearing by the rotor causes hemolysis, worse with malposition, suction or a high P-level. Checking position and lowering speed are first steps.
items.a: Hemolysis from pump malposition or high pump speed
w: Rhabdomyolysis from groin ischemia
Contrast nephropathy after the procedure
Acute tubular necrosis from the purge solution

items.q: An Impella supports the left ventricle. A patient on one develops a rising CVP, falling Impella flow and a falling MAP while the LV looks small on ultrasound. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: A left-sided device can only move what reaches the LV. Rising right-sided pressure with a small LV points to RV failure; options include inotropes, pulmonary vasodilators or a right-sided device (such as an Impella RP).
items.a: Right ventricular failure that is not delivering enough blood to the left side
w: Cardiac tamponade compressing the left ventricle more than the right
Impella pump thrombosis limiting forward flow despite good LV filling
Over-diuresis causing both ventricles to collapse around the inlet

items.q: Compared with an IABP, what is the main hemodynamic advantage of a left-sided Impella?
items.x: The IABP only augments what the heart does and relies on timing. The Impella is a microaxial pump that pulls blood from the LV into the aorta, unloading the ventricle and adding forward flow independently.
items.a: It moves blood forward actively and does not depend on the patient's own cardiac rhythm or output
w: It raises diastolic coronary perfusion more through timed counterpulsation
It lowers right ventricular afterload directly by venting the pulmonary artery
It works without any anticoagulation because the purge prevents clotting

items.q: A conscious LVAD patient (continuous-flow device) has no palpable pulse and a cuff that will not read a blood pressure. What is the best way to measure perfusion pressure?
items.x: Continuous-flow LVADs often abolish a palpable pulse. A manual cuff with Doppler: the pressure at which flow is first heard estimates the MAP (goal is usually around 70 to 90 mmHg).
items.a: Doppler opening pressure, which approximates the mean arterial pressure
w: The height of the pulse oximetry waveform, which tracks the systolic pressure
Capillary refill time, which reflects the mean arterial pressure on its own
An automated cuff on the thigh, which reads accurately without pulsatility

items.q: An LVAD patient is unresponsive, pale and apneic. The device makes no hum, and the controller shows a red heart alarm. What is the first priority?
items.x: Current guidance (AHA) supports compressions in an unresponsive LVAD patient with no perfusion, after a quick device check. Many arrests are from power loss, so batteries and connections are checked first.
items.a: Check power and connections, then start compressions if there is no perfusion
w: Avoid compressions entirely, because they will dislodge the pump from the apex
Defibrillate at once, before looking at the controller or the power source
Disconnect and reconnect the driveline to reset the controller's alarm

items.q: An LVAD patient's controller history shows a steady climb in power with a matching rise in the displayed (estimated) flow, while the patient feels worse. LDH is markedly elevated and the urine is tea-colored. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: Thrombus on the rotor makes the motor draw more power. Because the controller estimates flow from power, the displayed flow rises falsely even though real output may fall. Hemolysis raises LDH and plasma free hemoglobin and darkens the urine.
items.a: Pump thrombosis
w: Hypovolemia with suction events
Right ventricular failure
Driveline infection

items.q: An LVAD patient has repeated low-flow alarms after a day of vomiting and diarrhea, and is having runs of ventricular tachycardia. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: A dry LV collapses around the inflow cannula. The septum is pulled toward it, which can trigger ventricular arrhythmias. Careful fluid replacement usually resolves it.
items.a: Suction events from hypovolemia, with the inflow cannula pulling against the septum
w: Pump thrombosis slowing the rotor and lowering the displayed flow
Driveline fracture causing intermittent loss of power to the pump
Aortic insufficiency from the outflow graft recirculating blood

items.q: Why do patients with continuous-flow LVADs commonly develop gastrointestinal bleeding from arteriovenous malformations?
items.x: This is acquired von Willebrand syndrome plus angiodysplasia, made worse by anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy.
items.a: Low pulsatility promotes AV malformations, and high shear breaks down von Willebrand factor
w: The warfarin target is set very high to protect the pump, so the gut bleeds easily
Splanchnic flow is diverted to the pump, causing ischemic ulcers in the stomach wall
Tiny bubbles from the pump's bearings lodge in gut vessels and cause them to rupture

items.q: An LVAD patient's Doppler MAP is 118 mmHg. Why is this a concern specific to continuous-flow pumps?
items.x: Continuous-flow pumps are afterload sensitive: higher pressure reduces flow. Hypertension in LVAD patients is also strongly linked to hemorrhagic and ischemic stroke.
items.a: Pump flow falls as afterload rises, and high pressure raises the risk of stroke
w: High pressure makes the pump spin faster and cause hemolysis
High pressure prevents the aortic valve from closing
High pressure collapses the LV around the inflow cannula

items.q: A PA catheter reading shows CVP 18, PA 28/16, PAOP 8, cardiac index 1.8 and SVR 1,600. Which condition best fits?
items.x: A high CVP with a low wedge pressure means the right side is failing to fill the left. Low output and high SVR follow. Treat with careful volume and inotropes rather than diuresis or nitrates.
items.a: Right ventricular infarction or failure
w: Left ventricular cardiogenic shock
Hypovolemic shock
Septic shock

items.q: Which hemodynamic profile is most consistent with cardiac tamponade?
items.x: Fluid around the heart limits filling of all chambers equally, so diastolic pressures rise and equalize (often within a few mmHg) while output falls.
items.a: Equalization of CVP, PA diastolic and PAOP with low cardiac output
w: High PAOP with low CVP and low output
Low CVP and low PAOP with high cardiac output
High PA systolic with normal PAOP and normal output

items.q: A patient has a PA pressure of 60/34, a PAOP of 10 and a cardiac output of 3.1 L/min. What does the gap between the PA diastolic and the wedge suggest?
items.x: Normally PA diastolic is within about 5 mmHg of the wedge. A large gap means the resistance is in the pulmonary vessels themselves, not in the left heart.
items.a: Pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension, such as from massive PE or primary pulmonary vascular disease
w: Left heart failure with pressure backing up into the lungs
Mitral stenosis raising left atrial and pulmonary pressures
Volume overload from aggressive fluid resuscitation in transport

items.q: Using the formula MAP = CO x SVR, what is the most likely effect of starting a pure vasodilator in a patient with a fixed cardiac output?
items.x: If output cannot rise (fixed stroke volume, beta blockade, or stenotic valve), lowering SVR lowers pressure. In a failing heart that can respond, afterload reduction raises output and pressure may hold.
items.a: MAP falls because SVR falls with no rise in output
w: MAP rises because preload increases
MAP stays the same because the heart compensates instantly
MAP rises because afterload falls

items.q: An arterial line waveform shows a slurred upstroke, an absent dicrotic notch and a falsely narrow pulse pressure. What is the most likely problem?
items.x: Over-damped lines under-read the systolic and over-read the diastolic pressure; the MAP stays roughly accurate. A square-wave (fast flush) test shows fewer than one or two oscillations.
