items.q: A 3 kg newborn delivered in the field is jittery and cool to the touch with a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL, and vascular access is obtained. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: The neonatal dose is D10 2-4 mL/kg (6-12 mL for 3 kg) IV or IO. 30 mL is an older-child dose, D50 is too concentrated and too large, adult oral gel is not used, and a cool newborn is dried and kept warm, not left uncovered.
opts: Give D10 30 mL IV
Give D50 15 mL IV
Give D10 9 mL IV
Leave the infant uncovered for observation
Give oral glucose gel 15 g

items.q: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has deep rapid respirations, fruity breath and a glucometer reading of HI. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: This presentation suggests DKA with dehydration and possible potassium shifts, so fluids and ECG monitoring are appropriate. Dextrose is contraindicated in hyperglycemia, and glucagon or oral glucose would raise the glucose further.

Give a normal saline bolus per protocol
Give glucagon IM for confusion
Monitor the ECG for potassium-related changes
Give oral glucose gel for energy

items.q: A 20 kg 5-year-old with a peanut allergy has hives, wheezing and vomiting after a snack. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Children under 30 kg receive 0.01 mg/kg IM (0.2 mg here) or the 0.15 mg auto-injector (15-30 kg), repeated every 5-10 minutes as needed. The 1 mg/mL concentration is never pushed IV, and epinephrine is not delayed for antihistamines or for hypotension.

Wait for hypotension before giving epinephrine
Repeat in 5-10 minutes if there is no improvement

Give 0.2 mg IM of 1 mg/mL drawn from a vial
Repeat in 5-10 minutes if there is no improvement

items.q: A 70-year-old with coronary artery disease has anaphylaxis with hypotension and wheezing after a new antibiotic. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Epinephrine has no contraindication in anaphylaxis, so the IM dose is given, with ECG monitoring for dysrhythmias and chest pain. The 1 mg IV dose is for cardiac arrest, antihistamines do not replace epinephrine, and an arbitrary reduced dose would undertreat.

items.q: A 16 kg 4-year-old has itchy, localized hives after an insect bite, with clear lungs, no lip or tongue swelling and normal vital signs. Diphenhydramine is ordered per protocol. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: The EMS protocol dose is 1 mg/kg per dose (max 50 mg), 16 mg here, followed by reassessment for progression. Localized hives without airway, breathing or circulatory involvement are not anaphylaxis, and 50 mg and 160 mg are overdoses for this child.

Stop reassessing the child once he looks better

items.q: An 80-year-old man receives diphenhydramine 50 mg IV for generalized hives without airway or blood pressure involvement. Which reassessment steps are appropriate during transport? Select all that apply.
items.x: Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic and sedating, and older adults are prone to urinary retention, confusion, drowsiness and dizziness, so falls are prevented. It causes dry mouth and pupil dilation rather than salivation or miosis.

Check for pinpoint pupils
Check for new confusion
Watch for excess salivation
Do not let him walk unassisted

items.q: A 40-year-old with anaphylaxis improves after one IM epinephrine dose: BP 108/70 mm Hg, hives fading, mild wheeze remaining. Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV is given. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Corticosteroids are slow-acting adjuncts and never replace epinephrine, which is repeated if symptoms worsen; persistent bronchospasm can be treated with albuterol and reassessment continues. Diabetes is not a contraindication, though glucose may rise.

Repeat IM epinephrine if symptoms worsen
Withhold the steroid if the patient has diabetes
Keep reassessing for returning symptoms
Stop monitoring now that symptoms improved
Treat the remaining wheeze with albuterol
ok: Repeat IM epinephrine if symptoms worsen
Keep reassessing for returning symptoms
Treat the remaining wheeze with albuterol

items.q: A 12 kg 20-month-old has vomited 8 times from gastroenteritis, has had few wet diapers and is tachycardic. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: The ODT dose for 8-15 kg is 2 mg (IV would be 0.1-0.15 mg/kg, 1.2-1.8 mg), and a vomiting toddler needs hydration and glucose assessment. 8 mg ODT and 4 mg IV exceed the weight-based dose, and promethazine is contraindicated under 2 years.

Ondansetron ODT 2 mg
Ondansetron 4 mg IV
Check capillary refill, mucosa and glucose
Promethazine 6 mg IM
ok: Ondansetron ODT 2 mg
Check capillary refill, mucosa and glucose

items.q: A 60-year-old with repeated vomiting who takes methadone receives ondansetron 4 mg IV. Which actions are appropriate after the dose? Select all that apply.
items.x: QT prolongation and dysrhythmias are the key serious effects, made more likely by methadone and vomiting-related electrolyte loss; headache and dizziness are common, and a repeat dose may be considered at 10-15 minutes. Ondansetron does not cause respiratory depression or hypoglycemia.
opts: Watch the ECG for QT prolongation
Watch for respiratory depression from ondansetron
Reassess nausea in 10-15 minutes
Ask about a new headache or dizziness
Check glucose for ondansetron hypoglycemia
Report a new irregular rhythm
ok: Watch the ECG for QT prolongation
Reassess nausea in 10-15 minutes

Report a new irregular rhythm

items.q: A 34-year-old with a migraine and vomiting receives metoclopramide 10 mg IV over 15 minutes. Soon after, she says she cannot sit still and keeps trying to stand. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: Akathisia is a known adverse effect and a stop criterion, so further doses are held and the reaction reported. Repeating or pushing faster increases the risk, and labeling it anxiety misses the drug reaction.

Repeat 10 mg because nausea persists
Stop further metoclopramide doses
Push the next dose faster to shorten exposure
Report the reaction to medical direction

ok: Her restlessness is consistent with akathisia

items.q: A 45-year-old with epilepsy and prior abdominal surgery has repeated vomiting, a distended abdomen and no bowel movement for 3 days. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Suspected bowel obstruction and a seizure disorder both contraindicate metoclopramide by any route, and a patient with possible obstruction is kept NPO. Oral fluids worsen vomiting and aspiration risk.

Give metoclopramide 10 mg IV to speed emptying
Keep the patient NPO
Encourage oral fluids to rehydrate
Give metoclopramide IM instead of IV
ok: Withhold metoclopramide
Keep the patient NPO

items.q: Droperidol is being considered for a patient with nausea. Which findings make it inappropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Droperidol is contraindicated with known or suspected QT prolongation (QTc over 440 ms in men or 450 ms in women). A heart rate of 96/min, migraine history and a normal QTc do not prevent its use.

Heart rate of 96/min
History of migraine
Known congenital long QT syndrome
QTc of 410 ms in a woman

items.q: A severely agitated adult receives droperidol 5 mg IM per protocol. Which findings should the paramedic monitor for? Select all that apply.

Hypotension
Dystonia
Bronchospasm
Over-sedation
QT prolongation on the monitor

Dystonia
Over-sedation

items.q: Thirty minutes after haloperidol 5 mg IM for acute psychosis, a 22-year-old's neck is twisted to one side and his eyes are fixed upward. He is breathing normally. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Acute dystonia is a common haloperidol effect and a stop criterion; it is treated with diphenhydramine, and QT prolongation is a serious effect to monitor. More haloperidol worsens it, and naloxone has no role.

Give a second haloperidol dose
Give diphenhydramine per protocol
Give naloxone for the posturing
Monitor the ECG for QT prolongation

Give diphenhydramine per protocol

items.q: A 100 kg adult with extreme agitation is endangering himself and the crew, and ketamine IM is ordered per protocol. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
items.x: The protocol agitation dose is 4-5 mg/kg IM. Laryngospasm, apnea, hypersalivation and emergence reactions are known effects requiring continuous monitoring. Ketamine tends to raise, not lower, blood pressure.

Hypersalivation may occur

Prepare for laryngospasm or apnea
Hypersalivation may occur

items.q: A 70 kg adult has been seizing for 7 minutes and IV access is not available. Which actions are consistent with protocol? Select all that apply.
items.x: Adults over 40 kg receive 10 mg IM, or 5-10 mg IN, and respiratory depression is monitored. 0.3 mg/kg is an induction dose, treatment should not be delayed, and nothing is given by mouth to a seizing patient.

Give midazolam 21 mg IM (0.3 mg/kg)
Give midazolam 5-10 mg IN

Monitor SpO2 and ventilation after dosing

Give midazolam 5-10 mg IN

items.q: A 16 kg 4-year-old with epilepsy has been seizing for 6 minutes at home, and IV access is not available. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Rectal gel for ages 2-5 is 0.5 mg/kg (8 mg), and respiratory depression is anticipated. 16 mg is an overdose, IM diazepam absorption is erratic, and restraining a seizing child risks injury.

Rectal gel 8 mg (0.5 mg/kg)
Monitor breathing with a BVM ready
Diazepam 10 mg IM, since absorption is reliable

items.q: A 72-year-old with epilepsy has been seizing for 6 minutes. Which findings are contraindications to lorazepam? Select all that apply.
items.x: Acute narrow-angle glaucoma is a listed contraindication. A seizure lasting over 5 minutes is an indication, and epilepsy, older age and fever do not prevent use.

Known epilepsy on home medication
Acute narrow-angle glaucoma
Age of 72 years
Fever of 38.9 C (102 F)

items.q: Several patients are being evaluated for seizure activity. Which presentations are consistent with status epilepticus that needs a benzodiazepine? Select all that apply.
items.x: Status epilepticus is continuous seizure activity over 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery in between. A brief seizure with recovery, convulsive syncope or improving postictal confusion do not need a benzodiazepine.
opts: A 1-minute seizure, now postictal and breathing well
A generalized seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Brief limb jerking during a faint that stops at once
Two seizures without regaining consciousness between
A known epileptic now confused but improving after a seizure
ok: A generalized seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Two seizures without regaining consciousness between

items.q: A 67-year-old has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. BP is 196/104 mm Hg. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypoglycemia must be ruled out, and the last known well time decides thrombolysis eligibility. Aspirin is not given before imaging excludes hemorrhage, dextrose is not given without hypoglycemia, and rapid BP lowering can worsen ischemia.

items.q: A worker spilled hydrofluoric acid on his fingers and has severe pain with little visible burn. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

items.q: A 74-year-old on apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. The sending ED gave the andexanet alfa bolus, and the infusion is running at departure. Which actions belong in the transport plan? Select all that apply.

items.x: Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials) is the specific dabigatran reversal agent and has no listed contraindications, and serial neuro checks detect hematoma expansion. INR-based PCC and vitamin K are warfarin reversal, age is not a contraindication, and the head of the bed is usually raised about 30 degrees.

items.x: Methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension, preeclampsia and potent CYP3A4 inhibitors such as HIV protease inhibitors because of severe vasoconstriction. Asthma is a carboprost contraindication, and tachycardia from blood loss or oxytocin use does not prevent it.

Give lorazepam 2 mg IV

Give levetiracetam 1,200 mg IV if seizures persist

items.q: An 80-kg adult in status epilepticus stopped seizing after two doses of lorazepam but remains unresponsive with snoring respirations and an SpO2 of 89%. Levetiracetam is ordered before the flight. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: The airway is managed first, and levetiracetam 60 mg/kg is capped at 4,500 mg, infused over 10-15 minutes. Lorazepam is repeated only once, the second-line drug is not delayed for awakening, and glucose is checked in every seizing patient.

Infuse 4,500 mg IV over 10-15 minutes
Push 4,800 mg IV over 1 minute
Hold it until he is fully awake
Give a third 4 mg lorazepam dose now
Skip a glucose check since seizures stopped

Infuse 4,500 mg IV over 10-15 minutes

items.q: A 62-year-old in septic shock with lactic acidosis (pH 7.08) is breathing 36/min and tiring, and the sending physician asks about sodium bicarbonate before the flight. Which findings argue against giving it now? Select all that apply.
items.x: Bicarbonate is contraindicated with inadequate ventilation (the CO2 it generates accumulates, shown by a rising ETCO2), hypocalcemia (it worsens) and hypernatremia. The low pH is the reason it is being considered, and the HR and potassium are not contraindications.

Ionized calcium of 0.8 mmol/L

A pH of 7.08

ok: ETCO2 rising from 30 to 58 mm Hg

Serum sodium of 158 mEq/L

items.q: A 6-kg infant being transferred for sepsis becomes lethargic with a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Infants receive D10 5-10 mL/kg (30-60 mL for 6 kg), followed by a glucose recheck. D50 is too concentrated and too large a dose, oral glucose is unsafe with altered mental status, and treatment should not be delayed.

Give D10 30-60 mL IV or IO
Give oral glucose gel in the cheek
Recheck glucose after the dose
Withhold dextrose until a repeat check

Recheck glucose after the dose

items.q: A 70-kg patient with 45% TBSA burns from 6 days ago develops respiratory failure in a rural ICU and needs RSI for transfer. The potassium result is pending. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Succinylcholine is contraindicated from about 24 hours after a major burn, by any route, because of the risk of severe hyperkalemia; the risk peaks around 7-10 days, so 6 days is well within the danger window. Ketamine induction with rocuronium paralysis and preparation for airway edema are appropriate, and the airway cannot wait for a lab result.

Use succinylcholine since the burn is under 7 days old
Use ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV for induction
Give succinylcholine 4 mg/kg IM if IV access is lost
Prepare for a difficult airway from edema
Wait for the potassium before planning the airway
ok: Use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV for paralysis
Use ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV for induction
Prepare for a difficult airway from edema

items.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions has an HR of 48/min, peaked T waves and a widening QRS, and calcium chloride 1 g IV is ordered during transport. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Calcium chloride 1 g (10 mL of 10%) stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower potassium, so shifting therapy such as insulin with dextrose follows. Rapid push can cause bradycardia, extravasation can cause tissue necrosis, and ECG changes such as peaked T waves are an indication.

Expect the calcium to lower potassium
Push slowly while watching the monitor
Follow with potassium-shifting therapy as ordered
Withhold it because of peaked T waves
Watch the IV site for extravasation
ok: Give 10 mL of 10% through a patent large IV
Push slowly while watching the monitor

items.q: A 70-kg patient with suspected ethylene glycol ingestion is drowsy and breathing 32/min with a high anion gap acidosis, and he is being flown to a center with dialysis. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Fomepizole is loaded at 15 mg/kg IV for suspected poisoning and repeated every 12 hours, while gaps and mental status are followed. Waiting for a level delays the antidote, and a ventilator rate of 12 would remove his respiratory compensation and worsen acidosis.
opts: Give fomepizole 15 mg/kg (1,050 mg) IV now
Hold fomepizole until a confirmed level returns
Hand off the dose time for the 12-hour repeat
If intubated, set the ventilator rate to 12/min
Reassess mental status and breathing en route

ok: Give fomepizole 15 mg/kg (1,050 mg) IV now
Hand off the dose time for the 12-hour repeat

items.q: Thirty minutes into the IV acetylcysteine loading bag, a patient with acetaminophen overdose develops flushing, hives and mild wheezing. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Anaphylactoid reactions to IV acetylcysteine are managed by pausing the infusion, treating the reaction and restarting at a slower rate. Stopping antidote therapy for good would leave the liver unprotected, and charcoal is not a substitute.

Double the rate to finish the bag
Treat the reaction
Abandon all acetylcysteine therapy
Restart more slowly once it resolves
Use activated charcoal as sole therapy
ok: Pause the infusion
Treat the reaction
Restart more slowly once it resolves

items.q: A 60-kg patient with an unknown-time acetaminophen ingestion, right upper quadrant pain and rising LFTs is transferred during the 21-hour IV acetylcysteine regimen. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: The 21-hour regimen is 150 mg/kg over 60 minutes, 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours, so the bag in progress must be handed off accurately. An unknown ingestion time or elevated LFTs are indications to continue treatment, not reasons to stop or wait.
opts: Hand off the current bag, rate and start time
Run the 50 mg/kg second bag over 30 minutes
Run the 100 mg/kg last bag over 16 hours
Pause therapy until a timed level returns
Stop the drug because the LFTs are high

Run the 100 mg/kg last bag over 16 hours

items.q: A patient with digoxin toxicity and atrial fibrillation received digoxin immune Fab before transport. Which changes should the crew watch for after the dose? Select all that apply.
items.x: Once digoxin is bound, potassium shifts back into cells and can drop quickly, so it is checked every 1-2 hours. Removing digoxin's effect can also unmask heart failure and allow a rapid ventricular response in AF.
opts: A rapid fall in potassium
A rising serum potassium
Worsening heart failure
Rapid ventricular response in AF
QRS widening caused by the Fab
ok: A rapid fall in potassium
Worsening heart failure
Rapid ventricular response in AF

items.q: A farmworker has pinpoint pupils, wheezing, copious bronchial secretions and bradycardia after an organophosphate spill and is being prepared for a flight. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Decontamination protects the crew and aircraft, atropine is doubled every 5 minutes until bronchial secretions dry with no maximum (the 3 mg cap applies to bradycardia), and pralidoxime is added. Pupils are not a reliable endpoint, and succinylcholine can cause prolonged paralysis because cholinesterase is inhibited.
opts: Decontaminate before loading the aircraft
Titrate atropine until secretions dry
Cap atropine at a total of 3 mg
Use pupil size as the atropine endpoint
Add pralidoxime 1-2 g IV over 15-30 minutes
Use succinylcholine if RSI is needed
ok: Decontaminate before loading the aircraft
Titrate atropine until secretions dry
Add pralidoxime 1-2 g IV over 15-30 minutes

items.q: A patient who overdosed on verapamil has a BP of 70/40 mm Hg and an HR of 38/min despite fluids. Which therapies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Calcium chloride 1-2 g every 10-20 minutes, high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy and vasopressors support calcium channel blocker poisoning. Diltiazem and nicardipine are calcium channel blockers, and labetalol would worsen bradycardia and hypotension.
opts: Calcium chloride 1-2 g IV
Diltiazem infusion
High-dose insulin with dextrose
Labetalol 20 mg IV
Norepinephrine infusion
Nicardipine infusion
ok: Calcium chloride 1-2 g IV
High-dose insulin with dextrose
Norepinephrine infusion

items.q: A patient with metoprolol overdose is drowsy, with an HR of 40/min and a BP of 76/44 mm Hg, and glucagon is given IV during transport. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: For beta blocker overdose, glucagon is given 3-5 mg IV over 1-2 minutes and may be followed by a 2-5 mg/h infusion. Vomiting is common in a drowsy patient, so suction and airway protection are planned, and hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia, is expected.
opts: Give 3-5 mg IV over 1-2 minutes
Give 1 mg IM, as for hypoglycemia
Have suction ready for vomiting
Hold glucagon because of the hypotension
Follow with a 2-5 mg/h infusion if effective
Expect blood glucose to fall
ok: Give 3-5 mg IV over 1-2 minutes
Have suction ready for vomiting

items.q: A 62-year-old man with nausea and vomiting before a flight is alert and protecting his airway, with a BP of 118/72 mm Hg. His 12-lead shows a QTc of 490 ms, and droperidol is on the standing orders. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Droperidol is contraindicated with known QT prolongation (QTc over 440 ms in males), so it is held regardless of route and the provider is notified. An alert patient protecting his airway does not need intubation for nausea.
opts: Give droperidol 1.25 mg IV
Give droperidol 2.5 mg IM instead
Hold droperidol and notify the provider
Recheck the QTc only after the dose
Intubate him to protect the airway
ok: Hold droperidol and notify the provider

items.q: An intubated patient is paralyzed with a vecuronium infusion for a 2-hour flight. Which findings suggest inadequate sedation or analgesia? Select all that apply.
items.x: Vecuronium paralyzes without sedating, so awareness under paralysis must be watched for through sympathetic signs such as tachycardia, hypertension and tearing. Lack of movement is expected from the paralytic and does not show adequate sedation.
opts: Unexplained tachycardia
No patient movement
Rising blood pressure
SpO2 of 98%
Tearing
Equal, reactive pupils
ok: Unexplained tachycardia
Rising blood pressure
Tearing

items.q: A non-intubated 80-kg burn patient with an SBP of 92 mm Hg has severe pain despite fentanyl, and low-dose ketamine is ordered for the flight. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Analgesic ketamine is 0.1-0.3 mg/kg IV, and dysphoria or emergence reactions can occur, so pain and mental status are reassessed. It tends to raise BP rather than lower it, 4-5 mg/kg is an IM agitation dose, and continuous SpO2 monitoring continues.
opts: Give 8-24 mg IV (0.1-0.3 mg/kg)
Give 320-400 mg IV (4-5 mg/kg)
Watch for dysphoria and reassess pain
Withhold it because of the borderline BP
Remove the SpO2 probe once pain eases
ok: Give 8-24 mg IV (0.1-0.3 mg/kg)

items.q: Right after a large, rapid fentanyl bolus in an intubated patient, the crew cannot ventilate and the chest feels rigid. Tube position is confirmed. Which drug-related complications explain these findings? Select all that apply.
items.x: Chest wall rigidity is a serious effect of fentanyl that makes ventilation difficult. The other conditions do not cause sudden rigidity with inability to ventilate.
opts: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
Opioid-induced adrenal suppression
Drug-induced methemoglobinemia
Opioid-induced hypoglycemia
Opioid-induced hyponatremia

items.q: After intubation, a trauma patient in hemorrhagic shock has a BP of 84/50 mm Hg and needs ongoing sedation and analgesia for transport. Which choices are reasonable? Select all that apply.
items.x: Ketamine maintains BP and small titrated fentanyl doses limit hypotension. Full-dose propofol, large midazolam boluses and a dexmedetomidine load all commonly cause hypotension, which is dangerous in hemorrhagic shock.
opts: Ketamine for sedation
A full-dose propofol IV bolus
Small, titrated doses of fentanyl
Repeated large midazolam boluses
Dexmedetomidine with a full loading dose
ok: Ketamine for sedation
Small, titrated doses of fentanyl

items.q: A septic patient with a BP of 78/44 mm Hg and an SpO2 of 86% on a nonrebreather needs RSI before the flight. Which measures reduce the risk of peri-intubation cardiac arrest? Select all that apply.
items.x: Hypotension and hypoxia before RSI raise arrest risk, so resuscitation, a ready push-dose pressor, a reduced induction dose and thorough preoxygenation are used. Propofol in unstable patients is reduced to 0.5-1 mg/kg, and skipping preoxygenation worsens hypoxia.
opts: Resuscitate with fluids or pressors first
Give propofol 2.5 mg/kg for induction
Have push-dose epinephrine ready
Use a reduced induction dose
Skip preoxygenation to save time
Maximize preoxygenation before induction

Have push-dose epinephrine ready
Use a reduced induction dose
Maximize preoxygenation before induction

items.q: Right after intubation, a septic patient's BP falls to 68/40 mm Hg while a norepinephrine infusion is being prepared, and push-dose epinephrine is ordered. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Push-dose epinephrine is 10-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes as a bridge to an infusion. 1 mg is the arrest dose, 0.3 mg IM is the anaphylaxis dose, higher PEEP lowers venous return and BP, and profound post-intubation hypotension should not go untreated.
opts: Give the full cardiac-arrest dose by IV push
Give small diluted boluses IV every few minutes
Give the anaphylaxis dose IM in the thigh
Increase PEEP to raise the BP
Give fluids only until the drip is ready

items.q: A 66-year-old with low-output heart failure (BP 94/60 mm Hg, cool extremities, rising creatinine) is transferred on a milrinone infusion. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Milrinone commonly causes hypotension and ventricular ectopy, and new ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension or declining urine output require stopping or notifying. A large bolus worsens congestion, a higher rate deepens hypotension, the label load runs over 10 minutes, and continuous monitoring is required.

Trend BP and urine output
Bolus 1 L of saline for the SBP of 94
Double the rate if BP falls

Stop cardiac monitoring once stable
ok: Stop and notify for new runs of VT
Trend BP and urine output

items.q: A patient with stable monomorphic VT received amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes, converted to sinus rhythm, and is transferred on the maintenance infusion with a BP of 108/70 mm Hg. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: After the load, amiodarone runs at 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min, and AV block, hypotension or QT prolongation are reasons to stop and notify. Pads stay on in case VT recurs; recurrent stable VT receives 150 mg over 10 minutes, while 300 mg push is the arrest dose.

Run the infusion at 1 mg/kg/min
Keep defibrillation pads applied

items.q: A 70-year-old in AF with RVR at 150/min has a BP of 82/50 mm Hg, diaphoresis and new confusion before transfer. IV diltiazem was suggested by the sending clinic. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: This patient is unstable from the tachycardia, so synchronized cardioversion with sedation when feasible is indicated, and SBP under 90 is a contraindication to diltiazem. Adenosine does not convert AF and is not used for an irregular rhythm.
opts: Withhold diltiazem because SBP is under 90
Apply pads and prepare to cardiovert
Sedate before cardioversion if time allows
Use synchronized, not unsynchronized, shocks
Give diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes
Give adenosine 6 mg rapid IV
ok: Withhold diltiazem because SBP is under 90
Apply pads and prepare to cardiovert
Sedate before cardioversion if time allows
Use synchronized, not unsynchronized, shocks

items.q: A patient on a heparin infusion for PE has a platelet count that has fallen 60% from baseline, and a new leg clot is suspected. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: A platelet drop of 50% or more with new thrombosis suggests HIT, so heparin is stopped and the provider notified. Increasing heparin worsens HIT, and four-factor PCC contains heparin and is contraindicated in HIT.

Increase the rate to treat the clot
Notify the provider of possible HIT
Give four-factor PCC to reverse heparin
Continue if the aPTT is in range

Notify the provider of possible HIT

items.q: A 75-kg patient with an acute ischemic stroke 2 hours from last known well has a BP of 172/96 mm Hg and a glucose of 124 mg/dL, and is a lytic candidate before the flight to a thrombectomy center. Which orders are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Stroke tenecteplase for 70-79 kg is a single 20 mg bolus over 5 seconds, and a BP under 185/110 is acceptable. 40 mg is the STEMI dose for that weight, 0.9 mg/kg with a 10% bolus is alteplase, BP is not normalized, and antiplatelets are withheld for 24 hours after a lytic.
opts: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
Tenecteplase 40 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds
0.9 mg/kg with 10% given as a bolus
Lower BP below 120/80 mm Hg first
Aspirin 324 mg with the bolus
ok: Tenecteplase 20 mg IV bolus over 5 seconds

items.q: A crew prepares to move a patient on norepinephrine, propofol and heparin infusions from the ICU bed to the aircraft. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Tracing, labeling and verifying concentration and rate for every infusion prevents wrong-line and wrong-dose errors during handoff. Interrupting a vasopressor or pushing drugs through its line can cause abrupt swings in BP.
opts: Trace each line from bag to patient
Label each line and pump channel
Pause norepinephrine during the move
Confirm each concentration with the sending nurse
Push IV meds through the norepinephrine line
Verify each rate against the current order

Label each line and pump channel

Verify each rate against the current order

items.q: A 130-kg patient with an open tibia fracture is being transferred, and cefazolin is ordered before departure. He reports a childhood rash with amoxicillin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Cefazolin is 2 g IV, or 3 g for patients 120 kg or more, and the open wound is covered with a sterile dressing. Only penicillin anaphylaxis is a relative contraindication, and the routes are IV and IM.
opts: Give cefazolin 3 g IV
Give 1 g IV, the standard adult dose
Withhold it because of the rash history
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing
Give it by mouth to avoid reactions
ok: Give cefazolin 3 g IV
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing

items.q: A patient with an acute ischemic stroke is a candidate for alteplase, but the BP is 204/118 mm Hg. Which statements about BP management are accurate? Select all that apply.
items.x: Uncontrolled BP over 185/110 is a contraindication to alteplase for stroke, so BP is lowered below that level first, with agents such as labetalol or nicardipine. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated, and normalizing BP is not the goal.
opts: BP must be under 185/110 before alteplase
Alteplase may be given if BP is under 220/120
A sublingual nifedipine capsule is preferred
BP must be lowered under 120/80 first
BP is treated only after the bolus
ok: BP must be under 185/110 before alteplase

items.q: A 4-kg infant becomes bradycardic at 50/min with poor perfusion during transport despite effective oxygenation and ventilation, and atropine is ordered for suspected increased vagal tone. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.x: An infant with HR under 60 and poor perfusion despite effective ventilation needs CPR. PALS atropine is 0.02 mg/kg with a 0.1 mg minimum, so a 4-kg infant receives 0.1 mg; 0.5 mg is the maximum single pediatric dose, and ventilation should not be interrupted.
opts: Begin chest compressions
Give atropine 0.1 mg IV
Give atropine 0.08 mg IV (0.02 mg/kg)
Give atropine 0.5 mg IV
Withhold atropine because of age
Pause ventilation to recheck the rhythm
ok: Begin chest compressions
Give atropine 0.1 mg IV

items.q: In cardiac arrest, which effect of epinephrine is mainly responsible for improving coronary perfusion pressure during CPR?
items.x: Epinephrine's alpha effect constricts peripheral vessels, raising aortic diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion during compressions. It does not convert ventricular fibrillation; defibrillation does that.
items.a: Alpha-adrenergic peripheral vasoconstriction
w: Beta-2 mediated bronchodilation
Direct electrical conversion of fibrillation
Reduction of myocardial oxygen demand

items.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has no peripheral IV, and attempts at access have failed. Which route is an accepted alternative for giving epinephrine during resuscitation?
items.x: The intraosseous route reaches the central circulation about as reliably as IV access and is the preferred alternative in arrest. Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable when there is no spontaneous circulation.
items.a: Intraosseous
w: Subcutaneous
Sublingual
Oral

items.q: For which cardiac arrest rhythm is epinephrine recommended as early as possible, because no shock is indicated?
items.x: In nonshockable rhythms such as asystole and PEA, epinephrine is given as soon as feasible. In VF and pulseless VT, defibrillation comes first and epinephrine follows after initial shocks.
items.a: Asystole
w: Ventricular fibrillation
Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia

items.q: Epinephrine belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Epinephrine is an endogenous catecholamine that stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors. Atropine, not epinephrine, is the anticholinergic used in emergency care.
items.a: Sympathomimetic catecholamine
w: Parasympatholytic anticholinergic
Cardiac glycoside
Beta-adrenergic blocker

items.q: After return of spontaneous circulation in a patient who received several doses of epinephrine, which finding is an expected drug effect to monitor for?
items.x: Epinephrine's beta-1 stimulation raises heart rate and myocardial irritability, so tachycardia and ectopy are common after ROSC. It causes bronchodilation, not bronchospasm.
items.a: Tachycardia and ventricular ectopy
w: Bradycardia and heart block
Pinpoint pupils and miosis
Bronchospasm and wheezing

items.q: How does aspirin benefit a patient with a suspected acute coronary syndrome?
items.x: Aspirin blocks cyclooxygenase and thromboxane A2 production, keeping platelets from clumping onto the clot. It is not a fibrinolytic and does not break down existing fibrin.
items.a: It irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation
w: It dissolves the existing fibrin clot
It dilates the coronary arteries directly
It lowers myocardial oxygen demand directly

items.q: When aspirin is given for suspected acute coronary syndrome, how should the patient take the tablets?
items.x: Chewing speeds absorption through the oral and gastric mucosa so platelet inhibition begins sooner. Sublingual placement is the route for nitroglycerin, not aspirin.
items.a: Chew them before swallowing
w: Swallow them whole with water
Let them dissolve under the tongue
Hold them between cheek and gum

items.q: A patient with chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome reports which history that is a contraindication to aspirin?
items.x: A true aspirin hypersensitivity is a contraindication because it can trigger urticaria, bronchospasm or anaphylaxis. Prior aspirin use earlier in the week does not prevent its use now.
items.a: Known aspirin allergy with prior hives and wheezing
w: Daily use of a cholesterol-lowering medication
Taking a baby aspirin earlier in the week
History of controlled high blood pressure

items.q: A patient with chest pain has ST elevation in the inferior leads and is hypotensive. Why is nitroglycerin used with great caution in this patient?
items.x: Inferior MI often involves the right ventricle, which depends on preload to fill the left heart; venodilation can cause profound hypotension. The concern is preload, not resistance to the drug.
items.a: Possible right ventricular infarction makes the patient preload dependent
w: Inferior infarction makes the patient resistant to vasodilators
Nitroglycerin increases the risk of ventricular fibrillation here
Nitroglycerin worsens platelet clumping in inferior infarction

items.q: Before each dose of sublingual nitroglycerin for ischemic chest pain, which assessment is most essential?
items.x: Nitroglycerin's vasodilation can drop blood pressure sharply, so blood pressure is checked before every dose and reassessed after. Glucose is useful in many patients but does not determine whether nitroglycerin is safe.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Blood glucose level
Pupil size and reactivity
Capillary refill in the toes

items.q: A hypertensive patient presents with acute pulmonary edema. What is the main way nitroglycerin relieves the respiratory distress?
items.x: Nitroglycerin dilates veins, pooling blood peripherally and lowering the volume returning to the congested lungs. It is not a diuretic; fluid is redistributed, not excreted.
items.a: Venodilation reduces preload and pulmonary congestion
w: Bronchodilation opens constricted small airways
Diuresis removes excess fluid through the kidneys
Increased contractility strengthens the left ventricle

items.q: A patient with very high blood pressure and chest pain says he took a medication for erectile dysfunction yesterday. Why is this important before nitroglycerin?
items.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil potentiate nitrate vasodilation and can cause life-threatening hypotension. The interaction lowers, not raises, blood pressure.
items.a: Combined use can cause severe, prolonged hypotension
w: Combined use can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure
The combination blocks nitroglycerin from being absorbed
The combination causes rapid bleeding from the gums

items.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported after a patient takes nitroglycerin?
items.x: Dilation of cerebral blood vessels commonly produces a pounding headache. Yellow-tinted vision is associated with digoxin toxicity, not nitrates.
items.a: Throbbing headache
w: Severe constipation
Slowed respirations
Blurred yellow vision

items.q: Which teaching point helps a patient keep prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin tablets effective?
items.x: Nitroglycerin tablets lose potency with exposure to light, heat, air and moisture, so they belong in the original closed glass container. Plastic pill organizers and humid bathrooms speed degradation.
items.a: Keep them in the original tightly closed container
w: Store them in a moist bathroom cabinet
Transfer them to a plastic weekly pill box
Keep them open in a sunny window sill

items.q: A patient becomes lightheaded and hypotensive a few minutes after nitroglycerin. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
items.x: Nitroglycerin-induced venodilation can cause hypotension; laying the patient flat and reassessing vital signs is appropriate, along with reporting the change. This is a predictable effect, not anaphylaxis or hypoglycemia.
items.a: Recognize an expected vasodilator effect, place supine, and reassess
w: Recognize an allergic reaction and give glucagon
Recognize hypoglycemia and give oral glucose
Recognize opioid toxicity and give naloxone

items.q: In anaphylactic shock, which epinephrine effect most directly counters the drop in blood pressure?
items.x: Alpha-1 stimulation tightens dilated, leaky vessels and raises systemic vascular resistance. Beta-2 effects open the airways but do not restore blood pressure.
items.a: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction
w: Beta-2 bronchodilation
Muscarinic receptor blockade
Histamine-1 receptor blockade

items.q: What is the preferred initial route for epinephrine in a patient with anaphylactic shock in the field?
items.x: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. Nebulized epinephrine does not treat systemic shock.
items.a: Intramuscular injection in the lateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection in the upper arm
Inhaled by small-volume nebulizer
Sublingual tablet under the tongue

items.q: A patient in hemorrhagic shock remains hypotensive. Why is epinephrine not the primary treatment?
items.x: Hemorrhagic shock is a volume problem; controlling bleeding and restoring circulating volume address the cause. Vasoconstrictors cannot fill an empty vascular space.
items.a: The problem is lost volume, which needs bleeding control and fluids
w: Epinephrine is absorbed too slowly in trauma patients
Epinephrine causes too much bronchodilation in trauma
The problem is vasodilation, which needs antihistamines

items.q: A patient in anaphylaxis takes a beta-blocker daily. How might this affect the response to epinephrine?
items.x: Beta-blockade can blunt epinephrine's cardiac and bronchial effects, leading to persistent hypotension; glucagon is sometimes used in this situation. Alpha effects are not blocked by beta-blockers.
items.a: The response may be blunted, causing refractory hypotension
w: The response is usually exaggerated, causing hypertension
The beta-blocker fully prevents any alpha effects
The beta-blocker has no effect on epinephrine response

items.q: After epinephrine is given for shock, which combination of reassessments is most appropriate?
items.x: Epinephrine changes blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, and the response should show in perfusion and mental status. The other choices do not track its hemodynamic effect.
items.a: Blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm, and mental status
w: Pupil size, temperature, and capillary glucose only
Skin turgor, bowel sounds, and urine color
Grip strength, pupil size, and pain score

items.q: Albuterol belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as rescue therapy for bronchospasm. Inhaled corticosteroids control inflammation but do not provide rapid relief.
items.a: Short-acting beta-2 agonist
w: Long-acting anticholinergic
Inhaled corticosteroid
Leukotriene receptor antagonist

items.q: A patient receiving nebulized albuterol becomes shaky and reports a racing heart. How should these findings be interpreted?
items.x: Tremor and tachycardia are common albuterol effects from beta-receptor stimulation; they should be monitored and reported if significant. They do not indicate an allergy.
items.a: Common expected side effects of beta stimulation
w: Signs of a severe allergic reaction
Signs of opioid withdrawal
Signs of acute hypoglycemia

items.q: After a nebulized albuterol treatment for wheezing, which finding best shows the treatment is working?
items.x: Better air movement with less accessory muscle use shows reversal of bronchospasm. Wheezing that fades into silent breath sounds signals worsening obstruction, not improvement.
items.a: Improved air movement and decreased work of breathing
w: Wheezing disappears and breath sounds become absent
Heart rate rises well above baseline
Patient becomes drowsy and difficult to arouse

items.q: How does ipratropium produce bronchodilation?
items.x: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic that blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Beta-2 stimulation is how albuterol works, which is why the two are often combined.
items.a: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the airways
w: It stimulates beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle
It blocks histamine release from mast cells
It reduces airway inflammation like a corticosteroid

items.q: In the emergency treatment of moderate to severe bronchospasm, ipratropium is most often given in which way?
items.x: Ipratropium is an inhaled drug and is commonly nebulized with albuterol because the two act on different pathways. It is not given by injection.
items.a: Nebulized together with albuterol
w: Injected intramuscularly in the thigh
Chewed and swallowed as a tablet
Injected by slow intravenous push

items.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported with inhaled ipratropium?
items.x: As an anticholinergic, ipratropium reduces secretions and commonly causes dry mouth. Excess salivation would be the opposite, cholinergic effect.
items.a: Dry mouth
w: Hypoglycemia
Excess salivation
Slowed heart rate

items.q: How is levalbuterol related to albuterol?
items.x: Levalbuterol is the R-isomer of albuterol and works the same way, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle by stimulating beta-2 receptors. It is used for acute bronchospasm, not as a steroid or anticholinergic.
items.a: It is the active isomer of albuterol, also a beta-2 agonist
w: It is a long-acting form used only for prevention
It is an anticholinergic combined with albuterol
It is an inhaled steroid derived from albuterol

items.q: A patient with asthma receives nebulized levalbuterol. Which adverse effects should be monitored for?
items.x: Like albuterol, levalbuterol is a beta agonist and can cause tachycardia, tremor and nervousness. Bradycardia and drooling are cholinergic effects not expected with this drug.
items.a: Tachycardia, tremor, and nervousness
w: Bradycardia, miosis, and drooling
Hypertension, hives, and fever
Constipation, sedation, and slowed breathing

items.q: A patient in severe asthma exacerbation is too fatigued to use a nebulizer effectively. Why may intramuscular epinephrine be considered under protocol?
items.x: Systemic epinephrine reaches bronchial smooth muscle through the blood, so it works even when air movement is too poor to deliver inhaled drugs. It is not a sedative or anti-inflammatory.
items.a: It causes bronchodilation without depending on inhalation
w: It sedates the patient to reduce air hunger
It reduces airway inflammation over several hours
It thins mucus so it can be coughed up

items.q: A child with croup improves after nebulized epinephrine. Why is continued observation important?
items.x: Nebulized epinephrine shrinks swollen airway tissue only temporarily, so symptoms can return once it wears off. Delayed hypoglycemia and hives are not the expected concern.
items.a: Stridor can return as the drug's effect wears off
w: The drug commonly causes delayed hypoglycemia
The drug commonly causes delayed hives
Stridor typically worsens permanently after epinephrine

items.q: What is the first-line medication for a patient with anaphylaxis?
items.x: Epinephrine reverses vasodilation, airway swelling and bronchospasm and is the only first-line drug for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines relieve itching and hives but do not reverse shock or airway compromise.
items.a: Epinephrine
w: Diphenhydramine
Albuterol
Methylprednisolone

items.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
items.x: Auto-injectors are labeled for the anterolateral thigh, which provides rapid intramuscular absorption and can be reached through clothing. The abdomen is a common site for other injected drugs, not auto-injectors.
items.a: Anterolateral thigh
w: Deltoid muscle of the arm
Abdominal wall near the navel
Dorsal gluteal muscle

items.q: A patient's hives and wheezing resolve after self-administered epinephrine. Why does the patient still need emergency department evaluation?
items.x: Epinephrine is short-acting and symptoms may recur, including in a biphasic reaction hours later, so observation is needed. There is no antidote that must be given after epinephrine.
items.a: Symptoms can return as epinephrine wears off or in a biphasic reaction
w: Epinephrine routinely causes delayed liver injury
Epinephrine must be reversed with an antidote
Hives always progress to shock within one hour

items.q: Which epinephrine effect relieves the upper airway swelling of anaphylaxis?
items.x: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction decreases capillary leak and swelling in airway tissues. Blocking H1 receptors is how antihistamines work.
items.a: Vasoconstriction that reduces mucosal edema
w: Blocking histamine at H1 receptors
Increased mucus production in the airway
Relaxation of the skeletal muscles of the neck

items.q: A patient with anaphylaxis has received epinephrine but still has wheezing. What role does albuterol play?
items.x: Albuterol can relieve lower-airway bronchospasm that persists after epinephrine. It does not raise blood pressure or reduce upper-airway edema, so it never replaces epinephrine.
items.a: An adjunct for persistent bronchospasm
w: A replacement for epinephrine in anaphylaxis
The primary treatment for hypotension
A treatment for laryngeal swelling

items.q: Why is albuterol alone inadequate treatment for anaphylaxis?
items.x: Albuterol is a selective beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle but lacks the alpha effects needed for hypotension and swelling. It acts quickly on wheezing.
items.a: It does not reverse vasodilation or airway edema
w: It worsens hives by releasing histamine
It acts too slowly to relieve wheezing
It is only effective in children

items.q: During nebulized albuterol for an allergic reaction, which finding should the AEMT recognize as a common drug effect rather than worsening allergy?
items.x: Fine tremor is a common beta-agonist effect. Tongue swelling, spreading hives and hypotension suggest progression of the allergic reaction.
items.a: Mild tremor of the hands
w: New swelling of the tongue
Spreading hives on the chest
Dropping blood pressure

items.q: A patient in anaphylaxis who takes a beta-blocker remains hypotensive after repeated epinephrine. Which medication may be used for this situation?
items.x: Glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through a pathway that does not use beta receptors, so it may help when beta-blockade blunts epinephrine. The other drugs do not address this problem.
items.a: Glucagon
w: Naloxone
Ondansetron
Aspirin

items.q: Why can glucagon work when beta-blockers blunt the response to epinephrine?
items.x: Glucagon binds its own receptors on heart cells and raises cAMP, bypassing the blocked beta receptors. It does not bind or clear the beta-blocker.
items.a: It increases cardiac cAMP without using beta receptors
w: It directly blocks the beta-blocker in the blood
It stimulates alpha receptors more strongly
It speeds the liver's removal of the beta-blocker

items.q: Which common side effect of glucagon requires the AEMT to be prepared to protect the airway?
items.x: Nausea and vomiting are frequent after glucagon, so suction and positioning should be ready, especially in a patient with altered mental status. Bronchospasm is not a typical effect.
items.a: Vomiting
w: Bronchospasm
Seizures
Jaw rigidity

items.q: Acetaminophen is best described by which set of properties?
items.x: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has minimal anti-inflammatory action and does not affect platelets. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are the anti-inflammatory choice.
items.a: Analgesic and antipyretic with little anti-inflammatory effect
w: Opioid analgesic with strong sedating effects
Anti-inflammatory that strongly inhibits platelets
Local anesthetic that blocks nerve conduction

items.q: What is the most serious toxic effect of an acetaminophen overdose?
items.x: Excess acetaminophen overwhelms normal metabolism and produces a metabolite that damages the liver. Respiratory depression is typical of opioid overdose, not acetaminophen.
items.a: Liver injury
w: Respiratory depression
Gastric ulcer bleeding
Bone marrow failure

items.q: Before giving acetaminophen, which question is most important to ask the patient?
items.x: Many cold, sleep and prescription pain combinations contain acetaminophen, so asking prevents unintentional excess intake. Shellfish allergy has no bearing on acetaminophen.
items.a: Whether they recently took any product containing acetaminophen
w: Whether they have ever had a tetanus shot
Whether they are allergic to shellfish or iodine
Whether they have had recent dental work

items.q: For a patient with a history of stomach ulcers who needs a mild pain reliever, why might acetaminophen be preferred over an NSAID?
items.x: Acetaminophen lacks the GI irritation and antiplatelet effects of NSAIDs, which can cause ulcer bleeding. It is not safer in severe liver disease, where acetaminophen requires caution.
items.a: It does not irritate the stomach lining or impair platelets
w: It is a stronger anti-inflammatory than NSAIDs
It works by coating and protecting the stomach
It is safer than NSAIDs in severe liver disease

items.q: Which patient history calls for the most caution with acetaminophen?
items.x: Chronic alcohol use and liver disease increase the risk of acetaminophen liver toxicity. The other conditions do not meaningfully raise that risk.
items.a: Chronic heavy alcohol use with liver disease
w: Seasonal allergies treated with nasal spray
Recent ankle sprain with swelling
Well-controlled hypothyroidism

items.q: Why are dextrose-in-water solutions a poor choice for volume replacement in hemorrhagic shock?
items.x: After the dextrose is used by cells, the remaining free water distributes into all body compartments and little stays in the vascular space. Isotonic crystalloids such as normal saline are used for volume.
items.a: Once the sugar is metabolized, the free water leaves the vessels
w: The sugar binds red cells and blocks oxygen delivery
The solution raises blood pressure too quickly
The solution causes immediate allergic reactions

items.q: Before giving concentrated IV dextrose, why must the AEMT confirm that the IV line is patent and well secured?
items.x: Hypertonic dextrose is irritating, and if it leaks into tissue it can cause necrosis. Checking flow and flushing before and during administration reduces that risk.
items.a: Extravasation can cause severe tissue damage
w: Dextrose clots quickly inside the IV catheter
Dextrose cannot be pushed through a saline lock
A patent line prevents low blood sugar from recurring

items.q: During IV dextrose administration, the site becomes swollen, cool, and painful. What should the AEMT recognize?
items.x: Swelling, coolness and pain at the site indicate the solution is entering tissue rather than the vein, which must be recognized and managed per protocol. These are local signs, not systemic overload.
items.a: Infiltration of the IV
w: An expected drug effect
Hyperglycemic crisis
Fluid volume overload

items.q: Why is a large, proximal vein preferred when giving concentrated dextrose?
items.x: Concentrated dextrose is hypertonic and can cause phlebitis; larger veins with more blood flow dilute it faster. Vein size does not change how the body absorbs glucose.
items.a: Hypertonic solution irritates small veins
w: Dextrose is absorbed only by large veins
Small veins remove dextrose too quickly
Large veins prevent rebound hyperglycemia

items.q: After IV dextrose is given for hypoglycemia, which assessment confirms the treatment effect?
items.x: Rechecking the glucose level and the patient's mental status shows whether hypoglycemia has been corrected. Lung sounds and urine output do not reflect the response to dextrose.
items.a: Repeat blood glucose with mental status check
w: Repeat pupil check with grip strength
Repeat lung sounds with oxygen saturation
Repeat skin turgor with urine output

items.q: How does albuterol lower serum potassium in hyperkalemia?
items.x: Beta-2 stimulation drives potassium into cells, temporarily lowering serum levels. It does not remove potassium from the body, which requires the kidneys, binders or dialysis.
items.a: It shifts potassium from the blood into cells
w: It increases potassium excretion in urine
It binds potassium in the intestines
It removes potassium through the lungs

items.q: Why is albuterol considered only a temporary measure for hyperkalemia?
items.x: Albuterol moves potassium into cells but does not eliminate it, so serum levels can rise again as the effect fades. Definitive removal is needed afterward.
items.a: Total body potassium is unchanged and levels can rebound
w: Its effect lasts only seconds after inhalation
It causes the kidneys to retain more potassium
It is quickly neutralized by stomach acid

items.q: Which patient is at highest risk for hyperkalemia, a condition sometimes treated with albuterol?
items.x: Kidney failure with missed dialysis prevents potassium excretion, causing hyperkalemia. Vomiting, diarrhea and loop diuretics tend to cause low potassium.
items.a: A dialysis patient who missed treatments
w: A runner with prolonged vomiting
A patient taking a loop diuretic
A patient with ongoing diarrhea

items.q: Repeated high-dose albuterol can cause which electrolyte disturbance?
items.x: Because albuterol shifts potassium into cells, heavy use can lower serum potassium. It does not raise sodium, calcium or magnesium.
items.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
Hypermagnesemia

items.q: While albuterol is given to a patient with suspected hyperkalemia, which monitoring is most important?
items.x: Potassium abnormalities cause dysrhythmias, and albuterol itself raises heart rate, so cardiac monitoring is essential. Peak flow measures airflow, not the potassium effect.
items.a: Continuous cardiac rhythm and heart rate
w: Hourly temperature measurements
Pupil size and reactivity
Peak flow every few minutes

items.q: How does naloxone reverse opioid toxicity?
items.x: Naloxone displaces opioids from mu receptors and blocks them, reversing respiratory and CNS depression. It does not change how quickly the opioid is metabolized.
items.a: It competitively blocks opioid receptors
w: It speeds liver breakdown of the opioid
It binds the opioid in the stomach
It directly stimulates the breathing center

items.q: When giving naloxone to an unresponsive patient with suspected opioid overdose, what is the primary goal?
items.x: The aim is adequate ventilation; full awakening is unnecessary and risks abrupt withdrawal and agitation. Naloxone does not cause vomiting of pills.
items.a: Restore adequate spontaneous breathing
w: Restore full alertness and orientation
Induce vomiting of any pills swallowed
Lower the heart rate to normal

items.q: After naloxone reverses an opioid overdose, why must the patient be monitored closely?
items.x: Many opioids, especially long-acting or high-potency ones, outlast naloxone, so respiratory depression can return. Liver failure and hypoglycemia are not expected naloxone effects.
items.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, causing re-sedation
w: Naloxone often causes delayed liver failure
Naloxone often causes delayed anaphylaxis
Naloxone causes a late drop in blood glucose

items.q: A patient who uses opioids daily becomes agitated, vomits, and has goosebumps right after naloxone. What should the AEMT recognize?
items.x: Naloxone abruptly reverses opioid effects in a dependent patient, producing withdrawal with agitation, vomiting and piloerection. These signs are not an allergic reaction.
items.a: Acute opioid withdrawal
w: Allergic reaction to naloxone
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemic reaction

items.q: How does activated charcoal reduce the absorption of an ingested poison?
items.x: Activated charcoal's large surface area binds many drugs in the GI tract so less is absorbed. It is not an emetic or a receptor antagonist.
items.a: It adsorbs the toxin on its surface in the gut
w: It neutralizes acids by chemical reaction
It induces vomiting of stomach contents
It blocks the toxin at its receptor site

items.q: Which patient has a contraindication to activated charcoal?
items.x: Charcoal given to a patient with decreased consciousness or an unprotected airway risks aspiration. An alert patient with a recent ingestion is the typical candidate if ordered.
items.a: A drowsy patient who cannot protect the airway
w: An alert adult who swallowed pills recently
An alert patient who took an acetaminophen overdose
An alert patient with nausea but no vomiting

items.q: Activated charcoal binds poorly to which ingested substance?
items.x: Metals such as iron and lithium, alcohols and caustics are poorly adsorbed by charcoal. Aspirin, acetaminophen and tricyclics bind well.
items.a: Iron
w: Aspirin
Acetaminophen
Tricyclic antidepressants

items.q: Glucagon may be used as an antidote for an overdose of which medication class?
items.x: Glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through its own receptors, bypassing blocked beta receptors in beta-blocker overdose. Opioid overdose is reversed with naloxone.
items.a: Beta-blockers
w: Benzodiazepines
Opioids
Anticholinergics

items.q: A patient with beta-blocker overdose has bradycardia and hypotension. Which effect of glucagon makes it useful?
items.x: Glucagon has positive chronotropic and inotropic effects independent of beta receptors, countering beta-blocker toxicity. Blocking calcium entry would worsen the problem.
items.a: Increases heart rate and contractility
w: Lowers heart rate and contractility
Causes peripheral vasodilation
Blocks calcium entry into cardiac cells

items.q: When glucagon is given for beta-blocker toxicity, which side effect should the AEMT be prepared to manage?
items.x: Vomiting is a common glucagon effect, so suction and airway positioning should be ready. Bronchospasm and pinpoint pupils are not expected glucagon effects.
items.a: Vomiting with aspiration risk
w: Severe bronchospasm
Muscle rigidity
Pinpoint pupils

items.q: Before IV dextrose is given to a patient with altered mental status, which finding should be confirmed?
items.x: Dextrose is indicated for documented hypoglycemia, so a glucose check guides its use. Blood pressure and pulse do not determine the need for dextrose.
items.a: A low blood glucose reading
w: A high blood glucose reading
A normal blood pressure
A slow pulse rate

items.q: Why is IV dextrose preferred over oral glucose for a hypoglycemic patient who is unresponsive?
items.x: Oral glucose requires an intact gag reflex and ability to swallow; an unresponsive patient could aspirate. IV dextrose bypasses the airway.
items.a: The patient cannot safely swallow, risking aspiration
w: Oral glucose raises blood sugar too much
Oral glucose is only for children
IV dextrose lasts longer than any food

items.q: A known diabetic is confused, pale, and sweaty. Which finding most strongly supports hypoglycemia as the cause?
items.x: Taking insulin without eating commonly causes rapid hypoglycemia with diaphoresis and confusion, which dextrose treats. Fruity breath and Kussmaul breathing suggest DKA.
items.a: Rapid onset after skipping a meal following insulin
w: Gradual onset over days with heavy thirst
Fruity breath with deep, rapid breathing
Frequent urination with dry mucous membranes

items.q: A hypoglycemic patient is unresponsive and no IV access can be obtained. How can glucagon be given?
items.x: Glucagon is available for IM injection and as an intranasal powder, so it can be given without IV access. It is not effective by mouth.
items.a: Intramuscularly or by the intranasal form
w: Orally as a chewable tablet
Sublingually as a dissolving film
Rectally as a suppository

items.q: Why may glucagon be less effective in a malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use?
items.x: Glucagon raises blood sugar by releasing glucose from liver glycogen; if those stores are low, the response is weak. IV dextrose supplies glucose directly.
items.a: Liver glycogen stores may be depleted
w: Alcohol blocks glucagon receptors directly
Alcohol speeds glucagon excretion by kidneys
Alcohol inactivates glucagon in the blood

items.q: Ondansetron belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and brainstem vomiting center. H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors reduce acid but do not treat nausea directly.
items.a: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist
w: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
Histamine H2 receptor blocker
Proton pump inhibitor

items.q: Which cardiac effect of ondansetron is listed as a warning in its labeling?
items.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval and, rarely, cause torsades de pointes, so caution is needed in patients with long QT or electrolyte problems. ST elevation is not an expected effect.
items.a: QT interval prolongation
w: Sudden heart block
Marked hypertension
ST segment elevation

items.q: How should an orally disintegrating ondansetron tablet be given?
items.x: The orally disintegrating tablet dissolves on the tongue in seconds and is swallowed with saliva, useful for nauseated patients. It does not need to be swallowed whole with water.
items.a: Placed on the tongue to dissolve, then swallowed
w: Crushed and inhaled through a nebulizer
Swallowed whole with a large glass of water
Chewed thoroughly with a meal

items.q: Which side effect is commonly reported after ondansetron?
items.x: Headache is among the most common ondansetron side effects; constipation is another. Hallucinations are not a typical effect.
items.a: Headache
w: Hallucinations
Hypoglycemia
Excess tearing

items.q: Which patient history calls for the most caution before ondansetron?
items.x: Ondansetron's labeling advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome because of the risk of dangerous rhythms. The other histories do not raise this risk.
items.a: Congenital long QT syndrome
w: Seasonal pollen allergies
Recent knee replacement surgery
Well-controlled asthma

items.q: A child stung by a bee develops hives, wheezing, and lethargy. What is the priority medication?
items.x: Hives with respiratory involvement and altered mental status indicate anaphylaxis, for which IM epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines do not reverse airway or circulatory compromise.
items.a: Intramuscular epinephrine
w: Oral diphenhydramine
Nebulized ipratropium
Oral acetaminophen

items.q: When helping a parent use a child's epinephrine auto-injector, which teaching point is correct?
items.x: Auto-injectors go into the anterolateral thigh and are held in place for the labeled time so the full amount is delivered; they can be given through clothing. Labeling warns against injecting into the buttocks.
items.a: Press firmly into the outer thigh for the labeled time
w: Inject into the buttock for faster absorption
Remove clothing completely before injecting
Inject into the upper arm muscle

items.q: An infant is jittery, poorly feeding, and has a weak cry. Which assessment should guide whether dextrose is given?
items.x: Signs of hypoglycemia in infants are vague, so a glucose check confirms the need for dextrose. Temperature and head size do not establish hypoglycemia.
items.a: Blood glucose measurement
w: Temperature measurement
Head circumference
Pupil response

items.q: A school-age child with asthma is wheezing. Which device helps the child get more albuterol into the lungs from a metered-dose inhaler?
items.x: A spacer keeps the medication in a chamber so the child can inhale it with less need for coordination, improving delivery to the lungs. A peak flow meter measures airflow but delivers no medication.
items.a: A spacer attached to the inhaler
w: A nasal cannula
A bag-valve mask with reservoir
A peak flow meter

items.q: A toddler is found drowsy with slow, shallow breathing and pinpoint pupils near a grandparent's pill bottle. Which medication addresses the likely cause?
items.x: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression suggest opioid toxicity, which naloxone reverses; ventilation support comes first. Glucagon is for hypoglycemia or beta-blocker toxicity.
items.a: Naloxone
w: Glucagon
Ondansetron
Albuterol

items.q: A child with type 1 diabetes is unresponsive with a low glucose reading and no IV access. Which medication can be given?
items.x: Glucagon by IM injection or intranasally raises blood sugar without IV access. Oral glucose is unsafe because an unresponsive child cannot protect the airway.
items.a: Glucagon
w: Oral glucose gel
Ondansetron
Activated charcoal

items.q: Why is ondansetron given to some children with vomiting from gastroenteritis?
items.x: Controlling vomiting allows the child to keep down oral fluids and may avoid IV therapy. Ondansetron does not treat the infection or replace fluid itself.
items.a: To reduce vomiting so oral rehydration can succeed
w: To cure the underlying viral infection
To slow diarrhea by firming the stool
To treat dehydration directly by adding fluid

items.q: Why is acetaminophen preferred over aspirin for fever in a child with a viral illness?
items.x: Aspirin use in children with viral illnesses such as influenza or chickenpox is associated with Reye syndrome, a dangerous liver and brain disorder. Acetaminophen does not treat the infection.
items.a: Aspirin is linked to Reye syndrome in children
w: Aspirin does not reduce fever in children
Acetaminophen also treats the viral infection
Acetaminophen has stronger anti-inflammatory effects

items.q: Which teaching point helps a parent avoid giving too much liquid acetaminophen to a child?
items.x: The dosing device packaged with the product matches its labeled concentration and reduces measuring errors. Kitchen spoons vary in size and commonly lead to dosing mistakes.
items.a: Use the measuring device that comes with the product
w: Use a household kitchen spoon
Mix it into a full bottle of formula
Give an adult tablet cut into pieces

items.q: A child has had several days of vomiting and diarrhea with very little urine output. Why is ibuprofen a concern?
items.x: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys, and in a dehydrated child this can contribute to acute kidney injury. Liver failure is the major concern with acetaminophen overdose, not ibuprofen.
items.a: Dehydration increases its risk of kidney injury
w: Dehydration makes it cause liver failure
It worsens diarrhea by speeding the gut
It causes dangerous drops in blood sugar

items.q: A resident takes amlodipine for high blood pressure. Which change is a common side effect a nursing assistant should report to the nurse?
items.x: Amlodipine often causes swelling (edema) in the ankles and feet, which should be reported. It does not change urine color or cause mouth patches.
items.a: Swelling in the ankles and feet
w: Bright orange-colored urine
Increased hunger at night
White patches inside the mouth

items.q: A resident who takes atorvastatin to lower cholesterol complains of new, unexplained muscle pain and weakness. What should the nursing assistant do?
items.x: Statins like atorvastatin can rarely cause serious muscle damage, so new muscle pain or weakness must be reported. It should not be brushed off as normal soreness.
items.a: Report the muscle pain to the nurse
w: Give the resident a warm bath and recheck tomorrow
Tell the resident this is normal for everyone
Encourage extra exercise to work out the soreness

items.q: A resident on digoxin says food has lost its appeal, feels sick to the stomach, and sees yellow-green halos around lights. What do these changes suggest?
items.x: Nausea, loss of appetite, and vision changes such as yellow-green halos can mean digoxin levels are too high. These must be reported to the nurse right away, not treated as normal aging.
items.a: Possible signs of too much digoxin
w: Expected signs the medicine is working
Normal changes from aging eyes
Signs of a mild seasonal allergy

items.q: Why is furosemide usually given in the morning rather than at bedtime?
items.x: Furosemide is a strong water pill that makes the person urinate a lot for several hours. Morning timing helps avoid nighttime trips to the bathroom and falls.
items.a: It causes frequent urination for several hours
w: It works better on an empty stomach at night
It causes sleepiness during the day
It must be taken with the evening meal

items.q: A resident who takes hydrochlorothiazide feels lightheaded when getting out of bed. What is the safest action for the nursing assistant?
items.x: Water pills can lower blood pressure, especially when standing up. Sitting first and rising slowly lowers fall risk; standing quickly makes dizziness worse.
items.a: Have the resident sit on the edge of the bed before standing
w: Help the resident stand up quickly to get it over with
Have the resident walk to the bathroom alone
Lay the resident flat and leave the room

items.q: A resident who recently started lisinopril has a dry, tickly cough that will not go away. What should the nursing assistant know?
items.x: Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) commonly causes a dry, nagging cough, which should be reported to the nurse. It is not a sign the medicine is working.
items.a: A dry cough is a known side effect to report
w: A dry cough means the dose is working well
A dry cough is caused only by a cold
A dry cough means the resident needs more fluids

items.q: A resident taking lisinopril suddenly has swelling of the lips, tongue, and face. What should the nursing assistant do?
items.x: Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue (angioedema) is a rare but dangerous reaction to lisinopril that can block the airway. It is an emergency, not something to report later.
items.a: Call for the nurse right away and stay with the resident
w: Offer cold water and check back in an hour
Apply lotion to the lips and face
Write it down to report at the end of the shift

items.q: When taking vital signs on a resident who takes metoprolol, which finding is most important to report to the nurse?
items.x: Metoprolol slows the heart rate, so an unusually slow pulse can mean too strong an effect. Readings that match the resident's normal values are not a concern.
items.a: A pulse that is much slower than usual
w: A pulse that is the same as yesterday
A temperature that is normal
A blood pressure that is unchanged

items.q: Metoprolol belongs to which group of heart medicines?
items.x: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that slows the heart and lowers blood pressure. It is not a water pill; furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide are diuretics.
items.a: Beta blockers
w: Water pills (diuretics)
Blood thinners
Cholesterol-lowering statins

items.q: A resident with chest pain is given nitroglycerin by the nurse. Which side effect is common and should be expected?
items.x: Nitroglycerin widens blood vessels, which commonly causes headache and dizziness from lower blood pressure. The resident should stay seated or lying down to prevent falls.
items.a: Headache and feeling lightheaded
w: Increased appetite and thirst
Itchy rash on the arms

items.q: What is digoxin commonly used to treat?
