items.q: How does docusate help with constipation?
items.x: Docusate is a stool softener that lets water and fat mix into stool so it is easier to pass. Stimulant laxatives like senna are the ones that push the bowel muscles.
items.a: It softens stool by letting water mix into it
w: It strongly squeezes the bowel muscles
It neutralizes stomach acid
It slows the bowel to reduce diarrhea

items.q: A resident takes docusate. Which daily care action helps it work best, if allowed by the care plan?
items.x: Stool softeners work better when the person drinks enough fluids. Activity and fiber, as allowed, also help prevent constipation.
items.a: Offering fluids throughout the day
w: Limiting fluids at meals
Keeping the resident in bed all day
Serving only low-fiber foods

items.q: Omeprazole belongs to which group of medicines?
items.x: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that reduces stomach acid for heartburn and ulcers. It is not a laxative or antibiotic.
items.a: Proton pump inhibitors that lower stomach acid
w: Stimulant laxatives
Antihistamines for allergies
Antibiotics for infection

items.q: When is omeprazole usually taken for best effect?
items.x: Omeprazole works best when taken before a meal, commonly before breakfast. It is not a quick-acting antacid for sudden heartburn.
items.a: Before a meal, often before breakfast
w: Right after a large dinner
Only when lying down at night
Only during a heartburn attack

items.q: How is polyethylene glycol powder usually taken?
items.x: Polyethylene glycol powder is dissolved in a beverage such as water or juice before drinking. It is not taken dry or inhaled.
items.a: Mixed and dissolved in a glass of liquid
w: Sprinkled dry on the tongue
Rubbed onto the skin
Inhaled with a mouthpiece

items.q: How does polyethylene glycol relieve constipation?
items.x: Polyethylene glycol is an osmotic laxative that keeps water in the bowel, making stool softer and easier to pass. It does not work by irritating the bowel.
items.a: It keeps water in the bowel to soften stool
w: It irritates the bowel lining to cause cramping
It coats the stool with oil
It adds bulk by soaking up fat

items.q: A resident received magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) and now has many loose, watery stools. What should the nursing assistant do?
items.x: Magnesium hydroxide is a laxative, and too strong an effect can cause frequent watery stools and fluid loss. This should be reported.
items.a: Report the diarrhea to the nurse
w: Offer another laxative
Limit the resident's fluids
Ignore it because it is expected

items.q: Magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) is used for which purposes?
items.x: Milk of magnesia works as a laxative for constipation and as an antacid for acid indigestion. It does not treat motion sickness or allergies.
items.a: Constipation and upset stomach from acid
w: Nausea from motion sickness and vertigo
Allergies and itchy eyes
Pain and fever

items.q: Meclizine is used to prevent or treat which problem?
items.x: Meclizine is an antihistamine that helps prevent nausea, vomiting, and dizziness from motion sickness. It is not an antacid or laxative.
items.a: Nausea and dizziness from motion sickness
w: Heartburn from stomach acid
Constipation from pain pills
Diarrhea from antibiotics

items.q: A resident takes calcium carbonate often for heartburn. Which side effect should the nursing assistant watch for?
items.x: Calcium carbonate antacids commonly cause constipation. Magnesium-containing antacids are more likely to cause diarrhea.
items.a: Constipation
w: Diarrhea
Increased urination
Hair loss

items.q: A pregnant woman has heartburn. Calcium carbonate is often used for this. How does it work?
items.x: Calcium carbonate is an antacid that neutralizes stomach acid to relieve heartburn, which is common in pregnancy. It also provides calcium.
items.a: It neutralizes stomach acid
w: It speeds up the bowels
It numbs the throat
It reduces allergic swelling

items.q: Besides relieving heartburn, calcium carbonate is a source of a mineral that is important for which body part?
items.x: Calcium carbonate supplies calcium, which helps build and keep strong bones and teeth. During pregnancy, calcium supports the mother's and baby's bones.
items.a: Bones and teeth
w: Hair and nails only
Eyes and ears
Lungs and airways

items.q: Why is ferrous sulfate (iron) often given during pregnancy?
items.x: Pregnancy increases the body's need for iron, and low iron can cause anemia. Ferrous sulfate supplies iron to build healthy red blood cells.
items.a: To treat or prevent iron-deficiency anemia
w: To prevent morning sickness
To lower blood pressure
To prevent urinary infections

items.q: Which drink taken with iron pills can help the body absorb the iron better?
items.x: Vitamin C in orange juice helps the body absorb iron. Milk, coffee, and tea can reduce how much iron is absorbed.
items.a: Orange juice
w: Milk
Coffee
Tea

items.q: A woman is taking nitrofurantoin for a bladder infection. Which symptom shows the infection may not be improving and should be reported?
items.x: Burning, urgency, and frequent urination are signs of bladder infection. If they continue or get worse, the nurse needs to know.
items.a: Continued burning and urgency when urinating
w: Urine that is pale yellow and clear
Normal number of bathroom trips
Feeling more energetic each day

items.q: Besides seasonal allergies, levocetirizine may also be used to relieve which skin problem?
items.x: Levocetirizine is an antihistamine labeled for chronic hives (urticaria) as well as allergies. It does not heal pressure ulcers or fungal rashes.
items.a: Itchy hives
w: Pressure ulcers
Fungal skin rash
Sunburn blisters

items.q: Why is levocetirizine usually taken in the evening?
items.x: Levocetirizine can make people sleepy, so it is labeled for evening use. Being drowsy at night is safer than during daytime activities.
items.a: It can cause drowsiness
w: It must be taken with dinner
It keeps people awake
It works only in the dark

items.q: Loratadine belongs to which group of medicines?
items.x: Loratadine is an antihistamine that blocks histamine to relieve allergy symptoms. It is less likely to cause sleepiness than older antihistamines.
items.a: Antihistamines
w: Antibiotics
Steroids (corticosteroids)
Blood thinners

items.q: A resident who takes loratadine for allergies suddenly has swelling of the lips and trouble breathing. What should the nursing assistant do?
items.x: Lip swelling and trouble breathing can be a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is an emergency. Antihistamines like loratadine are not enough to treat it.
items.a: Call for the nurse immediately and stay with the resident
w: Give the resident another allergy pill
Wait to see if the swelling goes away
Have the resident lie down and rest alone

items.q: Meclizine belongs to which group of medicines?
items.x: Meclizine is an antihistamine used for motion sickness and dizziness. Like other antihistamines, it can cause drowsiness and dry mouth.
items.a: Antihistamines
w: Antibiotics
Opioid pain relievers
Water pills (diuretics)

items.q: During cardiac arrest, ALS providers give epinephrine. What is its main intended benefit during CPR?
items.x: Epinephrine's alpha effects constrict blood vessels, raising the pressure that drives blood to the heart and brain during compressions. It does not dissolve clots or reliably convert a rhythm on its own.
items.a: Constricting blood vessels to improve blood flow to the heart and brain
w: Dissolving the clot that caused the arrest
Converting the rhythm back to normal by itself
Opening the airway by relaxing the throat muscles

items.q: An EMT crew arrives first at a witnessed cardiac arrest. ALS with epinephrine is several minutes away. What should the crew focus on?
items.x: Survival from cardiac arrest depends most on early high-quality CPR and defibrillation; epinephrine supports these but never replaces them. An epinephrine auto-injector is not an EMT treatment for cardiac arrest.
items.a: High-quality CPR and early use of the AED
w: Waiting for ALS before starting compressions
Giving the patient's epinephrine auto-injector first
Placing the patient in the recovery position

items.q: Epinephrine belongs to which group of medications?
items.x: Epinephrine is a catecholamine that stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, mimicking the sympathetic nervous system. Beta-blockers have the opposite effect on beta receptors.
items.a: Sympathomimetics (adrenergic agonists)
w: Beta-blockers
Opioid antagonists
Anticholinergics

items.q: Which effect of epinephrine on the heart comes from stimulating beta-1 receptors?
items.x: Beta-1 stimulation increases heart rate and the force of contraction. This raises the heart's oxygen demand, which is why chest pain or palpitations can follow a dose.
items.a: Faster heart rate and stronger contractions
w: Slower heart rate and weaker contractions
Relaxation of the coronary smooth muscle only
No change in rate but lower blood pressure

items.q: A patient with anaphylaxis improves after an epinephrine auto-injector but then reports new chest pain and a racing heart. What is the best interpretation and action?
items.x: Epinephrine increases heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand and can cause chest pain or dysrhythmias, especially in older adults or those with heart disease. New chest pain needs reassessment and prompt reporting, not simple reassurance.
items.a: Recognize a possible cardiac side effect, reassess, and report it to ALS
w: Expect this as proof the dose was too small and repeat it now
Treat this as anxiety and reassure the patient only
Assume a new allergic reaction and ignore the vital signs

items.q: How does aspirin help a patient with a suspected heart attack?
items.x: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that blocks thromboxane production, limiting further clot growth. It does not dissolve an existing clot; that is the role of fibrinolytics or catheter procedures.
items.a: It reduces platelet clumping so the clot is less likely to grow
w: It dissolves the existing clot in the coronary artery
It dilates the coronary arteries to relieve chest pain
It slows the heart rate to lower oxygen demand

items.q: Why are patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome told to chew aspirin rather than swallow it whole?
items.x: Chewing breaks the tablet up so it is absorbed more quickly, speeding the antiplatelet effect. It does not activate the drug or prevent allergic reactions.
items.a: Chewing allows faster absorption and quicker antiplatelet effect
w: Chewing prevents the tablet from irritating the stomach
Chewing is needed to activate the medication
Chewing reduces the risk of an allergic reaction

items.q: Which finding in a patient with chest pain is a contraindication to giving aspirin?
items.x: A known aspirin allergy (or active GI bleeding) is a contraindication. Hypertension, diabetes and chest pain at rest are common in heart attack patients and are not reasons to avoid aspirin.
items.a: A known allergy to aspirin
w: A history of high blood pressure
Chest pain that began while resting
A history of type 2 diabetes

items.q: Which finding is a contraindication to assisting a chest pain patient with nitroglycerin?
items.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil or tadalafil combined with nitroglycerin can cause severe, prolonged hypotension. High blood pressure and typical cardiac pain are not contraindications.
items.a: Recent use of an erectile dysfunction medication such as sildenafil
w: A blood pressure higher than the patient's usual
Chest pain that radiates to the left arm
A history of a previous heart attack

items.q: Before an EMT assists a patient with nitroglycerin, which condition must generally be met?
items.x: At the EMT level, nitroglycerin is an assisted medication: it must be the patient's own prescription and given with online or protocol-based medical direction. Another person's prescription does not qualify.
items.a: It is prescribed to the patient and medical direction approves
w: The patient has taken aspirin within the past day
The patient's pain has lasted longer than usual
A family member has a prescription for it

items.q: Nitroglycerin lowers blood pressure and cardiac workload mainly by which action?
items.x: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that mainly dilates veins, reducing preload and the heart's oxygen demand. It is not a beta-blocker or a diuretic.
items.a: Dilating veins so less blood returns to the heart
w: Blocking beta receptors to slow the heart
Causing the kidneys to remove extra fluid
Constricting arteries to redirect blood flow

items.q: Shortly after taking nitroglycerin, a patient reports a pounding headache. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Headache is a common, expected side effect caused by vasodilation of blood vessels in the head. It is not a sign of allergy, and a headache actually suggests the tablet is active.
items.a: An expected side effect from dilation of blood vessels
w: A sign of an allergic reaction to the tablet
Proof that the tablets have lost their potency
A sign that the patient is having a stroke

items.q: Which vital sign is most important for an EMT to reassess after each nitroglycerin dose?
items.x: The main danger of nitroglycerin is hypotension from vasodilation, so blood pressure is checked before and after each dose. Temperature and glucose are not directly affected.
items.a: Blood pressure
w: Body temperature
Pupil size
Blood glucose

items.q: A patient has a very high blood pressure and a headache but no chest pain. Why is nitroglycerin not an EMT treatment here?
items.x: EMTs assist with nitroglycerin for chest pain of suspected cardiac origin under medical direction. Treating severe hypertension is an ALS and hospital decision; nitroglycerin lowers, not raises, blood pressure.
items.a: At the EMT level it is used for suspected cardiac chest pain, not high blood pressure alone
w: Nitroglycerin raises blood pressure and would make this worse
Nitroglycerin only works when blood pressure is low
Nitroglycerin is only given by injection in hypertension

items.q: How is a nitroglycerin tablet given?
items.x: Nitroglycerin tablets and spray are given sublingually for rapid absorption through the mucosa. Swallowing exposes the drug to first-pass liver breakdown, which greatly reduces its effect.
items.a: Placed under the tongue and allowed to dissolve
w: Swallowed whole with a full glass of water
Chewed and swallowed like aspirin
Placed between the cheek and gum and chewed

items.q: Anaphylactic shock is classified as which type of shock?
items.x: In anaphylaxis, widespread vasodilation and leaky capillaries cause distributive shock. Hypovolemic shock comes from fluid or blood loss, and cardiogenic shock from pump failure.
items.a: Distributive shock
w: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Obstructive shock

items.q: Which action of epinephrine most directly raises blood pressure in anaphylactic shock?
items.x: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction reverses the vasodilation of anaphylaxis and raises blood pressure. Beta-2 bronchodilation helps breathing but does not raise blood pressure; epinephrine is not an antihistamine.
items.a: Alpha-1 stimulation that constricts blood vessels
w: Beta-2 stimulation that relaxes the airways
Blocking histamine at its receptors
Increasing urine output by the kidneys

items.q: A patient in anaphylactic shock takes a beta-blocker daily. What should the EMT anticipate after giving epinephrine?
items.x: Beta-blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine and make anaphylaxis harder to treat, so early ALS backup is important. The effect is reduced, not absent, and the beta-blocker does not treat the reaction.
items.a: The response may be weaker, so call for ALS early
w: The patient will be unusually sensitive to epinephrine
Epinephrine will have no effect at all on breathing
The beta-blocker will fully reverse the reaction

items.q: A patient's blood pressure and breathing improve after an epinephrine auto-injector. Why is continued transport and monitoring still needed?
items.x: Epinephrine wears off quickly and symptoms may recur, including biphasic reactions hours later. Improvement after epinephrine supports, rather than rules out, anaphylaxis.
items.a: Epinephrine's effects are short-lived and symptoms can return
w: Epinephrine causes lasting low blood pressure later
The improvement shows the reaction was not anaphylaxis
A second injection is required by law after any use

items.q: After giving epinephrine to a patient in shock, how should the EMT reassess?
items.x: A patient in shock is unstable and needs frequent reassessment of vital signs, mental status, breathing and skin to detect improvement or deterioration. Waiting for new complaints can miss a decline.
items.a: Repeat vital signs, mental status and skin findings frequently, as for an unstable patient
w: Recheck vital signs once on arrival at the hospital
Reassess only if the patient reports new symptoms
Check blood glucose first, then vital signs at the hospital

items.q: How does albuterol relieve wheezing in an asthma attack?
items.x: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and opens the airways. It does not reduce inflammation like a corticosteroid or block histamine.
items.a: It stimulates beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
w: It blocks histamine to reduce airway swelling
It thins mucus so it can be coughed up
It reduces airway inflammation like a steroid

items.q: Which step is part of correct metered-dose inhaler technique?
items.x: The patient should exhale, seal the lips on the mouthpiece or spacer, activate the inhaler during a slow deep breath, and hold the breath. Spraying during exhalation or shallow breaths delivers little drug to the lungs.
items.a: Breathe out fully, then press the inhaler while inhaling slowly and deeply
w: Press the inhaler while breathing out forcefully
Take quick, shallow breaths while spraying
Spray into the air first and then breathe it in

items.q: An asthma patient who was wheezing loudly now has very quiet breath sounds, is drowsy, and is still working hard to breathe. What does this most likely mean?
items.x: A quiet or silent chest with fatigue and altered mental status signals severe obstruction and impending respiratory failure. Improvement would show easier breathing and better alertness, not drowsiness.
items.a: Airflow is worsening; prepare to assist ventilations and call ALS
w: The inhaler has worked and the attack is ending
The patient is relaxing and can be reassured
The wheezing was caused by anxiety alone

items.q: Which finding in a patient having an allergic reaction shows airway involvement that calls for epinephrine?
items.x: Hoarseness, stridor and throat tightness suggest upper airway swelling, a sign of anaphylaxis that needs epinephrine. Localized hives or mild local reactions alone do not meet anaphylaxis criteria.
items.a: Hoarse voice, stridor, or a feeling of throat tightness
w: Itchy hives limited to the arms
Watery eyes and a runny nose
Mild redness around an insect sting

items.q: A patient in anaphylaxis is wheezing and has throat swelling. Why is epinephrine preferred over an albuterol inhaler as the first medication?
items.x: Epinephrine counters the whole systemic reaction: airway edema, bronchospasm and vasodilation. Albuterol only relaxes bronchial muscle and does not treat swelling or shock, though it can be used as an add-on.
items.a: Epinephrine treats airway swelling, bronchospasm and low blood pressure together
w: Albuterol is not safe in any allergic reaction
Epinephrine works only on the lungs and acts faster
Albuterol would make the throat swelling worse

items.q: Where is an epinephrine auto-injector given?
items.x: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh, where absorption is reliable, and can be given through clothing. Injection into the buttock or other sites is not recommended.
items.a: Into the outer (anterolateral) thigh
w: Into the upper arm deltoid muscle
Into the abdominal wall near the navel
Into the buttock's upper outer area

items.q: After an epinephrine auto-injector, which set of effects should the EMT expect as common side effects?
items.x: Epinephrine stimulates the sympathetic system, causing tachycardia, tremor, anxiety and pallor. Slowing of the heart or breathing is not expected.
items.a: Fast heart rate, shakiness, anxiety and pale skin
w: Slow heart rate, drowsiness and flushed skin
Pinpoint pupils and slowed breathing
Low blood sugar and sweating

items.q: Which patient best meets the criteria for anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine?
items.x: Anaphylaxis involves more than one body system, such as skin signs plus respiratory compromise or hypotension. Local swelling, contact rashes and seasonal allergy symptoms are not anaphylaxis.
items.a: Hives after a bee sting with difficulty breathing and low blood pressure
w: Swelling and pain only at the bee sting site
Itchy rash on one arm after touching a plant
Sneezing and watery eyes during pollen season

items.q: After epinephrine, a patient with anaphylaxis still has some wheezing. What is the role of an albuterol inhaler here?
items.x: Albuterol may help persistent bronchospasm, but it does not treat airway swelling or shock. Epinephrine remains the first-line drug for anaphylaxis.
items.a: An add-on for remaining bronchospasm, not a replacement for epinephrine
w: The main treatment that makes epinephrine unnecessary
A treatment for the low blood pressure of anaphylaxis
A way to reverse the side effects of epinephrine

items.q: After assisting an allergic patient with an albuterol inhaler, what should the EMT reassess first?
items.x: Albuterol targets bronchospasm, so its effect is judged by breathing effort, wheezing and oxygenation. Pupils and glucose are not the main markers of response.
items.a: Work of breathing, breath sounds and oxygen saturation
w: Pupil size and reaction to light
Blood glucose and skin temperature
Bowel sounds and abdominal tenderness

items.q: Acetaminophen is best described as which type of medication?
items.x: Acetaminophen is an analgesic and antipyretic but has minimal anti-inflammatory action and does not affect platelets. It is not an NSAID or an opioid.
items.a: A pain reliever and fever reducer with little anti-inflammatory effect
w: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that thins the blood
An opioid pain reliever that can slow breathing
A sedative that reduces anxiety and causes sleep

items.q: Which organ is most at risk from acetaminophen overdose?
items.x: Excess acetaminophen produces a toxic metabolite that damages the liver. Stomach irritation and bleeding are more typical of NSAIDs such as aspirin or ibuprofen.
items.a: Liver
w: Kidneys
Lungs
Stomach lining

items.q: A patient took a large amount of acetaminophen a few hours ago and feels only mildly nauseated. What is important to understand?
items.x: Early acetaminophen poisoning often causes few or mild symptoms, while liver injury appears a day or more later. Transport for evaluation is needed regardless of how well the patient appears.
items.a: Serious liver damage can develop later even if the patient looks well now
w: Mild symptoms mean the amount taken was not harmful
Acetaminophen overdose mainly causes immediate breathing problems
The patient can be observed at home if symptoms stay mild

items.q: Why should an EMT ask about all cold remedies and prescription pain pills when a patient reports taking acetaminophen?
items.x: Acetaminophen is in many cold and flu products and some opioid combination pills, so accidental overdose is common. These products add to the total exposure rather than block it.
items.a: Many combination products also contain acetaminophen, adding to the total amount
w: Cold remedies block acetaminophen so it stops working
Prescription pain pills cancel out acetaminophen's effects
Acetaminophen cannot be taken with any other medication

items.q: Which medication is used in the hospital as the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning?
items.x: Acetylcysteine replenishes the liver's protective glutathione and prevents liver injury. Naloxone reverses opioids, not acetaminophen, even in combination products.
items.a: Acetylcysteine
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Atropine

items.q: ALS arrives for an unresponsive patient with a very low blood sugar. Which form of dextrose is appropriate for this patient?
items.x: An unresponsive patient cannot protect the airway, so oral glucose risks aspiration; ALS gives dextrose intravenously. Dextrose is not given intramuscularly.
items.a: Intravenous dextrose
w: Oral glucose gel between cheek and gum
Intramuscular dextrose into the thigh
Dextrose tablets dissolved under the tongue

items.q: Why is it important to watch the IV site closely when concentrated dextrose is given?
items.x: Concentrated dextrose is irritating, and extravasation can injure or kill surrounding tissue. Allergy to dextrose is not a typical concern.
items.a: Leakage into surrounding tissue can cause serious tissue damage
w: Dextrose often causes a severe allergic rash at the site
Dextrose makes the vein clot and stops all flow
Dextrose leaking out causes the blood sugar to drop

items.q: Before giving glucose to a diabetic patient with altered mental status, which assessment should be done if local protocol allows?
items.x: A glucometer reading confirms hypoglycemia and gives a baseline to judge the response to treatment. Temperature and bowel sounds do not guide glucose administration.
items.a: Check the blood glucose level with a glucometer
w: Check the core body temperature
Measure the patient's urine output
Listen for bowel sounds in each quadrant

items.q: A diabetic patient takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication such as glipizide. After oral glucose, the patient is alert and wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
items.x: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycemia that outlasts a single glucose dose. This is why medical direction and hospital observation are strongly encouraged.
items.a: Blood sugar may fall again hours later as the medication keeps working
w: The glucose will cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure
The medication will make the glucose ineffective right away
Glipizide causes an allergy to glucose after treatment

items.q: A known diabetic is confused but can swallow, and blood sugar cannot be measured. Why is giving oral glucose still considered reasonable?
items.x: The brief rise from oral glucose is unlikely to harm a hyperglycemic patient, while untreated hypoglycemia can quickly cause brain injury. Glucose does not lower blood sugar.
items.a: A small amount of sugar will not harm a high-sugar patient but may help a low-sugar one
w: Oral glucose lowers blood sugar if it is already too high
Confusion in diabetics is always caused by high blood sugar
Oral glucose has no effect unless blood sugar is low

items.q: What effect does albuterol have on blood potassium levels?
items.x: Beta-2 stimulation drives potassium into cells, temporarily lowering the blood level. It does not remove potassium from the body.
items.a: It lowers blood potassium by shifting potassium into the cells
w: It raises blood potassium by releasing it from cells
It removes potassium from the body through the urine
It has no effect on potassium at any amount

items.q: Hospitals sometimes give nebulized albuterol for high potassium. What is a limitation of this treatment?
items.x: Albuterol shifts potassium into cells for a short time, so other treatments such as dialysis are needed to remove it from the body. It does not need wheezing to work.
items.a: The effect is temporary because potassium is moved, not removed
w: It permanently removes potassium from the body
It only works if the patient is wheezing
It raises potassium briefly before lowering it for good

items.q: ALS may give albuterol for suspected high potassium. Which patient history most suggests this problem?
items.x: Missed dialysis allows potassium to build up, which can cause weakness and dangerous slow rhythms. Vomiting, diarrhea and diuretics more often cause low potassium.
items.a: A dialysis patient who missed treatments and now has weakness and a slow pulse
w: A young athlete with leg cramps after a long run
A patient with vomiting and diarrhea for several days
A patient taking a water pill who feels thirsty

items.q: A patient with severe asthma has used albuterol repeatedly for hours. Which electrolyte problem might cause muscle weakness and irregular heartbeats?
items.x: Repeated albuterol doses shift potassium into cells and can cause hypokalemia, leading to weakness and dysrhythmias. Albuterol does not raise potassium.
items.a: Low potassium
w: High potassium
High calcium
Low sodium

items.q: Which medication taken together with frequent albuterol most increases the risk of low potassium?
items.x: Loop diuretics like furosemide cause potassium loss in the urine, adding to albuterol's potassium-lowering effect. Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors tend to raise potassium.
items.a: Furosemide, a loop diuretic
w: Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic
Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor
Acetaminophen, a pain reliever

items.q: How does naloxone reverse an opioid overdose?
items.x: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that pushes opioids off their receptors. Binding drugs in the gut describes activated charcoal, not naloxone.
items.a: It blocks opioid receptors and displaces the opioid from them
w: It speeds up the liver's breakdown of opioids
It stimulates the breathing center directly like caffeine
It binds the opioid in the stomach so it is not absorbed

items.q: A patient wakes and breathes normally after naloxone, then refuses care. Why is continued monitoring important?
items.x: Many opioids, especially long-acting or potent ones, last longer than naloxone, so re-sedation and respiratory depression can return. Naloxone does not remove the opioid.
items.a: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so breathing may slow again
w: Naloxone causes delayed breathing problems of its own
The patient will now be immune to further opioid effects
Naloxone permanently removes the opioid from the body

items.q: A patient with a suspected opioid overdose is breathing a few shallow breaths per minute and is cyanotic. What should the EMT do first?
items.x: Inadequate breathing is immediately treated with airway management and ventilation; naloxone follows but takes time to work. Charcoal is unsafe in a patient who cannot protect the airway.
items.a: Open the airway and ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
w: Give naloxone and wait for the patient to wake up
Place the patient in the recovery position and observe
Give activated charcoal to absorb the opioid

items.q: How does activated charcoal work in some oral poisonings?
items.x: Activated charcoal binds many substances in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing absorption. It does not act on poison already absorbed and is not an emetic.
items.a: It adsorbs the poison in the gut so less is absorbed
w: It neutralizes poisons already in the bloodstream
It causes vomiting to empty the stomach
It coats the stomach to stop pain and burning

items.q: For which patient is activated charcoal contraindicated?
items.x: Charcoal given to a patient with altered mental status risks vomiting and aspiration into the lungs. It is considered only for alert patients who can swallow and protect the airway, per medical direction.
items.a: A drowsy patient who cannot protect the airway
w: An alert adult who swallowed pills recently
An alert patient who agrees to drink it
An alert patient with a known ingestion and stable vitals

items.q: Which patient meets the usual criteria for oral glucose?
items.x: Oral glucose is for a patient with a history of diabetes and altered mental status who can swallow and protect the airway. Unresponsive or seizing patients risk aspiration.
items.a: A known diabetic with altered mental status who can swallow
w: An unresponsive diabetic with no gag reflex
A diabetic who is alert with no complaints
A confused patient who is actively seizing

items.q: Why is oral glucose contraindicated in a patient who cannot swallow?
items.x: A patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway may aspirate the gel. The danger is airway compromise, not a rapid rise in blood sugar.
items.a: The patient could aspirate the gel into the airway
w: The gel will not absorb unless it is swallowed whole
It will raise blood sugar dangerously fast
It causes vomiting in unresponsive patients

items.q: How is oral glucose gel given?
items.x: Oral glucose is placed between the cheek and gum (or on a tongue depressor) a little at a time so it can be absorbed and swallowed safely. Giving it all at once raises the risk of choking.
items.a: Placed between the cheek and gum or on the tongue in small portions
w: Injected into the muscle of the outer thigh
Sprayed into the nostrils with an atomizer
Swallowed all at once as a single large mouthful

items.q: Several minutes after oral glucose, a diabetic patient's mental status has not improved. What should the EMT consider?
items.x: Lack of improvement suggests the hypoglycemia is severe or something else, such as stroke, head injury or overdose, is causing the altered mental status. ALS and further assessment are needed.
items.a: Other causes of altered mental status and the need for ALS
w: That the glucose was absorbed and no change is expected
That the patient must have high blood sugar instead
That transport is unnecessary since glucose was given

items.q: Which presentation in a diabetic patient most suggests low blood sugar rather than high blood sugar?
items.x: Hypoglycemia comes on quickly with sympathetic signs such as cool, clammy skin. Gradual onset, fruity breath and deep rapid breathing suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.a: Sudden confusion with cool, pale, sweaty skin
w: Gradual onset with warm, dry skin and fruity breath
Deep rapid breathing and several days of thirst
Frequent urination and slowly worsening fatigue

items.q: A child with a peanut allergy has hives, wheezing and vomiting after a snack. The child has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best interpretation?
items.x: Skin signs plus respiratory and GI symptoms after a known allergen meet anaphylaxis criteria, and epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines and inhalers do not treat the systemic reaction.
items.a: Anaphylaxis; epinephrine is indicated per protocol
w: A mild reaction that only needs an antihistamine
Food poisoning that needs no medication
An asthma attack that needs only an inhaler

items.q: While using a parent's epinephrine auto-injector, a child accidentally injects it into his own thumb. What is the main concern?
items.x: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels and can reduce circulation to a finger or thumb, so the injury should be reported and evaluated. Allergy to epinephrine is not the concern.
items.a: Reduced blood flow to the thumb from vasoconstriction; report it
w: A severe allergic reaction to the epinephrine itself
Immediate cardiac arrest from the injection
Low blood sugar caused by the epinephrine

items.q: A young child with diabetes is suddenly irritable, sweaty and sleepy. What should the EMT suspect first?
items.x: Sudden behavior change, sweating and lethargy in a diabetic child are classic signs of hypoglycemia. High blood sugar usually develops more gradually with thirst and frequent urination.
items.a: Low blood sugar
w: High blood sugar
Simple tiredness
Dehydration from heat

items.q: Why should blood glucose be checked in a sick infant or child with altered mental status, even without diabetes?
items.x: Young children have limited glycogen reserves, so poor feeding or illness can cause hypoglycemia. Checking glucose helps identify a treatable cause.
items.a: Children have small glucose stores and can become hypoglycemic during illness
w: Children cannot develop low blood sugar unless diabetic
Glucose checks are required before any pediatric transport
Altered mental status in children is always from fever

items.q: Which finding in a child with asthma suggests significant respiratory distress?
items.x: Retractions, nasal flaring and use of accessory muscles show increased work of breathing. Talking in full sentences and clear lungs suggest mild or no distress.
items.a: Retractions between the ribs and nasal flaring
w: Clear breath sounds and normal skin color
A dry cough only at night
Talking in full sentences while playing

items.q: A young child cannot coordinate breathing with a metered-dose inhaler. What device helps deliver the medication?
items.x: A spacer holds the medication so the child can inhale it over several breaths, and a mask helps with young children. Oxygen masks and cannulas do not deliver inhaler medication.
items.a: A spacer with a face mask
w: A nasal cannula
A bag-valve mask alone
A nonrebreather mask

items.q: A toddler found near a grandparent's pain pills is very sleepy with slow, shallow breathing. Which additional finding suggests opioid poisoning?
items.x: Constricted pupils with respiratory depression and decreased responsiveness form the classic opioid toxidrome. Dilated pupils and agitation suggest stimulant or anticholinergic poisoning.
items.a: Pinpoint pupils
w: Widely dilated pupils
Hot, flushed, dry skin
Rapid heart rate and agitation

items.q: What is an advantage of giving naloxone by the intranasal route?
items.x: Intranasal naloxone is absorbed through the nasal mucosa and avoids needlestick risk. It still wears off, and airway and ventilation remain the first priorities.
items.a: It is absorbed through the nasal lining without needing a needle
w: It works only after it is swallowed
It lasts much longer than injected naloxone
It does not need the airway to be managed

items.q: A caregiver says a feverish child was given acetaminophen. What information is most important for the EMT to obtain?
items.x: Timing and use of multiple products help identify possible accidental overdose, which is common with children's fever and cold medicines. Brand and flavor do not change the risk.
items.a: When it was given and whether other medicines with acetaminophen were used
w: Which brand name and flavor of the product was used
Whether the child liked the taste of the medicine
Whether the bottle was bought at a pharmacy or a store

items.q: Compared with acetaminophen, ibuprofen also has which effect?
items.x: Ibuprofen is an NSAID that relieves pain, fever and inflammation. Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory effect.
items.a: It reduces inflammation as well as pain and fever
w: It reverses opioid effects as well as pain
It raises blood sugar as well as fever
It causes sleep as well as reducing pain

items.q: During an amiodarone infusion for stable wide-complex tachycardia, which adverse effects are most important to watch for?
items.x: IV amiodarone commonly causes hypotension and bradycardia through vasodilation and its beta-blocking and calcium-channel effects. It does not typically cause hypertension or tachycardia.
items.a: Hypotension and bradycardia
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Hypoglycemia and seizures
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves

items.q: Amiodarone is primarily classified as which type of antiarrhythmic?
items.x: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarization and the refractory period, though it also has Class I, II and IV effects. Lidocaine, not amiodarone, is the Class IB agent.
items.a: Class III agent that prolongs repolarization by blocking potassium channels
w: Class IB agent that shortens repolarization by blocking sodium channels
Class II agent that works only by blocking beta-1 receptors
Class IV agent that works only by blocking L-type calcium channels

items.q: How is adenosine administered for stable narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia?
items.x: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must be pushed rapidly through a proximal IV and flushed right away to reach the heart. A slow push lets it be metabolized before it reaches the AV node.
items.a: Rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush
w: Slow IV push over several minutes
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid
Diluted continuous infusion titrated to rate

items.q: Which patient factor may blunt the effect of adenosine, so the expected response may not occur?
items.x: Methylxanthines such as theophylline and caffeine block adenosine receptors and can reduce its effect. Dipyridamole and a transplanted heart do the opposite and increase sensitivity to adenosine.
items.a: Recent theophylline use or heavy caffeine intake
w: Current dipyridamole therapy
History of heart transplant
Current carbamazepine therapy

items.q: In which patient with rapid atrial fibrillation is IV diltiazem contraindicated?
items.x: Blocking the AV node in pre-excited atrial fibrillation can speed conduction down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation. COPD is not a contraindication; diltiazem is often chosen over beta blockers in these patients.
items.a: Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation
w: Atrial fibrillation in a patient with COPD
Atrial fibrillation in a patient with diabetes
New atrial fibrillation with narrow QRS and normal blood pressure

items.q: Which ECG change is most important to monitor during a procainamide infusion?
items.x: Procainamide is a sodium-channel blocker with Class III effects, so it widens the QRS and lengthens the QT, raising the risk of torsades. Peaked T waves with a short QT point to hyperkalemia, not procainamide toxicity.
items.a: Widening of the QRS complex and prolongation of the QT interval
w: Shortening of the PR interval
New ST elevation in the inferior leads
Peaked T waves with a shortened QT interval

items.q: Why is a central line or large, secure IV preferred when giving calcium chloride?
items.x: Calcium chloride is very irritating to tissue, and extravasation can cause necrosis and sloughing. It works when given peripherally in an emergency; a secure line is chosen for safety, not effectiveness.
items.a: Extravasation can cause severe tissue necrosis
w: It precipitates when exposed to light
It is only effective when given into a central vein
It causes anaphylaxis when given peripherally

items.q: In cardiac arrest, sodium bicarbonate is reasonable in which situation rather than as routine therapy?
items.x: Current guidelines advise against routine bicarbonate in arrest, but it is reasonable in special cases such as hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker overdose. Arrest length alone is not an indication.
items.a: Known pre-existing hyperkalemia
w: Any arrest that lasts longer than ten minutes
Asystole of unknown cause
Pulseless electrical activity from hypovolemia

items.q: The main benefit of epinephrine during cardiac arrest comes from which effect?
items.x: Epinephrine's alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises aortic diastolic pressure and improves coronary and cerebral perfusion during CPR. It does not convert VF by itself, and its beta-1 effect speeds rather than slows conduction.
items.a: Alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction that raises coronary perfusion pressure
w: Beta-2 bronchodilation that improves oxygenation
Direct conversion of ventricular fibrillation to sinus rhythm
Beta-1 slowing of conduction through the AV node

items.q: Atropine raises heart rate by blocking the vagus nerve. In which patient with symptomatic bradycardia will it have little effect?
items.x: Atropine works by blocking vagal input, and a transplanted heart has no vagal innervation, so atropine has little effect. Vagally mediated bradycardia, such as during vomiting or suctioning, usually responds well.
items.a: A heart transplant recipient with a denervated heart
w: Sinus bradycardia during vomiting
Bradycardia from increased vagal tone
Sinus bradycardia during endotracheal suctioning

items.q: How does aspirin reduce clot formation in acute coronary syndrome?
items.x: Aspirin permanently inactivates platelet cyclooxygenase, lowering thromboxane A2 and platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. P2Y12 blockade describes drugs like clopidogrel and ticagrelor.
items.a: Irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2
w: Reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor
Directly inhibits thrombin in the clot
Converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve the clot

items.q: Why is aspirin chewed rather than swallowed whole in suspected acute coronary syndrome?
items.x: Chewing a non-enteric-coated tablet allows faster absorption through the oral and gastric mucosa, so platelet inhibition starts sooner. It does not prevent GI bleeding.
items.a: Chewing speeds absorption and the onset of platelet inhibition
w: Chewing prevents gastrointestinal bleeding
Swallowed tablets are inactivated by stomach acid
Chewing lowers the risk of an allergic reaction

items.q: Which recent medication use is a contraindication to nitroglycerin in a patient with chest pain?
items.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil combined with nitrates can cause severe, refractory hypotension. Statins, metformin and ACE inhibitors are not contraindications.
items.a: Sildenafil taken for erectile dysfunction
w: Atorvastatin taken for high cholesterol
Metformin taken for diabetes
Lisinopril taken for hypertension

items.q: A patient has ST elevation in II, III and aVF plus ST elevation in V4R. Why is nitroglycerin used with great caution?
items.x: ST elevation in V4R suggests right ventricular involvement, and these patients rely on preload to maintain output, so venodilation from nitroglycerin can cause profound hypotension. Nitroglycerin relieves, rather than causes, vasospasm.
items.a: Right ventricular infarction makes the patient preload dependent
w: Nitroglycerin causes coronary artery vasospasm
Nitroglycerin increases left ventricular afterload
Nitroglycerin is ineffective in inferior wall ischemia

items.q: During transfer, a patient on a heparin infusion has a platelet count that has fallen by more than half from baseline and a new leg clot. What should be recognized?
items.x: A platelet drop of more than half with new thrombosis is classic for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which should be reported to the provider right away. It is a paradoxically prothrombotic immune reaction, not an expected effect.
items.a: Possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
w: Dilutional thrombocytopenia from IV fluids
Expected heparin effect needing no action
Immune reaction to aspirin given earlier

items.q: What is a concern with giving morphine for chest pain in acute coronary syndrome?
items.x: Opioids slow gastric emptying, which can delay absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors such as ticagrelor and clopidogrel. Morphine tends to lower, not raise, myocardial oxygen demand.
items.a: It may delay absorption and onset of oral P2Y12 inhibitors
w: It directly increases myocardial oxygen demand
It causes coronary artery vasospasm
It inactivates heparin in the IV line

items.q: Why might fentanyl be preferred over morphine for ischemic chest pain in a patient with borderline blood pressure?
items.x: Fentanyl releases little histamine, so it is less likely than morphine to cause vasodilation and hypotension. It is shorter acting than morphine and still causes respiratory depression.
items.a: It causes less histamine release and less hypotension
w: It has a longer duration so fewer doses are needed
It has added antiplatelet effects
It does not cause respiratory depression

items.q: Which finding makes early IV metoprolol inappropriate in a patient with STEMI?
items.x: Early IV beta blockade increases the risk of cardiogenic shock in patients with heart failure, low output or other shock risk factors. Hypertension with ongoing ischemia is a setting where it may be reasonable.
items.a: Signs of heart failure or a low-output state
w: Sinus tachycardia with hypertension
Ongoing ischemic chest pain
History of hyperlipidemia

items.q: How is tenecteplase given for STEMI?
items.x: Tenecteplase is given as one weight-based IV bolus, which is convenient in transport. The bolus-plus-infusion regimen describes alteplase.
items.a: As a single weight-based IV bolus
w: As a bolus followed by a 90-minute infusion
As a continuous infusion over a full day
As an intracoronary injection only during PCI

items.q: Which is an absolute contraindication to alteplase for STEMI?
items.x: Any history of intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis. Advanced age and chronic hypertension are factors to weigh, not absolute contraindications.
items.a: Any prior intracranial hemorrhage
w: Hypertension controlled on medication
Age older than 75 years
Current daily aspirin use

items.q: Nicardipine belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that mainly dilates arterioles with little effect on the AV node. Nondihydropyridines such as diltiazem slow AV conduction.
items.a: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
w: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Organic nitrate vasodilator
Selective beta-1 blocker

items.q: Which adverse effects should be monitored during a nicardipine infusion?
items.x: Arterial vasodilation from nicardipine can cause headache and reflex tachycardia. It has little effect on the AV node, so heart block is unlikely.
items.a: Reflex tachycardia and headache
w: Bradycardia and heart block
Bronchospasm and wheezing
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves

items.q: How does labetalol lower blood pressure?
items.x: Labetalol combines alpha-1 blockade, which lowers vascular resistance, with nonselective beta blockade, which limits reflex tachycardia. A pure beta-1 blocker would be something like metoprolol.
items.a: Blocks alpha-1 receptors and beta receptors
w: Blocks only beta-1 receptors
Stimulates central alpha-2 receptors
Directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle

items.q: Which history makes labetalol a poor choice for a hypertensive emergency?
items.x: Labetalol's nonselective beta blockade can worsen bronchospasm in asthma. It is a first-line choice in severe preeclampsia, aortic dissection and stroke blood pressure control.
items.a: Severe asthma with active bronchospasm
w: Pregnancy with severe preeclampsia
Acute aortic dissection
Acute ischemic stroke before thrombolysis

items.q: In which hypertensive emergency is IV nitroglycerin especially useful?
items.x: Nitroglycerin quickly reduces preload, and afterload at higher doses, which helps in hypertensive pulmonary edema. In aortic dissection it should not be used alone because it can cause reflex tachycardia that raises shear stress.
items.a: Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema
w: Eclampsia
Hypertensive intracranial hemorrhage
Aortic dissection as the only agent

items.q: How does hydralazine lower blood pressure?
items.x: Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator, which is why reflex tachycardia is common. It does not block beta receptors or ACE.
items.a: Directly relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle
w: Blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart
Blocks calcium channels in the AV node
Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme

items.q: Which allergy is a contraindication to clevidipine?
items.x: Clevidipine comes in a lipid emulsion that contains soy and egg components, so these allergies are contraindications. Sulfa and penicillin allergies are unrelated.
items.a: Allergy to soy or egg products
w: Allergy to sulfonamide antibiotics
Allergy to penicillin
Allergy to iodinated contrast

items.q: What property makes clevidipine easy to titrate?
items.x: Clevidipine is broken down by esterases within minutes, so blood pressure responds quickly to rate changes. A long half-life would make it harder, not easier, to titrate.
items.a: Ultra-short half-life from breakdown by blood and tissue esterases
w: Long half-life that keeps levels steady
Elimination unchanged by the kidneys
Liver metabolism into long-acting active metabolites

items.q: In acute aortic dissection, why is esmolol started before a vasodilator?
items.x: Lowering heart rate and contractility first reduces the force on the aortic wall and prevents the reflex tachycardia a vasodilator would cause. Esmolol decreases, not increases, contractility.
items.a: To prevent reflex tachycardia and reduce shear stress on the aorta
w: To increase cardiac contractility
To raise preload before vasodilation
To reverse vasodilator toxicity

items.q: After a prolonged nitroprusside infusion, a patient develops worsening metabolic acidosis and confusion. What should be suspected?
items.x: Nitroprusside releases cyanide as it is metabolized, and accumulation causes metabolic acidosis and altered mental status. Report these findings to the provider promptly.
items.a: Cyanide toxicity
w: Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Thyroid storm

items.q: Per Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, which vasopressor is first-line for septic shock in adults?
items.x: Norepinephrine is the recommended first-line vasopressor in septic shock. Vasopressin is usually added to norepinephrine rather than used first.
items.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Vasopressin

items.q: Norepinephrine is infusing through a peripheral IV and the site becomes blanched and cool. Which agent is infiltrated into the area?
items.x: Phentolamine is an alpha blocker that reverses local vasoconstriction from norepinephrine extravasation. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasopressor extravasations.
items.a: Phentolamine
w: Hyaluronidase
Dexrazoxane
Sodium thiosulfate

items.q: Which lab change is an expected effect of an epinephrine infusion and can complicate lactate interpretation?
items.x: Epinephrine stimulates beta-2 receptors on muscle, increasing glycolysis and lactate even when perfusion is adequate. It tends to raise glucose and lower potassium.
items.a: Rising lactate from beta-2 stimulated glycolysis
w: Falling lactate from improved perfusion alone
Hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Hyperkalemia from potassium leaving cells

items.q: Compared with norepinephrine in shock, dopamine is associated with which outcome?
items.x: Trials comparing the two found more arrhythmias with dopamine, and a subgroup of cardiogenic shock patients did worse. Low-dose dopamine does not protect the kidneys.
items.a: More tachyarrhythmias
w: Fewer tachyarrhythmias
Better protection of kidney function
Lower mortality in cardiogenic shock

items.q: How does vasopressin raise blood pressure?
items.x: Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction independently of adrenergic receptors. This is why it still works when catecholamine receptors respond poorly.
items.a: Stimulates V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: Stimulates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
Stimulates beta-1 receptors to increase contractility
Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 in cardiac muscle

items.q: In septic shock, how is vasopressin typically used?
items.x: Guidelines suggest adding vasopressin to norepinephrine rather than using it as first-line therapy. It has no inotropic effect.
items.a: Added to norepinephrine to raise MAP or reduce norepinephrine need
w: As the first-line single vasopressor
As an inotrope for low cardiac output
As a treatment for symptomatic bradycardia

items.q: A patient in cardiogenic shock is started on dobutamine. Which effect may cause blood pressure to fall?
items.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 inotrope but also has beta-2 effects that dilate vessels and can lower blood pressure. It increases, not decreases, contractility.
items.a: Beta-2 mediated peripheral vasodilation
w: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction
Activation of vasopressin receptors
Negative inotropy on the myocardium

items.q: Which effect is expected after phenylephrine is given for hypotension?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist, so rising blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that slows the heart. It has essentially no beta activity.
items.a: Reflex bradycardia as blood pressure rises
w: Marked tachycardia from beta-1 stimulation
Bronchodilation from beta-2 stimulation
Increased myocardial contractility

items.q: Which patient factor increases the risk of milrinone accumulation and hypotension?
items.x: Milrinone is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so it accumulates in renal impairment and can cause hypotension and arrhythmias. Because it works beyond the beta receptor, beta blockers do not raise its levels.
items.a: Renal impairment
w: Hepatic impairment
Current beta-blocker therapy
Obesity

items.q: Before methylene blue is given for refractory vasoplegic shock, which medication history raises concern?
items.x: Methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase and carries a boxed warning for serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. Statins and PPIs do not share this risk.
items.a: Use of an SSRI or other serotonergic drug
w: Use of a statin
Use of a proton pump inhibitor
Use of a loop diuretic

items.q: During continuous albuterol for severe bronchospasm, which electrolyte change should be monitored?
items.x: Beta-2 stimulation shifts potassium into cells, so repeated or continuous albuterol can lower serum potassium. Albuterol is actually used to treat hyperkalemia.
items.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia

items.q: How can albuterol be delivered to an intubated patient during transport?
items.x: Albuterol is delivered as an aerosol placed in the ventilator circuit, by nebulizer or an inhaler with an adapter. IV albuterol is not available in the US.
items.a: In-line nebulizer or inhaler with spacer in the ventilator circuit
w: Direct liquid instillation down the endotracheal tube
Continuous IV infusion through a central line
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen

items.q: How does ipratropium produce bronchodilation?
items.x: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic that blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. Beta-2 stimulation describes albuterol.
items.a: Blocks muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle
w: Stimulates beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle
Blocks leukotriene receptors
Stabilizes mast cells to prevent histamine release

items.q: Why is a corticosteroid such as methylprednisolone given early in a severe asthma exacerbation?
items.x: Steroids treat the inflammation behind the exacerbation, but the effect takes hours, so they are given early alongside bronchodilators. They are not rapid bronchodilators.
items.a: It reduces airway inflammation, with benefit developing over hours
w: It causes bronchodilation within minutes
It thins and clears mucus plugs
It suppresses the cough reflex

items.q: During an IV magnesium infusion for severe asthma, which adverse effects should be watched for?
items.x: Magnesium relaxes smooth muscle, including blood vessels, so hypotension and flushing are common. Tremor and tachycardia are typical of beta agonists.
items.a: Hypotension and flushing
w: Tremor and tachycardia
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
Hypertension and seizures

items.q: After nebulized racemic epinephrine for croup, why must the child be observed for a period of time?
items.x: Racemic epinephrine reduces airway swelling for a limited time, so stridor can come back once it wears off. That is why observation after treatment is standard.
items.a: Symptoms can return as the effect wears off
w: It can cause delayed hypoglycemia
It can trigger a delayed allergic reaction
It causes late-onset bronchospasm

items.q: Levalbuterol is best described as which of the following?
items.x: Levalbuterol is the R-isomer of albuterol and is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used for acute bronchospasm. It is not a long-acting maintenance agent.
items.a: The active R-enantiomer of albuterol
w: A long-acting beta-2 agonist for maintenance
An inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator
A methylxanthine bronchodilator

items.q: In severe asthma when inhaled therapy is not reaching the airways, by which route is terbutaline given?
items.x: Injectable terbutaline is given subcutaneously, reaching the airways through the bloodstream when bronchospasm limits inhaled delivery. It is not available as an inhaler in the US.
items.a: Subcutaneous injection
w: Rectal suppository
Intranasal spray
Inhaled dry powder

items.q: Why is dexamethasone used for a child with croup?
items.x: Dexamethasone reduces subglottic inflammation for a prolonged period and decreases return visits and severity. Immediate vasoconstriction describes racemic epinephrine.
items.a: It is a long-acting steroid that reduces airway swelling
w: It causes immediate vasoconstriction of the airway
It has direct antiviral activity
It causes bronchodilation through beta-2 receptors

items.q: In anaphylaxis with wheezing, how does epinephrine relieve bronchospasm?
items.x: Epinephrine's beta-2 effect relaxes airway smooth muscle, while its alpha-1 effect reduces mucosal swelling and raises blood pressure. Alpha-1 stimulation does not relax bronchial smooth muscle.
items.a: Stimulates beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
w: Stimulates alpha-1 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airway
Blocks histamine-1 receptors in the airway

items.q: Which adverse effect is associated with etomidate?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, briefly reducing cortisol production. It is chosen for induction precisely because it rarely causes hypotension.
items.a: Transient adrenal suppression
w: Profound hypotension on induction
Triggering of malignant hyperthermia
Bronchospasm from histamine release

items.q: Why is etomidate often selected for induction in a hypotensive trauma patient?
items.x: Etomidate is hemodynamically neutral, making it useful in unstable patients. It provides no analgesia and is short acting, so analgesia and sedation must follow.
items.a: It has minimal effect on blood pressure and heart rate
w: It provides strong analgesia
It has a long duration of sedation
It causes significant bronchodilation

items.q: Why is ketamine a good induction agent for a patient intubated for severe asthma?
items.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects relax bronchial smooth muscle, which helps in severe bronchospasm. It increases, rather than reduces, secretions.
items.a: It has bronchodilating properties
w: It reduces airway secretions
It lowers heart rate
It never causes emergence reactions

items.q: Which agent rapidly reverses rocuronium neuromuscular blockade?
items.x: Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroid blockers such as rocuronium and vecuronium, reversing them quickly. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, not paralysis.
items.a: Sugammadex
w: Flumazenil
Dantrolene
Naloxone

items.q: After RSI with rocuronium, why is early post-intubation sedation and analgesia critical?
items.x: Rocuronium has no sedative or analgesic effect and lasts much longer than etomidate or ketamine induction doses, so a paralyzed patient may be awake. Paralysis also hides signs of distress, so sedation must be given proactively.
items.a: Paralysis outlasts the induction agent, risking awareness
w: Rocuronium itself lowers the seizure threshold
Rocuronium has sedative effects that wear off quickly
Sedation speeds the metabolism of rocuronium

items.q: Which patient has a contraindication to succinylcholine?
items.x: After denervation injuries, burns or crush injuries older than a few days, extra acetylcholine receptors develop and succinylcholine can cause dangerous hyperkalemia. An acute fracture does not carry this risk.
items.a: A patient with a spinal cord injury from two weeks ago
w: A patient with a femur fracture from one hour ago
A patient with a history of asthma
A patient intubated for an ongoing seizure

items.q: After succinylcholine, a patient develops jaw rigidity, a rapidly rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia and then fever. What should be recognized?
items.x: Succinylcholine can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients, and a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics and develops over days.
items.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Anaphylaxis

items.q: Which hemodynamic effect is most common after propofol induction?
items.x: Propofol dilates vessels and depresses the heart, so hypotension is common, especially in volume-depleted patients. Hypertension and tachycardia are more typical of ketamine.
items.a: Hypotension from vasodilation and myocardial depression
w: Hypertension and tachycardia
Bradycardia with a rise in blood pressure
No significant change in blood pressure

items.q: Vecuronium belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Vecuronium is a nondepolarizing aminosteroid paralytic that competes with acetylcholine at the motor end plate. Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing blocker in common use.
items.a: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker
w: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker
Benzodiazepine sedative
Dissociative anesthetic

items.q: Why might atropine be given around RSI in a young infant receiving succinylcholine?

items.q: When cefazolin is ordered for suspected infection, what is best practice regarding blood cultures?
items.x: Cultures drawn before antibiotics are more likely to identify the organism, but antibiotics should not be meaningfully delayed. Waiting for results would delay treatment.
items.a: Obtain cultures before the first dose if this does not delay it
w: Obtain cultures only after the first day of therapy
Skip cultures because they do not change care
Wait for culture results before giving the antibiotic

items.q: Before an insulin infusion is started for diabetic ketoacidosis, which lab must be confirmed?
items.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells, so starting it with low potassium can cause dangerous hypokalemia and arrhythmias. Potassium is replaced first if low.
items.a: That serum potassium is not low
w: That blood glucose has normalized
That ketones have cleared
That serum calcium is normal

items.q: During DKA treatment, glucose falls toward the target range but the anion gap is still open. What is the usual approach?
items.x: Insulin is needed to clear ketoacidosis, so dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycemia while insulin keeps closing the gap. Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA.
items.a: Add dextrose to IV fluids while the insulin infusion continues
w: Switch to subcutaneous insulin right away
Give a bolus of sodium bicarbonate
Give a large bolus of IV insulin

items.q: During transport of a patient on an insulin infusion for DKA, how often is glucose usually checked?
items.x: Insulin infusions can lower glucose quickly, so hourly checks are standard. Waiting for symptoms would miss hypoglycemia in a sedated or altered patient.
items.a: About every hour by point-of-care testing
w: Only once on arrival
About every six hours
Only if the patient has symptoms

items.q: A hypoglycemic patient wakes up after IV dextrose. What is the next step?
items.x: IV dextrose works quickly but briefly, so glucose is rechecked and complex carbohydrates are given when safe. Insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.
items.a: Recheck glucose and give a longer-acting carbohydrate when able to eat
w: Assume the problem is resolved
Give insulin to prevent rebound
Give a second bolus without rechecking

items.q: Why is unnecessary hyperglycemia from dextrose-containing fluids avoided in acute stroke or brain injury?
items.x: High glucose is associated with larger infarcts and worse outcomes after stroke and brain injury. Treat confirmed hypoglycemia but avoid unneeded dextrose.
items.a: Hyperglycemia is linked to worse neurologic outcomes
w: Hyperglycemia lowers intracranial pressure
Hyperglycemia improves outcomes
Glucose level has no effect on the brain

items.q: A hypoglycemic patient is unconscious and has no IV access. Which routes can be used for glucagon?
items.x: Glucagon is approved for IM, SC and, as a nasal powder, intranasal use. An unconscious patient should never receive anything by mouth.
items.a: Intramuscular, subcutaneous or intranasal
w: Oral, sublingual or buccal
Rectal or transdermal only
Inhaled by nebulizer only

items.q: In which patient is glucagon less likely to raise blood glucose?
items.x: Glucagon works by releasing stored liver glycogen, which is depleted in starvation and chronic alcohol use. IV dextrose is preferred in these patients.
items.a: A patient with chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition
w: A patient with type 1 diabetes on insulin
A patient who ate a meal recently
A school-age child

items.q: Which adverse effect is common after glucagon, and how should the crew prepare?
items.x: Vomiting is common after glucagon, especially as the patient wakes up. Positioning and suction reduce aspiration risk.
items.a: Nausea and vomiting, so protect the airway
w: Bradycardia, so prepare atropine
Hypokalemia, so prepare potassium
Bronchospasm, so prepare albuterol

items.q: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder has confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which deficiency should be suspected?
items.x: Confusion, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities are the classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. It is treated with IV thiamine.
items.a: Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy
w: Vitamin B12 deficiency causing anemia
Folate deficiency causing neural tube defects
Vitamin K deficiency causing bleeding

items.q: A hypoglycemic patient with chronic alcohol use needs dextrose. How should thiamine fit in?
items.x: Glucose metabolism uses thiamine, so at-risk patients should receive thiamine too, but hypoglycemia is treated right away. Delaying dextrose is more dangerous.
items.a: Give thiamine as well, without delaying dextrose
w: Delay dextrose until thiamine levels return
Give dextrose only, since thiamine has no role
Give thiamine only, since dextrose is harmful

items.q: How does ondansetron prevent nausea and vomiting?
items.x: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and brainstem. Dopamine blockade describes metoclopramide and droperidol.
items.a: Blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors
w: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors
Blocks histamine H1 receptors
Blocks neurokinin-1 receptors

items.q: Which adverse effect warrants caution with ondansetron in a patient with long QT syndrome?
items.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, and its labeling advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome. Extrapyramidal effects are more typical of dopamine blockers.
items.a: QT prolongation
w: Extrapyramidal symptoms
Tissue necrosis at the IV site
Hypoglycemia

items.q: Which adverse effects of ondansetron are most common?
items.x: Headache and constipation are the most frequent side effects. Restlessness and spasms are typical of metoclopramide.
items.a: Headache and constipation
w: Diarrhea and excess salivation
Drowsiness and dry mouth
Restlessness and muscle spasms

items.q: How does metoclopramide relieve nausea?
items.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and speeds gastric emptying. 5-HT3 blockade describes ondansetron.
items.a: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors and increases gut motility
w: Blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors only
Blocks histamine H1 receptors
Blocks muscarinic receptors

items.q: After rapid IV metoclopramide, a patient feels intense restlessness and cannot sit still. What should be recognized?
items.x: Akathisia is an extrapyramidal effect of dopamine blockade and is more common with rapid IV push. Report it so it can be treated.
items.a: Akathisia
w: Panic attack
Serotonin syndrome
Hypoglycemia

items.q: In which patient is metoclopramide contraindicated?
items.x: Metoclopramide increases gut motility, which can be harmful with obstruction, perforation or GI bleeding. Gastroparesis is an approved indication.
items.a: A patient with a suspected mechanical bowel obstruction
w: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis
A patient with a migraine headache
A patient with nausea after surgery

items.q: What does the boxed warning for injectable promethazine describe?
items.x: Injectable promethazine is very irritating and can cause severe tissue injury and gangrene. Deep IM injection is the preferred route.
items.a: Severe tissue injury, including gangrene, from extravasation or arterial injection
w: Severe liver failure
Torsades de pointes
Serotonin syndrome

items.q: Promethazine is contraindicated in which population?
items.x: Promethazine has a boxed warning for fatal respiratory depression in children under 2. Motion sickness is one of its indications.
items.a: Children younger than 2 years
w: Adults older than 65 years
Pregnant patients
Patients with motion sickness

items.q: Which adverse effects can droperidol share with metoclopramide?
items.x: Both drugs block dopamine receptors and can cause akathisia and dystonia. Constipation and headache are typical of ondansetron.
items.a: Akathisia and other extrapyramidal symptoms
w: Constipation and headache
Red skin and urine
Bradycardia and bronchospasm

items.q: Where does droperidol act to relieve nausea?
items.x: Droperidol is a butyrophenone that blocks dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Serotonin blockade in the gut describes ondansetron.
items.a: Dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
w: Serotonin receptors in the gut wall
Histamine receptors in the inner ear
Neurokinin receptors in the vomiting center

items.q: How does oxytocin control postpartum hemorrhage?
items.x: Most postpartum hemorrhage is from uterine atony, and oxytocin makes the uterus contract and clamp down on vessels. It does not affect clotting factors.
items.a: It stimulates uterine contraction, compressing bleeding vessels
w: It promotes clotting factor production
It relaxes the uterus to reduce bleeding
It causes widespread systemic vasoconstriction

items.q: After a prolonged oxytocin infusion, a patient develops headache, confusion and low sodium. What should be suspected?
items.x: Oxytocin resembles vasopressin and in prolonged infusions can cause water retention and hyponatremia. Report these findings promptly.
items.a: Water intoxication from oxytocin's antidiuretic effect
w: Preeclampsia with severe features
Amniotic fluid embolism
Magnesium toxicity

items.q: What is the main purpose of magnesium sulfate in severe preeclampsia?
items.x: Magnesium is the drug of choice for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures. Separate antihypertensives are used for blood pressure.
items.a: To prevent eclamptic seizures
w: To lower blood pressure as the main agent
To strengthen uterine contractions
To prevent postpartum hemorrhage

items.q: A patient on a magnesium infusion has a respiratory rate of 8 and absent reflexes. Which medication reverses magnesium toxicity?
items.x: Calcium antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and heart. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.
items.a: Calcium gluconate
w: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Sodium bicarbonate

items.q: Which maternal adverse effects are most important to monitor after terbutaline?
items.x: Terbutaline is a beta agonist, and its boxed warning cites serious maternal heart problems with prolonged tocolysis. It raises, not lowers, glucose.
items.a: Tachycardia, chest pain and arrhythmias
w: Bradycardia and hypotension
Hypoglycemia and sweating
Respiratory depression

items.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid in postpartum hemorrhage?
items.x: TXA reduces fibrinolysis and is given alongside uterotonics, not instead of them. It has no effect on uterine tone.
items.a: An adjunct to uterotonics that slows clot breakdown
w: A replacement for oxytocin
A drug that contracts the uterus
A reversal agent for anticoagulants

items.q: Which condition is a contraindication to methylergonovine?
items.x: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and can raise blood pressure sharply. Asthma is the main contraindication for carboprost.
items.a: Preeclampsia or chronic hypertension
w: Asthma
Type 2 diabetes
Prior cesarean delivery

items.q: Which condition is a contraindication to carboprost?
items.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that can cause bronchospasm. Hypertension is the main concern with methylergonovine.
items.a: Asthma
w: Chronic hypertension
Type 2 diabetes
Prior cesarean delivery

items.q: Misoprostol belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog. Carboprost is the F2-alpha analog and methylergonovine is the ergot alkaloid.
items.a: Prostaglandin E1 analog
w: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analog
Ergot alkaloid
Synthetic oxytocin

items.q: A patient at 34 weeks gestation has severe-range blood pressure. Which IV agent is first-line?
items.x: Labetalol, hydralazine and nifedipine are first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat are contraindicated because of fetal harm.
items.a: Labetalol
w: Nitroprusside
Enalaprilat
Furosemide

items.q: An infant has a heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. Along with CPR, which medication is given first?
items.x: Pediatric bradycardia is usually caused by hypoxia, and epinephrine is the first drug when it persists despite good ventilation. Atropine is reserved for vagal causes or primary AV block.
items.a: Epinephrine
w: Atropine
Adenosine
Amiodarone

items.q: In which child is atropine preferred over epinephrine for bradycardia?
items.x: Atropine treats bradycardia from vagal stimulation or primary AV block. Hypoxic bradycardia is treated with ventilation and epinephrine.
items.a: A child whose bradycardia is from increased vagal tone during intubation
w: A child whose bradycardia is from hypoxia
A child in pulseless electrical activity
A child in ventricular fibrillation

items.q: Why is glucose checked often in a sick neonate during transport?
items.x: Newborns, especially when sick or stressed, use up limited glycogen stores fast. Frequent checks catch hypoglycemia before it causes harm.
items.a: Neonates have small glycogen stores and become hypoglycemic quickly
w: Neonates cannot metabolize glucose
Dextrose is contraindicated in neonates
Neonates are prone to severe hyperkalemia

items.q: A child with asthma has less wheezing after albuterol but now has poor air movement and is tired. What does this suggest?
items.x: A quiet chest with poor air movement and fatigue means too little air is moving to wheeze. This is an ominous sign that needs immediate reporting.
items.a: Worsening obstruction with impending respiratory failure
w: Improvement from the albuterol
Expected albuterol side effect
Anxiety now resolving

items.q: A child becomes agitated and combative after receiving midazolam. What should be recognized?
items.x: Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical agitation, especially in children. It is not an allergy and should be reported.
items.a: A paradoxical reaction to the benzodiazepine
w: Expected effect of correct sedation
A sign of opioid withdrawal
An allergic reaction to midazolam

items.q: Why is naloxone avoided in a newborn whose mother uses opioids long term?
items.x: Infants exposed to opioids in the womb can have abrupt, severe withdrawal and seizures after naloxone. Ventilatory support is the priority.
items.a: It can precipitate acute withdrawal, including seizures
w: It causes severe neonatal hypoglycemia
It is ineffective in newborns
It worsens respiratory depression

items.q: An infant has a regular, narrow-complex heart rate too fast to count with no visible P waves. Why is adenosine given?
items.x: These findings suggest SVT, and adenosine briefly blocks AV conduction to break the reentry circuit. Sinus tachycardia is treated by addressing the cause.
items.a: To briefly block the AV node and end the SVT
