items.q: An older patient on digoxin is admitted with acute kidney injury, nausea, yellow-tinged vision, and new bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Digoxin is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so AKI raises levels; GI symptoms, visual changes, and bidirectional VT are classic for toxicity. Digoxin is not primarily cleared by the liver, so hepatic failure is the less likely cause.
items.a: Digoxin toxicity from reduced renal clearance
w: Hypercalcemia from a thiazide diuretic
Hepatic failure impairing digoxin metabolism
Hypermagnesemia from an antacid

items.q: A patient on lisinopril develops swelling of the lips and tongue without hives or itching. What mechanism best explains this reaction?
items.x: ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibition lets bradykinin build up and cause angioedema, often without urticaria. Because it is not histamine- or IgE-driven, antihistamines and steroids work less well than they do for allergic angioedema.
items.a: Accumulation of bradykinin from ACE inhibition
w: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Complement activation by drug immune complexes
Direct histamine release from basophils

items.q: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on lisinopril is being switched to sacubitril-valsartan. Which precaution is required?
items.x: Combining neprilysin inhibition with an ACE inhibitor greatly increases angioedema risk because both raise bradykinin, so a washout period is required. Overlapping the drugs is contraindicated for the same reason.
items.a: Allow a washout after the last ACE inhibitor dose
w: Give the first dose with the last ACE inhibitor dose
Add a potassium supplement with the first dose
Overlap both drugs for several days before switching

items.q: Spironolactone is added to lisinopril for a patient with heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Which labs are most important to follow after starting it?
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and with an ACE inhibitor and reduced kidney function the risk of hyperkalemia and worsening renal function is high. Sodium can change, but potassium is the dangerous abnormality to watch.
items.a: Serum potassium and creatinine
w: Serum sodium and glucose
Liver enzymes and bilirubin
Uric acid and calcium

items.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response also has acutely decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Why is IV diltiazem a poor choice for rate control?
items.x: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers reduce contractility and can worsen decompensated HFrEF. Diltiazem slows, rather than speeds, AV nodal conduction, which is why it is used for rate control in other patients.
items.a: Its negative inotropy can worsen systolic heart failure
w: It speeds conduction through the AV node
It causes reflex tachycardia from vasodilation
It is contraindicated in patients with diabetes

items.q: Before giving sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain, which home medication is most important to ask about?
items.x: Nitrates combined with PDE-5 inhibitors can cause profound, refractory hypotension, so recent use must be asked about. The other drugs do not have a dangerous hemodynamic interaction with nitrates.
items.a: A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil
w: A proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole
A statin such as atorvastatin
An SSRI such as sertraline

items.q: Clopidogrel must undergo which process before it can inhibit platelets?
items.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that needs CYP2C19-dependent activation in the liver, so poor metabolizers and some interacting drugs reduce its effect. It is not activated by the kidney or by gut flora.
items.a: Hepatic activation, largely through CYP2C19
w: Renal conversion to an active metabolite
Cleavage by gut bacteria in the colon
None; the parent drug is fully active

items.q: A patient receiving aggressive IV furosemide for volume overload is most likely to develop which pattern of lab changes?
items.x: Loop diuretics increase potassium and hydrogen ion loss and cause contraction alkalosis. They also increase calcium and magnesium excretion, so high calcium or magnesium would not be expected.
items.a: Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis
w: Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis
Hypercalcemia and hypermagnesemia
Hyperkalemia and hypercalcemia

items.q: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is recommended first-line?
items.x: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock because it raises vascular tone with modest inotropy and fewer arrhythmias than dopamine. Phenylephrine is an alternative in select cases, not the routine first choice.
items.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Isoproterenol

items.q: A peripheral IV running norepinephrine infiltrates, and the surrounding skin becomes pale and cool. Which agent is used locally to limit tissue injury?
items.x: Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic blocker that reverses the local vasoconstriction caused by extravasated norepinephrine. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasoactive extravasations, and cold would worsen vasoconstriction.
items.a: Phentolamine infiltrated into the affected area
w: Hyaluronidase injected into the affected area
Protamine injected into the affected area
Ice packs applied over the affected area

items.q: Vasopressin added to norepinephrine in septic shock raises blood pressure mainly by acting on which receptor?
items.x: Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through V1 receptors, independent of adrenergic receptors, which is why it can reduce catecholamine needs. V2 receptors mediate water reabsorption, not vascular tone.
items.a: V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct
Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on arterioles
Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart

items.q: A hospitalized patient develops anaphylaxis with wheezing and hypotension after a new antibiotic. What is the preferred initial route for epinephrine?
items.x: Intramuscular epinephrine in the thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection and is the first-line initial treatment for anaphylaxis. Inhaled or oral routes do not treat the systemic reaction.
items.a: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Nebulized inhalation through a face mask
Oral administration as a liquid solution

items.q: A patient on an epinephrine infusion has a rising lactate despite improving blood pressure and perfusion. What best explains this?
items.x: Epinephrine's beta-2 effects drive glycolysis in muscle and raise lactate even when tissue perfusion is adequate. Lactate is not a metabolite of epinephrine itself, so that explanation is wrong.
items.a: Beta-2 stimulation increases aerobic glycolysis and lactate production
w: Epinephrine is metabolized directly into lactic acid
Epinephrine always causes mesenteric ischemia
Alpha-1 stimulation blocks lactate uptake by the liver

items.q: A patient becomes hypotensive and receives IV phenylephrine. Which heart rate response is expected?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist; the rise in blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that slows the heart. It has no meaningful beta-1 activity, so tachycardia is not expected.
items.a: Reflex slowing of the heart rate
w: Marked sinus tachycardia from beta-1 stimulation
No change because it acts only on veins
New atrial fibrillation from atrial stimulation

items.q: Dobutamine is started for low-output cardiogenic shock. Which adverse effects should the team watch for most closely?
items.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 agonist with some beta-2 vasodilation, so it can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, and a drop in blood pressure. It does not cause strong alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.
items.a: Tachyarrhythmias and possible hypotension
w: Bradycardia and complete heart block
Severe hypertension from alpha stimulation
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves

items.q: Milrinone is being considered for a patient with low-output heart failure and acute kidney injury. What is the main concern?
items.x: Milrinone is eliminated mainly by the kidneys, so it builds up in renal impairment and its vasodilating and proarrhythmic effects become stronger. It lowers, not raises, blood pressure.
items.a: It accumulates because it is renally cleared, raising hypotension and arrhythmia risk
w: It is hepatically cleared and causes liver failure in kidney injury
It is cleared by plasma esterases, so kidney injury has no effect
It accumulates and causes hypertensive crisis in kidney injury

items.q: Compared with norepinephrine as the first vasopressor in shock, dopamine is associated with which outcome?
items.x: Trials comparing the two found more arrhythmias with dopamine and no renal benefit, which is why norepinephrine is preferred. The idea that dopamine protects the kidneys has not been supported.
items.a: More arrhythmic events
w: Better protection of kidney function
Lower overall mortality
Less tachycardia

items.q: A patient is started on midodrine for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Which counseling point is most important?
items.x: Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist prodrug that can cause significant supine hypertension, so doses are timed while the patient is upright during the day. Bedtime dosing is exactly what raises that risk.
items.a: Take doses during the day, not near bedtime, to limit supine hypertension
w: Take the last dose at bedtime to prevent morning dizziness
Take each dose lying flat to improve absorption
Take doses only when dizzy to avoid tolerance

items.q: For a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, argatroban is generally preferred over bivalirudin when the patient has which condition?
items.x: Argatroban is cleared by the liver, so it is a good choice when kidney function is poor. In hepatic impairment it accumulates, which is where bivalirudin is often favored.
items.a: Severe kidney impairment
w: Severe hepatic impairment
Active gastrointestinal bleeding
Planned percutaneous coronary intervention

items.q: On day seven of unfractionated heparin, a patient's platelet count falls by more than half and a new DVT appears. What process best explains this?
items.x: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction against PF4-heparin complexes that activates platelets, causing both low counts and thrombosis. Marrow suppression would not explain the new clot.
items.a: Antibodies to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes activate platelets
w: Heparin directly suppresses megakaryocytes in the marrow
Platelets are diluted by large-volume IV fluids
Platelets are sequestered in an enlarged spleen

items.q: Enoxaparin is ordered for VTE prophylaxis in a patient with severely reduced kidney function. What is the main concern?
items.x: Enoxaparin is cleared by the kidneys, so it accumulates in severe renal impairment and needs adjustment or an alternative such as unfractionated heparin. It does not lose effect in renal failure.
items.a: It accumulates and raises bleeding risk without adjustment
w: It is inactivated faster and loses its effect
It causes hyperkalemia through aldosterone activation
It requires conversion by the kidney to work

items.q: A patient on warfarin is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. What effect is expected?
items.x: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, which clears the more potent warfarin isomer, so the INR rises. This is one of the most common clinically important warfarin interactions.
items.a: A higher INR and increased bleeding risk
w: A lower INR and increased clot risk
No change in INR but more bruising
A lower INR from increased vitamin K intake

items.q: A patient has a mechanical mitral valve and needs long-term anticoagulation. Which oral agent is appropriate?
items.x: Warfarin is the oral anticoagulant used for mechanical heart valves. Direct oral anticoagulants are not approved for mechanical valves, and dabigatran caused more clots and bleeding in a trial in this group.
items.a: Warfarin
w: Apixaban
Rivaroxaban
Dabigatran

items.q: A patient on warfarin has an intracranial hemorrhage and an elevated INR. Which approach reverses the anticoagulation most rapidly?
items.x: Four-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX, and X within minutes, and IV vitamin K keeps the correction going. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
items.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate with IV vitamin K
w: Fresh frozen plasma alone without vitamin K
Protamine sulfate with IV vitamin K
Oral vitamin K alone

items.q: Which oral anticoagulant's clearance depends most heavily on kidney function?
items.x: Dabigatran is cleared mostly by the kidneys, so its levels rise sharply in renal impairment. Apixaban has the least renal clearance of the direct oral anticoagulants.
items.a: Dabigatran
w: Apixaban
Rivaroxaban
Warfarin

items.q: How does idarucizumab reverse the effect of dabigatran?
items.x: Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity. A decoy factor Xa describes a different reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors.
items.a: It is an antibody fragment that binds dabigatran tightly
w: It supplies clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X
It acts as a decoy factor Xa that binds inhibitors
It neutralizes heparin through ionic binding

items.q: Protamine most completely reverses the anticoagulant effect of which agent?
items.x: Protamine binds unfractionated heparin and fully neutralizes it. It only partially reverses enoxaparin and has no meaningful effect on fondaparinux or apixaban.
items.a: Unfractionated heparin
w: Enoxaparin
Fondaparinux
Apixaban

items.q: A patient on rivaroxaban for VTE is started on rifampin. What is the expected effect?
items.x: Rifampin strongly induces both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which lowers rivaroxaban exposure and can lead to treatment failure. Rifampin is an inducer, not an inhibitor.
items.a: Lower rivaroxaban levels and higher risk of clotting
w: Higher rivaroxaban levels and higher risk of bleeding
No change because rivaroxaban is renally cleared only
Higher levels because rifampin inhibits CYP3A4

items.q: Which patient is at highest risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia if succinylcholine is used for intubation?
items.x: After burns, crush injuries, or denervation, extra acetylcholine receptors spread across muscle, and succinylcholine can release large amounts of potassium. The other conditions do not upregulate these receptors.
items.a: A patient with a crush injury several days ago
w: A patient with a COPD exacerbation
A patient with acute appendicitis
A patient with an asthma attack

items.q: Shortly after intubation with succinylcholine, a patient develops jaw rigidity, rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, and fever. What should be recognized?
items.x: Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis treated with dantrolene. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after dopamine blockers, not minutes after anesthesia.
items.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Anaphylaxis

items.q: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium-induced paralysis?
items.x: Sugammadex is a modified cyclodextrin that binds steroidal blockers like rocuronium and vecuronium directly. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is how neostigmine works, not sugammadex.
items.a: It encapsulates rocuronium and removes it from the receptor
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the junction
It blocks muscarinic receptors to limit side effects
It competes with rocuronium as a direct agonist

items.q: A patient who takes an oral hormonal contraceptive received sugammadex during surgery. Which counseling point applies?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen and reduce contraceptive exposure, similar to missing a dose, so backup contraception is advised for a period. Doubling doses is not the recommended approach.
items.a: Use a nonhormonal backup method for a period afterward
w: No change is needed because there is no interaction
Double the next contraceptive dose to compensate
Switch permanently to an intrauterine device

items.q: For rapid sequence intubation in a patient with severe hyperkalemia, why is rocuronium preferred over succinylcholine?
items.x: Rocuronium blocks the receptor without depolarizing the muscle, so it does not release potassium. It actually lasts longer than succinylcholine, which is why a reversal plan matters.
items.a: It is nondepolarizing and does not raise serum potassium
w: It has a much shorter duration than succinylcholine
It directly lowers serum potassium
It does not need to be reversed

items.q: Which adverse effect is a key concern with etomidate used for induction?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase and temporarily suppresses cortisol production. It is chosen in unstable patients precisely because it usually preserves blood pressure.
items.a: Transient adrenal suppression from blocked cortisol synthesis
w: Profound hypotension in most patients
Severe bronchospasm from histamine release
Malignant hyperthermia triggering

items.q: Ketamine is a useful induction agent for a patient with hypotension or severe bronchospasm mainly because it:
items.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects tend to maintain blood pressure, and it relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. It increases, rather than reduces, airway secretions.
items.a: Supports blood pressure and causes bronchodilation
w: Lowers blood pressure and reduces airway secretions
Causes profound bradycardia and bronchoconstriction
Has no effect on heart rate or airway tone

items.q: Which lab should be monitored periodically during a prolonged propofol infusion in the ICU?
items.x: Propofol is delivered in a lipid emulsion, so prolonged infusions can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Triglycerides are the standard lab to follow.
items.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum ammonia
Serum uric acid
Serum amylase only

items.q: A sedated ICU patient with kidney failure stays oversedated long after a midazolam infusion is turned off. What best explains this?
items.x: Midazolam's active metabolite, alpha-hydroxymidazolam glucuronide, is renally cleared and builds up in kidney failure, prolonging sedation. Kidney failure slows, rather than speeds, its elimination.
items.a: An active glucuronide metabolite accumulates in kidney failure
w: Midazolam is converted to a longer-acting opioid
Kidney failure speeds midazolam clearance
Midazolam inhibits its own metabolism permanently

items.q: Why is cisatracurium often chosen for neuromuscular blockade in patients with liver and kidney failure?
items.x: Cisatracurium breaks down spontaneously in plasma by Hofmann elimination, so it does not depend on the liver or kidneys. Sugammadex does not reverse benzylisoquinolines like cisatracurium.
items.a: It undergoes Hofmann elimination, independent of organ function
w: It is excreted unchanged by the kidneys
It is cleared only by hepatic metabolism
It is reversed by sugammadex

items.q: A patient receives frequent nebulized albuterol during a severe asthma exacerbation. Which lab change is most expected?
items.x: Beta-2 agonists stimulate the sodium-potassium pump and shift potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium. This is the same effect used to treat hyperkalemia.
items.a: Hypokalemia from potassium shifting into cells
w: Hyperkalemia from potassium release from cells
Hypercalcemia from bone resorption
Hyponatremia from water retention

items.q: Ipratropium is added to albuterol during a COPD exacerbation. How does it improve airflow?
items.x: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks vagal bronchoconstriction, adding to the effect of a beta-2 agonist. Beta-2 stimulation is how albuterol, not ipratropium, works.
items.a: It blocks muscarinic receptors to reduce bronchoconstriction
w: It stimulates beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle
It blocks leukotriene receptors in the airway
It inhibits phosphodiesterase in airway cells

items.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes is started on oral prednisone for a COPD exacerbation. Which problem is most likely?
items.x: Glucocorticoids raise glucose by increasing insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis, and with morning dosing the rise peaks in the afternoon and evening. Hypoglycemia is not expected.
items.a: Hyperglycemia, often most prominent later in the day
w: Hypoglycemia, especially overnight
Hyperkalemia from mineralocorticoid effects
Hypercalcemia from increased absorption

items.q: A patient admitted for a COPD exacerbation can swallow and absorb oral medications. How does oral prednisone compare with IV methylprednisolone?
items.x: In patients who can take oral medications, oral corticosteroids work as well as IV for COPD exacerbations. Hospitalization alone does not require the IV route.
items.a: Oral therapy is generally as effective as IV therapy
w: IV therapy is required for any hospitalized patient
Oral therapy works only after several weeks
IV therapy has fewer side effects at any dose

items.q: A patient on chronic theophylline is started on ciprofloxacin and develops nausea, tachycardia, and a seizure. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range and is cleared by CYP1A2, which ciprofloxacin inhibits, so levels rise and cause GI, cardiac, and seizure toxicity. Ciprofloxacin is an inhibitor, not an inducer.
items.a: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, raising theophylline levels
w: Ciprofloxacin induces CYP1A2, lowering theophylline levels
Theophylline raises ciprofloxacin levels into the toxic range
The drugs bind each other and form a toxic compound

items.q: IV magnesium sulfate is given during a severe asthma exacerbation. How does it help?
items.x: Magnesium inhibits calcium entry into airway smooth muscle, producing bronchodilation in severe exacerbations. It does not have direct anti-inflammatory steroid-like effects.
items.a: It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by opposing calcium
w: It reduces airway inflammation like a corticosteroid
It thins mucus by breaking disulfide bonds
It blocks leukotriene synthesis in the airway

items.q: For which patient should tiotropium be used with particular caution?
items.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, and anticholinergic effects can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention from prostate enlargement. The other conditions are not specific concerns.
items.a: A patient with narrow-angle glaucoma or urinary retention
w: A patient with well-controlled hypertension
A patient with type 2 diabetes
A patient with osteoarthritis of the knee

items.q: Which serious adverse effect carries a boxed warning for montelukast?
items.x: Montelukast carries a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events, so patients and families should report mood or behavior changes. Liver injury is rare and is not the boxed warning.
items.a: Neuropsychiatric events such as agitation, depression, or suicidal thoughts
w: Liver failure requiring transplantation
Severe hypokalemia and arrhythmias
Bone marrow suppression with agranulocytosis

items.q: For a patient hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia, azithromycin is commonly added to a beta-lactam mainly to cover which organisms?
items.x: Beta-lactams do not cover atypical organisms, so a macrolide is added for Legionella, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydophila. Azithromycin does not reliably cover MRSA or Pseudomonas.
items.a: Atypical organisms such as Legionella and Mycoplasma
w: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Anaerobes from aspiration

items.q: A patient is discharged on budesonide-formoterol inhaler. Which teaching point helps prevent a common local side effect?
items.x: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause oral thrush and hoarseness, and rinsing and spitting reduces deposition in the mouth. Taking it with meals does not reduce this risk.
items.a: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
w: Use a nasal decongestant before each dose
Take each dose with a full meal
Swallow the dose quickly without inhaling deeply

items.q: A patient with IV access is in convulsive status epilepticus. Which medication is the preferred first-line treatment?
items.x: A benzodiazepine such as IV lorazepam is first-line for status epilepticus. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate are second-line agents if seizures continue.
items.a: Intravenous lorazepam
w: Intravenous levetiracetam
Intravenous phenobarbital
Oral lamotrigine

items.q: What is an advantage of fosphenytoin over IV phenytoin?
items.x: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug that is less irritating to veins, reducing tissue injury. It is still converted to phenytoin and can still cause hypotension and arrhythmias, so monitoring is still needed.
items.a: Lower risk of infusion-site injury such as purple glove syndrome
w: No need for cardiac monitoring during infusion
No risk of hypotension during infusion
It does not convert to phenytoin in the body

items.q: A malnourished patient with low serum albumin has a total phenytoin level within the usual range but shows nystagmus and ataxia. What explains this?
items.x: Phenytoin is highly protein bound, so low albumin raises the free, active fraction even when the total level looks acceptable. A free phenytoin level or corrected value gives a better picture.
items.a: The unbound fraction is higher than the total level suggests
w: Low albumin lowers the unbound phenytoin fraction
The level must be falsely high from lab interference
Nystagmus is unrelated to phenytoin levels

items.q: A patient on valproic acid becomes lethargic and confused, but liver enzymes are normal. Which lab should be checked?
items.x: Valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy even when liver tests are normal. Pancreatitis is another valproate toxicity, but it presents with abdominal pain rather than isolated confusion.
items.a: Serum ammonia
w: Serum lipase
Serum magnesium
Serum creatine kinase

items.q: A patient whose seizures are controlled on valproic acid is started on meropenem and then has breakthrough seizures. Why?
items.x: Carbapenems can drop valproate concentrations rapidly and substantially, causing loss of seizure control; the combination is generally avoided. Simply increasing the valproate dose does not reliably overcome this interaction.
items.a: Carbapenems sharply lower valproic acid levels
w: Meropenem directly lowers the seizure threshold alone
Valproic acid inactivates meropenem in the blood
Meropenem raises valproic acid to toxic levels

items.q: Which adverse effect should patients and families be told to report when levetiracetam is started?
items.x: Levetiracetam commonly causes behavioral and mood effects, including irritability and, rarely, suicidal thoughts. Gingival overgrowth is a phenytoin effect, not a levetiracetam effect.
items.a: Irritability, mood changes, or behavioral symptoms
w: Gingival overgrowth and coarse facial features
Weight gain and hair loss
Kidney stones and metabolic acidosis

items.q: Before starting carbamazepine in a patient of Asian ancestry, which test is recommended?
items.x: HLA-B*15:02, which is more common in many Asian populations, is strongly linked to carbamazepine-induced SJS and TEN. TPMT testing applies to thiopurines such as azathioprine.
items.a: HLA-B*15:02 to assess risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
w: TPMT activity to assess risk of myelosuppression
G6PD activity to assess risk of hemolysis
CYP2C19 genotype to assess drug activation

items.q: How is nimodipine given to a patient after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage?
items.x: Nimodipine is given by mouth or feeding tube; injecting capsule contents IV has caused cardiac arrest and death. It is used to improve neurologic outcomes after aneurysmal SAH.
items.a: Orally or by feeding tube, never intravenously
w: Intravenously as a continuous infusion
Intrathecally through a ventricular drain
Intramuscularly into the deltoid

items.q: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use is confused and hypoglycemic. Why is thiamine given before or with dextrose?
items.x: Glucose metabolism uses thiamine, and giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamine does not change how fast dextrose is absorbed.
items.a: To prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
w: To speed absorption of the dextrose
To prevent rebound hypoglycemia
To reverse alcohol intoxication directly

items.q: Which finding is an absolute contraindication to IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke?
items.x: Any hemorrhage on imaging rules out thrombolysis because it would worsen bleeding. Controlled hypertension and statin use are not contraindications.
items.a: Intracranial hemorrhage on head CT
w: History of well-controlled hypertension
Mild headache at symptom onset
Daily statin use at home

items.q: Why is morphine a poor choice for a patient with severe kidney failure?
items.x: Morphine's glucuronide metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate in kidney failure, causing prolonged sedation, respiratory depression, and myoclonus. It is not a renal prodrug.
items.a: Active metabolites accumulate and cause sedation and neurotoxicity
w: It is inactive until converted by the kidneys
Kidney failure speeds its clearance and shortens its effect
It directly damages the remaining nephrons

items.q: Which opioid is generally preferred in severe kidney impairment because it lacks clinically important active metabolites?
items.x: Fentanyl is metabolized by the liver to inactive metabolites, making it a safer choice in kidney failure. Meperidine forms normeperidine, which accumulates and can cause seizures.
items.a: Fentanyl
w: Morphine
Codeine
Meperidine

items.q: A patient with opioid-induced respiratory depression responds well to naloxone but becomes drowsy and hypoventilates again later. Why?
items.x: Naloxone's duration is often shorter than that of long-acting or extended-release opioids, so sedation can return. Patients need ongoing monitoring and may need repeat doses or an infusion.
items.a: Naloxone's effect can wear off before the opioid's effect
w: Naloxone itself causes delayed respiratory depression
The opioid was converted into naloxone
Naloxone increases opioid absorption from the gut

items.q: A patient's methadone was recently titrated up for pain, and several days later they become very sedated. What best explains the delay?
items.x: Methadone's long and unpredictable half-life means levels keep rising for days after a dose change, so respiratory depression can appear late. That is why titration is slow and monitoring continues after changes.
items.a: Its long, variable half-life lets it accumulate over days
w: It is a prodrug that activates only after a week
It causes delayed allergic reactions
Its effect is limited to the first dose

items.q: A patient on sertraline is prescribed tramadol after surgery and develops agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, and fever. What should be recognized?
items.x: Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake, and combined with an SSRI it can cause serotonin syndrome with clonus and hyperreflexia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome features rigidity and slow reflexes after dopamine blockers.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Opioid withdrawal
Anticholinergic toxicity

items.q: Which hospitalized patient is the poorest candidate for IV ketorolac?
items.x: Ketorolac is an NSAID that reduces renal blood flow and can worsen kidney injury, so it is contraindicated in renal impairment or volume depletion. It is commonly used for renal colic when kidney function is normal.
items.a: A patient with acute kidney injury
w: A patient with renal colic and normal kidney function
A patient with postoperative pain and normal labs
A patient with a migraine and normal labs

items.q: A patient's home medications include hydrocodone-acetaminophen and an over-the-counter cold product. What is the main concern?
items.x: Many combination and OTC products contain acetaminophen, and taking several can exceed safe daily totals and cause hepatotoxicity. Acetaminophen does not affect platelets the way NSAIDs do.
items.a: Unintended cumulative acetaminophen intake causing liver injury
w: Severe kidney injury from hydrocodone
Additive bleeding risk from acetaminophen
Serotonin syndrome from the combination

items.q: An older patient with chronic kidney disease on gabapentin becomes increasingly drowsy and confused with myoclonus. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Gabapentin is cleared unchanged by the kidneys, so it accumulates in CKD and causes sedation, confusion, and myoclonus. It is not hepatically metabolized.
items.a: Gabapentin accumulation from reduced renal clearance
w: Gabapentin-induced liver failure
Serotonin syndrome from gabapentin
Gabapentin-induced hypoglycemia

items.q: A patient is sedated with dexmedetomidine in the ICU. Which adverse effects need the closest monitoring?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone, causing bradycardia and hypotension. It causes little respiratory depression, which is one of its advantages.
items.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Respiratory depression and apnea
Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity
Hypertensive crisis and tachycardia

items.q: Why is flumazenil used cautiously in a patient with long-term benzodiazepine use or an unknown mixed overdose?
items.x: Flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine receptor and can trigger seizures in dependent patients or those who took proconvulsant drugs such as tricyclics. It does not cause respiratory depression.
items.a: It can precipitate withdrawal seizures
w: It causes profound respiratory depression
It worsens opioid toxicity
It has no effect on benzodiazepines

items.q: Before giving IV haloperidol for agitated delirium, which assessment is most important?
items.x: IV haloperidol can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes, so a baseline ECG and correction of potassium and magnesium are important. Metabolic labs matter for long-term antipsychotic use, not this acute decision.
items.a: An ECG for the QTc interval and electrolytes
w: A lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c
A urine pregnancy test only
Thyroid function tests

items.q: Two days after starting haloperidol, a patient develops fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure, and a very high CK. What should be recognized?
items.x: Fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and high CK after a dopamine blocker point to NMS. Serotonin syndrome develops faster and features clonus and hyperreflexia instead of lead-pipe rigidity.
items.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia
Acute dystonic reaction

items.q: A patient on stable lithium is started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. What is the main risk?
items.x: Thiazides increase proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption, raising lithium levels; ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs do the same. Lithium is not hepatically cleared.
items.a: Lithium toxicity from reduced renal lithium clearance
w: Subtherapeutic lithium from increased excretion
Hypokalemia that blocks lithium's effect
Hepatotoxicity from the combination

items.q: A patient on clozapine is admitted with fever and a sore throat. Which lab is most urgent?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia and agranulocytosis, and fever or sore throat may be the first sign. The absolute neutrophil count guides urgent management.
items.a: Absolute neutrophil count
w: Serum lithium level
Serum ammonia
Thyroid-stimulating hormone

items.q: Which combination raises the most concern for cardiorespiratory depression in an agitated patient?
items.x: Labeling advises against combining IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines because of reports of hypotension, bradycardia, and respiratory depression. The other combinations do not carry this risk.
items.a: IM olanzapine given with a parenteral benzodiazepine
w: Oral olanzapine given with oral acetaminophen
IM olanzapine given with oral docusate
Oral olanzapine given with a nicotine patch

items.q: A patient with Parkinson disease develops distressing hallucinations in the hospital. Why is quetiapine often preferred over haloperidol?
items.x: Quetiapine binds D2 receptors loosely, so it is less likely to worsen parkinsonism. Haloperidol's strong D2 blockade can markedly worsen motor symptoms.
items.a: Its weak dopamine D2 blockade causes less motor worsening
w: It increases dopamine release in the striatum
It has strong D2 blockade that reduces tremor
It works without crossing the blood-brain barrier

items.q: A patient taking sertraline needs linezolid for a resistant infection. Which risk should the team watch for?
items.x: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor, and combining it with an SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome. When the combination is needed, the patient is monitored closely for agitation, clonus, and fever.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome because linezolid inhibits monoamine oxidase
w: Lithium toxicity from reduced renal clearance
Hypertensive crisis from tyramine in hospital food
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from dopamine blockade

items.q: A patient with cirrhosis is admitted in alcohol withdrawal. Why is lorazepam often chosen over chlordiazepoxide?
items.x: Lorazepam is conjugated directly and has no active metabolites, so it accumulates less in liver disease. Chlordiazepoxide relies on oxidative metabolism and has long-acting active metabolites.
items.a: It is cleared by glucuronidation without active metabolites
w: It has a much longer half-life than chlordiazepoxide
It is the only benzodiazepine that treats seizures
It undergoes extensive oxidative liver metabolism

items.q: For which patient is bupropion contraindicated?
items.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated with seizure disorders, eating disorders, and abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal. It is used for smoking cessation and seasonal depression.
items.a: A patient with a seizure disorder
w: A patient with well-controlled hypertension
A patient who smokes cigarettes
A patient with seasonal depression

items.q: A patient who recently used heroin develops sudden severe withdrawal after the first dose of buprenorphine. What explains this?
items.x: Buprenorphine binds opioid receptors tightly but activates them only partly, so it can push off a full agonist and precipitate withdrawal. That is why induction usually waits for withdrawal signs or uses a low-dose start.
items.a: Its high-affinity partial agonism displaces full agonists
w: It is a full agonist that causes overdose
It blocks serotonin reuptake
It is converted to naloxone in the liver

items.q: A patient with hyperkalemia has peaked T waves on ECG. What is the purpose of IV calcium gluconate?
items.x: Calcium protects the heart from arrhythmia within minutes but does not change serum potassium. Insulin and beta-agonists shift potassium into cells, and binders or diuretics remove it.
items.a: It stabilizes the cardiac membrane without lowering potassium
w: It shifts potassium into cells
It removes potassium through the gut
It increases urinary potassium excretion

items.q: When IV regular insulin is used to treat hyperkalemia, what is the main risk and how is it addressed?
items.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but also lowers glucose, so dextrose is usually given unless glucose is high, and glucose is monitored for hours. Insulin does not cause hypercalcemia.
items.a: Hypoglycemia, so dextrose is given and glucose is checked
w: Hypercalcemia, so calcium levels are checked
Hypernatremia, so sodium levels are checked
Hyperkalemia rebound, so insulin is repeated hourly

items.q: Which adverse effect is most important to monitor in a patient with heart failure receiving sodium zirconium cyclosilicate?
items.x: Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate exchanges sodium for potassium, and edema is a recognized adverse effect, especially in fluid-sensitive patients. Intestinal necrosis is linked to sodium polystyrene sulfonate.
items.a: Edema from its sodium content
w: Intestinal necrosis
Hypercalcemia
Severe constipation and bowel obstruction

items.q: A patient is started on patiromer for chronic hyperkalemia and takes several other oral medications. Which teaching point is most important?
items.x: Patiromer can bind other oral drugs in the gut and reduce their absorption, so doses are spaced apart. Taking everything together is exactly what causes the interaction.
items.a: Separate patiromer from other oral medications
w: Take patiromer with all other medications at once
Take patiromer only on an empty stomach at bedtime
Crush other medications into the patiromer suspension

items.q: Which serious adverse effect is associated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate?
items.x: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has been linked to colonic necrosis, particularly with sorbitol or in patients with bowel dysfunction. It does not cause hypercalcemia.
items.a: Intestinal necrosis
w: Severe hypercalcemia
Acute pancreatitis
Hemorrhagic cystitis

items.q: A patient's hypokalemia does not improve despite repeated potassium chloride replacement. Which other electrolyte should be checked and corrected?
items.x: Low magnesium increases renal potassium wasting, so hypokalemia is often refractory until magnesium is repleted. Phosphate and calcium do not have this direct effect.
items.a: Magnesium
w: Phosphate
Calcium
Chloride

items.q: When hypertonic saline is used for symptomatic chronic hyponatremia, what is the main risk of correcting sodium too quickly?
items.x: Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia, and overly rapid correction pulls water out of cells and damages myelin. Cerebral edema is the danger of hyponatremia itself or overly rapid lowering of sodium, not of correction.
items.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome
w: Cerebral edema from water shifting into neurons
Severe hypokalemia from sodium loading
Acute kidney injury from tubular necrosis

items.q: A patient receives large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride during resuscitation. Which acid-base disorder is most likely?
items.x: Normal saline has more chloride than plasma, and large volumes lower bicarbonate, causing a hyperchloremic acidosis with a normal anion gap. It does not add unmeasured anions.
items.a: Hyperchloremic non-anion gap metabolic acidosis
w: High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis

items.q: An older patient taking desmopressin for nocturia is admitted with confusion and nausea. Which lab abnormality is most likely?
items.x: Desmopressin is a V2 agonist that increases free water reabsorption and can cause hyponatremia, especially in older adults. Hypernatremia is what it is used to prevent in diabetes insipidus.
items.a: Hyponatremia
w: Hypernatremia
Hyperkalemia
Hypercalcemia

items.q: Why is nitrofurantoin a poor choice for cystitis in a patient with markedly reduced kidney function?
items.x: Nitrofurantoin needs adequate kidney function to reach effective urine concentrations, and accumulation raises the risk of neuropathy and other toxicity. Hyperkalemia is a trimethoprim concern, not nitrofurantoin.
items.a: Urine levels are inadequate while systemic toxicity rises
w: It is converted to a nephrotoxin by the liver
It causes severe hyperkalemia in kidney disease
It is only active in alkaline urine

items.q: A patient taking azathioprine after a transplant is started on allopurinol for gout. What is the main risk?
items.x: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which inactivates azathioprine and mercaptopurine, so levels rise and can cause life-threatening marrow suppression. Azathioprine levels rise, not fall.
items.a: Severe myelosuppression from reduced azathioprine breakdown
w: Gout flares from rapid uric acid lowering only
Transplant rejection from lower azathioprine levels
Kidney stones from increased uric acid excretion

items.q: Before starting allopurinol in a patient of Korean descent with chronic kidney disease, which test is recommended?
items.x: HLA-B*58:01 is strongly linked to allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, SJS, and TEN and is more common in some Asian and African American populations. HLA-B*15:02 is the marker used for carbamazepine.
items.a: HLA-B*58:01 to assess risk of severe skin reactions
w: HLA-B*15:02 to assess risk of severe skin reactions
G6PD activity to assess risk of hemolysis
TPMT activity to assess risk of myelosuppression

items.q: A patient on colchicine for gout is started on clarithromycin and develops diarrhea, weakness, and low blood counts. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising colchicine to toxic levels that affect the GI tract, muscles, and marrow. Low counts are not explained by C. difficile.
items.a: Colchicine toxicity from CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition
w: Clostridioides difficile infection from clarithromycin alone
Allergic reaction to clarithromycin
Colchicine levels falling below the effective range

items.q: An older patient with chronic kidney disease on long-term colchicine develops proximal muscle weakness and an elevated CK. What should be recognized?
items.x: Colchicine is partly renally cleared, and accumulation in CKD can cause myopathy and neuropathy, especially with statins or interacting drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica does not raise the CK.
items.a: Colchicine-induced neuromyopathy from accumulation
w: Polymyalgia rheumatica unrelated to medications
Expected gout progression
Hypothyroidism from colchicine

items.q: Which boxed warning applies to febuxostat?
items.x: In a trial against allopurinol, febuxostat was associated with higher cardiovascular death in patients with known cardiovascular disease. HLA-B*58:01 hypersensitivity is an allopurinol concern.
items.a: Higher cardiovascular death in patients with established cardiovascular disease
w: Severe hypersensitivity linked to HLA-B*58:01
Fatal hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Osteonecrosis of the jaw

items.q: Before giving rasburicase for tumor lysis syndrome, which condition must be screened for?
items.x: Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide while breaking down uric acid, which can cause severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency. TPMT affects thiopurine drugs.
items.a: G6PD deficiency
w: TPMT deficiency
HLA-B*58:01 carrier status
Pseudocholinesterase deficiency

items.q: Which teaching point is most important for a patient starting oral alendronate?
items.x: Alendronate is poorly absorbed and can cause esophageal injury, so it is taken fasting with plain water while remaining upright. Food, calcium, and iron block its absorption.
items.a: Take it with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright afterward
w: Take it with milk and a meal to protect the stomach
Take it at bedtime while lying down
Take it with calcium and iron for better effect

items.q: Before IV zoledronic acid is given, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Zoledronic acid can cause kidney injury and hypocalcemia, so renal function is checked and low calcium or vitamin D is corrected first. Liver tests are not the main concern.
items.a: Kidney function and calcium status
w: Thyroid function and lipid panel
Liver enzymes and ammonia
Platelet count and INR

items.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease receives denosumab. Which adverse effect is of greatest concern?
items.x: Denosumab blocks RANKL and bone resorption, and patients with advanced CKD are at high risk of severe hypocalcemia. It is not cleared by the kidneys and is not directly nephrotoxic.
items.a: Severe hypocalcemia
w: Severe hypercalcemia
Hyperkalemia
Acute kidney injury from the drug itself

items.q: In severe hypercalcemia of malignancy, what is the role of calcitonin?
items.x: Calcitonin lowers calcium within hours, but its effect fades within a few days, so it is paired with IV fluids and a bisphosphonate for durable control. Its benefit is speed, not durability.
items.a: Rapid but short-lived calcium lowering due to tachyphylaxis
w: Slow but durable calcium lowering over weeks
Calcium lowering by increasing gut absorption
Permanent cure by blocking tumor PTHrP release

items.q: How does N-acetylcysteine protect the liver after an acetaminophen overdose?
items.x: NAC restores glutathione, which binds NAPQI, the toxic metabolite of acetaminophen. Activated charcoal, not NAC, is what limits gut absorption.
items.a: It replenishes glutathione to detoxify the toxic metabolite
w: It blocks acetaminophen absorption in the gut
It inhibits CYP2E1 permanently
It increases renal excretion of acetaminophen

items.q: How does fomepizole treat ethylene glycol or methanol poisoning?
items.x: Fomepizole competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase so ethylene glycol and methanol are not converted to toxic acids. Hemodialysis, not fomepizole, removes the toxins and acids.
items.a: It inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, blocking toxic metabolite formation
w: It binds the alcohol directly in the bloodstream
It speeds conversion to the toxic metabolites
It increases renal excretion of the toxic acids

items.q: In acute digoxin overdose, which finding is an indication for digoxin immune Fab?
items.x: Digoxin Fab is indicated for life-threatening arrhythmias, significant hyperkalemia from acute toxicity, or end-organ effects. Mild symptoms with a normal ECG are usually observed.
items.a: A life-threatening arrhythmia or marked hyperkalemia
w: Mild nausea with a normal ECG
Isolated first-degree AV block
A single loose stool

items.q: A patient with a tricyclic antidepressant overdose has a widened QRS on ECG. Which treatment is first-line?
items.x: Sodium loading and alkalinization overcome tricyclic sodium channel blockade and narrow the QRS. Procainamide is also a sodium channel blocker, and physostigmine can cause asystole in tricyclic toxicity.
items.a: IV sodium bicarbonate
w: IV procainamide
IV physostigmine
IV flumazenil

items.q: A patient with sulfonylurea overdose keeps becoming hypoglycemic despite dextrose. How does octreotide help?
items.x: Sulfonylureas trigger insulin release, and dextrose can drive even more; octreotide suppresses that release and prevents recurrent hypoglycemia. Glucagon, not octreotide, raises hepatic glucose output.
items.a: It inhibits insulin release from the pancreas
w: It increases hepatic glucose output directly
It blocks sulfonylurea absorption in the gut
It increases renal excretion of the sulfonylurea

items.q: How does glucagon help in beta-blocker overdose with bradycardia and hypotension?
items.x: Glucagon activates its own receptor on cardiac cells, raising cAMP and contractility even when beta receptors are blocked. It does not act on beta receptors itself.
items.a: It raises cardiac cAMP through a non-beta receptor pathway
w: It directly stimulates beta-1 receptors
It blocks calcium channels in the heart
It increases vagal tone to the heart

items.q: A patient taking an SSRI needs methylene blue for methemoglobinemia. Which risk should the team anticipate?
items.x: Methylene blue is a potent MAO-A inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs. It can also cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome from its MAO inhibition
w: Hypertensive crisis from tyramine release
Severe hypoglycemia from insulin release
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

items.q: A smoke-inhalation patient with suspected cyanide poisoning receives hydroxocobalamin. How does it work?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin combines with cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which the kidneys excrete. Inducing methemoglobin is how nitrites work, which is risky in smoke inhalation with carbon monoxide.
items.a: It binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted
w: It induces methemoglobin, which binds cyanide
It speeds conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate
It displaces carbon monoxide from hemoglobin

items.q: Before giving physostigmine for suspected anticholinergic delirium, which finding should be ruled out?
items.x: Physostigmine can cause bradycardia and asystole in tricyclic toxicity, so a widened QRS is a reason to avoid it. Dilated pupils, dry skin, and tachycardia are expected features of anticholinergic toxicity.
items.a: QRS widening suggesting tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
w: Dilated pupils on exam
Dry, flushed skin
Mild sinus tachycardia

items.q: Which route of vitamin K is least reliable and generally not recommended for reversing warfarin?
items.x: Subcutaneous vitamin K is absorbed unpredictably, so oral is used for non-urgent correction and IV for serious bleeding. IV is reliable and fast but carries a small risk of anaphylactoid reactions.
items.a: Subcutaneous
w: Oral
Intravenous
Through a feeding tube

items.q: Combining IV vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam is associated with which problem?
items.x: Observational data show more AKI with vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam than with vancomycin plus other beta-lactams, so kidney function is followed closely. The combination does not protect the kidneys.
items.a: Higher rates of acute kidney injury
w: Higher rates of hearing loss only
Lower rates of kidney injury than vancomycin alone
Severe liver injury in most patients

items.q: For treatment of Clostridioides difficile infection, how must vancomycin be given?
items.x: Oral vancomycin stays in the gut lumen where C. difficile lives; IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon. Poor oral absorption is exactly why the oral route works for this infection.
items.a: Orally, because IV vancomycin does not reach the colon
w: Intravenously, because oral vancomycin is not absorbed
Intramuscularly into the gluteal muscle
Topically as a rectal cream

items.q: A patient with kidney injury on cefepime becomes confused with myoclonus. What should be recognized?
items.x: Cefepime is renally cleared and can accumulate, causing encephalopathy, myoclonus, and nonconvulsive seizures. Unadjusted dosing in kidney injury is the classic setup.
items.a: Cefepime neurotoxicity from accumulation
w: Expected sepsis-associated delirium only
Cefepime-induced hypoglycemia
Serotonin syndrome from cefepime

items.q: Which property makes ceftriaxone convenient in patients with kidney failure?
items.x: Ceftriaxone is eliminated through both bile and urine, so it generally does not need renal adjustment. Most other cephalosporins such as cefepime do require adjustment.
items.a: Dual biliary and renal elimination, so routine renal adjustment is not needed
w: Complete renal elimination, requiring dialysis dosing
No elimination by any route, so it lasts weeks
Elimination only through the lungs

items.q: Why is daptomycin not used to treat pneumonia?
items.x: Surfactant binds and inactivates daptomycin in the alveoli, so it fails in pneumonia despite good activity against S. aureus. That activity makes it useful for bacteremia and skin infections.
items.a: It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
w: It does not cover Staphylococcus aureus
It causes bronchospasm when given IV
It is only available as an oral tablet

items.q: A patient will receive linezolid for several weeks. Which lab should be monitored regularly?
items.x: Linezolid can cause myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, with longer courses, so the CBC is monitored. It does not need renal adjustment and is not typically nephrotoxic.
items.a: Complete blood count for thrombocytopenia
w: Serum creatinine for nephrotoxicity
Thyroid function for hypothyroidism
Serum uric acid for gout

items.q: A patient on lisinopril and spironolactone is started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which risk is most important?
items.x: Trimethoprim blocks sodium channels in the collecting duct like amiloride, reducing potassium excretion; with an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, hyperkalemia can be severe. TMP-SMX can cause hypoglycemia, but hyperkalemia is the key danger here.
items.a: Hyperkalemia from trimethoprim's amiloride-like effect
w: Hypokalemia from increased potassium excretion
Hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Hypercalcemia from increased bone resorption

items.q: Which toxicities are most important to monitor with gentamicin?
items.x: Aminoglycosides damage the proximal tubule and the inner ear, so kidney function and drug levels are followed and hearing or balance changes are reported. Liver toxicity is not a main concern.
items.a: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
w: Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis
Cardiotoxicity and QT prolongation
Myelosuppression and hemolysis

items.q: An older patient taking prednisone is prescribed levofloxacin. Which adverse effect is of particular concern?
items.x: Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, and the risk is higher in older adults and with corticosteroids. Patients should report heel or tendon pain.
items.a: Tendinitis and tendon rupture
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Gingival overgrowth

items.q: A patient receiving high-dose IV acyclovir for HSV encephalitis develops a rising creatinine. What is the likely mechanism?
items.x: IV acyclovir can crystallize in renal tubules, especially with dehydration, so adequate hydration and renal monitoring are important. Glomerulonephritis is not the typical mechanism.
items.a: Crystal nephropathy from drug precipitating in the tubules
w: Immune-mediated glomerulonephritis
Prerenal injury from vasoconstriction
Rhabdomyolysis from muscle toxicity

items.q: A patient on metformin is admitted with sepsis and acute kidney injury. Which complication is the main concern?
items.x: Metformin is renally cleared, and AKI plus hypoperfusion increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia because it does not stimulate insulin secretion.
items.a: Lactic acidosis from metformin accumulation
w: Hypoglycemia from increased insulin secretion
Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin deficiency
Hyperkalemia from aldosterone blockade

items.q: A patient on empagliflozin is admitted after surgery with nausea, an anion gap acidosis, and a glucose only mildly elevated. What should be recognized?
items.x: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, particularly around surgery, illness, or reduced intake. Hyperosmolar state involves very high glucose without significant ketoacidosis.
items.a: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
w: Lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Starvation ketosis without acidosis

items.q: Compared with glipizide, why is glyburide riskier in a patient with chronic kidney disease?
items.x: Glyburide has long-acting active metabolites that accumulate in CKD and cause prolonged hypoglycemia. Glipizide's metabolites are inactive, making it the safer sulfonylurea in CKD.
items.a: Its active metabolites are renally cleared, prolonging hypoglycemia
w: It does not stimulate insulin release
It causes more weight loss than glipizide
It is cleared only by the kidneys unchanged

items.q: A hospitalized patient with type 2 diabetes has persistently high glucose and is eating. Which regimen is preferred?
items.x: Inpatient guidelines favor scheduled basal insulin, plus prandial and correction doses when eating, over sliding scale alone, which reacts to highs and lows rather than preventing them.
items.a: Scheduled basal insulin with prandial and correction insulin
w: Correction-only sliding scale insulin
Starting a new sulfonylurea
Oral metformin despite kidney injury

items.q: Before starting an IV insulin infusion for diabetic ketoacidosis, which lab must be checked?
items.x: Insulin drives potassium into cells, and DKA patients often have total body potassium depletion; if potassium is low, it must be replaced first to avoid dangerous hypokalemia. Magnesium matters but is not the key gating lab.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum magnesium
Serum lipase
Serum calcium

items.q: A patient's medication list includes levothyroxine and calcium carbonate, taken together each morning. Which counseling point applies?
items.x: Calcium, iron, and some binders reduce levothyroxine absorption, so doses are spaced apart and levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. Food reduces, rather than improves, absorption.
items.a: Separate the doses because calcium reduces levothyroxine absorption
w: Take them together because calcium improves absorption
Take levothyroxine only with a high-fat meal
Take calcium before bed with levothyroxine

items.q: A patient on long-term prednisone is admitted with vomiting, confusion, and hypotension that does not respond to fluids. What should be recognized?
items.x: Long-term glucocorticoids suppress the HPA axis, and illness, vomiting, or missed doses can cause adrenal crisis. It is treated with stress-dose IV hydrocortisone and fluids.
items.a: Adrenal crisis from a suppressed HPA axis
w: Primary hyperaldosteronism
Thyroid storm
Pheochromocytoma crisis

items.q: In thyroid storm, why is propylthiouracil often preferred over methimazole?
items.x: Both drugs block thyroid hormone synthesis, but PTU also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3. PTU carries a boxed warning for severe liver injury, so it is not safer for the liver.
items.a: It also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
w: It is safer for the liver than methimazole
It works by destroying thyroid tissue
It has a much longer duration of action

items.q: A patient on methimazole presents with fever and a sore throat. Which lab is most urgent?
items.x: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, and fever or sore throat may be the first sign, so neutrophil counts are checked right away. The TSH does not identify this emergency.
items.a: Complete blood count with differential
w: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum calcium
Hemoglobin A1c

items.q: A patient on weekly semaglutide is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. What should be considered?
items.x: GLP-1 receptor agonists have been associated with acute pancreatitis, which presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back. The finding should be reported to the provider and a lipase checked; DKA would not be caused by insulin excess.
items.a: Acute pancreatitis
w: Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin excess
Hypoglycemic seizure
Thyroid storm

items.q: Which adverse effect should be considered before giving IV ondansetron to a patient already on several QT-prolonging drugs?
items.x: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval in a dose-related way, and the risk adds up with other QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte problems. Tardive dyskinesia is a concern with metoclopramide.
items.a: QT prolongation
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Hemorrhagic cystitis
Agranulocytosis

items.q: A patient with Parkinson disease has postoperative nausea. Why is metoclopramide a poor choice?
items.x: Metoclopramide blocks central D2 receptors and can worsen parkinsonism or cause other extrapyramidal effects, including tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use. It promotes, rather than slows, GI motility.
items.a: Its dopamine blockade can worsen parkinsonism
w: It causes severe constipation
It strongly prolongs the QT interval more than any antiemetic
It blocks serotonin receptors in the gut

items.q: Which ICU patient has an established indication for stress ulcer prophylaxis?
items.x: Prolonged mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy are major risk factors for stress-related GI bleeding. Routine prophylaxis in low-risk ward patients increases risks such as C. difficile without clear benefit.
items.a: A mechanically ventilated patient with coagulopathy
w: A ward patient with community-acquired pneumonia
A stable patient admitted for cellulitis
A postoperative patient eating a regular diet

items.q: How does IV pantoprazole reduce acid secretion in upper GI bleeding?
items.x: Proton pump inhibitors bind the H+/K+ ATPase covalently, raising gastric pH and helping clot stability. H2 receptor blockade describes famotidine.
items.a: It irreversibly inhibits the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase
w: It blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
It coats the ulcer base with a protective barrier
It neutralizes acid already in the stomach

items.q: A patient with cirrhosis is on lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. What is the usual titration target?
items.x: Lactulose is titrated to two to three soft stools daily to reduce ammonia absorption. Excessive diarrhea can cause dehydration and electrolyte problems that worsen encephalopathy.
items.a: Two to three soft stools per day
w: One formed stool every other day
Six or more watery stools per day
No stool output until confusion resolves

items.q: In which situation is loperamide inappropriate for diarrhea?
items.x: Slowing gut motility in C. difficile or invasive infection can trap toxins and organisms, raising the risk of toxic megacolon. Uncomplicated noninfectious or mild traveler's diarrhea is an appropriate use.
items.a: Suspected C. difficile infection or bloody invasive diarrhea
w: Chronic diarrhea after a confirmed negative workup
Traveler's diarrhea without fever or blood
Diarrhea from irritable bowel syndrome

items.q: Which serious risk is associated with IV promethazine?
items.x: Promethazine carries a boxed warning for severe tissue injury, including gangrene, with perivascular extravasation or intra-arterial injection. Deep IM injection is the preferred parenteral route.
items.a: Severe tissue injury and gangrene if it extravasates
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Severe hypercalcemia

items.q: A patient takes sucralfate and is prescribed oral levofloxacin. What is the concern?
items.x: Sucralfate contains aluminum, which binds fluoroquinolones in the gut and lowers their absorption, so doses are separated. It does not raise fluoroquinolone levels.
items.a: Sucralfate reduces levofloxacin absorption
w: Sucralfate raises levofloxacin to toxic levels
Levofloxacin dissolves the sucralfate coating
The two drugs cause severe hyperkalemia

items.q: An older patient with chronic kidney disease on IV famotidine becomes confused. What should be considered?
items.x: Famotidine is renally cleared, and accumulation in CKD or older age can cause confusion and delirium. It does not cause hepatic encephalopathy.
items.a: CNS effects from famotidine accumulation
w: Hepatic encephalopathy from famotidine
Famotidine-induced hypoglycemia
Serotonin syndrome from famotidine

items.q: Misoprostol is prescribed to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers in a patient of reproductive potential. Which counseling point is essential?
items.x: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog that can cause uterine contractions and pregnancy loss, so it is contraindicated in pregnancy for ulcer prevention. Its common GI side effect is diarrhea, not constipation.
items.a: It can cause miscarriage, so pregnancy must be avoided
w: It causes severe constipation in most patients
It increases the risk of tendon rupture
It must be taken with antacids to work

items.q: A patient with preeclampsia is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding is typically the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity?
items.x: Reflexes fade before respiratory depression and cardiac effects, so reflexes, breathing, and urine output are checked regularly. Seizures are what magnesium prevents, not a sign of toxicity.
items.a: Loss of deep tendon reflexes
w: Respiratory arrest
Cardiac arrest
Seizure activity

items.q: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia develops respiratory depression. Which agent is used to counteract magnesium?
items.x: Calcium antagonizes the neuromuscular and cardiac effects of magnesium. Naloxone reverses opioids and has no effect on magnesium toxicity.
items.a: IV calcium gluconate
w: IV naloxone
IV flumazenil
IV sodium bicarbonate

items.q: For postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony, methylergonovine is contraindicated in which patient?
items.x: Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction and can trigger severe hypertension, stroke, or seizures in hypertensive patients. Asthma is the main contraindication for carboprost, not methylergonovine.
items.a: A patient with preeclampsia or hypertension
w: A patient with asthma
A patient with group B strep colonization
A patient with gestational diabetes

items.q: For postpartum hemorrhage, carboprost should be avoided in which patient?
items.x: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog that can cause bronchospasm, so asthma is a key contraindication. Hypertension is the main contraindication for methylergonovine.
items.a: A patient with asthma
w: A patient with chronic hypertension
A patient with gestational diabetes
A patient with hypothyroidism

items.q: Which IV medication is a first-line option for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy?
items.x: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, and oral immediate-release nifedipine are first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat are contraindicated because of fetal harm.
items.a: Labetalol
w: Nitroprusside
Enalaprilat
Esmolol

items.q: Betamethasone is given to a patient at risk of preterm delivery. What is the main purpose?
items.x: Antenatal corticosteroids speed fetal lung development and reduce respiratory distress and other neonatal complications. They are not tocolytics.
items.a: Accelerate fetal lung maturity
w: Stop uterine contractions
Prevent maternal seizures
Prevent neonatal group B strep infection

items.q: An RhD-negative patient delivers an RhD-positive infant. What is the purpose of Rho(D) immune globulin?
items.x: Rho(D) immune globulin clears fetal RhD-positive cells from the mother's blood before she makes anti-D antibodies, protecting future pregnancies. It is given to the mother, not used to treat the newborn.
items.a: Prevent maternal alloimmunization against fetal RhD
w: Treat hemolytic disease in the newborn
Prevent postpartum hemorrhage
Boost the newborn's immune response

items.q: Which adverse effect can occur with prolonged high-dose oxytocin infusion with large volumes of IV fluid?
items.x: Oxytocin is structurally similar to vasopressin and can cause water retention and hyponatremia, which may lead to seizures. Uterine tachysystole is another key risk to monitor.
items.a: Hyponatremia from its antidiuretic effect
w: Hypernatremia from sodium retention
Hyperkalemia from cell lysis
Hypercalcemia from bone resorption

items.q: Tranexamic acid is given early in postpartum hemorrhage. How does it work?
items.x: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that blocks plasminogen's conversion to plasmin, stabilizing clots. It does not contract the uterus, so uterotonics are still needed.
items.a: It blocks plasminogen activation to reduce fibrinolysis
w: It increases uterine muscle contraction
It replaces fibrinogen and clotting factors
It activates platelets directly

items.q: Why is IV penicillin G given during labor to a patient colonized with group B streptococcus?
items.x: Intrapartum penicillin reduces transmission of GBS to the newborn and prevents early-onset sepsis. It is not given to treat or prevent maternal infection.
items.a: Prevent early-onset GBS infection in the newborn
w: Treat maternal urinary tract infection
Prevent postpartum endometritis only
Speed cervical ripening

items.q: A transplant patient on cyclosporine is started on rifampin. What is the main concern?
items.x: Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, lowering cyclosporine levels and raising the risk of rejection. Levels are monitored closely and adjusted.
items.a: Lower cyclosporine levels and risk of rejection
w: Higher cyclosporine levels and nephrotoxicity
Severe hyperkalemia from the combination
No interaction because they use different pathways

items.q: A transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on fluconazole. Which effect should the team anticipate?
items.x: Azole antifungals inhibit CYP3A4, raising tacrolimus levels and the risk of kidney injury, tremor, hyperkalemia, and hyperglycemia. Rejection would be the concern with an inducer, not an inhibitor.
items.a: Higher tacrolimus levels with nephrotoxicity and tremor
w: Lower tacrolimus levels with rejection
No change in tacrolimus levels
Lower fluconazole levels with fungal relapse

items.q: A patient on weekly low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is given trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. What is the main risk?
items.x: Trimethoprim also inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and sulfamethoxazole reduces methotrexate clearance, so marrow toxicity can be severe. This combination is generally avoided.
items.a: Pancytopenia from additive antifolate effects
w: Loss of methotrexate efficacy
Severe hypoglycemia
Acute hepatic failure within hours

items.q: Before starting azathioprine, which testing helps identify patients at high risk of severe myelosuppression?
items.x: Low TPMT or NUDT15 activity causes thiopurine metabolites to build up and can cause life-threatening marrow suppression. HLA-B*58:01 relates to allopurinol hypersensitivity.
items.a: TPMT and NUDT15 activity or genotype
w: HLA-B*58:01 genotype
G6PD activity
CYP2C19 genotype

items.q: Before starting infliximab, which screening is required?
items.x: TNF inhibitors raise the risk of reactivating latent TB, so screening is required and latent TB is treated before or during therapy. Hepatitis B screening is also recommended.
items.a: Testing for latent tuberculosis
w: Testing for HLA-B*15:02
Baseline pulmonary function tests
Baseline bone density scan

items.q: Before rituximab is given, which screening is required because of a boxed warning?
items.x: Rituximab can reactivate hepatitis B, causing fulminant hepatitis, so HBsAg and anti-HBc are checked before treatment. The other tests are not tied to a boxed warning.
items.a: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
w: Thyroid function tests
Hemoglobin A1c
Urine drug screen

items.q: Which counseling point is essential for a patient of reproductive potential starting mycophenolate?
items.x: Mycophenolate carries a boxed warning for embryofetal toxicity, including miscarriage and congenital malformations. Pregnancy testing and contraception are required.
items.a: It causes birth defects and pregnancy loss, so reliable contraception is required
w: It causes hyperthyroidism, so thyroid tests are needed monthly
It causes tendon rupture, so exercise must be limited
It causes photosensitivity only, so sunscreen is enough

items.q: Why is diphenhydramine a poor choice as a hospital sleep aid for an older adult?
items.x: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and is on the Beers list because it causes confusion, constipation, and urinary retention in older adults. It does cause drowsiness, which is why it is often misused for sleep.
items.a: Its anticholinergic effects contribute to delirium and urinary retention
w: It causes severe hypertension in older adults
It is ineffective at causing drowsiness
It causes hyperkalemia in older adults

items.q: A patient on pembrolizumab develops several days of watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. What should be recognized?
items.x: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related adverse events, and colitis is a common one that may need corticosteroids. It should be reported promptly rather than treated as routine diarrhea.
items.a: Immune-mediated colitis
w: Expected tumor response
Lactose intolerance unrelated to therapy
Neutropenic fever

items.q: Which monitoring is recommended for a patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine?
items.x: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinopathy, so screening exams are done at baseline and periodically. It can also prolong the QT interval.
items.a: Baseline and periodic eye exams for retinal toxicity
w: Monthly liver biopsies
Periodic bone marrow biopsies
Annual pulmonary function tests only

items.q: Which toxicity is most important to prevent and monitor with cisplatin?
items.x: Cisplatin damages renal tubules, so aggressive hydration and monitoring of creatinine and magnesium are standard. Hemorrhagic cystitis is linked to cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide.
items.a: Nephrotoxicity with magnesium wasting
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary fibrosis

items.q: Before doxorubicin is started, which baseline study is most important?
items.x: Doxorubicin causes cumulative, dose-related cardiomyopathy, so ejection fraction is checked at baseline and during treatment. Pulmonary function testing is used for bleomycin.
items.a: Assessment of left ventricular ejection fraction
w: Pulmonary function testing
Audiometry
Bone density scan

items.q: Which toxicity of high-dose cyclophosphamide is reduced by giving mesna and hydration?
items.x: The metabolite acrolein irritates the bladder lining; mesna binds it in the urine. Neuropathy and ototoxicity are not prevented by mesna.
items.a: Hemorrhagic cystitis
w: Peripheral neuropathy
Cardiomyopathy
Ototoxicity

items.q: How must vincristine be given?
items.x: Vincristine given intrathecally causes fatal ascending neurotoxicity, so it carries strict labeling and is often prepared in minibags. Its common dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral neuropathy.
items.a: Intravenously only, because intrathecal use is fatal
w: Intrathecally only, to reach the CSF
Intramuscularly into a large muscle
Subcutaneously into the abdomen

items.q: Which toxicity is most characteristic of bleomycin?
items.x: Bleomycin causes pneumonitis and fibrosis, so pulmonary function and new cough or dyspnea are watched closely. Unlike most chemotherapies, it causes little myelosuppression.
items.a: Pulmonary toxicity that can progress to fibrosis
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Cumulative cardiomyopathy
Severe myelosuppression

items.q: Shortly after starting capecitabine, a patient develops severe mucositis, diarrhea, and neutropenia. Which enzyme deficiency should be suspected?
items.x: DPD breaks down fluorouracil, the active form of capecitabine, so deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal toxicity. TPMT deficiency affects thiopurines, not fluoropyrimidines.
items.a: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase
w: Thiopurine methyltransferase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Pseudocholinesterase

items.q: A patient taking tamoxifen is admitted with leg swelling. Which serious adverse effect should be considered?
items.x: Tamoxifen has estrogen-like effects on clotting and raises the risk of DVT and PE, along with endometrial cancer. Leg swelling in this setting warrants evaluation for DVT.
items.a: Venous thromboembolism
w: Hemorrhagic cystitis
Pulmonary fibrosis
Peripheral neuropathy

items.q: What is the purpose of leucovorin after high-dose methotrexate?
items.x: Leucovorin is a reduced folate that does not need DHFR, so it restores folate-dependent processes in healthy cells. It does not remove methotrexate; glucarpidase breaks down methotrexate in delayed clearance.
items.a: It bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to rescue normal cells
w: It speeds renal excretion of methotrexate
It neutralizes methotrexate in the blood
It prevents methotrexate-induced nausea

items.q: Which factor most increases the risk of toxicity from high-dose methotrexate?
items.x: Methotrexate is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so impaired renal function causes delayed clearance and severe marrow, mucosal, and kidney toxicity. Alkalinization, hydration, and level monitoring are used to protect clearance.
items.a: Reduced kidney function
w: Mildly elevated blood glucose
A history of hypothyroidism
Well-controlled hypertension

items.q: During an irinotecan infusion, a patient develops cramping, diarrhea, sweating, and salivation. Which treatment is appropriate?
