items.x: Irinotecan inhibits acetylcholinesterase and can cause early cholinergic symptoms that respond to atropine. Loperamide is used for the separate delayed diarrhea that starts later.
items.a: Atropine for the acute cholinergic syndrome
w: Loperamide for delayed diarrhea
Ondansetron for nausea
Diphenhydramine for allergy

items.q: An older patient is admitted with symptomatic bradycardia. Which home eye drop could be contributing?
items.x: Ophthalmic timolol is absorbed systemically and can cause bradycardia, heart block, and bronchospasm. Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost do not cause beta-blocker effects.
items.a: Timolol ophthalmic solution
w: Latanoprost ophthalmic solution
Artificial tear drops
Ketotifen ophthalmic solution

items.q: A patient on acetazolamide for glaucoma has an abnormal chemistry panel. Which acid-base change is expected?
items.x: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate loss and a hyperchloremic acidosis, along with hypokalemia. It does not add unmeasured anions.
items.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
w: Metabolic alkalosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis

items.q: A burn patient treated with silver sulfadiazine cream has a low white blood cell count a few days later. What should be recognized?
items.x: Silver sulfadiazine is associated with a transient drop in white cells that often recovers. It should be recognized and monitored rather than assumed to be lab error.
items.a: Transient leukopenia associated with silver sulfadiazine
w: Expected sign of burn wound sepsis only
Allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
Lab error caused by the cream

items.q: Before certain surgeries, nasal mupirocin may be applied. What is its purpose?
items.x: Intranasal mupirocin reduces S. aureus carriage, including MRSA, which lowers surgical site and other infection risk. It is not a treatment for sinusitis.
items.a: Decolonize the nose of Staphylococcus aureus to reduce infection
w: Treat bacterial sinusitis
Relieve nasal congestion
Prevent viral upper respiratory infections

items.q: Scabies is diagnosed in a hospitalized adult. Which teaching about permethrin cream is correct?
items.x: Permethrin is applied to all skin from the neck down, left on for the recommended time, and close contacts are treated at the same time. Treating only itchy spots misses mites elsewhere.
items.a: Apply to the whole body from the neck down and treat close contacts
w: Apply only to itchy areas and wash off after a minute
Apply to the face and scalp only
Take it by mouth with food

items.q: Why is a topical lidocaine patch useful for localized pain in an older inpatient?
items.x: Lidocaine patches act locally on peripheral nerves with little systemic absorption, avoiding sedation and kidney effects. They should be applied to intact skin, not open wounds.
items.a: It gives local pain relief with minimal systemic absorption
w: It provides strong systemic opioid-like effects
It reduces inflammation like an oral NSAID
It is safe to apply to broken or open skin

items.q: Which areas should generally be avoided when applying clobetasol, a superpotent topical steroid?
items.x: Thin skin absorbs more steroid and is prone to atrophy and striae, so superpotent steroids are generally avoided on the face and skin folds. Thick-skinned areas like palms and soles often need stronger steroids.
items.a: The face, groin, and armpits
w: The palms and soles
The elbows and knees
The scalp

items.q: What is the most important safety requirement for a patient of reproductive potential prescribed isotretinoin?
items.x: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen and is available only through the iPLEDGE program with pregnancy testing and contraception. The other measures are not required.
items.a: Pregnancy prevention under a restricted program
w: Annual chest radiography
Weekly kidney function testing
Avoiding all dairy products

items.q: Why is proparacaine eye drop not given to patients for home use?
items.x: Topical ocular anesthetics delay healing and can cause corneal ulceration with repeated use, while removing pain that signals worsening injury. They are used only for brief exams and procedures.
items.a: Repeated use damages the corneal epithelium and masks injury
w: It causes systemic hypertension
It is ineffective after a single dose
It permanently dilates the pupil

items.q: Which skin finding in an obese inpatient is best treated with topical nystatin?
items.x: Bright red rash in skin folds with satellite lesions suggests Candida, which nystatin treats. Honey-crusted lesions suggest impetigo, which needs an antibacterial.
items.a: Beefy red intertrigo with satellite pustules in skin folds
w: Honey-crusted lesions on the face
Silvery plaques on the elbows
Painful vesicles in a band on one side

items.q: A resident taking lisinopril reports a persistent dry, hacking cough. How should the LVN interpret this?
items.x: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril commonly cause a dry cough from bradykinin buildup, and it should be reported so the provider can decide on therapy. It is not a sign of the drug working or of low potassium.
items.a: A common ACE inhibitor side effect to report to the provider
w: An expected sign of the drug working that needs no follow-up
An early sign of digoxin toxicity to report to the provider
A symptom of low potassium that needs a dietary change

items.q: Before giving oral metoprolol to a resident, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Metoprolol is a beta blocker that slows heart rate and lowers blood pressure, so both are checked before each dose. Potassium and urine output matter more for diuretics.
items.a: Apical pulse and blood pressure
w: Blood glucose and temperature
Serum potassium and urine output
Pain level and bowel sounds

items.q: Which lab value does the LVN check to monitor the effect of warfarin?
items.x: Warfarin is monitored with the PT/INR. The aPTT is the test used for unfractionated heparin, which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.
items.a: International normalized ratio (INR)
w: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Platelet count
Serum potassium

items.q: Which electrolyte imbalance is the most common concern with furosemide?
items.x: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that causes loss of potassium in the urine, so low potassium is the classic concern. High potassium is a concern with potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, not loop diuretics.
items.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia

items.q: A patient taking atorvastatin reports new, unexplained muscle pain and weakness. What is the best action by the LVN?
items.x: Statins can cause myopathy and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis, so unexplained muscle pain or weakness must be reported. It should not be dismissed as harmless.
items.a: Report the symptoms promptly to the RN or provider
w: Reassure the patient that this is expected and harmless
Apply a heating pad and recheck the next week
Suggest taking an extra dose at bedtime instead

items.q: A patient with angina uses sublingual nitroglycerin. Which other medicine can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure if taken with it?
items.x: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil greatly increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitrates and the combination is contraindicated. Atorvastatin is often taken by the same patients but does not cause this interaction.
items.a: Sildenafil
w: Atorvastatin
Acetaminophen
Metformin

items.q: Which teaching is most important for a patient taking spironolactone?
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing and can cause hyperkalemia, so potassium-based salt substitutes and extra potassium should be avoided. Encouraging high-potassium foods is teaching for loop or thiazide diuretics.
items.a: Avoid salt substitutes that contain potassium
w: Eat extra bananas and oranges every day
Take a potassium supplement with each dose
Limit fluids to prevent low sodium

items.q: Apixaban belongs to which drug class?
items.x: Apixaban directly blocks factor Xa. Dabigatran is the oral direct thrombin inhibitor, and warfarin is the vitamin K antagonist.
items.a: Direct factor Xa inhibitor
w: Vitamin K antagonist

items.q: Which side effect is very common with everolimus?
items.x: Stomatitis is one of the most common everolimus side effects, and alcohol-free mouth care is encouraged. Hearing loss and blue-tinted vision are not typical.
items.a: Mouth sores and ulcers
w: Excess salivation
Hearing loss
Blue-tinted vision

items.q: Which side effect is common with erlotinib?
items.x: EGFR inhibitors such as erlotinib commonly cause an acneiform rash, along with diarrhea. The other effects are not typical of this drug.
items.a: An acne-like rash on the face and chest
w: Hair darkening
Weight gain from fluid retention
Very slow heart rate

items.q: Which history should be reported before a patient starts enzalutamide?
items.x: Enzalutamide can lower the seizure threshold, so a seizure history or seizure risk factors must be reported. Allergies and arthritis do not affect its use.
items.a: A history of seizures
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
Lactose intolerance

items.q: Which effect should a patient be taught to expect with latanoprost eye drops?
items.x: Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost can increase brown pigment in the iris and lengthen and darken eyelashes. Constricted pupils with poor night vision are typical of pilocarpine.
items.a: Gradual, possibly permanent darkening of the iris
w: Constricted pupils and dim vision at night
Bright orange discoloration of tears
Rapid loss of eyelashes

items.q: Which history should be reported before a patient starts timolol eye drops?
items.x: Timolol is a nonselective beta blocker that can be absorbed into the bloodstream and trigger bronchospasm or slow the heart. It is contraindicated in asthma and severe COPD.
items.a: Asthma or severe COPD
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Mild osteoarthritis
Recent sunburn

items.q: How is permethrin cream applied to an adult for scabies?
items.x: For scabies, permethrin is massaged into all skin from the neck down and washed off after the labeled time. Short scalp application with rinsing is how it is used for head lice.
items.a: Over the whole body from the neck to the soles of the feet
w: Only on the visible bumps and burrows
On the scalp only, then rinsed off quickly
Only on the hands and wrists

items.q: Which history is a contraindication to silver sulfadiazine cream?
items.x: Silver sulfadiazine is a sulfonamide, so sulfa allergy is a concern. Penicillin allergy is not a cross-reaction with sulfonamides.
items.a: A known allergy to sulfa drugs
w: A known allergy to penicillin
A history of type 2 diabetes
A history of seasonal allergies

items.q: Which effect of isotretinoin should be reported promptly?
items.x: Isotretinoin has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts, which require prompt reporting. Dry lips and skin are very common and expected.
items.a: Depressed mood or thoughts of self-harm
w: Dry, chapped lips
Mild dry skin
Mild nosebleeds in dry weather

items.q: Which teaching is correct for a patient using topical tretinoin?
items.x: Topical tretinoin increases sun sensitivity, so sunscreen and sun protection are important. Applying it to wet skin or using thick layers increases irritation.
items.a: Use sunscreen daily since the skin burns more easily
w: Apply it to wet skin right after washing
Use it with a tanning bed for faster results
Apply a thick layer several times a day

items.q: Which teaching is correct for clobetasol cream?
items.x: Clobetasol is a super-high-potency steroid that can thin skin, so it is avoided on the face, groin, and underarms and used for limited periods. It is not used as a moisturizer.
items.a: Avoid applying it to the face, groin, or underarms
w: Apply it thickly under a tight bandage daily
Use it long term as an everyday moisturizer
Apply it to the eyelids for eczema

items.q: Which effect should a patient using pilocarpine eye drops expect?
items.x: Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, which reduces vision in dim light. Dilated pupils are the opposite of its effect.
items.a: Trouble seeing in dim light, such as night driving
w: Darkening of the iris color
Dilated pupils and sensitivity to light
Yellow discoloration of the skin

items.q: How is lidocaine-prilocaine cream applied before a needle procedure?
items.x: The cream needs time under an occlusive dressing to numb the skin. Rubbing it in just before the needle stick does not allow enough time for it to work.
items.a: As a thick layer under an occlusive dressing, ahead of time
w: Rubbed in thoroughly right before the needle stick
Applied only after the procedure for pain
Swabbed on and rinsed off right away

items.q: Mupirocin ointment is used to treat which condition?
items.x: Mupirocin is a topical antibacterial used for impetigo. Fungal infections such as ringworm need an antifungal.
items.a: Impetigo caused by staph or strep bacteria
w: Ringworm and other fungal skin infections
Cold sores caused by herpes virus
Scabies infestation

items.q: What is the primary mechanism by which digoxin increases myocardial contractility?
items.x: Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, which raises intracellular sodium, slows the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and leaves more calcium for contraction. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition is how milrinone works, not digoxin.
items.a: Inhibition of the Na+/K+ ATPase, raising intracellular calcium
w: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in myocytes
Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-3 in cardiac muscle

items.q: A patient taking digoxin for atrial fibrillation is started on a loop diuretic. Which electrolyte change most increases the risk of digoxin toxicity?
items.x: Digoxin competes with potassium at the Na+/K+ ATPase, so low potassium enhances its binding and toxicity. Hyperkalemia can be a result of acute digoxin overdose, but it does not predispose to toxicity.
items.a: Hypokalemia
w: Hyperkalemia
Hypernatremia
Hypophosphatemia

items.q: Which group of tests is classically monitored during long-term amiodarone therapy because of its organ toxicities?
items.x: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and lipophilic, causing hypo- or hyperthyroidism, hepatotoxicity, and pulmonary fibrosis. Creatine kinase monitoring is associated with statins, not amiodarone.
items.a: Thyroid function, liver enzymes, and pulmonary function
w: Serum uric acid, amylase, and lipase
Creatine kinase, audiometry, and serum calcium
Complete blood count, ferritin, and vitamin B12

items.q: Atorvastatin lowers LDL cholesterol primarily by which mechanism?
items.x: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors. Blocking NPC1L1 is the mechanism of ezetimibe.
items.a: Inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase in the liver
w: Blocking intestinal NPC1L1 cholesterol transporters
Activating PPAR-alpha to increase lipoprotein lipase
Binding PCSK9 to prevent LDL receptor degradation

items.q: A patient develops a persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril. What is the mechanism of this adverse effect?
items.x: ACE also degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin levels, causing cough and contributing to angioedema. AT1 receptor blockade is how ARBs work, and ARBs rarely cause cough.
items.a: Accumulation of bradykinin due to reduced breakdown by ACE
w: Direct blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor
Histamine release from airway mast cells
Beta-2 receptor blockade causing bronchoconstriction

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of ezetimibe?
items.x: Ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 on the intestinal brush border, decreasing cholesterol absorption. Binding bile acids describes bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine.
items.a: Blocks the NPC1L1 transporter, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption
w: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis
Binds bile acids in the gut, interrupting enterohepatic circulation
Inhibits hepatic VLDL secretion by reducing lipolysis in fat tissue

items.q: Which adverse effect is classically associated with verapamil?
items.x: Verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, commonly causes constipation by relaxing intestinal smooth muscle. Dry cough is associated with ACE inhibitors.
items.a: Constipation
w: Dry cough
Hirsutism
Hypoglycemia

items.q: Why is nitroglycerin contraindicated in a patient who recently took sildenafil?
items.x: Nitrates increase cGMP production through nitric oxide, and PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown, so together they cause profound vasodilation and hypotension. The interaction is pharmacodynamic, not a CYP3A4 effect.
items.a: Both raise cGMP, risking severe hypotension
w: Sildenafil blocks the conversion of nitroglycerin to nitric oxide
Both prolong the QT interval, risking torsades de pointes
Sildenafil inhibits CYP3A4, causing nitroglycerin to accumulate

items.q: Hydralazine shares which classic adverse effect with procainamide and isoniazid?
items.x: Hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid are classic causes of drug-induced lupus, especially in slow acetylators, often with anti-histone antibodies. Angioedema is linked to ACE inhibitors instead.
items.a: Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome
w: Angioedema
Gingival hyperplasia
Ototoxicity

items.q: A patient starting niacin for dyslipidemia reports facial flushing and warmth. What explains this, and what can reduce it?
items.x: Niacin-induced flushing is mediated by prostaglandins, so pretreatment with aspirin reduces it. It is not primarily histamine-mediated, so antihistamines are not the classic answer.
items.a: Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation, reduced by taking aspirin beforehand
w: Histamine release from mast cells, reduced by taking an antihistamine
Serotonin release from platelets, reduced by taking ondansetron
Bradykinin accumulation in skin, reduced by taking an ARB

items.q: Which receptor profile best describes norepinephrine?
items.x: Norepinephrine potently stimulates alpha-1 (vasoconstriction) and beta-1 (inotropy) receptors but has minimal beta-2 effect. A selective alpha-1 agonist describes phenylephrine.
items.a: Strong alpha-1 and beta-1 agonist with little beta-2 activity
w: Strong beta-1 and beta-2 agonist with little alpha activity
Selective alpha-1 agonist with no beta activity
Selective beta-1 agonist with no alpha activity

items.q: Norepinephrine extravasates from a peripheral IV, causing local blanching and ischemia. Which agent is classically infiltrated into the area?
items.x: Phentolamine is a nonselective alpha antagonist that reverses local vasoconstriction from vasopressor extravasation. Hyaluronidase is used for some other extravasations but does not counter alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.
items.a: Phentolamine
w: Hyaluronidase
Atropine
Dexrazoxane

items.q: IV phenylephrine raises blood pressure in a hypotensive patient. What change in heart rate is expected?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist; the rise in blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor-mediated reflex bradycardia. It has no meaningful beta-1 activity to raise heart rate directly.
items.a: Decreased heart rate from a baroreceptor reflex
w: Increased heart rate from direct beta-1 stimulation
Increased heart rate from beta-2 mediated vasodilation
No change because it has no effect on vascular tone

items.q: Dobutamine is used in cardiogenic shock mainly because of which action?
items.x: Dobutamine is predominantly a beta-1 agonist that increases contractility and cardiac output. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition is the mechanism of milrinone.
items.a: Beta-1 agonism that increases myocardial contractility
w: Alpha-1 agonism that strongly raises vascular resistance
V1 receptor agonism that constricts vascular smooth muscle
Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition that increases cAMP

items.q: Besides adrenergic receptors, dopamine stimulates which receptor type in the renal and mesenteric vasculature?
items.x: Dopamine activates D1 receptors in renal and splanchnic vessels, as well as beta-1 and alpha-1 receptors depending on dose. Vasopressin V1 receptors are the target of vasopressin.
items.a: Dopamine D1 receptors
w: Vasopressin V1 receptors
Histamine H2 receptors
Angiotensin AT1 receptors

items.q: In vasodilatory shock, vasopressin raises blood pressure mainly by stimulating which receptor?
items.x: Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through Gq-coupled V1 receptors, independent of adrenergic receptors. V2 receptors in the collecting duct mediate its antidiuretic effect, not its pressor effect.
items.a: V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: V2 receptors on renal collecting duct cells
Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
Beta-1 receptors on cardiac myocytes

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of milrinone?
items.x: Milrinone inhibits PDE3, raising cAMP to increase contractility and cause vasodilation, so it is called an inodilator. Beta-1 stimulation also raises cAMP but is how dobutamine works.
items.a: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3, increasing cAMP in heart and vessels
w: Stimulates beta-1 receptors, increasing cAMP in the heart
Inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, increasing cardiac calcium
Blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing vascular smooth muscle

items.q: For anaphylaxis outside a monitored setting, what is the preferred route of epinephrine?
items.x: IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. IV push epinephrine is reserved for monitored settings because it can cause dangerous arrhythmias and hypertension.
items.a: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Intravenous push through a peripheral line
Inhaled through a nebulizer mask

items.q: Midodrine is used for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Which adverse effect is most characteristic?
items.x: Midodrine's active metabolite is an alpha-1 agonist, so it can raise blood pressure excessively when the patient lies down. It tends to cause reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia.
items.a: Supine hypertension
w: Reflex tachycardia
Hypoglycemia
Hypokalemia

items.q: Why does repeated dosing of ephedrine produce a progressively smaller blood pressure response?
items.x: Ephedrine is a mixed-acting sympathomimetic that releases norepinephrine from nerve terminals, so stores deplete and tachyphylaxis develops. It is not metabolized by plasma cholinesterase.
items.a: It acts partly by releasing stored norepinephrine, which becomes depleted
w: It irreversibly downregulates alpha-1 receptors after one exposure
It is rapidly metabolized by plasma cholinesterase after each dose
It induces its own hepatic metabolism through CYP enzymes

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of warfarin?
items.x: Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Enhancing antithrombin is how heparin works.
items.a: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing active factors II, VII, IX, and X
w: Enhances antithrombin activity against thrombin and factor Xa
Directly and reversibly inhibits factor Xa
Irreversibly acetylates platelet cyclooxygenase

items.q: A patient with a stable INR on warfarin starts fluconazole. What effect on the INR is expected?
items.x: S-warfarin is mainly metabolized by CYP2C9, which fluconazole inhibits, so warfarin levels and INR rise. Induction leading to a lower INR is the classic effect of rifampin.
items.a: INR rises because fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9
w: INR falls because fluconazole induces CYP2C9
INR falls because fluconazole binds warfarin in the gut
INR is unchanged because the drugs share no pathway

items.q: Unfractionated heparin produces its anticoagulant effect mainly by which mechanism?
items.x: Heparin works as a cofactor, greatly enhancing antithrombin's inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa; its effect is monitored with the aPTT. Direct thrombin binding without a cofactor describes argatroban or dabigatran.
items.a: Binding antithrombin and accelerating inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa
w: Inhibiting vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of clotting factors
Directly binding the active site of thrombin without a cofactor
Blocking the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor

items.q: Several days into heparin therapy, a patient's platelet count falls by half and a new deep vein thrombosis develops. What is the underlying mechanism?
items.x: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is caused by IgG antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes that activate platelets, causing both thrombocytopenia and thrombosis. Marrow suppression would not explain the new clot.
items.a: IgG antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes activate platelets
w: Heparin directly suppresses megakaryocytes in the bone marrow
Heparin causes vitamin K deficiency, impairing clotting factors
Antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa cause platelet sequestration in the spleen

items.q: Compared with unfractionated heparin, how does enoxaparin differ in mechanism?
items.x: Low-molecular-weight heparins still work through antithrombin, but their shorter chains favor factor Xa inhibition over thrombin. They still require antithrombin, so they are not direct thrombin inhibitors.
items.a: It acts more selectively against factor Xa than thrombin
w: It directly inhibits thrombin without needing antithrombin
It inhibits vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis
It acts more selectively against thrombin than factor Xa

items.q: Which agent specifically reverses the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran?
items.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban.
items.a: Idarucizumab
w: Andexanet alfa
Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione

items.q: Rivaroxaban belongs to which anticoagulant class?
items.x: Rivaroxaban binds and inhibits factor Xa directly without needing antithrombin. Fondaparinux is the classic indirect factor Xa inhibitor because it works through antithrombin.
items.a: Direct factor Xa inhibitor
w: Direct thrombin inhibitor
Vitamin K antagonist
Indirect factor Xa inhibitor

items.q: A patient with reduced-function CYP2C19 alleles takes clopidogrel after a coronary stent. What is the main concern?
items.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 to irreversibly block the P2Y12 receptor; poor metabolizers form less active drug and have higher risk of stent thrombosis. Bleeding from accumulation would occur with a drug inactivated, not activated, by the enzyme.
items.a: Less conversion to the active metabolite, reducing antiplatelet effect
w: Accumulation of the active metabolite, increasing bleeding risk
Faster renal clearance of the drug, shortening its action
Increased conversion to a hepatotoxic metabolite

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of alteplase?
items.x: Alteplase is a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts fibrin-bound plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin. Inhibiting plasminogen activation is the action of antifibrinolytics such as aminocaproic acid.
items.a: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin
w: Inhibits plasminogen activation to stabilize clots
Blocks glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on platelets
Directly inhibits thrombin bound within the clot

items.q: Why does a single dose of aspirin affect platelet function for the life of the platelet?
items.x: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis, and anucleate platelets cannot synthesize new enzyme. Irreversible P2Y12 blockade describes clopidogrel and prasugrel.
items.a: It irreversibly acetylates COX-1, and platelets cannot make new enzyme
w: It reversibly binds COX-2, and platelets clear it slowly
It irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 receptor on platelets
It permanently depletes platelet stores of vitamin K

items.q: Succinylcholine is avoided in a patient several days after a major burn injury because of which risk?
items.x: Burns, crush injuries, and denervation upregulate extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors, so depolarization releases large amounts of potassium. Prolonged paralysis relates to pseudocholinesterase deficiency, not liver metabolism.
items.a: Severe hyperkalemia from upregulated acetylcholine receptors
w: Severe hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Prolonged paralysis from reduced liver metabolism
Severe hypocalcemia from muscle calcium uptake

items.q: A patient remains paralyzed for hours after a standard intubating dose of succinylcholine. Which inherited condition best explains this?
items.x: Succinylcholine is hydrolyzed by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase; atypical or deficient enzyme leads to prolonged apnea. Slow acetylation affects drugs like isoniazid and hydralazine, not succinylcholine.
items.a: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency
w: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Slow N-acetyltransferase activity
Thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency

items.q: How does rocuronium produce neuromuscular blockade?
items.x: Rocuronium is a nondepolarizing agent that competes with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors. Persistent depolarization describes succinylcholine.
items.a: Competitively blocks nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate
w: Persistently depolarizes the motor end plate
Inhibits acetylcholine release from motor nerve terminals
Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

items.q: Sugammadex reverses rocuronium-induced blockade by which mechanism?
items.x: Sugammadex is a modified cyclodextrin that binds and encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium, removing it from the neuromuscular junction. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is how neostigmine reverses blockade.
items.a: Encapsulating rocuronium molecules in the plasma
w: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase at the end plate
Directly stimulating nicotinic receptors
Increasing acetylcholine release from nerve terminals

items.q: Propofol produces sedation and anesthesia mainly by which action?
items.x: Propofol enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing inhibitory chloride currents. NMDA receptor antagonism is the mechanism of ketamine.
items.a: Potentiating GABA-A receptor chloride currents
w: Blocking NMDA glutamate receptors
Stimulating central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors
Activating mu opioid receptors

items.q: Which mechanism is primarily responsible for ketamine's dissociative anesthesia?
items.x: Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors, producing dissociative anesthesia while largely preserving airway reflexes and respiratory drive. GABA-A potentiation is how propofol and benzodiazepines act.
items.a: NMDA receptor antagonism
w: GABA-A receptor potentiation
Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonism
Kappa opioid receptor antagonism

items.q: Which adverse effect of etomidate results from inhibition of 11-beta-hydroxylase?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits adrenal 11-beta-hydroxylase, transiently reducing cortisol synthesis. It is chosen for its hemodynamic stability, so marked hypotension is less typical than with propofol.
items.a: Adrenal suppression with reduced cortisol
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Severe hypotension from vasodilation
Hyperkalemia from potassium release

items.q: How does midazolam modify GABA-A receptor function?
items.x: Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening and need GABA present. Increasing the duration of opening is the classic description of barbiturates.
items.a: Increases the frequency of chloride channel opening
w: Increases the duration of chloride channel opening
Directly opens the channel without GABA present
Blocks GABA reuptake into presynaptic neurons

items.q: During sevoflurane anesthesia, a patient develops rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, and hyperthermia. What is the underlying mechanism?
items.x: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by inherited ryanodine receptor defects that release excess calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when exposed to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine; dantrolene treats it. D2 blockade describes neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
items.a: Uncontrolled calcium release through a defective ryanodine receptor
w: Excess serotonin activity in the central nervous system
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the hypothalamus
Direct thyroid hormone release from the gland

items.q: Why is cisatracurium often chosen for patients with both liver and kidney failure?
items.x: Cisatracurium breaks down spontaneously in plasma by Hofmann elimination, which depends on pH and temperature rather than the liver or kidneys. Pseudocholinesterase hydrolysis describes succinylcholine.
items.a: It undergoes Hofmann elimination independent of organ function
w: It is cleared entirely by the kidneys unchanged
It is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4 to inactive products
It is hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase

items.q: Albuterol relieves acute bronchospasm through which mechanism?
items.x: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 receptors, increasing cAMP and relaxing airway smooth muscle; tremor and tachycardia are common effects. Muscarinic antagonism is the mechanism of ipratropium and tiotropium.
items.a: Beta-2 agonism that raises cAMP and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle
w: Muscarinic antagonism that blocks bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Leukotriene receptor blockade that reduces airway inflammation
Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition that reduces neutrophil activity

items.q: In asthma, how should salmeterol be used according to its labeling?
items.x: Long-acting beta agonist monotherapy in asthma has been linked to asthma-related deaths, so LABAs are used with an inhaled corticosteroid. Its slow onset also makes it unsuitable as a rescue inhaler.
items.a: Only together with an inhaled corticosteroid
w: As the first-line rescue inhaler for acute attacks
As monotherapy for mild intermittent asthma
Only during an acute exacerbation requiring hospitalization

items.q: Tiotropium improves airflow in COPD by which mechanism?
items.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction. Long-acting beta-2 agonism describes salmeterol or formoterol.
items.a: Long-acting antagonism of M3 muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle
w: Long-acting agonism of beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle
Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase in airway inflammatory cells
Stabilization of mast cells to block mediator release

items.q: Which adverse effect is most expected with inhaled ipratropium?
items.x: Ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist, so local anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth are common. Oral candidiasis is associated with inhaled corticosteroids.
items.a: Dry mouth
w: Oral candidiasis
Hypokalemia
Hyperglycemia

items.q: What is the mechanism of action of montelukast?
items.x: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist; its labeling carries a boxed warning about neuropsychiatric events. Inhibiting 5-lipoxygenase is the mechanism of zileuton.
items.a: Blocks the cysteinyl leukotriene CysLT1 receptor
w: Inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, blocking leukotriene synthesis
Binds free IgE, preventing mast cell sensitization
Inhibits phosphodiesterase-4 in inflammatory cells

items.q: Zileuton reduces asthma symptoms by inhibiting which enzyme, and which lab test is monitored during therapy?
items.x: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, blocking leukotriene synthesis, and can cause hepatotoxicity, so liver enzymes are monitored. Phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition is the mechanism of roflumilast.
items.a: 5-lipoxygenase; liver enzymes
w: Cyclooxygenase-2; serum creatinine
Phosphodiesterase-4; blood glucose
Phospholipase A2; complete blood count

items.q: A patient on theophylline is started on ciprofloxacin and develops tremor, tachycardia, and a seizure. What explains this?
items.x: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and is cleared by CYP1A2, which ciprofloxacin inhibits, causing toxicity with arrhythmias and seizures. CYP induction would lower, not raise, theophylline levels.
items.a: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, raising theophylline levels
w: Ciprofloxacin induces CYP1A2, producing a toxic metabolite
Theophylline raises ciprofloxacin levels by blocking renal secretion
Both drugs block adenosine reuptake in the brain

items.q: What should a patient be taught to reduce the risk of oral thrush with inhaled fluticasone?
items.x: Inhaled corticosteroids deposit in the oropharynx and suppress local immunity, so rinsing and spitting reduces candidiasis. Inhaled corticosteroids are controller medicines, not rescue medicines for acute attacks.
items.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each use
w: Use the inhaler only during acute attacks
Take the inhaler with a full meal
Inhale a short-acting beta agonist afterward

items.q: Omalizumab is used in allergic asthma because of which mechanism?
items.x: Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody that lowers free IgE and prevents binding to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. Blocking IL-5 describes mepolizumab, a different biologic.
items.a: Binds free IgE, preventing it from attaching to mast cell receptors
w: Blocks the IL-5 cytokine, reducing eosinophil survival
Blocks the IL-4 receptor alpha subunit on T cells
Inhibits leukotriene synthesis in mast cells

items.q: Roflumilast is used to reduce COPD exacerbations. What is its mechanism?
items.x: Roflumilast selectively inhibits PDE4, raising cAMP in inflammatory cells and reducing lung inflammation. PDE5 inhibition describes sildenafil used for pulmonary hypertension.
items.a: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-4, increasing cAMP in inflammatory cells
w: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, increasing cGMP in pulmonary vessels
Antagonizes M3 muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle
Stimulates beta-2 receptors in airway smooth muscle

items.q: What is the primary mechanism of phenytoin's antiseizure effect?
items.x: Phenytoin stabilizes inactivated sodium channels, limiting high-frequency repetitive firing. T-type calcium channel blockade is the mechanism of ethosuximide.
items.a: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state
w: Blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons
Increases the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening
Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A to reduce release

items.q: A small increase in phenytoin dosing causes a large rise in serum level and toxicity. Which pharmacokinetic property explains this?
items.x: Phenytoin's hepatic metabolism saturates at therapeutic levels, so elimination becomes zero-order and levels rise disproportionately. Autoinduction is the classic property of carbamazepine.
items.a: Saturable metabolism that shifts to zero-order kinetics
w: Very high renal clearance of unchanged drug
Strong induction of its own metabolism over time
Large first-pass effect that varies with meals

items.q: Before starting carbamazepine in patients of Asian ancestry, which genetic test is recommended to reduce the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
items.x: HLA-B*15:02 carriers have a much higher risk of carbamazepine-induced SJS and toxic epidermal necrolysis. HLA-B*57:01 screening is used before abacavir.
w: HLA-B27

items.q: Valproic acid use in early pregnancy is most classically associated with which birth defect?
items.x: Valproate is strongly teratogenic and classically causes neural tube defects. Ebstein anomaly is classically linked to lithium.
items.a: Neural tube defects such as spina bifida
w: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Tooth discoloration and enamel defects
Gray baby syndrome

items.q: Ethosuximide is effective for absence seizures because of which mechanism?
items.x: Absence seizures arise from thalamocortical oscillations driven by T-type calcium currents, which ethosuximide blocks. Irreversible GABA transaminase inhibition is the mechanism of vigabatrin.
items.a: Blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons
w: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in cortical neurons
Irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase
Antagonizes AMPA glutamate receptors

items.q: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly, especially when given with valproate, to reduce the risk of which serious reaction?

Current atorvastatin therapy

items.q: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is recommended first-line?
items.x: Surviving Sepsis guidelines recommend norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor for septic shock. Dopamine causes more tachyarrhythmias and is no longer preferred.
items.a: Norepinephrine
w: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Dobutamine

items.q: A patient receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV develops a cool, pale, blanched area around the insertion site. Which agent is used to treat this extravasation?
items.x: Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that reverses local vasoconstriction from norepinephrine extravasation and limits tissue necrosis. Hyaluronidase is used for some non-vasopressor extravasations, not alpha-agonist injury.
items.a: Phentolamine infiltrated into the affected area
w: Hyaluronidase infiltrated into the affected area
Topical nitroglycerin applied to the hand only
Subcutaneous epinephrine near the site

items.q: Vasopressin is added to norepinephrine in a patient with refractory septic shock. What is its mechanism of raising blood pressure?
items.x: Vasopressin causes vasoconstriction through V1 receptors, independent of adrenergic receptors, which helps lower catecholamine requirements. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition describes milrinone, which tends to lower blood pressure.
items.a: Activation of V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
w: Stimulation of beta-1 receptors on the myocardium
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-3 in vascular tissue
Direct activation of alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem

items.q: A patient develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension minutes after a bee sting. What is the preferred route for the first dose of epinephrine?
items.x: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous dosing and is first-line for anaphylaxis. IV bolus epinephrine is reserved for cardiac arrest or carefully titrated infusions because of arrhythmia risk.
items.a: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Slow intravenous push through a peripheral line
Nebulized inhalation through a face mask

items.q: A patient with an acute anterior MI has cool extremities, low urine output, and low cardiac output with borderline blood pressure. Which agent primarily increases myocardial contractility through beta-1 stimulation?
items.x: Dobutamine is a predominantly beta-1 agonist inotrope used in low-output cardiogenic shock. Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that raises afterload without improving contractility.
items.a: Dobutamine
w: Phenylephrine
Vasopressin
Midodrine

items.q: A patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy develops low-output decompensated heart failure. Why might milrinone be chosen over dobutamine?
items.x: Milrinone raises cAMP by inhibiting PDE-3, so its inotropic effect does not depend on beta receptors occupied by a beta-blocker. Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition is digoxin's mechanism.
items.a: It inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 and bypasses beta receptors
w: It stimulates alpha-1 receptors to raise vascular tone
It blocks the sodium-potassium ATPase in myocytes
It activates dopamine receptors to improve renal flow

items.q: Shortly after a phenylephrine infusion is started for hypotension, the patient's heart rate falls. What best explains this finding?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist; the rise in blood pressure triggers a baroreceptor-mediated reflex slowing of heart rate. It has no beta-blocking or direct muscarinic activity.
items.a: Reflex bradycardia from increased vascular resistance
w: Direct beta-1 receptor blockade at the sinus node
Drug-induced complete heart block from conduction toxicity
Muscarinic receptor stimulation at the AV node

items.q: A patient with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is started on midodrine. Which adverse effect is most important to monitor for?
items.x: Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist prodrug that can cause marked supine hypertension, so patients are taught to take it during daytime upright hours and avoid lying flat afterward. Bronchospasm is a beta-blocker concern.
items.a: Supine hypertension
w: Severe hypokalemia
Bronchospasm
Profound bradycardia at rest

items.q: Compared with norepinephrine in septic shock, dopamine is associated with which disadvantage?
items.x: Trials comparing the two agents found more arrhythmic events with dopamine, which is why norepinephrine is first-line. Dopamine does raise blood pressure, and both agents can cause peripheral ischemia.
items.a: Higher rate of tachyarrhythmias
w: Greater risk of digital ischemia
Inability to raise mean arterial pressure
Need for administration through an arterial line

items.q: Synthetic angiotensin II is added for a patient with refractory vasodilatory shock. Which adverse effect requires concurrent prophylaxis?
items.x: Angiotensin II was associated with more thromboembolic events in its pivotal trial, so the label recommends concurrent VTE prophylaxis. Hypoglycemia and pancreatitis are not characteristic effects.
items.a: Venous and arterial thromboembolism
w: Severe hypoglycemia
Acute pancreatitis
Drug-induced lupus

items.q: On day seven of IV heparin, a patient's platelet count has fallen by more than half and a new DVT is found. Heparin has been discontinued. Which anticoagulant is most appropriate now?
items.x: Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requires a non-heparin anticoagulant such as the direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban. Low-molecular-weight heparins cross-react with HIT antibodies, and starting warfarin alone in acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene.
items.a: Argatroban
w: Enoxaparin
Warfarin
Dalteparin

items.q: A patient on a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion develops major bleeding. Which agent reverses the anticoagulant effect?
items.x: Protamine is a positively charged protein that binds and neutralizes heparin rapidly. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
items.a: Protamine sulfate
w: Vitamin K
Idarucizumab
Desmopressin

items.q: Enoxaparin is being considered for VTE treatment. Which patient factor most warrants adjustment or an alternative anticoagulant?
items.x: Enoxaparin is renally cleared, so it accumulates in severe renal impairment and raises bleeding risk; dose adjustment or unfractionated heparin is used. Mild liver disease and the other conditions do not significantly alter its clearance.
items.a: Severe renal impairment
w: Mild hepatic steatosis
History of penicillin allergy
Well-controlled hypothyroidism

items.q: A patient taking warfarin presents with an intracranial hemorrhage and a markedly elevated INR. Which is the most appropriate reversal strategy?
items.x: 4F-PCC rapidly replaces factors II, VII, IX, and X, and IV vitamin K sustains reversal as the liver makes new factors. Oral vitamin K alone is far too slow for life-threatening bleeding.
items.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K
w: Protamine sulfate plus fresh frozen plasma
Oral vitamin K alone with repeat INR
Idarucizumab plus IV tranexamic acid

items.q: A patient taking dabigatran needs emergency surgery for a perforated bowel. Which agent specifically reverses dabigatran?
items.x: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity. Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban.
items.a: Idarucizumab
w: Andexanet alfa
Protamine sulfate
Phytonadione

items.q: A patient with a DVT has triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. Why is rivaroxaban not recommended for long-term anticoagulation?
items.x: In triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, rivaroxaban was associated with higher rates of recurrent thrombosis than warfarin, so warfarin is preferred. Rivaroxaban does not require INR monitoring.
items.a: It was linked to more thrombotic events than warfarin
w: It cannot be given to patients with lupus anticoagulant tests
It requires frequent INR monitoring in this population
It causes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia in these patients

items.q: A patient after coronary stenting has a CYP2C19 poor-metabolizer genotype. Why is clopidogrel likely to be less effective?
items.x: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated mainly by CYP2C19, so poor metabolizers generate less active metabolite and get weaker P2Y12 inhibition. An alternative such as ticagrelor or prasugrel is often chosen.
items.a: Reduced conversion of the prodrug to its active metabolite
w: Faster renal elimination of the active drug
Increased binding of the drug to plasma albumin
Upregulation of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors

items.q: A patient with acute coronary syndrome is undergoing PCI. Which history is a contraindication to prasugrel?
items.x: Prasugrel carries a boxed warning and is contraindicated in patients with prior stroke or TIA because of increased intracranial bleeding. Asthma is a caution with ticagrelor because of dyspnea, not prasugrel.
items.a: Prior transient ischemic attack
w: Prior hip replacement
Well-controlled asthma
History of gout

items.q: A patient with iron deficiency anemia is starting oral ferrous sulfate. Which counseling point is accurate?
items.x: Oral iron commonly darkens stools and causes constipation or GI upset. Calcium, antacids, and dairy decrease iron absorption, and bright red blood suggests bleeding that needs evaluation.
items.a: Dark stools and constipation are expected effects
w: Take it together with calcium carbonate for absorption
Take it with milk to improve absorption
Bright red blood in stool is an expected effect

items.q: A patient with CKD-related anemia is being evaluated for epoetin alfa. What should be assessed before starting therapy?
items.x: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents need adequate iron to work, so iron deficiency is assessed and corrected first. Hemolysis tests and hemoglobin electrophoresis are not routine prerequisites.
items.a: Iron stores, including ferritin and transferrin saturation
w: Serum uric acid and lactate dehydrogenase
Hemoglobin A2 by electrophoresis
Serum haptoglobin and direct antiglobulin test

items.q: Rapid sequence intubation is planned. In which patient is succinylcholine contraindicated?
items.x: After denervation injury, upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors can release large amounts of potassium with succinylcholine and cause fatal hyperkalemia. A full stomach is an indication for rapid sequence intubation, not a contraindication to succinylcholine.
items.a: A patient with a spinal cord injury two weeks ago
w: A patient with a full stomach after a meal
A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient with a history of migraine

items.q: After succinylcholine for intubation, a patient develops masseter rigidity, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, tachycardia, and fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.x: Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients through uncontrolled RyR1 calcium release; dantrolene is the treatment. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows antipsychotics and develops over days.
items.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Thyroid storm

items.q: How does sugammadex reverse rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade?
items.x: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that binds rocuronium and vecuronium, pulling them away from the neuromuscular junction. Neostigmine reverses blockade by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.
items.a: It encapsulates rocuronium in plasma
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the junction
It competitively blocks nicotinic receptors
It enhances renal excretion of rocuronium

items.q: A woman using an oral hormonal contraceptive receives sugammadex after surgery. Which counseling point is most important?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen, so the label advises treating its use like a missed pill and using backup nonhormonal contraception for the following seven days. The effect is temporary, not permanent.
items.a: Use a backup nonhormonal contraceptive method for a week
w: Expect permanent loss of contraceptive effect
Double the next contraceptive pill to compensate
No interaction with hormonal contraception occurs

items.q: Etomidate is chosen as an induction agent for a hemodynamically unstable patient. Which adverse effect is characteristic of this drug?
items.x: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, which transiently suppresses cortisol synthesis. It is chosen precisely because it causes little hypotension.
items.a: Transient adrenal suppression
w: Malignant hyperthermia
Marked hypotension
Bronchospasm from histamine release

items.q: A hypotensive trauma patient with a history of severe asthma needs rapid sequence intubation. Which induction agent is most appropriate?
items.x: Ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, tends to preserve blood pressure through sympathetic stimulation and causes bronchodilation. Propofol often causes significant hypotension in hemodynamically unstable patients.
items.a: Ketamine
w: Propofol
Methohexital
Thiopental

items.q: A ventilated patient has been sedated with a propofol infusion for several days. Which laboratory value should be monitored because of the drug's formulation?
items.x: Propofol is delivered in a lipid emulsion, so prolonged infusions can cause hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis. Ammonia monitoring relates to valproate or liver disease, not propofol.
items.a: Serum triglycerides
w: Serum ammonia
Serum lithium level
Serum uric acid

items.q: Midazolam is given for procedural sedation. Which effect is most characteristic of this drug?
items.x: Benzodiazepines such as midazolam produce sedation, anxiolysis, and anterograde amnesia but no meaningful analgesia. Dissociative anesthesia with nystagmus describes ketamine.
items.a: Anterograde amnesia
w: Dissociative anesthesia with nystagmus
Prolonged neuromuscular paralysis
Significant analgesia without sedation

items.q: A rapid IV bolus of fentanyl is given during induction, and bag-mask ventilation suddenly becomes very difficult. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Rapid administration of potent opioids such as fentanyl can cause chest wall and glottic rigidity that impairs ventilation; it responds to neuromuscular blockade or naloxone. Fentanyl causes little histamine release compared with morphine.
items.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: Histamine-mediated anaphylaxis
Tension pneumothorax from positive pressure
Malignant hyperthermia crisis

items.q: A patient has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension and dizziness. Which medication is first-line?
items.x: Atropine blocks vagal muscarinic tone at the sinus and AV nodes and is the first-line drug in ACLS bradycardia algorithms. Adenosine, metoprolol, and diltiazem all slow the heart rate further.
items.a: Atropine
w: Adenosine
Metoprolol
Diltiazem

items.q: A patient receives repeated albuterol nebulizer treatments for an asthma exacerbation. Which laboratory change is expected?
items.x: Beta-2 stimulation activates Na+/K+-ATPase and shifts potassium into cells, which lowers serum potassium. Beta-agonists tend to raise, not lower, serum glucose.
items.a: Decreased serum potassium
w: Increased serum sodium
Decreased serum glucose
Increased serum calcium

items.q: Budesonide-formoterol can be used as both daily maintenance and as-needed reliever therapy in asthma. Which property of formoterol makes this possible?
items.x: Formoterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist with a fast onset, so it relieves symptoms quickly while the paired corticosteroid treats inflammation. Salmeterol has a slower onset and is not used as a reliever.
items.a: Rapid onset of bronchodilation
w: Antimuscarinic action on airway smooth muscle
Absence of any systemic absorption
Inhibition of leukotriene synthesis

items.q: A patient with persistent asthma starts inhaled fluticasone. Which counseling point best prevents its most common local adverse effect?
items.x: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia; rinsing and spitting, plus using a spacer, reduces this. ICS are controllers and are not used as rescue therapy.
items.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each use
w: Use it only during acute wheezing episodes
Take it with food to reduce stomach upset
Inhale it immediately before exercise

items.q: Why must salmeterol be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid in a patient with asthma?
items.x: Long-acting beta-agonist monotherapy in asthma was associated with increased severe exacerbations and asthma-related death, so it is used only with an ICS. Oral candidiasis is a corticosteroid effect, not a salmeterol effect.
items.a: LABA monotherapy in asthma increases asthma-related deaths
w: Salmeterol is inactive without a corticosteroid present
Corticosteroids are needed to prevent salmeterol tolerance
Salmeterol monotherapy causes severe oral candidiasis

items.q: A patient with COPD is being started on tiotropium. Which coexisting condition warrants the most caution?
items.x: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and can worsen urinary retention and narrow-angle glaucoma. Hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis are not affected by anticholinergic bronchodilators.
items.a: Urinary retention from prostatic hyperplasia
w: Hypothyroidism on replacement therapy
Mild chronic kidney disease
Osteoarthritis of the knees

items.q: A teenager with asthma and allergic rhinitis is taking montelukast. Which adverse effect carries an FDA boxed warning?
items.x: The FDA added a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events such as agitation, sleep disturbance, depression, and suicidality with montelukast. Hepatotoxicity is associated with zileuton, another leukotriene modifier.
items.a: Neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts
w: Severe hepatotoxicity requiring liver transplant
Cardiac arrhythmias with QT prolongation
Agranulocytosis with severe infection

items.q: A patient with COPD on long-term theophylline develops nausea, tachycardia, and a seizure after starting a new antibiotic. Which antibiotic most likely caused this?
items.x: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme that metabolizes theophylline, so levels rise into the toxic range. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and toxicity causes arrhythmias and seizures.
items.a: Ciprofloxacin
w: Amoxicillin
Cephalexin
Doxycycline

items.q: Roflumilast is added for a patient with severe COPD, chronic bronchitis, and frequent exacerbations. What is its mechanism of action?
items.x: Roflumilast inhibits PDE-4, increasing cAMP in inflammatory cells and reducing exacerbations. It is not a bronchodilator; M3 blockade describes tiotropium.
items.a: Selective inhibition of phosphodiesterase-4
w: Blockade of muscarinic M3 receptors
Antagonism of cysteinyl leukotriene receptors
Binding and neutralizing circulating IgE

items.q: A patient with severe allergic asthma and an elevated serum IgE is started on omalizumab. What should be done after each injection?
items.x: Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis, so patients are observed after administration and taught to recognize symptoms. It does not affect theophylline levels or the QT interval.
items.a: Observe the patient for anaphylaxis
w: Check a serum theophylline level
Obtain an ECG to check the QT interval
Measure blood glucose over several hours

items.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis is starting elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor. Which laboratory test requires routine monitoring?
items.x: CFTR modulators can raise transaminases and bilirubin, and serious liver injury has been reported, so liver tests are checked at baseline and periodically. Thyroid and uric acid monitoring are not required.
items.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum lithium levels
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum uric acid

items.q: A patient on phenytoin for epilepsy presents with horizontal nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech after a recent dose increase. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics at therapeutic levels, so small dose increases can cause large rises in serum level and cerebellar signs such as nystagmus and ataxia. Stroke is possible but less likely given the timing with a dose change.
items.a: Phenytoin toxicity from saturable metabolism
w: New posterior circulation stroke
Expected effect of subtherapeutic dosing
Vitamin B12 deficiency from phenytoin

items.q: Fosphenytoin is chosen instead of IV phenytoin in a patient with status epilepticus. What is a key advantage of fosphenytoin?
items.x: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug with less infusion-site injury, including purple glove syndrome, and it can be given IM. Cardiac monitoring is still needed because hypotension and arrhythmias can occur.
items.a: Less risk of local tissue injury at the infusion site
w: No need for cardiac monitoring during infusion
No effect on hepatic enzyme metabolism
No risk of hypotension during infusion

items.q: A patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting several minutes and has IV access. Which medication is the first-line treatment?
items.x: Benzodiazepines such as IV lorazepam are first-line for status epilepticus. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate are second-line agents if seizures continue, and propofol is reserved for refractory status.
items.a: Intravenous lorazepam
w: Intravenous levetiracetam
Intravenous phenobarbital
Intravenous propofol

items.q: A woman of reproductive age with generalized epilepsy is considering valproic acid. Which risk is most important to discuss?
items.x: Valproate carries a boxed warning for major congenital malformations, especially neural tube defects, and reduced IQ after in utero exposure. Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are typical of phenytoin.
items.a: Neural tube defects and other major birth defects
w: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism
Kidney stones and metabolic acidosis
Stevens-Johnson syndrome in carriers of HLA-B*1502

items.q: A patient on valproic acid has lamotrigine added. Why does this combination require especially slow lamotrigine titration?
items.x: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, roughly doubling its levels and raising the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. A slower, lower titration schedule is used.
items.a: Valproate raises lamotrigine levels and serious rash risk
w: Valproate lowers lamotrigine levels and causes seizures
Lamotrigine induces valproate metabolism and causes hepatotoxicity
The combination causes severe QT prolongation

items.q: Before starting carbamazepine in a patient of Han Chinese ancestry, which test is recommended?
items.x: Patients with HLA-B*1502, common in many Asian populations, have a much higher risk of carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. TPMT testing applies to thiopurines.
items.a: HLA-B*1502 genotyping
w: TPMT enzyme activity
G6PD enzyme activity
CYP2C19 genotyping

items.q: Which patient with migraine has a contraindication to sumatriptan?
items.x: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that can cause coronary vasoconstriction, so they are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease, prior stroke, and uncontrolled hypertension. Asthma does not limit triptan use.
items.a: A patient with known coronary artery disease
w: A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient with mild chronic kidney disease
A patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis

items.q: A patient presents with acute ischemic stroke symptoms within the treatment window. Which finding is an absolute contraindication to alteplase?
items.x: Any intracranial hemorrhage on CT rules out thrombolysis. Advanced age and controlled hypertension are not absolute contraindications, and blood pressure must simply be controlled before treatment.
items.a: Intracranial hemorrhage on noncontrast head CT
w: Age older than eighty years
Mild facial droop on the affected side
History of well-controlled hypertension

items.q: A patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage is started on nimodipine. What is the purpose of this therapy?
items.x: Nimodipine improves neurologic outcome after subarachnoid hemorrhage by reducing delayed ischemic deficits. It is given orally or by feeding tube only; IV administration of the capsule contents can cause cardiac arrest.
items.a: To improve outcomes from delayed cerebral ischemia
w: To lower blood pressure to normal levels quickly
To prevent rebleeding from the aneurysm
To prevent early post-hemorrhage seizures

items.q: A patient with an overdose of extended-release morphine awakens after IV naloxone. Why does this patient still need prolonged observation?
items.x: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, especially extended-release or long-acting agents, so sedation and respiratory depression can recur. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
items.a: Naloxone's effect may wear off before the opioid's
w: Naloxone causes delayed respiratory depression itself
Naloxone enhances later absorption of the opioid
Naloxone blocks the liver's metabolism of morphine

items.q: Which patient factor most increases the risk of hepatotoxicity from acetaminophen within the usual dosing range?
items.x: Chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione, increasing toxic NAPQI and liver injury. Peptic ulcer disease is a concern with NSAIDs, not acetaminophen.
items.a: Chronic heavy alcohol use
w: Concurrent use of omeprazole
Mild chronic kidney disease
History of peptic ulcer disease

items.q: In which postoperative patient should ketorolac be avoided?
items.x: Ketorolac is a potent NSAID that reduces renal prostaglandins and can worsen kidney injury; it is also avoided in active GI bleeding and for perioperative pain in CABG. The other conditions do not limit its use.
items.a: A patient with acute kidney injury after surgery
w: A patient with well-controlled hypothyroidism
A patient with mild seasonal allergies
A patient with controlled hyperlipidemia

items.q: A patient taking sertraline is prescribed tramadol for back pain. Which adverse effect is of greatest concern?
items.x: Tramadol inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake in addition to its opioid effect, so combining it with an SSRI raises serotonin syndrome risk. Tramadol also lowers the seizure threshold.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Severe hypertensive crisis
Agranulocytosis

items.q: A patient is starting methadone for opioid use disorder. Which test is most important to monitor for its cardiac risk?
items.x: Methadone prolongs the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes, particularly at higher doses or with other QT-prolonging drugs. It does not reduce ejection fraction or cause ischemia.
items.a: Electrocardiogram for QT interval
w: Echocardiogram for ejection fraction
Serum troponin for myocardial injury
Exercise stress test for ischemia

items.q: A patient with opioid use disorder who used heroin a few hours ago requests buprenorphine induction. What is the main risk of giving it now?
items.x: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial mu agonist that displaces full agonists and can precipitate withdrawal, so induction usually waits until mild-to-moderate withdrawal is present. Its ceiling effect makes respiratory depression less likely than with full agonists.
items.a: Precipitated opioid withdrawal
w: Severe respiratory depression
Serotonin syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: A patient with end-stage renal disease received repeated meperidine and now has tremor and myoclonus followed by a seizure. What is the cause?
items.x: Normeperidine is a renally cleared metabolite that causes CNS excitation and seizures, which is why meperidine is avoided in renal impairment and older adults. Morphine-6-glucuronide is morphine's metabolite.
items.a: Accumulation of the metabolite normeperidine
w: Accumulation of morphine-6-glucuronide
Opioid-induced hypoglycemia
Direct histamine release in the brain

items.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease needs an opioid for severe pain. Why is morphine a poor choice?
items.x: Morphine's glucuronide metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate in kidney failure, causing sedation, respiratory depression, and neurotoxicity. Fentanyl or hydromorphone with caution are often preferred.
items.a: Its active metabolites accumulate and cause toxicity
w: It is only available by the intravenous route
It is eliminated mainly by the liver unchanged
It has no effect on visceral pain

items.q: Compared with nonselective NSAIDs such as naproxen, celecoxib is associated with which characteristic?
items.x: Selective COX-2 inhibition spares gastric protective prostaglandins, but celecoxib carries the same boxed warnings for cardiovascular thrombotic events and GI bleeding as other NSAIDs. It has no meaningful antiplatelet effect.
items.a: Lower GI ulcer risk with similar cardiovascular warnings
w: Higher GI ulcer risk with no cardiovascular warnings
No renal effects and no cardiovascular warnings
Strong antiplatelet effect similar to aspirin

items.q: A mechanically ventilated patient is sedated with dexmedetomidine. Which adverse effect is most common?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow, causing bradycardia and hypotension with relatively little respiratory depression. Hypertriglyceridemia is a propofol effect.
items.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Severe respiratory depression
Hypertriglyceridemia
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: A patient stable on lithium for bipolar disorder develops coarse tremor, confusion, and ataxia after starting a new medication for hypertension. Which medication most likely caused this?
items.x: Thiazides increase proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption, raising lithium levels into the toxic range. ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs have a similar effect, while amlodipine does not meaningfully change lithium clearance.
items.a: Hydrochlorothiazide
w: Amlodipine
Hydralazine
Doxazosin

items.q: Which laboratory tests should be monitored periodically in a patient on long-term lithium?
items.x: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and chronic kidney effects, including nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so TSH and renal function are checked along with drug levels. Lithium tends to cause leukocytosis rather than cytopenias.
items.a: Renal function and thyroid function
w: Liver enzymes and serum lipase
Complete blood count and haptoglobin
Serum prolactin and fasting lipids

items.q: A patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is starting clozapine. Which monitoring is required?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so the absolute neutrophil count is monitored on a set schedule. Myocarditis, seizures, and metabolic effects are other important clozapine risks.
items.a: Absolute neutrophil count
w: Serum lithium level
Serum ammonia level
Thyroid antibodies

items.q: A patient has generalized anxiety disorder without other psychiatric conditions. Which medication is an appropriate first-line long-term treatment?
items.x: SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line maintenance therapy for generalized anxiety disorder. Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam carry dependence and misuse risks and are not first-line long-term therapy.
items.a: Sertraline
w: Alprazolam
Hydroxyzine
Propranolol

items.q: A patient with major depression asks about bupropion. Which history is a contraindication?
items.x: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia nervosa. SSRI-related sexual dysfunction and smoking are reasons bupropion may be preferred.
items.a: Current bulimia nervosa
w: Prior SSRI-related sexual dysfunction
Current tobacco use
History of hypothyroidism

items.q: A few hours after receiving IM haloperidol, a patient develops sustained neck twisting and upward eye deviation. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.x: This is acute dystonia from dopamine blockade, treated with an anticholinergic such as benztropine or with diphenhydramine. Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and propranolol for akathisia.
items.a: Benztropine
w: Bromocriptine
Dantrolene
Propranolol

items.q: A patient with schizophrenia is starting olanzapine. Which monitoring is most important for its major long-term adverse effects?
items.x: Olanzapine has high risk of weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, so metabolic monitoring is essential. Weekly neutrophil monitoring is specific to clozapine.
items.a: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipid panel
w: Absolute neutrophil count each week
Serum lithium and creatinine levels
Liver biopsy before therapy

items.q: A patient taking phenelzine eats aged cheese and develops a severe occipital headache and very high blood pressure. What is the mechanism?
items.x: MAO inhibitors prevent breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, and tyramine then releases norepinephrine, causing a hypertensive crisis. Patients are counseled to avoid aged, fermented, and cured foods.
items.a: Tyramine is not broken down and releases norepinephrine
w: Serotonin reuptake is blocked in the brainstem
Dopamine receptors are blocked in the hypothalamus
Histamine is released from intestinal mast cells

items.q: A patient with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis also takes daily oxycodone for chronic pain. Which medication for alcohol use disorder is most appropriate?
items.x: Acamprosate is renally cleared and does not interact with opioids, making it suitable in liver disease. Naltrexone would precipitate opioid withdrawal, and disulfiram is risky in cirrhosis.
items.a: Acamprosate
w: Naltrexone
Disulfiram
Chlordiazepoxide

items.q: How does varenicline help with smoking cessation?
items.x: Varenicline partially stimulates nicotinic receptors to reduce cravings and withdrawal while blocking the rewarding effect of nicotine from smoking. Dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition describes bupropion.
items.a: Partial agonism at alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptors
w: Inhibition of dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake
Full agonism at nicotinic receptors in muscle
Antagonism of mu opioid receptors in the brain

items.q: A patient with severe hyperkalemia has peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which medication should be given first to stabilize the cardiac membrane?
items.x: IV calcium antagonizes the membrane effects of potassium and acts within minutes but does not lower potassium. Binders and diuretics remove potassium too slowly to be the first step.
items.a: IV calcium gluconate
w: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
IV furosemide
Oral patiromer

items.q: IV regular insulin is given with dextrose to treat hyperkalemia. Which monitoring is most important afterward?
items.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but can cause delayed hypoglycemia, especially in kidney disease, so glucose is checked frequently. The other effects are not expected from this treatment.
items.a: Frequent blood glucose checks for hypoglycemia
w: Serum magnesium checks for hypermagnesemia
Urine output for osmotic diuresis
Serum calcium checks for hypercalcemia

items.q: A patient with CKD on an ACE inhibitor is started on patiromer for chronic hyperkalemia. Which electrolyte abnormality should be monitored?
items.x: Patiromer exchanges calcium for potassium and also binds magnesium, so hypomagnesemia is a recognized adverse effect. Other oral drugs should be separated in time from patiromer to avoid binding.
items.a: Hypomagnesemia
w: Hypernatremia
Hypercalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia

items.q: A patient with heart failure on high-intensity furosemide therapy is most likely to show which laboratory pattern?
items.x: Loop diuretics increase distal sodium delivery and potassium and hydrogen ion loss, causing hypokalemic contraction alkalosis. They also increase calcium excretion, unlike thiazides.
items.a: Hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis
w: Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis
Hypercalcemia with metabolic acidosis
Hypernatremia with respiratory acidosis

items.q: A patient develops an acute gout flare a few weeks after starting hydrochlorothiazide. What explains this?
items.x: Thiazides compete with uric acid for proximal tubular secretion and cause volume contraction, both raising serum urate. Thiazides can also cause hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, and hyperglycemia.
items.a: Decreased renal excretion of uric acid
w: Increased purine production in the liver
Direct crystal deposition of the drug
Increased intestinal absorption of purines

items.q: A patient with cirrhosis has new moderate ascites. Which diuretic regimen is first-line?
items.x: Secondary hyperaldosteronism drives sodium retention in cirrhosis, so the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is the foundation, often paired with furosemide. Thiazides add hyponatremia risk without targeting the mechanism.
items.a: Spironolactone with or without furosemide
w: Hydrochlorothiazide alone
Acetazolamide alone
Mannitol with furosemide

items.q: A patient taking acetazolamide for prevention of acute mountain sickness has which expected acid-base change?
items.x: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes bicarbonate loss in the urine, producing a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap acidosis that stimulates ventilation. Hypochloremic alkalosis is seen with loop and thiazide diuretics.
items.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
w: High anion gap metabolic acidosis
Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
Primary respiratory acidosis

items.q: A man taking tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia is scheduled for cataract surgery. What is the most important counseling point?
items.x: Alpha-1A blockade affects the iris dilator muscle and can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, so the surgeon needs to know in advance. Pupil dilation tends to be poorer, not better.
items.a: Inform the eye surgeon about tamsulosin before surgery
w: Expect the drug to lower intraocular pressure
Tamsulosin has no relevance to eye surgery
Expect improved pupil dilation during surgery

items.q: A man has taken finasteride for benign prostatic hyperplasia for a year. How does it affect prostate cancer screening?
items.x: Finasteride, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, lowers PSA by about half after several months, so values are doubled for interpretation. Any confirmed PSA rise on finasteride warrants evaluation.
items.a: It lowers PSA, so measured values should be doubled
w: It raises PSA, so measured values should be halved
It has no effect on PSA results
It makes PSA undetectable and unusable

items.q: An older adult with mild dementia has overactive bladder. Which medication is preferred to avoid anticholinergic cognitive effects?
items.x: Mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist that relaxes the detrusor without anticholinergic effects; blood pressure should be monitored. Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen confusion in older adults.
items.a: Mirabegron
w: Oxybutynin
Tolterodine
Trospium

items.q: A patient is starting oral alendronate for osteoporosis. Which counseling point is correct?
items.x: Alendronate is poorly absorbed and can cause pill esophagitis, so it is taken first thing in the morning with plain water, fasting, and the patient stays upright before eating. Calcium and food greatly reduce absorption.
items.a: Take with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright
w: Take with milk at bedtime to reduce nausea
Take with breakfast and a calcium supplement
Lie down after taking to improve absorption
