w: Prone with hands restrained behind the back
Face down with a backboard on top
Seated upright with no further monitoring

items.q: What advantage does ketamine offer when sedating a severely agitated, violent patient without IV access?
items.x: Ketamine given IM produces dissociative sedation within minutes, which improves safety for patient and crew. All sedated patients still need monitoring.
items.a: Rapid onset after intramuscular injection
w: Slow onset that avoids oversedation
It requires no further monitoring
It works only by the oral route

items.q: Which uncommon airway complication must be prepared for when ketamine is used for agitation?

w: Epiglottitis

Foreign body obstruction

items.q: An agitated, tremulous, sweating patient is in alcohol withdrawal. Why is a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam preferred?

items.a: It treats the withdrawal itself and reduces seizure risk
w: It reverses alcohol intoxication
It prevents liver damage from alcohol
It replaces thiamine lost in alcohol use

items.q: Hours after haloperidol, a patient has sustained neck twisting, eyes rolled upward and tongue protrusion. Why is diphenhydramine given?
items.x: Acute dystonia from dopamine blockade responds to anticholinergic agents such as diphenhydramine. It is not an allergy, and diphenhydramine does not treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
items.a: To treat an acute dystonic reaction
w: To treat an allergic reaction
To sedate further agitation
To treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome

items.q: How does tranexamic acid reduce bleeding in trauma?

It reverses the effect of anticoagulants like warfarin
It constricts bleeding vessels at the injury site

items.q: Why does the time since injury matter when tranexamic acid is considered for a bleeding trauma patient?
items.x: Trials show TXA reduces bleeding deaths when started early, with the most benefit within about 3 hours, and later use may cause harm. It does not need to wait for blood products.
items.a: Benefit is greatest when given within 3 hours of injury

It must be delayed until blood products are given
Its effect is the same regardless of timing

items.q: Why is fentanyl often preferred over morphine for analgesia in a trauma patient with borderline blood pressure?

w: It raises blood pressure through vasoconstriction
It cannot cause respiratory depression

items.q: A patient with a traumatic brain injury receives fentanyl for pain. Which monitoring is most important?

w: Urine output every few minutes
Skin color for signs of jaundice
Pupil response to confirm opioid effect

items.q: Why is ketamine useful for analgesia in a hypotensive trauma patient?
items.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects usually preserve blood pressure, and patients generally keep their airway reflexes and breathing. It does not treat the shock itself.
items.a: It tends to maintain blood pressure and airway reflexes
w: It strongly lowers heart rate and blood pressure
It reverses hemorrhagic shock
It causes complete muscle paralysis

items.q: What is a benefit of adding low-dose ketamine to opioids for severe fracture pain?

It prevents infection at the fracture site

items.q: Why is 5% dextrose in water a poor fluid for resuscitating hemorrhagic shock?

It causes the blood to clot too quickly
It is too thick to infuse rapidly

items.q: Before and during administration of concentrated IV dextrose, what is most important to confirm?

When the patient is actively seizing

items.q: Why are dextrose-containing IV fluids generally not given routinely to a patient with acute stroke unless the glucose is low?

w: Dextrose dissolves the clot too quickly
Dextrose raises the blood pressure dangerously
Dextrose interferes with the stroke scale

items.q: When IV insulin is used to treat hyperkalemia, why is dextrose usually given with it?
items.x: Insulin shifts potassium into cells but also lowers blood glucose, so dextrose is given to prevent hypoglycemia unless glucose is already high. Calcium, not dextrose, stabilizes the cardiac membrane.
items.a: To prevent hypoglycemia caused by the insulin
w: To push potassium into the urine
To stabilize the cardiac membrane
To make the insulin work more slowly

items.q: Which finding suggests hypocalcemia that calcium chloride would treat?
items.x: Low calcium increases nerve and muscle excitability, causing tingling, cramps, carpopedal spasm and a long QT. Loss of reflexes and flushing suggest high magnesium.
items.a: Carpopedal spasm and tingling around the mouth
w: Peaked T waves and muscle weakness
Flushing and loss of deep tendon reflexes
Polyuria and excessive thirst

items.q: During IV administration of calcium chloride, what monitoring is most important?
items.x: Rapid calcium can slow the heart and cause arrhythmias, so it is given slowly with the ECG monitored. Glucose and peak flow are not affected.
items.a: Continuous ECG for bradycardia and arrhythmias
w: Pupil checks for constriction
Blood glucose every few minutes
Peak flow measurements

items.q: A patient with hyperkalemia has wide QRS complexes and peaked T waves. What does IV calcium gluconate do?
items.x: Calcium protects the heart from the effects of high potassium within minutes but does not change the potassium level. Other treatments such as insulin, albuterol and dialysis lower potassium.
items.a: It stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does not lower potassium
w: It removes potassium from the body through the kidneys
It shifts potassium into the cells
It binds potassium in the gut

items.q: A patient with a long QT interval develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that twists around the baseline and has a pulse. Which drug is indicated?
items.x: Torsades de pointes is treated with IV magnesium, which suppresses early afterdepolarizations. Adenosine and diltiazem are for narrow-complex rhythms.
items.a: Magnesium sulfate
w: Adenosine
Diltiazem
Metoprolol

items.q: Why is low magnesium corrected in a patient whose hypokalemia does not respond to potassium replacement?
items.x: Magnesium deficiency increases renal potassium wasting, so potassium stays low until magnesium is replaced. The lab values are real, not false.
items.a: Low magnesium causes ongoing potassium loss through the kidneys
w: Magnesium is converted into potassium in the liver
Magnesium blocks potassium absorption in the gut
Low magnesium causes falsely low lab readings

items.q: How does sodium bicarbonate help lower serum potassium in severe hyperkalemia with acidosis?
items.x: As pH rises, hydrogen ions leave cells and potassium moves in, lowering serum potassium. Calcium, not bicarbonate, stabilizes the cardiac membrane.
items.a: Raising blood pH drives potassium into the cells
w: It binds potassium in the bloodstream
It increases potassium loss in stool
It stabilizes the cardiac membrane directly

items.q: Which problems can result from giving too much sodium bicarbonate?
items.x: Excess bicarbonate raises pH and delivers a large sodium load, which can cause alkalosis, low potassium and fluid overload. It treats acidosis rather than causing it.
items.a: Metabolic alkalosis and sodium overload
w: Metabolic acidosis and dehydration
Hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia
Hypercalcemia and kidney stones

items.q: Furosemide belongs to which class of diuretics?
items.x: Furosemide blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending loop of Henle, making it a potent loop diuretic. Thiazides act in the distal tubule.
items.a: Loop diuretic acting on the loop of Henle
w: Thiazide diuretic acting on the distal tubule
Potassium-sparing diuretic acting on aldosterone
Osmotic diuretic acting throughout the nephron

items.q: Which electrolyte disturbance is most important to monitor after furosemide?
items.x: Loop diuretics cause loss of potassium, magnesium and calcium in the urine, so hypokalemia is a major concern. They do not raise potassium.
items.a: Low potassium
w: High potassium
High sodium
High calcium

items.q: How does nebulized albuterol help lower potassium in hyperkalemia?
items.x: Albuterol stimulates beta-2 receptors that drive the Na-K pump, moving potassium into cells temporarily. It does not remove potassium from the body.
items.a: Beta-2 stimulation activates the sodium-potassium pump, shifting potassium into cells
w: It increases potassium loss through the kidneys
It binds potassium in the airway lining
It blocks potassium absorption from the gut

items.q: When giving naloxone to a patient with suspected opioid overdose, what is the goal of treatment?
items.x: Naloxone is titrated to restore effective breathing; aiming for full wakefulness can trigger abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation. Pupil size is not the treatment goal.
items.a: Adequate spontaneous breathing
w: Full alertness and orientation
A heart rate above normal
Dilated pupils

items.q: After a patient wakes up following naloxone, why is continued monitoring important?
items.x: Many opioids, especially long-acting or high-potency ones, last longer than naloxone, so breathing can decline again. Repeat doses may be needed.
items.a: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, causing re-sedation
w: Naloxone causes delayed seizures in all patients
Naloxone causes rebound hypertension hours later
Naloxone leads to delayed liver failure

items.q: In a tricyclic antidepressant overdose, which finding is a key indication for sodium bicarbonate?
items.x: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels and widen the QRS, and bicarbonate overcomes this blockade with sodium and alkalinization. Sinus tachycardia, not bradycardia, is typical.
items.a: Widening of the QRS complex
w: Sinus bradycardia
Peaked T waves
ST depression in the lateral leads

items.q: How does sodium bicarbonate help in salicylate (aspirin) poisoning?
items.x: Alkaline urine traps salicylate in its ionized form so it is excreted, and alkaline blood keeps it out of the brain. Activated charcoal, not bicarbonate, binds drug in the gut.
items.a: It alkalinizes the urine to increase salicylate excretion
w: It binds salicylate in the stomach
It reverses the antiplatelet effect
It blocks salicylate absorption from the gut

items.q: A 22-year-old swallowed an unknown number of carbamazepine tablets 40 minutes ago. He is drowsy, answers slowly and gags weakly. HR 104, BP 118/70, SpO2 96%. Which feature of this presentation is a contraindication to activated charcoal?
items.x: Charcoal that is vomited and aspirated causes severe lung injury, and a drowsy patient with a weak gag cannot protect the airway. Charcoal is still useful within about an hour, and recirculating drugs such as carbamazepine are bound well by it.
items.a: Depressed consciousness with an unprotected airway
w: Ingestion more than thirty minutes before arrival
A drug that recirculates through the gut and liver
Sinus tachycardia with a normal blood pressure

items.q: After hydroxocobalamin is given for suspected cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation, which finding is expected?
items.x: Hydroxocobalamin is a deep red compound that binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, and it turns the skin and urine red. This is expected and can interfere with some lab tests.
items.a: Red discoloration of the skin and urine
w: Blue discoloration of the lips
Yellowing of the eyes
Black, tarry stools

items.q: When treating organophosphate poisoning with atropine, what is the main endpoint for giving more?
items.x: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects, so it is titrated to clear airway secretions and improve breathing. It does not reverse nicotinic effects such as muscle twitching, and pupils are an unreliable endpoint.
items.a: Drying of bronchial secretions and easier breathing
w: Return of normal pupil size
Resolution of muscle twitching
A heart rate below normal

items.q: What does pralidoxime do in organophosphate poisoning?
items.x: Pralidoxime removes the organophosphate from acetylcholinesterase, restoring the enzyme and improving muscle weakness. Atropine, not pralidoxime, blocks muscarinic receptors.
items.a: It reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given before the bond ages
w: It blocks muscarinic receptors to dry secretions
It binds the organophosphate in the gut
It increases acetylcholine release at synapses

items.q: Why can glucagon help a patient with a beta blocker overdose who is bradycardic and hypotensive?
items.x: Glucagon activates its own receptors on heart cells, increasing cAMP, heart rate and contractility even when beta receptors are blocked. It does not compete at the beta receptor.
items.a: It raises cardiac cAMP through a pathway that bypasses beta receptors
w: It blocks the beta blocker from binding receptors
It stimulates the vagus nerve to slow the heart
It increases absorption of the beta blocker

items.q: For which overdose is calcium chloride most specifically used?
items.x: Calcium can partly overcome calcium channel blockade, improving contractility and blood pressure. Opioid overdose needs naloxone and cyanide needs hydroxocobalamin.
items.a: Calcium channel blocker overdose with hypotension
w: Opioid overdose with apnea
Organophosphate exposure
Cyanide toxicity from smoke

items.q: Before giving IV dextrose to a patient with altered mental status, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Confirming hypoglycemia with a glucose check guides treatment and avoids unnecessary dextrose. The other assessments do not confirm low blood sugar.
items.a: A point-of-care blood glucose level
w: A 12-lead ECG
A serum potassium level
A pulse oximetry reading

items.q: A patient with hypoglycemia from a sulfonylurea overdose improves after IV dextrose. What should be anticipated?
items.x: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release for many hours, so glucose often drops again after dextrose is used. These patients need repeated glucose checks and observation.
items.a: Recurrent hypoglycemia as the dextrose is used up
w: Permanent correction after a single dose
Severe hyperkalemia within minutes
Rebound hypertension and bradycardia

items.q: Which presentation most strongly suggests hypoglycemia that should respond to dextrose?
items.x: Sweating, tachycardia and confusion reflect the adrenaline response and brain glucose shortage of hypoglycemia. Fruity breath and deep breathing suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.a: Sweating, confusion and fast heart rate in a patient using insulin
w: Fruity breath, deep breathing and thirst in a new diabetic
Slow onset of thirst and frequent urination over days
Fever, stiff neck and a rash in a young adult

items.q: A combative patient with known diabetes has low blood glucose and no IV access. Which route can be used for glucagon?
items.x: Glucagon can be given IM, subcutaneously or as a nasal powder when an IV is not available. It is not given orally, sublingually or rectally.
items.a: Intramuscular injection
w: Oral liquid
Sublingual tablet
Rectal suppository

items.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose by releasing stored liver glycogen. In which patient are those stores most likely depleted?
items.x: Glucagon works by releasing glycogen stores from the liver, which are depleted in starvation and chronic alcohol use. IV dextrose is more reliable in these patients.
items.a: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use
w: A well-nourished patient on insulin
A young adult with type 1 diabetes
An athlete who skipped one meal

items.q: How does glucagon raise blood glucose?
items.x: Glucagon triggers hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, releasing stored glucose. Unlike dextrose, it does not contain glucose itself.
items.a: It stimulates the liver to break down glycogen into glucose
w: It provides glucose directly into the bloodstream
It increases insulin release from the pancreas
It blocks glucose uptake by the kidneys

items.q: Why is thiamine given before or with dextrose to a malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use?
items.x: Glucose metabolism uses thiamine, and in thiamine-deficient patients a glucose load can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. Treating hypoglycemia should not be delayed, though.
items.a: To help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
w: To prevent rebound hypoglycemia
To treat alcohol withdrawal seizures
To speed alcohol metabolism

items.q: Which combination of findings is classic for Wernicke encephalopathy?
items.x: The classic triad is confusion, unsteady gait and ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, though all three are often not present. Tremor and hallucinations suggest alcohol withdrawal.
items.a: Confusion, ataxia and abnormal eye movements
w: Fever, rash and stiff neck
Tremor, sweating and hallucinations
Chest pain, dyspnea and leg swelling

items.q: What is thiamine's role in the body?
items.x: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is needed by key enzymes in glucose metabolism, so deficiency harms energy-dependent tissues like the brain. It is not a hormone or electrolyte.
items.a: It is a cofactor for enzymes that metabolize carbohydrates
w: It is a hormone that lowers blood glucose
It is an electrolyte that controls heart rhythm
It is a clotting factor made by the liver

items.q: Besides chronic alcohol use, which patient is at risk for thiamine deficiency?
items.x: Poor intake and absorption, as with persistent vomiting, bariatric surgery or hyperemesis, can deplete thiamine. Well-nourished patients are not usually at risk.
items.a: A patient with prolonged vomiting after bariatric surgery
w: A patient with well-controlled high blood pressure
A healthy adult who takes a daily multivitamin
A patient recovering from a simple ankle sprain

items.q: How does ondansetron relieve nausea and vomiting?
items.x: Ondansetron is a selective 5-HT3 antagonist acting in the gut and the brain's vomiting center. Dopamine blockade describes metoclopramide and droperidol.
items.a: It blocks 5-HT3 serotonin receptors
w: It blocks dopamine D2 receptors
It blocks histamine H1 receptors
It blocks muscarinic receptors

items.q: Which ECG effect is a labeled warning for ondansetron?
items.x: Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, especially with other QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte problems. Delta waves suggest an accessory pathway.
items.a: QT interval prolongation
w: ST segment elevation
Delta waves
Peaked T waves

items.q: A patient taking an SSRI becomes agitated with tremor, clonus, sweating and fever after receiving ondansetron. What should be recognized?
items.x: Serotonin syndrome has been reported when ondansetron is used with serotonergic drugs and shows clonus, hyperthermia and agitation. It should be reported and the patient supported.
items.a: Possible serotonin syndrome
w: An expected effect of ondansetron
Acute dystonic reaction
Hypoglycemia

items.q: What is metoclopramide's mechanism as an antiemetic?
items.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and speeds stomach and upper intestinal movement. Ondansetron is the 5-HT3 blocker.
items.a: Dopamine receptor blockade and increased gastric emptying
w: Serotonin 5-HT3 blockade only
Histamine H1 blockade only
Opioid receptor stimulation in the gut

items.q: Soon after IV metoclopramide, a patient feels intensely restless and cannot sit still. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Akathisia is an extrapyramidal effect of dopamine blockers such as metoclopramide, felt as inner restlessness. It should be recognized and reported.
items.a: Akathisia
w: Anxiety disorder
Hypoglycemia
Opioid withdrawal

items.q: In which patient is metoclopramide contraindicated?
items.x: Metoclopramide increases gut motility and can be harmful when there is obstruction, perforation or GI bleeding. Gastroparesis and migraine are common uses.
items.a: A patient with suspected bowel obstruction
w: A patient with migraine and nausea
A patient with diabetic gastroparesis
A patient with nausea after surgery

items.q: Because of its boxed warning for severe tissue injury, what is the preferred route for injectable promethazine?
items.x: Promethazine can cause gangrene with IV extravasation or accidental intra-arterial or subcutaneous injection, so deep IM is preferred. Subcutaneous use is contraindicated.
items.a: Deep intramuscular injection
w: Rapid IV push
Intra-arterial injection
Subcutaneous injection

items.q: Promethazine is contraindicated in which group because of fatal respiratory depression?
items.x: Promethazine carries a boxed warning against use in children under 2 years because of fatal respiratory depression. Older adults need caution but are not absolutely excluded.
items.a: Children younger than 2 years
w: Adults older than 65 years
Pregnant patients
Patients with migraine

items.q: How does droperidol relieve nausea and vomiting?
items.x: Droperidol is a dopamine antagonist that acts in the brain's chemoreceptor trigger zone. Serotonin blockade describes ondansetron.
items.a: It blocks dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
w: It blocks serotonin receptors in the gut wall
It neutralizes stomach acid
It increases stomach emptying through cholinergic action

items.q: Which effect should be expected when droperidol is given with opioids or benzodiazepines?
items.x: Droperidol is sedating and adds to the CNS depression of opioids and benzodiazepines, so patients need close monitoring. It does not reverse opioids.
items.a: Additive sedation and central nervous system depression
w: Reversal of the opioid's effects
Marked increase in heart rate
Excessive alertness and insomnia

items.q: When is oxytocin given in the field to control postpartum bleeding?
items.x: Oxytocin can trap an undelivered twin or placenta, so it is given after delivery once another fetus is ruled out. Giving it during labor in the field can cause dangerous uterine contractions.
items.a: After the placenta delivers and no other fetus is present
w: Before the baby's head is delivered
As soon as contractions begin
Before the umbilical cord is clamped

items.q: How does oxytocin control postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony?
items.x: The uterus stops bleeding mainly by contracting around its vessels, and oxytocin strengthens those contractions. It does not act on clotting factors.
items.a: It makes the uterine muscle contract, compressing bleeding vessels
w: It activates clotting factors in the blood
It constricts vessels throughout the body
It relaxes the uterus so the placenta can separate

items.q: A pregnant patient with severe preeclampsia has a seizure. Which drug is the treatment of choice to stop and prevent eclamptic seizures?
items.x: Magnesium sulfate is more effective than other anticonvulsants for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures. Phenytoin was inferior in trials.
items.a: Magnesium sulfate
w: Phenytoin
Valproic acid
Phenobarbital

items.q: While receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia, which finding is often the first sign of toxicity?
items.x: Reflexes disappear before respiratory depression and cardiac arrest, so they are checked regularly. Decreased, not increased, urine output raises toxicity risk.
items.a: Loss of deep tendon reflexes
w: Increased urine output
Rising blood pressure
Tachycardia and tremor

items.q: How does terbutaline act when used to briefly slow preterm contractions?
items.x: Terbutaline is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes uterine as well as bronchial smooth muscle. Its injectable form carries a boxed warning against prolonged use for preterm labor.
items.a: Beta-2 stimulation relaxes uterine smooth muscle
w: Alpha-1 stimulation tightens the cervix
Calcium channel blockade stops contractions
Oxytocin receptor blockade in the uterus

items.q: Which maternal adverse effects of terbutaline should be monitored and reported?
items.x: Beta stimulation causes maternal tachycardia and can lead to arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia and pulmonary edema. Bradycardia is not expected.
items.a: Tachycardia, palpitations and chest pain
w: Bradycardia and heart block
Hypotension from vagal stimulation
Constricted pupils and drowsiness

items.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid in postpartum hemorrhage?
items.x: TXA reduces fibrin breakdown and lowers bleeding deaths when given early, but it does not make the uterus contract. Fundal massage and uterotonics such as oxytocin remain essential.
items.a: An adjunct to uterotonics and fundal massage, not a replacement
w: The first and only drug needed for atony
A uterotonic that makes the uterus contract
A replacement for blood products in severe bleeding

items.q: Why is IV tranexamic acid given slowly rather than as a rapid push?
items.x: The labeling notes that hypotension has occurred with rapid IV injection of tranexamic acid. It is not inactivated by fast administration.
items.a: Rapid injection can cause hypotension
w: Rapid injection causes hypoglycemia
Rapid injection inactivates the drug
Rapid injection causes severe bradycardia

items.q: Which IV agent is a first-line choice for severe hypertension in a patient with preeclampsia?
items.x: Labetalol, along with hydralazine and oral nifedipine, is first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal harm.
items.a: Labetalol
w: Enalaprilat
Nitroprusside
Furosemide

items.q: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate develops slow, shallow breathing and absent reflexes. Why is calcium gluconate given?
items.x: Calcium counteracts magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and heart, temporarily reversing toxicity while ventilation is supported. It does not remove magnesium from the body.
items.a: It antagonizes magnesium's effects on nerves and muscle
w: It increases kidney excretion of magnesium
It binds magnesium and inactivates it
It sedates the patient to reduce oxygen need

items.q: An infant's heart rate remains below normal with poor perfusion despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. Which drug is first-line?
items.x: Pediatric bradycardia is usually caused by hypoxia, and when it persists with poor perfusion despite good ventilation, epinephrine is the first drug. Atropine is for vagal causes or primary AV block.
items.a: Epinephrine
w: Atropine
Adenosine
Amiodarone

items.q: During intubation, a child's heart rate suddenly drops. Which cause of bradycardia is atropine most appropriate for?
items.x: Atropine blocks vagal effects, so it is appropriate for vagally mediated bradycardia or primary AV block. Hypoxic bradycardia is treated first with oxygenation and ventilation.
items.a: Increased vagal tone from airway manipulation
w: Hypoxia from a failed airway attempt
Hypothermia after cold-water drowning
Hyperkalemia from kidney failure

items.q: Why are lower concentrations of dextrose used for infants and young children than the concentrated form used in adults?
items.x: Highly concentrated dextrose is very hypertonic and can injure small veins and tissues, so diluted forms are used in children. Lower concentrations do not work faster.
items.a: Concentrated solutions are hypertonic and can damage small veins
w: Children cannot metabolize concentrated glucose
Concentrated dextrose causes seizures in children
Lower concentrations raise glucose faster

items.q: A child is having a prolonged seizure and no IV can be started. Which route of midazolam is commonly used?
items.x: Intranasal midazolam is absorbed quickly through the nasal mucosa and is effective for pediatric seizures without IV access. Oral and transdermal routes are not practical during a seizure.
items.a: Intranasal via a mucosal atomizer
w: Oral liquid
Transdermal patch
Inhaled nebulizer

items.q: Why is caution needed with naloxone in a newborn whose mother has used opioids regularly during pregnancy?
items.x: Abrupt reversal in an opioid-dependent newborn can trigger severe withdrawal and seizures, so ventilation support is the priority. Naloxone does work in newborns.
items.a: It can cause abrupt, life-threatening withdrawal including seizures
w: It has no effect in newborns
It causes severe hypoglycemia
It blocks the newborn's breathing reflex

items.q: An infant has a very fast, narrow-complex rhythm. Which feature suggests SVT that may respond to adenosine rather than sinus tachycardia?
items.x: SVT starts and stops abruptly, has little rate variability and usually lacks visible P waves. Sinus tachycardia varies with activity, has P waves and usually has a cause such as fever.
items.a: Abrupt onset with a fixed rate and absent P waves
w: Gradual rise in rate with fever and dehydration
Rate that varies with crying and activity
Visible P waves before every QRS complex

items.q: How does ondansetron help a child with vomiting from gastroenteritis?
items.x: By reducing vomiting, ondansetron helps children tolerate oral fluids and may avoid an IV. It does not treat the infection or replace fluids.
items.a: It reduces vomiting so oral rehydration can succeed
w: It cures the underlying viral infection
It stops diarrhea by slowing the gut
It replaces lost electrolytes

items.q: What should caregivers be taught when giving liquid acetaminophen to a child?
items.x: Kitchen spoons are inaccurate and many combination products also contain acetaminophen, so mixing them risks overdose and liver injury. The supplied device and weight-based dosing reduce errors.
items.a: Use the measuring device supplied and dose by weight
w: Use a kitchen spoon for convenience
Combine it with adult cold medicines
Give extra doses if the fever persists

items.q: Which child needs provider guidance before receiving ibuprofen?
items.x: NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys and can cause kidney injury in dehydrated children. The other children are common, appropriate uses.
items.a: A child with severe vomiting and signs of dehydration
w: A child with a fever and earache
A child with a sprained ankle
A child with teething discomfort

items.q: A child in severe asthma has diminished breath sounds and no audible wheezing after albuterol. How should this be interpreted?
items.x: A quiet or silent chest in severe asthma means too little air is moving to produce wheezing, which is ominous. Improvement would include better air movement and less work of breathing.
items.a: Worsening obstruction with very little air movement
w: Full recovery from the asthma attack
An expected side effect of albuterol
A sign the child is ready for discharge

items.q: During transport of a patient with norepinephrine running through a peripheral IV, what is essential?
items.x: Peripheral norepinephrine is acceptable short term in a large, proximal vein, but extravasation can cause tissue necrosis, so the site must be checked often. Sharing or flushing the line risks boluses.
items.a: Frequent checks of the IV site for infiltration
w: Flushing the line hourly to keep it open
Hanging it on the same line as the antibiotic
Checking the site only at arrival

items.q: Which finding suggests excessive vasoconstriction from a norepinephrine infusion?
items.x: Intense alpha-1 vasoconstriction can reduce blood flow to the extremities and organs, causing cool, mottled skin. Warm, flushed skin suggests vasodilation.
items.a: Cold, mottled fingers and toes with poor perfusion
w: Warm, flushed skin and bounding pulses
Low blood pressure with a slow heart rate
Increased urine output and thirst

items.q: Why should a norepinephrine infusion run through a dedicated line that is not flushed?
items.x: Norepinephrine is potent and short acting, so pushing the drug remaining in the line can cause a sudden rise in blood pressure. A dedicated line prevents unplanned boluses.
items.a: Flushing would deliver an unintended bolus and spike the blood pressure
w: Flushing would dilute it and make it inactive
Flushing would cause the drug to crystallize
Flushing would cause a drop in heart rate

items.q: Why may a fentanyl infusion have a longer effect than expected after several days?
items.x: Fentanyl is highly lipophilic, so it builds up in fat and muscle and is slowly released, prolonging its effect. Its short duration applies to single doses.
items.a: It is fat soluble and accumulates in tissues during prolonged infusion
w: It is converted into a long-acting toxic metabolite
It is excreted unchanged only by the lungs
It loses potency the longer it is infused

items.q: An intubated patient is fighting the ventilator. Why does an analgesia-first approach often start with fentanyl?
items.x: Many ventilated patients are agitated from pain, so treating pain first can reduce the need for deeper sedation. Fentanyl does not cause paralysis.
items.a: Pain often drives agitation, and treating it may reduce sedative needs
w: Fentanyl paralyzes the patient so they cannot fight
Fentanyl has no effect on breathing in ventilated patients
Fentanyl prevents delirium completely

items.q: Why may a patient with kidney failure remain sedated long after a midazolam infusion ends?
items.x: Midazolam's active metabolite is cleared by the kidneys and accumulates in renal failure, prolonging sedation. Prolonged infusion also causes accumulation in fat.
items.a: An active metabolite builds up when kidney function is poor
w: Midazolam is not removed by the liver at all
Kidney failure makes midazolam more water soluble
Midazolam converts into an opioid in kidney failure

items.q: What concern is linked to prolonged benzodiazepine sedation such as a midazolam infusion in critically ill patients?
items.x: Critical care guidelines prefer non-benzodiazepine sedation where possible because benzodiazepines are associated with delirium and longer ventilation. They do not cause hypertension.
items.a: Increased risk of delirium and longer time on the ventilator
w: Increased risk of high blood pressure
Increased risk of hypoglycemia
Increased risk of excessive alertness

items.q: How should the depth of sedation be assessed during a midazolam infusion?
items.x: Validated scales such as the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale give an objective measure to avoid under- or over-sedation. Heart rate and pupils are unreliable sedation markers.
items.a: Use a validated sedation scale such as the RASS
w: Rely on the heart rate alone
Check pupil size only
Assume sedation if the patient is quiet

items.q: In which patient should ketamine be used with caution due to its cardiovascular effects?
items.x: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects raise heart rate and blood pressure, which can worsen severe hypertension or myocardial ischemia. In hypotension or asthma these effects can be helpful.
items.a: A patient with severe, uncontrolled hypertension or active ischemia
w: A patient with septic shock and low blood pressure
A patient with asthma who needs sedation
A patient with a long bone fracture

items.q: Which effect of ketamine may require more frequent suctioning?
items.x: Ketamine increases salivary and airway secretions, which may need suctioning. It tends to relax, not tighten, bronchial smooth muscle.
items.a: Increased salivation and airway secretions
w: Dry mouth and thick mucus
Decreased gag reflex
Bronchospasm

items.q: Before giving a scheduled dose of digoxin, which assessment is most important for the nurse to perform?
items.x: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node, so a full apical count is needed to detect bradycardia before giving it. A brief radial check can miss irregular beats and undercount the rate.
items.a: Count the apical pulse for one full minute
w: Check the radial pulse for fifteen seconds
Measure blood pressure in both arms
Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants

items.q: A patient taking digoxin and furosemide reports nausea, poor appetite, and yellow-green halos around lights. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: GI upset and visual changes are classic signs of digoxin toxicity, and loop diuretics can lower potassium, which makes toxicity more likely. These are not expected effects and should be reported along with a digoxin level and potassium.
items.a: Possible digoxin toxicity, which low potassium can worsen
w: Expected adjustment effects of digoxin therapy
An allergic reaction to furosemide
Dehydration from drinking too much water

items.q: A patient is on long-term amiodarone. Which set of tests does the nurse expect to be monitored periodically?
items.x: Amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction, liver injury, and pulmonary toxicity, so these organs are monitored over time. The other panels do not target its known organ toxicities.
items.a: Thyroid, liver, and lung function tests
w: Amylase, lipase, and uric acid levels
Hemoglobin A1c, lipase, and bone density
Creatine kinase, ammonia, and lactate levels

items.q: Before a scheduled dose of oral metoprolol, the nurse finds a heart rate well below the patient's usual rate and the patient reports dizziness. What is the priority action?
items.x: Beta blockers slow the heart rate, and symptomatic bradycardia needs provider review before more drug is given. Giving the dose and rechecking later could worsen the bradycardia.
items.a: Notify the provider before giving the dose
w: Give the dose and recheck vital signs later
Give the dose with a full glass of water
Have the patient walk to assess tolerance

items.q: A patient taking lisinopril develops sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema at any time during therapy, and tongue or throat swelling can block the airway. It is not a first-dose blood pressure effect and needs urgent airway assessment and provider notification.
items.a: Angioedema, a possible airway emergency
w: Expected first-dose low blood pressure
A mild contact allergy to a food
Fluid overload from heart failure

items.q: Which laboratory value is the nurse's priority to monitor in a patient receiving furosemide?
items.x: Loop diuretics cause loss of potassium, and low potassium can trigger dangerous dysrhythmias. Furosemide tends to lower, not raise, sodium and calcium.
items.a: Serum potassium, for hypokalemia
w: Serum calcium, for hypercalcemia
Serum sodium, for hypernatremia
Blood glucose, for hypoglycemia

items.q: A patient prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin for angina asks about other medicines. Which medicine should the nurse teach the patient to avoid combining with it?
items.x: Nitrates combined with PDE-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension. Aspirin is commonly used together with nitroglycerin in coronary disease.
items.a: Sildenafil or other PDE-5 inhibitors
w: Acetaminophen for headaches
Aspirin for heart protection
Atorvastatin for cholesterol

items.q: A patient takes spironolactone and lisinopril. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?
items.x: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and ACE inhibitors also raise potassium, so hyperkalemia is the key risk. Low potassium is the concern with loop and thiazide diuretics, not this combination.
items.a: High serum potassium with muscle weakness
w: Low serum potassium with leg cramps
A mild increase in daytime urination
Mild breast tenderness that is unchanged

items.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and a rapid ventricular rate is receiving IV diltiazem. Which monitoring is the priority?
items.x: IV diltiazem slows AV conduction and dilates vessels, so bradycardia, heart block, and hypotension can develop quickly. Intake and output alone would miss these changes.
items.a: Continuous heart rhythm and frequent blood pressure
w: Hourly bedside blood glucose checks
Daily serum digoxin level
Strict intake and output only

items.q: The nurse is preparing a patient for IV adenosine to treat SVT. Which expected effect should the nurse explain?
items.x: Adenosine is given by rapid IV push with a saline flush and briefly blocks the AV node, often causing a few seconds of very slow or absent heartbeat, flushing, or chest discomfort. Its effects last seconds, not hours.
items.a: A few seconds of very slow heartbeat with flushing or chest pressure
w: Drowsiness that lasts for several hours
A sustained rise in blood pressure
Gradual slowing of the heart over a day

items.q: During a peripheral norepinephrine infusion, the nurse notes blanching, coolness, and swelling at the IV site. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Norepinephrine extravasation causes intense local vasoconstriction, and phentolamine, an alpha blocker, is infiltrated into the area to limit tissue damage. Protamine reverses heparin and has no role here.
items.a: Phentolamine infiltrated into the affected area
w: Protamine given by IV push
Naloxone given intramuscularly
Vitamin K given subcutaneously

items.q: Which route is preferred for a continuous norepinephrine infusion whenever possible?
items.x: A central line lowers the risk of tissue injury from extravasation of this potent vasoconstrictor. Small hand veins carry the highest risk of infiltration.
items.a: A central venous catheter
w: A small vein in the back of the hand
An intramuscular injection site
A subcutaneous infusion site

items.q: A patient in anaphylactic shock needs epinephrine right away and has no IV access. Which route is recommended?
items.x: Intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous injection. Undiluted IV push epinephrine can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.
items.a: Intramuscular injection into the outer thigh
w: Subcutaneous injection into the upper arm
Undiluted IV push through a new line
A dissolving tablet under the tongue

items.q: A patient receiving a dopamine infusion develops a new rapid, irregular heart rhythm. How does the nurse interpret this finding?
items.x: Dopamine stimulates beta-1 receptors and can cause tachydysrhythmias, which should be reported promptly. A new dysrhythmia is not a marker of therapeutic effect.
items.a: A known adverse effect that needs prompt reporting
w: An expected sign that the drug is working
A sign of low blood volume only
An allergic reaction to the IV diluent

items.q: Which statement best describes how dobutamine helps a patient in cardiogenic shock?
items.x: Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 agonist that strengthens contraction and raises cardiac output. Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition describes milrinone, another inotrope.
items.a: It increases heart contractility through beta-1 stimulation
w: It constricts arteries through alpha-1 stimulation
It blocks calcium channels in vascular muscle
It inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 in heart muscle

items.q: A patient receives IV phenylephrine for hypotension. Which change in vital signs should the nurse watch for as blood pressure rises?
items.x: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist, and the rise in blood pressure can trigger a reflex slowing of the heart. It lacks the beta effects that would cause tachycardia.
items.a: Reflex bradycardia
w: Marked tachycardia
Rising respiratory rate
Falling body temperature

items.q: How does vasopressin raise blood pressure in septic shock?
items.x: Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction without beta-adrenergic effects. It does not directly increase heart rate.
items.a: It constricts blood vessels through V1 receptors
w: It speeds the heart through beta-1 receptors
It dilates renal arteries through dopamine receptors
It boosts contractility by inhibiting PDE-3

items.q: A patient with decompensated heart failure is started on milrinone. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Milrinone is an inotrope and vasodilator, so hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias are the main risks. It does not cause respiratory depression.
items.a: Blood pressure and heart rhythm
w: Blood glucose for hyperglycemia
Respiratory rate for depression
Temperature for malignant hyperthermia

items.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient taking midodrine for orthostatic hypotension?
items.x: Midodrine can cause supine hypertension, so doses are taken while upright during the day and not near bedtime. Lying flat after a dose increases that risk.
items.a: Take doses during daytime hours, not close to bedtime
w: Take the last dose at bedtime for overnight effect
Lie flat for an hour after each dose
Take each dose only while lying down

items.q: Which adverse effect is the main safety concern with droxidopa, and what does the nurse teach?
items.x: Droxidopa carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension, so patients sleep with the head of the bed elevated and supine blood pressure is monitored. Hypoglycemia is not a known effect.
items.a: Supine hypertension; rest with the head of the bed raised
w: Hypoglycemia; carry a fast-acting sugar source
Bradycardia; check the pulse before standing
Hyperkalemia; avoid salt substitutes

items.q: Which laboratory test does the nurse use to evaluate the therapeutic effect of warfarin?
items.x: Warfarin is monitored with the INR, which reflects its effect on vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. The aPTT is used for unfractionated heparin.
items.a: International normalized ratio (INR)
w: Activated partial thromboplastin time
Anti-factor Xa level
Platelet count

items.q: Which dietary teaching is appropriate for a patient starting warfarin?
items.x: Vitamin K in leafy greens counters warfarin, so a steady intake keeps the INR stable. Cutting out greens entirely is unnecessary and can make the INR swing when intake changes.
items.a: Keep intake of leafy green vegetables consistent
w: Avoid all green vegetables completely
Eat extra leafy greens when bruising occurs
Take a vitamin K supplement every morning

items.q: Several days after starting heparin, a patient's platelet count has dropped by more than half and a new clot is suspected. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction that lowers platelets and paradoxically causes clotting, and it must be reported right away. Dilution would not explain a large drop with new thrombosis.
items.a: Possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
w: Expected dilution from IV fluids
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis

items.q: Which laboratory test is commonly used to monitor a continuous IV infusion of unfractionated heparin?
items.x: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with the aPTT (or an anti-Xa level by facility protocol) to keep it in the therapeutic range. The INR is used for warfarin.
items.a: Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
w: International normalized ratio (INR)
Serum fibrinogen level
Bleeding time

items.q: Which technique is correct when giving enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe?
items.x: Enoxaparin is given by deep subcutaneous injection, usually in the abdomen, and the air bubble in the prefilled syringe is not expelled. Rubbing the site increases bruising.
items.a: Inject subcutaneously in the abdomen without expelling the air bubble
w: Inject intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Rub the site firmly afterward to reduce bruising
Expel the air bubble, then inject into the thigh muscle

items.q: Which statement by a patient taking apixaban shows correct understanding?
items.x: Bleeding is the main risk with apixaban, so signs like black stools or easy bruising should be reported. Apixaban does not need routine INR monitoring, unlike warfarin.
items.a: "I will report black stools or unusual bruising."
w: "I need weekly INR checks to adjust my dose."
"I will double my next dose if I miss one."
"I can take ibuprofen freely for pain."

items.q: A patient with acute ischemic stroke symptoms is being considered for alteplase. Which finding must be confirmed before it is given?
items.x: Alteplase dissolves clots and is contraindicated in intracranial hemorrhage, so imaging must rule out bleeding first. A lipid panel has no bearing on eligibility.
items.a: A head CT showing no bleeding in the brain
w: A normal lipid panel
A recent urine culture result
That the patient has been fasting

items.q: While giving protamine to reverse heparin, which adverse effects should the nurse watch for?
items.x: Protamine can cause hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylaxis-like reactions, especially if given too fast. It does not cause hypertension or seizures.
items.a: Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and allergic reaction
w: High blood pressure and seizures
High potassium and peaked T waves
Low blood glucose and sweating

items.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease receives epoetin alfa. Which finding should the nurse report?
items.x: Epoetin raises the risk of hypertension, clots, and stroke, especially when hemoglobin rises quickly or too high. A rising reticulocyte count is an expected sign it is working.
items.a: A rapid rise in hemoglobin or new high blood pressure
w: A gradual rise in reticulocyte count
Mild tenderness at the injection site
Improved energy over several weeks

items.q: Which medicine can reduce the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel and is generally avoided with it?
items.x: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can reduce its effect. Acetaminophen has no meaningful interaction with clopidogrel.
items.a: Omeprazole
w: Acetaminophen
Levothyroxine
Metformin

items.q: Which patient is at the highest risk for dangerous hyperkalemia if given succinylcholine?
items.x: After major burns, crush injuries, or denervation, extra receptors on muscle allow succinylcholine to release large amounts of potassium. Mild dehydration does not create this risk.
items.a: A patient with a severe burn injury several days ago
w: A patient with mild dehydration
A patient with well-controlled asthma
A patient who takes a daily multivitamin

items.q: Shortly after succinylcholine is given, the patient develops jaw rigidity, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, and a fast heart rate. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Masseter rigidity with rising end-tidal CO2 and tachycardia are early signs of malignant hyperthermia, which is treated with dantrolene. Fasciculations are brief twitches, not sustained rigidity.
items.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Expected fasciculations
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Latex anaphylaxis

items.q: After intubation, a patient is receiving rocuronium. Which nursing priority applies?
items.x: Neuromuscular blockers paralyze muscles but do not affect awareness or pain, so sedation and analgesia must be given. A paralyzed patient cannot breathe or report pain.
items.a: Ensure adequate sedation and pain control, since it provides neither
w: Reduce sedation, since rocuronium causes deep sleep
Expect the patient to breathe well without support
Ask the patient to rate pain on a numeric scale

items.q: How does sugammadex reverse neuromuscular blockade?
items.x: Sugammadex forms a tight complex with rocuronium or vecuronium, removing it from the junction. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is how neostigmine works.
items.a: It binds and encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium
w: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
It blocks nicotinic receptors on muscle
It stimulates muscarinic receptors in the heart

items.q: A patient who takes oral hormonal contraceptives received sugammadex during surgery. Which teaching is appropriate?
items.x: Sugammadex can bind progestogen and lower contraceptive effect, so labeling advises a backup method for seven days. It is not true that contraceptives are unaffected.
items.a: Use a backup nonhormonal method for the next week
w: No change is needed; contraceptives are unaffected
Take two contraceptive pills the next day
Skip the next week of contraceptive pills

items.q: Which adverse effect is associated with etomidate used for rapid sequence intubation?
items.x: Etomidate briefly inhibits cortisol production, a concern in critically ill or septic patients. It is not a trigger for malignant hyperthermia.
items.a: Temporary adrenal suppression
w: Severe hypertension
Histamine-related bronchospasm
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: Why may ketamine be chosen for induction in a patient with low blood pressure?
items.x: Ketamine's sympathetic stimulation usually supports blood pressure and heart rate while preserving respiratory drive. It has no specific reversal agent.
items.a: It tends to maintain blood pressure and breathing drive
w: It lowers heart rate and blood pressure
It reliably abolishes all airway reflexes
It has a specific reversal agent

items.q: Which handling practice is important when giving propofol?
items.x: Propofol is a lipid emulsion that can grow bacteria, so aseptic technique and timely disposal of opened product are required. It is given IV, not intramuscularly.
items.a: Use strict aseptic technique, since the lipid supports bacterial growth
w: Shake the vial and give it intramuscularly
Mix it with other drugs in the same syringe
Save an opened vial in the refrigerator for tomorrow

items.q: A patient becomes oversedated after midazolam. Which reversal agent should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines such as midazolam. Naloxone reverses opioids, not benzodiazepines.
items.a: Flumazenil
w: Naloxone
Sugammadex
Neostigmine

items.q: After a rapid IV push of fentanyl, ventilation becomes difficult because the chest feels stiff. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Rapid, large IV doses of potent opioids like fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity that impairs ventilation. Fentanyl is not a malignant hyperthermia trigger.
items.a: Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
w: A severe hypertensive reaction
Malignant hyperthermia
Hyperkalemia from muscle injury

items.q: Which side effects should the nurse teach a patient to expect after using albuterol?
items.x: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist, and some beta stimulation causes tremor and tachycardia. Thrush and hoarseness are linked to inhaled corticosteroids.
items.a: Tremor, nervousness, and a fast heart rate
w: Drowsiness and a slow heart rate
Oral thrush and hoarseness
Constipation and dry eyes

items.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient using an inhaled fluticasone inhaler?
items.x: Rinsing and spitting lowers the risk of oral thrush from inhaled corticosteroids. Fluticasone is a daily controller and does not relieve sudden wheezing.
items.a: Rinse the mouth and spit after each use
w: Use it first for sudden wheezing
Swallow the rinse water after each use
Use it only on days with symptoms

items.q: Which teaching is correct about salmeterol?
items.x: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta agonist with slow onset for maintenance, not rescue. In asthma it should be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid, never used alone.
items.a: It is not used to relieve a sudden asthma attack
w: It works within seconds for acute wheezing
It can be used alone without a controller in asthma
It may be used several times every hour as needed

items.q: Which history should the nurse report before a patient starts tiotropium?
items.x: Tiotropium is an anticholinergic that can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention. Seasonal allergies are not a concern.
items.a: Narrow-angle glaucoma or urinary retention
w: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Osteoarthritis of the knees
Treated hypothyroidism

items.q: Which effect should the nurse teach patients and families to report while taking montelukast?
items.x: Montelukast has a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events. Yellow-green halos are a sign of digoxin toxicity.
items.a: Mood changes, agitation, or suicidal thoughts
w: Black, tarry stools
Yellow-green halos around lights
Gum overgrowth

items.q: A patient on theophylline starts ciprofloxacin and then reports nausea, restlessness, and a racing heart. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Ciprofloxacin slows theophylline clearance, and theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range, so toxicity can follow. A theophylline level should be checked and the provider notified.
items.a: Possible theophylline toxicity from a drug interaction
w: Expected adjustment to the antibiotic
An allergic reaction to ciprofloxacin
Worsening asthma control

items.q: A patient with diabetes is started on a short course of prednisone for an asthma flare. Which change should the nurse anticipate?
items.x: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose, so closer monitoring is needed in diabetes. Prednisone tends to lower potassium and raise the white cell count.
items.a: Higher blood glucose levels
w: Lower blood glucose levels
Higher serum potassium
Lower white blood cell count

items.q: When is oseltamivir treatment most effective for influenza?
items.x: Oseltamivir works best when started within 48 hours of symptoms, though it may still be used later for hospitalized or high-risk patients. Waiting for culture results delays benefit.
items.a: When started within two days of symptom onset
w: Only after a fever has lasted a full week
After a culture confirms flu several days later
Only if pneumonia has already developed

items.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient prescribed benzonatate capsules?
items.x: Releasing benzonatate in the mouth numbs the throat and can cause choking or severe reactions. It should also be stored away from children, for whom accidental ingestion can be fatal.
items.a: Swallow capsules whole without chewing or sucking
w: Chew the capsules for faster relief
Open the capsule and mix it in applesauce
Let the capsule dissolve under the tongue

items.q: Which history should the nurse report before a patient takes pseudoephedrine for congestion?
items.x: Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic decongestant that can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Seasonal allergies are a common reason it is used.
items.a: Uncontrolled high blood pressure
w: Seasonal allergies
Mild osteoarthritis
Iron deficiency

items.q: Which IV fluid is compatible for flushing before and after IV phenytoin?
items.x: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions, so the line is flushed with normal saline. It should not be mixed with other fluids or drugs.
items.a: Normal saline
w: Dextrose in water
Lactated Ringer's with dextrose
Any fluid already running in the line

items.q: Which teaching helps a patient manage a common long-term effect of phenytoin?
items.x: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, and good oral hygiene reduces it. Phenytoin levels are also monitored by name since it has a narrow therapeutic range.
items.a: Brush and floss carefully and see a dentist regularly
w: Expect hair thinning and use a mild shampoo
Avoid all dairy products to protect the liver
Take it with grapefruit juice to improve absorption

items.q: Which new symptom in a patient taking carbamazepine should be reported right away?
items.x: Carbamazepine can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which need urgent attention. Mild early drowsiness is common and usually fades.
items.a: Skin rash with blisters, fever, or mouth sores
w: Mild drowsiness during the first days
Mild nausea relieved by taking with food
Slight dizziness that improves with time

items.q: Which effect should the nurse teach a patient and family to watch for with levetiracetam?
items.x: Levetiracetam is linked to behavioral changes, and antiepileptics carry a warning for suicidal thoughts. Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin.
items.a: Irritability, mood changes, or thoughts of self-harm
w: Overgrowth of the gums
Excess facial and body hair
Yellowing of the skin and eyes

items.q: Which instruction is most important for a patient starting lamotrigine?
items.x: Lamotrigine has a boxed warning for serious rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially early in therapy. Gum overgrowth is a phenytoin effect.
items.a: Report any new rash, since it may signal a serious skin reaction
w: Expect weight gain during the first month
Have gum checks for overgrowth
Expect a fine hand tremor as it starts working

items.q: Which laboratory tests does the nurse expect to be monitored for a patient taking valproic acid?
items.x: Valproic acid can cause hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia, so liver tests and platelets are checked, along with valproic acid levels. A lithium level is unrelated.
items.a: Liver function tests and platelet count
w: Thyroid panel and lipid panel
Serum lithium and sodium
Serum magnesium and phosphate

items.q: After IV lorazepam is given for status epilepticus, which assessment is the nurse's priority?
items.x: Benzodiazepines can depress breathing, especially after repeated doses, so airway and breathing are monitored closely. Hypertension is not a typical effect.
items.a: Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
w: Blood pressure for hypertension
Hourly bedside blood glucose
Bladder for urinary retention

items.q: Which history is a contraindication to sumatriptan?
items.x: Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease and uncontrolled hypertension. Seasonal allergies do not affect triptan use.
items.a: Coronary artery disease
w: Seasonal allergies
Iron deficiency anemia
Osteoarthritis

items.q: Which finding should the nurse report in a patient taking donepezil?
items.x: As a cholinesterase inhibitor, donepezil increases vagal tone and can cause bradycardia and syncope. Dry mouth and constipation are anticholinergic effects, the opposite of its action.
items.a: Slow heart rate or fainting
w: Dry mouth and constipation
Increased appetite
Thinning hair

items.q: Before giving IV morphine, which assessment is most important?
items.x: Respiratory depression is the most dangerous opioid effect, and increasing sedation usually comes before it. Bowel sounds matter for constipation but are not the priority.
items.a: Respiratory rate and level of sedation
w: Presence of bowel sounds
Pupil response to light only
Oral temperature

items.q: After naloxone reverses an opioid overdose, what must the nurse continue to monitor for?
items.x: Naloxone often wears off before longer-acting opioids, so sedation and slow breathing can return. Repeat doses may be needed.
items.a: Return of respiratory depression as naloxone wears off
w: Persistent hypertensive crisis
Severe hypoglycemia
Prolonged muscle paralysis

items.q: Which teaching helps prevent accidental acetaminophen overdose?
items.x: Many combination products contain acetaminophen, and taking several at once can cause liver injury. Over-the-counter status does not make any amount safe.
items.a: Check cold and sleep products for hidden acetaminophen
w: Take it with alcohol to improve its effect
Any amount is safe because it is sold over the counter
Combine it freely with other pain relievers

items.q: Which finding should the nurse report in a patient receiving ketorolac?
items.x: Ketorolac is a potent NSAID with boxed warnings for kidney injury and GI bleeding, and its total course is limited. Improved pain is the intended effect.
items.a: Decreased urine output or black stools
w: Mild drowsiness after a dose
Improved pain scores
Slight warmth at the injection site

items.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient using a fentanyl transdermal patch?
items.x: Heat increases fentanyl absorption from the patch and can cause a fatal overdose. Cutting the patch damages the release system.
items.a: Avoid heating pads, hot tubs, and direct heat over the patch
w: Cut the patch in half for a smaller effect
Apply each new patch to the same spot
Cover the patch with a heating pad at night

items.q: Why is hydromorphone considered a high-alert medicine?
items.x: Hydromorphone is several times more potent than morphine, and look-alike names and products have led to fatal errors. Naloxone does reverse it.
items.a: It is far more potent than morphine, so mix-ups can cause overdose
w: It has no reversal agent
It causes severe hypertension
It is given only by the intrathecal route

items.q: Which adverse effect requires ECG monitoring in a patient taking methadone?
items.x: Methadone can prolong the QT interval and cause torsades de pointes. It does not cause hyperkalemia.
items.a: QT prolongation and dysrhythmias
w: Hyperkalemia
Gum overgrowth
Malignant hyperthermia

items.q: A patient taking warfarin asks about using ibuprofen for back pain. Which response is accurate?
items.x: NSAIDs impair platelet function and irritate the GI tract, adding to warfarin's bleeding risk. They do not make warfarin weaker.
items.a: It increases bleeding risk when combined with warfarin
w: It lowers the INR and makes warfarin weaker
It has no interaction with warfarin
It speeds up clotting and raises clot risk

items.q: Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for during a dexmedetomidine infusion?
items.x: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone, so bradycardia and hypotension are its most common effects. It usually causes little respiratory depression.
items.a: Bradycardia and hypotension
w: Hyperthermia and muscle rigidity
Hyperkalemia and peaked T waves
Severe hypertension and fast heart rate

items.q: Which interaction is a concern when tramadol is given to a patient taking an SSRI?
items.x: Tramadol has serotonergic activity, and combining it with SSRIs raises the risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures. Hyperkalemia is not linked to this combination.
items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Neutropenia

items.q: A patient taking lithium has vomiting, diarrhea, coarse hand tremor, and confusion. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: GI symptoms, coarse tremor, and confusion are signs of lithium toxicity, which has a narrow therapeutic range. A fine tremor can be expected, but a coarse tremor with confusion is not.
items.a: Possible lithium toxicity needing a lithium level
w: Expected side effects that will pass
Anxiety that needs a benzodiazepine
Food poisoning unrelated to lithium

items.q: Which teaching helps keep lithium levels stable?
items.x: Low sodium or dehydration causes the kidneys to retain lithium and raises levels. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen also raise lithium levels.
items.a: Keep salt and fluid intake consistent day to day
w: Follow a very low-salt diet
Limit fluids to reduce urination
Use ibuprofen freely for headaches

items.q: Which symptom should a patient taking clozapine report right away?
items.x: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia, so signs of infection need urgent evaluation with an ANC. Weight gain and drooling are common but not emergencies.
items.a: Fever, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms
w: Mild weight gain over months
Drowsiness after evening doses
Increased saliva at night

items.q: A patient on haloperidol develops high fever, rigid muscles, confusion, and unstable blood pressure. What does the nurse recognize?
items.x: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability define neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency. Tardive dyskinesia causes involuntary movements without fever.
items.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Acute dystonia
Akathisia

items.q: A young adult is starting sertraline for depression. Which monitoring is most important early in treatment?
items.x: Antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children and young adults, especially early or after dose changes. Routine sertraline levels are not used.
items.a: Watch for worsening depression or suicidal thoughts
w: Check blood glucose before each dose
Monitor for gum overgrowth
Check a sertraline level weekly

items.q: Which foods should a patient taking tranylcypromine avoid?
items.x: MAOIs block the breakdown of tyramine, and high-tyramine foods can trigger a hypertensive crisis. Fresh meats and fish are low in tyramine.
items.a: Aged cheeses, cured meats, and tap beer
w: Fresh chicken, rice, and apples
Plain yogurt, oatmeal, and bananas
Fresh fish, pasta, and green beans

items.q: Which monitoring is most important for a patient taking olanzapine long term?
items.x: Olanzapine commonly causes weight gain, hyperglycemia, and high lipids, so metabolic monitoring is routine. Lithium levels are unrelated.
items.a: Weight, blood glucose, and lipid levels
w: Thyroid function and calcium
Lithium level and sodium
Uric acid and creatine kinase

items.q: Which teaching is correct for a buprenorphine-naloxone sublingual film?
items.x: The film is designed to be absorbed under the tongue, and swallowing or chewing it lowers absorption. Naloxone is included to discourage injection misuse.
items.a: Let the film dissolve fully under the tongue
w: Swallow the film whole with water
Chew the film for a faster effect
Dissolve the film in juice and drink it

items.q: Which teaching is essential for a patient taking disulfiram?
items.x: Even small amounts of alcohol, including in mouthwash or cooking, can cause flushing, vomiting, and a racing heart. Any form of alcohol can trigger the reaction.

w: Adenosine
Atropine
Diltiazem

items.q: Which drug is an accepted alternative to amiodarone for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation?

Sodium bicarbonate
Calcium chloride

items.q: A patient on long-term amiodarone reports increasing dyspnea and dry cough, and DLCO has fallen. What should be suspected?

items.q: During an arrest, neither IV nor IO access can be obtained, but the patient is intubated. Which drug can be given through the endotracheal tube?

items.q: After sodium bicarbonate is given during resuscitation, what change should the respiratory therapist anticipate?

items.a: A transient rise in ETCO2 and PaCO2
w: A sharp fall in ETCO2
Immediate bronchospasm
A drop in serum sodium

items.q: A patient with opioid overdose has a respiratory rate of 4. After IV naloxone, when is improvement in rate and depth typically seen?
items.x: IV naloxone acts within a couple of minutes; intranasal and IM routes take a few minutes longer. Breathing rate, depth, SpO2 and ETCO2 are reassessed.

w: After about 20-30 minutes

Only after a second dose

items.q: An overdose patient breathes normally after naloxone, then an hour later becomes drowsy with shallow respirations. What best explains this?
items.x: Naloxone's effect typically lasts about 30-90 minutes, shorter than many opioids, including long-acting and some synthetic opioids. Continued monitoring is essential.

w: Naloxone itself causes delayed sedation
The patient developed naloxone tolerance
Naloxone triggered benzodiazepine release

items.q: Shortly after naloxone, a patient with heroin overdose develops frothy sputum, crackles and worsening hypoxemia. What is the most likely cause?

items.a: Pulmonary edema associated with abrupt opioid reversal
w: Aspiration of naloxone into the airway

Methemoglobinemia from naloxone

items.q: An apneic patient with suspected opioid overdose has a pulse. What is the first priority?

items.a: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
w: Wait for naloxone to restore breathing
Begin chest compressions immediately
Obtain an arterial blood gas

items.q: Why is flumazenil used cautiously in a patient who takes benzodiazepines daily?
items.x: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but can trigger seizures in chronic users and in mixed overdoses involving tricyclic antidepressants.
items.a: It can precipitate withdrawal seizures
w: It causes severe opioid withdrawal
It produces prolonged neuromuscular blockade
It causes rebound pulmonary hypertension

items.q: After procedural sedation with midazolam, flumazenil restores alertness, but 45 minutes later the patient is drowsy with slow, shallow breathing. What explains this?
items.x: Flumazenil acts within 1-2 minutes but lasts roughly an hour or less, so re-sedation can occur. Respiratory rate, depth and SpO2 are monitored afterward.
items.a: Flumazenil's effect ended before midazolam's
w: Flumazenil causes delayed respiratory depression
Midazolam was converted into an opioid
Flumazenil raises the effect of midazolam

items.q: A patient sedated with midazolam and fentanyl receives flumazenil. He wakes slightly, but his respiratory rate stays at 6. Why?

Flumazenil worsens respiratory depression
The midazolam blocks flumazenil's receptor site

items.q: A client started sertraline 8 days ago and says, "This isn't working, I still feel down." Which response is most accurate?
items.x: SSRIs often cause side effects before benefit. Full antidepressant effect commonly takes 4-6 weeks, so early teaching supports adherence.
items.a: Full benefit usually takes about 4 to 6 weeks of regular use.
w: Sertraline should work within the first 2 to 3 days if effective.

items.q: The boxed warning on fluoxetine and other antidepressants concerns which risk?
items.x: All antidepressants carry a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents and young adults, especially early in treatment.
items.a: Increased suicidal thoughts in children, teens and young adults
w: Life-threatening liver failure in adults over age 65
Sudden cardiac death in people with heart disease
Severe low white blood cell counts in all age groups

items.q: A 19-year-old begins escitalopram for depression. When is close monitoring for suicidal thoughts most important?
items.x: Risk is highest early in treatment and around dose changes. Energy may return before mood improves, giving a window of increased risk.

w: Only after the medicine reaches full effect at 6 weeks

Only if the client has a prior suicide attempt

items.q: Duloxetine belongs to which class, which also explains its use for chronic nerve pain?

items.a: Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI)
w: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)
Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor

items.q: A client on an SSRI asks about side effects that may affect a relationship. Which effect is common and worth discussing openly?

Loss of taste for sweet and salty foods
Gradual darkening of the skin and nails

items.q: Which finding in a client taking lithium most strongly suggests toxicity?
items.x: Fine tremor, thirst and frequent urination are expected. Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, slurred speech, unsteady gait and confusion signal toxicity and need prompt reporting.
items.a: Coarse hand tremor with slurred speech and confusion
w: Fine hand tremor and mild thirst in the first week
Gradual weight gain over several months
Increased urination at night with normal thinking

items.q: A client on lithium mentions taking over-the-counter ibuprofen daily for back pain. Why is this important to report?
items.x: NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors reduce lithium clearance by the kidneys and can raise levels into the toxic range.
items.a: NSAIDs can raise lithium levels toward toxicity.
w: Ibuprofen makes lithium work much more slowly.
NSAIDs lower lithium levels and cause relapse.
Ibuprofen and lithium together cause severe rash.

items.q: Which teaching about fluids and diet is most appropriate for a client taking lithium?
items.x: Lithium is handled like sodium. Low salt intake, dehydration or heavy sweating raise lithium levels, so steady intake helps keep levels stable.
items.a: Keep fluid and salt intake steady from day to day.
w: Cut back sharply on salt to protect the heart.
Limit fluids so the medicine stays concentrated.
Eat a high-salt diet on days with low mood.

items.q: Besides lithium levels, which labs are monitored periodically during long-term lithium therapy?
items.x: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and affect kidney function, so thyroid and kidney tests are checked at baseline and periodically.
items.a: Kidney function and thyroid function
w: Liver enzymes and blood ammonia
Platelet count and clotting times
Creatine kinase and serum potassium

items.q: When is a blood sample for a routine lithium level usually drawn?
items.x: Lithium levels are trough levels, typically drawn about 12 hours after the last dose, so results can be compared reliably over time.
items.a: About 12 hours after the last dose, before the next one
w: Within 1 hour after swallowing the last dose
Any time of day, since timing does not matter
Right after a meal to reflect peak absorption

items.q: A client on lithium has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days from a stomach virus. What is the main concern?
items.x: Dehydration and sodium loss reduce lithium excretion and raise levels. Illness with vomiting or diarrhea should be reported to the prescriber.
items.a: Fluid and sodium loss may push lithium to toxic levels.
w: The virus will make lithium completely ineffective.
Lithium will cause the virus to last much longer.
Diarrhea means the client is allergic to lithium.

items.q: A client taking valproate for bipolar disorder reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting. What should be suspected?
items.x: Valproate carries boxed warnings for pancreatitis, liver injury and birth defects. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting needs prompt reporting.
items.a: Pancreatitis, a boxed warning for valproate
w: Expected stomach upset that fades in days
A sign that the dose is too low to work
Lithium-like toxicity from dehydration

items.q: Why is valproate use in people who could become pregnant a major counseling topic?
items.x: Valproate is strongly teratogenic, with risk of neural tube defects and lower IQ in exposed children. Pregnancy plans should be discussed with the prescriber.
items.a: It carries a high risk of birth defects such as neural tube defects.
w: It reliably causes birth control pills to fail.
It causes infertility that is usually permanent.
It is safe in pregnancy but not while breastfeeding.

items.q: A client taking phenelzine is planning lunch. Which choice is of greatest concern?
items.x: Aged cheeses and cured or fermented meats are high in tyramine, which can trigger a hypertensive crisis with an MAOI. Fresh dairy and fresh meats are low in tyramine.
items.a: Aged cheddar cheese and salami on crackers
w: Grilled chicken breast with steamed rice
Fresh cottage cheese with sliced peaches
Scrambled eggs with toast and fresh milk

items.q: A client on phenelzine suddenly develops a severe headache at the back of the head, stiff neck and pounding heartbeat. What does this suggest?
items.x: Occipital headache, stiff neck, palpitations and sweating are classic signs of MAOI hypertensive crisis, an emergency to report immediately.
items.a: Hypertensive crisis from a tyramine or drug interaction

Lithium toxicity from poor fluid intake
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from dopamine block

items.q: Combining phenelzine with which medicine poses the highest risk of serotonin syndrome?
items.x: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, meperidine, tramadol or dextromethorphan can cause serotonin syndrome. A washout period is required between them.

w: Acetaminophen
Docusate
Loratadine

items.q: A client recently had an antidepressant added to another serotonergic drug and now has agitation, sweating, fever, diarrhea and jerking reflexes in the legs. Which condition fits best?

items.a: Serotonin syndrome
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Lithium toxicity
Acute dystonic reaction

items.q: A young adult received haloperidol for the first time 6 hours ago. The neck is twisted to one side and the eyes are rolled upward. What is this?

items.a: Acute dystonic reaction
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Akathisia

items.q: Which medicine is commonly used to treat acute dystonia caused by an antipsychotic?

w: Buspirone
Lithium
Trazodone

items.q: A client started on fluphenazine paces the hall and says, "I can't sit still, I feel jittery inside." Which effect is most likely?
