items.a: Akathisia
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Serotonin syndrome
Catatonia

items.q: After years of fluphenazine, a client has repeated lip smacking, tongue thrusting and grimacing. What is the most likely condition?
items.x: Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect of long-term dopamine blockade, with involuntary orofacial movements that may be permanent.
items.a: Tardive dyskinesia
w: Acute dystonia
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Akathisia

items.q: Which tool is used to screen clients on antipsychotics for tardive dyskinesia?
items.x: The AIMS is a structured exam for involuntary movements, done at baseline and periodically during antipsychotic treatment.
items.a: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS)
w: Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)
Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA-Ar)
Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale

items.q: A client on haloperidol for several weeks now has a shuffling gait, masklike face, stiff arms and a pill-rolling tremor. What is this?
items.x: Dopamine blockade can mimic Parkinson disease, usually appearing after weeks. It is a form of EPS and often responds to anticholinergic treatment.
items.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome

items.x: High-potency first-generation agents like haloperidol and fluphenazine cause the most EPS. Quetiapine and clozapine have very low EPS risk.

Clozapine
Olanzapine

items.x: Olanzapine has high risk of weight gain, diabetes and high lipids. Metabolic monitoring is recommended at baseline and regularly afterward.

w: Thyroid function, kidney function, and sodium
Liver enzymes, ammonia, and platelet count
Absolute neutrophil count every week

items.q: A client recently started on quetiapine reports feeling very sleepy and dizzy when standing up. These effects are best explained by:
items.x: Quetiapine is strongly sedating and blocks alpha receptors, causing orthostatic hypotension. Teach rising slowly and report fainting or falls.
items.a: Sedation and orthostatic hypotension, common with quetiapine
w: Early neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Acute dystonia affecting the inner ear
An allergic reaction needing epinephrine

items.q: A client taking risperidone reports breast enlargement and milky nipple discharge. What is the likely cause?

items.a: Elevated prolactin from dopamine blockade
w: Low thyroid hormone from the medicine
High blood sugar from metabolic effects
Low sodium from fluid retention

items.q: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 104 F, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and a fluctuating blood pressure. What is the priority?
items.x: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability suggest NMS, a life-threatening emergency needing immediate medical care.
items.a: Report immediately as possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Recheck vital signs at the next routine round.
Offer fluids and reassess in a few hours.

items.x: Muscle rigidity and breakdown raise CK, sometimes dramatically. White blood cell count is often elevated as well.
items.a: Creatine kinase (CK)

Serum lithium level
Hemoglobin A1c

items.q: Which finding favors neuroleptic malignant syndrome over serotonin syndrome?
items.x: NMS develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slowed movement. Serotonin syndrome starts within hours with clonus, hyperreflexia and GI symptoms.

w: Clonus and hyperreflexia within a few hours
Diarrhea with shivering soon after a new SSRI
Dilated pupils and agitation after tramadol

items.q: What is a main advantage of haloperidol decanoate over daily oral tablets?
items.x: Long-acting injectable antipsychotics release medicine over weeks, helping people who struggle with daily pills. Side effect risks remain.
items.a: It supports adherence because one injection lasts for weeks.
w: It has no risk of extrapyramidal side effects at all.
It works within minutes for acute agitation.
It cannot cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

items.q: A client taking clozapine reports a sore throat and fever. Why is this important to report promptly?
items.x: Clozapine carries a boxed warning for severe neutropenia. ANC is monitored, and signs of infection need prompt evaluation.
items.a: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia and serious infection.
w: Clozapine commonly causes seasonal allergies.
Fever means the clozapine level is too low.
Sore throat is an early sign of tardive dyskinesia.

items.q: What is the boxed warning shared by all antipsychotics?
items.x: Antipsychotics are not approved for dementia-related psychosis because they raise mortality in older adults with dementia, largely from cardiovascular and infectious causes.
items.a: Increased death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis
w: Increased suicidal thoughts in children and teenagers
Fatal liver failure in the first months of therapy
Life-threatening rash in people of Asian ancestry

items.q: A client prescribed lorazepam says they still drink a few beers every evening. What is the main concern?
items.x: Benzodiazepines and alcohol are both CNS depressants. Together they can cause deep sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.
items.a: Additive sedation and dangerously slowed breathing
w: Alcohol will make lorazepam stop working entirely

Alcohol triggers a disulfiram-like flushing reaction

items.q: The boxed warning for alprazolam highlights danger when it is combined with which drugs?

items.a: Opioids
w: SSRIs
Antacids
Stimulants

items.q: A client who has taken alprazolam daily for years wants to quit abruptly on their own. What is the most serious risk?

items.a: Withdrawal seizures
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Serotonin syndrome
Hypertensive crisis

items.q: Why does alprazolam carry a higher risk of rebound anxiety and dependence than longer-acting benzodiazepines?
items.x: Short-acting, fast-onset benzodiazepines produce stronger reinforcement and more interdose rebound symptoms, increasing misuse and dependence risk.

It blocks serotonin reuptake like an SSRI.

w: Rapid weight gain and new-onset diabetes
Hypertensive crisis with aged cheese
Uncontrollable lip smacking and grimacing

items.x: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. In dependent patients it can provoke acute withdrawal and seizures, so it is used cautiously.

w: Naloxone
Naltrexone
Benztropine

items.q: A client wants to use buspirone only when a panic attack starts. Which teaching is accurate?

items.a: It works only with regular daily use and takes weeks to help.
w: It works within minutes, just like lorazepam.
It is most effective when taken only at bedtime.
It should be chewed for faster relief of panic.

items.x: Buspirone does not cause dependence, euphoria or significant withdrawal and is not a controlled substance.

It works faster than any benzodiazepine.

w: Lithium levels for toxicity
Weekly absolute neutrophil counts
AIMS exams for involuntary movements

items.q: Where is methadone dispensed for treatment of opioid use disorder?

items.a: Through federally certified opioid treatment programs
w: At any retail pharmacy with a routine prescription
Only in hospital emergency departments
Through online pharmacies by mail order

items.q: A client used heroin 4 hours ago and has no withdrawal signs. Why is starting buprenorphine now a concern?
items.x: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist. Given while a full agonist is still active, it displaces it and triggers sudden withdrawal; induction usually waits for mild to moderate withdrawal.

It causes severe rebound high blood pressure.

items.q: Why is naloxone included in buprenorphine-naloxone films and tablets?

w: To make buprenorphine absorb faster under the tongue
To treat constipation caused by the buprenorphine
To lower the risk of liver injury from buprenorphine

items.q: A client being considered for naltrexone used opioids two days ago. What is the concern?

items.a: Naltrexone can cause sudden, severe opioid withdrawal.

Naltrexone causes a disulfiram-like reaction.
Naltrexone will be absorbed too slowly to help.

items.q: Which safety teaching applies to people who have been taking naltrexone and later return to opioid use?
items.x: After a period of opioid blockade, tolerance falls. Using previous amounts of opioids can cause fatal overdose; naloxone access is important.

items.q: Which product should a client on disulfiram be taught to check labels on because it may contain alcohol?

w: Toothpaste

Sunscreen

items.q: Which two side effects are most common when a child starts methylphenidate?
items.x: Stimulants commonly cause insomnia and appetite suppression, along with headache and stomach ache.
items.a: Trouble sleeping and decreased appetite
w: Weight gain and daytime sleepiness
Hair loss and dry cough
Increased thirst and frequent urination

items.q: Why are stimulant doses for ADHD usually scheduled in the morning?
items.x: Stimulants increase alertness for hours. Doses taken later in the day commonly interfere with falling asleep.

w: Stimulants are absorbed only on an empty stomach.
Morning doses prevent tardive dyskinesia.

items.q: Which routine monitoring is especially important for a school-age child on amphetamine salts?
items.x: Stimulants can slow growth through appetite suppression. Height and weight are tracked, and slowed growth is reported to the prescriber.

w: Weekly white blood cell counts
Lithium levels every three months
Thyroid function before each refill

items.q: Methylphenidate and amphetamine products are in which controlled substance schedule?
items.x: Stimulants for ADHD are Schedule II because of their high potential for misuse and dependence, which limits refills.

Not controlled

items.q: The boxed warning for amphetamine products focuses on which risk?

Severe low white blood cell counts
Fatal liver failure in young children

items.q: Before starting a stimulant, which history is most important to ask about?

items.a: Heart disease, fainting, or sudden death in the family

Prior childhood ear infections
Lactose intolerance or food allergy

items.q: A teen on methylphenidate notices fingers turning white and painful in the cold. What should be done with this information?
items.x: Stimulants carry a warning for peripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud's phenomenon. New color changes, pain or sores in fingers or toes should be reported.

Treat it as an allergy to the medicine's dye.
Assume it is a sign of low blood sugar.

items.q: A college student on a stimulant says friends keep asking for pills during exams. Which response is most appropriate?
items.x: Diversion of Schedule II stimulants is common on campuses, illegal and dangerous. Secure storage and open discussion reduce misuse.
items.a: Sharing is illegal and risky; keep the medicine stored securely.

Giving pills to friends is legal if no money changes hands.

items.q: Which group of findings suggests stimulant misuse or overdose?
items.x: Stimulant toxicity causes sympathetic overdrive: agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and sometimes psychosis or seizures.

Low blood pressure, slow pulse and drowsiness
Lip smacking, tongue thrusting and grimacing

items.q: A child on methylphenidate begins hearing voices and becomes very suspicious. What is the best interpretation?

items.q: How does atomoxetine differ from methylphenidate?
items.x: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. It is not controlled and builds benefit over weeks, unlike stimulants.
items.a: It is a non-stimulant that takes several weeks for full effect.
w: It is a stimulant that works within one hour.
It is a Schedule II drug with high misuse risk.
It is an injectable used only in hospitals.

items.q: For an adolescent with ADHD and a history of substance misuse, which medicine is often preferred?
items.x: Atomoxetine has negligible misuse potential and is not a controlled substance, making it a common choice when misuse is a concern.
items.a: Atomoxetine
w: Methylphenidate
Dextroamphetamine
Lisdexamfetamine

items.q: Atomoxetine carries a boxed warning for which risk?
items.x: Like antidepressants, atomoxetine has a boxed warning for increased suicidal ideation in children and adolescents. Mood changes should be monitored.
items.a: Suicidal thoughts in children and adolescents
w: Abuse, misuse and addiction
Sudden cardiac death in adults
Severe neutropenia and infection

items.q: A teen on atomoxetine reports dark urine, itching and yellowing of the eyes. What is the concern?
items.x: Rare severe liver injury has been reported with atomoxetine. Jaundice, dark urine or right upper abdominal pain need prompt evaluation.
items.a: Possible liver injury, which should be reported promptly
w: Expected dehydration from reduced appetite
A harmless color change from the capsule dye
Normal effect of the medicine reaching full strength

items.q: What makes lisdexamfetamine different from immediate-release amphetamine?
items.x: Lisdexamfetamine is converted to dextroamphetamine in the blood, giving smooth, long action and less appeal for snorting or injecting. It remains Schedule II.
items.a: It is a prodrug activated in the blood after absorption.
w: It is not a controlled substance in the US.
It is a non-stimulant that acts on serotonin.
It works only when applied as a skin patch.

items.q: Extended-release clonidine for ADHD has which important safety issue?
items.x: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that causes drowsiness and low blood pressure; abrupt cessation can cause rebound hypertension, so changes are tapered by the prescriber.
items.a: Rebound high blood pressure if it is ended abruptly
w: Severe insomnia and appetite loss
High misuse risk as a Schedule II drug
Tardive dyskinesia after long-term use

items.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury has an intrathecal baclofen pump. During therapy he has high fever, itching, rebound spasticity and confusion. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Abrupt loss of intrathecal baclofen causes fever, rebound spasticity, pruritus, altered mental status and can progress to seizures and death. It is a medical emergency.
items.a: Baclofen withdrawal from pump failure or an empty reservoir
w: Autonomic dysreflexia from a full bladder
Malignant hyperthermia from exercise
Expected response to increased activity

items.q: Baclofen reduces spasticity mainly by acting at which site?
items.x: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist that inhibits reflexes at the spinal level.
items.a: GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord
w: Calcium release in skeletal muscle
Acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem only

items.q: A patient with hemiplegia uses extensor tone in the affected leg to stand. After oral baclofen is started, what change should the therapist anticipate?
items.x: Spasticity reduction can unmask weakness, and some patients rely on extensor tone for standing and transfers.
items.a: Reduced ability to bear weight through the affected leg during transfers
w: Improved standing because of increased leg strength
Greater extensor tone during gait
No change in function, only in reflexes

items.q: Which statement about suddenly running out of oral baclofen is correct?
items.x: Abrupt withdrawal of oral baclofen can cause hallucinations, seizures and severe rebound spasticity, so missed supplies should be reported.
items.a: It can cause hallucinations, seizures and rebound spasticity
w: It is harmless because baclofen has a short half-life
It only causes mild muscle soreness
It improves strength within a day

items.q: A patient on tizanidine reports dizziness when standing at the start of each session. Which effect of the drug best explains this?
items.x: Tizanidine is a central alpha-2 agonist like clonidine and commonly causes hypotension and sedation.
items.a: Hypotension from central alpha-2 agonist action
w: Hypoglycemia from increased insulin release
Bradykinesia from dopamine blockade
Vestibular damage from ototoxicity

items.q: Which laboratory value is monitored in patients taking tizanidine long term?
items.x: Tizanidine can cause liver injury, so liver tests are monitored.
items.a: Liver function tests
w: Serum creatine kinase only
Thyroid stimulating hormone
Hemoglobin A1c

items.q: Which antispasticity drug works directly on skeletal muscle rather than in the central nervous system?
items.x: Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so it causes generalized muscle weakness with less sedation.
items.a: Dantrolene
w: Baclofen
Tizanidine
Diazepam

items.q: Besides spasticity, dantrolene is used to treat which emergency condition?
items.x: IV dantrolene is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia triggered by certain anesthetics.
items.a: Malignant hyperthermia
w: Autonomic dysreflexia
Neuroleptic-induced tardive dyskinesia
Status asthmaticus

items.q: Which adverse effect of dantrolene is most important to report?
items.x: Dantrolene carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity; jaundice and dark urine suggest liver injury.
items.a: Yellowing of the skin or dark urine
w: Mild dry mouth
Brief tingling in the feet
Slight increase in appetite

items.q: After botulinum toxin injection into the elbow flexors for spasticity, when is the peak effect usually seen?
items.x: Effect begins in several days, peaks in a few weeks and wears off over about 3 months, so stretching and splinting are timed to the peak.
items.a: About 2 to 6 weeks after injection
w: Within the first hour
On the first day only
About 6 months after injection

items.q: Botulinum toxin reduces focal spasticity by which mechanism?
items.x: The toxin cleaves proteins needed for acetylcholine release; nerve sprouting restores function over months.
items.a: Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
w: Blocking calcium release inside muscle fibers
Stimulating GABA-B receptors in the cord
Destroying the motor nerve permanently

items.q: Which intervention best complements botulinum toxin injection for a spastic plantarflexor?
items.x: The window of reduced tone is used to lengthen tissue with stretching, casting or splinting and to train the antagonist.
items.a: Serial casting or stretching to gain dorsiflexion range
w: Vigorous strengthening of the injected calf
Heat over the injection site for the first day
Complete rest of the limb for a month

items.q: Cyclobenzaprine is structurally similar to which drug class, explaining its sedation and dry mouth?
items.x: Cyclobenzaprine resembles tricyclics and has anticholinergic effects, making it a Beers Criteria drug for older adults.
items.a: Tricyclic antidepressants
w: Benzodiazepines
Opioid agonists
Beta-blockers

items.q: For which condition is cyclobenzaprine most appropriate?
items.x: Cyclobenzaprine is labeled for acute musculoskeletal spasm, not for spasticity from upper motor neuron lesions.
items.a: Acute muscle spasm from a back strain
w: Spasticity after spinal cord injury
Spasticity in multiple sclerosis
Rigidity in Parkinson disease

items.q: An older adult takes diazepam for muscle spasm. Which therapy concern is greatest?
items.x: Benzodiazepines cause sedation, slowed reaction time and falls, especially in older adults, and add to opioid sedation.
items.a: Sedation and impaired balance increasing fall risk
w: Rapid heart rate during exercise
Excess muscle tone after sessions
Low risk of interaction with opioids

items.q: Which skeletal muscle relaxant carries the greatest concern for misuse and dependence?
items.x: Carisoprodol is metabolized to meprobamate and is a controlled substance with misuse potential.
items.a: Carisoprodol
w: Metaxalone
Methocarbamol
Chlorzoxazone

items.q: A patient takes immediate-release oral oxycodone for post-op knee pain. When is a therapy session most likely to coincide with peak pain relief?
items.x: Oral immediate-release opioids peak in roughly 30 to 60 minutes, so coordinating with nursing for timing improves participation.
items.a: About 1 hour after the dose
w: About 5 minutes after the dose
About 8 hours after the dose
Right before the next dose is due

items.q: A patient on opioids says pain is zero during aggressive range of motion after a tendon repair. What is the main concern?
items.x: Analgesics blunt protective pain; the therapist should follow protocol limits rather than pain alone.
items.a: Pain relief may mask warning pain and allow tissue overstress
w: Opioids speed tendon healing
The patient cannot be on an opioid
Pain-free motion confirms the repair is strong

items.q: Which opioid side effect most directly increases fall risk when moving from supine to standing?
items.x: Opioids cause vasodilation and sedation, so check vitals with position changes and guard during early mobility.
items.a: Orthostatic hypotension and sedation
w: Constipation
Pruritus
Urinary retention

items.q: Which opioid side effect usually persists with ongoing use and should be asked about often?
items.x: Tolerance develops to most opioid effects but not to constipation; mobility and fluids help, and changes should be reported.
items.a: Constipation
w: Sedation
Nausea
Respiratory depression

items.q: A patient wears a fentanyl transdermal patch on the low back. What is the main concern with using a hot pack over that area?
items.x: FDA labeling warns that external heat raises fentanyl absorption and can cause fatal respiratory depression.
items.a: Heat increases drug absorption and can cause overdose
w: Heat makes the patch stop working
Heat causes the patch to lose adhesion only
There is no interaction between heat and the patch

items.q: Which finding during a session in a patient on opioids should be reported right away?
items.x: Excess sedation and slowed breathing signal opioid-induced respiratory depression.
items.a: Difficult to arouse with slow, shallow breathing
w: Mild itching of the forearms
Report of a dry mouth
Pain rated lower than yesterday

items.q: A patient takes tramadol and an SSRI. Which symptom pattern should be reported as a possible drug interaction?
items.x: Tramadol adds serotonin effects and can lead to serotonin syndrome; it also lowers the seizure threshold.
items.a: Agitation, tremor, sweating and fast heart rate
w: Slow heart rate and dry skin
Gradual weight gain and fatigue
Improved mood and energy

items.q: A patient with osteoarthritis takes ibuprofen daily. Which adverse effect is most important to ask about?
items.x: NSAIDs can cause GI ulcers and bleeding; black stools suggest upper GI bleeding.
items.a: Black, tarry stools or stomach pain
w: Increased muscle tone
Excessive thirst and hunger
Sudden hair loss

items.q: Long-term NSAID use can affect cardiovascular status in therapy because NSAIDs can:
items.x: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins, leading to sodium and water retention, edema and higher blood pressure.
items.a: Raise blood pressure and cause fluid retention
w: Lower blood pressure dramatically
Slow heart rate response to exercise
Increase red blood cell production

items.q: Compared with nonselective NSAIDs, celecoxib mainly offers which advantage?
items.x: COX-2 selective drugs spare stomach protection, but cardiovascular and kidney risks remain.
items.a: Lower risk of stomach ulcers
w: No cardiovascular risk
No effect on the kidneys
Stronger anti-inflammatory effect

items.q: Which statement about acetaminophen is correct for a patient with knee osteoarthritis?
items.x: Acetaminophen is analgesic and antipyretic but not anti-inflammatory; liver toxicity is the main risk with excess use.
items.a: It relieves pain but has little anti-inflammatory effect
w: It reduces joint swelling more than NSAIDs
It causes significant stomach bleeding
It is a strong muscle relaxant

items.q: A patient has taken oral prednisone for a year for rheumatoid arthritis. Which complication is most important to consider when planning manual therapy and resistance exercise?
items.x: Chronic glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase fracture risk, especially in vertebrae.
items.a: Osteoporosis with fracture risk
w: Increased bone density
Hypertrophy of type II fibers
Faster ligament healing

items.q: A patient on long-term prednisone has trouble rising from a chair but normal grip strength. What is the most likely cause?
items.x: Steroid myopathy causes painless proximal weakness, mainly of the hip and shoulder girdle.
items.a: Steroid myopathy affecting proximal muscles
w: Peripheral neuropathy of the hands
Upper motor neuron spasticity
Cerebellar ataxia

items.q: After repeated corticosteroid injections near the Achilles tendon, what is the main tissue concern?
items.x: Corticosteroids inhibit collagen synthesis and fibroblast activity, so loading should progress cautiously.
items.a: Weakened tendon with higher rupture risk
w: Calcification that improves strength
Increased collagen synthesis
Permanent nerve block of the calf

items.q: Which wound finding is expected in a patient on chronic corticosteroids?
items.x: Steroids blunt inflammation and slow collagen formation, so infection signs may be muted.
items.a: Slower healing with fewer signs of inflammation
w: Faster healing with more redness
Excess granulation tissue
Healing that is unaffected

items.q: A patient on pramipexole falls asleep suddenly while seated during a session. What is the best explanation?
items.x: Dopamine agonists can cause sudden sleep attacks without warning, which also matters for driving.
items.a: Sudden sleep onset is a known dopamine agonist effect
w: It is a sign of low blood glucose from the drug
It indicates the drug is not working
It is caused by a high-protein meal

items.q: A family member reports that a patient on ropinirole has begun gambling and shopping compulsively. What is the correct response?
items.x: Dopamine agonists are linked to impulse-control disorders such as gambling, shopping and binge eating.
items.a: Report it to the provider as a possible impulse-control side effect
w: Reassure them it is unrelated to medicines
Recommend higher activity levels to distract him
Document it only as a personality change

items.q: Apomorphine is used in Parkinson disease mainly for:
items.x: Apomorphine works within minutes; orthostatic hypotension and nausea are common.
items.a: Rapid rescue from sudden 'off' episodes
w: Long-term prevention of dementia
Lowering blood pressure
Treating constipation

items.q: Which drug is commonly used to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia?
items.x: Amantadine, an NMDA antagonist, reduces dyskinesia; it can cause leg edema, livedo reticularis and confusion.
items.a: Amantadine
w: Trihexyphenidyl
Entacapone
Selegiline

items.q: Why is trihexyphenidyl often avoided in older adults with Parkinson disease?
items.x: Anticholinergic drugs are on the Beers Criteria list because of cognitive and autonomic side effects.
items.a: Anticholinergic effects cause confusion, constipation and urinary retention
w: It causes severe dyskinesia
It raises blood pressure sharply
It blocks levodopa absorption

items.q: Rasagiline improves Parkinson symptoms by:
items.x: MAO-B inhibitors prolong dopamine activity and can interact with meperidine, tramadol and some antidepressants.
items.a: Inhibiting MAO-B to slow dopamine breakdown
w: Blocking peripheral dopa decarboxylase
Directly releasing acetylcholine
Blocking NMDA receptors

items.q: A patient on metoprolol begins cardiac rehab. What is the best way to set exercise intensity?
items.x: Beta-blockers blunt resting and exercise heart rate, so heart-rate targets underestimate effort; RPE is preferred.
items.a: Use the rating of perceived exertion or talk test
w: Use the age-predicted maximum heart rate formula
Target a heart rate rise of 50 beats
Use blood glucose response

items.q: During exercise, a patient on atenolol has a heart rate that barely rises despite heavy breathing. Best interpretation?
items.x: Beta-blockers limit heart rate increase; monitor symptoms, RPE and blood pressure instead.
items.a: An expected blunted chronotropic response from the beta-blocker
w: The patient is not working hard enough
The pulse oximeter is malfunctioning
The patient has developed heart block from exercise

items.q: In a patient with diabetes on propranolol, which hypoglycemia sign may be masked?
items.x: Beta-blockers hide adrenergic signs such as tachycardia and tremor; sweating usually remains.
items.a: Rapid heart rate and tremor
w: Sweating
Confusion
Hunger

items.q: A patient started lisinopril this week and feels dizzy after rising from the mat table. What is the best action?
items.x: Antihypertensives commonly cause orthostatic hypotension, especially early; slow position changes and documentation help.
items.a: Return to sitting, check orthostatic vitals and report the findings
w: Have the patient walk briskly to raise blood pressure
Ignore it because ACE inhibitors do not affect blood pressure
Perform vigorous neck stretching

items.q: Why is an extended cool-down important for a patient on amlodipine?
items.x: Abrupt stop of exercise plus drug-induced vasodilation can pool blood in the legs and drop blood pressure.
items.a: Vasodilation increases the risk of post-exercise hypotension
w: It raises the heart rate too much
It causes hypoglycemia after exercise
It causes bronchospasm after exercise

items.q: A patient on furosemide reports leg cramps and palpitations during exercise. Which lab value is most relevant?
items.x: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, which can cause cramps, weakness and arrhythmias.
items.a: Serum potassium
w: Serum calcium only
Hemoglobin A1c
Serum albumin

items.q: Which concern is most relevant for an older adult on hydrochlorothiazide exercising in a warm room?
items.x: Diuretics reduce fluid volume, which adds to heat stress and lightheadedness on standing.
items.a: Dehydration and orthostatic hypotension
w: Fluid overload and pulmonary edema
Low heart rate from beta blockade
Increased bleeding risk

items.q: A patient injects rapid-acting insulin before breakfast and comes to therapy about an hour later. Which is the main exercise risk?
items.x: Rapid-acting insulin peaks within about 1 to 2 hours, and exercise further lowers glucose.
items.a: Hypoglycemia near the time of peak insulin action
w: Hyperglycemia from the meal
Ketoacidosis from exercise
Hyperkalemia from insulin

items.q: During a session, a patient on insulin becomes shaky, sweaty and confused. What is the best first response?
items.x: These are classic signs of hypoglycemia; fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck follow facility protocol.
items.a: End exercise, check glucose if possible and give a fast-acting carbohydrate per protocol
w: Continue exercise to raise blood sugar
Give a high-fat snack and resume exercise
Have the patient lie down and rest without checking glucose

items.q: Why should a patient who injected insulin into the thigh be monitored closely before a vigorous leg workout?
items.x: Increased blood flow to working muscle speeds absorption from nearby sites, raising hypoglycemia risk.
items.a: Exercise of that limb can speed insulin absorption
w: Leg exercise destroys insulin at the site
The thigh absorbs insulin more slowly during exercise
Exercise raises blood glucose after injection

items.q: A patient on warfarin slips and strikes her head but feels fine. What is the best action?
items.x: Anticoagulated patients can develop delayed intracranial bleeding; head strikes need prompt evaluation.
items.a: Report the fall promptly for medical evaluation
w: Document it and recheck next week
Apply ice and continue the session
Reassure her because she has no symptoms now

items.q: Which lab value best reflects anticoagulation level for a patient on warfarin?
items.x: Warfarin is monitored with the PT/INR; a high INR increases bleeding risk with manual therapy or falls.
items.a: INR
w: Platelet count
Hemoglobin A1c
Serum creatinine

items.q: A patient on apixaban develops a swollen, painful knee without injury. What should the therapist suspect?
items.x: Anticoagulants raise risk of hemarthrosis and soft-tissue bleeding; avoid vigorous manual therapy and report it.
items.a: Spontaneous joint bleeding (hemarthrosis)
w: Normal response to exercise
Gout from the drug
Tendon rupture from the drug

items.q: An older adult takes zolpidem at bedtime. Which fall risk should be addressed in home safety training?
items.x: Sedative-hypnotics impair balance and alertness, especially when getting up at night to toilet.
items.a: Night-time and early-morning falls from sedation and poor balance
w: Falls only during afternoon exercise
Falls caused by low blood glucose
Falls caused by high heart rate

items.q: Which over-the-counter drug in an older adult is a Beers Criteria concern for confusion and falls?
items.x: First-generation antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic, causing confusion, urinary retention and falls in older adults.
items.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Acetaminophen
Topical diclofenac
Calcium carbonate

items.q: Xerostomia caused by medications most often results from blocking which receptors?
items.x: Salivary secretion is driven by parasympathetic muscarinic stimulation. Anticholinergic drugs block these receptors and reduce saliva flow.
items.a: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
w: Dopamine D2 receptors
Beta-adrenergic receptors
Serotonin 5-HT3 receptors

items.q: An 80-year-old with overactive bladder reports a sticky mouth and difficulty chewing bread. Which of her medicines is the most likely contributor?
items.x: Oxybutynin is a bladder antispasmodic with strong anticholinergic effects; dry mouth is its most common side effect.
items.a: Oxybutynin
w: Famotidine
Lisinopril
Levetiracetam

items.q: Which antidepressant is known for strong anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and constipation?
items.x: Tertiary-amine tricyclics like amitriptyline block muscarinic receptors strongly, causing xerostomia, constipation and confusion.
items.a: Amitriptyline
w: Trazodone
Famotidine
Ramelteon

items.q: A patient takes an over-the-counter sleep aid nightly and complains of morning dry mouth. Which ingredient is the likely cause?
items.x: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic activity, causing dry mouth and next-day sedation.
items.a: Diphenhydramine
w: Melatonin
Acetaminophen
Calcium carbonate

items.q: How does reduced saliva most directly affect the oral preparatory phase?
items.x: Saliva moistens food and binds particles into a cohesive bolus. Without it, chewing is prolonged and the bolus falls apart, leaving residue.
items.a: Poor bolus cohesion with prolonged chewing
w: Premature spillage of thin liquids
Delayed laryngeal vestibule closure
Reduced upper esophageal sphincter opening

items.q: A patient with xerostomia has dry crumbly solids scattered in the oral cavity after the swallow. Which compensation is most commonly recommended?
items.x: Liquid washes help moisten and clear dry solids when saliva is reduced. Moist, sauced foods also help.
items.a: Alternating bites of solid with sips of liquid
w: Chin tuck with every liquid swallow
Supraglottic swallow for solids only
Head rotation toward the weaker side

items.q: Pilocarpine improves dry mouth by which mechanism?
items.x: Pilocarpine is a cholinergic (muscarinic) agonist, a sialogogue that stimulates remaining salivary tissue.
items.a: Stimulating muscarinic receptors on salivary glands
w: Coating the oral mucosa with a lubricant
Blocking histamine release in the mouth
Increasing fluid absorption from the gut

items.q: Cevimeline is FDA-approved for dry mouth associated with which condition?
items.x: Cevimeline is a muscarinic agonist approved for dry mouth in Sjogren's syndrome.
items.a: Sjogren's syndrome
w: Parkinson's disease
Myasthenia gravis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

items.q: Which side effect is most commonly reported with pilocarpine tablets?
items.x: Because pilocarpine stimulates muscarinic receptors throughout the body, sweating is the most common side effect.
items.a: Sweating
w: Dry eyes
Constipation
Urinary retention

items.q: Why might a saliva substitute help a patient when pilocarpine does not?
items.x: Sialogogues need functioning glands to stimulate. Saliva substitutes simply coat and moisten the mouth, so they work after extensive gland damage.
items.a: Substitutes lubricate even without working salivary tissue
w: Substitutes regenerate damaged salivary glands
Substitutes block anticholinergic drug effects
Substitutes stimulate muscarinic receptors more strongly

items.q: A child with cerebral palsy is prescribed a medicine to reduce drooling. Which drug is commonly used for this purpose?
items.x: Glycopyrrolate is an anticholinergic used to reduce chronic drooling; it can also thicken secretions and cause constipation.
items.a: Glycopyrrolate
w: Pilocarpine
Cevimeline
Donepezil

items.q: A hospice patient has a patch placed behind the ear to dry secretions. Which drug is this most likely?
items.x: Transdermal scopolamine is an anticholinergic patch sometimes used to reduce secretions; it can cause dry mouth and confusion.
items.a: Scopolamine
w: Fentanyl
Rotigotine
Pilocarpine

items.q: Which oral health problem is a long-term consequence of chronic medication-induced xerostomia?
items.x: Saliva buffers acid and clears bacteria; chronic dryness raises the risk of caries and oral candidiasis.
items.a: Dental caries
w: Gingival overgrowth
Tooth discoloration from staining
Excessive tooth enamel thickening

items.q: The term anticholinergic burden refers to which concept?
items.x: Several mildly anticholinergic medicines can add up to a large total effect, especially in older adults.
items.a: The cumulative effect of several drugs with anticholinergic activity
w: The single strongest anticholinergic drug in a regimen
The length of time an anticholinergic stays in the body
The dose needed to treat anticholinergic toxicity

items.q: Which inhaled medicine for COPD commonly causes dry mouth?
items.x: Tiotropium is an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist; dry mouth is its most common side effect.
items.a: Tiotropium
w: Albuterol
Budesonide
Fluticasone

items.q: Unlike most antipsychotics, which one commonly causes excessive salivation rather than dry mouth?
items.x: Clozapine frequently causes sialorrhea, especially at night, despite its anticholinergic properties.
items.a: Clozapine
w: Chlorpromazine
Olanzapine
Quetiapine

items.q: Shortly after receiving haloperidol, a patient has sustained tongue protrusion and difficulty swallowing. What is this most likely?
items.x: Acute dystonia appears within hours to days of starting a high-potency antipsychotic and can involve the tongue, jaw and larynx. It needs prompt medical attention.
items.a: Acute dystonic reaction
w: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome

items.q: Tardive dyskinesia most commonly produces which oral-motor finding?
items.x: TD causes repetitive involuntary orofacial movements that can disrupt bolus control and the oral phase.
items.a: Involuntary lip smacking and tongue writhing
w: Fixed tongue deviation to one side
Fasciculations with tongue atrophy
Flaccid lips with loss of tone

items.q: Compared with acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia typically appears when?
items.x: TD is a late complication of long-term dopamine blockade and may persist even after the drug changes.
items.a: After months to years of exposure
w: Within hours of the first dose
Only after the drug is withdrawn
Within the first week of therapy

items.q: Which medication is FDA-approved to treat tardive dyskinesia?
items.x: Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors approved for TD. Anticholinergics like benztropine are not effective for TD.
items.a: Valbenazine
w: Benztropine
Haloperidol
Metoclopramide

items.q: Which GI medicine carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia?
items.x: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine receptors and has a boxed warning for TD, with risk rising with long-term use.
items.a: Metoclopramide
w: Famotidine
Omeprazole
Pantoprazole

items.q: Drug-induced parkinsonism from antipsychotics most often affects swallowing by causing which finding?
items.x: Dopamine blockade can produce bradykinesia and rigidity of oral and pharyngeal muscles, much like Parkinson's disease.
items.a: Reduced tongue movement and delayed swallow initiation
w: Premature velopharyngeal closure
Increased pharyngeal contraction strength
Hyperactive gag reflex with spasm

items.q: A college student takes a pill at bedtime with a small sip of water and wakes with sharp pain when swallowing. Which drug is a classic cause?
items.x: Doxycycline is acidic and a classic cause of pill esophagitis, especially when taken lying down with little water.
items.a: Doxycycline
w: Famotidine
Levetiracetam
Lisinopril

items.q: Alendronate labeling directs patients to remain upright for 30 minutes after a dose mainly to lower which risk?
items.x: Bisphosphonates irritate the esophagus; staying upright with a full glass of water helps the pill clear quickly.
items.a: Esophageal irritation and ulceration
w: Orthostatic low blood pressure
Aspiration of the tablet
Rebound bone loss

items.q: Solid potassium chloride tablets are a known cause of which swallowing-related injury?
items.x: Potassium chloride can injure the esophageal mucosa if it lodges in place, causing odynophagia or ulceration.
items.a: Pill-induced esophageal injury
w: Vocal fold paralysis
Tongue fasciculations
Oral candidiasis

items.q: Which patient factor most increases the risk of pill esophagitis?
items.x: Recumbent position and low fluid volume let pills stall in the esophagus. Upright posture and adequate fluid aid clearance.
items.a: Taking pills lying down with little fluid
w: Taking pills with a full glass of water
Taking pills while seated upright
Taking pills spaced through the day

items.q: Odynophagia means which symptom?
items.x: Odynophagia is painful swallowing, a hallmark of pill esophagitis; dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
items.a: Pain with swallowing
w: Difficulty initiating a swallow
Food sticking without pain
Coughing during a swallow

items.q: A patient with dysphagia has trouble swallowing an extended-release tablet. What is the best SLP action?
items.x: Many extended-release or enteric-coated products cannot be crushed; the pharmacist can identify a safe alternative form.
items.a: Ask the pharmacist or prescriber about alternative forms
w: Crush the tablet into applesauce
Cut the tablet into small pieces
Dissolve the tablet in hot water

items.q: Two weeks after neck injections for cervical dystonia, a patient reports new trouble swallowing. What is the most likely explanation?
items.x: Dysphagia is a known effect of cervical botulinum toxin injection due to spread to nearby pharyngeal muscles; distant spread carries a boxed warning.
items.a: Spread of botulinum toxin to swallowing muscles
w: An allergic reaction to the injection
Tardive dyskinesia of the pharynx
